This verse summarizes the six auspicious omens in this land, though it further adds that a fragrant wind arose and the earth became pure, yet no Dharma was preached.

The one who enters meditative concentration is the Teacher himself. This is because his ability to guide others through preaching the Dharma and entering concentration is itself the act of preaching the Dharma while in concentration.
Wind is fundamentally odorless, yet its fragrance is extraordinary, serving as an auspicious sign.
Since celestial flowers are most wondrous, how could they have color without fragrance? This symbolizes that the movement from cause to fruit is like a flower possessing fragrance within the wind.
Since the flowers have gathered upon the ground, the ground is thus adorned and purified; since the cause tends toward the fruit, the fruit is thus adorned, purified, and radiant.
Because clouds of merit gather to adorn the Buddha-body, these two matters manifest and establish the four kinds of flowers.
△ Second, the inquiry regarding the six auspicious omens in other lands. Part one: the inquiry regarding the six realms of existence.
The radiance from between his eyebrows illuminated eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, making them all appear like gold.

From the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence above, within all these worlds, the transitions through birth and death of sentient beings in the six realms, the karmic conditions of their good and evil deeds,
and the beauty or ugliness of the retributions they received— all were clearly seen therein.
Sentient beings are those who go; birth and death are the place to which they go; the conditions of good and evil karma are the cause of going;
and the receiving of retribution, whether favorable or unfavorable, is the fruit of going. △ Second, the question regarding seeing that Buddha preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, I behold the Buddhas, the Holy Sovereign Lions, expounding the sutras that are subtle, wondrous, and supreme.
Their voices are pure, emitting gentle sounds; they instruct the bodhisattvas with countless billions of Brahma-voices, profound and exquisite, which all delight in hearing.
In their respective worlds, they preach the True Dharma through various causes and conditions, illuminating the Buddha-dharma with immeasurable parables.
Awakening sentient beings, he directly beholds the Buddha;
this extensively clarifies the characteristics of the preaching of the Dharma, namely the teaching of the sudden doctrine (sudden teaching) suited to those of great capacity—the Lion-like Holy Lord.
This is like the image of Rocana in this land, expounding the subtle and wondrous chapters of the sutras.
First, just as in this land the sun shines upon the high mountains to manifest the *Avataṃsaka*, so too does he teach the bodhisattvas;
just as in this land there are no śrāvakas across the seven locations and eight assemblies, so too does he illuminate the Buddha-dharma to awaken sentient beings;
just as in this land one first beholds the Buddha-body and enters the wisdom of the Tathāgata. △ Third, the question regarding the assembly in other lands, part three: first, the opening.
Regarding the Śrāvaka Vehicle:
if a person encounters suffering and becomes weary of old age, sickness, and death, the Buddha teaches them *nirvāṇa* as the exhaustion of the limits of all suffering.

If one encounters suffering and becomes weary of its accumulation, and further becomes weary of the fruits of dependent origination, such a person is able to [attain] the *nirvāṇa* taught by the Buddha.
This is merely to bring an end to all suffering. △ Second, opening the path for those of the Middle Vehicle:
If there are people who have merit from having previously made offerings to the Buddha and who aspire to the supreme Dharma, one preaches the Pratyekabuddha vehicle for them.
If they have made many offerings to the Buddha, although they may encounter suffering, they will thereby attain merit; thus it is said that Śrāvakas plant the seeds of merit over three lifetimes.
Because Pratyekabuddhas have cultivated merit for a hundred kalpas, they surpass Śrāvakas in terms of their physical form; thus it is said they possess "merit.

Those who "seek the supreme Dharma" are the Pratyekabuddhas seeking the Way; by practicing and deeply investigating the profound and wondrous principle of dependent origination, they open the Middle Vehicle in other lands.
△ Third, opening the Mahāyāna.
If there are sons of the Buddha who cultivate various practices to seek unsurpassed wisdom, for their sake the pure path is taught.

Because they employ true compassion and are able to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas, they are called "sons of the Buddha. Because they cultivate the six perfections, they are said to engage in "various practices.
Because they aspire to the path of the Buddha, it is called "unsurpassed wisdom. Within these six perfections, the six obscurations are absent.

Just as one says a medicinal preparation is "pure" because it contains no disease, yet this refers to a path of purity that is not ultimate purity. △ Fourth, concluding the preceding and opening the subsequent:
"Mañjuśrī, dwelling here, I have seen and heard such things as these, numbering in the thousands of billions;
though they are thus numerous, I shall now speak of them briefly."
"Seeing and hearing such as this" concludes what preceded; "in such great numbers" opens up what follows.
△ Fifth, the question regarding the cultivation of practice by bodhisattvas in other lands, part one: the general question.
I see bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in that land seeking the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions.
△ Second, the sequential questioning of the six [perfections]. First, the questioning of *dāna* (generosity). Third, first, the questioning of the relinquishing of wealth.
There may be those who practice giving gold, silver, coral, pearls, mani-jewels, conch shells, agate, diamonds, and various other treasures;

or slaves, vehicles, precious ornaments, and palanquins—giving these with joy and dedicating the merit toward the Buddha-way, wishing to obtain this vehicle, the foremost in the three realms praised by all Buddhas.
Or there may be bodhisattvas who possess precious chariots drawn by four horses, complete with railings and flowered canopies.

Adorning one's carriage and giving away precious jewels or slaves are acts of giving that both the noble and the humble are capable of performing. However, as for such things as chariots drawn by four horses, these are what a king bestows;
because one practices *dāna* (generosity) through such means, it is called "giving. △ Second, the question regarding the renunciation of the body.
Furthermore, he saw Bodhisattvas giving their own flesh, hands, feet, wives, and children to those who sought the Unsurpassed Way.
Their own flesh and so forth constitute the "inner body," while their wives and children constitute the "outer body. △ Third, the question regarding the relinquishing of life.
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas joyfully giving away their heads, eyes, and bodies to seek the wisdom of a Buddha.

The relinquishing of the head and eyes is equivalent to relinquishing life itself; yet, the "Dharma-gift" (dharma-dāna) is not explicitly mentioned here because it is reserved for the subsequent *prajñāpāramitā*.
Moreover, when body, life, and wealth are understood to be equal to the future limit of saṃsāra, attaining that which is indestructible and eternally abiding—this is precisely the Dharma.
[The Buddha spoke of] giving. △ Second, the inquiry regarding precepts:

Mañjuśrī, I have seen various kings who, having gone to the presence of the Buddha to inquire about the unsurpassed path, immediately abandoned their pleasant lands, palaces, ministers, and concubines, shaved off their hair and beards, and donned the dharma robes.
For those living at home, giving is easy while observing the precepts is difficult; for those who have left the home life, observing the precepts is easy while giving is difficult.

Therefore, with reference to the bhikṣu, the *Ji* (Record) states: "Going forth" signifies departing rather than remaining elsewhere; "approaching the Buddha's dwelling" indicates that the object of inquiry is supreme;
"the unsurpassed path" refers to what is relinquished being no light matter; and "the land of bliss" signifies that both body and mind are detached; thus it says "shaving."
As the *Pañcarājāsūtra* states: "In the past, there were five kings who were mutual friends. One king was named Puhuan (Universal Peace), who practiced the bodhisattva path;
the other four kings held intense wrong views. Puhuan took pity on them, summoned them to his palace for seven days of entertainment, and then escorted them back to their respective kingdoms.
On the way, halfway through the journey, the Great King himself questioned them, saying: 'You [ministers]...'"
"Each of you, what do you find pleasing? The Four Kings each replied, "We find pleasure in the joys of the world. The King then turned the question back to them, asking, "What do you find pleasing?
The King answered, "That which I find pleasing is neither born nor extinguished, neither suffering nor pleasure;
it is mastery over both existence and non-existence. The Four Kings asked, "Where does such pleasure exist? The King said, "My teacher is called the Buddha."
Recently, at the Jetavana, various kings were filled with joy and together proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling.

The Buddha preached on the eight sufferings, and the kings along with their retinues—numbering hundreds of thousands of myriads—attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. Having renounced their kingdoms to enter the Way, they donned the dharma robes.
As the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* states: "If a dragon obtains even a single thread of this kashaya robe, the golden-winged Garuda will not swallow it. It is as clear as this.
*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. △ Third, the inquiry into patience (*kṣānti*).
One may see a bodhisattva who has become a bhikṣu dwelling alone in a secluded and quiet place, delighting in the recitation of the sūtras.

There are three kinds of patience: becoming a bhikṣu is the patience of ascetic practice (*duṣkaracaryā-kṣānti*), while dwelling alone in a secluded and quiet place is the patience of birth (*upapatti-kṣānti*).
Delighting in the recitation of the sūtras is the foremost patience of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-kṣānti). △ Fourth, the inquiry into diligence:
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas who, with courageous and vigorous diligence, enter deep mountains to contemplate the Buddha-way.
Now, deep mountains are fearsome and are not the dwelling place of those who are indolent or timid; only those who are courageous and resolute can find peace therein.

With an air of indifference toward external things, they contemplate the cultivation of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), never ceasing moment by moment as they advance in their quest for the Buddha-way.
△ Fifth, Questions on Dhyāna, Part Two: First, Questions on the Cultivation of Fundamental Dhyāna (according to the *Zàng* and *Tōng* teachings).

Furthermore, one sees those who, having become free from desire, constantly dwell in seclusion and deeply cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
These powers universally possess fundamental cultivation. Those who attain the five powers by becoming free from desire do so through the concentration of the Shared Teaching (*paryāya-yāna*).

In the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), one is simultaneously free from the desires of the two vehicles; furthermore, within the Middle Way, one is free from the desire for the dharma that accords with the Path, and thus deeply cultivates [concentration].

Regarding the first dhyāna, from its first grade up to its ninth grade, as they are transmitted and successively deepen, one attains mastery over transformation and can manifest the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
While ordinary beings possess five supernormal powers and those of the Two Vehicles possess six, the Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching yield their portion to the Buddha;

though they possess them, they are not called "untainted" (*anāsrava*), and thus they are also termed "five supernormal powers. In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), both the beginning and the end are fully endowed with the six supernormal powers. △ Second, the question regarding supramundane [powers].
Regarding the superior dhyāna (the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles]):
one also sees Bodhisattvas in peaceful dhyāna with palms joined, praising the Kings of All Dharmas with ten million gāthās.
This peaceful dhyāna and the chanting of gāthās represent the supreme dhyāna of the Separate and Perfect Vehicles; because stillness and movement do not obstruct one another, it is thus.

Arising from and entering the meditative absorption of cessation, he manifests all modes of deportment; like the lute of the asuras, it produces melody without being struck, appearing through resonance when there is no object or thought.
△ Sixth: Questions on Prajñā, Part One: First, the question regarding his own practice.
Furthermore, one sees that the Bodhisattvas possess profound wisdom and firm resolve, such that they are able to question the Buddhas and, having heard [the teachings], receive and uphold them all.
"Profound wisdom" means reaching the ultimate source of principles; "firm resolve" refers to the vastness of their vows.
Thus, through these two kinds of adornments, they are able both to question and to maintain [the Dharma]. △ Second, questioning regarding the transformation of others.
Furthermore, they see sons of the Buddha, endowed with meditative concentration and wisdom, expounding the Dharma for the multitude through immeasurable parables;
delighting in the teaching of the Dharma, they transform various bodhisattvas, shatter the armies of Māra, and beat the drum of the Dharma.

In the stage of "not yet arrived" (*anāgamya*), wisdom is predominant; in the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the four dhyānas, and so forth, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is predominant. Furthermore, in the liberations (*vimokṣa*), wisdom is predominant; in the nine concentrations (*navasamādhi*), concentration is predominant;

and in the ten spheres of totality (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*), both are moderate. Moreover, in the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), concentration is predominant; in Bodhisattvas, wisdom is predominant; and in the Buddha, they are equal. Regarding the subduing of Māra:

the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) subdues the four Māras; the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*) subdues the eight Māras in succession; and the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*) subdues them perfectly.

He who beats the drum that shatters the eight māras, the ten māras, and all māras, attains perfect enlightenment upon the initial arousal of the thought of awakening (*prathama-cittotpāda*), manifests as a hundred Buddhas throughout the Buddha-fields, and fully beats the Dharma-drum of the Brahma-wheel. △ Third: Questions on the Non-sequential [Teachings], Part Seven.
First, questions on dhyāna; 2.1. Questions on entering the dhyāna of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Furthermore, he saw that when the Bodhisattva remained in silent tranquility, the devas and nāgas paid him reverent homage, yet he did not feel joy because of this.
△ Second, the question regarding entry into the samādhi of compassion:
Furthermore, he saw the Bodhisattva dwelling in the forest, emitting light to relieve the sufferings of those in the hells and causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
"Successive questioning" refers to a gradual, single path; "non-successive questioning" does not follow a fixed, single path.
Now, the first line of questioning concerns entry into the *śānta-dhyāna* (equanimity meditation). The self-cultivation record states that "equanimity meditation" refers to the fourth dhyāna.

Alternatively, it may refer to the equanimity of forgetting both the distinct and the perfect [teachings]; because one forgets that dhyāna, it is called "equanimity. Next, one line concerns entry into the *karuṇā-dhyāna* (compassion meditation).

This refers to the transformation of others; furthermore, the Bodhisattva enters meditative concentration and emits light to bring about various benefits, as fully detailed in the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saṃcayagāthā*.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "It is easy to cultivate compassion (*karuṇā*) in the first dhyāna, joy (*muditā*) in the second dhyāna, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in the third dhyāna, and equanimity (*upekṣā*) in the fourth dhyāna.
These four—loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity—cultivated within the four dhyānas are called the Four Immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
The mind is the practice of the Bodhisattva. △ Second, the inquiry regarding diligence:
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha who never sleep, but instead walk in meditation within the groves, diligently seeking the Buddha-way.
This refers precisely to such dharma-gates as *pratyutpanna-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Standing Before the Buddhas). "Pratyutpanna" translates as "standing before the Buddha.
This is cited here because it is practiced constantly for ninety days; since one never sleeps during this time, one's diligence can be known.
△ Third, the question on precepts.
Furthermore, one sees those who possess the precepts and whose majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) is without deficiency, pure like a precious gem, as they seek the Buddha-way.
"Eportment without deficiency" refers to the first, the non-deficient precept; "pure like a precious gem" refers to the tenth, the ultimate precept.
These are cited from among the ten precepts, taking the first and the last. The names of these ten precepts appear in the *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise) and the *Mahā-sūtra* (Great Sūtra). △ Four.
Questioning on patience:
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha who, abiding in the power of patience, are able to endure all the insults and beatings of arrogant people as they seek the path to Buddhahood.
Question: Regarding the two types of patience (*kṣānti*) that arise from the Dharma, the *Āgama* states that there are six kinds of power:
first, the power of a child’s crying; second, the power of a woman’s anger; third, the power of a king’s arrogance; fourth, the power of an Arhat’s progress;
fifth, the power of the Buddhas’ compassion; and sixth, the power of a bhikṣu’s patience. △ Fifth, further questioning on meditation (*dhyāna*).
Furthermore, they see bodhisattvas who have abandoned all frivolous laughter and foolish companions, and who, having approached wise ones,
single-mindedly eliminate distraction and collect their thoughts in mountain forests for hundreds of thousands of millions of years in order to seek the Buddha-way.
It removes the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*): abandoning frivolous laughter removes the hindrance of restlessness and remorse;

abandoning the company of the deluded removes the hindrance of ill-will; associating with the wise removes the hindrance of doubt; single-mindedness that eliminates distraction removes the hindrance of sensual desire;
and withdrawing the mind to the mountain forests removes the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness. [Section] Six: Questions on Generosity (*dāna*). Part One: Explaining the Fourfold Giving.
In some instances, one sees a bodhisattva bestowing a hundred kinds of fine foods and medicinal decoctions upon the Buddha and the Sangha;

or bestowing named robes and superior garments worth ten million, or even priceless robes, upon the Buddha and the Sangha; or bestowing ten thousand *koṭis* of sandalwood jewel pavilions and various exquisite bedding upon the Buddha and the Sangha;
or bestowing pure gardens with flourishing flowers and fruits, flowing springs, and bathing pools upon the Buddha and the Sangha.
He gives to the Buddha and the Sangha.
△ Second, the conclusion of the giving:
Through such various kinds of subtle and wondrous giving, he gives with joy and without weariness, seeking the unsurpassed path.
The first three lines clearly explain the four types of material gifts, namely: food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
The fourth line explains the gift of gardens and so forth. The fifth line concludes by clarifying the purpose of these gifts.
Regarding what is called "clothing," the Āgamas state that when Kāśyapa went forth into the homeless life, he selected the lowest garments from his home and obtained a tattered robe.
Its value was one hundred thousand taels of gold; it was used to make the *saṃghāṭī* robe, as well as various pickled vegetables and fine delicacies.
△ Seventh, the inquiry into Prajñā, Part One: Prajñā that cannot be spoken yet is spoken.
There may be bodhisattvas who preach the dharma of quiescence, providing various instructions to countless sentient beings.
△ Second, the contemplation of the unobservable Prajñā:
Or one may see a bodhisattva contemplating the nature of all phenomena as being without dual characteristics, just like empty space.
Third, explaining and contemplating the *Prajñāpāramitā*, one further sees that the sons of the Buddha have minds free from attachment, seeking the unsurpassed path through this wondrous wisdom.
These three categories of the text have already been clarified; as for the third category, it is where the path of language is cut off and the activities of the mind are extinguished.
Thus, it is by speaking that which cannot be spoken and contemplating that which cannot be contemplated that one discusses Prajñāpāramitā. △ Sixth, the inquiry concerning Nirvāṇa.
Part One: A general indication of the erection of stūpas.
Mañjuśrī again saw bodhisattvas making offerings to the śarīra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
△ Second, the number of stupas:
Furthermore, one sees the sons of the Buddha constructing countless stupas and temples, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, adorning the realms.
△ Third, the dimensions of the stupas.
The precious stupa was five thousand yojanas in height and exactly two thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
△ Fourth, the characteristics of the stupas:
each individual stupa-temple featured a thousand banners and streamers, with jeweled lattices and canopies, while precious bells chimed harmoniously.
△ Five: Offerings.
Devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans constantly make offerings of incense, flowers, and music.
△ Six: Summary.
Mañjuśrī and the sons of the Buddha, in order to make offerings to the śarīra, adorned the stūpas and temples so that the realms naturally became exceptionally sublime and wondrous,
like the celestial king of trees with its flowers in full bloom.

Now, seeing that in other lands the Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa, their disciples, longing for their virtue, erect stupas and temples; this signifies that the immeasurable [Buddhas] all return to the One.
In Sanskrit it is called *stūpa*, here translated as "square mound. Regarding the planting of kings: this refers to the *pārijāta* tree.
As for the offerings of śarīra relics, the adornments of the Buddha-lands by devas, nāgas, music, and so forth—it is because of the stupa.
Because he conceals his physical form, the merit of one who makes offerings to him is vastly different from that of offering to a temple structure or a dwelling place.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, there was a bhikṣu named Brahmamāla standing before the Buddha fanning him with a whisk.
The Buddha pushed it away. Ānanda thought to himself: "This bhikṣu has constantly attended upon the Buddha; why is it that at this final moment, he has been dismissed?"
"What is the reason for this? The Buddha told Ānanda: "Now, the city of Kuśinagara is twelve yojanas in extent and is crowded with devas.
All these devas wish to make offerings, but because this bhikṣu possesses great majestic power and his radiance outshines them, they are prevented from approaching him.
It is for this reason that they have been driven back. Ānanda asked: "By what causes and conditions has this come to pass?"
The Buddha Śarīraprabha said: "In the past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, with a heart of joy, I held a torch in my hand to illuminate that Buddha’s stūpa.
Because of this merit, my radiance is thus. Since the illumination by fire was such, the rest may be known accordingly.
△ Second, the request for an answer, in two parts: first, raising the matter of doubt to state the request; third, first, citing what was seen in this land.
The Buddha emitted a single ray of light, and I, along with the assembled multitude, beheld this realm in all its various and wondrous splendor.
△ Second, the account of seeing other lands:
Through the inconceivable power of the Buddhas' spiritual wisdom, they emit a single pure light that illuminates immeasurable lands.

First, the events of this land are presented; because the white tuft of hair is the primary basis, it is mentioned first, and because various other matters are involved, they are described as "various.

Second, the events of other lands are presented; because the Buddhas are the primary basis, they encompass the remaining five auspicious signs. △ Third, the request for an answer to resolve the doubts of the assembly.
"We have seen this unprecedented occurrence; O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, we pray that you resolve the doubts of the assembly.
△ Second, the explanation of four latent difficulties, part one: the direct explanation.
"The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy and reverence; why, O World-Honored One, do you emit this radiance?"
Regarding the three lines at the end that resolve four latent difficulties: Mañjuśrī internally formulated these challenges and did not immediately provide answers for three reasons:

first, these auspicious signs were rare and extraordinary, and thus could not be hastily or lightly adjudicated; second, the assembly of the wise was as vast as the ocean, and he wished to show humility by deferring to them;

third, he intentionally withheld his response to provoke the assembly’s thirst for the teaching, thereby causing them to look toward him with longing. For these reasons, he set aside the questions to "suppress" them.
It is difficult to conceal and reject [the doubt]; Maitreya’s clarification of the intent behind these objections also consists of three points: first, the omens were great and the doubts were great;

if they were not explained, the anxiety would remain in his breast, hindering his hearing of the True Teaching. Second, the assembly is as vast as the ocean, yet their spiritual capacities reside in the benevolent one.
Third, the entire multitude gazes upon the benevolent one; thus we know that his sincere devotion is profound and earnest, which is why he speaks clearly to provide an explanation.

Regarding the request for an answer to the initial objection: because the objection arises from the formal request, the request says, "O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, please resolve the doubts of the assembly.
Mañjuśrī then raises the initial objection: "You say there are doubts in the assembly, yet the assembly has never doubted.
If they were in doubt, they should have asked; since the assembly does not doubt, what is there for me to resolve? Maitreya then employs the first [reasoning].
The verse commentary says: "The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy, looking toward both you and me;
they wish for me to question you and desire that you provide the answer.
O Son of the Buddha, answer now to resolve our doubts and bring us joy. For what benefit do you manifest this radiance?"
Because of this, Mañjuśrī raised a second challenge: "The assembly all harbors doubts that are not easily answered;

we shall wait until the Buddha emerges from his meditative absorption before resolving these uncertainties. Maitreya then explained with a second verse: "If there are doubts lingering in one's breast, the mind will be as uneasy as a rhinoceros;
one should answer them at the proper time, while also knowing when the Tathāgata will arise from his absorption."
The Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment and attained the wondrous Dharma; is he now about to preach it, or is he about to bestow a prophecy?
Because of this, Mañjuśrī again raised a third objection: "I and you, O Venerable One, dwell together on the stage of training;
we wish to fathom the Buddha’s intention and deliberate upon it together, yet for you alone to answer me would be unreasonable. Maitreya then... [the text continues].

The three verses explain that I too, with a subtle mind, hesitated below [the tree] for two *yama*s, wondering whether he was preaching the wondrous Dharma or whether he was about to bestow a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*);
thus it says, "The Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment" (and so forth), up to "whether he was about to bestow a prediction."
To manifest the various Buddha-lands adorned with myriad jewels and pure, and to cause one to behold the Buddhas—this is no small matter.
Mañjuśrī, on this account, raised the fourth objection: "If it is as you say, then this would merely be the dispelling of a doubt;
why trouble yourself to answer me? Maitreya then used the fourth verse to explain: "How can you judge [the matter] based on my hesitant mind?"
The statement "Great matters" indicates that the manifestation of the various Buddha-lands is not a minor cause.
Since Wenshu’s refutation of the objection has reached its conclusion, the humble light [of the response] also ceases. The final verse concludes the request for an answer.

These four objections were received by Guangzhai from his immediate teacher, who in turn received them from Master Zhao (pronounced zhāo) of Jiangbei. As these were former sages, they were skillful in expressing their insights beyond the literal text.

Because [the Buddha] has reflected upon this, he now employs it; in the subsequent passage where Mañjuśrī provides a definitive answer, clearly resolving the matter at the point of response, he cuts through these four latent doubts, the principle of which is consistent with the preceding. △ Second, the conclusion of the request.
Mañjuśrī, you should know that the fourfold assembly, the nāgas, and the spirits are all gazing upon you, wondering what you will say.
△ Fifth, the introduction to the response to the question, which has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part [the prose] further has four sections.
First, the reflection prior to the response, which has two sub-sections. First, the presentation of the topic.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya and the other great beings, sons of good family, saying:
"As I reflect and deliberate—'reflect' meaning to weigh and consider—I see that the present is like the past and the past is like the present. How could Mañjuśrī not have been an ancient Buddha?"
One should understand that this indicates the contemplation of the traces [of the Buddha]. △ Second, the actual deliberation:
"Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, desires to preach the Great Dharma, rain down the Great Dharma, blow the Great Dharma conch, beat the Great Dharma drum, and expound the Great Dharma meaning."
"One who wishes to preach the Great Dharma" answers the auspicious sign of preaching the Dharma; "one who rains down the great rain of the Dharma" answers the auspicious sign of raining down flowers;
"one who blows the great Dharma conch" answers the auspicious sign of the great assembly’s hearts rejoicing; "one who beats the great Dharma drum" answers the auspicious sign of the earth shaking;

"one who expounds the great meaning of the Dharma" answers the auspicious sign of emitting light. As for "one who wishes to preach the Great Dharma," this refers exclusively to what the Buddhas of the past have preached.
Following the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, the provisional teachings were opened and the ultimate reality was revealed, gathering the immeasurable back into the One;

reflecting on this, since the Buddha has now finished preaching the Dharma, he too should open the provisional and reveal the real, uniting the immeasurable to return to the One—the One being the Great Dharma.
That which rains down the rain of the Great Dharma is precisely that which all Buddhas of the past entered universally after raining down flowers.
The Bodhisattvas of the stages of practice, dwelling, and heading toward the grounds reflect that the present Buddha is likewise so;

those who blow the great Dharma-conch are none other than the fourfold assembly of former times, who, seeing the auspicious signs, rejoiced with unprecedented delight. When obstacles are removed and the faculties are stirred, human conduct is transformed;

both teaching and principle are one and the same. They reflect that the joy of the present assembly is likewise so; those who beat the great Dharma-drum are none other than those for whom the earth shook in the past.
Subsequently, there were six instances of destroying the thief of ignorance; one may infer that it is the same for the present Buddha as well.

Because his vocal teaching is supremely wondrous, those who expound the great Dharma-principle do so because the Buddhas of the past emitted light from the white tuft between their brows and immediately thereafter preached the Lotus Sūtra;

one may infer that it is the same for the present Buddha as well. Since he extensively clarifies that the Way of the five Buddhas is identical, and because it is indeed the Buddha-way, it is said that he "expounds" it.

This is the Great Dharma-meaning. Although it mentions only the single auspicious sign of entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), all five signs are without exception derived from the intent of entering concentration;
thus, the meaning is inclusive. Furthermore, to explain this separately: "desiring to preach the Great Dharma" is the general statement, while the following four phrases are the specific details.
These—rain, wind, striking, unfolding, revealing, awakening, and causing entry—are correlated with the stages of *caryā*, *vihāra*, *pratipatti*, and *bhūmi*. This is as explained at the beginning.
1. When the seeds receive rain, the sprouts emerge; this corresponds to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision being revealed at the stage of the Ten Abidings (*daśabhūmi*). 2.

Next, like blowing a conch shell to change one's designation, one hears the Dharma upon attaining the Ten Abidings and is transformed to enter the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), wherein the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is shown. 3. Third, like striking a drum, the soldiers of the precepts follow;

hearing the Dharma upon attaining the Ten Practices, one is transformed to enter the Ten Transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*), thereby awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The term "to unfold" (*yan*) means to spread horizontally.

"Vertical, broad, and deep" refers to the meaning of unfolding and manifesting; having heard the Dharma in the Ten Dwellings and entered the Ten Grounds, one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, exhausting the source and reaching the limit, such that depth and breadth are fully perfected. △ Second, the brief answer regarding what was previously seen.
"O sons of good family, in the past, when I saw this omen under various Buddhas—namely, the emission of this light—I immediately preached the Great Dharma.
Therefore, you should know that the present Buddha’s manifestation of light is likewise so;
he manifests this omen because he desires to cause all sentient beings to hear and know the Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe."
Initially, one reflects using one’s own wisdom; now, one answers questions regarding other lands based on what has been briefly seen.

Seeing now as it was in the past, and the past being exactly like the present, that which is intended to cause sentient beings to hear and know is precisely the two types of wisdom—listening and contemplation—and the two modes of practice—faith and the Dharma.
△ Third, answering questions based on what was extensively seen, part three: first, citing one Buddha to illustrate the same principle. First.
Clarifying the time and season: "O sons of good family, as in the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago,
Maitreya asked about horizontal vision based on the light, and Mañjuśrī answered by citing vertical vision from the past, just as in the past."
Since the kalpas are said to be immeasurable and boundless, they are truly inconceivable. △ Second, the designation of the name:

At that time, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.
"Identical in title" means that their common designations are the same. The sun is wisdom (*prajñā*) and the moon is concentration (*samādhi*);

concentration and wisdom are the virtues of one's own practice, while the lamp-light is the virtue of transforming others. Furthermore, the sun, moon, and lamp represent the three types of knowledge (*trividya*);

since the present Buddha also possesses these three knowledges, they are said to be identical. The Record states: "Regarding 'common designations,' the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) possesses all ten titles; therefore, it is so named."
From the perspective of the pervasive Dharmakāya, it is also appropriate to establish the meaning [of the name] by saying, "This body of mine is itself the Dharmakāya";
thus, the title should be the "Name Corresponding to the Dharma. However, in explaining the Name Corresponding to the Dharma, it must be established based on the Dharma. As the *Zhiguan* says:
"Coming by means of non-dual wisdom to accord with perfect enlightenment is called 'Tathāgata' (Thus-Come One); because non-dual principle universally enters all dharmas, it is named..."
The Worthy One (*Arhat*) possesses the wisdom that realizes non-duality; because the essence of this wisdom is impartial, he is called the Perfectly All-Knowing One (*Samyaksaṃbuddha*).

Knowing the non-dual dharma, his cognition interpenetrates the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); although there is no coming or going, it universally enters the three periods of time, and thus he is called the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct (*Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*).

Because the non-dual nature of phenomena is darkly harmonized with the three virtues (*triguṇa*), he is called the Well-Gone One (*Sugata*). Because his principle pervades all things and encompasses the three worlds, he is called the Knower of the World (*Lokavid*).

One who can understand this principle has no further superior above them and is thus called the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*). Because they understand this principle, they are able to discipline those difficult to discipline;
they discipline the ten dharma realms and are thus called the Tamer (*vināyaka*). They comprehend the phenomena of the dharma realm and are thus called the Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).

Because they accord with this principle, all honor and look up to them, surpassing the levels of humans and devas, and are thus called the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). Because they awaken to this principle...
He is named Buddha because he has realized this principle; therefore, he is revered by the three periods of time and is thus called the World-Honored One (*Lokanātha*).
△ Third, the exposition of the Dharma: first, the initial teaching of the Sudden Vehicle is the same [as the preceding].

He expounds the true Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its meaning is profound and far-reaching, its phrasing is skillful and exquisite, it is pure and unadulterated, and it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure, holy life.
The initial opening of the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna constitutes the seventh excellence. Regarding "excellent in the beginning, middle, and end":

the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination of the Sudden Teaching are called "excellence of timing. Its meaning being profound and far-reaching refers to the principle of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the Sudden Teaching; this is called "excellence of meaning.

Its phrasing being skillful and wondrous refers to that which is uttered by the eightfold voice of the Sudden Teaching; this is "excellence of expression. To penetrate these principles is [the excellence of practice].

To speak directly so as to gladden the minds of Bodhisattvas is called "excellence of speech. Being pure and unmixed means not being shared with the followers of the Two Vehicles; this is the Sudden Teaching.
Being uniquely and fully endowed with excellence clarifies the *mañjuṣā* (full) Dharma both within and beyond the realms;
this is the perfection of the Sudden Teaching. Being pure and stainless means being free from the defects of the two extremes; this is the flexibility of the Sudden Teaching.

It is well said that Nanyue [Huisi] stated, "This is merely practicing goodness. The characteristics of the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) are precisely the unconditioned compassion of the Sudden Teaching.
△ Second, the opening of the gradual after the sudden is the same:
for those seeking the state of a *śrāvaka*, he taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to deliver beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death, ultimately leading them to *nirvāṇa*.
For those seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha, one should teach the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; for Bodhisattvas, one should teach the Six Pāramitās.
The Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is precisely what the Buddhas of the past taught after the sudden [teaching] to open the way for the gradual—this is the same answer given to the question above.
The teaching on *nirvāṇa* and the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) answers the previous question regarding the explanation for the *pratyekabuddhas*.

The teaching on the six *pāramitās* answers the previous question regarding the cultivation of various practices. △ Third, the opening of the provisional and the manifestation of the real are identical.
"Causing them to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and achieve all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā).
This clarifies the teaching of the ancient Buddhas who, after opening the gates of the sudden and gradual [teachings], subsequently revealed the ultimate reality.
From beginning to end, this concludes the answer to Maitreya’s questions regarding the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas in other lands and the construction of stupas following their nirvāṇa. △
In the second period of invitation, twenty thousand Buddhas were identical [in name].
Next, there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa; next, there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa.
In this way, these twenty thousand Buddhas all shared the same single title, Candrasūryapradīpa, and also shared the same clan name, which was Bharadvāja.
Rāḍha, Maitreya, you should know that from the first Buddha to the last Buddha, they were all of one name, Sūryagandhottamapradīpa, fully endowed with the ten epithets;
the Dharma they preached was excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.

In the first citation, one Buddha is mentioned who fully enumerates both sudden and gradual teachings; in the second citation, twenty thousand Buddhas are mentioned, but only the sudden teaching is cited.
Therefore, it is said that they are "good in the beginning, middle, and end. In the subsequent citation, only one Buddha is mentioned who cites only the opening of the gradual teaching.

The reason for this is that these are cited alternately; the reference to the preceding [passage] makes the meaning clear. As for the surname *Pāraśava*, this refers to the tenth [class] of the Brahmins.
One of the eight clans; in the *Benxing ji jing* (Sūtra on the Collection of Past Deeds), his name is translated as "Heavy Banner" (*Chongdang*).
△ Third, citing the final Buddha, the fact that he previously witnessed [the same event] is identical to what has occurred now.
When that last Buddha had not yet left the household life, there were eight princes:

the first was named Meaningful Intent, the second Good Intent, the third Immeasurable Intent, the fourth Jewel Intent, the fifth Increasing Intent, the sixth Doubt-Dispelling Intent, the seventh Resonant Intent, and the eighth Dharma Intent.
These eight princes possessed sovereign majesty and virtue, each governing four continents.
When the princes heard that their father had left the household life and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
they all renounced their royal positions and likewise followed him into the homeless life. They resolved upon the Mahāyāna, constantly practiced the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*),
and all became Dharma-preachers who had already planted roots of goodness under tens of millions of Buddhas.
In the past, the Buddha had eight sons; now, the Buddha has one son. Although their numbers are unequal, both were born in lands where they dwell together.

These lands possess both *darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* afflictions, and thus both manifest having sons. The fact of having sons is the same in both cases; however, the specific manifestations differ according to conditions.
The birth of one son symbolizes the purity of the One Path, while the birth of eight sons symbolizes the Eightfold Noble Path. Though the numbers differ, the underlying meaning is the same.
△ Second, the similarity between past events witnessed and the present; second, the initial appearance of identical signs. First, clarifying the six auspicious omens in this land:
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa was preaching a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Anantārtha*, which teaches the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas. The Buddha...

Having finished preaching this sutra (the same as in the "Teaching the Dharma" section), he immediately sat cross-legged in the midst of the great assembly and entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings,
his body and mind unmoving (the same as in the "Entering Samādhi" section). At that time, it rained *māndārava* flowers,
*mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers from the sky, scattering over the Buddha.
As well as the great assembly (the rain of flowers is the same), the entire Buddha-world shook in six ways (the earthquake is the same). At that time, within the assembly—
monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and various minor kings and wheel-turning [kings]— [all were present].

The Holy Kings and this great assembly attained what they had never experienced before; with joy, they joined their palms and gazed at the Buddha with single-minded devotion. (The assembly rejoiced together.

At that time, the Tathāgata emitted a light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminated eighteen thousand buddha-fields in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception.
(The emission of light was the same for all directions.)
△ Second, clarifying the six auspicious omens in other lands.

As it is said, "What is seen now is like the various Buddha-lands," this implies that by what is seen now, one knows that the six auspicious omens in the other lands of past Buddhas were also identical to those of the present. △
The second point, regarding their shared doubt, is as follows:
Maitreya, you should know that at that time there were twenty billion bodhisattvas in the assembly who desired to hear this Dharma.
When these bodhisattvas saw this light universally illuminating the Buddha above them, they attained what they had never experienced before and wished to know the purpose of this light.
The causal conditions.
At that time, the doubts in the minds of the bodhisattvas in the assembly were identical to those of Maitreya now. △ Second, the events witnessed in the past will be the same as those occurring now;
first, the identity of the persons involved.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Prabhāsa who had eight hundred disciples.

Just as the former Buddha, when entering meditative concentration, caused the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa to preach the sutra, so too does the present Buddha, when entering meditative concentration, cause Śāriputra to preach the sutra;
thus, the persons upon whom he relies are the same. Furthermore, the eight sons of the former Buddha were disciples of the Tathāgata Prabhāsa during his period of meditative concentration.
When [the Buddha] arose from his meditation, he addressed Miao Guang (Prabhāpāla) and entrusted him; now, the Buddha’s disciple Rāhula also takes Śāriputra as his teacher.
When the Buddha arises from meditation, he again addresses Śāriputra until the conclusion of the "Trace Gate" (Ji-men), where he once more entrusts him to him.
Thus, the ancient and the modern are identical. Those who doubt may say that Miao Guang is a bodhisattva while Śāriputra is a śrāvaka.
How should we understand this? One must know that while past events have already been revealed, his present deeds have not yet unfolded;

thus he is called a Bodhisattva for now. As for the statement that he is compared to a Śrāvaka, this refers to his manifest traces. Śāriputra was indeed a great Bodhisattva—how could he be anything else?

Why did the former Miaoguang (Wonderful Light) descend as a trace-manifestation? It was surely because Mañjuśrī skillfully employed the expedient means of concealment by appearing specifically as a Śrāvaka.
[This] reveals the ears. △ Second, the identity of the names of the Dharma taught:

At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa arose from samādhi and, for the sake of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, preached a Mahāyāna sūtra named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which teaches the Dharma to bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.
To say that the names of the sutras are identical means that the wondrous Dharma itself is identical. △ Third, the identity of the time:

for sixty minor kalpas, [the Buddha] did not rise from his seat; those in the assembly who were listening also sat in one place for sixty minor kalpas, their bodies and minds unmoving as they listened to what the Buddha preached, perceiving it as if it were the duration of a single meal. During this time, there was not a single person among the multitude...
Whether in body or mind, they may give rise to weariness and fatigue.
△ Fourth, the proclamation of extinction is the same:
After the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had preached this sutra for sixty intermediate kalpas, he immediately, before the Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, and...
In the midst of the assembly of brahmins, devas, and asuras, he proclaimed these words:
"This very day, at midnight, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa without remainder.
Just as when the Buddha previously preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he immediately announced his entry into extinction; it was likewise with Kāśyapa Buddha, because his land was pure.
Regarding the "proclamation of extinction" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this refers to entering extinction immediately;

it means that in the current *Ratnakoṭi-parivarta*, the Tathāgata clarifies that he shall soon enter nirvana, as his work of transformation and guidance is complete and the matter of proclaiming extinction has been fulfilled. △ Fifth, the equality of bestowing predictions.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakośa. The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa immediately bestowed upon him a prediction of enlightenment, declaring to the bhikṣus:
"This bodhisattva Guṇakośa shall next become a buddha, titled Viśuddhakāya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

In the past, the Buddha bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon the Bodhisattva Guṇasaṃbhava; now, the Buddha bestows a prediction upon the Śrāvaka Śāriputra. How could these two cases be the same?

Since the events of the past were already accomplished, it is said that the prediction for a bodhisattva is precisely the convergence of the three vehicles into a single vehicle, wherein a śrāvaka attains the prediction.
If one were to say that the prediction for a śrāvaka was bestowed in the past, then once the Buddha has arisen from samādhi, what further would there be to discuss?
It is because Mañjuśrī speaks with such skillful art that he does not reveal his origins; his failure to reveal them clarifies his underlying intention, which awaits a definitive prediction.
*Tathāgata* is translated here as "Thus-Come One" (*Rulai*); *Arhat* as "Worthy of Offerings" (*Yinggong*);
and *Samyaksaṃbuddha* as "Perfectly All-Knowing" (*Zhengbianzhi*). Among these ten titles, three are cited here.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "If I were to analyze these three [aspects], I would not reach their end even after the exhaustion of an eon.
△ Sixth, regarding the period after his parinirvāṇa, it accords with the five [periods] throughout the sūtras; first, it clarifies the timing:
having received the prophecy, the Buddha entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* during the middle watch of the night.
△ Second, identifying the person:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light (Prabhūtaratna) shall uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
△ Third, clarifying the duration: [The period of time.]
For eighty full minor kalpas, he preached the Dharma for the sake of humans.
△ Fourth, clarifying the assembly of those transformed [by the Buddha], in two parts: first, clarifying those who were already his disciples.
The eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa all took Subhāṣita as their teacher; Subhāṣita taught and transformed them, causing them to become firm in the Path.
Having made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of buddhas, these princes all attained the Way of the Buddha;
the last among them to attain Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara.

Those who have already attained perfection are the eight sons whose practices were perfected and who have long since become Buddhas. △ Second, explaining those who will attain perfection as disciples:
Among the eight hundred disciples, there was one named Seeking Fame (Yaśaskāma), who was greedy for gain and offerings.

Although he recited many scriptures, he did not penetrate their meaning and forgot much of what he had learned; therefore, he was called "Seeking Fame. This person also planted various [roots of merit]...

By virtue of the causes and conditions of their roots of goodness, they encountered immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, and praising them.
Regarding the "Eight Sons" and the "Eight Hundred," the former clarifies doubts directly, while the latter reveals the secret *āyus-pramāṇa* (lifespan) to clarify doubts. As for those who might say:
Maitreya is one who has attained the position of the Successor (Upapadya), whereas Mañjuśrī is not a Successor; thus, the former is "great" and the latter is "small.
Because the great should not answer and the small should not question, it is appropriate that Maitreya raise the matter of the eight hundred [disciples], as there must indeed be a question.

Furthermore, because Miaoguang (Prabhāsa) previously personally encountered the Buddha and was formerly his teacher, his resolution of doubts is not erroneous. In secretly revealing the *āyus-pramāṇa* (lifespan), the youngest of the eight sons attains [the realization].
The Buddha who attained enlightenment under the name Dīpaṃkara was none other than Dīpaṃkara (Radiant Light); this very Radiant Light is Mañjuśrī, who is the ninth-generation patriarch of Śākyamuni.

While the grandson has now become the patriarch and the patriarch has become his disciple, this lack of fixed status between teacher and disciple conveys the meaning that birth is not truly born and extinction is not truly extinguished.
Question: In the past, when Maitreya saw various Buddhas, did he ever hear the Dharma?
Regarding the question "What now? and the answer, one must strike and awaken the faculties and capacities of the assembly at that time. *Miaole* states:
As for the "Nine Generations of Patriarchs," if we rely on the fact that all eight sons were disciples of Miaoguang, then Miaoguang occupies the head of the eight generations.
The last of the eight sons was named Randideng; since Randideng was the teacher of Śākyamuni, therefore [it is] Miaoguang... [the text continues].

Kāśyapa was the ancestor of nine generations. Regarding the statement that "birth is non-birth" and so forth, since master and disciple are mutually related in this way, one should know that the birth of master and disciple is in truth non-birth;
likewise, their prior extinction was in truth non-extinction. This is because they had long ago realized the principle of the eternal abiding that is neither born nor extinguished;
therefore, they now manifest traces of birth and extinction. Furthermore, these traces are difficult to fathom.
Arising is not arising because its fundamental principle is wondrous; cessation is not cessation because its origin and manifestation, though distinct, are inconceivably one.
△ Fifth, the conclusion that unites the ancient and the present:
Maitreya, you should know that the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light at that time—could he have been anyone else? It was my own self. [He who was] Seeking Fame...
"Bodhisattva, it is you yourself.
△ Fourth, the clear and definitive answer:
"Now seeing this auspicious omen, which is no different from that of old, I therefore reflect that today the Tathāgata shall preach the Mahāyāna."
The title of this sutra is *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.
Since the six auspicious omens of both the past and the present are identical, one may reflect that they are certainly not erroneous; whether abbreviated or detailed, they are all determined.
When it says "I shall preach the Mahāyāna," this refers to the previously mentioned omen of preaching the Dharma; its name is *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

The phrase "the certainty" refers to what was previously called the omen of the rain of flowers; "the teaching of the Dharma for Bodhisattvas" refers to what was previously called the omen of universal joy;
and "that which is protected by the Buddha's mindfulness" refers to what was previously called the omen of the earth’s trembling.

These are all included within the collective entry into meditative concentration. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts: first, the verse summary of the detailed answer regarding what was previously seen. First...
The first verse of the hymn is the same [as the prose].
At that time, Mañjuśrī, wishing to restate this meaning within the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"I recall that in the past, through immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, there was a Buddha, a Honored One among Men, named Candrasūryapradīpa."
The World-Honored One expounds the Dharma, delivering immeasurable sentient beings and innumerable billions of bodhisattvas, causing them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
△ Second, the verse on the final Buddha; third, the three points of commonality. First, the verse on how past events are identical to the present.
When the Buddha had not yet left the household life, his eight princes saw the Great Sage renounce the world and likewise followed him in practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
II. Verses on Past Events Being Identical to the Present (2): A. Verses on the Identity of the Six Auspicious Omens Here and There (2):
1. The Six Auspicious Omens in This Land.
At that time, the Buddha preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled "The Immeasurable Meanings" (*Ananta-nirdeśa*), extensively analyzing it for the great assembly.
Having finished preaching this sūtra, he sat cross-legged upon the Dharma-seat in a samādhi called "The Station of Immeasurable Meanings.
Heavenly *māndārava* flowers rained down, celestial drums resounded spontaneously, and devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts made offerings. △ The Honored One in the Center.
All Buddha-lands immediately shook with a great trembling, and the Buddha emitted light from between his eyebrows, manifesting various rare and wondrous events.
Among these, the spontaneous sounding of celestial drums signifies that he speaks of himself without being questioned.
The manifestation of these rare and wondrous events is a general summary of all the auspicious omens. △ Second, the six omens in other lands (part five): first, the six visions.
The destinies are the same.
This light shines upon eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, revealing to all sentient beings the places where they undergo the retribution of birth and death through their karma;
it is seen that these various Buddha-lands are adorned with myriad jewels, possessing the colors of lapis lazuli and crystal, all because of the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
Furthermore, he saw the various devas, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras each making offerings to that Buddha.

The three lines constitute the first half-verse of the *saṃgīti* (repeated verse) summarizing the auspicious omens; the next single line specifically mentions the six destinies, hence the term "all" (*sarva*).
The subsequent single line generally clarifies the causes and effects of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), where the two characters "birth-and-death" (*shengsi*) serve as a general heading.
This is the heading. Regarding the section on the causes of karma and the fruits of retribution, there are twenty items in sequence. The first line clarifies the land upon which they rely;
this was not mentioned in the preceding prose passage or within the questions and answers, and it is only here that it is stated.

One should know that the preceding [sections] were indeed present, as the subsequent line clarifies the intent of making offerings across the various realms of existence (*gati*), thereby manifesting the maturation of the spiritual capacities (*indriya*) of those to be trained. Thus, it should be understood that the preceding [text] was not lacking.
Question: It is also not the case that they do not exist. Since you have already stated that adornment is itself the Pure Land, why do you say their "ways are the same"?
Answer: Purity arises from the radiance of light; fundamentally, the six realms are the Pure Land, and thus there is no name for the evil paths.

Therefore, one knows that it is not only the physical forms that are pure, but by means of this light, all manner of jewels are also fully present. Each offering refers to the eighteen thousand lands.
△ Second, the verses on seeing the Buddhas are the same.
Furthermore, one sees all Tathāgatas spontaneously attaining the path of Buddhahood, their physical forms like mountains of gold, majestic and exceedingly subtle,
like pure lapis lazuli with the image of true gold appearing within it.
Regarding "spontaneously attaining the Buddha-way": the path of skillful means involves applying the mind to cultivation until the True Way is manifested;

this is precisely what is meant by spontaneity (*zìrán*), wherein one accords with principle through effortless operation. Furthermore, spontaneously attaining the Buddha-way refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body);

the lapis lazuli represents the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) which is fundamentally pure, while the golden image represents the manifestation of form in response to sentient beings. △ Third, the verse explains the sudden sameness.
The World-Honored One expounds the profound meaning of the Dharma amidst the great assembly.
This refers to applying the Dharma to persons; since the Dharma is already profound and mysterious, one should know that it must move those with great capacities to open the Sudden Teaching.
This verse praises the aforementioned state of being purely singular and without admixture. △ Fourth, the verse on the commonality of the three vehicles.
In each and every buddha-field, the assemblies of śrāvakas were countless; through the illumination of the Buddha’s light, they all beheld those great congregations.
Some bhikṣus were seen in mountain forests, diligently maintaining pure precepts as if guarding a bright pearl;
others were seen as bodhisattvas practicing generosity, patience, and so forth, their number equaling the sands of the Ganges—all this was due to the radiance of the Buddha’s light.

This refers to individuals in relation to the Dharma; since those of the Two Vehicles must necessarily understand that the Three Piṭakas were taught as an expedient opening, this verse summarizes what was previously stated for those seeking the state of a Śrāvaka:
the teaching of the Four Noble Truths. Although the Pratyekabuddhas are not explicitly mentioned in the verse, they are included therein by implication.
The following two lines summarize the Mahāyāna of the Six Pāramitās. Regarding the practice of giving, patience, and so forth...
The remaining two perfections—meditation (dhyāna) and wisdom (prajñā)—are already established;

however, regarding the designation of a bhikṣu as a bodhisattva of the six perfections, since the preceding verse of inquiry already states, "I also see bodhisattvas acting as bhikṣus," there is no contradiction in this sense of a bhikṣu being a bodhisattva.
△ Fifth, the verse on the equality of the bodhisattva’s practice.
Furthermore, I see various bodhisattvas who have deeply entered various meditative concentrations, their bodies and minds tranquil and unmoving, seeking the unsurpassed path;
and I also see various bodhisattvas who, knowing the mark of the quiescence of all phenomena, preach the Dharma in their respective lands, seeking the Buddha-way.
△ Second, the doubts of the fourfold assembly are the same.
At that time, when the fourfold assembly saw the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa manifesting such great supernormal powers, their hearts were filled with joy,
and they each asked one another about the causes and conditions for this matter.

The verse concerning the fourfold assembly’s doubts regarding the former Buddha may be understood according to the text. △ Third, the verse on the fact that what was previously seen will be the same as what occurs now, in six parts;
first, the verse on the identity of the persons involved.
The Honored One, revered by devas and humans, having just arisen from samādhi, praised the Bodhisattva Wondrous Light: "You are the eye of the world, the refuge and object of faith for all.
You are able to uphold the treasury of the Dharma; as I have taught the Dharma, only you are able to realize and know it.
Having thus praised him, the World-Honored One caused Wondrous Light to rejoice.
The "Eyes of the World" refers to the Bodhisattvas acting as the eyes of both the mundane and supramundane worlds to guide and transform humanity.
△ Second, the verse on the identity of preaching the Dharma:
"When this Lotus Sūtra is preached..."
△ The three verses indicate that the duration was the same:
for sixty full intermediate kalpas, the Dharma Master Sublime Light was able to receive and uphold all of this most sublime Dharma taught while remaining seated upon this very throne without rising.
This refers to the wisdom that perceives the inconceivable extension and brevity of kalpas; through his wondrous light, he has fully received and upheld the Buddhas' teachings of the past.
This is also like Śāriputra receiving the Buddha’s entrustment. △ Fourth, the verse on proclaiming the extinction, which is in four parts; first, the proclamation of extinction.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and had gladdened the assembly, he immediately on that very day addressed the multitude of devas and humans:
"I have already explained for you the meaning of the true reality of all dharmas; tonight, at midnight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
This is the same as when the Buddhas of the past proclaimed their parinirvāṇa, which has now been followed in succession by the present Buddha. △ Second, the entrustment:
"You must practice with single-minded diligence and remain far removed from negligence; for the Buddhas are extremely difficult to encounter, appearing but once in hundreds of millions of kalpas."
This was the entrustment given by the Buddhas of the past, which is identical to that of the present Buddha. As the *Śāriputra-śīla-sūtra* (Yijiao jing) states:
"You bhikṣus, after my parinirvāṇa, you should treasure and revere the *prātimokṣa*. It is like encountering light in the darkness, or like a poor man finding a treasure.
You should know that this is your Great Teacher; whether I remain in the world or not, there is no difference. △
Third, weeping with grief:
when the sons of the World-Honored One and others heard that the Buddha had entered nirvana, each harbored sorrow and distress, exclaiming, "How swift is the extinction of the Buddha!
At that time, the assembly, hearing of the Buddha’s entry into extinction, gave rise to weeping and grief just as they do now; it is as described in the Mahā-sūtra.

It is said that with tears filling his eyes and blood appearing over his entire body like *pārijāta* flowers, this was the resolve of one who deeply reveres the Dharma and yearns for it. △ Fourth, the consolation:
"O Sovereign Lord, King of the Dharma, you comfort immeasurable multitudes: 'When I enter parinirvāṇa, you should not grieve or be afraid.'"

In the past, when the Buddha consoled the assembly, he did so in the same manner as the present Buddha; as the *Śāsanānuśāsanī-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) says: "O Bhikṣus, do not harbor grief or distress.
Even if I were to remain in this world for one kalpa or two kalpas, the assembly would still eventually disperse.
To meet and never part again is ultimately impossible. My Dharma, which fully accomplishes both self-benefit and the benefit of others, is already complete. If I were to remain for long..."

There is no further benefit [to be gained]; this is analogous to the present Buddha entrusting [the Dharma] to Maitreya (the meaning of which is seen in the *Jì*). △ Fifth, the verse on the bestowal of the prediction is the same:
This Bodhisattva Guṇagarbha has already attained thorough penetration of the mind of the untainted true mark (*anāsrava-lakṣaṇa*);
he shall next become a Buddha named Viśuddhakāya and shall likewise deliver immeasurable multitudes.

The "outflow-free true reality" (*anāsrava-tattva-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the dharma of the three perfectly wondrous truths (*triratna*). "Outflow-free" means that the three truths are gathered and subsumed without any loss or leakage.
"True reality" means being free from the characteristics of false conceptualization; it is called "true reality" because it is the characteristic of formlessness (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*). △ Six:
Verses on the Propagation of the Sūtra After Extinction, identical to the five [preceding sections]. First: Verses on the Time After Extinction.
The fourfold assembly attained benefits.
That night, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa like a fire extinguished when its fuel is exhausted; his relics were distributed and immeasurable stupas were erected.
The bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, redoubled their diligence in seeking the unsurpassed path.
Regarding the phrase "when the fuel is exhausted, the fire is extinguished," the interpretations differ between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
In the Hīnayāna, the Buddha takes the body of retribution (*vipākakāya*) as the fuel and wisdom as the fire; when the body perishes, the wisdom ceases.

In the Mahāyāna, the Buddha takes the capacities of sentient beings as the fuel and the manifestation of response (*nirmāṇa*) as the fire; when the capacities of sentient beings are exhausted, the responsive form likewise vanishes. One must apply oneself with even greater diligence.
Those who advance are those who should deliver others through *nirvāṇa*. △ Second, a verse on the person capable of propagating the sutra:
"This Dharma Master Wonderful Light upholds the treasury of the Buddha's Dharma.
△ Third, a verse on the time period for propagating the sutra.
During eighty minor kalpas, he extensively proclaimed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
△ Fourth, verses on the disciples benefited; part one: verses on disciples already perfected.
These eight princes, transformed and enlightened by Prabhāsa, have become firm in the unsurpassed Way and shall behold countless Buddhas.

Having made offerings to all the Buddhas, he followed and practiced the marks of the Great Path, succeeding one after another in attaining Buddhahood and receiving successive predictions of enlightenment.
Finally, the God among Gods, known as Dīpaṃkara Buddha—the guide of all sages—delivered immeasurable multitudes across to liberation.
△ Second, the verse on becoming a disciple:
At that time, Dharma Master Miaoguang had a disciple whose mind was constantly filled with indolence and who was greedily attached to fame and profit.

Seeking fame and profit without satiety, he frequently visited the homes of the noble families; he abandoned what he had practiced and recited, falling into forgetfulness so that his mastery was lost.

For these reasons, he is named Seeking Fame (Yaśaskāma). Having also performed various wholesome deeds, he has seen countless Buddhas, made offerings to those Buddhas, followed their practice of the Great Vehicle, and fulfilled the six *pāramitās*. Now he beholds the Lion of the Śākyas;
hereafter he shall become a Buddha named Maitreya, who will extensively deliver sentient beings in numbers beyond measure.
△ Fifth, a summary connecting the ancient and the modern:
"After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you who were indolent are now the Dharma Master Miaoguang; I myself am he.
△ Third, the clear judgment and answer in verse, in three parts: first, the verse on preaching the Mahāyāna sūtras.
"I see that the Buddha Dīpaṃkara manifested such a sign of his original radiance; by this I know that the present Buddha intends to preach the Lotus Sūtra.
This verse explains the structural outline of the sūtra as already seen. Furthermore, previously Maitreya resolved four latent difficulties so that Mañjuśrī would certainly provide an answer;
here, it is Mañjuśrī who cuts off these four latent doubts so that Maitreya shall not raise them again.
Question: Regarding the first doubt concerning the initial passage, Mañjuśrī extensively cites that previous Buddhas had already preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Maitreya harbors a latent doubt, wishing to ask: "The times when various Buddhas respond to conditions differ; although the ancient Buddha was named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, why must the present Buddha be likewise?
Mañjuśrī immediately cuts through this with the first verse: "I saw the Lamp-Luminous [Buddha]..."
The Buddha’s original light-omen was such as this; by this, one knows that the Buddha now intends to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This [section] cuts off their doubts, and is thus called "The Question. △ Second, the verse on the teaching for bodhisattvas.
The present signs are like the original auspicious omens; these are the skillful means of all Buddhas. Now the Buddha emits light to assist in elucidating the meaning of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Maitreya, because of this, further doubts whether there are cases where both the name and the meaning are the same, and cases where the name is the same but the meaning differs;
what, then, does this name signify? Mañjuśrī immediately resolves this with the second verse, stating: "The present signs are like the original auspicious omens."
These are the skillful means of all Buddhas; now this Buddha emits light to assist in elucidating the meaning of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This is the answer to the question regarding the substance of their doubts.
All you people should now know: join your palms and wait with single-mindedness for the Buddha, who shall rain down the Dharma-rain to satisfy those who seek the Way.
Maitreya then further doubted who could realize the signless nature of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
therefore, Mañjuśrī used this third verse to sever the doubt underlying his fundamental inquiry. △ Third, the verse on being protected by the Buddha’s mindfulness.
If there are those seeking the three vehicles who harbor doubts or regrets, the Buddha shall eliminate and sever them so that none remain.

Because Maitreya subsequently harbored further doubts—namely, that while the Buddha rains down the rain of Dharma to thoroughly moisten the bodhisattvas, it also moistens those of the two vehicles—Mañjuśrī immediately severed his doubts with the fourth verse.
This was used as a question, and Maitreya followed in succession, constructing further doubts.
Since Mañjuśrī repeatedly resolved these matters until their affairs were exhausted and their principles fully realized, he internalized them;

this may be called being skilled in question and answer, possessing both forms of adornment. Guangzhai only knew to recount Master Zhao’s explanation of the four hidden difficulties, thereby manifesting Maitreya’s excellence, yet he failed to see how Mañjuśrī’s resolution of the four hidden doubts allowed [Maitreya] to shine.
Maitreya did not question [the Buddha] regarding the capacity of Miaode (Wondrous Virtue); this interpretation originates from Tiantai and is not derived from other commentaries.
This is the second chapter, "Expedient Means," of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
This chapter is the primary teaching of the entire sutra and the confluence of all dharmas; it serves as both the testimony of faith (*samyag-adhimukti*) and the introduction (*nidāna*).
This parable illustrates this [teaching], and even extends to its circulation; it explains the title of this chapter in two parts: first, briefly, and second, extensively.
Briefly, there are three kinds of skillful means (*upāya*); extensively, there are ten pairs of provisional and real.

The three kinds of skillful means refer to the Dharma, the function, and the ability to penetrate the secret and wondrous. Regarding "the Dharma and the function": *fang* (方) refers to the Dharma, and *bian* (便) refers to the function.
The Dharma has both square and round aspects, and its applications have points of divergence and convergence. The three provisional means (triyāna) are the square and the ruler;
the one reality is the compass and the circle. This principle may be used to explain other sutras, but it is not the intended meaning of this present chapter.

That which is called "ability to penetrate," "expedient means" (upāya), and "gate" (mukha)—the term "gate" signifies that which can penetrate what is to be penetrated. Expedient means and skillful stratagems are all introductory preludes for the sake of the Truth.
The true manifestation of the gateway of reality is achieved through skillful means (*upāya*); it is named "gateway" because it is derived from that which reveals [the truth].

Thus, "gateway" explains "skillful means. As the Sūtra says: "Opening the gateway of skillful means to reveal the aspect of reality. This meaning may be explained in other sūtras, but it is not the intended sense of this chapter.
Regarding the term "secret and subtle": "secret" (*pi*) refers to the hidden; "convenient" (*bian*) refers to the subtle. It is the subtle penetration [of the truth].
