Regarding the directions, this is precisely the true secret point: the pearl within the robe and the jewel upon the king’s crown are non-dual and indistinguishable;
the hired laborer and the son of the elder are likewise non-dual and indistinguishable. The method and the gate are the Secret and Sublime Sūtra, which says:
"Only I know these marks; the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so. Cease, cease! There is no need for further [discourse].
Because it is said that my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable, the term "esoteric subtlety" (*guhyamāhātmya*) is used to explain "skillful means" (*upāya*);

this is precisely the intended meaning of the present chapter, and thus it is called the "Chapter on Skillful Means. Regarding the ten pairs of provisional and real: first, phenomena and principle; second, principle and teaching; third, teaching and practice;
fourth, bondage and liberation; fifth, cause and fruit; sixth, essence and function; seventh, gradual and sudden; eighth, opening and closing; ninth, penetration... [and so forth].

Regarding the ten distinct *siddhāntas*, within these ten, they are further explained in detail through eight perspectives—such as the sequence of arising, the provisional and the real, and the fundamental and the trace—yet they do not transcend the meaning of the causes and effects of one’s own practice, and the subject and object of transforming others.
△ Second, regarding the main exposition, it is divided into two parts: first, a brief opening of the three to reveal the two; second, an extensive opening of the three.

The first section of the initial passage further divides into two parts: first, the opening of the three [topics]; second, the manifestation of the two superior doubts that lead to a request for instruction.
The first of these again divides into two: first, the prose section together with seventeen and a half verses praising the two wisdoms;

second, two and a half verses that explicitly and briefly reveal [the truth], thereby shaking one's attachments and giving rise to doubt. The first of these [sub-sections] again divides into two: first, the prose section consisting of twenty-seven and a half lines.

The opening text of the verse is further divided into two parts: first, praising the two wisdoms by means of words; second, praising the two wisdoms beyond words. The first part is further divided into two:
first, clarifying the provisional and real aspects of all Buddhas; second, clarifying the provisional and real aspects of Śākyamuni.

The first of these is further divided into three: first, a double praise; second, a double explanation; third, a double conclusion. The first of these is further divided into two: first, the scribe’s introductory record.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose serenely from samādhi and addressed Śāriputra.
Śāriputra asked, "The Buddha is always in meditative concentration; for what reason do you say he has 'arisen'? The Buddha replied, "There is a specific purpose for this demonstration.
When the Buddhas of the past preached this sūtra, they would invariably first enter the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings, which is to say, the Lotus Samādhi; now, the present Buddha does likewise."

However, while entering meditative concentration one contemplates principle to settle the mind in the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), and upon emerging from concentration, one causes others to likewise settle their minds in the true reality.
[The Buddha] addressed Śāriputra because, among those of the Lesser Vehicle, he was foremost in wisdom;

intending to use him to break down limited wisdom and reveal Great Wisdom, the Buddha first addressed him to stir the assembly. △ Second, the formal praise of the two wisdoms, in two parts: First, the praise.
Ultimate wisdom.
The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable;
the wisdom of all Buddhas is precisely ultimate wisdom. The essence of this wisdom is the one mind as the threefold wisdom. It is profound indeed.
"Profoundly immeasurable" means that the Buddha’s true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) penetrates vertically to the very bottom of reality, and thus is called "profound";
it extends horizontally to the limits of the *dharmadhātu*, and thus is called "immeasurable. △ Second, praising the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
This gate of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter; it is something that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know.

This "gate of wisdom" refers to *upāya-jñāna* (expedient wisdom). It is essentially the preliminary skillful means (*pūrvopāya*) for the path of self-cultivation, possessing the power of progressive advancement;

therefore, it is called a "gate. Entering through this gate constitutes the Middle Way. Within the Middle Way, it is called "reality" (*tattva*); prior to the Middle Way, it is called "expediency" (*upāya*).

Regarding "difficult to understand and difficult to enter": the seven kinds of skillful means cannot fathom it; the Ten Abodes constitute the beginning of understanding, while the Ten Grounds constitute entry.
By citing the beginning and the end, one may know that the intermediate stages are difficult to demonstrate and difficult to awaken to.

As for the separate mention of those who cannot know according to the Hīnayāna, it is because their attachments are heavy; thus, they are specifically refuted. Furthermore, because they lack the capacity and flee, it is said that they do not know.

Because [the followers of] the Avataṃsaka are like the deaf, the mute, and the blind, it is said they do not know; because [the followers of] the Vaipulya are disparaged and [the followers of] the *Pratītyasamutpāda* dwell in thatched huts, it is said they do not know;
because [the followers of] the Prajñā have turned the teaching and their minds are free from longing or grasping, it is said they do not know.

Now, as the great capacity has been awakened, light is emitted and the earth shakes; since the Way of the Buddhas of both this and other ages is identical, yet [you] still harbor doubts, it is therefore said: "You do not know."
Not knowing that a bodhisattva of sharp faculties can, through their various capacities, know those of dull faculties who are the same as the two vehicles—this too is a case of not knowing.
△ Second, the dual explanation: first, the explanation of real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Why is this? Because the Buddha has personally attended upon hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of countless Buddhas and fully practiced the immeasurable Dharma of all Buddhas.

Having encountered many Buddhas in the external world, he received and inherited their most essential teachings; thus, his realization of true wisdom is profoundly deep and his internal practice is pure and substantial.
The reason the true wisdom (*jñāna*) of the Dharma-practice is immeasurable is as follows. △ Second, the explanation of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*):
His valorous diligence brings his fame to universal renown.
Because of this valorous diligence, he is able to enter gates that are difficult to enter; having entered these gates, he [benefits] the world.
Because he was revered for his transformative virtue by beings of boundless reach, his fame and reputation were heard everywhere. △ Third, the double conclusion in two parts:
first, concluding the wisdom of reality.
He has accomplished the profound and unprecedented Dharma.

Because it accords with principle and is ultimate, it is called "accomplished"; because it reaches the very bottom of the other shore, it is called "profound. △ Second, the conclusion regarding provisional wisdom:
that which is taught according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand in its underlying intent.

Because it accords with capacities and meets the occasion, it is said to be "taught according to what is appropriate"; because it is not something known by those at the stage of the seven expedient means (*saptopāya*), it is said to be "difficult to understand.
△ Second, explaining the provisional and the real of Śākyamuni; first, the double praise; first, praising his wisdom.

Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood, if true wisdom were not perfected, the Way of the Buddha would not be accomplished. Since it is said that once one becomes a Buddha, all things are accomplished.
2. Praising the Provisional and the Real.

Through various causes and conditions and various parables, he extensively expounded his verbal teachings; by means of countless skillful means, he guided sentient beings to cause them to leave behind all attachments.

For more than forty years, because he used the three kinds of provisional and real transformations to harmonize with sentient beings according to their capacities, it is said that they were "various."
Regarding causes, conditions, and parables: the Hīnayāna uses the plantain tree and water bubbles as metaphors, while the Mahāyāna uses the city of the gandharvas, mirrors, illusions, and so forth.
"Extensively expounding" means being able to produce immeasurable meanings from a single dharma.
"Innumerable skillful means" refers to the seven stages of expedient means. "Guiding [beings] to leave behind all attachments" refers to teaching the ten wholesome actions to bring about detachment.
To speak of stillness while attached to the three miserable realms; to speak of the Dharma of the Tripitaka while detached from the desires of the desire realm;

to speak of the Bodhisattva Dharma while detached from views and afflictions; and to speak of the Buddha-Dharma while detached from attachment to the love of the dharma that accords with the Path—these constitute the detachment from such attachments.
△ Second, the dual explanation.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata has already fully perfected the *pāramitās* of skillful means (*upāya*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and vision (*darśana*).
The two characters "Tathāgata" explain true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*), for he attained perfect enlightenment by coming forth from the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
"Skillful means" explains provisional wisdom (*prajñā-upāya*), while "knowledge and vision *pāramitās*" refer to the simultaneous presentation of both provisional and ultimate wisdom.

It is so; however, "all-knowledge" (*sarvākārajñatā*) is called true knowledge, the "Buddha-eye" is called true seeing, and the "knowledge of the paths" (*mārgajñatā*) is called provisional knowledge, while the "Dharma-eye" is called provisional seeing.
Because both reach the ultimate limit of phenomena and principle, they are called *pāramitā* (perfection);
being "fully endowed" means that both the provisional and the real are completely consummated. △ Third, the double conclusion of the two [knowledges], first concluding the real wisdom.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast and profound.
Their vastness and brightness extend horizontally; their profundity and brightness extend vertically. Such true wisdom is neither horizontal nor vertical;

it is expressed through words as a praise of its transcendence, yet when discussing its horizontal and vertical illumination, it is limitless and infinite—like a box and its lid, both being equally large. △ Second, the conclusion regarding provisional means.
Wisdom, immeasurable and unimpeded powers, fearlessnesses, meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis, entering deeply into the boundless and accomplishing all unprecedented dharmas.
"Immeasurable" refers to the four immeasurables of the Buddha-ground; "unimpeded" refers to the four analytical knowledges of the Buddha-ground.
The power to produce infinite, inexhaustible eloquence from a single word or a single meaning is the ten powers; "fearlessness" refers to the four fearlessnesses.
"Dhyāna" is the true mark of all dhyānas; "samādhi" is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; "samāpatti" is the King of Samādhis.
"Profoundly entering the boundless" forms the vertical depth; "accomplishing [the lower]" forms the horizontal breadth.
△ Second, praising the two wisdoms beyond words, part one: the initial section on the reasons for praising them beyond words, subsection one: citing the reasons for praising them beyond words.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is able to skillfully analyze and eloquently expound all dharmas with supple and gentle speech that delights the hearts of the multitude.
To cite once more the provisional and the ultimate is merely to express extreme admiration and to manifest his profound respect and earnestness; he is truly capable of skillful discernment.
"Skillfully expounding all dharmas" refers to the wisdom of expedient means (*upāya-jñāna*); "speech that delights the hearts of the multitude" refers to the wisdom of reality (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Second, pointing to the realm beyond words:
Śāriputra, to speak of it in brief, the Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas.
To state the essentials: the beginning of this pointing is toward the immeasurable and boundless;

pointing to the provisional refers to the unprecedented Dharma, while pointing to the real refers to these two dharmas which the Buddha has fully accomplished through the cultivation of the path. How could these be described?
If one were to clarify only a single matter, one should not say "fully"; since both the provisional and the real are pointed out together, the meaning is clear. △ Second, the definitive exclusion.
Regarding the two types of praise [praise by words and praise by silence], first is the praise by silence.
[The Buddha] stops Śāriputra, saying there is no need for further explanation.
Master Yin says this is intended to cause doubt to arise from that cessation, thereby generating a mind of inquiry. Master Guan says it concerns the reality of dharmas (*bhūta-dharma*).
Because it is difficult to understand, [the Buddha] first restrains [his speech] to startle common sentiments;

now, clarifying that this Dharma is profoundly quiescent, beyond the path of language, and its essence is inexpressible, he therefore restrains himself and offers praise. He establishes compassion to preach for others, yet if they hear it and cannot understand, it would damage their roots of goodness;
thus, he restrains himself. △ Second, explaining the intent behind the restraint and praise, in two parts: first, clarifying that the Buddha is...

The supreme person cultivates and attains the supreme Dharma, which is unspeakable; first, it clarifies that the provisional and ultimate [teachings] of the supreme person are horizontally fulfilled and thus unspeakable. Why is this so?
Because the Dharma accomplished by the Buddha is the foremost, most rare, and difficult-to-understand teaching.
△ Second, it clarifies that the ultimate authority and reality of the supreme person are vertically profound and ineffable;
only Buddha-to-Buddha can fully exhaust them.

This explains the intent of the cessation of praise, establishing the contrast between the accomplished and the unaccomplished, and even the contrast between the difficult to understand and the not difficult to understand.

To explain this: it is taught horizontally that [the fruit] is attained through the cultivation of the path; therefore, it cannot be said that only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom its limits and depths.

Just as the body of the moon on the fifteenth day is not incomplete in its form and its light is not non-pervasive, so too is this attainment through the vertical and profound cultivation of the path;
for this reason, it cannot be spoken of. △ Second, explaining that the profound realm is ineffable.
Because it is beyond conceptualization, it cannot be described in two ways: first, a brief indication of the chapters on the provisional and the real;

the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is the "real," while the provisional aspects of all phenomena are the "provisional. Second, a detailed explanation of the characteristics of the provisional and the real.
That which is called all dharmas having such characteristics, such natures, such essences, such powers,
such functions, such causes, such conditions, such fruits, and such retributions, being thus equal from beginning to end.

The "true reality of all phenomena" (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*) briefly indicates the profound realm of the provisional and the real. "All phenomena" refers to the thousand suchnesses of the hundred realms;
this is the provisional aspect of the real. "True reality" refers to the essence of the Middle Way principle; this is the real aspect of the provisional.

The phrase "so-called 'all phenomena are equal'" extensively explains the profound realm of the provisional and the real. As for "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), they are to be observed from the perspective of external appearances.

Furthermore, one may distinguish their natures by designating that which occupies the internal self-division without changing its primary substance as the "substance" (*tī*), its functional capacity as "power" (*bala*), its structural formation as "activity" (*kriyā*),

the cause of habituation as the "causal cause" (*hetu-hetu*), the assisting cause as the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*), the fruit of habituation as the "fruit" (*phala*), the retributive fruit as the "retribution" (*vipāka*),
the initial manifestation as the "root," the subsequent retribution as the "branch," and the ultimate destination as the "consummation" (*niṣṭhā*), and so forth. If one acts in this manner...

If "like" (ru) is taken in the sense of the beginning and end both being empty, it is "equal"; if it is taken in the sense of the characteristics of nature, where the characteristics of the beginning and end exist, it is "equal";
if it is taken in the sense of the middle, where the real characteristics of both beginning and end are present, it is "equal. Now, we do not rely on these;
rather, the perfection of all three dharmas constitutes ultimate equality. Master Nanyue read this passage as "ru" (like) in all instances, and thus it is called the "Ten Suchnesses" (shi ru).
Tiantai also said that reading the text according to its meaning involves three shifts: first, "this mark is suchness," up to "this retribution is suchness";
second, "such a mark," up to "such a retribution"; third, "the mark is thus," up to "the retribution is thus.
If all are termed "suchness" (*tathatā*), then "suchness" means non-differentiation, which is the meaning of emptiness. If...
To designate names for the characteristics of emptiness through such descriptions as "forming characteristics" and so forth is the meaning of the provisional (*prajñapti*).
To act according to such characteristics as they truly are, in accordance with the Middle Way and the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), is the meaning of the middle (*madhyama*).

For the sake of making the analysis easy to understand, the aspects of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are clarified; yet, if one grasps the intended meaning, emptiness is itself the provisional and the middle. Regarding the true nature (*tathatā*), it is explained that emptiness is one.
All emptiness, the characteristic of the empty dot, and the characteristic of clarity are one; all that is provisional is one. This is the "One" within the Middle Way, wherein all is the Middle.
It is neither one, two, nor three, yet it manifests as one, two, and three. Being neither vertical nor horizontal, this is called the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
If one follows the meaning, one may conveniently analyze it according to these three intentions; if one follows the reading, one should rely on the verse text, which says:
Such are the meanings of the various natures and characteristics of these great fruits and retributions; only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively realize this Dharma.
These ten "thusnesses" (yǒurúshì) are the dharmas of cause and effect upon the ten realms. These ten dharmas encompass all phenomena.
Furthermore, within a single dharma-realm there are ten suchnesses; within the ten dharma-realms there are one hundred suchnesses; and within yet another single dharma-realm...
When the nine dharma-realms are fully present, there are one hundred dharma-realms; thus, these nine realms constitute the provisional (expedient), while the Buddha-realm constitutes the real.
To discuss this in detail, each realm possesses its own provisional and real aspects (as each single realm contains all nine). However, this provisional and real nature is inconceivable;
it is the domain of the two wisdoms of the Buddhas. Taking this as the object, what dharma would not be subsumed? This very object gives rise to wisdom.
Regarding why wisdom does not arise, Jingxi says, "The pointing to the wondrous realm originates from the *Lotus Sūtra*";
this refers precisely to this passage. The *Wenju* states: "Now, fourfold explanations are made: first, in terms of the ten dharma-realms; second, in terms of the Buddha-dharma realm;

third, in terms of separation and combination; and fourth, in terms of stages. The Sūtra speaks of "all dharmas," and thus the ten dharma-realms are used to explain it. The Sūtra says: [text continues].

Because the Buddha has accomplished rare and marvelous dharmas, the *Sūtra* uses the "Dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu) interpretation; it says: "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak, for my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable.

Because [the Buddha] is both distinct from and identical to [all beings], the *Sūtra* uses the "separation-and-union" (li-he) interpretation; it says: "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust [this].

Because [the Buddha] occupies the supreme rank, the *Sūtra* uses the "position" (wei) interpretation. Regarding the first point, concerning the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātavaḥ*), this refers to the six ordinary realms and the four noble realms.
Although dharmas are immeasurable in number, they do not transcend these eleven; although within each single realm there may be many branches, they do not transcend ten.

Thus, the specific characteristics and nature of the hell realm—including its beginning and end—are fully present therein; likewise, the characteristics and nature of the animal realm—including its beginning and end—are fully present;
and so on until the characteristics and nature of the Buddha-dharma realm—including its beginning and end—are fully present, without any deficiency.
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the path of the hells accomplishing the dharmas of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is a prime example of this;
one should know that the same applies to the other nine dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). Within each individual realm, all ten suchnesses (*tathatā*) of the other nine realms are mutually present.

When these are reflected upon from the perspective of their own respective positions, the nine realms and their ten suchnesses are all termed "expedient" (*upāya*); it is only when reflecting upon their own specific position that they are so designated.
The ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm are called the "Real. Within the one, there are the immeasurable; within the immeasurable, there is the one. For this reason, they are termed "inconceivable.

Although ordinary beings possess them, their emotions are deluded and they are cut off from principle. Although those of the Two Vehicles possess them, they abandon them in their quest for liberation.
Although Bodhisattvas possess them, their illumination is not all-pervasive; thus it is called "not yet clear. Only the Tathāgata [penetrates] them thoroughly.
Examining this, it is complete in both horizontal and vertical dimensions; it is understood solely by oneself alone and is not seen by others.

Because it cannot be proclaimed or demonstrated, it is simply "stopping, stopping," where speech is cut off. This was already explained in the section on the "Excellence of the Realm" (*dharmadhātu*) within the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning);

it will not be recorded here in full. Second, regarding the explanation according to the Buddha-dharmadhātu: the Buddha-realm is neither characterized nor uncharacterized, yet it is named as having such characteristics, pointing toward the myriad phenomena.
Because it is a virtuous causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the subsequent text says, "adorned with various jewels.

The Buddha-realm is neither a nature (*svabhāva*) nor a non-nature, yet it is called "such a nature" because it refers to wisdom as the revealing cause (*vidyā-hetu*); hence the subsequent text says, "there is a great white ox," and so forth.
The Buddha-realm is neither beginning nor end, nor is it not beginning and not not-end, yet it is spoken of in terms of beginning and end. This is the beginning.

The "end of the Buddha’s marks" (*buddha-lakṣaṇa-paryanta*) is precisely the "retribution of the Buddha" (*buddha-vipāka*); this is the provisional aspect of one's own practice (*svayam-caryā-vaśika*).

Since the Buddha-realm is neither equal nor unequal, yet is said to be ultimately equal, it refers to the true reality (*dharmatā*). Therefore, the heading states that "true reality" is the reality of one's own practice.
Because it is the provisional within the real, it is called "beginning and end"; because it is the real within the provisional, it is called "equality. This is...

The Tathāgata himself practices the provisional and the ultimate, which are most supreme; from the supreme characteristic up to the supreme retribution, they are broad horizontally and deep vertically, being without superior.
Therefore, the heading states "the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas.
By analogy, one should also say "the true nature (*bhūtadharmatā*), the true substance (*bhūtadravya*), and even the true ultimate," but for brevity, only one is cited to represent them all.
The Tathāgata’s various ears are all-pervasive, illuminating both horizontally and vertically, encompassing everything as clearly as observing a fruit in the palm of one's hand.

Yet, for ordinary beings, it is like two people born blind; for those of the Two Vehicles, it is like a person with a squint; and for Bodhisattvas, it is like seeing at night—dim and unclear, beyond comprehension.

Because it cannot be described, it is "Cease, cease! It is beyond words. Third, regarding the explanation by way of separation and conjunction: if one considers the ten [realms] as observed within the Buddha’s own mind...
The ten suchnesses of the realm are all supreme characteristics, up to and including supreme retribution; they are solely the single Buddha-dharmadhātu.
Like the ocean that gathers all rivers, or like a thousand chariots sharing the same track—this constitutes the provisional and the real of one's own practice (*svayam-ācāra*).

If, however, one follows the intentions of others, there are the nine dharma-realms; their ten suchnesses, characteristics, and natures constitute the provisional and the real of transforming others (*parārtha*).
Whether transforming oneself or others, following the provisional or the ultimate, according to others one opens [the teaching], while according to oneself one synthesizes it.
Transversally and vertically, it illuminates all; its opening and closing are sovereign. Only Buddha after Buddha can exhaustively fathom this;
ordinary people slander and do not believe, those of the Two Vehicles are bewildered and do not accept it, and Bodhisattvas have not yet clarified the "dust and stumps. For these reasons, stop, stop!

This transcends words. Fourth, the explanation by way of defining the stages: such "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refer to the fact that all sentient beings possess the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) which is inherently present;
this is the manifestation of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Such "nature" (*svabhāva*) is the wisdom of inherent virtue, the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Such "essence" (*dharmatā*) is the principle of the Middle Way, the *dharmatā* of reality.
These three virtues are also universally present across all ten dharma-realms and at every stage.
Therefore, they are inconceivable and cannot be expressed; thus, [the Buddha] ceased speaking, for words are cut off. Miaole (妙樂) says:

"The reason there are four explanations is that it clarifies how the principle encompasses everything, hence the explanation in terms of the ten realms; it clarifies the ultimate nature of self-realization, hence the explanation in terms of the Buddha-realm."

Because it clarifies the Buddha’s transformative function, it is explained by way of separation and conjunction; because it clarifies the pervasiveness of the three virtues, it is explained by way of the various stages.

If one considers *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in relation to one another, each has its own breadth and narrowness. Now, if one possesses all four modes of explanation, then this [the former] is broad while that [the latter] is narrow;

this refers only to the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vipāka*) and does not speak of the three thousand realms, whereas that is narrow while this is broad. Although their designations differ, in principle they must be equal. Therefore—
The fruit must necessarily be complete, and there must necessarily be a basis for it. △ Twenty-seven and a half verses in gāthā form praise the prose section in two parts:
first, praising the two wisdoms by means of words; second, first, praising the two wisdoms of the Buddhas through combined verses; second, first, praising the two wisdoms of all Buddhas in verse.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Hero of the World is immeasurable; among all classes of beings—gods, humans, and all other sentient creatures—none are able to know the Buddha."
The "Hero of the World" praises the wisdom of the Buddhas above as being immeasurable;
this praises their profound and infinite [wisdom], which is the true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) of all Buddhas. The subsequent three lines praise the expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) of all Buddhas.
△ Second, praising the two types of wisdom of Śākyamuni.
The Buddha’s powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), various samādhis, and all other dharmas of a Buddha cannot be measured by anyone.
"Buddha" here praises my attainment of Buddhahood; the verses on the powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth praise his qualities of true wisdom (*jñāna*);
and the "other dharmas" refer to the skillful means (*upāya*) for transforming others, which are the remainder of true wisdom.
This serves as a supplementary verse for the various causes and conditions mentioned above. △ Second, the combined verse of the two Buddhas’ explanation, praise, and concluding eulogy:
"Originally following countless Buddhas, they have fully practiced all paths; the profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma is difficult to see and difficult to comprehend."
The first two lines of this verse summarize the preceding passage on how the Buddhas have personally attended hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and fully practiced the path of the Dharma;

it praises the profound and subtle Dharma. It summarizes the preceding conclusion praising the accomplishment of true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*), which is a profound and unprecedented phenomenon difficult to see and difficult to comprehend.
It summarizes the preceding conclusion praising the intent of expedient wisdom (*upāyajñāna*), which is difficult to fathom.
This is the explanation.
Having practiced these various paths for immeasurable billions of kalpas, I have fully known and seen the attainment of the fruit at the site of enlightenment.
The verse above [describes] Śākyamuni’s perfection of knowledge and vision; having already attained full completion, it cites the cause by stating that he has completed the practice of the path.
Having fully realized the fruits and being complete in the manifestation of those fruits, I have thoroughly known and seen them; I know and see them as vast and profound.
△ Second, the praise beyond words for the two wisdoms, in five parts: first, a verse on the inconceivable realm.
Such are the meanings of the various natures and characteristics of these great fruits and retributions.
In the preceding verse on the inconceivable realm, the ten suchnesses were presented;

here, by citing only the first and the last, the meaning of the intermediate stages can be understood through the single character "yi" (one/meaning), which also encompasses the ultimate stage and so forth. △ Second, the verse following upon the ineffable realm.
Only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions can know this matter.
To summarize the essential points in verse: the Buddhas have fully accomplished [all these qualities]. △ Third, a verse summarizing the praise that transcends words.
This Dharma cannot be shown; its characteristics are quiescent.

The verse follows by stating "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak," because the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) has no spatial location and thus cannot be shown, and because it transcends the path of language, its characteristics are said to be quiescent.
△ Fourth, the verse on those who do not know [the Dharma], in eight parts: first, a general exclusion of those who do not enter.
No other classes of sentient beings are able to understand it;
these are the people of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*). △ Second, distinguishing those who can enter:
excluding the assembly of Bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm and solid.
This refers to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); thus, it is said that "the power of faith is firm and solid.

While the prose section clarifies the ultimate knowledge of the Buddha, the present verse clarifies the knowledge of the initial stage of faith; these are cited alternately for mutual illustration. △ Third, distinguishing the ignorance of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
The disciples of the Buddhas who have made offerings to all the Buddhas, whose outflows are entirely exhausted, and who dwell in their final bodies—
even such persons as these cannot withstand its power.
△ 4. Citing Śāriputra’s ignorance:
Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, and they all exhausted their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
"Exhausting one's thoughts to measure" means to apply the utmost effort and deplete one's thinking; the rest should be understood accordingly. △ 5. Citing all...
The disciples do not know it.
Even if the ten directions were filled with beings like Śāriputra and all other disciples,
and they were to exhaust their thoughts together to measure it across all the lands of the ten directions, they still could not know it.
△ Sixth, the raising of the branch of the Pratyekabuddha’s ignorance:
Even the Pratyekabuddhas— those of sharp wisdom, free from outflows, in their final bodies, and as numerous as the bamboos filling the ten directions—
if they were to focus their minds with one accord for immeasurable billions of kalpas, they would be unable to know even a small fraction of the Buddha’s true wisdom.
△ Seventh, it is raised that bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds do not know this.
Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds have made offerings to countless Buddhas, fully comprehend all meanings and principles, and are moreover skilled in preaching the Dharma;
like rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds, they fill the lands of the ten directions, and with a single mind and wondrous wisdom, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...
All together reflect that they cannot know the Buddha’s wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "generating the mind" (*cittotpāda*): it may refer to Bodhisattvas on the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) who have not yet severed their afflictions (*kleśa*) after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;
or it may refer to the aforementioned devas and worldly people who, having themselves attained the six perfections, generate the resolve.
These words distinguish between the provisional and the perfect teachings; those at the initial stage of both are equally called "bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.
△ Eighth, distinguishing those bodhisattvas who have not yet attained non-retrogression from those who do not know [this].
Even if Bodhisattvas who have attained non-retrogression were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and sought to contemplate it with a single mind, they would still be unable to know it.
This is because those in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) who have attained non-retrogression have only severed the delusions within the realm of desire; thus, they do not know the distinct principle.

Furthermore, even those on the stages prior to the [first] ground in the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), who possess the non-retrogression of the position of realization and practice, likewise do not know it. △ Fifth, the verse on the Dharma that is difficult to understand: Only...
The Buddha is able to know the realm of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
He further addressed Śāriputra: "I have now fully attained the untainted, inconceivable, profound, and subtle-dharmas;
only I know these marks, and the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise."
The "Inconceivable One" refers to the realm where the verses abide—the profound and wondrous Dharma, the first and most rare, difficult-to-understand teaching.
The three subsequent lines of the verse—“Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom it”—clarify that the paths of all Buddhas are identical and all reach ultimate perfection;
therefore, it says, “Only I know this mark, as do the Buddhas of the ten directions.”
It is likewise. △ Two and a half lines: The main section briefly elucidates the movement of attachments and the arising of doubts. Part One: All Buddhas Reveal the Reality.
Sub-part One: Clarifying that the Paths of All Buddhas are Identical.
Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas do not differ.
This treatise shows that the Buddhas’ way of transforming beings is identical. △ Second, the exhortation to believe:
One should give rise to great power of faith regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
△ Third, the actual revelation of reality:
"The Dharma of the World-Honored One must, after a long time, reveal the truth.
This means that by revealing the truth, he shakes former attachments and gives rise to present doubts; therefore, the text below says, "Could this not be Māra?"
That one becomes a Buddha depends precisely upon hearing these words. Since the Buddha has already exhorted belief through such words of truth as they are, why would he instead provoke doubt?
To prevent slander arising from doubt, he exhorts belief and reveals the truth. △ Second, Śākyamuni’s Opening of the Three;
first, the actual explanation of opening the three.

When [the Buddha] addresses the assembly of śrāvakas and those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas—those whom I have caused to be liberated from the bonds of suffering and attain nirvāṇa—it is to reveal that the two vehicles previously realized that which is "neither of the two" (ubhayānta-vinirmukta). Thus it is said they "attain nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, this can be compared to the bodhisattva vehicle of the six perfections. How is this known? Because by practicing the conduct of the six perfections, one is immediately freed from the bonds of the four miserable destinies.
Being unable to enter parinirvāṇa immediately, one attains nirvana only after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas and a hundred kalpas; "reaching" (dài) means that it is attained only after a long interval.
Furthermore, regarding the practice of the six pāramitās: because the former [stages] involve delivering others, it is said "I cause them to be liberated from the bonds of suffering";

because the latter involves attaining the untainted (anāsrava), it is said "one reaches and attains nirvāṇa. By inferring this meaning, one knows this refers to the vehicle of the six pāramitās. Moreover, below...
The verse states: "The Buddha, by the power of skillful means, reveals the teachings of the three vehicles. If this were not indicated, on what basis would there be "three"?
One should not redundantly count the two vehicles as the three vehicles. △ Second, the direct refutation of the three vehicles.
The Buddha, through the power of skillful means, demonstrates the teachings of the Three Vehicles;
these are all provisional and illusory. △ Third, the purpose for establishing the Three [Vehicles]:
to lead sentient beings who are attached to various places so that they may attain liberation.
The mind is a provisional means for leading [beings] away from all sufferings; it is not the ultimate reality, but merely a gateway of skillful means.

△ Second, raising doubts to request instruction, in two parts: first, the narration of the doubts, in two parts: first, the doubts of the twelve hundred [disciples]. First, the narration by the sūtra compiler. First, the doubts of the twelve hundred.
At that time, within the great assembly were twelve hundred śrāvakas, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others, who were arhats with out-flows exhausted.
△ Second, the doubts of the fourfold assembly.
As for the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who have resolved their minds upon becoming śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas:
since the preceding section has already rejected all three vehicles as being merely provisional expedients, why is it that the present narration of doubts concerns only the two vehicles?
It is because their attachments are heavy and their doubts are deep; therefore, they are singled out for mention. In the subsequent passage where the doubts are set forth, it says:
The Bodhisattvas who seek Buddhahood know that those of the three vehicles all harbor doubts. △ Second, the actual arising of doubt, in two parts:
first, doubting the Buddha’s two kinds of wisdom; second, first, a general doubt regarding the two kinds of wisdom.
Each of them had this thought: "Why does the World-Honored One now so earnestly praise skillful means?
△ Second, the specific doubts regarding the two kinds of wisdom. First, the doubt concerning true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*).
They spoke thus: "The Dharma attained by the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to understand."
△ Second, the doubt regarding provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
"Whatever he speaks, his underlying intent is difficult to discern; it is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

These three passages express doubts concerning the two types of wisdom—provisional and ultimate—both collectively and individually, primarily because [the bodhisattvas] have heard the words of the Buddhas.

There is no difference; one must speak of the truth. Why is there doubt? It is because the Buddha previously taught that the wisdom of the three vehicles is identical in realization and not distinct, differing only in that some residual habits (*vāsanā*) have been exhausted while others have not.
Now, he suddenly praises the Tathāgata’s two kinds of wisdom as being beyond his own reach; therefore, he doubts the Buddha’s two kinds of wisdom. △ Second, doubting what he himself has attained.
The Buddha has taught that there is but one meaning of liberation, and we too have attained this Dharma and reached Nirvana;
yet we do not know where this meaning leads.
Regarding "one liberation," the three types of persons in the Tripiṭaka teachings share the same liberation; this is our own doubt concerning what has been attained.
Riding upon the Noble Path is the true means of transcendence; by practicing this principle, one likewise reaches Nirvana.

Now, you suddenly state that all these are merely expedient means (*upāya*). I do not yet know which dharma is the ultimate reality; therefore, it is said that "I do not know where this meaning leads.
II. The Main Request for a Decision. This section has three parts: three requests and three refusals. First, the first request. Part two: the extended [explanation].
The first part of the second practice presents the doubt:
At that time, Śāriputra, knowing that the fourfold assembly harbored doubts and that he himself had not yet fully understood, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, for what cause and by what condition do you so earnestly praise the foremost skillful means of all Buddhas as being profound, subtle, wondrous, and difficult to comprehend?"
The Dharma.
△ Second, the formal request:
"Since ancient times, I have never heard such a teaching from the Buddha; now the fourfold assembly all harbor doubts."

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this matter. For what reason does the World-Honored One so earnestly praise this profound, subtle, wondrous, and difficult-to-understand Dharma?
Within this formal request, there are three requests and two refusals; when combined with the preceding [refusal], they constitute three refusals. (Yao)

Master Longyi said: "The first *zhǐ* (cessation) was for the sake of the profound principle that is difficult to understand; the first *qǐng* (request) was for the sake of seeking a resolution for oneself and others.
The second *zhǐ* was for those who were startled, doubtful, or lacked faith; the second *qǐng* was for those who had long planted the seeds [of virtue] and would surely understand.

The third *zhǐ* was for those who would surely slander and fall into suffering; the third *qǐng* was for those of sharp faculties to obtain benefit. Tiantai said: "The Buddha knew in advance that there would be benefits for the three assemblies throughout the three weeks."
Because they did not do so together later on, the three [Buddhas] waited for their third request. △ Second, the verse summary in six parts;
first, the verse summarizing the doubt regarding true wisdom.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
The Great Holy Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, has finally proclaimed this Dharma after a long time.
△ Second, the verse on doubting expedient wisdom:
[The Buddha] himself declares that he has attained such inconceivable dharmas as the powers, the fearlessnesses, the samādhis, the dhyānas, and the liberations.
Regarding the Dharma attained at the site of enlightenment, there is no one capable of posing a question; my own intention is difficult to fathom, and there is no one who can inquire.
Without being asked, I shall speak of my own accord, praising the path I have practiced—the wisdom that is most subtle and profound, which has been attained by all Buddhas.
△ [This section] clarifies the doubts of those with the three types of knowledge, the three vehicles, and the fourfold assembly.
Those Arhats free from outflows and those seeking nirvana have now all fallen into the net of doubt; why has the Buddha spoken thus?
This also includes those seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others.
Gazing at one another with lingering hesitation, we look up to the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings: what is the meaning of this matter? We pray that the Buddha will explain it for us.
The first line clarifies the śrāvakas; the latter two lines clarify the pratyekabuddhas;

and those who seek nirvāṇa in the middle clarify the bodhisattvas of the six perfections. How is this known? Because it was stated above that they "have attained nirvāṇa," whereas here [it refers to] these.

Regarding the phrase "and those who are called [to it]," this indicates that because these bodhisattvas seek nirvana for themselves and also lead others [to it], they are distinguished from the two vehicles;
thus one knows them to be bodhisattvas. △ Fourth, clarifying the doubts of Śāriputra.

Among the assembly of śrāvakas, the Buddha declared me to be the foremost; yet now, regarding my own wisdom, I am filled with doubt and unable to discern whether this is the ultimate Dharma or merely the path I am currently practicing.
"Venerable Śāriputra, you now doubt whether the cultivation and realization based on the teachings of the three vehicles has ever been erroneous.
If you say that these are merely skillful means and not ultimate reality, is it that the fruit realized is not real, or is it that the cause practiced is not true?"
○ As for "Wisdom," it is based on the authentic scriptures and belongs to Śāriputra. △ Fifth, clarifying the doubts of the Buddha’s sons:
"The sons born from the Buddha’s own mouth join their palms, gaze upward, and wait, wishing that you would utter a subtle and wondrous sound and speak according to reality at this time."
△ Sixth, a general explanation of the request made by those with shared doubts:
The number of devas, nāgas, spirits, and others is like the sands of the Ganges; the number of bodhisattvas seeking Buddhahood is eighty thousand;
furthermore, there are the wheel-turning sage-kings from ten trillion lands who, joining their palms with a reverent heart, desire to hear the complete path.
△ Second, the cessation.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra: "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak further.
If this matter were explained, all the devas and humans in the entire world would be struck with alarm and doubt."
The intention behind this cessation is the fear that doubts may arise. △ Second Request:
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha once more, saying, "World-Honored One, we pray that you will speak; we pray that you will speak. Why is this?
Because in this assembly there are countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya sentient beings who have previously seen various Buddhas and whose faculties [are matured]."
Those with sharp and penetrating wisdom who clearly understand what the Buddha has taught will be able to revere and believe it.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Dharma King, the Unsurpassed Honored One, please speak; have no concern. Among the immeasurable multitude in this assembly, there are those capable of revering and believing."
△ Third Intermission.
The Buddha again stopped Śāriputra, saying: "If one were to speak of this matter, all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—would be struck with alarm and doubt;
those bhikṣus of overweening pride would fall into a great abyss. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses once more:
The Buddha then stopped him, out of concern for those with overweening pride, saying: "Stop, stop;
there is no need to speak. My Dharma is subtle and inconceivable; if those with overweening pride were to hear it, they would certainly not show respect or faith."
△ Third Request.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will speak it; we pray that you will speak it!

In this assembly, there are those like us, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, who throughout successive lifetimes have already received transformation and instruction from the Buddha."
These people will certainly be able to generate respectful faith, which will bring them peace and security for a long night and provide great benefit.

That which is called the darkness of ignorance is the "long night"; if they can generate respectful faith, they will surely emerge from the ocean of birth and death, which is called "peace and security."
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Unsurpassed One, Honored among Two-legged Beings, I pray you will proclaim the foremost Dharma. I am the eldest son of the Buddha; may you deign to analyze and explain it for me.
The immeasurable multitude in this assembly is able to respect and believe in this Dharma, for the Buddha has already taught and transformed such as these throughout his successive lives."
With single-minded devotion and palms joined, we—these twelve hundred and others who seek Buddhahood—desire to hear and receive the Buddha’s words.
For the sake of this assembly, we pray that you will deign to analyze and expound these teachings; upon hearing this Dharma, they will give rise to great joy.
△ Second, the extensive explanation of "Opening the Three to Reveal the One" consists of seven chapters and a half, which is divided into three cycles.
First, the Dharma-exposition for those of superior faculties; second, the parable-exposition for those of middling faculties (entering the *Upamā-parivarta*);

third, the causal-condition exposition for those of inferior faculties (entering the beginning of the *Purāṇa-nagara-parivarta*). The first section further has five parts: first, the actual Dharma-exposition; second, Śāriputra’s realization and understanding (beginning the parables).

(At the beginning of the Simile Chapter: 1) The three Buddhas’ confirmation; 2) the bestowing of predictions; 3) the joy of the fourfold assembly. Regarding the first [section], there are again two parts:
first, the prose; second, the verses. Regarding the first [of these], there are again three parts: first, the promise to speak; within this, first, the favorable assent.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: "Since you have already made your earnest request three times, how could I not speak?
First, he acceded to the request; second, he granted the permission."
"Listen now attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.

'First, listen attentively' refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); 'reflect well' refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and 'contemplate it' refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
△ Third, the selection and permission."
When these words were spoken, five thousand bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās in the assembly immediately rose from their seats, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew.
Why was this? Because the roots of transgression for these individuals were deep and heavy, and they possessed overweening pride;
they claimed to have attained what they had not attained, and claimed to have realized what they had not realized. Possessing such faults, they did not remain.
The World-Honored One remained silent and did not restrain him.

When he spoke these words, it was to distinguish the assembly and permit five thousand [monks] who were seated there; for while the Tathāgata had previously issued three prohibitions, he now intended to permit the teaching by using his majestic spiritual power to dispatch them away.
Therefore, this is called "distinguishing the assembly. Because the obstacles of the five turbidities are numerous, their offenses are heavy, and they cling to the Lesser Vehicle.

To obscure one’s great name while its roots remain deep, to claim to have attained what has not been attained, and to harbor overweening pride (*adhimāna*)—to fail to realize the three fruits and to remain unenlightened as an adept (*aśaikṣa*)—such are the faults known as the three types of obstructive grasping and pride.

If these are not restrained, then upon hearing the higher teaching that reveals the One Vehicle through the opening of the Three Vehicles, the concise meaning will remain hidden; thus, even before slander arises, it is sufficient to act as a bond.

If the causes and conditions for the jewel depart, there will be benefit; yet if one hears the extensive opening of the three to reveal the one, and this offends one's sentiments and gives rise to slander, there will be harm while remaining—this is what is not restrained.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra: "In this assembly of mine now, there are no longer branches or leaves; it consists purely of the firm and the real."
"Ānanda, such persons of overweening pride may either fall back or remain stationary; listen well now, for I shall explain this to you.
Just as twigs, leaves, and fine fragments are unfit for use as vessels, so too those who cling to the expedient means of expedient means are not fit vessels for the Great [Vehicle].
As the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra says: 'To grasp at branches and leaves while abandoning the root—such a person is not wise. This refers precisely to this."

"It is fitting that you withdraw; it would indeed be best. This means that since [Subhūti] was already concealing himself with his own minor [attainments], he further obstructed the great light of others.
Now, by withdrawing, he incurs no fault of slandering the Dharma, nor does he commit the transgression of hindering others; therefore, it is said to be "best.

While the upper branches and leaves have not yet been removed, the Tathāgata’s three pauses were intended for the earnest desire to hear the reality. Thus, Śāriputra made four requests; master and disciple discerned the capacity of the audience, which was not [yet ready].
This is merely a matter of being reserved; "you" here refers to the conclusion of the permission granted. △ Second, receiving the mandate.
Śāriputra said, "So be it, World-Honored One; I wish and desire to hear it.
To "receive the mandate" means to respectfully follow and accept the command. △ Third, the actual exposition, in two parts: first, clarifying the four Buddhas.
The detailed exposition of the two aspects—expedient and real—of all Buddhas, and the detailed exposition of the two aspects—expedient and real—of Śākyamuni.
The first section further divides into two parts: first, the general exposition of all Buddhas; second, the enumeration of the Buddhas of the three periods.
The first of these further divides into four sections, the first of which is the praise of the rarity of the Dharma.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Such a wondrous Dharma as this is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at rare intervals, just as the udumbara flower appears but once in a long while.
By praising both the Dharma and its parable, he indicates that it is preached only at such times; for when all Buddhas appear amidst the five turbidities, they must first open the Three Vehicles."
Now, for more than forty years since the World-Honored One first appeared, he has revealed the truth only rarely and at long intervals;

thus it is said that he speaks only when the time is right. That he did not speak for so long was because people were not yet capable, the time had not yet arrived, and the five thousand had not yet withdrawn.
Now that people are capable, the time has arrived, and the five thousand have departed; therefore, he will definitively expound the Mahāyāna.

The *udumbara* flower—here translated as "spiritually auspicious"—appears once every three thousand years, and its appearance coincides with the emergence of a Golden Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*).
This symbolizes that only after the beings of the Three Vehicles have been fully matured does one preach the Sublime Dharma and bestow the prediction of Buddhahood (*vyākaraṇa*) upon the Dharma King.
△ Second, [the section on] how the teaching is not false.
Śāriputra, you all should believe what the Buddha has spoken; his words are not false.
When I say "you should believe," I am exhorting you to have faith that they are not false. This principle is most profound, for this principle differs from what was taught in the past.
These words are most subtle, for these words contradict what was said before. This practice is most universal, for this practice diverges from what was practiced in the past. This person is most...
That which was previously inferior is now superior; what was once referred to as the four kinds of coarse labor is now all considered sublime.
Fearing that sentient beings might give rise to slander, he exhorts them to have faith. Faith is not false; it is the person who speaks the non-false Dharma.
△ Third, the opening of the expedient means, in three parts: first, the opening.
"Śāriputra, the Buddhas teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; their underlying intent is difficult to understand.
Because the Buddhas teach by means of skillful expedients according to three types of capacities, it is said they "teach according to what is appropriate.
Because the meaning of the Buddha's intent cannot be understood in terms of substantial entities, it is said that "the underlying intent is difficult to understand. △ Second, the explanation.
Why is this? It is because I have expounded all dharmas through countless skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and verbal expressions;
I am merely citing the present Buddha’s power of expedient means to explain the skillful means of all Buddhas, for their skillful wisdom is identical. Thus, I borrow [this example].
This explains that "I have used innumerable skillful means" refers to how the Buddhas also reveal provisional teachings just as I do. △ Third, the conclusion.
Fourth, the revelation of the true reality. Fifth, first, the designation of the superior person and the Dharma.

This Dharma cannot be understood through conceptualization or discrimination; only the Buddhas can know it. Regarding this statement that "this Dharma is not [accessible to] conceptualization and the like," there are two meanings:
either it serves as a conclusion to the provisional and an opening toward the real, or it directly reveals the ultimate reality.

As for concluding the provisional and opening toward the real: the Buddha’s intent is difficult to fathom, such that only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully comprehend it; those who receive the teaching, however, say:
Third, regarding "the Buddhas know that the one ear is the manifestation of reality": this refers to the subsequent text. First, it identifies the person and the dharma;

by citing the dharma of non-discrimination, it indicates that this is known only by the Buddhas. That the Buddhas, through non-discriminative wisdom, understand the dharma of non-discrimination is precisely the meaning of manifesting reality.
△ Second, identifying the intent for appearing in the world.
Why is this so? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great causal matter.
First, a general explanation; second, a detailed explanation of each term. Regarding the general explanation:

the Buddhas awaken to the marks of reality as it truly is, and by means of this true path, they appear in response to the world, solely to enable sentient beings to attain this true path; they have never done anything other than this.

Regarding "other matters," all things other than the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena are termed demonic activities (*mārakarman*). Next, as for the word-by-word analysis: "One" refers to the single true reality;
because it is not three, five, seven, or nine, it is called "one. Its nature is vast and expansive;
because it encompasses three, five, seven, and nine, it is named "Great. Because it is the ritual procedure for the appearance of all Buddhas in the world, it is named "matter" (*vastu*).

Because sentient beings possess the capacity (indriya) to respond to the Buddha, he is called the "cause" (hetu); because the Buddha responds by acceding to that capacity, he is called the "condition" (pratyaya).
This constitutes the fundamental intent of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world. △ Third, the summary statement.
Śāriputra, as for what is called "the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
appear in the world solely for the sake of one great causal matter," this is intended to be analyzed and further raised up as the starting point for an explanation. △ Fourth, the actual explanation.
Regarding the four [aspects], first, the principle: first, the direct explanation.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and to attain purity;

they appear in the world because they desire to demonstrate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings; they appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge...
He appears in the world because he wishes to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; he appears in the world for this purpose.
This explanation is of a single principle, yet it is further divided into four meanings: first, in terms of the four stages; second, in terms of the four wisdoms; third, in terms of the four gates;
and fourth, in terms of contemplating the mind. First, regarding the explanation in terms of the four stages: the realm of the Truth (satya) is not something that can be known or seen; it is only...
Only the Buddha’s wisdom and the Buddha’s eye can know and see; if one possesses only two types of wisdom or four types of eyes, one cannot know or see.
Now, by taking the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), one who attains the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom through the stages of abiding, advancing, and entering is able to know and see.

Therefore, these four stages are employed to explain the oneness of principle (*liyi*); this is to manifest the principle by means of the stages. "Opening" refers specifically to the ten abidings (*shizhu*).

Initially, by destroying ignorance and opening the *tathāgatagarbha*, one perceives the principle of the true reality (*dharmatā*), like the sun rising and darkness vanishing so that the eyes become functional;
therefore, it is called "opening. Through the cultivation of conditions, delusions are destroyed, and thus it is said that [the mind] is made pure.

"Manifesting" refers to the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*): once the obstacles of delusion are removed, the essence of knowledge and vision is revealed, and the manifold virtues of the *dharmadhātu* are clearly displayed.

Therefore, it is called "demonstrating and awakening": this refers to the removal of obstacles during the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*), wherein the essence is manifested and the practices of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) clarify the integration of phenomena and principle;
because there is no longer any dualistic course, it is called "awakening and entering. This refers to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*):
since phenomena and principle are already integrated, one acts with sovereign non-obstruction, spontaneously proceeding from *A* to *Ta* to enter the ocean of *sarvajñā*. Therefore, it is so named.

As for "entering": ○ Second, the explanation according to the four wisdoms: First, the wisdom of the path (*mārgajñatā*) perceives the true nature of the path; within this true nature, one attains the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).

Second, the wisdom of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) knows the distinct characteristics of the various paths and seeds within the ten dharma-realms, as well as the aspects of their delusions and awakenings, and reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision in each and every instance. Third, the all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*) knows all dharmas.
The realization that the single characteristic is quiescent extinction is precisely awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Fourth, the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) which knows all phenomena as having the characteristic of quiescent extinction in their single characteristic—recognizing all various types of activities and appearances—is precisely entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Third, the horizontal explanation according to the four gates of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): The gate of emptiness—where all is empty—is the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The gate of existence—where all exists—is the revealing of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The gate of both emptiness and existence—where all is both empty and existent—is the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The gate of neither emptiness nor existence...

Entering through the gate that all things are neither empty nor existent, one immediately enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*). "Being able to penetrate" refers to the four [phases], while "that which is penetrated" refers to the One.
"Opening, showing, awakening, and entering" are the gates by which one penetrates; "that which is known" and "that which is seen" are the principles (*tattva*) thus penetrated.
Fourth, the explanation by way of contemplating the mind (*citta) is as follows: one contemplates the principle of the three truths within the nature of the mind (*cittatathatā*), which cannot be...

To contemplate this gate of observation as pure is called "opening"; although it is inconceivable, one is able to discern emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, such that they are perfectly distinct without confusion—this is called "indicating.
That the middle of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle is three yet one, and one yet three—this is called "realizing.
That the middle of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle is neither emptiness, nor the provisional, nor the middle, yet simultaneously illuminates emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
The middle stage is called "entry," which constitutes the single mind’s threefold contemplation; yet, these are distinguished as the specific stages of seeing, discerning, awakening, and entry.
Thus, they are explained through four aspects: [the stages] are established by reason, reason is established by position, position is established by wisdom, and wisdom is established by the gates.
Because the gates are penetrated, wisdom is perfected; because wisdom is perfected, the positions are established.
Because they are established in their respective positions, they perceive the principle; because they perceive the principle, it is called the "Unity of Principle. △ Second, the conclusion:
Śāriputra, this is why all Buddhas appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter.

The conclusion is that the principle is one. Although the former provisional teachings also provide expositions on the meanings of opening, showing, awakening, and entering, they are not the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
therefore, they are provisional. Now, because this clarifies the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it is the real. The real is precisely the unity of principle.
△ Second, the identity of persons.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas.

If one speaks according to the provisional means of the past, it is said that they teach and transform the three vehicles; yet in terms of the ultimate truth, this is actually the transformation of bodhisattvas.
It is like that impoverished son who considered himself a lowly hired laborer, whereas from the perspective of the elder, he was truly his own son."
This is precisely the oneness of persons. △ Third, the oneness of practice:
"Whatever is performed is always for one purpose; it is solely through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision that sentient beings are shown and awakened.

The various practices of the Three Vehicles are termed "various" (zhū), yet because they are for the sake of the Perfect [Vehicle], these "various" are in fact a single matter. What, then, is this practice?
Wherever he arrives, he proceeds solely toward the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; this is precisely the practice of a single intention. △ Fourth, the teaching on the One [Vehicle]:
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for sentient beings solely by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle;
there is no other vehicle, whether two or three."

The teaching of the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun) is called the Single Buddha Vehicle (ekabuddhayāna); thus, the "Introductory Chapter" states that "preaching the Mahāyāna sūtra" refers precisely to this doctrinal meaning.
From the Distinct Teaching (biejiao) onwards, all are termed "with remainder," which means they are not of definitive meaning and are not the Buddha’s Single Vehicle.

Now, when it says "only by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle," it refers exclusively to the preaching of the Buddha-dharma, the vehicle of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao). As for "no other vehicles," it means there are no other vehicles apart from this.
There is no separate teaching that involves expedient means with remainder and lacks duality; there is no [teaching] within the *Prajñāpāramitā* that involves duality;
and there is no [teaching] within the Vaipulya (*Vaipulya*) that confronts the three.
Since these two and three are all absent, how much more so the three found within the Tripiṭaka? △ Fifth, the summary of the identity of the Dharma.
Śāriputra, the Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions is also like this.
△ Second, the section listing the Buddhas of the three periods, in three parts: first, the Buddhas of the past; second, first, the opening of the provisional.
Śāriputra, the Buddhas of the past, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions,
parables, and modes of expression, have expounded all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
△ Second, revealing the reality:

These dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle; therefore, all these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, will ultimately attain all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā).
All are for the sake of the One Buddha Vehicle; the teaching is one, the Dharma heard from the Buddha is one—this refers to who hears the Dharma.
It encompasses sentient beings and includes the attainment of the person; all ultimately attain the All-Knowledge (sarvajñā).

That which is known by this All-Knowledge is the Oneness of Principle (li-yi), and that which knows it is the Oneness of Practice (xing-yi). Although these four onenesses are not sequential, they are simultaneously complete. △ Second, the Buddhas of the Future.
Second, first opening the provisional: Śāriputra,
future Buddhas who shall appear in the world will likewise, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means,
various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, expound all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
△ Second, revealing the reality:

Because these dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle, all these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
△ Third, regarding the Buddhas of the present: first, the intention for appearing in the world is indicated.

Śāriputra, in the present, throughout the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddha-lands in the ten directions, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, extensively benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings.
Just as in the chapter on the Buddhas it is said that they appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition, so too is it here:
he appears in the world solely for the purpose of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings. △ Second, the disclosure of the provisional.
These Buddhas likewise, through immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, expound all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
△ Third, revealing the reality, in two parts: first, specifically clarifying the present teaching, in one section, in one paragraph.
"These dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle; thus, these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately all attain the Knowledge of All Modes.
This passage fully contains the fourfold "Onenesses. △ Third, a general clarification that the three periods of time share one principle and one reality.
Śāriputra, these Buddhas teach and transform bodhisattvas solely because they wish to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings,
because they wish to awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and because they wish to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
"However, in teaching and transforming bodhisattvas, this person’s single desire and below are one in principle. △ Second, the Chapter of Śākyamuni, Part Five:
First, Opening the Provisional.
"Śāriputra, I now likewise do so; I know that all sentient beings have various desires and deep-seated inclinations."
Adapting to their respective natures through various causes, conditions, parables, and modes of expression, I employ skillful means to preach the Dharma for them.
I am none other than the present Śākyamuni Buddha; because my former three [past lives] and my subsequent one [present life] are no different from those of the four Buddhas, it is so stated.
It is also thus: knowing that sentient beings have various desires refers to the faculties, inclinations, and natures of the five vehicles.
"Past" refers to the faculty (*indriya*); "present" refers to the desire (*chanda*); and "future" refers to the nature (*gotra*). That which is deeply attached to in the mind is the faculty.
"Expedient means" (*upāya*) refers to the provisional teachings of the three vehicles opened according to what is appropriate. △ Second.
This reveals the reality.
Śāriputra, it is because all these [teachings] are for the sake of attaining the One Buddha Vehicle and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Such statements as these indicate that the provisional is itself the real; the Buddha Vehicle is the teaching, and the knowledge of all modes is that which is known.

The single principle of knowing is itself the single practice of attaining the Buddha-vehicle; that one can attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā) is simultaneously the personification of this principle.
△ Third, citing the five turbidities to explain the skillful means, in two parts: first, stating the intent.
Śāriputra, in the worlds of the ten directions there are not even two vehicles, let alone three.

This is intended to introduce the five turbidities; previously, it was explained that the Buddhas open up the provisional to reveal the ultimate, but it has not yet been clarified how they conceal the ultimate to establish the provisional.
That Dharma is pure and serene, like the single void; therein there is not even a trace of the second [vehicle], much less a trace of the third.

If even the provisional [teachings] of the Vaipulya are thus, how much more so the provisional teachings of the single Three [Vehicles] and the single Five [Vehicles]—which include the addition of the devas?

It is solely because the obstacles of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) are so heavy that the ultimate reality cannot be proclaimed; therefore, one must employ the provisional teachings of the single Three and the single Five, as well as the provisional teachings that retain elements of both the Three and the Two.
Thus it is said: "Within the One Buddha Vehicle, he distinguishes and teaches the Three. △ Second, citing the five turbidities, part four.
Chanting the number:
Śāriputra, all Buddhas appear in the five turbidities of the evil world.
△ Second, listing their names.

These are what are called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), and the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
△ Third, the essential nature and characteristics.
Thus it is.
The *kalpa-kṣaya* (degeneration of the eon) has no separate substance; an eon (*kalpa*) is a long duration, while a *kṣaṇa* (instant) is a short duration.

This conventional designation "degeneration of the eon" is established solely in reference to the four degenerations. The text states, "In the period of turmoil during the degeneration of the eon," which conveys this very meaning.
