As for the "degeneration of sentient beings" (*sattva-kṣaya*), it is merely a conventional designation established by taking the retributive fruits of those [afflictions such as] views and pride; thus it is called the "degeneration of sentient beings. Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*):...

The turbidity of affliction (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) has the five dull proclivities (*pañca-mṛdu-anuśaya*) as its essence; the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) has the five sharp proclivities (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-anuśaya*) as its essence;

and the turbidity of life-span (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) has the continuity of form and mind (*rūpa-citta*) as its essence. Regarding the characteristics of these five turbidities, they intensify and converge during this period:
when hatred reaches its peak, weapons arise; when greed reaches its peak, famine arises; and when delusion reaches its peak... [the pestilence arises].
Because pestilence arises and the three calamities emerge, afflictions flourish doubly and various views burn ever more fiercely.

Coarse and debased form and mind, evil reputations, and foul appellations destroy years and diminish lifespans; the various turbidities combine to scorch all, like waters rushing toward darkness where wind and waves rage and fish and dragons are tossed about, such that not one finds any reliance.
It is caused by the power of time, just as it was at the beginning of the kalpa during the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

When the heavens fall to earth, it causes beings to harbor desires, just as the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter the Rough and Astringent Garden (Karkaśavana) and give rise to hearts of contention;
this is called the mark of the kalpa-turbidity (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). The ocean of greed receives all streams yet is never satisfied; the venomous snake of anger drinks poison and disturbs the world;
the darkness of ignorance is more stubborn and dull than pitch blackness; and arrogance is so high that it looks down upon others with boundless contempt.
The net of doubt and lack of faith renders one incapable of being told the truth; this is the characteristic of the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).

To claim there is a person where there is no person, or to claim there is a self where there is no self—such views as these sixteen types of knowledge and sixty-two [wrong views] are like a net and resemble a dense forest;

they entangle and distort one so that one cannot emerge on one's own. This is the characteristic of the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Grasping at form and mind, it establishes [these false notions].
First, the analogy of the sovereign is like sticky glue: there is nothing it does not adhere to, causing one to drift through the six realms of existence and take birth everywhere;

this is the characteristic of the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). To be born in the morning and perish in the evening, to emerge by day and die by night—like waves turning and smoke swirling, remaining unstilled for even a moment—this is the characteristic of the turbidity of life-span (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).
If we consider them in their sequence, taking afflictions and views as the root, [it proceeds from there].
These two turbidities (kaṣāya) constitute the nature of sentient beings. From these sentient beings arises the maintenance of life;
when these four pass through time, it is called the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the turbidity of the eon). Thus, this clarifies the essence and characteristics of the five turbidities.

As for their essence and characteristics, they cannot be fully detailed here; therefore, it is stated briefly as "thus. Although the sūtra does not provide them in full, the commentary describes them in brief. △ Four.

Explanation of the Conclusion: Śāriputra, because during the period of the defilement of the kalpa, sentient beings have heavy impurities, being stingy, greedy, and jealous, and have thus perfected all roots of unwholesomeness,
the Buddhas, by the power of skillful means, differentiate and teach the three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
The turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) refers to the time of chaos; the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) refers to the heavy defilements of sentient beings;

stinginess and greed are the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*); jealousy is the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*); unwholesome speech pertains to both the turbidity of afflictions and the turbidity of views;

and the full development of the sense faculties is the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). It is precisely because the five turbidities obstruct sentient beings in this land so heavily that they are able to hinder the Mahāyāna.

Therefore, the Tathāgata distinguishes and teaches three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle. △ Fourth, distinguishing the false to strengthen faith, in two parts: first, distinguishing the true from the false;
second, [the section on] "If one has not heard and known [this], they are not true disciples. First, if one has not heard and known [this], they are not true disciples.
Śāriputra, if my disciples claim to be arhats or pratyekabuddhas, yet do not hear or know that all buddhas,
the Tathāgatas, solely teach and transform bodhisattvas, they are not disciples of the Buddha, nor are they arhats, nor are they pratyekabuddhas.
If a disciple of the Buddha can personally believe and understand [the Dharma], yet another does not believe or understand, the latter is neither a true disciple nor an Arhat;
therefore, the assembly is earnestly exhorted to believe, accept, and understand. The text is divided into two parts: first, distinguishing the true from the false.
If one has neither heard nor known [the Dharma], they are not a true disciple, just as a worldly disciple follows and succeeds to the teacher’s methods.

That is to say: first, not hearing the teaching leads to ignorance; second, being ignorant leads to a lack of practice; third, lacking true practice leads to a lack of principle; fourth, lacking principle leads to not being a disciple;
fifth, not being a disciple leads to not being a person. △ Second, failing to believe and accept what one has heard results in the formation of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, these bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs claim for themselves that they have already attained arhatship, that this is their final body, and that they have reached ultimate nirvāṇa;
thus, they no longer aspire to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
You should know that such people are all those of overweening pride (adhimāna). Why is this? If there were a bhikṣu who had truly attained...
It is impossible for an Arhat not to believe this Dharma;
this second point clarifies that disbelief constitutes overweening pride (*abhimāna*). To encourage them toward faith, it is said:

"You claim for yourself that this is your final birth, yet your births are actually immeasurable; you are truly not in your final birth. You claim for yourself that you have reached the ultimate goal, yet you have truly not reached the ultimate goal."

To claim what has not been attained as having been attained—is this not the pride of overestimation (*adhimāna*)? A true Arhat, whose defilements have been eliminated and whose faculties are sharp, knows that [the path] is not ultimate and thus does not give rise to such pride.
Knowing it is not ultimate yet placing faith in the ultimate is to place faith in the principle;

this is the first instance of non-pride, which constitutes the first instance of practice. To have faith is to have faith in the teaching; this is the first instance of the teaching. Such a person is a disciple of the Buddha.
The disciple is thus one and the same as the person [of the Buddha]. △ Second, the opening and removal of doubts, in two parts: first, the opening and removal;
second, first, the removal regarding after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. This removes the notion that there is no Buddha present after the Buddha has passed into extinction.

If, while the Buddha is in the world, one does not believe or accept this sutra when it is correctly preached, yet claims to be a true Arhat, this constitutes the arrogance of overestimation (*adhimāna*).

However, if one attains Arhatship only after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, and thus adheres exclusively to the provisional teachings while not believing in the perfect Dharma, such a person is permitted [to claim the title] and is not considered arrogant.
△ Second, the difficulty of finding good people.
Why is this? After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and understand the meaning of such sutras as these will be difficult to find.

Even though the Buddha has entered extinction, if this sutra still exists and yet one does not believe or accept it, should this not be considered the arrogance of overweening pride? One will immediately [realize this].
[The Buddha] provides an exemption, noting that although this sutra exists after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who can understand its meaning are difficult to encounter;
thus, even if Arhats do not believe or understand it, they should be permitted as not being of overweening pride. △ Second, resolving doubts.
If one encounters another Buddha, one will attain definitive understanding within this Dharma.

Regarding the question of whether those who understand the sutras after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—who have attained arhatship and entered parinirvāṇa forever—will not meet [another Buddha], the commentary explains:
although such persons conceive the thought that they have attained extinction, after their lives have ended, they are born outside the realms.
There are those in other lands who, encountering other Buddhas, hear this sutra and immediately attain decisive understanding.
Nanyue said that "other Buddhas" refers to the four reliances (*catur-yoni*). Furthermore, arhats may encounter them and, upon hearing the sutra, attain decisive understanding;

or, by practicing the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), they may see the Buddhas of the ten directions, who preach this sutra for them, whereby they immediately attain decisive understanding. Moreover, there are ordinary practitioners (*pṛthagjana*)...

Through repentance with utmost sincerity, one sees the Buddhas of the ten directions who preach for them, and thus also attains definitive understanding. △ Fifth, explaining that there is no falsehood:
Part One, exhorting faith in Śākyamuni.
"Śāriputra, you all should with a single mind believe, understand, receive, and uphold the Buddha’s words."
△ Second, exhorting faith in all Buddhas:
The words of the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are not false;
since the path of all Buddhas is the same, one should further believe and accept it. △ Third, concluding that it is not in vain.
There is no other vehicle; there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle.

△ Second, the verse summary has two parts: first, the verse summary of the initial promise to answer; second, the verse summary of the selection and the promise. First, the verse summary of the five thousand who withdrew from their seats.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs harboring overweening pride; upāsakas with arrogance and upāsikās lacking faith—these four assemblies numbered five thousand.
They did not perceive their own faults, for they were deficient in the precepts.”
To cherish and protect one's own faults is the mark of small wisdom; such people have already been winnowed out from among the assembly by the Buddha’s majestic power.
Because they lack merit, they are unable to receive this Dharma.

The four assemblies all commonly possess the pride of superiority (*adhimāna*) and the pride of self (*māna*), yet they are absent in those who have attained the fruits of the path through extensive cultivation of the Way.

Among monastics, there is a tendency to falsely claim the fruits of sainthood upon attaining meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), giving rise specifically to the pride of superiority; among laypeople, those who boast of their own excellence frequently give rise to the pride of self.

Women, having shallow wisdom, often produce deviant and perverse views; those who do not perceive their own faults suffer from three losses: their minds are shrouded, their flaws are concealed, and they broadcast their own virtues.
One who cannot reflect upon their own virtues is a person without shame (*anapatrāpya*); one who recognizes their own faults is a monk with a sense of modesty (*hrī*).

One who has deficiencies in the precepts (*śīla*) is said to have "defects" (*chidra*) in their discipline (*vinaya-saṃvara*); one who has lapses in the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) associated with the Path is said to have "leaks" (*srotas*), because they lack the concentration and other qualities of the Path.
Thus, when evil thoughts arise within like a jade containing flaws, it is because there is no discipline externally.
Moving the body and mouth like jade or dew-drops, one covers over transgressions and thus naturally acquires [retribution]; this is called "protecting and cherishing.

Those of small wisdom do not possess the knowledge of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) or those still in training (*śaikṣa*), but instead possess worldly, minor wisdom. They falsely claim that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) to be without outflows;
because it is the smallest among the small, it is called "small wisdom. As for "dregs and chaff," these refer to the five thousand [monks] and others who possess only worldly [wisdom].

Because their interim meditation lacks the moisture of untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative concentration, it is like dregs; because they possess only a literal understanding of the words without the reality of realization, it is like husks.
Furthermore, these dregs and husks serve as metaphors for their lack of great capacity. 2. Verse on the Assembly Being Purified.
This assembly has no branches or leaves, but consists only of the pure and solid.
"Branches and leaves" are a metaphor for those who are not good vessels; since they are entirely unfit for service, they must be sent away. △ Second, the verse on the admonition and permission.
Śāriputra, listen well. I exhort you to listen well.
△ Second, the verse of the formal answer, which has two parts: first, the verse on the four Buddhas; second, the verse on Śākyamuni Buddha.
The first section [of the former] further has four parts: first, the verse on the Buddhas in general; second, the verse on the past Buddhas; third, the verse on the future... [text fragmentary].
Chapter on the Buddhas of the Future, Verse 4. Chapter on the Buddhas of the Present, Part One, Section One: Five Sections. First, the verse on the employment of skillful means. Subsection One:
The verse on the actual employment of skillful means.
"The Dharma attained by all Buddhas is taught to sentient beings through immeasurable powers of expedient means, according to what the minds of sentient beings contemplate."
The Buddha fully knows the various paths traversed, the diverse dispositions of desire, and the good and evil karma of previous lives;
having known these, he employs the power of skillful means—through various conditions, parables, and modes of speech—to cause all beings to rejoice.
He preaches the sūtras, gāthās, itivṛttakas, jātaka tales, and accounts of marvelous events, as well as nidānas, avadānas, and geyas.
The *Upadeśa-sūtra* states:
"The Dharma attained by all Buddhas" refers to attaining the various provisional dharmas through the cultivation of the Path.

"Immeasurable power of skillful means" refers to the subsequent verse which explains that he has preached all dharmas through countless skillful means and various causes and conditions. [This concerns] the minds of sentient beings.

"What is contemplated" refers to the preceding verse on preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate (*yathā-yogam*). Within this verse, the characteristics of "what is appropriate" are extensively set forth;

that is, teaching according to the capacities of those in the nine dharma-realms (*navadharmadhātu*) by means of the seven skillful means (*saptopāya*). Since it cannot be definitively determined as either nine or seven, it is said to be "various" (*aneka*).
That which was practiced in the past is called "nature" (*prakṛti*); that which is now delighted in is called "desire" (*chanda*); and these refer to wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
Regarding the phrase "The Buddha fully knows those who are equal to himself among the seven stages of practice, which are transmitted and alternate between good and evil":

the Buddha, through his wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), illuminates the dispositions and desires of all beings; he then teaches the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-śāsana*) according to what is appropriate for each.

*Sūtra*—here translated as "Scripture of Accord" (*kīngiēng*)—has both general and specific meanings. Generally, it is the collective name for the holy teachings; specifically, it refers to the twelve divisions [of the scriptures].

Within these divisions, those that directly explain the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are called *sūtra-gāthā*; these are the "isolated verses" (*gūqǐ*), which do not consist of repeated stanzas.
The *itivṛttaka* (Past Events) explains matters such as the world in former times. The *jātaka* (Birth Stories) explains matters concerning the Buddha's previous births.
The *adbhutadharma* (Marvelous Events) refers to the various supernatural powers manifested by the Buddha, which cause sentient beings to marvel.
The "Marvelous" (Adbhuta-dharma) refers to all matters concerning the origins of the Buddha’s words; "Origins" (Nidāna) refers to events involving supernatural causes.

"Parables" (Avadāna) are, for example, like the saying that when the moon is hidden behind heavy mountains, one uses a fan as a metaphor for it, or when the wind ceases in the great void, one instructs by means of a moving tree.
"Geya" (Gāthā) is translated here as "Repetitive Verses"; these repetitive verses restate the Sūtras previously spoken in prose. "Udāna" [is...]

*Vaipulya* (波提舍) here means "treatise" (*śāstra*). The nine divisions mentioned above are said to have been taught in the past as provisional expedients for those at the seven stages of skillful means.
If there are further [divisions] among the twelve, such as *vaipulya*, *avaivartika* (unasked discourse), *svayambhū* (self-spoken), and *vyākaraṇa* (prediction), [they are included].
△ Second, the verse concludes the intent of the provisional application of skillful means.
For those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings, who are attached to the cycle of birth and death, who do not practice the profound and wondrous path under the countless Buddhas,
and who are distressed and distracted by manifold sufferings— for these he preaches nirvāṇa.
Because their faculties were dull in previous lives and they lack the capacity in this life to hear the Great [Vehicle], it is said that they do not practice the profound and wondrous Way.
Because they were attached to greed in previous lives and their obstructions are heavy, and they are tormented by manifold sufferings in this life, they can only hear the Small [Vehicle];
therefore, it is said that for them he preaches *nirvāṇa*. △ Second, the verse clarifying the reality, in four parts; first, the verse on the single principle.
I have established these skillful means to enable you to enter the Buddha-wisdom;

I have never said before that you shall all attain the Buddha-way because the time for such a proclamation had not yet arrived. Now is precisely that time, and I shall definitively proclaim the Mahāyāna.

These nine divisions of my Dharma were taught in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, with the entry into the Mahāyāna as their fundamental purpose; it is for this reason that I preach this sutra.

"Causing them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom" refers to the first great causal condition of this matter. "Decisively expounding the Mahāyāna" is the general verse that reveals, awakens, and causes entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
These nine divisions of my Dharma—some say they are the teachings of the Hīnayāna—whereas the Mahāyāna consists of twelve divisions.
This is because the Hīnayāna is a teaching of extinction like ashes, lacking the body of the wish-fulfilling jewel.
Because there are no Vaipulya [sūtras] and no spontaneous sounding of the celestial drum, there is no "unasked self-exposition.
Although there are prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), they are so few that there is no [distinct category of] prophecy. This has been explained according to the specific [classification];

however, speaking generally according to the broad [classification], both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna possess twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga*). "Division" (*aṅga*) means a category; it is also called the "Twelvefold Teaching. These are the nine [categories].
The name of the section has already been explained above. △ Second, the verse on the person (the recipient of the teaching), in one stanza:
There is a son of the Buddha whose mind is pure, supple, and sharp; who, in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, has practiced the profound and wondrous path.
For these sons of the Buddha, I preach this Mahāyāna sūtra; I prophesy that such a person shall attain the path of Buddhahood in a future age.
Because they recollect the Buddha with a profound mind and practice the pure precepts, these individuals, upon hearing [this teaching], attain great joy that pervades their entire bodies.

Knowing their mental activities, the Buddha preaches the Mahāyāna for them; whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, having heard even a single verse of the Dharma I preach, they will all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
In the preceding verses, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach only the Bodhisattvas; the "person of clear understanding" (mingren) mentioned above refers directly to this.
The verses on the teaching and transformation of Bodhisattvas extensively set forth various skillful means (*upāya*). All these people become persons of true reality (*satpuruṣa*).

When a son of the Buddha possesses a pure mind, he is a person of the distinct teaching (*biejiao*). For such a son of the Buddha, the Mahāyāna sūtras are preached, and upon receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), his heart rejoices. This is as follows:

Those who have become true persons of the Perfect Teaching—whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas—the śrāvakas also include pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattvas encompass those of the Six Perfections as well as the bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching; all shall undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
Thus, these seven kinds of skillful means are none other than sons of the Buddha. △ Third, the verse on the teaching (one verse).
Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma; there is no second and no third, except for the Buddha’s skillful means.
He uses only provisional names to guide sentient beings, speaking thus for the sake of revealing the Buddha’s wisdom.
The verse above states that because the Tathāgata possesses only the single Buddha Vehicle, he teaches the Dharma for sentient beings without any other vehicles—neither two nor three.
If the Buddhas of the ten directions teach only this one Dharma, this constitutes the teaching of the One; it is a provisional name used as a guide, which is the teaching of skillful means.
By citing these three provisional names of teachings, it reveals that the Buddha’s wisdom is the teaching of the One. The text is clear on this point.
Second, there is no duality of the "half" and "full" teachings within the absence of supernatural powers; third, there is no triad within the Three Piṭakas.
These are all provisional names used to guide sentient beings; now, because there is only the single Buddha’s Perfect Vehicle, it is said that he "expounds the Buddha-wisdom.
△ Fourth, the verse on practice (one).
When the Buddhas appear in the world, this alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. They never deliver sentient beings by means of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
The Buddha himself abides in the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), adorned with the power of the Dharma and wisdom he has attained, and thereby delivers sentient beings.
Having personally realized the unsurpassed path—the equal Dharma of the Great Vehicle—if he were to transform others through the Lesser Vehicle...
"Even toward a single person, I would fall into stinginess; this is not permissible.
This verse means that all actions performed are always for one purpose, and that purpose is practice; it never concerns the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and so forth.
This expresses the meaning of "always performing one thing" mentioned above. "The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna," and so on, is the subsequent verse.

The preceding section solely uses the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to instruct and awaken sentient beings; the following single line explains the intention of not delivering them by means of the Lesser Vehicle.
△ Third, the verse on exhorting faith has two parts: first, exhorting faith by citing the fruit; second, first, citing the inner mind.
If a person places their faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Tathāgata— who is neither deceptive nor possessed of greed or envy, and who has severed all evils within all phenomena—
then that person shall, like the Buddha, alone be free from fear throughout the ten directions.
This clarifies that the Buddha’s mind is pure; because he has already severed ignorance, stinginess, and all evils, and speaks from within this pure mind, his words are trustworthy.
△ Second, citing external forms:
"I adorn my body with marks, and my radiance illuminates the world; honored by immeasurable multitudes, I preach for them the seal of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*)."
His physical marks are radiant and distinct, his appearance is dignified and majestic; within he is free from the darkness of delusion, and without he possesses luminosity.
His speech is free from deception, and as one revered by the multitude, he speaks the seal of the Mahāyāna, which may be trusted and accepted.
△ Second, exhorting faith by citing causes, in two parts: first, citing past vows.
"Śāriputra, you should know that I originally established a vow desiring to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself.
My former vow was not merely a personal pledge for my own enlightenment, but also a pledge that all sentient beings should together enter the Buddha’s wisdom;
now, because I am fulfilling that vow, this teaching is spoken, and it should be believed. 2. Explaining that the present vow is fulfilled.
“As my original vow was, it is now fulfilled; I have transformed all sentient beings and caused them all to enter the Buddha-way.
Now that Bodhi is complete and sentient beings have entered [the path], and you yourself have personally realized the Buddha-wisdom, you can verify that my vow was not in vain.
[The interlocutor] asked: “Since your original vow was universal and sentient beings are still so numerous, how can your vow be fulfilled? The Buddha replied three times: [as follows].
The benefit of the world through things now clarifies the fulfillment of the vow regarding the present discourse. △ Fourth, the raising of the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya).
First, a general clarification that the five turbidities obstruct the Great [Vehicle]:
"If I were to encounter sentient beings and teach them all the Buddha-way, those without wisdom would become confused and deluded, and would not accept the teaching."
Sentient beings undergo suffering, and thus all Buddhas give rise to compassion; because compassion and suffering correspond to one another, they are said to "meet.

Once they meet, [the Buddhas] cause them all to enter the Buddha-way; therefore, the five turbidities cannot obstruct [them]. Because those with great wisdom do not accept [obstruction], it is said that [the turbidities] "obstruct the Great.
△ Second, specifically explaining the obstructions of the five turbidities, part one: the turbidity of sentient beings.
I know that these sentient beings have never cultivated the roots of goodness; because they are stubbornly attached to the five desires and deluded by craving, they give rise to affliction.
Due to the causes and conditions of various sensual desires, they fall into the three evil realms and transmigrate through the six destinies, undergoing all manner of bitter poisons and suffering.
The "roots of goodness" refer to the true nature of reality (*tathatā*); because one is unable to plant roots of goodness here, one cannot attain greatness.
To be stubbornly attached to the five desires is the very root of all evils. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"From delusion and craving, my illness arises. △ Second, the defilement of the lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
The subtle form of the conceived embryo constantly grows from lifetime to lifetime for those of meager virtue and little merit who are oppressed by manifold sufferings.

According to the interpretation of the contemplation of the mind (*citta-vipaśyanā*), the arising of a single thought-moment constitutes the karma for future existence; this karma is the embryo, and the embryo is karma.

This cycle is inexhaustible, continuing without interruption from life to life, whereby the physical form increases. This form consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and these aggregates are also termed "worldly lifespan."
Because it connects the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) from the initial stage of thin curd (*dadhi*) through to old age and death, it is called "the world" (*loka*).
The latter two phrases clarify the characteristics of the defilement of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). △ Third, the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
Entering the dense forest of wrong views—whether regarding existence or non-existence—one relies upon these various views which comprise the sixty-two [types].
The five views intersect like a thick and luxuriant forest; "existence" refers to the view of eternalism, while "non-existence" refers to the view of annihilationism.
Based on these two views, the sixty-two arise, such as when non-Buddhists reckon that the self is the fourfold [categories], beginning with "form is [the self]."
"I am separate from form; form is me; I am great and form is small; I dwell within form; I am great and form is small; form dwells within me.
The same applies to the other four aggregates (*skandha*). These constitute twenty-three views.
Together with the sixty [views] and the two fundamental views of annihilationism and eternalism, they total sixty-two. △ Fourth, the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
Deeply attached to illusory dharmas, stubbornly clinging to them so as not to relinquish them, conceited and arrogant due to their own pride, with a crooked and insincere mind.
△ Fifth, the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*):
For thousands of millions of billions of eons, such people have not heard the name of the Buddha, nor have they heard the True Dharma; they are difficult to deliver.

The long absence of the Buddha-dharma is precisely the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the defilement of the age). Furthermore, because the aforementioned four defilements (*kaṣāya*) are concentrated within this period, it is called the *kalpa-kaṣāya*.
Such people as these are difficult to deliver because they are obstructed by the five defilements; if they do not believe in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), they cannot be delivered.
△ Third, [the teaching of] the Lesser Vehicle is expounded for the sake of the five defilements.
Therefore, Śāriputra, I have established skillful means to teach the path for the exhaustion of suffering and to point toward it with Nirvāṇa.
I have taught the Three Piṭakas and the Four Noble Truths: suffering is the Truth of Suffering; that suffering must have a cause is the Truth of Origination;
the path is the Truth of the Path; and Nirvāṇa is the Truth of Cessation. △ Fourth: Teaching the Great through the Small.
Although I speak of nirvana, it is not a true extinction; all dharmas have, from the very beginning, been characterized by constant and inherent quiescence.
O Son of the Buddha, having practiced the Way, you shall in a future age attain Buddhahood.

If one merely suppresses the delusions of the three realms and extinguishes form to attain emptiness, this is not true extinction. If one realizes that ignorance is fundamentally non-existent and eternally quiescent, this is true extinction.
Although it is fundamentally non-existent and eternally quiescent, if one does not cultivate the Way, there is no means by which to realize union with it;
therefore, it is said: "O Son of the Buddha, having practiced the Path, you shall become a Buddha in a future age. △ Fifth, the verse on the non-futility [of practice], part one.
First, it clarifies that Śākyamuni first opened the way for the three [vehicles]:
"I possess the power of skillful means to reveal and teach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
Second, it clarifies that all Buddhas subsequently manifest the reality: [the verse continues].
All World-Honored Ones preach the single vehicle (ekayāna) path.

Śākyamuni opens up the three vehicles while the various Buddhas reveal the reality; these are merely mutual manifestations of one another. △ Third, the correct clarification that [the teaching] is not false.
Now, this great assembly should all eliminate their doubts and delusions; the words of the Buddhas do not differ, being only the single, non-dual vehicle.
What was provisional before and what is real now are truthful words that are not false; the Way of the Buddhas is the same, so do not give rise to doubt.
△ Second, the Chapter on Past Buddhas, in two parts: first, the verse on the opening of the three [vehicles].

Throughout incalculable kalpas in the past, there have been immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa—hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of billions in number, their total count beyond measure.
Such World-Honored Ones have expounded the characteristics of all dharmas through various causes and conditions, parables, and countless powers of skillful means.
△ Second, the two verses clarify the one and the two; first, the brief verse summarizes the preceding three points.
All these World-Honored Ones equally preach the One Vehicle Dharma to transform immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
"All preach the Dharma of the One Vehicle" praises the unity of the teaching; "transforming immeasurable sentient beings" praises the unity of the person;
"causing them to enter the Buddha-way" praises the unity of the principle, while also attaining the unity of practice. II. Extensively revealing the one through the five vehicles. 1.
First, a general revelation of the one through the five vehicles.
Furthermore, the Great Holy Lords, knowing the deep-seated desires of all beings among the devas and humans in the world,
employ various other skillful means to assist in manifesting the ultimate truth.
The phrase "the multitudes of devas and human beings" here raises various vehicles to clarify the oneness of persons;

furthermore, by means of diverse skillful means, it raises various practices to manifest the oneness of practice while simultaneously attaining the oneness of teaching. The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is precisely the oneness of principle (*li*).
If one employs the perfect and wondrous right contemplation, this is the skillful means of the true aspect (*dharmatā*); this is not called "diverse. If one employs...

The seven expedient contemplations that assist in revealing the ultimate truth are called "alternative expedients. △ Second, specifically distinguishing the five vehicles to reveal the one and the three:
first, opening the Bodhisattva vehicle.
If there are any classes of sentient beings who encountered the various Buddhas of the past, and whether they heard the Dharma, practiced giving, observed the precepts,
practiced patience, diligence, meditation, or wisdom— engaging in such various cultivations of merit— all such persons have already attained the path to Buddhahood.

If one explains this according to the five vehicles, it refers only to the Bodhisattva Vehicle of the six perfections. If one explains it according to the seven expedient means, it encompasses both the general and specific Bodhisattva Vehicles.

Why is this? While all three teachings of the Mahāyāna practice the six perfections, there are differences in how the mind is directed. Practicing the six perfections with a conceptual mind is the Bodhisattva of the Tripitaka [Teaching];
practicing them without signs (*animitta*) is the Bodhisattva of the General Teaching; and practicing them without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*) is the Bodhisattva of the Specific Teaching.

The sequential practice of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) within the signless (animitta) is the distinct teaching (biejiao) for bodhisattvas; however, as this text merely lists the six perfections here, it is not yet known to which [category] they definitively belong.

Referring back to the previous passage, which states, "furthermore, by means of diverse skillful means (upāya)," these skillful means refer not only to the bodhisattvas of the six perfections, but to the skillful means of the bodhisattvas of all three teachings.
Those who heard the Dharma in the past have all already attained realization; thus, the "one" of the "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna) refers to the six [perfections] of the past.
Their practices of deliverance are all already perfected; their conduct is one and the same. Thus, these people have all already become persons of the Way;
they have all already attained the Buddha-way; they have all already realized the One Principle. △ Second, the opening of the two vehicles.
"Even after the Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, if there are people with virtuous and gentle minds, all such sentient beings have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
This passage opens the way for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to all enter the One Vehicle. How is this known?

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is praised that the mind of an arhat is harmonious, supple, and gentle; furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti Nirdeśa Sūtra* states that "dwelling in a disciplined mind is the practice of the noble ones. Therefore, [this is established].
To know this: those who formerly possessed a good and gentle heart have all accomplished the practice of the One; that all sentient beings shall become Buddhas is the single principle.

△ Third, opening the paths of humans and devas, in two parts: first, regarding how the minor virtues of humans and devas form the seeds of the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause) to manifest the Reality, in ten sections.
First, building stupas to clarify the path of devas.
After the various Buddhas have passed into parinirvāṇa, those who make offerings to their relics erect billions of kinds of stupas—
made of gold, silver, crystal, *śaṅkha* (conch), *musāragalva* (amber), *muktikā* (pearl), and *vaiḍūrya* (lapis lazuli)— purely, extensively, and magnificently adorned and ornamented.
Some may erect stone temples, or those made of *candana* (sandalwood), *agaru* (aloewood), *khadira* (catechu), or other timbers, as well as bricks, tiles, clay, and earth.

If one piles up earth in the midst of a wilderness to construct a Buddhist temple, because at that time one’s mind is directed with sincerity toward the renunciation of wealth and treasures, one naturally and spontaneously experiences bliss as a result;

therefore, this belongs to the vehicle of humans and devas (*manuṣya-deva-yāna*). As for the *mùqián* (wooden *mùqián*), there is a type of wood in Chang’an called *mù* which is also suitable for making images, as stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
It is said that placing even a portion of the Buddha’s relics the size of a mustard seed within a small stupa results in natural karmic rewards in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
this is precisely the meaning [of the teaching]. △ Second, building a stupa from sand clarifies the human vehicle.
Even those who, in childhood play, gathered sand to make stūpas for the Buddha—all such people as these have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Building stūpas from sand in childhood play is a human karmic cause;

because at the time of the action one acts with a mind that is expansive and serene, seeking the diligent attainment of happiness when the fruit of goodness arises, this is human karma. △ Third, the section on creating images with a sincere mind clarifies the heavens.
Karma: If a person, for the sake of the Buddha, establishes various images, carving them with all the marks and signs so that they are fully completed as Buddhas—
whether made of the seven treasures, brass, red or white copper, pewter, lead, tin, iron, wood, or even clay.
Or those who used cloth stiffened with glue to create images of the Buddha—such people as these have all already attained the path to Buddhahood;
or those who painted images of the Buddha, adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings, whether doing so themselves or employing others—they have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* does not permit the use of glue, as doing so incurs the offense of transgression (*āpatti*); yet this sūtra [permits] its use.
Regarding this, the ancient masters say that in foreign lands they use tree resin. Miaole states that the *Sūtra on the Merit of Image Making* says there are eleven kinds of merit from making images:
first, the eyes will be pure in every lifetime; second, one will be born in places free from evil.
Third, one is always born into a noble family; fourth, one’s body is like the color of purple-polished gold; fifth, one possesses an abundance of rare treasures and playthings;
sixth, one is born into a family of the wise and virtuous; seventh, one is born to become a king; eighth, one becomes a golden-wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*);
ninth, one is born in the Brahma Heaven with a lifespan of one kalpa; tenth, one does not fall into the evil realms; eleventh, ...
Those born in future lives will still be able to revere and honor the Triple Gem.

It is further said that if, at the time of death, a person speaks the words for making an image—even one as small as a grain of wheat—it can eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas across the three periods of time.
△ Fourth, the karma of the person who clarifies the Buddha through playful drawing:
even if a child plays at drawing an image of the Buddha using grass, wood, a brush, or even their fingernails.
△ Fifth, the conclusion that reveals the reality:
Thus, these various persons gradually accumulated merit, became fully endowed with the mind of great compassion, and have all already attained the Buddha-way;
they merely transform bodhisattvas and deliver immeasurable multitudes.
All these people together constitute the "person" (the practitioner). Gradually accumulating merit and fulfilling the mind of great compassion constitutes the "practice.
Attaining the Way of the Buddha constitutes the "principle. Having already attained Buddhahood, one is further able to transform others;
transforming only Bodhisattvas constitutes the "teaching. 6. Explaining the karmic activity of the mind by means of offerings to various sensory objects.
If a person, with a heart of reverence, makes offerings of flowers, incense, banners, and canopies to stupas, shrines, precious images, or painted images;

or if they cause others to perform music—sounding drums, blowing horns and conchs, playing flutes, pipes, lutes, harps, *pi-pa* lutes, gongs, and cymbals—and offers all such exquisite sounds as an offering;
or if, with a joyful heart, they sing hymns and praises in glorification of the Buddha’s virtues.
Even down to a single small sound, all have already attained the Way of the Buddha.
*Bai* (貝) refers to the large conch shell; *bei* (唄) is sometimes called *beini* (唄匿), which is translated here as "praise and hymn.
△ Seventh, explaining human karma by means of offerings made with the sensory objects while in a distracted state of mind.
If a person, even with a distracted mind, makes an offering of a single flower to a painted image, they will gradually come to see countless Buddhas.
In the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, there was an elder who fathered a son named Tianhua (Celestial Flower);
because he had scattered grass flowers upon the Sangha in a previous life, he left the household life and realized the fruit of Arhatship. △ Eighth: Clarifying Offerings in Terms of Bodily Action.
The karma of devas and humans:
there may be those who prostrate, or perhaps merely join their palms, or even raise a single hand, or slightly bow their heads, or cast their five limbs to the ground.
This supreme form of worship is the karma of devas; joining the palms and bowing the head is the middling form of worship, which is that of humans.
Karma. △ Ninth, the conclusion of the offering reveals the reality:

by means of this offering to the image, one gradually beholds immeasurable Buddhas, personally attains the Unsurpassed Way, and extensively delivers countless multitudes, entering nirvana without remainder like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
Not only does one enter the Buddha-way oneself, but one is also able to transform and deliver sentient beings so that they enter nirvana.

When the bonds of the seeds and fruits are exhausted, it is called "without remainder" (anupadhiśeṣa). Since the firewood is exhausted, the responding fire perishes; therefore, it is said that "the fire is extinguished when the wood is spent."
△ Tenth, regarding the karma of making offerings to enlightened persons through verbal action:
If a person with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple and utters "Namo Buddha" even once, they have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
*Namo* (or *namo*), sometimes translated as "taking refuge" or "deliver me. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha said: If there is a person who utters 'Namo Buddha' even once, their merit shall not be exhausted until the end of suffering.
2. Clarifying the reality through the seeds of the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*).
Regarding all the Buddhas of the past—whether currently existing or having entered parinirvāṇa—if there are those who hear this Dharma, they have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.

Following the previous analogy, whether it be with marks, without marks, non-marks, or neither mark nor non-mark; whether with a sincere mind or a distracted mind—these seeds of the five vehicles are now all opened and integrated into the One Reality.
Hearing even a single phrase with a sincere mind is the karma of a celestial being; hearing even a single [phrase] with a distracted mind is [the karma of a human].
Question: What is the intention behind this passage, which extensively explains through the gateway of past Buddhas that all five vehicles enter into reality?

Answer: All Buddhas of the three periods of time possess the opening of provisional means (*upāya*). However, because future Buddhas have not yet arisen and present Buddhas have only recently begun their practice, their realization of this meaning is weak.

In contrast, the Buddhas of the past opened the provisional means long ago; thus, those who received transformation under them have all achieved the "Fourfold Identity" (*catur-eka-tva*) and are [already] in accord with reality.

The empty words fabricated by those who insist on proving their doctrines through the expedient means and ultimate reality manifested throughout the ten directions are not as good as verifying them through actual fact;
therefore, the Buddhas of the past extensively expounded the five vehicles. △ Third, the verse on the Buddhas of the future, in two parts:
first, the verse on the opening of the three [vehicles].
The future World-Honored Ones will be immeasurable in number; these Tathāgatas likewise teach the Dharma through skillful means, for all Tathāgatas employ immeasurable expedient means.
△ Second, two verses clarify the oneness of the four [aspects]. The first verse concerns the person:
"If there are those who hear the Dharma, there shall be not one among all sentient beings whom I do not deliver and lead into the Buddha’s untainted wisdom."
△ Second, one verse on practice:
"The original vow of all Buddhas is that the Buddha-way which I have practiced, I desire all sentient beings to likewise attain.
△ Third, one verse on teaching:
Although the Buddhas of future ages shall preach hundreds of thousands of billions of countless Dharma-gates, in reality they are but the One Vehicle.

The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, know that all phenomena are eternally devoid of intrinsic nature and that the Buddha-seed arises from conditions; therefore, they preach the One Vehicle.
To know that phenomena are eternally devoid of intrinsic nature means that the true mark (*dharmatā*) is eternally abiding and lacks self-nature, even to the point of lacking causal nature;
this absence of nature, wherein even "naturelessness" itself is absent, is called "naturelessness.

That which arises from conditions as the seed of the Buddha refers to the Middle Way of naturelessness, which is precisely the seed of the Buddha. Those who are deluded regarding this principle give rise to the notion of sentient beings due to ignorance acting as a condition.
This principle is that because the practice of the teachings serves as the condition, right awakening arises; to give rise to the Buddha-seed, one requires the teaching of the One Vehicle.
This is the first verse concerning the teaching. △ Fourth, the single verse on the principle.

This Dharma abides in its fixed position; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. Having realized this at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the Teacher explains it through skillful means.
"This Dharma abides in its fixed position" means that the true awakening of sentient beings is of one suchness and not two;

none transcend suchness, for all are established in their positions as being in accordance with suchness. "The characteristics of the world are eternally constant" means that supramundane true awakening also takes suchness as its position.
Taking *tathatā* (suchness) as the characteristic, sentient beings are likewise so; since the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding, is this not the oneness of principle?
Furthermore, it is explained that "the world" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*); "eternally abiding" refers to the direct cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).

Now, this direct cause is not identical to the six dharmas, yet the conditional and contributory causes (*pratyaya-hetu* and *hetu-hetu*) are not separate from them. Because the direct cause is eternal, the conditional and contributory causes [are likewise eternal].

Because it is also eternal, it is said that "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. Regarding the phrase "knowing this at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*), this cites the fruit to explain and reveal [the teaching]:
the site of enlightenment is luminous, its principle has long been pervasive, yet because sentient beings' afflictions are heavy, expedient means were employed to bestow the three [vehicles].
4. Verse on the Chapter on Present Buddhas (3 sections): First, stating the intent of manifesting transformation.

The Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who are honored by devas and humans, have appeared in the world for the sake of bringing peace and stability to sentient beings;
they, too, preach this very Dharma.
This is precisely the intent behind the provisional teachings: to bring peace and security to sentient beings. △ Second, the verse reveals the ultimate truth:
Knowing the supreme quiescence, by the power of skillful means, although various paths are displayed, in reality they are for the Buddha-vehicle alone.
The first [verse] on "tranquility" (*śānti*) praises the single principle of reality as the Buddha-vehicle; alternatively, it praises the single teaching or the single practice.
△ Third, the verse on "opening the provisional":
It knows the various practices of sentient beings, what their deep minds contemplate, the karma they have practiced in the past, their dispositions, natures, and the power of their diligence.

Furthermore, he taught by means of various causes, conditions, parables, and verbal expressions, employing skillful means appropriate to the sharpness or dullness of the faculties [of sentient beings].

△ Second, the verse on the chapter of Śākyamuni has two parts: first, a brief verse summarizing the aforementioned provisional and ultimate teachings to serve as the basis for the general parable below; second, the verse clarifying the ultimate truth.
First, the verse clarifying the ultimate truth:
Now I am also like this: for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, I proclaim the Buddha-way through various Dharma-gates.
"Now I am also like this" means that I, Śākyamuni, the sovereign of a single transformation, teach sentient beings through the same single reality;
thus it is said "like this. This serves as the basis for the following parable of the elder. "Peace and security" refers to the Great [Vehicle].
Nirvana is the eternal and blissful abode; because this place is tranquil and free from the obstacles of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), it is called "peaceful and secure.

"Peace" is contrasted with "insecurity," meaning that the three realms, possessing the obstacles of the five turbidities, are termed "insecure"—this serves as the basis for the subsequent parable of the burning house.
"Sentient beings" refers to those in the five destinies who are the disciples to be transformed—this serves as the basis for the subsequent parable of the five hundred people.
The creation of the various fundamental dharma-gates corresponds to the non-various [reality] below; there is only one gate as the analogy for the fundamental basis.
II. Verse on the Opening of the Provisional:
"By the power of my wisdom, I know the dispositions and desires of sentient beings, and through skillful means I preach all dharmas so that they may all attain joy."

The power of wisdom is precisely the power of skillful means (*upāya*). To know the dispositions and desires of sentient beings refers to the root-natures of the five destinies and their distinctions among the three vehicles;
this serves as the basis for the analogy of the thirty children. "All phenomena" refers to the teachings of the three vehicles.
"Knowing" means discerning the capacities of those with inferior faculties. "Teaching through skillful means" refers to the correct application of provisional methods to cause all [beings] to...

Those who attain joy do so according to their capacity and suitability. Although these two verses are brief, they encompass the Buddha’s entire career of transformation—opening up provisional means and revealing the ultimate reality, tracing the origin and reaching the end—leaving nothing out; thus, they are called "Brief Verses" and serve as the general basis for the subsequent metaphors.
II. Extensive Verses on the Six Meanings Above, Serving as the Basis for the Subsequent Specific Metaphors (6 sections). First, the verses on the first five [meanings].

The first section [of the initial passage] further consists of three parts: first, clarifying that the Buddha is able to see with his eyes. [The text continues: Two verses clarify the defilements; three verses reveal the skillful means of transformation; four verses manifest the reality; five verses praise the rarity of the Dharma;

six verses show that what is above is not in vain; and six verses encourage faith in what is above. Regarding the first [of these], there are again three [subsections]. First, it clarifies that the Buddha is able to see with his eyes.
Śāriputra, you should know that I observe with the Buddha-eye.
Observing with the Buddha-eye, I see that for the sake of the lower-ranking elder, I manifest as the Prabhūtaratna Buddha as a fundamental illumination.

Abiding in the stage of the Dharma-body, I employ the eternally quiescent Buddha-eye to mirror the various capacities of sentient beings; if their faculties are sharp and their defilements light, I appear in the form of Vairocana.

When preaching the Dharma of the One Vehicle, if the faculties [of beings] are dull, turbid, and heavy, he removes his jeweled necklace and assumes the form of an aged bhikṣu to enter the burning house, employing skillful means to open the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. At that time, because he discerns their capacities, he says:
"I, with my Buddha-eye, behold [them]. II. Explaining what is seen: the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*). First, the corruption of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
Seeing the sentient beings of the six realms who are impoverished and lacking in merit and wisdom.
*Miaole* says: "They are 'impoverished' because they lack merit, and 'deluded' because they lack wisdom;
because these impoverished and deluded sentient beings gather together in one place, it is called the defilement of sentient beings. △ Second, the defilement of lifespan (*āyus-kāṣāya*).
Entering the perilous path of birth and death, the continuity of suffering is unceasing.
*Miaole* (The Sublime Joy) states: "Within birth and death, there is further the 'perilous path';

because life is easily severed within this perilous path, it is a place of short lifespan, yet the continuity persists as the turbidity of life. △ Third, the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
They are deeply attached to the five desires, like a yak that loves its tail; shrouded by their own craving and greed, they are blind and see nothing.

The yak is a beast resembling an ox with a long tail; the ox loves its tail so much that it moves its body to protect it, and people covet its tail so much that they kill it for banners and streamers.
It is just the same when a person covets the five desires and thereby harms their own body.
△ Four verses on the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*):
"They do not seek the Buddha of Great Power nor the Dharma that severs suffering.

The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "Because there is no Buddha within the eon, it is called a 'defilement. Since the four defilements arise therein, there is likewise nothing to be sought."
If there is a Buddha in an eon, even though it is turbid, he can destroy it; thus the Sūtra says: "I alone am able to provide rescue and protection.
△ Fifth, the verse on the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*):
Deeply entering into various false views, they seek to abandon suffering through suffering.
All views are sensation (*vedanā*), and sensation is itself the practice of suffering. Since this suffering is caused by desire, how could one possibly abandon suffering? Miaole says:
"Because there are many [views], numbering sixty-two, they are called 'all' (*sarva*). Because of these views, there are the three types of sensation;
thus it is said that "view is itself sensation. Since all three sensations are suffering, those who wish to abandon suffering through this sensation of suffering—[how can they succeed?]
There is no such place. △ Third, the manifestation of great compassion in response:
for the sake of these sentient beings, he gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Having previously raised the subject of the "seer," he next clarifies the "seen"; now he clarifies how great compassion permeates the mind so that he may enter the triple world to bestow [benefits].
This is because they employ skillful means to lead others toward the Buddha-wisdom. △ Second, the verse on the skillful means of transforming through giving has two parts.
First, the initial thought of employing the Mahāyāna to propose it to those who are not yet ready has three parts. First, clarifying the employment of the Mahāyāna to propose it to them.
When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, observing the tree and also walking to and fro for twenty-one days, I contemplated these matters:
the wisdom I have attained is subtle, wondrous, and supreme.

Regarding "first sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*): from the perspective of ultimate truth, there is no time; however, because one employs time to transform sentient beings as the beginning of that transformation, it is called "first.

From the perspective of explaining according to phenomena (*dharma*), it is called the "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) because one cultivates and attains the Way in this place for the first time.

It is called the "Bodhi Tree" because one attained *samyaksambodhi* while sitting beneath this tree. From the perspective of contemplating the mind, the "tree" refers to the twelve [links of dependent origination].
Because he deeply contemplates dependent origination under the great tree of causes and conditions, he naturally attains *bodhi*.

Desiring to provide the shade of the forest of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas for all sentient beings, he speaks the *Vṛkṣapracchāyā-sūtra*. The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) of the Mahāyāna are the dharma for practicing the Path;
by personally traversing all stages (*bhūmi*) via these factors of the Path, one attains the Buddha-way. Desiring to transform others through this Dharma, [he teaches it].
It is for the sake of delivering sentient beings that he undertakes this practice. Regarding the "three periods of seven days," the *Past Causes and Effects Sūtra* (*Guoqu yinguo jing*) states:
"In the first week after attaining enlightenment, the Buddha contemplated that his Dharma was so subtle and profound that no one would be able to receive it.

In the second week, he contemplated the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of sentient beings. In the third week, he contemplated who should hear it first, and thus he proceeded toward Vārāṇasī."
To preach the Four Noble Truths and so forth to the five bhikṣus by means of the three vehicles for those of the three capacities is an explanation according to the Hīnayāna.
Now, to clarify the truth: while the Buddha abides in the stage of the Dharmakāya, he is quiescent yet ever-illuminating, constantly surveying all things with the Buddha-eye without omission.
How could it be that only upon reaching the site of enlightenment did he linger for twenty-one days before finally contemplating this matter? Thus, it is said to be "twenty-one days."

This clarifies that there is something being indicated. If one explains this according to the general approach of the Mahāyāna: the first seven contemplations intend to teach the Perfect Teaching (Eka-yāna);
the next seven contemplations intend to teach the Distinct Teaching; and the final seven contemplations intend to teach the Shared Teaching.

Since there was no spiritual capacity [for these teachings] among the listeners, he ceased the exposition of the Great [Teachings] and instead taught the Tripitaka and the Three Vehicles as a provisional transformation.
...so it is. △ Second, clarifying that sentient beings lack the capacity [to receive the teaching], in three parts: First, clarifying that their obstructions are heavy.
"The faculties of sentient beings are dull; they are attached to pleasure and blinded by ignorance.
△ Second, clarifying that they are incapable of hearing [the teaching].
How can such beings as these be delivered? △ Third, the entreaty of the various devas:
At that time, the Brahma kings, Śakra, Lord of Devas, the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, and Maheśvara...
Furthermore, the various hosts of devas and their retinues, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, reverently joined their palms and entreated me to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Although the Brahmās made this request, the Buddha, knowing that there were no [suitable] vessels for it, did not preach it. Why is this? As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha* asks: "How..."

Regarding the fact that the Brahmā King invited [the Buddha] to preach the Great [Vehicle], it is known from the Buddha’s response—“If one merely praises the Buddha-vehicle,” and so forth—that this was an invitation for the Great [Vehicle].
If one considers a single four-continent world system (*cāturmahādvīpaka*), there is only one Brahmā King who serves as the lord of the three realms;
however, the present mention of “all Brahmā Kings” indicates that the Tathāgata governs a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*), which contains ten billion sets of four continents.
Below, there are ten billion Brahma Kings; furthermore, since each dhyāna level has its own Brahma King, they are referred to as "the various [Brahmas].
If one discusses the actual invitation to hear the Dharma, it concerns the Lord of the Three Realms in the First Dhyāna. △ Third, the three knowledges regarding the desire to cease transformation;
first, the absence of receptive capacity.
I then reflected to myself: "If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would be unable to believe this Dharma;
because they would reject the Dharma and lack faith, they would fall into the three evil realms."
It is clear that if one forcefully preaches to those who lack the capacity, it will cause harm. △ Second, the cessation of the transformation [of the teaching]:
"I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter nirvana;
for if I preach, there will be destruction and extinction, and no benefit. This reflection serves as the foundation for the subsequent employment of expedient means.

...Furthermore, △ Second, reflecting upon how he employs the same means as all Buddhas to transform beings according to their suitability, in two parts: First, the formal explanation of the transformation;
Fourth, clarifying the suitability of the three vehicles.
He reflects: "Seeking the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past, I too, having now attained the Way, should likewise preach the three vehicles."

Regarding "seeking and reflecting": although [the beings] lack the great capacity [for the One Vehicle], they must not be abandoned forever; rather, they are to be guided and saved through skillful means.
It is not that [the Buddhas] are unaware of this, for they open the three vehicles with the intent to lead [beings] to be equal to all Buddhas;

thus it is called "seeking and reflecting. △ Second, explaining that there are those with small capacity, in two parts: first, explaining the praise of the various Buddhas, with five initial sections; first, Śākyamuni’s own narration of the various Buddhas.
Manifestation.
When I was reflecting in this way, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared and consoled me with Brahma-sounds.

Their manifestation occurs due to the power of the skillful means of mindfulness of the Buddha; their appearance is further due to two meanings: the correspondence with the Dharma-assembly and the suitability of the capacity [of the practitioner].
Therefore, the Buddha manifests. △ Second, the Buddhas truly praise Śākyamuni’s ability to conceal the real and manifest the provisional:
"Excellent, Śākyamuni, foremost guide! You have attained this unsurpassed Dharma and, following all Buddhas, employ the power of skillful means."
Because those at the highest level lacked the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) for a great transformation, the Buddhas did not praise [the teaching of] the Great Vehicle.

Now, wishing to preach the Small Vehicle to accord with their faculties and conditions, they ensure that these beings attain liberation from beginning to end; therefore, the Buddha praised them, saying, "Excellent! By bestowing one thing and introducing them to the three, he leads them into the Buddha-wisdom.
This is the foremost guide. One who attains this unsurpassed Dharma is one who has attained true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
It is subtle and supreme, yet those who employ the power of skillful means follow all Buddhas in concealing their true reality and utilizing provisional expedients.
△ Third, it clarifies that all Buddhas likewise conceal their true reality and utilize provisional expedients.
We, too, have all attained the most wondrous and supreme Dharma, and for the sake of the various classes of sentient beings, we distinguish and expound the three vehicles.
△ Fourth, a dual explanation of two meanings:

Those with little wisdom who delight in inferior dharmas do not believe they can become Buddhas; therefore, by means of skillful expedients, [the Buddha] distinguishes and expounds the various fruits.
Because sentient beings possess little wisdom and are unable to hear the Great [Vehicle], he conceals the reality; and because they delight in the Small [Vehicle], he employs expedient means.
△ Fifth, the dual conclusion regarding the two "selves":
although the three vehicles are taught, it is solely for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas.

Although three [vehicles] are spoken of, it is only for the purpose of revealing the reality. △ Second, explaining Śākyamuni’s response in accordance [with the request]. First, the speech that responds in accordance:
"Śāriputra, you should know: when I heard the profound, pure, subtle, and wonderful voice of the Holy Lion, I joyfully exclaimed, 'Namo Buddha!'"
Having heard the various Buddhas offer praise, he immediately replied: "Namo, Namo. This is translated as "reverently following";
it does not mean "delivering us," for that is not the intended sense. Second, he contemplated the capacities of sentient beings.
He further thought: "I have emerged from this world of turbid evil; as all Buddhas have taught, I too shall act in accordance with their instructions.
△ Third, the minor manifestation of transformative teaching:
Having contemplated these matters, he immediately proceeded to Vārāṇasī, [realizing that] the mark of the cessation of all phenomena cannot be expressed in words.
By the power of skillful means, he taught for the sake of the five bhikṣus that the mark of the quiescence of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words;
this is precisely the principle of the Middle Way and the seed of Buddhahood which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) as previously explained.
This principle is beyond calculation and moreover ineffable; now, by means of skillful means, it is taught as the three vehicles.
Furthermore, that which is neither arising nor ceasing is taught as arising and ceasing through skillful means;

likewise, the principle of partial truth cannot be expressed, yet it is taught through the four gates by skillful means. Initially, for the sake of the five bhikṣus, the gate of impermanence was taught.
△ Fourth, clarifying the practice and realization.
This is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma, whereby there arise the sounds of *nirvāṇa* and the distinct designations of the Arhat, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
To turn the Dharma within the Buddha’s mind that transforms others—causing it to enter the minds of others—is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma.

As stated previously, upon first attaining the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), one immediately severs the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) and partially realizes the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*); this is also called the partial attainment of *nirvāṇa with remainder*.
The sound of *nirvāṇa* arises from this; by virtue of this, one attains the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and thus receives the name of Arhat.
One who is able to expound the Three Vehicles is called a Buddha; the Three Vehicles that are expounded constitute the Dharma; those such as Arhats who have seen the Truths constitute the Saṅgha.
Thus, the Triple Gem manifests in the world. II. Resolving Doubts and Reflections.
"Since time immemorial, I have constantly taught that the Dharma of Nirvāṇa reveals the eternal exhaustion of the suffering of birth and death.

Fearing that [the disciples] might suspect the Teacher, thinking that the Buddha was initially unable to discern their capacities and only later came to know their faculties through reflection upon the Buddhas, I explain:
it is not that I did not know; rather, I employed skillful means, desiring specifically to lead them along the same path, and thus reflected upon the Buddhas."
Only upon first forming this thought did he realize that from time immemorial, seeing their attachment to the Lesser Vehicle, he had praised and shown them the way to bring all suffering to an end;
thus, upon hearing the Lesser Vehicle, they immediately attained liberation.

Fearing that his disciples might doubt how it is that sentient beings can momentarily hear [the teaching] in a single lifetime and yet realize Arhatship, he explains: "From time immemorial... and so forth.
By praising and manifesting [the truth] in accordance with their original practice, they quickly attain the Way. △ Third, the four verses that reveal the reality; first, one verse on the person:
"Śāriputra, you should know that I see my sons, those who equally aspire to seek the Buddha-way, numbering immeasurable thousands of millions."
All have come to the Buddha’s presence with hearts of reverence; they have previously heard from various Buddhas the Dharma taught through skillful means.
These two verses apply to those of both the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles, for all such practitioners are children of the Buddha.

Furthermore, these two verses are also called "the arousal of the Mahāyāna capacity" (*indriya*) or "seeking the fruit," clarifying that because the capacity is aroused, one seeks the fruit with resolve.

Those who seek the Buddha-way are precisely those seeking the Great [Vehicle] and not seeking the small fruit. There are three meanings to this "seeking": first, the sense that a great capacity has a resonance with its fruit;
"seeking" is discussed here within the context of this capacity. Second, it refers to the secret seeking within one's own sentiments regarding whether one will attain it or not;
this is the intended meaning here. Third, it refers to speaking out to seek it, which is the earnestness of the three requests. All [of these] are encompassed by two phrases.
The great capacities respond to the Buddha, each arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling. Regarding the two phrases "formerly followed" and so forth:

herein, the first flavor involves being tamed, disciplined, and practicing the three collections (Tripitaka), the six perfections, and the three teachings—both general and specific—which serve as skillful means.
Because one is matured through these means, hindrances are removed, the capacity is awakened, and one seeks the Great [Vehicle]. △ Second, the verse on the single principle.
I then had this thought: "The reason the Tathāgata has appeared is to expound the Buddha-wisdom; now is precisely the time for this.
This single line of verse is so called because its principle is one; "expounding the Buddha-wisdom" refers to the aforementioned seed-wisdom (*tathāgata-jñāna-darśana*).
Furthermore, from here down to the two lines and one phrase beginning with "Now I am joyful and fearless," is also called the "Buddha’s Joy."

Because sentient beings rejoice in obtaining the benefit of the Mahāyāna, and because the Buddha seeks to bring forth his Buddha-wisdom, he has appeared. Although in the past their hindrances were heavy and they lacked the capacity, the Buddha’s wisdom could not be taught;
now that their capacity has been awakened, it is precisely the time for its teaching. Thus it is said, "Now is truly the time.
Since those who hear this teaching will surely believe and understand, and will not fear slander or fall into the great evil realms, it is called "rejoicing without fear. △
The Three Teachings are One.
Śāriputra, you should know that those of dull faculties and small wisdom, who are attached to signs and possessed by pride, cannot believe in this Dharma.
Now I rejoice and am fearless; among all bodhisattvas, I directly abandon expedient means and speak only of the Unsurpassed Way.
Since these two lines of verse teach [the single path], it is said that "only the unsurpassed path" is taught;
the following three phrases are also rightly termed the "manifestation of reality. The five vehicles are circuitous rather than direct, and indirect or peripheral rather than central;
now, all such deviations are abandoned, and only the straight and upright single path is taught. (One line, four characters).
Upon hearing this Dharma, the net of doubt of the Bodhisattvas has been entirely removed, and the twelve hundred Arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas.

Because they practice this single line [of verse], it says "they shall all likewise become Buddhas. Furthermore, this single line is also called "receiving and practicing" and "awakening and entering";
it refers to the two types of Bodhisattvas who, upon first hearing this brief exposition, shake off their former attachments and thereby attain realization.
The new doubts have now all been eliminated; it is not only Bodhisattvas, but the followers of the Two Vehicles as well, who are thus [liberated].
As for the statement that "all Śrāvakas shall become Buddhas," the former teachings did not speak of the Two Vehicles becoming Buddhas, whereas now they are granted predictions (vyākaraṇa).

How could these predictions apply solely to the Two Vehicles? And how could the removal of doubts apply solely to Bodhisattvas? When both are preserved, then both are complete. △ Fourth, the verse praising the Dharma.
The first of the two [sections on] aspiration:
"In accordance with the ritual for teaching the Dharma by the Buddhas of the three times, I now likewise teach this non-conceptual Dharma, such as this wondrous Dharma mentioned above."

As for "being like those of the three periods," this refers to leading others to be the same as all Buddhas through the use of skillful means (*upāya*). This is because skillful means is the ritual form used to lead sentient beings.
To speak of the dharma of non-discrimination is to lead them to be the same as all Buddhas by revealing the reality (*tattva*).

Since reality transcends the path of words, how could it possess ritual forms? Furthermore, skillful means and reality are fundamentally without discrimination; they are only divided for those of dull faculties and small wisdom.

Distinguishing between the provisional and the ultimate, one now returns to realize the non-duality of the one and the three; one knows that the Buddha’s teaching of the three and the one is without distinction.
All Buddhas are thus; why should this alone be an exception? II. Verses on the previous section, "Only then does he speak it," in five parts.
First, raising the point that such persons are difficult to encounter.
The appearance of the Buddhas in the world occurs at vast intervals; it is difficult to encounter them.
After a long, protracted period, a Buddha appears—this illustrates the difficulty of meeting a person [who is a Buddha]. △ Second, illustrating the difficulty of the Dharma being taught.
Even more difficult than this is for such a Dharma to be preached once it has appeared in the world;
