it is only now that the Buddha, having appeared in the world for over forty years, has finally revealed the truth. △ Third, citing the difficulty of hearing the Dharma.
It is also difficult to hear this Dharma even throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas.
For those like the group of five thousand who rose from their seats and departed as the Brahma-sound filled their ears—was it not indeed difficult for them to hear?
△ Fourth, citing the difficulty of believing and accepting [the teaching].
Those who are able to hear this Dharma are likewise rare.
Among the assembly, only Śāriputra has attained realization; as for those of middling and inferior capacities, though they listen, they still cannot fully comprehend it.
△ Fifth, citing the analogy of flowers to illustrate these four difficulties.
For example, the udumbara flower is beloved by all; it is rare for gods and humans alike, appearing only once in a great while.
To hear the Dharma with joy and praise, even uttering but a single word, is to have already made offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Such a person is exceedingly rare, surpassing even the udumbara flower.

The single metaphor of the *tāṃ-puṣpa* (udumbara flower) illustrates the four preceding difficulties; now, we merely combine [the discussion of] the difficulty for the listener, while the remaining examples can be understood by analogy.
△ Fifth, the verse on "not being in vain" has two parts: first, do not harbor doubt toward a person who is trustworthy.

"You all should not harbor doubts regarding me. As the King of All Dharmas, I have universally addressed the great assembly, teaching and transforming all bodhisattvas through the single vehicle (ekayāna) alone; I have no śrāvaka disciples."
As for the Dharma King: since one who is a king of men speaks without duality, how could the Buddha, the Dharma King, ever permit false speech?
While skillful means may be provisional and expedient, how could that which is true and real possibly be deceptive? Upon hearing the Dharma King preach the Dharma, do not give rise to doubt.
△ Second, do not give rise to doubt regarding the trustworthy Dharma.
"Śāriputra, you śrāvakas and bodhisattvas should know that this wondrous Dharma is the secret essence of all Buddhas.
For more than forty years it has been stored within the Buddha’s mind, unknown to others; thus it is called 'secret.

Because the direct path of the One Vehicle subsumes all myriad ways, it is called 'essential. △ Sixth, the verse summarizing the preceding section on distinguishing the assembly and exhorting them to faith. Part one: the verse."
Regarding the first of the three stages of selecting the assembly: those who are not disciples are excluded.
Because in this world of the five turbidities, beings such as these take pleasure only in various desires and will never seek the Buddha-way.

If one delights in various sensual desires, this is the practice of Māra; therefore, it must be excluded. In the preceding text, even those attached to *nirvāṇa* were said not to be disciples of the Buddha;
here, those attached to *saṃsāra* are said to be disciples of the Buddha—this is merely a mutual exclusion of what they are not.

As for "those who ultimately do not seek the Buddha-way," this verse excludes those of *adhimāna* (overweening pride). One with overweening pride has not attained the supreme Dharma, yet claims to have attained it.
Because the aforementioned dharma is such, that person does not seek the Buddha-way. △ Second, it is difficult to find those who can explain the meaning after the Buddha’s extinction.
In future ages, evil people, hearing the Buddha preach the One Vehicle, will be deluded and fail to believe or accept it; they will destroy the Dharma and fall into the evil realms.

In future ages, those who are wicked will find it difficult to encounter someone capable of interpreting the meaning after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. △ Third, regarding those who meet other Buddhas and attain definitive understanding:
for those who possess a sense of shame and modesty, whose minds are pure, and who earnestly seek the Buddha-way, one should extensively praise the path of the One Vehicle for their sake.
△ Second, the two verses exhorting faith. First, exhorting faith in the provisional [teachings]:
"Śāriputra, you should know that the Dharma of all Buddhas is thus: by means of thousands of millions of skillful expedients, they preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
Those who have not practiced and studied cannot understand this."
△ Second, the exhortation to believe in the truth:
"Since you have already understood that all Buddhas, the Teachers of the World, employ skillful means according to circumstances, you should no longer harbor any doubts;
let your hearts give rise to great joy, knowing for yourselves that you shall become Buddhas."

The provisional application of skillful means is precisely for the sake of the ultimate reality; when there is no doubt regarding the provisional and the real, one knows for oneself that one will become a Buddha.
*Fahua jing kezhu*, Scroll One.
*Miaofa lianhua jing kezhu*, Scroll Two.
The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, Chapter Three: The Parable (in the original text, this chapter is titled "Appropriate to the Occasion").

Previously, the five Buddhas revealed the provisional teachings; those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom heard them in their entirety and attained awakening. However, those of middling and inferior capacities remained mired in delusion and failed to reach understanding;
their attachments were stirred and doubts arose, causing them to hesitate at the crossroads. Therefore, the parables of the three carts and the single cart are presented once more.
It is called the "Parable Chapter" because it employs metaphors to cause awakening and understanding. △ Second, Śāriputra’s Acceptance and Understanding, in two parts:
first, the narrator’s account of his internal realization; second, [the actual realization]. First, the account of his internal realization.
At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy and was filled with delight.
To have understanding arise within the mind is called "delight"; for this delight to move the physical form is called "leaping.

Having heard the sublime Dharma from the Sublime Person and attained sublime understanding, how could one not leap for joy when these three forms of joy are fully present? △ Second, describing his external demeanor.
He immediately rose, joined his palms, and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance.
The union of the provisional and the real is like the joining of two palms; gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance signifies the realization of the Real.

That the Real is the realm of the Buddha and not a method of expedient means is shown by gazing without reserve and contemplating with focused intent, which represents the opening of the Buddha-wisdom and vision. △ Second.
Śāriputra himself recounted his experience in two parts; first, the prose section, which begins with the indication of the three types of joy.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "Having now heard this Dharma-sound from the World-Honored One, I am filled with exultation, having attained what I have never experienced before."
Now, following the World-Honored One’s designation, I see the Buddha’s body; therefore, it is called "joy of the body.

Hearing this Dharma-sound and rejoicing upon hearing it from the Buddha’s own mouth is called "joy of the mouth. Attaining what was never before experienced and understanding the Buddha’s intent with my own mind is called "joy of the mind.
△ Second, explaining the loss has three parts; first, clarifying that not seeing the Buddha in the past constitutes the loss of the body.
"Alas! Why is this?
In the past, we heard such a Dharma from the Buddha, seeing various bodhisattvas receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, while we ourselves were not included in this matter;
we are deeply grieved at having lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision."

In the past, when the Buddha conferred the prediction of enlightenment upon the Bodhisattvas, I was not included in that matter. Seeing that the meaning of the Buddha was remote, and because I did not see the Buddha, I lacked the joy of embodiment.

Those who hear such a Dharma as this—just as when the sun shines upon a high mountain, its hidden meanings become manifest—are like those who are deaf or mute and cannot say they have heard it; hearing such a Dharma is merely hearing within the Vaipulya (Extensive) teachings.
Because the true wisdom of the Mahāyāna is no different from that of the present, it is said that "hearing such a Dharma" constitutes receiving a prediction (vyākaraṇa).

Furthermore, regarding those who receive predictions within the Vaipulya sūtras—where the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are excluded and left deeply moved by their own [inferiority]—this refers to those who, upon hearing the praise of the Great and the disparagement of the Small in texts such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, harbor internal doubts while outwardly feeling contempt;
this state of being inwardly suspicious yet outwardly disdainful is what is termed "being moved by grief. This would result in the loss [of the prediction].
Those who come now to seek knowledge and vision lose the seeing of the Buddha-eye and the knowing of the Buddha-wisdom.
△ Second, explaining the loss of speech due to not having heard the Dharma in the past:
"World-Honored One, whenever I dwelt alone in mountain forests or beneath trees, whether sitting or walking, I would constantly think: 'We..."
Since we have entered the same Dharma-nature, why is it that the Tathāgata delivers us by means of the Hīnayāna?
This is our own fault, not the World-Honored One’s.
Whether sitting or walking in the places of reflection among the mountains, forests, and beneath trees, our manner of contemplation has always been inferior.
If one dwells in mountain forests with a mind attached to the Lesser Vehicle, one will not hear the Dharma;
therefore, there is no joy of speech for those who enter the same Dharma-nature as Bodhisattvas—meaning those who together enter the correct path.

This fault of clinging to the Lesser Vehicle arises because they do not know that beyond the Dharma-nature of the Hīnayāna, there exists a further sublime principle which the Bodhisattvas have attained. Since they cling [to the Lesser Vehicle]...

When one enters into the single principle, one may doubt that the three teachings can serve as its gateway; when seeing the Buddha bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon a bodhisattva, one may doubt that the Buddha is partial and thus incur fault.
To say, "This is our own fault, arising from our delusion regarding the provisional [teachings]; how could it concern any partiality on the Buddha's part?
and to recount past errors while looking up with gratitude to the Tathāgata—this is precisely what is meant by "drawing forth one’s faults and returning to take refuge. △ Third, the Clarification.
In the past, our minds did not understand, which constitutes a failure of our resolve.
Why is this? If we had waited for [the Buddha] to explain the causes by which he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, we would certainly have been delivered and liberated by means of the Mahāyāna.
However, we did not understand his skillful means (*upāya*) employed according to what was appropriate.
"World-Honored One, regarding what has been taught, when I first heard the Buddha-dharma, I immediately believed and accepted it, reflecting upon it and seeking realization.
From the past until now, throughout both day and night, I have constantly reproached myself:
it was truly because I did not wait for the causes to be explained that I lacked genuine understanding; and because I did not recognize skillful means, I lacked expedient wisdom."
Because there is no "understanding" due to the absence of [a self], there is no mental joy. Since past losses have already been revealed, present gains manifest of themselves.
Regarding the two meanings of "waiting for an explanation of the cause": first, one does not accept the waiting-for-opposition; second, one does not abide in the waiting-for-subsequent.
First, the *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that the wisdom of the three truths is the cause for attaining Buddhahood; because this waits for opposition from me, I do not accept it.
This constitutes a loss in the former sense: among the teachings of all Buddhas, after a long time, one must necessarily proclaim the true self;

if one does not wait for this but hastily takes up the Lesser Vehicle, this is a loss in the latter sense. If one waits for this [teaching], then in both the former and latter stages, one will surely attain liberation through the Mahāyāna.
△ Third, the conclusion establishing the three joys, in two parts: first, the conclusion.
Now, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma never before heard, all doubts and regrets have been severed;
body and mind are at ease, and we have attained swift peace and security.
From the Buddha comes the joy of the body through this bond, the joy of the mouth through hearing this Dharma, and the joy of the mind through the severing of doubt. △
Next, the accomplishment [of the body]:
"Today I finally know that I am truly a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by birth from the Dharma, and having obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma.

Truly a son of the Buddha, I have realized the fulfillment of the Buddha’s meaning. This concludes the accomplishment of the body. "Born from the Buddha’s mouth" concludes the accomplishment of the mouth.

They are also born from the transformation of the Dharma, formed through the concentration of the mind. △ Second, the verse summary has three parts; first, the verse summarizes the proclamation of the three joys.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
Having heard this sound of the Dharma, I have attained what I never had before; my heart harbors great joy, and the net of doubt has been entirely removed.
△ Second, the verse commentary on the three types of joy, first: the joy of seeing the Buddha.
Since long ago I have been graced by the Buddha’s teaching and have not lost the Mahāyāna; the Buddha’s voice is most rare, for it can remove the afflictions of sentient beings.
Having already attained the exhaustion of outflows, hearing it further removes my sorrow and distress.

The prose section clarifies the loss of knowledge and vision, while the verse section clarifies that the Mahāyāna is not lost. The prose discusses the distant [cause] regarding the loss, whereas the verse discusses the immediate [cause] regarding the attainment;
thus, the texts manifest these points reciprocally. △ Second, the verse on not hearing the Dharma, in two parts:
first, the verse on not hearing because the upper body is distant.
Whether dwelling in mountain valleys or beneath forest trees, whether sitting or walking in meditation, I constantly contemplate this matter, sighing with deep self-reproach:
"How can we deceive ourselves? We too are sons of the Buddha, having entered together into the outflow-free Dharma;
yet we are unable to proclaim the unsurpassed path in the future—the golden body, the thirty-two marks, the ten powers, and the various liberations."

While sharing in the same Dharma, I have not attained these things—the eighty minor marks of excellence, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and other such merits—and thus I have lost them all.

When I am alone walking in meditation, I see the Buddha amidst the great assembly, his fame filling the ten directions and bringing vast benefit to sentient beings; reflecting on this, I think to myself that I have lost this advantage and have deceived myself.

This verse does not include the prediction regarding the loss of the Buddha’s merits: from the first of the thirty-two marks, the level soles of the feet, up to the final mark, the high and rounded crown of the head;

from the first of the ten powers, the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), up to the final power, the power of knowing the permanent eradication of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-samudghāta-jñānabala*);
and from the first of the eighty minor marks, the narrow and long fingernails, up to the mark on the chest.
The marks of the ten thousand characters and the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) are said to be "not shared" with the two vehicles.

Beginning from being naturally free of faults and culminating in the knowledge of events in the past, present, and future, they are characterized by non-attachment, non-obstruction, and wondrous bliss.

As for the golden color, the thirty-two marks, and so forth up to the eighteen unique qualities, these are all as explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation); the current text belongs to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), whereas the previous explanation was according to the Comparative Teaching (*bi*).
It can be seen that his inconceivable excellence is as described below in the section concerning Devadatta.
Day and night, I constantly contemplate this matter, wishing to ask the World-Honored One whether it is a failure or not;
for I have often seen the World-Honored One praise the various bodhisattvas, and thus I deliberate upon this matter day and night.
Now I hear the Buddha’s voice preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate; it is untainted and inconceivable, leading all beings to the site of enlightenment.
Regarding my constant contemplation day and night: is saṃsāra the night and nirvāṇa the day?
Is there nirvāṇa within saṃsāra, or is there nirvāṇa apart from saṃsāra? When awakening is attained, these two—
This verse dispels both doubts. 2. Verse on Not Hearing [the Teaching] Because of Entering the Dharma-nature:
"Originally I clung to false views as a teacher of the Brahmins; the World-Honored One, knowing my mind, uprooted my heterodoxy and preached Nirvana.
I completely eliminated all false views and attained realization within the Dharma of Emptiness. At that time, I thought to myself that I had reached extinction."

Wrong views are the attachment of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while entering into the *dharmatā* is the attachment of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Ordinary beings initially cling to wrong views;
for their sake, the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to uproot those wrong views.

Once the followers of the two vehicles have realized the Dharma of emptiness, each considers themselves to have attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, both ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles do not hear the Great [Vehicle].
This is also the vehicle of the Dharma-multiplication. ○ The Brahmins are the same as the Brāhmaṇas; their own lineage claims they were born from the mouth of Brahmā.
△ Third, the verse on attaining liberation of mind:
"Now he has realized for himself that this is not the true extinction; when he attains Buddhahood, he will be endowed with the thirty-two marks."
When the multitudes of devas, humans, yakṣas, nāgas, and spirits pay homage, it can then be said that [suffering] is eternally extinguished without remainder.
This is *nirvāṇa*, which is translated here as "extinction" (*mie*) or "crossing over" (*du*). The *nirvāṇa* previously realized was not the Great *Nirvāṇa*;
only when one attains Buddhahood and the fruits of retribution are exhausted and vanish does it truly bear the name of Mahāyāna *Nirvāṇa*.
When the Buddha was among the great assembly and said, "I shall become a Buddha," upon hearing such a sound of the Dharma, my doubts and regrets were entirely removed.
At first, when I heard what the Buddha had said, my heart was greatly startled with doubt: "Could it not be that a Māra has become a Buddha to disturb and confuse my mind?
But as the Buddha explained through various causes, analogies, and skillful words, my mind became as calm as the ocean; having heard this, the net of my doubts was severed.

Regarding the statement "I shall become a Buddha," this refers to the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means), which says: "I bestow a prediction upon such a person that they shall attain the Way of Buddhahood in a future life.

As for the phrase "having heard what the Buddha has said," etc., it refers to the initial hearing of the brief opening that reveals the One by means of the Three, which stirred their attachments and gave rise to doubt—doubting that the Buddha was a demon.
Now, one knows that the Buddha’s former explanations of causes and conditions and parables were all intended as provisional teachings (*upāya*) to establish the ultimate reality (*satya*).
Since Śākyamuni has already attained the state of reality, his mind is at peace and his doubts have been severed.
The Buddha said that in the past, immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa also dwelt in skillful means and all taught this Dharma;
the number of Buddhas in the present and future is likewise immeasurable, and they too expound such a Dharma through various skillful means.
"Now, the World-Honored One, from his birth, his renunciation, his attainment of the Way, and his turning of the wheel of Dharma, has likewise taught through skillful means.
The World-Honored One speaks the true Way; Pāpīyas could not have done this. Therefore, I am certain that this is not the Māra who has become a Buddha.
It was because I had fallen into a net of doubt that I thought this was the work of Māra."

The preceding prose section clarifies that [the realization] does not depend on external causes and does not involve the understanding of skillful means; this section clarifies that it does depend on causes and involves the understanding of skillful means.
Hearing that one shall become a Buddha is the cause; hearing that the paths of the five Buddhas are identical is the understanding of skillful means.
These are merely mutual explanations of two aspects. ○ *Pāpīyan* is the correct pronunciation of *Pāpiman*; this is translated as "Evil" (*Ē*).
Because one constantly harbors evil intentions, one accomplishes evil dharmas. △ Third, the conclusion in verse:
Hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice, profound, far-reaching, and most subtle, as he expounds the pure Dharma, my heart is filled with great joy;
doubt and regret are forever exhausted. Abiding in the midst of true wisdom, I am certain that I shall become a Buddha, revered by devas and humans.
He turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma to teach and transform all bodhisattvas.
The first one and a half verses conclude this section: the first three phrases conclude the joy of speech, and the latter three phrases conclude the joy of mind.
The next verse establishes [the conclusion]. △ Third, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and fulfillment, which has three parts: first, his past teaching of the Great [Vehicle].
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "I now declare before this great assembly of devas, humans, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas:
in the past, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, I have constantly taught and transformed you in the presence of twenty thousand koṭis of Buddhas.
You, too, have followed me through the long night to receive instruction. Because I have guided you by means of skillful expedients, you have been born within my Dharma."

In the preceding passage, Śāriputra personally recounted his attainment of awakening; now the Tathāgata describes how that understanding is not false. Regarding the "Unsurpassed Way," the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states:
"The unsurpassed body refers to the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*); the unsurpassed reception and maintenance refers to the fulfillment of self-benefit and benefiting others;
the unsurpassed life refers to view, precepts, and wisdom; and the unsurpassed [speech] refers to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)."
The unsurpassed in terms of contemplation refers to the six *pāramitās*. The unsurpassed in terms of liberation refers to the ability to destroy the two obstacles.

The unsurpassed in terms of practice refers to the noble practices (*ārya-caryā*) and the Brahma-practices (*brahma-caryā*). The *Śrī-mālā-sūtra* (Thirteenfold Ornament) states: "The path should be pure; impurity is not the path.
The path should be single-minded; manifold thoughts are not the path. The path should be contented; much desire is not the path. The path should be respectful..."
Respect is not the path; one should restrain the mind from pride. Heedlessness is not the path; one should illuminate it with clarity.
Self-concealment is not the path; one should cultivate continuity. Non-action is not the path; one should apply diligent effort. Laziness is not the path; one should awaken to it.
Delusion is not the path; one should transform it through instruction. Stinginess is not the path; one should draw near to virtuous friends.

Practicing evil and non-pathways—through various such [teachings] as these, the unsurpassed path is clarified; now, in this sutra, perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) is established as the unsurpassed path.
Whether partial or sequential, these are all discussed in other sutras.

Having followed me for a long night while receiving instruction, although they were once greatly transformed, they had not yet shattered the darkness of ignorance and delusion; because they received instruction from the Buddha within their own minds, it is called "long."
Even if one has not yet destroyed the afflictions of views and thoughts during the night and so forth, a single phrase heard becomes a seed of the cause;

once this seed is deposited within consciousness, it is never lost throughout eternal kalpas. Since even the perception of darkness in contrast to light is not erroneous, how much more so is true awakening—how could it possibly be false?
Therefore, by citing past teachings, he extensively describes that his vision of the Buddha was not in error. "By means of skillful expedients," and so forth, follows below.

Regarding the two directions of the meaning: first, because one was previously transformed by the Great [Vehicle] and now gives rise to great understanding, it is said that they are "guided to be born within my Dharma";

this belongs to the first instance of the general purport of the teaching. Second, if one were to avoid the evil realms through skillful means by being led by the Small [Vehicle], it is said that they are "guided to be born within my Dharma";
this belongs to the second instance of forgetting the Great and grasping the Small. △ Within the second [instance], forgetting...
"Take it as small.
Śāriputra, in the past I taught you to set your aspiration on the Buddha-way, yet now you have forgotten it all and instead claim for yourself that you have already attained nirvāṇa."
That you have now forgotten it all is what is meant by abandoning the Great Vehicle midway and practicing the Small;
this is called "forgetting it all midway. That you now claim to have already attained *nirvāṇa* is precisely what is meant by "forgetting it all now."
△ Third, now he returns to speak of the Great [Vehicle].
"I now wish to cause you to recall the path practiced according to your original vows;
therefore, for the sake of the śrāvakas, I shall preach this Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma*, which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas."

To cause them to recall their original vows is precisely to state that their attainment of understanding was not in vain. First, provisional teachings were bestowed to establish their intermediate minor virtues;
subsequently, the reality was revealed to fulfill their original vow and great aspiration. △ Fourth, the Buddha bestows predictions upon them.
Part One: The Prose Exposition. Ten sections. First: The Time Period.

"Śāriputra, in a future age, after immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas have passed—this section below is the bestowal of the prediction (vyākaraṇa)—if you attain great understanding and know for yourself that you shall become a Buddha, what need is there to wait for a prediction? There are four reasons for granting a prediction:

first, because in the past no prediction was given to those of the Two Vehicles; second, because now it is necessary to grant a prediction to them; third, because those of middling and lower capacities have not yet awakened [to this truth]; and fourth..."

[The purpose of] recording [this] is threefold: first, to encourage them; second, to establish a karmic connection for those who hear it; and third, to fulfill their original vows; therefore, they are recorded. ○ Miaole says: Question:
Since they have already received their predictions (vyākaraṇa), why must they still pass through further kalpas? Answer:

If the prediction were for bodhisattvas, it would generally be said that they have attained non-arising wisdom (anutpāda-jñāna) and so forth; however, since this prediction is for śrāvakas, it must be discussed in terms of kalpas and lands.
The place where a Buddha attains enlightenment must have the appropriate conditions and karmic affinity; these śrāvakas had never previously practiced the path to the Pure Land.
After receiving their predictions, they formed karmic connections with various beings, and because the capacities of those beings differed, the duration of the kalpas varied.

Furthermore, the reason why the times for these śrāvakas differ is that [the Buddha] accommodated what was suitable for each being according to the length of their respective capacities; thus, their karmic conditions were not equal from the beginning.
What is the distinction in their dwelling? △ Second, the cultivation of causes:
they made offerings to several thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, upheld the True Dharma, and fully perfected the path practiced by Bodhisattvas.
△ Third, attaining the fruit:
You shall become a Buddha named Flower Radiance (Puṣparāja) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

As for the name "Flower Radiance" (Huaguang), it refers to the wondrous Way of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. It originated with Dīpaṃkara, was transmitted by Prabhāsa, and was succeeded by Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Because these Buddhas extended their hands one after another in a continuous succession of light, Śāriputra received his prediction and was named Flower Radiance;
this was to illuminate this Way so that those with eyes might behold it together and follow its transformation. The authentic scripture refers to him as the Buddha Padmaprabha.
The meaning must be understood in both ways: some say he attained enlightenment upon seeing the rain of flowers and the emission of light;
others say it was because his country possessed flowers and fruits. Both contradict the authentic sutras and are therefore unworthy of adoption.

As for those who have received the Buddha’s prediction that they shall attain the fruit after kalpas, this demonstrates that when the myriad virtues are perfectly complete, one becomes a Buddha endowed with the ten titles. △ Four.
As for the land, the name of the country is Vimala (Free from Defilement). Its terrain is level and upright, pure, adorned, secure, and prosperous; gods and humans are numerous and flourishing.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli, with golden cords marking its boundaries at the intersections of the eight crossroads. Alongside each [road], there are...
The rows of trees made of the seven treasures are always in bloom and bear fruit.

The land is named "Free from Defilement" (*Vimalā*); this was established first as the name of the soil, indicating its lower characteristics. It is level, meaning it has no elevations or depressions;
it is upright, meaning it is neither biased nor slanted. To signify the excellence of the lower land, lapis lazuli is used, further clarifying its superior features through eightfold intersections.
As for "Dao" (the Way), according to the *Erya*, "eight thoroughfares" are called *chongqi*; it refers to four roads intersecting.
It is also said to refer to the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate points. △ Fifth, regarding the preaching of the Dharma:
The Tathāgata Padmaprabha likewise taught and transformed sentient beings by means of the Three Vehicles. Śāriputra, although when that Buddha appeared...
It is not that this is an evil age; rather, by virtue of his original vow, he teaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
Following the precedent of the present Śākyamuni, it is said, "In this [land] there is also a sūtra of the One Vehicle.

Although such a text does not exist here, since he has fulfilled his vow by teaching both the three and the one, these are taken as the primary and secondary aspects. The passage beginning with "Śāriputra" clarifies the intention behind teaching the Three Vehicles in this land.
Purity alone is the fulfillment; the threefold vow is both bestowal and relinquishment. Question: Where is this vow taught? Answer:
According to the *Mahākaruṇā-gaṇḍavyūha-sūtra*, Śāriputra practiced the bodhisattva path for sixty kalpas.

Once, when a brahmin begged for his eyes, Śāriputra spat upon them and stepped over them in anger, thereby regressing to the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). He then made a vow that on the day he attained Buddhahood, [the earth] would open up.
Because it pertains to the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, it is said, "by means of his original vows," and so forth.
△ Sixth, the name of the eon: Why is that eon named "Great Jewel Adornment"?
It is because within that land, bodhisattvas are regarded as the great jewels.
△ Seven: The Number of the Assembly.
Those bodhisattvas are immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, beyond the reach of calculation or analogy, and cannot be known except by the power of a Buddha’s wisdom.
When they wish to walk, precious flowers receive their feet. These bodhisattvas...

These are not bodhisattvas who have merely first resolved their minds; rather, they have long planted the roots of virtue, having purified their Brahma-conduct under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of buddhas.
They are constantly praised by all buddhas, always cultivate the wisdom of the buddhas, possess great supernormal powers, and are well-versed in the gateways of all dharmas.
They are upright and without guile, firm in their resolve and mindfulness—such bodhisattvas fill [this land].
Regarding that land:
△ Eighth, the lifespan.
Śāriputra, the lifespan of the Buddha Puṣparāja was twelve small kalpas, excluding the time when he was a prince and had not yet become a Buddha.
The people of that land have a lifespan of eight minor kalpas.
△ Ninth, the Stage of Succession:
After twelve minor kalpas have passed, the Tathāgata Padmaprabha confers the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi upon the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavati.
He bestowed the prediction of supreme enlightenment upon the bhikṣus, declaring:
"This Bodhisattva Sthiramati shall next become a Buddha named Puṣpadantapadavikrāmin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
his buddha-field shall likewise be such as this."
Because his resolve and mindfulness are firm and he well understands all dharma-gates, he is named "Firm-Filled Flower Feet-Settled.
The Sutra says: "Passing through the Lotus Realm, he arrives at that land. As for the bodhisattva practice, precious flowers receive his feet;
his dignified deportment is orderly and his Way-fragrance is rich and pervasive. Among those who follow his transformation, there are none who do not comply, whether they depart or remain."
To call this the "Practice of Peace and Bliss" is merely a failure to consult the original source text. △ Ten Stages of the Dharma’s Abiding:

Śāriputra, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Flower-Light, the True Dharma shall abide in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise abide in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Śāriputra, the True Dharma lasts for thirty-two small kalpas.

Regarding the term "small kalpa" (*antarakalpa*), it refers to the destruction of sentient beings by the three calamities—famine, disease, and warfare—or it simply denotes a duration of time as a "small kalpa," such as when it is said that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was preached for sixty small kalpas;
this does not mean that the external world is destroyed by the three calamities to constitute a small kalpa. △ Second, the verse summary (in two parts).
Regarding the first verse of the prose commentary, the attainment of the fruit is presented by way of anticipation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In a future age, Śāriputra shall become a Buddha, a Honored One of Universal Wisdom, whose name shall be Padmaprabha; he shall deliver immeasurable multitudes."
△ Second, the verse following the prose summarizes the causes of practice:
"Making offerings to countless Buddhas, fulfilling the bodhisattva practices, and attaining the qualities such as the ten powers, one realizes the unsurpassed path.

Regarding "the ten powers and so forth," these refer specifically to the fruit of Buddhahood, which is designated as "powers" (bala), whereas those attained at the initial stage [of the first bhūmi] are designated as "qualities" (guṇa).
Regarding the phrase "the virtues mentioned are equal," this does not refer merely to making offerings to the Buddha, but also includes the practice of purifying the Buddha-land;

alternatively, it may signify that by partially attaining the merit of the Ten Powers, one achieves the prediction of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*). △ Third, the names of the kalpas surpassed in the verses.
After the passage of immeasurable kalpas, there was a kalpa named Mahāratnavyūha.
△ Fourth, a verse on the purity of the land:
The world was named Vimalaviśuddha, free from all blemish and impurity; its ground was made of lapis lazuli, and its paths were demarcated by golden cords.
The trees of seven precious substances, variegated in color, are always laden with flowers, fruits, and seeds.
△ Fifth, the verse that transcends numerical categories:
The bodhisattvas in that land are always firm in their resolve and mindfulness, and they have all fully perfected the *pāramitā* of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Under countless Buddhas, he skillfully studied the Bodhisattva path.
"The perfection of supernormal powers" refers to the six supernormal powers and the six perfections. △ Sixth, a verse summarizing the teaching of the Dharma.
Such great beings as these were transformed by the Buddha Flower Light (*Puṣyarāja*).
△ Seventh, the verse on the transcendence of the lifespan:
When the Buddha was a prince, he abandoned his kingdom and worldly glory; in his very last body, he left the household life and attained the Way of Buddhahood.
The Buddha Flower-Light (Padmaprabha) shall dwell in the world for a lifespan of twelve minor kalpas, and the people of that land shall have a lifespan of eight minor kalpas.
△ Eighth, regarding the duration of the Dharma’s abiding:
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma (Saddharma) shall remain in the world for thirty-two minor kalpas, extensively delivering all sentient beings.
After the True Dharma has been extinguished, the Semblance Dharma shall last thirty-two [years].
△ Ninth, the offering to the relics:
the relics shall spread widely, and devas and humans shall all offer worship to them.
△ Second, the summary and praise:

All that was performed by the Buddha Padmaprabha was exactly like this; that Most Victorious One among two-legged holy beings is peerless and without equal—he is none other than your own self, and you should rejoice in this.

"Rejoicing within oneself" is the explanation for entering the initial stage of the Joyful Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). At the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), one is able to perform the Buddha-activities throughout a hundred Buddha-worlds;
at the second dwelling, it is double that amount. △ 5. The Fourfold Assembly’s Comprehension and Acceptance. Part One: The Long Discourse. Sub-part One:
The Scribe’s Account of the Assembly’s Joy.
At that time, the great assembly— the fourfold community of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as devas,
nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others—
seeing Śāriputra receive the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the presence of the Buddha, were filled with great joy in their hearts.
They were filled with immeasurable joy and exultation.
△ Second, the presentation of offerings:
Each person removed the upper garment they were wearing to offer it as an offering to the Buddha, Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā-deva-rāja, and the others.
Together with countless sons of gods, they also made offerings to the Buddha with celestial fine garments, celestial *mandārava* flowers, and *mahā-mandārava* flowers and so forth;
scattering these celestial garments while remaining suspended in mid-air, they whirled about themselves.
Hundreds of thousands of kinds of celestial music were performed simultaneously in the sky, raining down a multitude of celestial flowers.
"Each person shall take off their robes," etc.—this is a general instruction for the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings, as well as the two groups of renunciants.

Regarding the "upper robe" (*uttarāsaṅga*), it refers specifically to the *saṃghāṭī*. If one were to discuss the three robes (*tricīvara*) collectively, they must not be discarded, because in the Western [Indian] method, practitioners generally possess only these three robes.
However, when speaking of them in a general sense to include laypeople as well, turning them over oneself signifies that one has heard [the teaching].
When Śāriputra received his prediction, the Dharma-nature spontaneously transformed; cause and effect, the environment and its inhabitants, self and others—all were transformed.
Among these, the fact that the garments and offerings provided by the various devas were transformed into music in mid-air and that he attained understanding is according to the authentic sutras;
however, this wondrous transformation is actually the result of the resonance of his sincere dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
△ III. Correctly Understanding and Accepting the Teaching, Part Two:
First, accepting the opening of the provisional means, he spoke these words: "In the past, the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī.
△ Second, accepting the revelation of the ultimate reality.
Now, once again, you turn the unsurpassed and greatest wheel of Dharma.
This "greatest wheel of Dharma" refers to this very sutra, the most perfect among the perfect, which possesses the fourfold excellence of principle, teaching, practice, and person;
or the tenfold excellence of the realms and wisdom, and so forth; or the threefold excellence of the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—the wondrous Dharma.

This wheel is named the Wondrous Wheel of Dharma. △ Second, the verses in praise [of the preceding], which consist of two parts; first, the verses praising the opening of the provisional to reveal the real.
At that time, the various devaputras, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
In the past, at Vārāṇasī, you turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, analyzing and explaining the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates;
now, once again, you turn this most wondrous, unsurpassed, great wheel of the Dharma—a teaching so profound and subtle that few are able to believe it.
The Four Truths are explained as previously [in the *Āgamas*]. Regarding the "five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha*), this refers to the five *skandhas*.

The statement "formerly at Vārāṇasī, etc. refers to the teaching of the *Tripitaka* (the *Āgama* teachings). The statement "now again turning the most wondrous [Dharma], etc. refers to the teaching of the Perfect (*Vipula*) Dharma.

Because the *Lotus Sūtra* reveals and clarifies the relationship between the *Tripitaka* and the Perfect, it does not describe the intermediate stages of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā. △ Second, the description of attaining understanding.
We rejoice in this dedication.
From time immemorial, we have repeatedly heard the World-Honored One preach such profound, wondrous, and supreme Dharma as we have never heard before;
that the World-Honored One has preached this Dharma, we all rejoice in. Now, the one of great wisdom, Śāriputra, has received the honorable prediction.
We, too, shall likewise surely attain Buddhahood; we shall become the most honored and unsurpassed among all worlds.

The Buddha-way is inconceivable, and he teaches through skillful means according to what is appropriate. Whatever meritorious deeds we possess—whether of this life or past lives—and whatever merit we have gained from seeing the Buddha, we dedicate it all toward the Buddha-way.
The first line is a self-statement; the next two and a half lines express sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); and the final line is a dedication of merit.
"We also are likewise" refers to Śāriputra’s realization of understanding, his being affirmed by the Buddha, and his receiving of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
Question: Since even the great *śrāvakas* such as Kāśyapa and Subhūti have not yet attained liberation, how could the fourfold assembly [do so]?

Among humans, those who first attained awakening answered the fourfold assembly and the devas; they also possessed three grades of faculties, with those of superior capacity being equal to Śāriputra, while those of middling and inferior capacity may be known accordingly.

Furthermore, it is understood that both Śāriputra and Kāśyapa were manifestations of expedient practice; because their middling and inferior understandings had not yet been opened, Kāśyapa and Pūrṇa appeared as if they did not understand.
As the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says: "As long as sentient beings have not been healed, the Bodhisattva likewise [does not rest]."

"Unhealed," and so forth. △ Two chapters and a half constitute the parables for those of medium capacity. This section has four parts: 1. The first half-chapter provides the primary parable to reveal the truth; 2.
The "Faith and Understanding" chapter describes how those of medium capacity attain realization; 3. The "Herbs" chapter records the Tathāgata’s confirmation; 4.
The "Bestowal of Prophecy" chapter grants the prophecy to the great assembly. Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, the request; third, the initial narration.
"I have no further doubt.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I now have no more doubt or regret;
I have personally received from the presence of the Buddha the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

From here on, for the sake of those of middle capacity, there are four chapters that provide explanations through parables. This current chapter is precisely the "Parable" chapter, which opens up the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle;
the "Faith and Understanding" chapter clarifies how those of middle capacity attain understanding; the "Medicinal Herbs" chapter clarifies the Tathāgata’s confirmation and bestowal of predictions;
and the "Bestowal of Predictions" chapter clarifies the conferring of those predictions. These four sections all rely upon parables; this constitutes the completion of the "Parable" section.
The following four sections all explain, by means of causes and conditions, how Cienru (Kaundinya) attained understanding upon receiving the entrustment of the pearl;

they further cite the case of King Kongwang (Gaganarāja) obtaining a prediction, and provide an analogy for the Dharma-exposition that there should have been the joyful response of the fourfold assembly of middle-capacity practitioners, yet none is present here.

First, this is because the compiler of the sutra has omitted details; second, the pattern can be understood from preceding and succeeding passages; the subsequent text appears in the "Dharmabhāṇaka" chapter.
The middle section may be understood according to the text as it stands. △ Second, describing that others have afflictions:

These twelve hundred who have attained mastery over their minds formerly dwelt on the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), and the Buddha constantly taught them, saying, "My Dharma can bring about liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death, culminating in ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
These individuals, both those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), each likewise considered themselves to have already attained [liberation].

Those who held views of selfhood and views of existence or non-existence, thinking they had attained *nirvāṇa*, have now fallen into doubt and confusion upon hearing before the World-Honored One what they have never heard before.
The Buddha constantly teaches those of inferior capacity; "self-view" refers to the ignorance that fails to understand the aggregates (*skandhas*).

Regarding those who falsely conceptualize within the dharmas such as the sense bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) that there is a self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*), and who hold views of existence or non-existence—the view of existence being the eternalist view (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of non-existence being the nihilist view (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*)—and so forth, including views of both existence and non-existence:

the "now" below refers to the adherence to a single principle from the past. Previously, it was taught that the three [vehicles] were ultimate; now, furthermore, it is taught that the One is the true reality. Previously...

Third, because the current [teaching] and the previous [teachings] are as contradictory as a spear and a shield, leading to confusion, it is said that "all fall into doubt. ○ *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) says:
"Hearing what has never been heard before" refers to the four sections concerning Śāriputra within the *Fashuo* (Exposition of the Dharma), which were not present in the former teachings.
△ Third, universally for the fourfold assembly.
"Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be freed from doubt and regret.
These 'causes and conditions' refer to the causes and conditions of the three preceding [Buddhas] and the one subsequent [Buddha]. The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states:

"This refers to the fundamental origins from beginning to end regarding the three preceding and the one subsequent; therefore, it is called 'causes and conditions. The first four chapters on the Buddhas provide a brief explanation, while the chapter on Śākyamuni is somewhat more detailed."

Although Guang used the five turbidities to explain the beginning and end of the provisional [teaching], its full scope remained unclear; thus, those of medium capacity were not yet enlightened by this.

Therefore, the parable is explained in detail to clarify the characteristics of saṃsāra, to fully enumerate the reasons for the three carts leaving the house, and to simultaneously reveal the intent behind seeking three and then one.
By extensively describing the equal bestowal upon all sons and the equal mind toward them, this finally fulfills [the purpose].
This was at the request of the causal conditions. △ Second, the response, which has two parts: first, the initiation; second, the suppression intended to incite indignation and valor.

At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "Did I not previously say that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, through various causes, conditions, parables, and skillful means of speech, teach the Dharma all for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
All that has been taught is for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas.

Did I not previously state that "the lower pointing to the upper" refers to the opening of provisional means (*upāya*)—all for the sake of *bodhi*—and "pointing to the upper to reveal the real" refers to the manifestation of the ultimate truth—all for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas?
Whether provisional or real, all enter the path of the Buddha; since this has already been clearly stated, why do you persist in your attachment?
To instruct those who are deluded and ignorant by reproaching them in this manner is actually to suppress them so as to incite their indignation and courage.
△ Second, leading them to advance swiftly:
"However, Śāriputra, you should now further clarify this meaning through a parable; for those who possess wisdom rely upon parables [to understand]."
An analogy is used to facilitate understanding.
Having previously employed such urgent refutations to draw [the disciples] in and comfort them, there was fear that they might feel contemptuous and sink into despair;

thus, the permission to use analogies is granted to further clarify this meaning. If one can understand this, it may still be called "wisdom. △ Second, the analogies, in two parts: first, the prose section.
The first part of the two verses has two sections: first, the opening of the analogy; second, the application of the analogy. The first of these [the opening of the analogy] also has two parts:
first, the general analogy for the six [qualities]; first, the analogy of the elder, which has three parts: first, name and conduct.
Śāriputra, regarding kingdoms, cities, towns, and villages:

"kingdom" refers to that which is named after its ruler yet acts as if it were the subject; "city" refers to that which has names both near and far, and thus cites the location to clarify the name and the conduct.
A "kingdom" (rājya) is the most distant boundary; a "city" (nagara) is the central seat of governance; and a "village" (grāma) is [the settlement].

In the neighboring villages, there is an elder whose reputation for conduct extends throughout these three places. Though one does not see his minute failings when near him, from afar one merely admires his lofty character.

His speech is free of words that should be censured; his conduct is free of actions that should be censured; and his mind is free of thoughts that should be censured. His name and his conduct correspond perfectly; he is a true great man.
Now, let us take the Land of True Reward as the capital and the Land of Expedient Means as the neighboring village; they are analogous in this way.
The dwelling land constitutes the internal assembly where the Tathāgata’s three karmas accord with the movement of wisdom;
within these three lands, he bestows transformation according to the capacities of beings, such that his fame is universally heard and his virtue pervades the Dharma-realm. △ Second, the titles.
There is a great elder.
An elder is like a worldly elder who is endowed with ten virtues: first, noble lineage; second, high status; third, great wealth;
fourth, majestic power; fifth, profound wisdom; sixth, advanced age; seventh, pure conduct; eighth, complete etiquette; ninth, [superiority]...

In terms of reverence, they were descendants of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors; in terms of lineage, they belonged to families that adorned their headdresses with pheasant feathers on the left and right.

In terms of rank, they served as counselors, regents, prime ministers, stewards, and directors. In terms of wealth, they possessed copper hills and golden valleys, abounding in luxury and extravagance.

In terms of authority, they were as stern as frost, achieving results through gravity without the need for formal severity. In terms of wisdom, their minds were like armories, containing weapons of extraordinary and transcendent skill.
In his advanced years, he was hoary-headed and dignified, a figure before whom all things bowed; in his conduct, he was as flawless as white jade, acting exactly as he spoke.
In matters of ritual, he observed every degree of propriety with such decorum that he became a model for the world to gaze upon. Above, he was revered by the Sovereign;
below, he was the refuge of the four seas. Possessing these ten virtues, he was known as a Great Elder (Mahā-śreṣṭhin), a transcendent elder indeed.
The Tathāgata’s lineage is born from the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) throughout the three periods of time;

his rank is one in whom merit is perfected and the Way is manifest; his ten bodies are infinite; his wealth consists of the Dharma-treasures and all myriad virtues, which he possesses in full measure; his majesty is the fierce power of the ten strengths that subdues Māras and externalists;
his wisdom is the single mind and threefold knowledge, through which nothing is not thoroughly penetrated; and his years were those in which he attained realization early.
The Perfectly Awakened One has been thus for a vast eon; his three karmas move in accordance with wisdom without error.
In his deportment, he is fully endowed with the majestic bearing of a Buddha. Above, he is praised by the awakened ones of the ten directions;
below, those of the seven stages of expedient means come to rely upon him. This is called the World-transcending Buddha, the Great Elder, namely Śākyamuni.
He is the sole master of transformation. △ Third, his virtuous deeds:
His age was advanced and his wealth immeasurable; he possessed many fields, houses, and various servants.

Being of advanced years, he was profoundly versed in both the present and the past—this is like the Buddha’s wisdom-virtue. His physical decline and maturity of character were like the ripening of his faculties and resolve.
The Buddha’s wealth of severed defilements (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) is immeasurable; this serves as a general metaphor for his myriad virtues. Fields and houses are specific metaphors:

fields can nourish life, which is analogous to how meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) provides the sustenance for *prajñā*; houses provide a place for the body to dwell, which is analogous to how the true realm (*bhūtadhātu*) serves as the abode for true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
If one discusses his merit and virtue, there is no practice he has not cultivated; if one discusses his wisdom, there is no object he does not illumine.
Therefore it is said that he possesses many fields and houses, as well as servants and attendants; these are metaphors for his complete mastery of skillful means and insight.
By harmonizing his light within the six realms and responding flexibly to the myriad needs of sentient beings, he acts as the servant of true wisdom.
△ Second, the analogy of the house.
"The house is vast" is the analogy for the aforementioned security; "insecurity" is an analogy for the three realms (*tridhātu*), wherein sentient beings [dwell].
The multitudes all dwell within the triple world; the Tathāgata, through his responsive transformations, governs and makes it his home. Therefore, it is said to be "vast and great.
△ 3. The Parable of the Single Gate:
There is only one gate.

The "one gate" (*ekadvāra*) is a metaphor for the gate of proclaiming the Buddha-way above; the principle of the Buddha-way is one, serving as that which is elucidated by the teaching, and the teaching serves as the gate.
As the text says: "By means of the gate of the Buddha's teaching, one exits the suffering of the triple world and attains the realization of *nirvāṇa*.
This gate has two aspects: the gate of a house and the gate of a chariot. The "house" refers to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), while the "gate" refers to the essential path of exit.
This is the explanation of the teaching of skillful means (*upāya*). "Vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to the Mahāyāna Dharma; "gate" (*mukha*) refers to the explanation of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*).
Although the Great and Small Vehicles are similar in this regard, one must distinguish between the subject and object. There are two types of subjects: the provisional and the real.

If one recognizes these two subjects, then the objects corresponding to them are present. If one recognizes the real object, then both the provisional subject and its corresponding object become the real subject and object. △ Four.
The analogy of the five hundred people:
a great multitude of people, numbering one hundred, two hundred, or even up to five hundred, reside therein.
The five hundred people represent the sentient beings of the five upper realms. △ Fifth, the analogy of the fire breaking out, part two: first, the emergence of the source.
The simile of the burning house represents the retributive fruits of the six realms.
The hall and pavilion are dilapidated, the walls have collapsed, the bases of the pillars are rotten, and the beams and rafters are leaning precariously.
The hall represents the desire realm and the pavilion represents the form and formless realms; because all three realms are impermanent, they are described as "dilapidated walls."

The walls are like the four great elements; their crumbling represents decline and loss. The pillars and foundations represent life; their rot represents peril and the fact that it will not last long.

The beams and rafters represent the mental consciousness; their tilting and danger represent the ceaseless flux of change. This explanation applies universally to both one's own and others' experiences within the three realms, and thus pertains to objective phenomena (*vastu*).
If, however, one explains this by applying it to the contemplation of one's own body, the hall represents the lower part of the body.
The pavilion represents the upper parts of the body, such as the head; the walls represent the skin and flesh; their collapse represents decrepitude;
the rottenness of the pillar-base represents impermanence; the beams and rafters represent the backbone; and their tilting and peril represent the end of life.
△ Second, the fire that burns it illustrates the eight sufferings and the five turbidities.
Simultaneously, fire suddenly breaks out on all sides, burning down the house and its dwellings.

Because the eight sufferings pervade the four elements and the four modes of birth, it is said they "surround" [it]. Because all are equally impermanent, it is said they arise "simultaneously and suddenly.
This is a metaphor for that which was originally non-existent now existing; originally there was no such suffering, yet through ignorance it comes to be. △ Six.
The Parable of the Thirty Sons:
Just as the many sons of an elder—whether ten, twenty, or up to thirty—are within this house;

this illustrates that when one knows the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings, and their past cultivation of the Buddha-dharma and innate nature are mutually related, the meaning of "sons" is established.

Because their sexual natures differ, there are thirty; if ten are the sons of the Bodhisattvas and twenty are the sons of the Two Vehicles, these capacities are all able to escape from the house, and are thus called "sons.

Those lacking this capacity are the five hundred people who all say "ten," because they all possess the nature of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*); it is said that they merely lack [the realization] while possessing the nature of wisdom within.

It is simply the nature of knowledge as it truly is. △ Second, the four distinct analogies: first, the analogy of the elder seeing the fire; second, the analogy of abandoning the stools and using the carts;
third, the analogy of equally bestowing the great carts; fourth, the analogy of the elder not being false. In the first section, there are again four parts; first, clarifying the ability to see.
The elder sees this.
The phrase "stands out" serves as an analogy for my own act of beholding with the Buddha-eye. △ Second, explaining what is seen:
"This great fire breaks out from the four sides."
The description of what is seen illustrates the sentient beings of the six realms who are observed; the great fire represents the three realms, the five turbidities, and the eight sufferings;
the four sides represent the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena (*kāya*, *vedanā*, *citta*, *dharma*). These—the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena—are the four sides of the house:

the body gives rise to the inversion of purity, sensations give rise to the inversion of pleasure, the mind gives rise to the inversion of permanence, and phenomena give rise to the inversion of self.

Due to these four inversions, there arise birth, old age, sickness, death, separation from the beloved, union with the hated, failure to obtain what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates, which are like a great fire breaking out from all four sides.
If one knows that the body is impure, that this suffering is felt by the mind, and that phenomena are impermanent and without self, then the fire of afflictions will be extinguished.
Furthermore, according to the subsequent passage, [it concerns] birth and old age...
Sickness and death constitute its four sides. △ Third, the manifestation of terror:
he is seized with great alarm and fear, and thinks to himself, "Although I am able to emerge safely from this burning gate..."
The preceding analogy refers to the arousal of the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for the sake of these sentient beings.
"Greatly startled and terrified" means that one is mindful of their falling back from the Great [Vehicle] and deeply concerned that they will give rise to grave evils;

thus, "startled" corresponds to loving-kindness (*maitrī*), being mindful of their lack of happiness, while "terrified" corresponds to compassion (*karuṇā*), being concerned about their suffering. "Although I am inferior" is the explanation that establishes this compassion.

Although the meaning of "fear" (*bhaya*) is not yet fully exhausted here, it clarifies that the Buddha, by the power of his wisdom, is able to seek out the true teachings and perceive the truths they expound;
thus, he is not endangered by the five turbidities or the eight sufferings, and is therefore called "peaceful" (*kṣema*).

He is not moved by the violent winds of the four inversions, and is therefore called "stable" (*yogakṣema*). He is far removed from all burdens and external entanglements, and is therefore called "transcendent" (*niḥsaraṇa*). Yet sentient beings do not...
"You are being burned by fire," yet the Tathāgata, out of his great compassion, is likewise burned by the fire of anxiety;
therefore he says, "Although I am equal [to you]," and so forth. △ Fourth, expanding upon what was previously seen:
the sons, however, within that burning house, were attached to and delighted in their play; they did not perceive, did not know, and felt neither alarm nor fear.
When fire comes and presses upon the body, causing pain that cuts to the very core, the mind feels no aversion and has no desire to escape.
To be immersed in the five sensory objects is called "sporting in emptiness"; to gain nothing thereby is called "playing in emptiness.

One merely dies in vain without ever developing weary detachment, just like a child playing who never says, "There is fire here. This is called being neither aware of nor understanding that fire is a phenomenon of heat.
It is said that one who does not know fire does not fear it can harm the body, while one who is not startled or concerned by fire does not dread it because it can sever life.
This is used as a metaphor for sentient beings who are entirely unaware of the five aggregates and the eight sufferings, and do not recognize the four inversions or the three poisons.
Since they do not perceive these delusions, how could they feel anxiety or concern? Yet when delusions invade the Dharma-body and wound the life of wisdom, such is the case. Thus...

To be awakened to suffering while remaining ignorant of its origin, to feel no alarm at losing the Path, and to feel no dread at losing Cessation—these are the five consciousnesses that oppress the body.
The body is oppressed by the eight types of suffering; when turbidity resides within the five consciousnesses, it is called "oppression" because it cuts into one's very self.
This is because each and every suffering arises from the five consciousnesses as they engage with their respective objects. As for "the mind not being weary or distressed," this refers to the mind.
This refers to the sovereign mind-king of the *manovijñāna* (consciousness). It does not loathe the suffering of impermanence, nor is it troubled by the accumulation of afflictions (*kleśa*).
One who lacks the intent to seek liberation does not cultivate the Path to seek cessation. △ Second, the analogy of discarding the stool and using the carriage, in two parts.
First, the analogy of discarding the stool, in two parts. First, the gate of exhortation regarding the provisional suitability, in three parts. First, the provisional suitability.
Śāriputra, this elder thought to himself: "My own hands and body possess strength;
I shall carry him out from the house using my lap or a small table.

This is analogous to the aforementioned contemplation of employing great transformation during the twenty-one days of reflection. In the phrase "my hands and body possess strength," the body is used as a metaphor.

The supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) that bear the burden are likened to the hands; wisdom (*prajñā*) is the uprooting, and by relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one possesses the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), which gives rise to the supernatural powers.
By relying on wisdom, one possesses the virtue of knowledge (*jñāna-guṇa*), which gives rise to the preaching of the Dharma. Regarding the "garment-bag" (*yīkè*) and the "writing desk":
the Tripiṭaka Master says that the garment-bag is a vessel from foreign lands used for holding flowers; it was employed to store offerings presented to nobles, and is now being taken here.

The combined analogy states: "If I were to praise the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana-bala*) and his powers of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) using only the power of my supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi-bala*) and the power of my wisdom (*prajñā-bala*), sentient beings would not be able to attain liberation through them. The power of supernatural faculties is like the body;

the power of wisdom is like the hand—as explained above. The power of knowledge and vision is like a basket (*kośaka*); the powers of fearlessness are like the fingers; and the ten powers (*daśabala*) are like the table."
The Tathāgata employs supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to initiate these three dharmas and employs wisdom (*prajñā*) to proclaim these three dharmas.

When there is no receptive capacity (*bhājana*), the transformation is ceased; this should be understood as follows: "Knowledge and vision" (*jñānadarśana*) is like a basket—its name is brief, but its meaning is profound.

The "four fearlessnesses" (*vaiśāradya*) are like a small table; regarding the Dharma, they are somewhat broad. The "ten powers" (*daśabala*) are like a desk; regarding the Dharma, they are extensive. The Buddha contemplated for twenty-one days, desiring...
Having thus explained the Dharma of the Buddha both extensively and concisely, [the father realized] that sentient beings were unable to bear it;
therefore, he spoke of "garments, baskets, small tables, and desks. △ Second, the refusal to accept.
He further reflected: "This house has but a single door, and it is moreover narrow and small; my children are young and immature."
The objects of cognition are places of attachment and play.
It is like those superior sentient beings whose faculties are dull; how can they be delivered? There is only one gate (*dvāra*). The meaning of the "gate" is as explained above;
now it is further clarified in terms of the general and the specific. As for the specific: "one" refers to the single principle, the single path, the gate of purity.
This refers to the correct teaching (saddharma) which pervades all that is to be taught; because its principles and doctrines are vast and expansive, they are not narrow or limited.

Beings who cling to the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism, as well as those at the seven stages of the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), are unable to personally penetrate these principles and teachings through their own power. It is because they are said to lack the capacity for such realization that [the teaching] is described as "narrow.

As for "pervading" (*tong*): because the principle is pure and without admixture, it is called "one"; because this principle can lead one through to liberation, it is called a "gate" (*mukha*); and because it is subtle, it is called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*).

Because it is subtle and difficult to know, they are called "narrow-minded and immature. Having been taught the unsurpassed path of the Mahāyāna by twenty thousand Buddhas, yet having weak roots of goodness, they are termed "immature.
If, upon hearing the Mahāyāna, they are able to give rise to slander and revilement, they are said to be "those who have not yet attained true understanding" and are "attached to places of play.
What was previously clarified was the weakness of good; what is clarified here is the strength of evil—this refers to the time of the cause.
Because they are deeply attached to the fruits of views and craving, they are deeply attached to the "reliance" (the body) and the "corrected" (the environment) in the desire realm;

they are attached to the six sense objects in the form realm; and they are attached to the flavor of meditative absorption in the formless realm. Therefore, the preceding passage states: "The faculties of sentient beings are dull;
blinded by attachment to pleasure and ignorance, they are incapable of hearing the Mahāyāna. △ Third, relinquishment.
Or they may fall and be consumed by fire.

This is a parable for relinquishing [the teaching] when there is no capacity for superior guidance and one ceases the transformation [of beings]; it means: "I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter nirvana.
There are two kinds of falling: first, falling because the immature remember their former places of play.
Second, because there is no consciousness at all and one clings to things as not being solid, one falls [into suffering]. This is like a young child remembering a former place of play;

it is analogous to being attached to the five desires and falling into the three miserable realms. Second, when one’s goodness is weak and lacks consciousness, one slanders the Mahāyāna and falls into the three miserable realms.
△ Second, the section on admonitions has three parts; first, the preliminary proposal.
"I shall speak to you of matters that cause fear: this house is already burning; you should emerge quickly and do not let yourselves be consumed by the fire.
Having formed this thought, he informed his sons of everything exactly as he had reflected, saying, "All of you, come out at once!"
Because one has already entered a place of play, the matter of fear is mentioned so that one may escape being burned by the fires of the five turbidities within the house of the five aggregates;
one ought to abandon it, hence it says, "one should quickly depart at this time. If one remains attached for long, one will surely sever one's roots of goodness;
thus it says, "do not let yourself be burned and harmed by the fire. △ Second, not accepting [the invitation].
Although the father, out of compassion, enticed them with kind words and gentle persuasion, the sons took pleasure in their play and refused to believe or accept his advice;
they felt neither alarm nor fear, having no intention at all of escaping, nor did they know what fire was,
what the house was, or what it meant to lose it.
Those who are neither startled nor terrified do not give rise to the wisdom of hearing because they are not startled, and do not give rise to the wisdom of reflection because they are not terrified.
They fail to recognize the eight sufferings and the five turbidities that can burn away their roots of goodness, just as one who does not recognize fire [ignores its danger].

They do not recognize the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, which are instruments of all suffering, just as one who does not recognize a house [ignores its collapse]. They do not know the cause for the loss of the Dharma-body, just as one who does not know how to mourn a loss [fails to grieve].
Knowing what constitutes a transgression, he abandons it. Third, as for "releasing and letting go":
he merely runs about playing to the east and west, looking only at his father;
turning his back to the light and facing the darkness, he moves swiftly between birth and death in the east and west, like one galloping within that state.
Seeing and craving are like a play; although one employs great [means] to correspond to them, because they do not follow the Great Teaching, it is said that he merely looks upon his father.
△ Second, the analogy of the chariots, in four parts: first, the analogy of the three carts corresponding to what is appropriate.
At that time, the elder had this thought: "This house has already been consumed by a great fire;
if I and my sons do not emerge immediately, we shall surely be burned to death. I must now devise a skillful means to enable my sons to escape this calamity."

This is like the previous contemplation on the past Buddhas, which also describes the manifestation of the Three Vehicles. The preceding statement that "suffering and pain are cutting to one's very core" refers to a state where one has not yet died;
the present statement that "one will certainly be consumed by fire" carries the sense of death. Question:
In the preceding passage, it was said that one safely emerges from the gate of what is being burned; why now is it said that if one does not emerge in time, one will certainly be consumed by fire?
Regarding the meaning: it should be understood that what was previously described as "emerging" refers to the emergence of the *dharmakāya*.
The present statement, "if it does not emerge at the proper time," and so forth, refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* manifesting as if it were subject to illness in common with sentient beings.

If sentient beings possess wholesome roots and their capacities are matured such that they are ready for transformation, then the *nirmāṇakāya* emerges at the proper time; if sentient beings have severed their wholesome roots and lack the capacity, they do not receive [the teaching].
"Transformation [bodies] do not appear at the same time as the response bodies; thus, they are both subject to being burned.
"I shall now employ skillful means" refers to the desire to establish the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles. △ Second, the analogy for what the mind previously preferred.
The father knew that each of his sons had their own inclinations and were certain to take pleasure in various rare treasures and extraordinary objects.
This is like when the aforementioned thought arose, and the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared, clearly manifesting that there was a way for those of the Hīnayāna to attain deliverance.
This is the pivotal opportunity. Because he previously practiced the "Lesser" [Vehicle], he knows his former mind;

furthermore, because he knew he had previously practiced the "Great" [Vehicle], he knows that within his former mind there was weariness with old age and death, and each name has its own preference. △ Third, the analogy of the rare Three Chariots, part one:
