the exhortation to turn [the wheel].
And he addressed them, saying: "These toys for your play are rare and difficult to obtain; if you do not take them now, you will surely feel regret later.
This praises the rarity of the three vehicles as a metaphor for the aforementioned bestowal of the three vehicles; having reflected upon this matter, they immediately proceeded [toward them].
Vārāṇasī. △ Second, the demonstration of the turning [of the wheel].
"These various kinds of sheep-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts are now outside the gate, where you may play. The sheep-cart is a metaphor for the Śrāvaka-yāna;
the deer-cart is a metaphor for the Pratyekabuddha-yāna; and the ox-cart is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva-yāna. As it is said:

The following text explains why [the practitioner] is currently outside the gate: it is because one is now permitted to be outside the gate, having severed the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and emerged from the three realms (*traidhātuka*), only then attaining [this state]. △ Third, the proof of transformation.
"You all should quickly come out from this burning house; whatever you desire, I shall give it to you.
To say "I shall give it to you" means that having personally realized it oneself, one causes others to realize it as well; therefore, it is called "giving.
△ Fourth, the analogy of fulfilling the sons' wishes.
At that time, the sons, having heard their father speak of the rare and precious playthings that accorded with their desires, each felt their hearts brimming with vigor;
they pushed and shoved one another, racing together in competition to be the first to flee from the burning house.

For example, receiving, practicing, and awakening to the realization [of the Dharma] is called "turning the wheel of the Dharma" and so forth. While the previous verse was brief in its essence, this analogy is extensive in its details;

it extensively clarifies that from the cultivation of causes to the attainment of the fruit, those whose aspirations accord with their capacities experience a correspondence between the teaching and the recipient—this is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

"Each mind is courageous and sharp" refers to the movement of thought and deliberation—this is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). "Mutually pushing and shoving" refers to... [the wisdom of cultivation].
The principle of the Four Noble Truths suppresses the delusions of views; when the correct and the false have not yet been decided, it is called "mutual competition.
This stage belongs to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) and corresponds to the levels of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit). "Competing" means competing to grasp the supreme truth:

initially, one contemplates the eight truths across the upper and lower realms through sixteen aspects, vying for the true path; subsequently, the contemplation is contracted until it reaches the truth of suffering within the desire realm.
The "dharma-patience regarding the suffering of the lower realms" refers to the stage of the Dharma-patience (kṣānti-dharma-avasthā).

It is called "shared" because it is common to the Stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma), as there is no distinction between its contemplation of the Truth of Suffering in the Desire Realm and that of the stage of Patience; hence, it is said to be shared.

It is called "rushing forward" because one enters the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) and swiftly perceives the principle within the fifteen moments of mind; thus, it is called rushing forward. Having severed the delusions of seeing (darśana-heya-kleśa), one partially attains Nirvāṇa.
The "platform" (pan) above immediately suggests the sound of *nirvāṇa*. "Vying to emerge" refers to the stage of practicing the Path.

To vyingly emerge from the triple world, achieve the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), and exhaust the afflictions of thought (*kleśa*) is precisely what it means to emerge from the burning house;

this corresponds to the aforementioned [platform] as well as the distinct names for the Dharma and Saṃgha of the Arhat. △ Third, the analogy of the equal bestowal of the great chariots, part four: first, the vision.
The Parable of the Son’s Deliverance from Peril:
At that time, the elder saw that his sons had all emerged safely; they were sitting on the open ground at the crossroads, free from all obstacles.
His mind was serene, and he leaped for joy with great exultation.
This is like the aforementioned "I" who then had this thought, up until the two lines and one verse of the gāthā:
"If the son has not yet escaped the hardship, the father is anxious; if he succeeds in leaving the fire, his mind becomes serene.
Because the son rejoices, the father also rejoices. The "four crossroads" is a metaphor for the Four Noble Truths; they are distinguished by means of the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.

It is called "the crossroads" because although the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*) have been eliminated, the delusions of conduct (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) still remain; thus it is not yet called "the open ground.
When the delusions of conduct within the three realms are exhausted, one is said to "abide in the fruit upon the open ground," for one no longer advances.

Because the delusions of view and conduct are exhausted and the principle of the True Truth (*satyārtha*) is manifested, it is said that "there are no further obstructions. Because one is no longer constrained by the delusions of view and conduct, it is said that one "arises in a state of ease (*tai-ran*)."
Because they have extinguished the notion of seeking peace and security, it is said that they are filled with joy. △ Second, the parable of the sons requesting vehicles from their father:

At that time, each of the sons addressed their father, saying, "Father, we pray that you will grant us at this time the playthings previously promised by you—the sheep-carts, the deer-carts, and the ox-carts."
This is like the two lines of verse concerning those of the Great Vehicle potential who have awakened their aspiration and, as sons of the Buddha, seek the Buddha-way.
Regarding this, the text explaining the "seeking of the carriage" lacks the character "seek" (suo); it is based on these words of petition that the "seeking of the carriage" is clarified.

There are three meanings to "seeking": first, "seeking by potential," which refers to the period after the realization of the Small Vehicle at the Deer Park, when one subsequently enters the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras) with a latent [aspiration].

First, the "seeking by means of the physical body" (*kō-soku*): being rebuked [by the Buddha], one does not slander the principle; having the desire to seek the Mahāyāna is called seeking by means of the physical body. Second, the "seeking by means of the emotional mind" (*jō-soku*):

reaching the *Prajñāpāramitā* assembly, one realizes and knows the joy of the Great Dharma, and the Great Mind arises. Even if one does not express it explicitly, the meaning of seeking becomes increasingly earnest;

this is called seeking by means of the emotional mind. Third, the "seeking by means of the oral expression" (*ku-soku*): coming to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one relies on the skillful means (*upāya*).
At the beginning of this chapter, having heard the Buddha’s brief exposition, all [the sons] declared it to be a "skillful means" (upāya), thereby moving their long-standing doubts;
thus they spoke three times in request, which is termed "seeking with the mouth. △ Third, the analogy of bestowing great carts upon the sons, which has three parts:
first, the general heading of two sections; second, "the sons are equal," etc.
"Śāriputra, at that time the elder bestowed [gifts] upon each of his sons.
This passage below is an analogy for how, among all bodhisattvas, he directly abandons expedient means and teaches only the unsurpassed path.
This clarifies that "the sons and others" are an analogy for all sentient beings who equally possess buddha-nature; this buddha-nature is the original, natural state.
Because they come together as one, they are equally sons. △ Second, "the carts are equal": this means that all are equal in being the Great Vehicle.
This clarifies that the carts are equal because they are equal in terms of the Dharma; thus, there is nothing that is not the Buddha-Dharma, serving as a metaphor for how all dharmas are *mahā*.
Because the *vaipulya* and the *mahāvaipulya* are identical, they are equal and thus constitute the "great chariot" (*mahāyāna*).

Yet, it is said that each is "bestowed" because each follows their own original practice—whether the Four Truths, the Six Perfections, or the immeasurable dharmas—and reveals the reality [of those practices]. Since these former habits differ, it is said that each receives [the vehicle];
and because all are the *mahāvaipulya*, it is called the "great chariot. △ Second, the extensive explanation of the chariots and so forth, in two parts: first, the extensive narration.
Regarding the substance [of the chariot], first is the description of its height and breadth:
that chariot is high and broad, adorned with various jewels, with railings surrounding it on all sides and bells suspended from them;
furthermore, canopies and awnings are spread above it, likewise embellished with rare and miscellaneous gems, and draped with precious cords interlaced together.
Floral tassels are layered profusely and the elegant mats are arranged with crimson pillows.

These are provisionally named "vehicles" and possess the characteristics of height and breadth; they are like the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, which extend horizontally to the very limits of the Dharma-realm and penetrate vertically to the source and bottom of the Three Truths.
Therefore, they are called "high and broad. Adorned with myriad jewels, they are likened to the ten thousand [virtues].
The practice of adorning the surrounding balustrades is like the *dhāraṇīs*, which uphold all myriad virtues and ward off all evils.

The bells suspended on all four sides are like the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), used to transform sentient beings below. The spreading of canopies and awnings is like the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*);
among all virtues, compassion is supreme, universally covering all. That it is adorned with various rare and precious jewels refers to—
The *Great Sutra of Compassion Adorned with True and Universal Goodness* states: "If compassion is fully endowed with the ten powers and the fearlessnesses, it is called the Tathāgata’s Compassion.
It is likened to being entwined by the jeweled cords of the four universal vows; it is likened to hanging the flower tassels of the firm and great compassionate mind;

and it is also likened to the exquisite garland of the seven factors of enlightenment, which gladden and move sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)."
Laying out a double-layered, supple mat is like practicing all the various *dhyānas* through refinement and cultivation;

layering them with softness and placing a vermilion pillow—whether the pillow is on the outside or the inside—is like a carriage: when the carriage is driven and moving, it requires this support to remain upright.
This is a metaphor for being still while moving and moving while still; such movement and stillness are precisely contained within the Ten Modes of Practice (*daśayāna*).

This is the meaning of "penetration and obstruction. If there is a pillow within the carriage, it serves to rest the body and head; this is an analogy for the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (one-practice samādhi), which brings rest to all wisdom and all practices.
Furthermore, "vermilion" (*dan*) refers to the color red, which is an analogy for the dharma of non-discrimination. △ Second, the explanation of the white ox.
The vehicle is drawn by white oxen, whose skin and color are pure and clean, whose physical forms are beautiful and excellent, and who possess great strength and vigor;
their gait is level and upright, and they move as swiftly as the wind.
That it is drawn by white oxen is a metaphor for the untainted *prajñā* (wisdom), which can guide one through the objects of the truths and bring all myriad practices to fulfillment.

Upon reaching *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), one realizes that this form (*rūpa*) is fundamentally identical to primordial purity and associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*). Its essence is endowed with the ten thousand virtues;
it is like skin being full, yet undefiled by afflictions (*kleśa*), and like color being pure. Furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are like white oxen;

within the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the two types of future good are fulfilled like skin being full, and the two types of future evil are exhausted like color being pure. These are the four.

The "satisfactions of mind" (*iddhipāda*) correspond to the practitioner’s heart being as beautiful as the physical form; the "faculties" (*indriya*) are like the sinews, in the sense that they provide the basis for the arising [of wholesome states].

The "powers" (*bala*) are like the limbs, in the sense of their function to crush and subdue [the defilements]. "Walking with even steps" is a metaphor for the equilibrium of concentration and wisdom;

it also represents the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) being harmoniously balanced. "Moving as swiftly as the wind" is a metaphor for the rapid progress within the practice of the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
One swiftly reaches *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). △ Third, the attendants:
Furthermore, he has many attendants who serve and protect him.
These attendants are a metaphor for the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means), which can adapt and follow others to provide service and carry out their commands.
Because all Māras, non-Buddhists, and those of the Two Vehicles with limited practice follow the functional application of expedient wisdom, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"They are all my attendants. Furthermore, the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) of the stage of fruition can be deployed at will; thus, they are indeed servants.
△ Second, explaining the reason for having a carriage.
Why is this? It is because this great elder possesses immeasurable wealth, and his various treasuries are all overflowing. The "chariot" refers to the movement [of practice];
the "overflowing of the treasury of wealth" is used as a metaphor for the perfection of the storehouses of merit and wisdom on the stage of fruition.

The "storehouse of practice" and the "storehouse of principle" consist of all dharmas tending toward generosity (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), and so forth; these tendencies do not exceed these categories, which is explained in terms of practice.
Regarding the Tathāgatagarbha as the destination of all phenomena—the aggregates, sense bases, elements, faculties, objects, and so forth—there is no phenomenon that does not reach this destination.

This is established from the perspective of principle (*li*). To practice this path through one's own cultivation according to this principle is called "filling" (*chong*); to transform others by means of this is called "overflowing" (*yi*).
△ Third, the extensive explanation of the mind and so forth, in two parts. First, the extensive explanation of the mind and so forth:
He then had this thought: "My wealth and possessions are boundless; it would not be right to give inferior, small carts to my children.
Now these young children are all my sons, and my love for them is without partiality. I possess such great carts made of the seven treasures."
Their number is immeasurable; one should regard them with an equal mind and bestow [the gifts] upon each individually, without making distinctions.
This clarifies that the mind is equal because the material wealth is inexhaustible and the sons are without partiality; therefore, the mind is equal.
If one were wealthy but not a son, or a son but poor, then the mind could not be equal. As for the seven-jeweled great chariots, their number is immeasurable.
"Measure" refers to how this present sutra reveals that both the teaching and the practice are entirely Mahāyāna;

furthermore, various distinct names such as Vaipulya, Prajñā, the Foundations of Mindfulness, the Right Efforts, the Faculties, the Powers, the Factors of Enlightenment, and the Path all reveal the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
This applies equally across all dharmas, and for this reason it is called "immeasurable. To say that each is "equal to it" means they do not deviate from it.

By practicing their respective disciplines, they manifest the true reality: as Śāriputra opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through wisdom and possessed all Buddha-dharmas, and Maudgalyāyana opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through meditative concentration, so it was for others as well;
because their minds were equal, there should be no distinction between them. △ Second, the explanation of the equality of mind.
The reason for this is that if these goods of mine were distributed throughout an entire kingdom, they would still not be exhausted;

how much less so for my sons? First, the explanation of the abundance of wealth: if it can suffice for an entire kingdom, how much more so for the sons? This is like a great round cause that pervades both good and evil;

how much more so the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? Next, the explanation of "the sons and others": if even those who are not sons are sufficiently provided for, how much more so those who are actually my sons?

It is like the Buddha, who, even for those with no karmic connection, still delivers them; how much more so for his own sons who possess such a connection! △ Fourth, the analogy of the sons’ joy upon obtaining the carts:
At that time, each of the sons mounted a great cart, attaining what they had never experienced before and which was not what they had originally hoped for.
This is like the Bodhisattvas above who, upon hearing this Dharma, have all cleared away the net of doubt.

Those of the Three Vehicles originally sought the carts of sheep, deer, and water buffalo, hoping only to escape the realm of segmented birth (*bhavāgra*). Now, having obtained the great white ox-cart that exhausts the realm of transformation (*pariṇāma-nirvāṇa*), they exceed their original expectations;
would they not rejoice? △ Fourth, the Parable of the Elder’s Non-emptiness (3): First, the Question.
"Rise, Śāriputra!
What do you think? Would that elder be guilty of any falsehood in giving these precious great chariots to his sons?"
Regarding the first [section], the Buddha’s initial question was originally intended only to grant three [years], yet now he grants one; this is not a falsehood.
Because he did not wish for Śāriputra to grasp at reality, he asked with what appeared to be a falsehood. △ Second, the response and explanation has two parts:
first, avoiding the difficulty by showing it is not false (also called "exchanging the heavy for the light" to show it is not false); third, the heading of the section.
Śāriputra said, "No, World-Honored One. This elder merely enabled his children to escape the disaster of the fire and preserve their lives;
it was not a falsehood.
△ Second, the explanation.
Why is this? If one preserves one’s entire life, it is as if one has already obtained objects of play and enjoyment.
To preserve one’s whole body and escape the fire is as if one has already obtained great treasures; that the heavy lives of one’s children have been saved—how could the gain not be real?
○ *Miaole* says: "To preserve the fivefold dharma-body of the Lesser Vehicle and enter the life of wisdom in emptiness is to have already obtained [the goal]."
If even what we have indulged in from time immemorial is thus, how much more so the Great Original [Teaching] for rescuing suffering through skillful means within the burning house!
△ Third, the conclusion by way of comparison: How much more so when one uses skillful means to pull others out and rescue them from that burning house!
Having escaped the fires of the eight sufferings and preserved the body of the five aggregates is already a great treasure;

how much more so when, at the abodes of twenty thousand Buddhas, the life-force of Mahāyāna wisdom was perfected, the causes were fulfilled, and the Buddha’s knowledge and vision were opened—how could this possibly be false?
△ Second, not contradicting the original mind and not being false (also titled "Exceeding what was originally hoped for and not being false"). First, the heading of the section.
World-Honored One, even if the elder had not given so much as the smallest single chariot, he would still not have been guilty of falsehood.
His initial declaration did not contradict his original intention; from the beginning, he knew there were no three [kinds of] carts, thereby ensuring that no one would slander him.
Since there was no slander, it did not contradict his original intention. II. Explanation.
Why is this? Because that elder previously formed this intention: "I shall cause my children to escape by means of skillful means.
For this reason, there is no falsehood.

Although he originally knew they were not small, he consented to [the idea of] small [vehicles] with the intent that they might escape from the burning house through skillful means. Since ancient times, it has been thus.
This would not contradict the Buddha’s original intention; since he did not give small carts, how could it be a falsehood? △ Third, the conclusion by way of comparison:
How much more so when the elder, knowing his own wealth to be immeasurable, desires to satisfy his children and gives them great chariots?
Because they have been given a great carriage that exceeds their original expectations, it is therefore not in vain. △ Third, the praise:
The Buddha told Śāriputra, "Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said."
Second, the two "Excellent! [expressions] describe his avoidance of calamity and do not contradict the two [points of] non-falsity.

Question: Why does the Buddha not himself state that it is not false? Answer: The Buddha permits three [others] to speak, whereas speaking for oneself is difficult; it is easy for Śāriputra to speak so as to gain the faith [of others] regarding its non-falsity.
△ Second, combining the parables, part one: first, combining the general parable, section six: first, combining the previous "Elder. Third.
The title of the initial stage of union is as follows:
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is also like this.
From here below, the union with the aforementioned elder—regarding his name, conduct, stages, titles, virtuous deeds, and so forth—the Tathāgata is also likewise.
First, regarding the combination of titles and names: the titles of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable virtues have already been briefly explained above by means of ten meanings.
Second, regarding the combination of name and practice:
he is thus the father of all worlds.
Regarding the phrase "all worlds" (*sarvaloka*) as the locus where [the Tathāgata] will dwell:

whereas the previous section spoke of "kingdoms, cities, towns, and villages," here it is simply stated as "all worlds" to universally indicate the three lands—the land of common dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), the land of expedient means (*upāya-kṣetra*), and the land of true retribution (*vipāka-kṣetra*).
All of these are places of the fruition-recompense of wondrous form and wondrous mind. The Tathāgata’s universal response throughout these three locations constitutes "all worlds."
He is the Father. △ Third, the unification of virtues and deeds:
He has forever exhausted all fears, decays, afflictions, anxieties, and the darkness of ignorance without remainder;

he has fully accomplished immeasurable knowledge and vision, the powers, and the fearlessnesses; he possesses great supernormal power as well as the power of wisdom, and is endowed with skillful means.

The perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) signifies the exhaustion of all fears and ignorance, which corresponds to the aforementioned "decline" and manifests the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

The accomplishment of immeasurable knowledge and vision corresponds to the aforementioned "advanced age" and manifests the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). The powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth correspond to the aforementioned "external virtues."
Immeasurable wealth and spiritual power refer to the profound cultivation of dhyāna-samādhi through which one attains supernatural faculties (abhijñā); this corresponds to the aforementioned field.
The power of wisdom refers to the intellect necessarily illuminating its objects, just as a body relies upon its dwelling place; this corresponds to the aforementioned house.
Being fully endowed with the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā) corresponds to the aforementioned various servants. △ Second, the correspondence with the five hundred people.
With great kindness and great compassion, he is ever free from weariness and constantly seeks virtuous deeds to benefit all beings.

Compassion is the foundation of transformative teaching; "all" refers to those in the five realms of existence who are perpetually enveloped by his compassion—this totals five hundred people. △ Third, the analogy of the house.
Thus they are born into the decaying and dilapidated fire-houses of the triple world;
this corresponds to the aforementioned vastness of the house. Fourth, the gathering of the thirty sons corresponds to the saving of sentient beings.
Sentient beings have karmic relatives who were previously counted as thirty children. △ Fifth, the conflagration of fire:
the fires of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; the darkness of ignorance and the fires of the three poisons.
The sudden ignition of fire upon closing [the vessel] is a metaphor. △ This concludes the first section of the six sections:
teaching and transforming others so that they may attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because the teaching can express the principle, and by seeking that principle one gives rise to practice and thereby attains bodhi, we know that the teaching and the principle function together;

this corresponds to the preceding metaphor of there being only a single gate. △ Second, combining the individual metaphors [into four]; first, combining the metaphor of seeing fire, which has four parts.
First, combining the eye that is able to see.
"Seeing.
This means that the eye capable of seeing when closed is precisely the Tathāgata’s eye of tranquil illumination, which is able to see.
△ Second, merging with the fire that is seen.
All sentient beings are scorched and boiled by birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction;
they undergo various kinds of suffering for the sake of the five desires and material gain, and because of their greedy attachment and pursuit, they experience manifold sufferings in the present,
followed by the sufferings of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts in the future, as well as poverty and distress when born among gods or humans.

The suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hated, and various other such sufferings—when combined with the fire seen arising from the four directions—these clarify the eight sufferings as fire. As the text states, the four sufferings are:
the suffering of attachment and pursuit, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and subsequently, the five [sufferings] in the hells, heavens, and human realms.

The flourishing of the aggregates (*skandha*), suffering, separation from the beloved, and meeting with the hated—as described in the text—these eight sufferings arise from the four sides of the four inversions (*viparyāsa*).
△ Third, combining the broad observations:
sentient beings are submerged within them, playing and sporting with joy, neither perceiving nor knowing, neither startled nor terrified, nor even [aware of it].

They give rise to weariness [with the world] but do not seek liberation; though they run hither and thither within this triple-world house on fire, even when encountering great suffering, they do not regard it as a calamity.

This corresponds to what was previously seen regarding the analogy of the fire: that the children neither perceive nor know [the danger], because they do not contemplate suffering or its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
Because they do not give rise to revulsion nor contemplate the Path or Cessation, they do not seek liberation; thus, even when encountering great suffering, they do not regard it as a calamity.
This corresponds to the aforementioned state where the mind does not feel revulsion or distress and lacks the intent to seek deliverance. △ Fourth, combining this with the arousal of fear.
Śāriputra, having seen this, the Buddha thought: "I am the father of sentient beings;
I should uproot their suffering and distress, and grant them the immeasurable and boundless joy of the Buddha's wisdom so that they may sport therein."
Combining the above: although I am able to emerge safely from this burning gate, my mind should also uproot their suffering and distress;
this is the power of Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) that uproots the sufferings of the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya).

To "bestow the immeasurable" is the power of Great Benevolence (mahāmaitrī) that grants them great bliss. △ Second, combining the analogies of discarding the small bench and using the carriage, part two: first—
Regarding the three points of initial synthesis and intended suitability:

Śāriputra, the Tathāgata further reflects thus: "If I were to rely solely on the power of my supernormal faculties and the power of my wisdom, abandoning skillful means, to praise for the sake of sentient beings the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge and vision and his fearlessness, sentient beings would be unable [to understand it]."
By this, one attains deliverance.

In the preceding [passage], there was both exhortation and admonition; now, however, there is only exhortation and no admonition. This is because exhorting toward what is correct is primary, while admonishing against evil is secondary.
Here, the "power" intended is simply the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi-bala*), which corresponds to the aforementioned power of the body and the power of wisdom.
To join one's hands is to praise the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision; to join the strength of the robe-sleeve is to express fearlessness;
to join the strength of the desk or table—if a Buddha first appeared using these [gestures], they would be appropriate for sentient beings, yet they could not be used to deliver them.
△ Second, joining those who lack the capacity.

Why is this? Because these sentient beings have not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, and are being consumed by the burning house of the triple world;
how then could they possibly understand the wisdom of the Buddha?
The explanation that [Śāriputra] could not attain deliverance corresponds to the preceding point that his sons did not accept exhortation and parable.

This is precisely because the obstructions of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) were so heavy that he had not yet escaped the fires of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and thus could not enter the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna;
hence it is said, "How could he possibly understand the Buddha’s wisdom? This single phrase corresponds to the preceding point that there was only one gate, which was moreover narrow and small.
They are unable to understand the Buddha’s wisdom. △ Third, the combined cessation of transformation. Part one: restating the three preceding parables.
Part one: the parable of the father and son who cannot be saved by physical strength.
Śāriputra, it is as if that elder, though possessing great strength in his body and hands, did not employ it.
The phrase "having joined [the hands] above, he releases them" is a skillful exhortation for those who lack the capacity [to understand], signifying the cessation of his transformative activity.

Although this passage lacks explicit words regarding "releasing" or the metaphor itself, the intent behind the metaphor of ceasing the transformative activity is very clear. △ Second, citing the parable of bestowing the three carts.
He merely used earnest and skillful means to strive to rescue his children from the perils of the burning house.
△ Third, the analogy of the equal bestowal of great chariots:
subsequently, he gave each of them a precious, grand chariot.
△ Second, the correct application of the cessation of transformation.
The Tathāgata is also like this: although he possesses power and fearlessness, he does not employ them.
△ Second, the application of the four vehicles; first, the application of the three vehicles as appropriate.
Using wisdom and skillful means, he rescues sentient beings from the burning house of the triple world.
△ Second, in accordance with his sons' prior inclinations, he preaches the three vehicles:
the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha-vehicle.

The Three Vehicles take "conveying" as their essential meaning; each, by means of the truths, conditions, and deliverance, serves as a vehicle to transport one out of the triple world and back to nirvana.
△ Third, the combined praise of the rarity of the chariot, first showing the turning [of the wheel] in combination.
And he spoke these words: "You must not take pleasure in dwelling within this burning house of the triple world; do not crave coarse and inferior forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and tangibles.
If you become attached and give rise to craving, you will be consumed by it. You should quickly escape from the triple world, for you shall attain the three vehicles:
the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddhayāna."
The three realms demonstrate the Truth of Suffering; swiftly exiting the three realms demonstrates the two truths of Cessation and the Path.

Cessation and the Path demonstrate that beyond these three realms there are the fruits of the Three Vehicles resulting from wisdom and abandonment; thus, they cause one to swiftly exit the three realms so that one may attain the Three Vehicles.
The Three Vehicles take the Path and Cessation as their essential substance. This corresponds to the three carts above, which are now at the gate.
Externally, it may be used for play. △ Second, the combined proof of the turning [of the wheel].
"I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never be in vain. You should simply cultivate with diligence and vigor.
By these skillful means, the Tathāgata entices and advances sentient beings.
"I shall grant you whatever you desire. △ Third, the combined exhortation to turn [the wheel]:
He further spoke these words: "You should know that these vehicles of the Threefold Dharma are all praised by the sages;

they are sovereign, unbound, and free from dependence or seeking. By means of these three vehicles, one employs the untainted faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditative concentrations, and..."
Emerging from samādhi and so forth, he enjoys himself and thereby attains immeasurable peace and happiness.

This is in accord with the preceding praise of the rarity of these three vehicles, which are the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas for drawing in sentient beings; thus they are extolled by all the sages.
My "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*) constitutes mastery, and my "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*) constitutes freedom from bondage. My birth—
"Having exhausted [defilements], one does not receive further existence" means being without dependence;

"having accomplished what was to be done and established the holy life" means being without further seeking, as one diligently cultivates the factors of enlightenment through untainted effort. Because one abides in true emptiness and nirvana, it is called "peaceful, secure, and blissful.
△ Fourth, fulfilling the wishes of the sons: Part One, fulfilling the wish for the goat-drawn carriage.

Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings who possess the internal nature of wisdom and, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, receive it with faith and accept it with earnest diligence,
desiring to quickly escape the triple world and seek nirvāṇa for themselves— this is called the Śrāvaka Vehicle,
like those sons who left the burning house seeking the goat carts.
Those who possess the nature of wisdom within have previously cultivated the aspiration for the Three Vehicles and seek to realize the wisdom-nature of the Three Vehicles;

therefore, the Buddha bestows upon them the teachings of the Three Vehicles. "Possessing the nature of wisdom within" and so forth refers to hearing the Dharma from the Buddha and receiving it with faith;

this corresponds to the previous analogy of hearing about the precious playthings described by the father, which satisfied their wishes—this is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). "With earnest diligence" corresponds to the previous analogy.

Each mind is courageous and sharp; this refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). "Diligence" (*vīrya*) combines with the above: "pushing and shoving. "Pushing" means inferring the truth, and "shoving" means expelling evil;
because evil is removed, the refined principle becomes clear, and thus one advances in cultivating wisdom. "Desiring to exit quickly" combines with the below: they compete and run together.
This is called the Śrāvaka vehicle; it combines with the above: "striving to exit the burning house. This is the cultivation of the Three Vehicles.
All [of these] possess these four [qualities]; yet the śrāvakas cannot transform others, just as a sheep does not look back at its flock.
Therefore, the sheep-cart is used as a metaphor for the Śrāvaka-yāna. △ Second, combining it with the deer-cart.
If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, receive it with faith and accept it,

and who with earnest diligence seek spontaneous wisdom, delight in solitary tranquility, and deeply understand the causes and conditions of all phenomena— these are called those of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle,
like those sons who left the burning house seeking the deer cart.
In Sanskrit, *pratyekabuddha* means "solitary enlightened one" (*yuanjue*). Those who seek spontaneous wisdom enter through the gate of the twelve links of dependent origination.
A *pratyekabuddha* is a practitioner of the Dharma; because they hear little Dharma from others and mostly infer its meaning for themselves, they are compared to a deer.
Deer do not rely on humans. △ Third, the gift of the ox-cart.
If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, receive it with faith and diligently cultivate it with vigor,
seeking all-knowledge— the Buddha-knowledge, self-arisen knowledge, teacherless knowledge, the Tathāgata’s insight, powers, and fearlessnesses— and out of compassion for immeasurable sentient beings,
seek their peace and happiness, benefiting gods and humans and delivering all, this is called the Mahāyāna; the Bodhisattva seeks this.

Because they ride upon it, they are called *mahāsattvas*. Just as those sons left the burning house seeking ox-carts, the Bodhisattva’s aspiration for *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) differs from that of the two vehicles; this is the Buddha-wisdom.

The Bodhisattva’s cultivation of causes with this in view is precisely the intent of the Mahāyāna, which carries all beings simultaneously. The Bodhisattva’s compassion in transforming sentient beings is like that of the ox.

Because patience carries one across [the sea of suffering], the ox-cart is used as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva vehicle. However, there is a distinction between the small white ox and the large white ox:
the small ox-cart is a metaphor for the vehicle of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), while the large white ox-cart is a metaphor for the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).
△ Third, the equal bestowing of the great carts. Part One: Citing the two metaphors. Sub-part One: Citing the escape from danger.
Śāriputra, it is like that elder who saw his sons safely emerge from the burning house and reach a place of fearlessness.

Of the four preceding analogies, we now apply only two: the application of "escaping the calamity" encompasses the meaning of "seeking the vehicle," and the application of "bestowing equally" encompasses the meaning of "granting gifts."
And he rejoices. △ Second, citing the equal bestowal:
"Reflecting that his wealth was immeasurable," and so forth, he bestowed great chariots upon his sons.
△ Second, combining the two parables: first, combining the escape from danger.
The Tathāgata is likewise thus: he is the father of all sentient beings.

If he sees immeasurable billions of sentient beings emerge from the fearful and perilous paths of the triple world through the gates of the Buddha's teaching and attain the bliss of nirvana, [he rejoices].

The "gate" (*mukha*) has three meanings: entering, exiting, and distinction. If the triple world is taken as the house and the five aggregates as the dwelling, then by being deluded regarding a single instance of form-and-mind (*rūpa-citta*), one enters that very same form-and-mind; this is "entering the gate" of birth and death.

As for the meaning of "exiting," it refers to mounting [the vehicle] to depart from the triple world; this refers to receiving the two teachings of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared), wherein that which is elucidated beneath those teachings constitutes the gate.
If interpreted in a distinct sense, this refers to taking the principles elucidated under the Separate Teaching as the gate.

What is now called the "gate of the Buddha's teaching" specifically refers to the principles underlying the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings acting together as a gate to exit the three realms and escape suffering.
△ Second, the combined bestowal of the five [vehicles], first: the reason for providing the vehicles.
At that time, the Tathāgata thought to himself: "I possess the immeasurable and boundless treasury of all Buddha-dharmas, such as the power of wisdom and fearlessness.
"Immeasurable wisdom" corresponds to the aforementioned overflowing of the immeasurable treasuries of wealth. △ Second, the correspondence.
Broaden your mind and so forth:

all these sentient beings are my children; bestow upon them the Mahāyāna and do not allow anyone to attain extinction alone, but rather bring them all to extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata.
In summary, for me, things are infinite; it would not be appropriate to give inferior, small carts to my children.
"The Tathāgata’s extinction" refers to the Great Vehicle’s *nirvāṇa* of the three virtues. △ Third, the section on the chapter of equal mind.
These sentient beings who have escaped the triple world are collectively granted the aforementioned equal distribution to all the sons. △ Fourth, the section on the equalizing of the carts:
they are given all the implements for the enjoyment of the Buddhas’ meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and so forth.
These are combined into one great vehicle. △ Fifth, combining the correct and vast great vehicle:
all are of one characteristic and one kind, praised by the sages, and capable of producing pure, wondrous, and supreme bliss.

The combined description of its height, breadth, and even its attendants is a simile for the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). The "one mark" is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
the "one kind" is the seed-wisdom (*bījajñāna*), which is Prajñā. It can produce pure and wondrous bliss;
this bliss is the absence of suffering and is called liberation (*vimukti*). The three virtues (*triguṇa*) are high, broad, and fully adorned; they encompass all qualities and are thus named *ma*.
This is the Mahāyāna. △ Fourth, the analogy of the absence of falsehood, in one part: First, restating the concession that the Small Vehicle leads to the Great.

Śāriputra, it is like that elder who first used the three vehicles to entice his children, and subsequently gave them only the great vehicles, adorned with precious objects and foremost in security; yet that elder was not guilty of falsehood.

The three vehicles used as inducements were originally intended to eliminate the five turbidities; once the five turbidities are eliminated, the great goodness is naturally preserved, and therefore only the great vehicle is given.
△ Second, the synthesis showing that this does not contradict the original intention, part one: the synthesis and explanation.
The Tathāgata is also like this: he is without falsehood; first he teaches the three vehicles to guide sentient beings, and only thereafter does he deliver them by means of the Great Vehicle alone.
This corresponds to the previous statement: "I use skillful means to enable my sons to escape. △ Second, the correspondence of the conclusion with the illustration.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable power of wisdom, the fearlessnesses, and the treasury of all dharmas, and is able to bestow the Dharma of the Mahāyāna upon all sentient beings; yet they are not all able to receive it.
Śāriputra, for these reasons, you should know that through the power of the skillful means of the Buddhas, the One Buddha Vehicle is distinguished and taught as three.

This clarifies that the Tathāgata’s original intent in appearing in the world was to preach the Mahāyāna; however, because those of small wisdom delight in and are attached to the three realms, he employs skillful means to entice and lead them.
Once they have emerged [from the realms], he returns to bestow the Mahāyāna, which accords with their fundamental aspiration;
thus it is said that he can grant the Dharma of the Mahāyāna to sentient beings, though they may not be fully capable of receiving it. △ Second.

The verses consist of two parts: first, a reiteration of the preceding prose; second, an exhortation to believe and circulate [the teaching]. The first part further consists of two sections: first, the verses on the opening parable;
second, the verses on the application of the parable. The first of these further consists of two sections: first, the verses on the general parable; second, the verses on the specific parables.
The first of these further consists of four sections, the first of which is the verses on the elder.
The Buddha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"For example, there is an elder.

[This] eulogizes his high title, which encompasses both his name and his conduct, as well as his virtues and deeds; since he possesses the qualities of one who leads others, he is thus known by that name.
He travels everywhere, revered by states and cities; he knows both the internal and external, and is high in both years and virtue.
Internally, he accords with the title of Bhagavān, the Self-Knowing Buddha, fully endowed with wisdom, abandonment, compassion, and myriad virtues.
△ Second, the verse on the dwelling has two parts; first, the verse on the vastness of the dwelling.
There was a great house;
this is a metaphor for the triple world, which is not a great house. 2. A verse elaborating on the substance of the house:

That house was ancient and had become suddenly dilapidated; the halls and chambers were high and perilous, the bases of the pillars were decayed and rotten, and the beams and rafters were slanting and leaning.
The foundations and steps have collapsed, the walls have crumbled and split apart, the plaster has fallen away, and the thatched roof-covering lies in disarray;
the rafters and eaves are misaligned and detached, the surrounding enclosures are crooked, and all is filled with various impurities.

These three lines extensively describe the substance of the house to clarify the characteristics of what is being burned: the three realms have existed for a beginningless duration and are not merely of recent origin.
Because it is something produced, it is impermanent and base; its name is "sudden decay. The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is its hall and the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is its house;

that one does not escape falling from these is called "high danger. That the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) supports it is like a pillar; that it is shifted by the three marks (*trilakṣaṇa*) is called "ruinous collapse.
The consciousness (*manovijñāna*) acts as the structural framework, serving as the beams and rafters; that it is destroyed by various sufferings is like a structure leaning precariously.
Past actions serve as the foundation; the time of old age is its collapse. The four great elements are the walls, and the skin is the plaster.
The wrinkled and decayed skin is the crumbling and fissuring; the once-vibrant and pure complexion is like fresh plaster, while the withered appearance of old age is the falling away.
As hair and beard decay with age, they all fall out, like a thatched roof in disarray.

The tendons and bones have fallen away, and the limbs and joints are too weak to support one another; like rafters and eaves, the thirty-six constituent parts become dislodged and separated from one another, hence it is called "completely obstructed.
The stomach and intestines coil and twist within, hence it is called "curved and winding.

Not only is it subject to the transformations of impermanence, but it is also filled with impurity, suffering, and so forth; hence it is said that "filth and defilement pervade it entirely. △ Third, the five verses in verse form.
There are one hundred [trees], with five hundred people dwelling within them.
Those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) whose faculties (*indriya*) are subsumed under the five destinies (*pañcagati*) also correspond to the analogy of the thirty sons. △ Fourth Verse.
The arising of fire is a metaphor for the four [realms]; first, it clarifies the events on the ground, which is a metaphor for the arising of fire in the desire realm.

Regarding the four, first it clarifies the categories of things burned, which is a metaphor for the ten *anuśayas* (latent tendencies) of sentient beings. Within this, first it correctly clarifies what is burned.
First, it clarifies the burning of birds and beasts, which is a metaphor for the five dull *anuśayas*. Regarding the five, first is the metaphor for the *anuśaya* of pride (*māna*).
The owl, the screech-owl, the eagle, the vulture, the crow, the magpie, the pigeon, and the dove—these eight birds are used as metaphors for the eight types of pride (*māna*).
Because pride causes sentient beings to exalt themselves and disparage others, like the nature of these birds who soar high and look down from above, they are compared to them.
To disparage others is "pride" (*māna*), while to esteem oneself is "conceit" (*mada*). The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* clarifies these eight forms of conceit.
Now, using analogies for the eight types of pride: pride in physical vigor is like the *chī* bird; pride in lineage is like the *xiāo* bird; pride in wealth is like the *diāo* bird;
pride in power is like the vulture; pride in longevity is like the crow; pride in intelligence is like the magpie; pride in performing good deeds is like the pigeon;
and pride in physical appearance is like the dove. △ Second, the analogies for the latent tendencies of anger.
Vipers, snakes, vipers, scorpions, centipedes, and millipedes—these are metaphors for the latent tendency of anger (*dveṣānuśaya*).
There are three types of anger: first, irrational anger, which is a sudden arising of a mind of hatred regardless of whether an action is right or wrong;
second, anger in accordance with reason, which occurs when another person actually harms me; and third, anger regarding disputes, which occurs when one is attached to one's own [position].
To understand this is to say that while others speak of conduct as wrong, it is like a venomous snake whose poison is so potent that it can suck it out without being touched;

whereas anger arising from irrationality is like a viper or a scorpion that stings only when touched. Anger based on grasping at principles is like a centipede or a millipede—representing anger born of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
As worldly people say, those with red necks are centipedes, while those that are not red are millipedes.
Lizards, centipedes, weasels, badgers, mice, and various other evil insects scurried about in all directions;
excrement and urine created foul-smelling places where impurities overflowed, and dung beetles and other insects gathered upon them.
This analogy illustrates how the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*) fails to comprehend its objects; this "delusion" is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). There are two types of ignorance:
first, the independent (*kevala*), and second, the associated (*saṃprayukta*). The lizards, centipedes, and other such creatures, appearing dazed and motionless, illustrate independent ignorance.
The weasels, wildcats, and mice illustrate associated ignorance. As for the various species of evil insects, they represent all [afflictions] that arise from the root of delusion.

The phrase "the fetters and proclivities run to and fro" clarifies that the various proclivities (anuśaya) condition one another, or condition the three realms, arising as swiftly as they cross paths like running horses.
The mention of "excrement and urine" below clarifies that the objects to which the deluded mind clings are all impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;
thus it says, "in the foul-smelling place of excrement and urine, impurity flows forth," due to ignorance (moha).

Because they fail to understand this and instead calculate it as permanent, blissful, self, and pure, thereby giving rise to defiled attachment, it is said that "dung beetles and various insects gather upon it.
△ Fourth, the analogy for the latent tendencies of greed.
Foxes, wolves, and jackals chew, trample, and gnaw upon the corpses and their flesh and bones;
because of this, packs of dogs compete to seize them, while they themselves, emaciated by hunger and filled with terror, wander everywhere in search of food.
This is an analogy for the latent tendency of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*). Greed is of two kinds: first, that which possesses power; second, that which lacks power.
That which possesses power seizes by means of its majesty and force, like foxes, wolves, and the like. That which lacks power begs and solicits from others, like jackals and the like.
The following passage clarifies how greed seizes upon objects and draws things toward oneself, like chewing: it does not proceed by way of right principle, but rather like treading upon something.
The greedy mind grasps at objects, whether one thing or many, with a sense of boundary as if biting into them;
when bones and flesh are strewn in disarray, it amasses the five sensory objects (pañca-kāmaguṇa) without knowing contentment.
Regarding the phrase "a pack of dogs vying with one another," this refers to powerful greed that seizes and plunders those who are weak, namely kings and thieves; such greed knows no bounds.
The feet are like one who, being hungry, seeks but cannot obtain; they are like one who is emaciated and strives in various ways to find sustenance;

they are like a person of many desires who, though wealthy, is impoverished and in a state of panic; and those who seek food everywhere are those who rush about in pursuit of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
△ Fifth, the analogy for the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).
"Quarreling, seizing, pulling, snarling, and barking.

This is a metaphor for the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) and hesitation between two extremes, which is called "doubt" when one has not yet decided whether something is right or wrong.
To claim "this is correct" is called "seizing," while to claim "this is incorrect" is called "pulling. "Snarling and barking" refers to the act of engaging in verbal debate to reach a decision.
This is the principle of right and wrong. △ Second, the conclusion:
"The house was thus filled with terrors and strange transformations.

This concludes the explanation of the five dull afflictions (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). △ Second, the illustration of the spirits and ghosts being burned, representing the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-kleśa*). Part one.
This is a general explanation.
It means that in every place there are *chimei* (goblins) and *wangliang* (sprites).

This is a general metaphor for the five *drstis* (views), such as the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), which arise from the five bases of contact (*sparśāyatana*) and are constantly present even in moments of haste.
Because the "desire for gain and fame" (lābha-yaśas) universally conditions the Four Truths and the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), it is said that they exist everywhere.

Since ghosts and spirits possess intelligence while birds and beasts do not, the sharp fetters (tīkṣṇa-nīvaraṇa) are likened to ghosts and spirits, and the dull fetters (mṛdu-nīvaraṇa) are metaphorically compared to birds and beasts.
II. Specifically explaining the five [fetters]: first, the analogy for wrong views (mithyā-dṛṣṭi).
Yakṣas, malevolent spirits, and those who devour human flesh, as well as various venomous insects and predatory beasts, give birth and raise their young, each guarding them jealously.
When the yakṣas vie with one another to seize and eat them, their malice grows even more fierce once they have eaten their fill;
the sounds of their quarreling are truly terrifying.
This is a metaphor for wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): because one reckons in terms of annihilationism or eternalism and does not believe in cause and effect, it is called "wrong view.
*Yakṣa* (properly translated as *yàchā*) refers to a swift-moving ghost. Human flesh is "good" and poisonous insects are "evil.
The mind of wrong view negates the reality of good and evil causes and effects, just as a *yakṣa* devours human flesh or poisonous insects. This is the essence of the metaphor.
The production of milk represents the general teaching on both good and evil, wherein cause and effect function in mutual generation.
Being satiated after eating it signifies the fulfillment of a mind of false views. The intensification of the evil mind signifies the expansion of false views.
The sound of quarreling signifies that what was accomplished within the inner mind is manifested externally through verbal teachings proclaiming the absence of cause.
Because dharmas that yield no fruit cause those who hear them to fall into the three miserable realms, they are said to be truly terrifying.
△ Second, an analogy for the clinging to precepts and rituals:
The kumbhāṇḍa ghost crouches upon a mound of earth, or sometimes rises one or two feet off the ground, moving back and forth as it wanders about.
He frolics wantonly, seizing the two hind legs of a dog and pinning it down until it cries out, placing his foot upon its neck; he delights himself by terrifying the dog.

This is a metaphor for the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which grasps what is wrong as the path—namely, reckoning what is not a cause to be a cause—and refers to the "precepts of chickens and dogs" known as *śīlavrataparāmarśa*.
A *kumbhāṇḍa* (translated here as "jar-shaped" because its private parts resemble a jar) is a superior type of ghost.
This is a metaphor for how cultivating impure wholesome states can overcome all evils.

"Crouching on a mound of earth" refers to non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) practicing the ten wholesome precepts, which enables them to be reborn in the six heavens of the desire realm; these six heavens are high places within the desire realm, just like a mound of earth.

Alternatively, it means that by leaving the lower realms, one attains the meditative concentrations (dhyāna) of the form realm—as if reaching a height of one chi—or the formless realm concentrations—as if reaching two chi—thereby ascending.

The higher realms are like departing and falling back; the view of precepts and observances is like rising again. It is like a dog that has been let loose to play, yet its feet are caught as soon as it tries to run.
To slander the absence of a cause for suffering is like adding a foot to a neck already suffering from a cause;
having already obtained the fruit of suffering, one further slanders the absence of a fruit of suffering. Just as a dog makes a sound, so does the person of wrong views negate [the truth].
To say that there is no principle by which a cause of suffering can produce the fruit of suffering is like trying to silence someone by striking them;

since you thus slander both the cause and the fruit of suffering, it is like one who, fearing a dog, instead takes pleasure in [beating] it himself. △ Third, the analogy for the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Furthermore, there are various ghosts with bodies that are tall and large, naked, black, and emaciated, who constantly dwell within it, emitting a great evil sound and crying out for food.

This is an analogy for the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), which falsely calculates the aggregates and elements to be a self; this is called the "view of a self," which enters vertically throughout the three periods of time.

Conceptualizing the self as "long" refers to its pervading the five aggregates horizontally; conceptualizing the self as "great" refers to its vastness; conceptualizing the self as "sovereign" refers to its lack of cultivation of wholesome dharmas;
because it lacks shame and remorse, it is called "naked"; because it is adorned with evil, it is called "black"; because it lacks the provisions of merit, it is called "emaciated";
and because those who conceptualize the self do not transcend the three realms, they are said to "permanently dwell within them. This is what is meant by conceptualizing the self.
Because they speak from within their hearts, proclaiming the characteristics of a self, it is said that they "utter great evil cries.
Because they hope to attain the fruits of the Path through such speech, it is said that they "shout out seeking food. △ Fourth, the simile for the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose throats are like needles.

This is a metaphor for the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); it means that because these views extend [their reach] as far as the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), they are called "grasping at views. Although the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is impermanent, one reckons it to be *nirvāṇa*.
It is like [the ghost] whose throat is so narrow that life is precarious, yet who preserves its longevity; therefore, it is said that their throats are like needles.
△ Fifth, the simile for extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*):
Furthermore, there are various ghosts with heads like those of oxen, some eating human flesh and others devouring dogs;
their hair is disheveled and matted, and they are cruel and predatory, driven by hunger and thirst, crying out as they run about.

This analogy illustrates how, based upon the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one calculates either a self or [the world as] eternal or annihilated; adhering to one extreme is called the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

The two extremes of eternity and annihilation are like the horns of an ox. To give rise to the view of extremes—such as "this body is the self" or "this self is the body"—is like the two horns of an ox.
The fault of calculating annihilation or eternity can sever the roots of mundane and supramundane goodness, just as eating poison destroys a person.
Flesh can sever the roots of worldly goodness; some even eat dogs. They may reckon [the self] as eternal or reckon it as subject to annihilation, revolving back and forth like disheveled hair:
if they reckon it eternal, they destroy the doctrine of annihilation; if they reckon it annihilated, they destroy the doctrine of eternity.
Like those who are cruel and predatory, lacking wisdom or meditative concentration, they merely sustain themselves with food and drink, driven by hunger and thirst. Each...
Chen-er saw them as if crying out and fleeing in haste. △ Third, a summary of the sharp and dull faculties:
Yakṣas, hungry ghosts, and various evil birds and beasts, driven by the urgency of hunger, look toward the four directions and exhaustively search the windows and doors;
such calamities and fears are immeasurable.

This one and a half lines summarize the characteristics of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and also summarize the characteristics of sentient beings of sharp and dull faculties—the first line refers to the sharp, and the second to the dull.
The following two lines generally summarize both types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*):

because their minds are always tainted (*sāsrava*) and constantly lack the flavor of the Path (*mārga-rasa*), they are said to be "hungry and urgent. Looking through the window for light illustrates their false contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Although one may aspire to and admire the flavor of the Way and engage in contemplation, the mind remains mired in attachment and frequently fails to accord with the true principle;
it is like looking at the sky through a narrow window, unable to attain unimpeded vision. The latter two lines summarize the extensive discussion to conclude that this is not [the correct view].
△ Second, clarifying the cause for the arising of the fire.
This dilapidated old house belongs to a single person who has recently departed from it;

not long after his departure, he—being the Buddha who manifests within the three realms and having made a vow since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment to deliver all beings—may be said to "belong to one person.
While the elder was in the house, he was able to ensure they were careful regarding the fire, but after he had left, the sons remained ignorant.

Therefore, the arising of fire internally corresponds precisely to the time when the Tathāgata, during his era as the Great Penetrating Buddha, constantly instructed these beings to subdue the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya), just as one is cautioned against fire.
When these beings subsequently give rise to the five turbidities, it is like the fire breaking out.
Because the Buddha responds to conditions in other lands rather than departing forever, it is said that he will "soon emerge. △ Third, explaining the arising of fire.
In the aftermath,
a fire suddenly broke out within the residence; from all four sides, the flames simultaneously blazed up with such intensity that the ridgepoles,
rafters, and columns burst with a thunderous crack, splintering and collapsing, while the walls crumbled and fell.

The three realms are the dwelling, the five aggregates are the house; its four sides are the locations where the body, sensation, mind, and phenomena give rise to the four inversions, the five turbidities, and the eight sufferings.
Thus it is said that their simultaneous continuity and gradual increase are called "blazing together.
The wailing of suffering is called the "sound of bursting," the destruction of the sense faculties is "cracking," the severing of the breath and the separation of bones from tendons is "breaking."
Crushed and fallen, the four great elements disperse; the walls collapse and fall down. △ Fourth, the signs of being burned:
various spirits and ghosts raise their voices in loud cries, while eagles, vultures, birds, kumbhāṇḍas, and others are filled with panic and terror.
They cannot emerge on their own.

This is analogous to the aforementioned spirits and deities; it illustrates those who follow the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), who claim that dharmas are fixed as eternally existent, having existed and then returning to non-existence—yet because this non-existence is itself eternal, they hold to eternalism.
It also illustrates those who hold the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), who claim that dharmas are fixed as being annihilated, such that there is only this single death and nothing more.
Furthermore, they all continued to cry out, for the matter had already been clearly revealed; thus it is said they raised their voices and shrieked loudly.

Vultures and eagles represent the dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*), while the *kumbhāṇḍas* and others represent the sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*). Among these, the precept-and-observance grasping (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) represents the dull afflictions. As for the sharp afflictions of precept-and-observance grasping:
originally they did not conceive of annihilation, but now, seeing impermanence, they give rise only to doubt and fear, not knowing the means of deliverance.

Therefore, it is said that they are terrified and unable to escape on their own. △ Second, explaining the events within the hole as a metaphor for the fire arising in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), in four parts:
first, explaining the types of beings being burned.
Malevolent beasts and venomous insects hide and scurry within the holes and burrows, and piśāca demons also dwell therein.
The concentration of the four dhyānas is like a hollow; although it does not reach the open expanse outside the gate, one can still escape the fierce flames.
This is analogous to entering the concentration of the four dhyānas: though one has not yet exited the realm [of form], one can still escape the coarse evils of the desire realm.
To benefit sentient beings, one may also attain dhyāna-concentration, just as the piśāca spirits also dwell therein.
Middle. △ Second, the cause for the fire’s arising:
because of meager merit;
due to having little merit, one encounters suffering by being close to evil. △ Third, the momentum of the fire’s arising.
Being oppressed by fire:
although there is no fierce flame within the hollows, there is still the affliction of heat;

this is analogous to how the fourth dhyāna, though devoid of the evils of the desire realm, still possesses the subtle suffering of the attachment to the flavor of joy and bliss, and is therefore said to be "oppressed by fire. △ Four: Being Burned.

These creatures were mutually harming one another, drinking blood and devouring flesh; the jackals and their ilk had already died beforehand, while various great and fierce beasts vied with one another to come and eat them,
as foul-smelling smoke billowed forth, filling the four directions.
Sentient beings of sharp or dull faculties who attain dhyāna are identical in their attainment, yet their respective conceptions differ;
they mutually affirm and deny one another as if they were harming each other. Since they give rise to various views within dhyāna, they cannot produce untainted concentration and wisdom.
They merely cling to silence, like drinking blood, or cling to the five factors such as vitarka and vicāra, like jackals devouring flesh.

This is a metaphor for the craving of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Because one has already abandoned this craving by practicing the future concentration (*anāgata-samādhi*) within the desire realm, it is said that they have already died previously.
Furthermore, the craving for meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is called "devouring," just as a great predatory beast can swallow the craving of the desire realm;
thus, it is said that they come vying to devour the four inversions and eight sufferings of the desire realm, which are like the fierce flames of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The four inversions and eight sufferings are like foul smoke; because smoke precedes the flame, it is used as a metaphor for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
The realm of form also encompasses body, sensation, mind, phenomena, and the four great elements; because suffering pervades all four directions, it is said to be "pervasive."
△ Third, the analogy for events in the air: the arising of fire in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). Part one: the things being burned.
Centipedes, millipedes, and venomous snakes, scorched by the fire, scramble to exit their burrows.

Previously, in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the centipede was used as a metaphor for anger (*dveṣa*); now, in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the centipede is likewise used as a metaphor for anger.
Although the centipede is not explicitly mentioned in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the mention of "poisonous insects" includes the centipede;

thus, one knows that anger pervades all three realms. Regarding "poisonous snakes" and so forth: those who are weary of the meditative absorptions of the realm of form (*rūpadhyāna*) emerge toward the formless realm, being weary of form.
One contemplates coarse objects as formless phenomena, like a venomous snake or one emerging from its hole after being scorched by fire. △ Second, the signs of what is burned:
the *kumbhāṇḍa* spirits seize and devour them, while the various hungry ghosts have flames burning upon their heads, tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat.
They wander about in panic and distress.

Because one who attains the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*) must necessarily extinguish the objects of perception belonging to the lower realms, it is said that they consume whatever comes their way.

Even though the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is situated at the very summit, one still cannot escape the various sufferings of perversion, which are like a fire burning upon one's head. Thus, even the Peak of Existence is not free from suffering. The Peak of Existence...
Furthermore, there are the fires of the eight sufferings: the arising of divergent thoughts in the mind is the suffering of birth;

the non-abiding of mindfulness is the suffering of aging; the agitation of the mental faculty that obstructs concentration is the suffering of illness; the falling away from concentration is the suffering of death; failing to attain concentration despite seeking it is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
the presence of obstacles when seeking concentration is necessarily the suffering of encountering the hated; and the cultivation [of concentration]... [is the suffering of separation from the loved].
The superior losing the inferior is called the suffering of separation from what is loved; the four aggregates of mind are the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
Because there is no support from untainted food and drink, one is afflicted by hunger and thirst; as this is still within saṃsāra, one wanders about in confusion, obstructed and distressed.
△ Fourth, the summary: Thus the various perils within the three realms are not one;
such a house is extremely terrifying, with manifold calamities of poison, harm, and fire.
This concludes the general analogy. △ Second, the verses on the specific analogies (three parts); first, the verse on the elder seeing the fire (three parts). First:
The verse describes the one who can see.
At that time, the master of the house was standing outside the gate and heard someone say:
"The master of the house" refers to the elder, who is the one capable of seeing; "standing outside the gate" precisely corresponds to what was stated above regarding the location.

To burn [the house] means to emerge safely through the gate. "Standing" refers to the Tathāgata, who dwells in the stage of the Dharmakāya, constantly harboring great compassion and desiring to save sentient beings, rather than remaining seated upon the throne of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā). What was previously called "seeing" is here called "hearing";
"hearing" replaces "seeing. Hearing necessarily derives from another source; this refers to the Buddha as teacher, meaning the Dharma of samādhi. This is that Dharma.
The teacher is, in fact, another person; however, because he enters samādhi, he is able to perceive their capacities, and thus it is said that "there are people.
△ Second, the verse on what is seen:
"You, my children, previously came into this house while playing; being young and ignorant, you took delight in it and became attached to its pleasures."
Question: You previously stated that you had not yet emerged; how then can you say you have entered by means of playing? Answer:

It may be that during the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, you once gave rise to the Great Resolve (mahācitta) to be called "emerging from the triple world," yet subsequently regressed, which is termed "entering.

It is like a person who lifts their foot intending to go out, but upon reaching the side of the gate, turns back; this is both called "going out" and called "returning and entering. Furthermore, this is the principle.

The nature is fundamentally pure; it is not a dharma of the triple world. Because of ignorance (*avidyā*), conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) arises, and there is birth and death, which is called "entering.

Therefore, it is said that they first came to enter through play. In the past, their karmic connections were shallow and their great goodness was not yet manifest, so they were called "young and small.
After falling back from the Great Vehicle, they transmigrate through the triple world, shrouded by ignorance; this is called "non-existence" (*amūla*).
[He] knows. △ Third, the verse on alarm and fear:
Having heard this, the elder was startled and entered the burning house.

This verse corresponds to [the prose]: "Immediately struck with great alarm and fear, he gave rise to a heart of great compassion. △ Second, the verse on the simile of abandoning the small table and employing the carts.
Second, the first verse illustrates the abandonment of the couch as a metaphor. Part one: the initial verse describes the appropriate means of rescue.
Having devised a suitable method to provide relief so that no burning or harm occurs, he exhorts his sons by describing various afflictions and calamities:
evil spirits, venomous insects, the spreading of a disastrous fire, and manifold sufferings occurring in continuous succession; there are also poisonous snakes, vipers, and various *yakṣas*.
Kumbhāṇḍa ghosts, jackals, foxes, dogs, eagles, vultures, crows, owls, centipedes, and their like—afflicted by the urgency of hunger and thirst, they are most terrifying;
how much more so this place of suffering, let alone the great fire!

"Appropriate" (*fāngyí*) means to adapt the Great Teaching to the circumstances. "Exhorting" (*gàoyù*) refers to the meaning of explaining various afflictions and hardships and providing admonitions and instructions.
"The calamitous fire spreading like creeping vines" (*mànshèn*) describes a continuous and uninterrupted state; the *Xījīng fù* says, "its form spreads and creeps.
△ Second, the verse on not accepting [the gift].
The sons, being ignorant, though they heard their father’s instruction, still took pleasure in their attachments.
[This concludes] the verse on how the sons were unwilling to believe or accept it. △ Third, the verse on the cessation of the transformation:
they continued their play without ceasing.

The verse above describes looking toward the father and merely playing; this refers to the *saviṣaya-jñāna* (knowledge with objects) and the *kleśa-āvaraṇa* (afflictive obstructions). △ Second, the verse on the parable of using the carts, in three parts.
