First, the verse on the three carts as the provisional teaching (*nīyāna*).
At that time, the elder had this thought: "My sons are like this; it increases my sorrow and distress. Now, this house..."
There was not a single thing to be enjoyed, yet the sons were so immersed in their play that they would not accept my instruction and were about to be harmed by the fire;
he then contemplated and devised various skillful means.
The first line clarifies the intended purpose, while the next line explains the reason for employing these means: because of their attachment to views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
It is only by bestowing the small carriage that one acts with the intent of using it; if one does not use the small, then both the large and the small perish.
Thus it is said: "it will be harmed by fire. Because it is harmed by fire, one loses the body; because one loses the body, one loses life.
Bestowing the small carriage is precisely the contemplation of using the teachings of the Three Vehicles. △ Second, the verse praising the rarity of the carriage has four parts; first, the verse:
Exhortation to Turn [the Wheel]:
I tell my sons that I possess various kinds of rare playthings and excellent chariots made of wonderful jewels.

As for these "wonderful jewels," they still belong to the realm of skillful means (*upāya*), such as cessation, tranquility, excellence, and detachment; if they were truly ultimate wonders, why would [I] [speak of them otherwise]?
They all went to their father’s place and asked for the chariots. △ Second, the verse shows the turning [of the wheel]:
"The sheep-drawn carriage, the deer-drawn carriage, and the great ox-drawn carriage are now outside the gate.
Being "outside the gate" is like showing the Four Noble Truths so that one may know the transcendence of the world. △ Third, the repeated exhortation to turn [the wheel].
"Come forth, all of you!

This is the exhortation for them to act in accordance with the truth; they must observe the truths in order to escape from the house. △ Fourth, the verse on the realization of the turning [of the wheel]:
"I have fashioned these chariots for you, so that you may play and sport according to your own desires."
The meaning of the sutra passage is this: "I am skilled at constructing chariots to provide for all; let it be verified that I shall certainly not lack chariots.
This citation is without error, and the testimony granted is not false. △ Third, the verse on fulfilling the sons' wishes.
Upon hearing such words regarding the various chariots, the sons immediately vied with one another to rush out and reach the open space, thereby escaping all suffering and distress.

This verse on rushing forth refers to the realization of the Truths (*satyābhisamaya*); the "open space" refers to the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). △ Third, the verse on the equal bestowal of the great chariots.
The first four verses illustrate the joy of escaping danger; the first two verses illustrate the escape from danger itself.
When the elder saw that his sons had emerged from the burning house and were sitting upon lion thrones at the crossroads, he was filled with joy.

Regarding the sitting upon the lion throne, there are two interpretations. First, it is said that because these sons sit upon this throne, they have emerged from the three realms and are therefore fearless.
Second, it is said that this is the seat upon which the elder sits; having seen his sons escape calamity, he immediately attains fearlessness.
Previously, while still outside the gate, he still possessed anxiety and fear, hence it is said he was "standing"; now that they have emerged from the gate, he finally sits down.
Out of fear, the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta* says: "Now I rejoice, being free from fear. Second, the verse on rejoicing:
He expresses his own celebration, saying, "I am now happy! These sons of mine were so difficult to raise and nurture;
they were foolish and ignorant, entering this perilous house where many venomous insects and terrifying *chimei* (goblins) dwelt, and fierce, great fires blazed up from all four sides."
"These children were addicted to pleasure and play, yet I have rescued them and enabled them to escape this calamity;
therefore, O people, I am now joyful.
Thus he spoke words of self-congratulation because he had obtained those to be converted. Consequently, he was filled with joy and satisfaction at the abodes of twenty-two billion Buddhas.
Because he instructs them in the great conditions, it is said they are "born"; because they undergo minor ripening in the interim, it is said they are "nurtured.

Having passed through this long period, as they mature repeatedly and their upbringing is not easily accomplished, it is said it is "extremely difficult. Because the primary elements are subtle, the ignorant and small-minded give rise to the five turbidities;
because they invite results through causes due to ignorance, it is said they "enter the house" to greedily delight in play and sport.

That is to say, for those who are attached to the five desires, it enables them to attain liberation from calamity and causes them to be free from the eight sufferings. △ Second, the verse on the sons requesting the vehicles:
At that time, the sons, knowing their father was sitting at ease, all went to where their father was and addressed him, saying, "We pray that you will grant us..."
"The three kinds of precious chariots, as previously promised—come forth, my sons, and I shall give you these three chariots according to your desires;
now is the very time, so please grant them.

The first two phrases clarify that at the time of requesting the chariots, it was verified that the aforementioned person sitting above was indeed the father. All subsequent [passages] follow this pattern. The first [phrase] below... [end of fragment].
The first line describes the granting of the permission for the search; the following two lines conclude the search. △ Third, the verse on the equal bestowal of the great chariots:
first, the verse that anticipates the explanation of the causes for the great chariots.
The elder is immensely wealthy, possessing many treasuries of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, conch, and agate.

That which is contained within the house is called a "treasury" (kūṭa), while that which is stored in the ground is called a "storehouse" (kośa). Practicing all dharmas is called a "treasury," and the six sense organs, such as the eye, being complete with all dharmas is called a "storehouse.
Regarding this, Miaole says: "As for 'practicing all dharmas being called a treasury,' it is simply..."
Taking "containing and storing" as its meaning, the six sense organs are fully termed "treasuries," because while the "storehouse" (zàng) is broad, the "warehouse" (kù) is narrow;
they may also be discussed interchangeably. △ Second, the verse on the Great Vehicle.
With various precious objects, they construct great chariots, adorned and decorated with railings all around, with bells suspended on all four sides and crisscrossed with golden cords.

All phenomena pertaining to cause and effect are collectively termed "various jewels"; in terms of the provisional teachings, the meaning of cultivation and attainment is like the construction of these vehicles.

Because there are many offspring, the chariots are not of a single kind; thus, the various things created are moreover vast. Furthermore, one must demonstrate the direction [of practice] so that they may know how to initiate cultivation;
this is called "creation" (*zào*). When cultivation is extinguished within the nature, creation returns to what is originally possessed—this is the very substance of the chariot.
As for "the adornments below," it means being fully equipped with the [ten] perfections (*pāramitā*), as explained previously.
A net of pearls was spread over it, with golden flower tassels hanging down everywhere and various colorful ornaments encircling it on all sides.
These pearls and other elements manifest the appearance of a canopy; the gates of compassion are not one, just as each individual mesh of a net.
Within [the canopy], there is a single pearl, symbolizing that all gates of universal compassion are equally designated as reality.

While the preceding text merely mentions "hanging various flower-garlands," which simply causes those who see them to rejoice, the present passage states that they "hang down everywhere," clarifying that all capacities for awakening are universally gladdened.
The various colored ornaments serve as a metaphor for the different modes of responsive transformation established throughout the surrounding perimeter.
The surrounding enclosures are appropriately arranged to encompass all things without omission.
Soft silks and cotton fill the mattresses and cushions; exquisite, fine woolen cloth, worth hundreds of billions, is pure white and clean, used to cover them above.
Great white oxen, fat, strong, and of beautiful form, draw the precious chariot.
Many attendants and followers wait upon and guard it.

While the previous passage simply spoke of "layered spreadings," the present addition of the praise for its "softness" serves as a metaphor for mastery in the various *dhyānas*; thus it is called "soft.
Furthermore, the mention of a precious woolen cloth (*karpāsa*) covering its surface serves as a metaphor for the sublime crowning the coarse, like a fine coverlet placed over a thick mattress.

The *Shuowen* states that it refers to the layered cushions within a carriage; because the practice of dhyāna is superior to that of ordinary or inferior practitioners, it is described as "fresh, white, pure, and clean.
△ Third, the verse on the section concerning the carriage.
With these exquisite chariots.
△ Fourth, the verse on the chapter of the impartial mind:
he bestows them equally upon all his sons.
△ Fourth Verse: Attaining the Chariots and Rejoicing.

At that time, the sons were filled with joy and leaped for gladness as they mounted these precious chariots to travel through the four directions, sporting and delighting themselves with sovereign ease and without hindrance.

Those who roam in the four directions ride upon the wisdom of the Middle Way, traversing horizontally through the fourfold sets of the four gates and the fourfold sets of the Four Noble Truths, and ascending vertically through the forty-one stages to the ultimate virtue of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; therefore, it is said that they sport with sovereign ease.
△ Second, the verse on the synthesis of the parable, in two parts. First, the verse on the synthesis of the general parable, in four parts. First, the verse on the synthesis of the elder.
[The Buddha] said to Śāriputra: "I am also like this—the most honored among the assembly of sages and the father of the world.
The first two phrases correspond to his rank and title; the latter two phrases correspond to his name and conduct, while together they express the meaning of praising his virtues.
"Tathāgata" is the most honored among the seven kinds of expedient sages and saints, and the father of the nine kinds of worldly beings. (Miaole states:)
The nine types are merely the nine realms. When the seven are compared to the nine, one simply excludes the four miserable destinies and includes the Bodhisattvas;

this is because the sense of being a "son" applies universally [to the nine], whereas the sense of forming a karmic connection through conditions is restricted [to the seven] in the mundane world. Thus, there are only seven in terms of skillful means.
△ Second, the two verses summarize the five hundred people.
All sentient beings are my children; they are deeply attached to worldly pleasures and lack the mind of wisdom.
This summarizes the meaning of the five paths, while the thirty children additionally encompass the causal factors; all sentient beings [are these children].
To say that birth is the true cause [of suffering] for one who lacks the mind of wisdom is merely a conventional expression devoid of reality. △ Third, the verse on the analogy of the house:
"The three realms have no peace; they are like a burning house."
The verse correctly summarizes the meaning of the entire household as well as that of a single gate. △ Fourth, it summarizes the arising of fire:
"Filled with manifold sufferings, most terrifying, and constantly possessed of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, and affliction—such fires blaze forth without ceasing."
The first two lines provide a general heading; the next two lines offer an explanation; the following two lines combine these with the general analogy, which refers to awakening.
△ Second, the verse combines the specific analogies into four parts; first, the verse combines the analogy of the elder seeing the fire, specifically the first part combining the act of seeing.
The Tathāgata has already departed from the burning house of the triple world and dwells in serene seclusion, peacefully abiding in the forests and wilds.
The preceding verse states that the Tathāgata is able to see precisely because he dwells in serene seclusion;

it is by this means that he perceives the five turbidities and his children, who are then joined together upon hearing the words of someone. ○ *Miaole* says: "Serene seclusion" and so forth refers to the application of wisdom within the King Samādhi.
This is precisely what is meant by "establishing [them] securely. △ Second, the verse summarizes what was seen:
"Now these three realms are all mine; the sentient beings therein are all my children.
Yet, this place is full of many afflictions and hardships."
The preceding verses on the various sentient beings being scorched and boiled by birth, old age, sickness, and death correspond to the aforementioned analogy of fire.
△ Third, the verses on the correspondence with fear and terror.
"I alone am able to provide rescue and protection.
Having seen this, the Buddha then thought: "It is fitting that he should enter the burning house in alarm. II.
Verses on the analogy of abandoning the benches and employing the carts (2): A. Verses on the analogy of abandoning the benches (3): 1. Verses on the analogy of the intended suitability.
Although he instructed him with two verses,
[the disciple] lacked the necessary capacity;
thus, he did not believe or accept them.
△ Third Verse: Synthesizing the Cessation of Transformations.

Because their attachment to the defilements of desire is profound, this verse states that they have not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. △ Second Verse: Synthesizing the Application.
The first verse concerning the three carts is intended to represent the three vehicles;
by means of this expedient, the preceding verse simply uses wisdom and skillful means to represent them. △ Second, the verse praising the rarity of the carts.
There is. For their sake, he teaches the Three Vehicles, causing all sentient beings to know the suffering of the three realms and revealing and expounding the supramundane path.
△ Third, the verses fulfill the wishes of the worthy sons.

Among these sons, those whose resolve is firm— whether they possess the three knowledges (*traividya*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), or have attained the stage of a *pratyekabuddha* or a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva—
and who are "firm in resolve" from the stage of *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti* onwards, this constitutes true firm resolve; this single phrase summarizes [the preceding].
The verse on the stage of the three vehicles galloping forward consists of one full line; each [subsequent] line separately describes the stage of the three vehicles contending to emerge.

Regarding the "three knowledges" (*vidyā*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) knows the suffering of the past, and knowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) knows the suffering of the future;

both are able to bring about wearying detachment from birth and death. Knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is able to perform correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) and sever all afflictions. This...
The three types of supernormal knowledge consist merely of the power of the body, skillful arts, and the divine ear that hears sounds;

the knowledge of others' minds merely perceives their distinct thoughts. Therefore, they are not called "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*). For non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, the meaning of "non-retrogression" is comprehensive, encompassing both the Mahāyāna and the Tripiṭaka.
△ Third, the verse on the analogy of bestowing equal great chariots, in two parts: first, the verse on the analogy of bestowing equally.
The first four verses of the "Great Vehicle" chapter correspond to the section on the Great Vehicle.
"O Śāriputra, for the sake of sentient beings, I have taught this single Buddha-vehicle through these parables.
This verse corresponds to the preceding section on the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and so forth common to all Buddhas. △ Second, the verses corresponding to the section on the Equal Mind.
If you all can believe and accept these words, you shall all attain the path of Buddhahood.
This verse above [describes] how these sentient beings are liberated from the three realms. △ Third, the verse on the combined, correct, and vast great chariot.
This vehicle is subtle, wondrous, pure, and supreme; it is unsurpassed among all worlds, approved by the Buddhas, and worthy of being praised, honored, and prostrated to by all sentient beings.
The preceding verses all describe [the dharmas] as being of one characteristic and one kind, etc. △ Fourth, the combined explanation of the verses concerning the chariot and the oxen:
"Immeasurable billions of powers, liberations, dhyānas, wisdoms, and other Buddha-dharmas."
The verse above states, "I possess immeasurable and boundless wisdom," and so forth. △ Second, the verse on the shared joy of obtaining the carts, which has two parts:
first, clarifying that each obtains a great cart.
Having obtained such vehicles, it causes all the sons to constantly engage in play throughout days, nights, and kalpas, together with the various bodhisattvas.
Together with the assembly of śrāvakas, they mount this precious vehicle and proceed directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
"Day and night" means that when one first attains the Buddha’s wisdom and vision—the light of the middle-way wisdom—it is like the day; while ignorance remains, it is like the night.

When one personally attains the wisdom of the middle way, it is like the day; yet, through compassion, one enters into birth and death, which is like the night. Thus, one constantly practices these two dharmas.
Therefore, it is said that those who sport in the three vehicles enter equally into the Buddha-wisdom; hence, it is stated "together with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Furthermore, this clarifies one's own practice and the transformation of others: because one personally attains this vehicle, it is said "sporting day and night";
and because one transforms others through this, it is said "together with all bodhisattvas and śrāvakas," indicating that the capacity to transform others is common to all three vehicles.
To ride the precious vehicle directly to the site of enlightenment refers to the stage of wondrous awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). △ Second, the conclusion and exhortation to believe:
For this reason, if one seeks with utmost sincerity throughout the ten directions, no other vehicle exists, except for the skillful means of the Buddhas.

Regarding the statement that there is no third cause or condition for the One Vehicle (ekayāna), if one seeks it with thorough sincerity throughout the lands of the ten directions, there is only this One and not two;
except for the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*), it cannot even be expressed in words. △ Fourth, the correct verse on the analogy of the non-falsehood, in two parts:
First, the verse on the chapter of non-falsity, in three parts. First, establishing the father-son relationship to clarify the original intention to bestow the Great [Vehicle].
He addressed Śāriputra: "All of you, my followers, are my children, and I am your father.
Since it is said that you are all my children, by principle it should be equal and I should bestow [the Great Vehicle] upon you. △ Second, clarifying the intent behind teaching the three vehicles:
it is fundamentally for the purpose of removing obstacles.
"Throughout many kalpas you have been scorched by manifold sufferings; I have rescued and delivered you all, causing you to emerge from the triple world.
Now that the three obstacles have been removed, my original intention is fulfilled, and I shall bestow upon you the Great Dharma.
Although I previously said that you had attained nirvana, this was merely the exhaustion of birth and death; in truth, you were not yet extinguished. What you must now do is as follows:"
Only the Buddha’s wisdom.
The first line clarifies that although obstacles are removed and birth-and-death is exhausted, this refers only to the exhaustion of *paricchinna-janma-maraṇa* (segmented birth-and-death);

because *pariṇāmi-janma-maraṇa* (transformative birth-and-death) still remains, it is said that "in reality, they are not extinguished. The subsequent half-line speaks of fulfilling the original aspiration; therefore, it says "now."
That which ought to be performed is solely the wisdom of the Buddha. △ Second, the verse that explains in combination how [the teaching] is not in vain, in three parts:
First, explaining the principle that all are equally sons [of the Buddha], and thus should be equal.
If there is a bodhisattva who, amidst this assembly, can with a single mind listen to the true Dharma of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones...

Although those sentient beings transformed through skillful means are all bodhisattvas—if there are such bodhisattvas, then the sentient beings transformed by the three vehicles through skillful means are all former children of the Buddha with whom he established karmic connections;
because they likewise all equally possess the Buddha-nature of True Suchness (tathatā), it is said that "they are all bodhisattvas. △ Second.
Because beings were unable to be transformed [by the single vehicle], he taught the three vehicles.
For those of small wisdom who are deeply attached to craving and desire, he taught the Truth of Suffering for their sake;
sentient beings rejoiced at this, having attained what they had never experienced before, as the Buddha declared that the Truth of Suffering is real and without deviation.
Below this, it is correctly explained that those with limited wisdom who possess heavy obstacles regarding the four truths of conditioned existence do not immediately believe and accept them;
therefore, as a skillful means to guide those of limited wisdom, the Truth of Suffering is taught.

Among the three vehicles, the Śrāvaka is the most inferior, yet for those whose minds find joy by taking the Truth of Suffering as their initial gateway, it is said to accord with their original inclinations, and thus they rejoice.
Originally weary of birth and death, they sought nirvana for themselves; now, hearing of the escape from suffering, they immediately realize their past habitual tendencies.

Thus, their hearts rejoice in the truth, for there is no difference [between this and their original intent]. The *Śāsanānuśāsanī Sūtra* states: "The Buddha taught that the Truth of Suffering is truly suffering and cannot be made into pleasure.
The two lines following "all sentient beings" clarify the capacity (*mārga-sāmarthya*), while the two lines following "the Buddha" clarify the response (*pratisamvid*).

If there are sentient beings who do not know the root of suffering and are deeply attached to its causes, unable to abandon them even for a moment—for their sake, he employs skillful means to teach the Way, saying: "The cause of all sufferings has greed as its root."
The first line correctly elucidates the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*); since origination is the cause of suffering, it is called the "root of suffering.

Because sentient beings do not know this, they are deeply attached to it—this is shown by the following two lines. The subsequent two lines clarify that the Path (*mārga*) is able to remedy origination; the final two lines clarify the faults and afflictions (*ādīnava*) of origination.
If one extinguishes craving and has no further basis for existence, such that all suffering is utterly exhausted, this is called the Third Truth.

This clarifies the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): the first two phrases clarify the function of ceasing the origin of suffering (*samudaya*), namely that if the cause of the origin is extinguished, then suffering has no basis;
the latter two phrases clarify how the Truth of Cessation receives its name.
One cultivates the Path for the sake of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
This clarifies that the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) carries the meaning of "penetration," for it is able to penetrate through to the emptiness of true nirvana.
Briefly stated, this consists of morality, concentration, and wisdom; extensively stated, it comprises the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).
To be free from all bonds of suffering is called attaining liberation. From what does such a person attain liberation? Merely to be free from delusion is called liberation.

The first two phrases reiterate that attainment of liberation: "accumulation" (saṃskāra) is the binder, and "suffering" (duḥkha) is that which is bound; to be free from this suffering and its accumulation is [liberation].
The phrase "attaining liberation" refers to the latter two lines [of the verse], which inquire what kind of liberation is attained through the contemplation of the Truths.
The latter two lines provide the explanation: "merely departing from delusion" means that ignorance (*avidyā*) is already unreal;

since the afflictions of view and thought arise in dependence upon ignorance, they are termed "delusion. Some interpret this as meaning that one merely removes the four truths [from perception], and this is called liberation.

Because they have escaped the *paricchinna-udvartana* (segmented death) but have not yet escaped the *pariṇāma-udvartana* (transformational death), they are not sovereign. △ Third, explaining the latter:

"If they are capable of returning their [great] elements, in reality they have not attained all-encompassing liberation; the Buddha says that such persons have not truly entered parinirvāṇa, nor have they truly attained it."

Because of the Unsurpassed Way, it is not my intention that [beings] should enter parinirvāṇa; I have appeared in the world as the Dharma King, possessing mastery over the Dharma, for the sake of establishing sentient beings in peace and security.

All liberation is precisely the unconditioned Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya), and the Unsurpassed Way is precisely the unconditioned Truth of the Path (mārga-satya). This is the original intent of the Buddha.

I desire that all beings attain liberation; yet you have only now severed the bonds of the分段身 (pariccheda-deha) and realized the emptiness of true reality (śūnyatā), which is not yet the Great Nirvāṇa.
Because you have not attained universal liberation, it has never truly accorded with my original intention.
Therefore, I said, "It is not my wish for you to reach extinction"—this refers to the liberation of the Śrāvaka vehicle. Now, I shall instead cause you to attain the [Great] Nirvāṇa.

Entering Great Nirvana through the Supreme Path is the ultimate fulfillment of the Buddha’s original intention: the unconditioned path of cessation that shatters the unconditioned suffering and its origin.
Previously, the Buddha wished to preach this, but sentient beings were unable to bear it; now that their obstacles have been removed, he preaches it once more.
As the Dharma King, the Buddha has attained mastery over both provisional and ultimate teachings; thus, he opens the three provisional gates to reveal the One.
How could reality ever contain falsehood? △ Second, the exhortation to believe, which is also called the method for transmitting the sutra, has two parts.
First, the heading; second, the specific explanation. First, the heading:
"O Śāriputra, I have proclaimed this Dharma-seal of mine for the sake of benefiting the world."
The "Dharma Seal" (dharmamudrā) is precisely the aforementioned "Seal of True Reality" (bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā). The Tathāgata preached this Dharma Seal for the benefit of the world;
yet he did not preach it because for more than forty years it was not yet the time to do so, and because the five thousand [monks] had not yet departed. Thus, he did not preach it.
△ Second, the marking of what is universally applicable and what is not.
Wherever you travel, do not propagate [this teaching] recklessly.
If it is spoken to the wicked by force, they will fall into suffering; if it is not spoken to the good, they will lose their happiness through error.
If one has great compassion for the wicked, one should not transmit it; if one has great kindness for the good, one should indeed transmit it. △ Second, the explanation.
Second, first explaining what can be spoken and what cannot be spoken:
If there are those who hear this and rejoice in it, receiving it upon their heads, you should know that such persons are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive).
If there are those who believe in and accept the Dharma of this sutra, these persons have already seen past Buddhas, have reverently made offerings to them, and have also heard this Dharma.
If there are those who can believe what you have spoken, they shall see me, as well as you and the community of bhikṣus, along with all the bodhisattvas.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is taught for those of profound wisdom; those of shallow understanding, upon hearing it, will be confused and fail to comprehend it.
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are beyond the reach of its power within this sūtra, O Śāriputra.
If even they enter this sutra through faith, how much more so the other śrāvakas? Those other śrāvakas follow this sutra because they trust the Buddha’s words;
it is not within the scope of their own wisdom.
These eight lines of verse clarify the Tathāgata’s skillful means for benefiting the world, universally encompassing the benefit of the three periods of time.

A separate discussion states that it causes those of the Two Vehicles to enter faith; the first line concerns those who have attained *avaivartika*—translated here as "non-retrogression"—which refers to observing the present.
The phrase "those who have previously seen" refers to observing the past and is spoken for the sake of excellence.

The phrase "I believe you have seen me" refers to observing the future and is spoken for the sake of excellence. As the subsequent text says: "If one has deep faith and understanding, they see [the Buddha]."

"The Buddha is always on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa" is precisely that meaning. This passage from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—the single line concluding the "closing" (of the provisional) and opening the "below" (the ultimate)—is as follows:
"The Tathāgata perceives and knows the benefits of the three periods of time. Therefore, he preaches this to conclude the "above" (the provisional).
If those of shallow understanding hear it and are confused and fail to understand, then he does not preach this to open the "below" (the ultimate). This is the explanation of the Tathāgata.

This is the chapter on "Speaking and Not Speaking. △ Second, explaining what is communicable and what is not communicable. Part one: clarifying that the gate of great compassion does not involve speaking [to certain beings].

First, the explanation. First, clarifying that because they slander the sutra, they fall into the evil realms. Fourth: Great Compassion pities sentient beings and, fearing they will slander [the teaching], does not speak [to them].
Furthermore, Śāriputra, do not preach this sutra to those who are arrogant, indolent, or who harbor views of a self.
First, it is listed that those who are arrogant, indolent, or attached to a self and desires will inevitably give rise to evil slander and obtain evil retributions;
therefore, out of great compassion, one should not preach it to such evil persons.
Do not preach this to ordinary people of shallow understanding who are deeply attached to the five desires and cannot comprehend it upon hearing it.
△ Second, clarifying that those who slander it will fall into hell:
If a person does not believe and slanders this sutra, they sever the Buddha-seed of all the world.
Regarding those who sever the Buddha-seed of the world: the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* takes afflictions (*kleśa*) as the seed of the Tathāgata;

this [text] takes the three paths as its nature-seed, just as ice is the seed of water. The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* takes the study of prajñā for the sake of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) as the Buddha-seed;
this takes the nature of the efficient cause (*upādāna-hetu*) as the Buddha-seed. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* takes the principle of the mind-nature as [the Buddha-seed].

The nature of the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) for this grasping, which is never interrupted, constitutes the seed of Buddhahood; the present sutra clarifies that even minor wholesome deeds can lead to Buddhahood, and this grasping serves as the contributory cause (*pratyaya*) for the seed of Buddhahood.
If one does not believe that minor wholesome deeds can lead to Buddhahood, one severs the seed of Buddhas in the world.
Or again, those who frown and harbor doubts— listen now as I describe the retribution for the sins of such people. Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa,
if there are those who slander such a sutra as this, or who, upon seeing one reading,

reciting, copying, or upholding it, treat them with contempt, hatred, jealousy, and harbor resentment— the retribution for the sins of these people, listen further as I describe, shall follow when their lives come to an end.
They enter the Avīci Hell and remain there for a full kalpa; when that kalpa ends, they are reborn there again, continuing in this manner through incalculable kalpas.
△ Third, falling into the realm of animals:
having emerged from hell, they shall fall among animals, such as dogs or jackals, their forms emaciated, dark-complexioned, and afflicted with scabies and sores.
They are harassed by others and further despised and loathed by people; they are constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst until their flesh and bones wither away.
While alive they suffer agonizing torment, and at death they are struck by tiles and stones. Because they have severed the lineage of the Buddhas, they undergo this retribution for their sins.

The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "Among the animals, those said to 'sever the Buddha-seed' are precisely those who destroy the two causes—the conditional (*pratyaya*) and the direct (*hetu*).

The preceding passage refers to severing all worldly Buddha-seeds: lack of faith severs the Buddha-seed of the direct cause, while failing to practice even minor good deeds severs the Buddha-seed of the conditional cause.
This sutra universally opens the Buddha-seed for all six realms; yet if one slanders it..."
The meaning of this sutra should be understood as follows:
if one is reborn as a camel or among donkeys, their body must constantly carry heavy loads while being subjected to whips and beatings;
they think only of water and grass and know nothing else—this is because they have slandered this sutra and incurred such guilt. Furthermore, there are those who become jackals and enter villages.
With a body afflicted by scabies and leprosy, and missing one eye, he will be beaten and pelted by children, enduring various agonies that may even lead to death.
Having died there, he will further receive the body of a python, five hundred yojanas in length;
deaf, dull-witted, and footless, he will crawl on his belly and be devoured by small insects for slandering this sutra.
Such is the retribution for committing such offenses.

Because you disparaged the True Vehicle, you have summoned the retribution of being made to carry a donkey; because of your doubts and biased views, you have summoned the retribution of having one eye like a jackal.
That you now enter the village is driven by the power of your karma, seeking for yourself the blows and beatings you deserve.

The great python is by nature prone to much anger; this is the retribution for harboring resentment born of hatred and jealousy. Being deaf, it lacks hearing, and being dull-witted, it lacks understanding;
it is also of the class that does not believe. △ Fourth, clarifying those who fall into the state of lowly humans.
If one obtains a human birth, one's faculties will be dull and obscured; one will be short, deformed, lame, blind, deaf, or hunchbacked. Whatever one says, people will not believe or accept it;
one's breath will constantly smell foul, and one will be possessed by malevolent spirits. One will be poor, lowly, and treated as a servant by others;
plagued by many illnesses and emaciated, one will have no one to rely upon. Even when associating with others, they will pay one no heed; and whatever one may obtain—
Furthermore, they quickly forget what they have learned; if they practice medicine, they may treat illnesses according to prescriptions yet increase the patient's ailment or even cause death;
if they themselves fall ill, no one will provide relief, and even if they take excellent medicine, their condition worsens;
or they may suffer the calamitous consequences of such crimes as rebellion, plundering, or theft committed by others.
Because they despise the light of wisdom, their six sense faculties are dark and dull;

because they disparage the body of the True Dharma, they are short, deformed, and ugly, with hands that are cramped and feet that are lame. Whatever they say or speak is slander and defamation—the retribution for their verbal karma.
They are shunned and not befriended, even suffering calamities and offenses out of proportion; all such retributions are discordant because they do not accord with the correct principle.
The first part explains karmic retribution; the second explains retribution that is difficult to repay. △ Second, explaining how one fails to encounter a Buddha due to falling into the evil realms:
First, not encountering a Buddha.
Such a sinner shall never see the Buddha, the King of all Sages, preaching the Dharma to transform and teach them.
△ Second, they again enter the evil realms.
Such sinners are constantly born in difficult places; crazed, deaf, and mentally deranged, they never hear the Dharma for incalculable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
From birth after birth they are deaf and mute, their faculties incomplete, and they dwell perpetually in hell as if wandering through a pleasure garden.
In other evil realms, such as those of camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs—which are their dwelling places and spheres of activity—they incur such offenses because they slander this sutra.
"Constantly born in difficult circumstances" refers to the eight difficulties; "never seeing a Buddha" refers to the difficulty of being born either before or after a Buddha's appearance.
Never hearing the Dharma is the difficulty of worldly wisdom and eloquence; being suddenly deaf or mute is the difficulty of blindness, deafness, and muteness;
constantly dwelling in hell is the difficulty of hell; being a camel, a donkey, or the like is the difficulty of the animal realm;
and being in other evil destinies implies rebirth in Uttarakuru or among the long-lived devas. △ Third, furthermore, becoming a person of low status.
If they should obtain human form, they will be adorned with deafness, blindness, muteness, poverty, and various misfortunes;
they will have dropsy, consumption, scabies, leprosy, carbuncles, and so forth as their clothing; their bodies will constantly be foul-smelling, filthy, and impure;

they will be deeply attached to the view of self, increasing their anger, and their lust will blaze so fiercely that they do not distinguish between humans and beasts—this is because they slander this sutra.
The retribution for such offenses is as follows:
regarding illness, one speaks of it as a "garment" and finds it difficult to escape various decays;
the body is constantly impure, lust is fierce and indiscriminate, and by abandoning pure karma, one increases evil habits. △ Second, the conclusion.
I tell you, Śāriputra, that if one were to speak of the sins of those who slander this sutra, they could not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
For this reason, I say to you: do not preach this sutra among people who lack wisdom.
The *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) says: Question: "Is it the slander of the sutra that produces the transgression, or is the sutra itself the condition for the transgression?

Answer: "Transgressions and blessings arise from the mind; the sutra merely serves as a contributing condition. However, according to the Buddha’s original intent, [the teaching] is solely for the purpose of generating blessings.

Thus, this is the fault of the deluded person, not a defect in the path. II. Clarifying that the Gate of Great Compassion should preach [to them]. Part One: Directly clarifying that it may be preached to virtuous people. (5)
First, regarding the one pair of past and present [teachings]:
if there are those of sharp faculties whose wisdom is clear, who have heard much and possess strong memory, seeking the path of the Buddha—for such persons as these, one may then preach this.
Furthermore, if there are those who have previously seen hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, who have planted various roots of goodness, and whose deep resolve is firm and steadfast.
To such a person as this, one may preach.
Now, the essential point of propagating the Sūtra is to harmonize these two gates so that each finds its proper place; this is true propagation.
If they do not find their proper place, it is merely a false proclamation. Those of sharp faculties have planted roots of goodness in the present and possess strength from the past.
Consciousness is the present; that which was previously seen is the past. △ Second, the pair of "above and below":
If there is a person who is diligent and constantly cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, not begrudging even their own body or life, then for such a person one may preach it.

If there is a person who is respectful, free from divergent thoughts, and who has distanced themselves from all common fools to dwell alone in mountains and marshes—only for such a person may one preach it.
Cultivating loving-kindness is to have compassion for those below; showing reverence is to honor those above. △ Third, the pair of internal and external.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if you see someone who abandons evil associates and draws near to virtuous friends, such a person may be taught this.
If you see a son of the Buddha who maintains pure precepts like a polished bright pearl and seeks Mahāyāna sūtras...
For such a person, one may indeed preach this.
Abandoning evil and befriending the good is the external seeking of precepts; guarding them like a precious jewel is the internal protection. △ Fourth, the pair of self and others.
If there is a person who is free from anger, upright, gentle, and soft, who always has compassion for all beings and reveres all Buddhas—
only to such a person may you preach this. Furthermore, if there is a son of the Buddha who, amidst the great assembly, preaches the Dharma with a pure mind using various causes,
conditions, parables, and expressions without impediment— only to such a person may you preach this.
Being upright and sincere while revering the Buddha is the practice for oneself; teaching the Dharma through parables is for the transformation of others. △ Fifth, the pair of beginning and end:
If there is a bhikṣu who, for the sake of omniscience, seeks the Dharma in all four directions, receiving it with palms joined above his head and upholding it solely with joy.
To those who would not accept even a single verse from any other sutra, but only from the Mahāyāna scriptures—such persons may be taught.
Just as a person with a sincere heart seeks the relics of the Buddha, so too they seek these sutras; having obtained them, they receive them upon the crown of their head.
Such a person no longer aspires to seek other sutras, nor do they ever think of the texts of external paths. To such a person, one may indeed teach.

Seeking the Dharma in the four directions is the beginning of requesting instruction; receiving it upon the crown of one’s head and practicing it with single-minded devotion is the end of relying upon it.
△ Second, the summary of what may be said:
"Śāriputra, I say that for those who seek the Buddha-way according to these characteristics, even an entire eon would not suffice to describe them."
"Then you shall be able to believe and understand; I will preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for you.
This is the summary. As for the "characteristics," they refer to the characteristics of the five pairs and one single person—the virtuous ones mentioned above.
Although such virtuous characteristics are numerous, ten are briefly cited here to demonstrate the propagation [of the teaching].
△ Second, the attainment of understanding by those of middling faculties among those who have faith and resolve.
Part One: Title. *The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Four: "The Chapter on Faith and Resolve" (in the original text, this chapter is titled "The Chapter on Faith and Joy").
This chapter clarifies the faith and resolve of those with middling faculties. Indeed, faculties may be sharp or dull, and delusions may be thick or thin; likewise, the teachings spoken may vary.

For example, there is a sequence of awakening before and after [the teaching of the Lotus Sūtra]. Before the seat of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it was as if one were sitting upon broad beans; the text says:
"Since the Tathāgata had been preaching the Dharma for a long time, I was at that time seated in the assembly, my body weary and exhausted.

I contemplated only emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and regarding the Bodhisattva teachings, I lacked even a single thought of joy or inclination. When I first heard the brief exposition, my attachments were shaken and doubt arose; through hearing it extensively," [I attained realization].
The five Buddhas were obscured and had not yet awakened; now, hearing this parable, they leap for joy with exultation. (Worldly level) Faith arises and understanding is born;

(Human level) doubt is dispelled; (Counteractive level) the principle is clarified. Therefore, it is named the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (the causal condition). △ Second, the explanation of the text has two parts:
first, the sūtra-narrator describes the joy; second, the description of the internal mind. First, the description of the internal mind.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented teaching regarding the World-Honored One’s bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon Śāriputra,
gave rise to a rare and marvelous mind and leaped for joy.
Subhūti alone is called "Life of Wisdom" (*prajñājīvita*). The three times he is addressed as "Mahā" (Great One) can be discussed generally: in general, he is both great and wise;
in particular, Subhūti understands the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness as his life (in terms of practice). Among all forms of wisdom, the Buddha-wisdom is supreme.

Because the Buddha charged him with the *Prajñāpāramitā* to propagate the teaching, and because he was commissioned by those who possess wisdom, he is called "Life of Wisdom" (in terms of doctrine). As for the other three [disciples], they are not so designated.
It is not so because, being young when [the Buddha] was commanded, he did not take emptiness as the core of his practice.

The phrases "what he heard from the Buddha" and so forth describe the causes for attaining joy. Having heard from afar the Dharma taught in the "Expedient Means" chapter and seeing Śāriputra receive his prediction, he rejoices because he hears and sees what he has never experienced before.
To express the arising of this rare mind, the narrator states that he has recently heard it.
For example, because the rare mind gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, it is called "faith" (*śraddhā*);

by means of this faith, one enters [the path], specifically the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), which is the intended meaning of the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding. △ Second, the description of external veneration.
He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with a single-minded focus joined his palms.
Bowing his body in reverence, he gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance.

Following the example of Śāriputra above, he likewise attained realization through the three karmas; he gave rise to a rare and marvelous mind, which constitutes realization through the mind. That is to say:
Rising from his seat to receive the instruction, he addressed the Buddha, speaking these words of understanding.

△ Second, his own address to the Buddha, which has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part [the prose] also has two sections: first, the brief explanation by way of Dharma; second, the detailed explanation by way of analogy.

The first of these [the brief explanation] also has two sections: first, the actual teaching of the Dharma; second, the brief citation of analogies. The first of these [the actual teaching] also has two sections: first, the clarification...
In the past, because we received the three [privileges], we did not seek the two [others]. First, the three are presented:
first, because we occupy the headship of the Saṃgha, we said to the Buddha, "We occupy the headship of the Saṃgha.

This clarifies the three things we do not seek. To describe our former failure: first, regarding occupying the headship of the Saṃgha, our dharma-ordination years (*dharma-varṣa*) are already advanced, whereas those who study late...
Taking me as their model, they suddenly changed their path and altered their course, abandoning the small for the great; thus they incurred the resentment of those who came after.
Because they sought to protect themselves and others, they did not seek [the Way]. △ Second, because his secular age had advanced.
Both of us are advanced in years.
Regarding those in the secular world whose years have already declined: if one were to become a Bodhisattva, one should single-mindedly undertake the Great Way to extensively deliver sentient beings.
Now that we are decrepit and old, we are incapable of such tasks; therefore, we do not seek it. △ Third, because [the goal] has already been realized.
They claimed to have already attained *nirvāṇa* and were incapable of further striving for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"World-Honored One, when you had long been dwelling in the past teaching the Dharma, I was at that time seated among the assembly;

my body was weary and exhausted, and I thought only of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, rather than regarding the Bodhisattva teachings, the playful exercise of supernormal powers, the purification of Buddha-fields, or their accomplishment."
Sentient beings do not find joy in this.
Third, having already attained the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) state of parinirvāṇa, they are unable to give rise to the Great Mind;

just as lotuses do not grow on high plateaus or dry land, it is said that they lack the capacity [for it]. Having exhausted the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), they are established in a state of no further reliance or seeking.

Therefore, it is said that one no longer seeks further toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) are called the three gates of liberation.

Contemplating all phenomena as being without self or what belongs to a self is called the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). If the characteristics of male and female, identity and difference, and so forth, are truly unobtainable, this is called signlessness (*animitta*).
If one knows that all phenomena are signless and entirely without activity, this is called wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Furthermore, to have no aspirations or seeking within the three realms is called "wishlessness" (apraṇihita). △ Second, the explanation [of the two aspects]:
first, the explanation of attaining nirvana without seeking.
Why is this? The World-Honored One has caused us to emerge from the three realms and attain the realization of nirvana.
Why is this? [The text] explains the three "non-seekings," though the wording is not in sequential order; first, it explains the non-seeking of attaining *nirvāṇa*.
△ Second, it explains being advanced in years:
"Furthermore, we are now already decrepit in age regarding the Buddha’s transformation of bodhisattvas toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
He did not give rise to even a single thought of longing for the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*).

Next, regarding the interpretation of "advanced in years" (*vṛddha*), it implies that he does not seek the leadership of the Saṃgha; alternatively, it refers to the fact that because he has long been preaching the Dharma, his mind no longer finds joy in it.

This explains that although he resides at the head of the Saṃgha, he does not seek [such status]. Since it is said that he is already seated there, yet further mentions his being "aged," one knows this refers to Śāriputra.
The Head of the Sangha. △ Second, explaining that one naturally attains [the goal] because the present assembly is one.
"We who have now heard before the Buddha the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the śrāvakas feel great joy in our hearts;
we have attained what we never had before, for we did not expect to suddenly hear such a rare Dharma at this time."
I am deeply grateful and fortunate to have attained this great and wholesome benefit.
This account of how I attained understanding is based on what I heard from afar; it briefly presents two aspects and extensively unfolds three to reveal one.

Therefore, regarding "being deeply grateful and fortunate to have attained this great and wholesome benefit," this is the formal presentation of how I attained understanding based on what I heard nearby, consisting of four analogies.
This is a metaphor for obtaining the excellent benefit of awakening through the rare and marvelous Dharma. △ Second, a brief presentation of analogies:
immeasurable treasures obtained without seeking.

This is a metaphor for how, though not previously sought, one now spontaneously attains the rare treasure of the Dharma and its wondrous bliss. It says: "In the past, [one] did not seek it, yet now one spontaneously attains... [This refers to] the *Prajñāpāramitā* leading [the way].

The teaching refers to the Dharma for Bodhisattvas; who would have imagined that we would now receive this complete and equal bestowal? △ Second, the detailed explanation through parables, which has two parts:
first, opening the parable, and second, applying the parable. The first part [opening the parable] further has two sections: first, the inquiry and exhortation.
“World-Honored One, we now wish to speak by means of an analogy to clarify this meaning.

As it is said in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*, when one wishes to resolve a matter according to worldly etiquette, one must first consult and initiate the discussion. **Part Two: Expounding the Analogies (4)** 1.
The Analogy of Father and Son Losing Sight of Each Other; 2. The Analogy of Father and Son Meeting; 3. The Analogy of the Father’s Command to Pursue and Entice Him.
The analogy of entrusting the family business has four parts, corresponding to the first section of the text, which also has four parts: first, the son turns his back on the fire and departs;
second, he first turns his back on his father and departs.
It is as if there were a man who, being still young, abandoned his father and fled, dwelling in another country for ten or twenty years.

Reaching the age of fifty, it is like a person who has twenty sons; this illustrates how the stages and practices of the Bodhisattva path are difficult for those of the Two Vehicles to know, as they have merely attained a level of understanding that is still immature.
Since their years are young, ignorance is thick and heavy, obscuring and covering the mind of liberation.

Because they lack power, they are called "infants"; "fleeing from their father" refers to those who have regressed from the Great [Vehicle]. To "abandon" means to cast off ignorance; to "cover oneself" means to conceal it. To "flee" means to head toward birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Question: Does the Buddha abandon his response after sentient beings give rise to delusions? Is it that the father leaves the son, or that the son abandons the father? Answer: It is because sentient beings do not evoke the Buddha that he passes away; thus, the fault lies with them. Furthermore, it is established that when the Buddha appears in the world, he does so for the sake of those who can perceive him. If sentient beings do not perceive him, he likewise departs. Therefore, it is the sentient beings who fail to respond, not the Buddha who abandons them. Thus, the Buddha’s departure is due to the lack of conditions on the part of sentient beings. This is why it is said that the father leaves the son. Furthermore, the Buddha’s appearance in the world is like a great cloud covering the sky; if there is no rain, it is not the fault of the cloud, but rather the fault of the earth being parched and unable to receive it. Likewise, the Buddha’s teaching is like rain; if sentient beings do not receive it, it is not the fault of the Buddha, but rather the fault of the sentient beings themselves. Therefore, it is said that the father leaves the son. Moreover, the Buddha’s appearance in the world is like a great physician who possesses the medicine of the Dharma. If the patient does not take the medicine, it is not the fault of the physician, but rather the fault of the patient’s own illness. Likewise, if sentient beings do not follow the Buddha’s teachings, it is not the fault of the Buddha, but rather the fault of the sentient beings’ own afflictions.

Therefore, it is said that the father leaves the son. Finally, the Buddha’s appearance in the world is like a great king who bestows wealth upon his subjects. If the subjects do not accept the wealth, it is not the fault of the king, but rather the fault of the subjects’ own greed. Likewise, if sentient beings do not accept the Buddha’s gifts of merit and wisdom, it is not the fault of the Buddha, but rather the fault of the sentient beings’ own attachment. Therefore, it is said that the father leaves the son. Thus, the Buddha’s departure is established by the fact that sentient beings do not evoke him. It is not that the Buddha abandons them. This is the meaning of "the father leaves the son. Furthermore, the Buddha’s appearance in the world is like the rising of the sun. If there is no light, it is not the fault of the sun, but rather the fault of the darkness of the world. Likewise, if sentient beings do not see the Buddha, it is not the fault of the Buddha, but rather the fault of the darkness of ignorance within sentient beings. Therefore, it is said that the father leaves the son. Consequently, the Buddha’s departure is established by the lack of response from sentient beings; it is not that the Buddha abandons them. This is the definitive meaning.

The meaning of "the son leaves his father" and "dwells long in another country" is as follows: the *dharmadhātu* of *nirvāṇa* is the Buddha’s own country, whereas the five desires (*pañcakāma*) of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) constitute another country.
Because one originally sought liberation but subsequently fell back and did not return, it is said that he "dwells long in another country.
Alternatively, ten [years] refer to the heavenly realm, twenty to the human realm, and fifty to the five paths of existence; this is explained in terms of...
Because one person may be equipped with wheels for various paths, it is said that "there may be ten," and so forth. △ Second, returning toward the origin.
As his years grew and he became further impoverished, he traveled in all directions in search of food and clothing;
gradually wandering on, he encountered his way back to his native land.
When their roots of goodness have been gradually permeated and they begin to desire renown, they are called "grown up.
Yet, while within the three realms, they do not see the Buddha-Father and fail to obtain the essential method for liberation. Thus, they are impoverished by the eight sufferings and scorched by fire;
thus, they are distressed as they rush about in the four directions seeking food and clothing. Before the Buddha appeared, all ordinary worldlings relied upon body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
The Dharma arises from the four inverted views; to seek the Right Path therein is like seeking food, and to seek the Path of Assistance is like seeking clothing.

To seek the Principle through weariness with suffering constitutes the conditions for being transformable. This refers to the meaning that when the Buddha first appeared in the world, those of various non-Buddhist paths were all the first to attain deliverance.
The phrase "gradually traveling and encountering [them] as they head toward their own country" clarifies this point.

The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), weary of suffering and seeking liberation, falsely pursue nirvana; although this was not their original intention, they nonetheless encountered the Buddha, which is why it is said they "met" him.
Their native land is as described above. △ Second, the father’s search for his son and his halting midway, in two parts:
first, failing to find the son.
His father had previously come seeking his son but could not find him.

After those of the Two Vehicles had regressed from the Great Vehicle, the Buddha constantly sought a suitable capacity (the *mārga*), yet because no such capacity manifested, it is said that he "could not find him.
△ Second, stopping at a city.
He halts at one city.

To halt at one city means that one does not abandon the family business for the sake of a single son; likewise, the Buddha does not abandon the transformation of other regions because there is no potential for conversion in one place.
By means of skillful means, he takes the Land of Abundant Resources as his kingdom, while the Land of Common Dwelling is the reality.
The recompense for the two realms is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), while the remainder of *nirvāṇa* is the city. Abiding in this *nirvāṇa* is called the place of rest;
this is the home. Therein arise two types of responses, superior and inferior: the inferior response responds to śrāvakas, and the superior response responds to bodhisattvas.
Those five classes of people who have severed the pervasive delusions are reborn together in that land, all becoming bodhisattvas, and are trained solely in the family business of the Mahāyāna.
He caused them to train and study until they reached this point of seeking out the means to dwell together with their sons.
That family was immensely wealthy, possessing immeasurable treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and crystal beads;
all their granaries and treasuries were completely overflowing, and they had many servants, ministers, officials, and subjects, as well as elephants, horses, and carriages.
Cattle and sheep are innumerable, and the profits from their coming and going extend even to other countries; merchants and traders are likewise exceedingly numerous.

Taking the realm of true reality (*dharmatā*) as the household, the ten thousand virtues as wealth, the five perfections and merit as riches, and Prajñā-wisdom as treasure—leading all toward the Mahāyāna is what constitutes the immeasurable gold, silver, pearls, and so forth.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in the Mahāyāna correspond to the meaning of the Elder’s great wealth mentioned above.

A granary is for storing rice, while a storehouse is for storing goods; the granary is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), because it gives rise to the one hundred and eight samādhis, and the storehouse is a metaphor for the true nature (*dharmatā*), because it can produce the wisdom of the eighteen emptinesses (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*).
To provide for oneself is "overflowing" (internal abundance), and to transform others is "spilling over" (external diffusion); this corresponds to what was mentioned above.
"Having many fields and houses" signifies having many servants and attendants; this is a metaphor for being fully endowed with the perfections (*pāramitās*) of skillful means, knowledge, and insight.

"Bending and curving according to the occasion" means responding to circumstances and conforming to both phenomena and principle; it also carries the sense of having many followers and retinues. Speaking in terms of their respective positions:

the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), as well as the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) and the thirty minds of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-bhūmi*), are all like this.

The *tongpu* (attendants) correspond to the Separate Teaching; the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching correspond to ministers; the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*) correspond to assistants; the ten practices (*caryā*) correspond to clerks;
and the ten abidings (*vihāra*) correspond to commoners who have first entered the realm of the Buddha.

Although all those within the borders of the land are subjects of the king, even though they have attained the status of commoners, they are still distant compared to the clerks and assistants. In the ten practices, one cultivates various dharmas through distinct and sequential training.
Driving and galloping are like the officials of the tenth *pariṇāmanā*, for their engagement with principle and phenomena is somewhat deeper and their office is closer to that of the King.
Thus they are like the assistants (*zuo*). The ten stages (*bhūmi*) assist the Buddha in his transformative activities, subduing demons and overcoming adversaries; thus they are like ministers.

The threefold contemplation within a single mind is like an elephant carrying the Perfect Teaching Mahāyāna. The sequential threefold contemplation is like a horse carrying the Distinct Teaching Mahāyāna, which is "immediately empty."

The analytical contemplation of emptiness (*vibhāga-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is like the transport of oxen, such as those in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra* and other Mahāyāna teachings that employ the analytical method (*vibhāga-dharma-vipaśyanā*).

Self-cultivation is like the transport of deer, sheep, and so forth, referring to the methods of the Two Vehicles (*dvi-yāna*). As for the "innumerable," all provisional and ultimate teachings are called "vehicles" (*yāna*);
the provisional and ultimate contemplative wisdoms are called "elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep. Thus, not only are the teachings manifold, but the contemplative wisdoms are likewise innumerable.
Furthermore, "entering and exiting" means that duality is non-dual when one enters, and non-duality is dual when one exits.

Moreover, employing the power of transformation for others is "exiting," while employing the power of self-cultivation is "entering. Using the Dharma to benefit sentient beings is "exiting," and withdrawing the transformative function to return the merit to oneself is "entering.
To "pervade other lands" means to pervade the three lands; to "practice where there is no path" means to attain thorough penetration of the Buddha-way.
This is precisely its meaning: the Dharma-nature alone is one’s own country; all that lies outside the Dharma-nature is termed another country.

When Bodhisattvas of this land go to other quarters to hear the Dharma, or Great Beings of other quarters come to this land to hear the sutras, their coming and going to gather such benefits is like that of merchants.
Furthermore, they enter everywhere—the Land of True Reward, the Land of Expedient Means, and the Land of Common Residence—in order to seek [the Dharma].
It is said that they are "numerous" because of the benefits of the Dharma. △ Third, the son’s arrival at his father’s city. Part one: the reasons for arriving at the city.
At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages and passed through kingdoms and towns.
Because they lack the merit, qualities, and wealth of the Mahāyāna, they are called "poor sons. Having fallen away from the Great Vehicle, they have encountered all manner of sufferings;
they have developed a deep sense of revulsion toward them and sought liberation. However, their grasp of the principle was incorrect, leading them to fall into heterodoxy.
Although such false wisdom has permeated their minds, it is easy for them to enter the correct path. Their aspiration for transcendence serves as the very cause for encountering a Buddha.
With false wisdom, one observes the five aggregates as a village, the twelve bases as a town, and the eighteen elements as a kingdom;
seeking the principle through these is called "seeking food and clothing. △ Second, he eventually reaches his father’s city.
He then arrived at the city where his father resided.

Because he had previously relied on deviant wisdom to assist the conditions for the formation of the capacity for awakening and thereby invoked the Great Compassion of the Buddha, it is said that he "arrived at the city"; this city is none other than *nirvāṇa*.

Since *nirvāṇa* encompasses both the *Hīnayāna* (half) and the *Mahāyāna* (full), when the delusions of sentient beings are exhausted, there is the sense of being able to attain *nirvāṇa*; hence the statement.
He arrived at the city. △ Fourth, his father’s anxious thoughts, in two parts: First, the suffering of missing his son.
Every time the father thought of his son, he reflected on their separation for over fifty years; yet he had never spoken of such a matter to anyone.
He merely pondered it within himself, harboring regret and remorse. He thought to himself that he was old and infirm, yet possessed much wealth, gold, silver, and precious treasures.
His treasuries were overflowing with jewels, yet he had no offspring; once he passed away, his wealth would be dispersed and lost, as there was no one to whom it could be entrusted.
For this reason, he remembered his son with constant and earnest longing.
Because the Tathāgata has constantly contemplated his son’s great capacity from the past until now, he says, "I have always been mindful [of you].

Because he has wandered through the five realms since regressing from the Great Vehicle, he says, "I have been separated from my son for over fifty years. Because he reveals the realm of ghosts and brings forth those of the asuras, he says, "The rest.
"Never before spoken" means that he has never previously addressed the ministers, officials, and commoners within the lands of expedient means.

This explains the karmic conditions for having such a son. Furthermore, since his appearance in this world, during the various assemblies on the *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* sutras, he has never spoken to the great bodhisattvas that these śrāvakas were originally sons of the Mahāyāna.

Because they were not [aware of themselves as] sons of the Buddha, they did not understand the Buddha-dharma; some were like those who are deaf or mute, some left the flowers to prostrate at the seats, and others abandoned them.

The bowl was bewildered and utterly failed in its various functions; those whose hearts harbored regret and remorse repented that in the past they had not been diligent in instructing and admonishing, thereby causing [the child] to lack training and flee away.
They lamented that the child did not contemplate their kindness and righteousness, distancing himself from them to seek kinship with others.

Internally, this was like the Tathāgata repenting that he had not been earnest in leading [them] inward, allowing ordinary people to eventually cause him to lose his original understanding; they lamented that such was the case.
Because the mind was unable to exert diligence and firm resolve, fleeing into delusion without returning, it is said that there is regret and remorse.
To think of one's own decrepitude is to realize that the time for transformation is drawing to a close, yet there is no one to transmit the Great Dharma, like an old man who has no son.
△ Second, the joy of obtaining a son.
He further reflects: "If I were to obtain a son to whom I could entrust my wealth and possessions, I would be at ease and happy, free from further anxiety.
When there is a capacity for deliverance, it is called "obtaining a son"; bestowing upon him the prediction of Buddhahood is called "entrusting the Dharma-wealth," which accords with [the analogy].
The fundamental mind further speaks of the joy; this concludes the general analogy. △ Second, the analogy of father and son meeting, in two parts.
First, the son seeing his father, in four parts. First, the cause for seeing the father.
World-Honored One, at that time the impoverished son, wandering about in search of employment, happened to come upon his father’s house.

This clarifies the analogy of the father and son meeting: it refers proximately to seeing the fire within the burning house, and distantly to seeing the five turbidities within the *upāya* (expedient means).
This is the cause for the first meeting with the father; through weariness with suffering and a longing for joy, he gradually seeks out the flavor of the principle.
Because gradual accumulation and habituation eventually result in supramundane roots of goodness, it is said that "he works for hire.

Because he can, through these successive roots of goodness, strike upon the Buddha’s compassion, it is said that "he encounters his father's house. Here, the father is a metaphor for the Dharma-body after the Path;

the house is a metaphor for unconditional compassion (*nirālambana-karuṇā*). Thus, the two capacities—the Great and the Small—simultaneously strike this house. △ Second, the place where he sees his father.
Standing by the side of the gate, he saw his father from afar.

"By the side of the gate" is a metaphor for the two contemplations (*dvividha-vipaśyanā*) serving as the skillful means; that is, the capacity for the "round" [Middle Way] situated between the two sides of the gate.

Because the Two Vehicles perceive only the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*), they are said to be "by the side of the gate"; it refers to the emptiness samādhi and the biased wisdom-eye of partial truth looking on from the side.

Regarding "Peering at the Dharma-body and seeing his father from afar": this means that the great capacity has only just begun to arise, and the act of knocking upon and summoning [the Buddha] is distant;
hence it is called "from afar. Furthermore, because the capacity is subtle and not yet responsive, it is termed "distant. △ Third, the appearance of seeing the father.
Seated upon a lion throne with precious footstools supporting his feet, he was surrounded by all the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and householders who paid him respectful homage.
Adorning his body with pearl necklaces worth ten million, he was attended on both sides by officials, citizens, and servants holding white whisks;
a precious canopy was spread above him, various flower banners were hung down, and fragrant water was sprinkled upon the ground while a multitude of flowers was scattered about.
With rows of famous flowers and various precious objects displayed for taking and giving, such diverse adornments and majestic power are uniquely sublime.

As for "sitting upon the lion throne," it signifies that the perfect retribution body (*vipākaphala-dharmakāya*) dwells peacefully in the principle of emptiness, free from both the pervasive and specific delusions.

Because he is free from the fear of the eight māras and other such terrors, it is said that he sits upon a lion throne; the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* explains that the lion throne consists of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).

As for the jeweled footstool supporting his feet, the ultimate truth (*satyārtha*) serves as the stool, and the meditative concentration and wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda*) rely upon the realm of *tathatā*.
The term "Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) refers to a noble clan of pure conduct who are lofty and pure; this signifies the state of Equal Enlightenment (*samayaksa-bodhi*), which is free from defilement.
The Bodhisattvas who are Kṣatriyas of royal lineage are those from the first bhūmi up to the ninth bhūmi.
The laypeople (gṛhapati) who are wealthy but not of noble birth are those of the thirty minds (triṃśac-cittotpāda).
The pearl necklaces are the four necklaces of precepts, concentration, wisdom, and dhāraṇī. Their value of ten million is the merit of the forty stages (bhūmi).
Virtue serves to adorn the Dharma-body. Regarding the officials, commoners, and servants:

if they clarify the meaning according to the "different gate" (i.e., the distinct teachings), those who receive the two teachings of the *āgama* (Tripitaka) and *vaipulya* (Shared) and sever the delusions of the shared [realm] are called "commoners"; those who receive the *pratyekabuddha* (Distinct) teaching and sever the delusions of the shared [realm] are called "officials.
If they clarify the meaning according to the "same gate" (i.e., the Mahayana), this is still the *pāramitā* of skillful means. Internally, it provides...

True wisdom is identical to the external; it accords with conditions and serves as a metaphor for the relationship between officials and the common people, which carries the meaning of internal service and external labor.

The white fly-whisk represents the function of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). As for "left and right": the right refers to the function of the wisdom that enters emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which sweeps away the dust of the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*);
the left refers to the function of the wisdom that enters the conventional (*prajñapti*), which sweeps away the dust of ignorance. These two constitute the Middle Way.
Because it is a skillful means (*upāya*) of the Path, it is said that attending and standing by him while covering him with a jeweled canopy is true compassion (*karuṇā*).
Hanging various flowered banners: the flowers are the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and the banners are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Sprinkling fragrant water upon the ground is the water of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), used to sprinkle upon those whose minds are scattered. Scattering various named flowers means spreading the flowers of the seven purities (*saptaviśuddhi*), namely, morality (*śīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*).
