"Wisdom" refers to the purification of knowledge regarding what is the path and what is not the path, and the purification of knowledge through abandonment.

"Precepts" refer to the three types of precepts, such as the restraint of moral discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*). "Concentration" refers to samādhis such as the Śūraṅgama. "Wisdom" refers to ultimate wisdom (*prajñā*).

"Abandoning doubt" means having already transcended doubts concerning the two truths. "Purification regarding what is the path and what is not the path" means that while practicing on what is not the path, one penetrates [to the path].
"Attaining the Buddha-way" means that the purity of knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana-viśuddhi*) is perfected, clearly seeing the Buddha-nature.

"Purity of abandonment and knowledge" (*prahāṇajñāna-viśuddhi*) means the perfection of the virtue of abandonment, wherein ignorance is forever exhausted. "Arranging precious objects" means arranging the true merits of the various stages (*bhūmi*).
"Bringing forth and taking in" has the same meaning as the previous "entering and exiting"; it refers to the practice undertaken for oneself.
To transform others, one must manifest as the Honored One of Sovereign Power, with boundless radiance and a sea of boundless physical forms;
this principle necessitates that one become a Śākyamuni Buddha—how could it possibly be any other Śākya?
△ Fourth, the arising of a mind of fear and avoidance.
Upon seeing his father’s great power and majesty, the impoverished son was immediately seized by terror and regretted having come here; he thought to himself in secret:
"This man must be either a king or a royal official; this is no place for me to earn wealth through labor.

It would be better to go to the poor quarters where there is a place to exert my strength, and where food and clothing are easily obtained. If I remain here long, I may be coerced and forced [into servitude]."
Having formed this thought, I fled away in haste.
"Great Power" (Mahābala) refers to the greatness of wisdom; "Great Might" (Mahāsthāmaprāpta) refers to the greatness of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

This is in the same sense as having strength in one's hands and body above. "Terrified" means that those of small capacity, being weak and inferior, are timid and fearful of the Great Way. "Regret" [is as follows].

As for those who have come here, the Buddha originally intended to present them with the Great Dharma; however, as their faculties did not correspond to the teaching, they harbored a desire to retreat from the Great Vehicle.
Thus it is said that they "regret having come here" and "privately harbor such thoughts. These thoughts exist secretly within their faculties in a hidden and subtle manner;

they are not manifest before the eyes, yet they exist because they perceive the Victorious Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Therefore, it is said they "privately think," or perhaps it refers to the king.

The term "and so forth" refers to the followers of Pāpīyān, the king’s retinue; they are of inferior capacity who have severed all traces like ashes and maintain a path of wordlessness that transcends form and appearance.

Upon seeing the image of the Supreme Response Body—which is beyond the reach of gods and humans—and hearing the Dharma taught, which is utterly distinct from the limited wisdom of the Two Vehicles, these beings of meager merit, having never before seen or heard such things, immediately claim it is Māra and that it was spoken by Māra.
Furthermore, the Dharma-body is like a king and the Reward-body is like a king’s attendant;

these belong to the Mahāyāna teachings and rewards, not to the place where one gains benefit through the Hīnayāna. Therefore, [the Buddha] thought to himself: "Perhaps they are kings or their attendants, and not places where my laborers might obtain goods.
This is because those of small capacity cannot receive the Great Transformation. It would be better, therefore, to go to the poor quarters.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that one can deliver these inferior beings by means of the dharmas they delight in when impoverished. However, the principle of emptiness alone does not encompass the myriad virtues;

it is not the *tathāgatagarbha*. Therefore, it is said that the "poor district" is characterized by a partial emptiness, corresponding to the wisdom of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Thus, it is said that there is ground upon which to exert effort;
relying on this wisdom of the Small Vehicle, one may attain the nirvāṇa with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) and practice the conduct of untainted food and clothing.
Because practice is called clothing and wisdom is called food, it is said that "clothing and food are easily obtained.
Because those who dwell here for a long time travel the path of the Mahāyāna through immeasurable kalpas, it is said they "dwell for a long time.

Because I was originally weary of and terrified of birth and death, yet if one cultivates the Mahāyāna one must necessarily enter birth and death to extensively study the myriad practices, it is said that [this] "oppresses me," as I originally delighted in the Lesser Vehicle.
Now, to cause me to give rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna is to force me to abandon the Great and take up the Small; therefore, it is said that he "ran swiftly.
△ Second, the father sees his son, in four parts: First, the place where the father sees his son.
At that time, the wealthy elder was upon the lion throne—the lion throne being the place from which the son is perceived.
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body dwells in the realm of the first-principle emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) and fearlessness, illuminating the capacities of sentient beings.
△ Second, seeing the son and immediately recognizing him.
"Upon seeing his son, he recognized him.
"Upon seeing his son, he recognized him" means that the Tathāgata, discerning the capacities of beings, knew him to be a sentient being with whom he had established a karmic connection in the past.
△ Third, "seeing his son, he rejoiced."
The mind is filled with great joy.
As for "the mind is filled with great joy": the Buddha constantly observes his son's capacity; now that this capacity has arisen in accordance with his compassion, he is therefore joyful.
This is the arousal of great compassion following the previous discourse on the Dharma; it corresponds to the state of "great alarm and fear" within the parable.
That [the father] "is startled and afraid" indicates that he possesses great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for the purpose of uprooting suffering;
that he "rejoices" indicates that he possesses great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) for the purpose of bestowing happiness.
△ Fourth, seeing that his son’s wish has been fulfilled, he immediately thinks: "My wealth and treasuries now have someone to whom they may be entrusted; I have constantly longed for this son."
Upon seeing him, he suddenly came of his own accord, which was most agreeable to my wishes; though I am now advanced in years, I still cherish [this treasure].

In the past, I saw sentient beings decline from the Mahāyāna to take up the Hīnayāna, seeking food in impoverished neighborhoods and struggling to sustain their lives; I constantly desired to give them wealth, but finding no opportunity, I could not do so.
Today that opportunity has arrived, coinciding with my heart of great compassion; therefore, I say: "The treasury is now open."
That which I have been constantly mindful of as entrusted to me clarifies that it is not merely because [the beings] are poor and lack great wealth;
rather, they are tormented by the manifold sufferings of saṃsāra and are objects of my great compassion, and thus I am constantly mindful of them.

Yet, although I wish to rescue and deliver them, they lack the capacity and cannot be saved; therefore, it was said, "there is no way to see them. Now, however, the capacity for deliverance has arisen, and thus it is said, "and suddenly..."
"Because he has long been called 'Great Compassionate One,' it is said that this greatly accords with my wishes.
As for the reason why he says "I, though old in years, still cherish [this teaching]," it is because his period of transformation in this world has come to an end; thus he says he is "old in years.

Since he has not yet encountered a great vessel to whom the Dharma may be entrusted, from whom could those who are yet to be delivered find liberation? Therefore, [he cherishes it] so that there may be those who can be saved.
As for the statement, "I do not worry that those who are currently greedy and stingy will not come of their own accord; therefore, my wish is fulfilled," it is as follows:

△ Third, the analogy of pursuing and inducing [others], which has two parts. First, sending someone to seize [them]. First, receiving the previous section on the gate of exhortation to assess whether there is a receptive capacity (móu), which has two parts.
First, the assessment of suitability.
He immediately dispatched an attendant to pursue and bring him back; at that time, the messenger ran swiftly to seize him.

This refers to the present occasion of leading [the practitioner] through the *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra], where one now leads them through the "Gate of Exhortation" (*kuan-men*) above, which is the intended application. Regarding the phrase "dispatching an attendant":

wisdom is that which dispatches, and teaching is that which is dispatched; the principle is the primary, while the teaching is the secondary. From the Buddha, the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-buddhavacana*) emerge.
It is intended that sentient beings who lack the capacity will not receive [the teaching], just as milk is not accepted by them;
therefore, it is said that "attendants are sent away. Furthermore, "attendants" refers to ministers and assistants;

this means that Dharma-body Bodhisattvas are dispatched to preach the Mahāyāna, such as when the four Bodhisattvas are made to expound the forty stages (*bhūmi*) within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—this is what is meant by sending away the attendants.

Regarding "pursuing them urgently to bring them back," this means that the Great Teaching was intended for those of lesser capacity; thus it is said they were pursued urgently because they previously possessed great potential, hence the term "bringing them back.
Regarding "running swiftly to seize them," this refers to the clear and manifest meaning of the Mahāyāna, which is straightforward and direct.
By employing this to meet the needs of sentient beings, one causes them to hasten toward Bodhi; therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Vehicle) Sūtra says, "its speed is like the wind."
If one takes a bodhisattva as a bystander, that bodhisattva, possessing their own supernatural powers and further empowered by the Buddha, can also cause that person to swiftly enter Bodhi.
△ Second, those lacking the capacity [for enlightenment].
The impoverished son was startled and alarmed, crying out in resentment and shouting, "I have committed no offense against you; why do you seize me?

Because he lacked the capacity for the Gate of Encouragement at the beginning, and because his aspiration for the Great Vehicle—though perhaps once awakened in the past under the Lesser Vehicle—had long been abandoned and forgotten, he was shocked upon suddenly hearing the Great Teaching.

It was because it contradicted his mind that he was startled, and because he did not recognize it that he was alarmed; thus it is said, "the impoverished son was startled and alarmed" due to the Lesser Vehicle.
To take afflictions as enemies and birth-and-death as suffering, yet to exhort others that "afflictions are precisely bodhi," is like raising a great cry while accusing them of injustice.
To hear that "birth-and-death is precisely nirvana" is like raising a great cry while lamenting one's own pain; therefore, it is said: "Raising a great cry while accusing them of injustice.
[The Buddha asked: "I originally did not seek 'Great' (Mahāyāna); for what reason have you used 'Great' to transform me? Thus he said: "I do not recognize it."
"What offense has he committed that he is being seized? △ Second, accepting the aforementioned gate of admonition to prepare for those without the capacity, in two parts: first, preparing for them.
The messenger held him even more tightly, forcibly dragging him back.

Regarding the "Chapter on Admonitions," the Master’s instruction that one must apply oneself with ever-increasing urgency means that while the previous exhortations to do good were still characterized by complacency, I shall now explain matters of dread;
this constitutes an urgent admonition through harsh words intended to cause one to distance oneself from evil.
When there is no internal capacity [for understanding] yet one is externally constrained by the Great Transformation, this is what is meant by being forcibly led back. △ Second: Absence.
At that time, the impoverished son thought to himself, "I am innocent, yet I have been imprisoned; this must mean certain death.
He became even more terrified, fainted, and fell prostrate upon the ground.
In the "Chapter on Admonishing the Leaders," it is said that those who lack the karmic affinity and consider themselves sinless are, in fact, the truly sinful; this is the meaning of compassion.
Because sentient beings commit sins, they enter the prison of birth and death. Because Bodhisattvas possess compassion, they likewise incur the same "sin" and enter the prison.

Those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) lack compassion and are thus termed "sinless"; yet to cause them to enter the prison of birth and death is precisely to subject them to imprisonment.

Because one enters the cycle of birth and death without great skillful means, one will inevitably and forever lose the life-force of the wisdom of the Three Vehicles; therefore, it is said that one "will certainly die.
Because one contemplates such matters, it is said that one becomes "even more terrified. Because one lacks the small wisdom to comprehend the Great Teaching, it is said that one "faints.
Because one immediately gives rise to slander and will surely fall into the three miserable realms, it is said that one "collapses to the ground"; this is also delusion.
"Stupefaction and delusion" refers to the stage of ignorance. △ Third, summarizing the exhortations to cease the Mahāyāna transformation; Part Four:
First, reflecting on the cessation of the transformation; Sub-part One: First, knowing that his great aspiration is weak.
The father saw him from afar and said to his messenger, "There is no need for this man; do not force him to come.

That he saw him from afar is because his limited capacity is distant from the Mahāyāna; thus it is called "afar. That he saw him is because he is a child with whom [the father] has established a karmic connection.
As for saying to the messenger, this refers to the messenger of the teaching; it is explained that the fundamental wisdom of the teaching knows that there is nothing [to be grasped].
The Great Vehicle’s teachings should be appropriately simplified for the sake of people; thus, he spoke to the Bodhisattvas, saying:

"There is no need to manifest your sublime and wondrous bodies so that those of the Two Vehicles may see them. As in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, you should withdraw the fragrance of your bodies so as not to cause those sentient beings to give rise to delusive attachments.
Furthermore, when Samantabhadra entered this Sahā world, he contracted his body to make it small; all such instances are of this nature.

Regarding this meaning, "do not force" means that for those who have not yet developed a great capacity, if one were to manifest a superior body and preach the Mahāyāna Dharma, it might instead damage their roots of goodness;
therefore, it says "do not force. △ Second, knowing the strength of their lesser aspirations.
Sprinkle cold water on the face to cause them to awaken; do not speak with them further.

Sprinkling cold water on the face signifies that they possess limited aspirations and should employ the three types of ash to sever the principle of water and eliminate the heat of view-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought-delusions (*saṃjñā-kleśa*).
"Face" refers to the aversion toward birth and death and the turning toward Nirvana; this is what is meant by "face. "Awakening" means—
He opens the small teaching to accommodate those of small capacity, enabling them to leave behind their afflictions and delusions and realize the Four Noble Truths.
"Do not speak with them again" means that one must certainly cease the Mahāyāna teaching for them. △ Second, the explanation of the intention for ceasing the transformation.
Why is this? Because the father knows that his son’s disposition is inferior, and knowing himself to be noble and wealthy, he realizes that he is difficult for his son to accept;
yet, while he knows him to be his own son, he employs skillful means and does not tell others, "This is my son."
The followers of the two vehicles loathe suffering and aspire to emptiness; being intimately attached to what is inferior, they lack a heart of compassion and thus fear the great Dharma as difficult.
For the time being, their limited inclinations are permitted, which suppresses the Buddha’s original intent and causes him to cease his transformative activity.

However, knowing with certainty that these beings had previously resolved upon the Great Mind under twenty billion Buddhas, it is said, "I know for certain that you are my children. Regarding the phrase "by means of skillful expedients," etc.: [End of excerpt]
In the past, within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, there was speech according to the intentions of others—a skillful means used for protection—whereby one was called a Śrāvaka;
it did not speak according to one's own intention, saying that one is a Bodhisattva. △ Third, the explicit clarification of the cessation of transformation.
The messenger said to him, "I now release you; go wherever you please.
By saying "I now release you," he recognizes that the great capacity [for conversion] is weak; by saying "go wherever you please," he recognizes that the minor goodness [of the recipient] is strong.
For these two reasons, he ceases his great transformation. △ Fourth, the appropriateness of ceasing the transformation.
The impoverished son rejoiced at having attained what he had never experienced before; rising from the ground, he went to the poor quarters to seek food and clothing.
Because he was not coerced by the Great Teaching, he was filled with joy; because he was spared from the grave sin of slandering it, he was freed from the three miserable realms.

Thus it is said that "from the ground" there arose a small measure of goodness, and thus it is said that he "arose. Furthermore, previously, when confronted with the Great Dharma, he was bewildered and distressed.
Having awakened from the ground of ignorance while lying down, he now approaches [the world] so that awakening may be attained; thus it is said, "rising from the ground.
Because he desires to seek the Dharma of the Path within the Four Noble Truths, it is said, "going to a poor village to seek food and clothing.
Alternatively, because he seeks the Dharma of the Path among the four views (the four inversions), it is called a "poor village. △ Second, dispatching two people.
Section Two: Inducing [the Sons]—Part One: The Uniform Teaching; Section Four: Part One: Receiving the Superior [Teaching] and Proposing the Three Chariots.
At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his sons, established a skillful means and secretly dispatched two men who were haggard in appearance and devoid of majesty, saying:
"You may go to him and speak slowly to this impoverished son, 'There is work here; we shall pay you double wages.'"
"You are like a poor man who has come directly here; if you consent to come, I shall employ you. If you ask what you are to do, you may simply say:
'I will hire you to remove the dung; we two shall work together with you.'"

From this point downward, [the text] speaks of "intending to entice and lead" by means of the near provision of the three carts to save the children and the distant provision of the turning of the wheel at Vārāṇasī as a skillful means.

It says "intending to entice and lead" because he wishes to bring about the cessation of great suffering and will not allow anyone to be abandoned in isolation; it says "about to employ skillful means" for this reason.

As for the phrase "secretly dispatching two persons," it refers to the four great disciples who, being of equal standing, each take charge of a portion of the task, and since they do not involve the bodhisattvas, they are called "two persons."

In terms of the Dharma, it refers to the four truths of dependent origination; in terms of principle, it refers to the constructed (saṃskṛta) and the two truths of ultimate and conventional; in terms of persons, it refers to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Initially, for the sake of the Mahāyāna, it is said that "one immediately dismisses the bystanders" to symbolize the teaching of the One Great Vehicle and one bodhisattva person.

Now, it is clarified that the provisional means conceal the reality and thus constitute the "secret," while pointing to the partial truth constitutes "dismissal. In terms of the teachings, this conceals the *maṃtra* (full) syllables.

The term "esoteric" (*mi*) refers to the half-syllables (*ardha-akṣara*), while "expedient removal" (*kai*) refers to the concealment of the Bodhisattva practice within oneself; thus, it is called "esoteric" because one secretly maintains the conduct of a Bodhisattva, and "expedient removal" because one outwardly manifests as a Śrāvaka.

Within the teachings for the Two Vehicles, one does not cultivate the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), but merely speaks of suffering, impermanence, and impurity—this constitutes the physical appearance of being haggard and withered.
Regarding the person, this means that all Bodhisattvas conceal their original nature and manifest [as such].

Because the manifest forms are not teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), they lack the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and thus are said to be without majestic virtue (*an-avaivartika-tejas*).

When it says, "You may go to them," this means that the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) is adapted to those of lesser capacity. Because the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) clarifies principles directly and truly, it speaks of "running swiftly to seize";
because the principles clarified by the Lesser Vehicle are circuitous and obscure, it speaks of "speaking slowly. This [latter] has its place of application.
As for the Path of Seeing and the Path of Cultivation, these are the places where the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*) are severed; thus, they are worth twice as much to you.

Furthermore, while the five precepts and ten wholesome actions merely enable one to escape the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*), the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination can enable one to escape the triple world (*traidhātuka*);
this constitutes the first multiple. Moreover, while the six practices of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) can only suppress the afflictions, cultivating the Four Noble Truths can actually sever them.
To attain Nirvana constitutes the second type of "exhausted son. If [the Buddha] perceives a capacity [for the teaching], this is "granting permission," whereby he establishes the teaching;
if there is no capacity, this is "not granting permission," whereby he does not establish the teaching. What does he wish to accomplish?

Those of the Two Vehicles desire only to eliminate the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) and realize the proof of Nirvana; they do not concern themselves with purifying Buddha-lands or bringing sentient beings to maturity.
"To hire you with words to remove the filth, we two shall also work together with you.

This refers to the teaching for those of dull faculties among the Two Vehicles, who must rely on the teachings and perform practices before they can cultivate their karma; it refers to the principle where wisdom and the truth mutually support one another;
and it refers to the person where the provisional person practices together with the real person—hence the statement that "we two shall work together with you. △ Second, the acceptance.
The Superior One knew the son’s prior intention;
at that time, the two messengers sought out the impoverished son and, having found him, spoke of his being "found" because they knew he possessed the capacity [for the teaching].
△ Third, acknowledging the joy regarding the rare carriage mentioned above.
He related the aforementioned matters in detail, explaining how he had been hired to perform the work of removing filth. Fourth, [the father] fulfilled the son's previous wish:
at that time, the impoverished son first took his wages and immediately set about clearing away the refuse; when his father saw his son, he felt pity for him and marveled at this.
The two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) aspire to the fruit by practicing the cause; this is why they first inquire about the price.

Thus it is said that they first take the "filth" of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) to obtain the "price" of the path and its cessation (*mārga-nirodha*). Their father feels pity and wonder:

he pities them for taking [only] the state of an arhat, and he wonders at their failure to seek the Buddha-way. What is lost is great, while what is gained is meager; therefore, he speaks of his wonder. This concludes the section.
This concludes the section on "Comprehending the Meaning through Analogies. △ Second, Comprehending the Meaning (also called "Probing the Meaning"), Part Four:
First, he first employed provisional wisdom for a long time to gauge what was appropriate.
Furthermore, on another day, he saw his son’s body from afar through a window.
The word "furthermore" (*yòu*) is used here as a respectful term intended to express the intent of seeking out and grasping the meaning of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body;

it indicates that [the father] had long known the capacities of his son—whether great or small—and was reiterating the Buddha’s intention by employing the pedagogical methods of "one" and "three. Thus, the section is headed with "furthermore" (*yòu*). "On another day" (*tā rì*) refers to a subsequent occasion.
The term "two vehicles" refers to those who consider their own provisional means as their own path, while regarding the teachings of the two vehicles as belonging to others;

these "others" are precisely the Dharma-body. "Day" signifies time, and it also signifies wisdom. Because one relies on the temporal function of the Dharma-body to employ wisdom and illumine the capacities [of beings], it is said that "the other day.
When true wisdom illumines reality, it is "self"; when provisional wisdom illumines skillful means, it is "other. If...
The "Equalizing Teaching" (齊教) takes the activity of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) as its own day and the activity of the transformation body as the day of others.
If one probes this "receiving" (*ling*), it is the receiving [of wisdom] within the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) that illuminates the capacities of sentient beings.

At the time of the Dharma-body, the skillful means and wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*) used to transform others illuminate those provisional capacities—whether they exist or do not exist; whether the application of these provisional matters is appropriate or not—all are [illuminated].

Because this is illuminated by expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), it speaks of "another day" and "windows. "Partial vision" implies smallness; this expresses how expedient wisdom illuminates those with partial capacities.
"From afar" means being far removed from the Great; thus it is called "seeing from afar.

"I see you, my son"—in the past you once planted [the seeds of] the Great, hence you are called "son"; because the Great is used as a standard for comparison, it is called "seeing. The window is partial and narrow.

Because it was not yet appropriate for a great transformation, he ceased his grand displays and bestowed only minor favors. △ Second, having long known the skillful means, these became his cherished pastimes.
[He appeared] emaciated and haggard, covered in filth, dust, and impurities.
The Tathāgata first knows that the followers of the Two Vehicles have minor pleasures and pastimes; that their power of wisdom from cultivating causes is slight and thus they are weak;
that their power of merit from cultivating causes is slight and thus they are emaciated; that they are withered by internal fear of impermanence and external encounter with the eight sufferings;
that the four abidings are like dung and soil; and that ignorance is like dust and grime. △ Third, having known this for a long time, he joyfully offers the three carts as a rare boon.
There was one who immediately cast off his necklaces, fine soft upper garments, and ornaments, and instead put on coarse, tattered, and soiled clothes;
with dust covering his body and holding a refuse-basket in his right hand, he appeared as if filled with fear.

Removing the exquisite garments is a metaphor for concealing the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body), its immeasurable merits, the forty-two stages, the precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, *dhāraṇīs*, and so forth;
as well as the ornaments of the *śīla-saṃvara* and the subtle, soft, superior robes, and the adornments of the primary and secondary marks of a great being (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
If these majestic robes and forms were displayed, the followers of the two vehicles would be startled and fearful; they are not fit to behold such marks and signs. Therefore—

Having cast off [fine garments], he puts on coarse and tattered ones and manifests a body sixteen feet tall; this represents the coarse stage of *kṣānti* (patience) and the inferior stage of *dharma-kṣānti*.

His body being covered with dust and soil signifies the presence of afflictions (*kleśa*), conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), and outflows (*āsrava*). His left hand symbolizes the Real (*tattva*) and his right hand symbolizes Expedient Means (*upāya*);
through the ease and utility of these expedient means, he himself severs the fetters (*saṃyojana*) by means of this expedient dharma to attain Buddhahood, and further employs it.
This expedient teaching was intended to transform others; thus it is said that he holds a dung-removal vessel in his right hand. His "appearance of fear" is a semblance;
it demonstrates conformity with the Lesser Vehicle’s dread of birth and death, as well as the retributions of the cold wind and the horse-barley.
△ Fourth, having long known the son’s wish, he accepts and practices [the path]. Part seven: first, the analogy for the four foundations of mindfulness.
"Speak to all the laborers.
To speak to all the laborers means that this refers to the teaching of the Tripiṭaka which demonstrates the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni).

Because these are the vessel for removing filth and the sphere for severing the fetters (saṃyojana), the *Śāsanānuśāsana Sūtra* states: "If one constantly relies on the foundations of mindfulness to practice the Path, one can destroy the four inversions (catur-viparyāsa)."

This leading out from within the burning house, characterized by immediate aspiration and courageous vigor, corresponds to the stage of an ordinary person (*bālapṛthagjana*) who possesses the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
△ Second, the parable of the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*):
"You must all exert yourselves and not be indolent; by means of skillful methods (*upāya*), you shall come near your son."
"Do not allow for laxity" means to cause them to diligently cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
If laxity arises, one cannot eliminate the two evils (those already arisen and those yet to arise) nor produce the two virtues (those already arisen and those yet to arise).

Because of these two forms of diligence, one is able to ignite the fire of "warmth" (*ūṣmagata*) and, by pushing and shoving against the burning house, enter the stage of the warmth of cultivation-wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā-ūṣma-bhūmi*). By means of skillful means (*upāya*), this is attained.
Those who approach the "foundations of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna) have not yet attained the fire of principle to warm their hearts; they remain distant and cannot be approached.

However, by means of the "four right efforts" (samyakprahāṇa), which first attain the "warmth" (ūṣmagata) stage of skillful means, one can then be approached. △ Third, an analogy for the "four bases of psychic power" (ṛddhipāda).
Later, he spoke to him again, saying: "Ho! Man, you shall always work here; do not go elsewhere. I shall increase your wages.
Whatever you require—such as basins, vessels, rice, flour, salt, or vinegar—do not hesitate or find it difficult to ask for.
I also have old and worn-out servants who will provide whatever you need."

The exclamation "Tut! is used for startling awakening and also for reproaching and enumerating faults. Within the context of right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), agitation is a characteristic of wisdom (*prajñā*);
it is like a man, who possesses a masculine nature. Now, the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are the dharma of concentration (*samādhi*); they are like a woman, who possesses a feminine nature.

This is because when one is spurred on by right effort, one cannot yet correspond with true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Therefore, one uses "Tut" to startle and reproach, causing one to relinquish [agitation].

Because they are scattered and enter into stillness, it says, "O man! Regarding "you are always" and so forth: mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and right effort (*samyakpradhāna*) are not called "constant" when their movement is not single-minded.
Within the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), concentration does not differ from its object; thus, when one contemplates, there is concentration, and when one contemplates, there is abandonment.
Because concentration and abandonment are single-minded, it says, "You are constant. Because this activity is not distracted or agitated, it says, "Do not [be distracted]."
Furthermore, those others who remain here, still amidst mutual pushing and shoving, are at the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) dharma.

Regarding the statement "I shall increase your price": this refers to the inability to give rise to the true *yathābhūta* contemplation during the stage of right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), whereas within the stage of right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), one can give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Therefore, it is said that the price is increased. As for "whatever may be required," this includes all wholesome factors—both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*)—whether they be auxiliary paths (*pratyekamārga*) or the direct path (*mukhyamārga*).

If one seeks from within the contemplation of the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), whatever is desired shall be obtained immediately. The essence of the four dhyānas contains the various branches and elements like a basin;
the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*) is coarse like rice, while the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmatāśūnyatā*) is fine like flour—this is the Right Path.
The sixteen contemplations of the Four Noble Truths regard impermanence as salt and suffering as vinegar—these are the Aids to the Path, which are as difficult to master as rice and flour.
When eating, one must mix it with salt and vinegar; the Right Path is difficult to manifest and requires the assistance of the Auxiliary Path.

Do not harbor doubts regarding this assistance. Because the preceding discussion of the Right and Auxiliary Paths was examined within the *Yirui guan* (Contemplation of Accomplishing One's Wishes), do not doubt that [the goal] can certainly be achieved.

Since one should regard it as one's own property, it is said "do not find it difficult. If you wish to directly attain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) to serve as hands and feet, then [proceed as follows]:
Regarding those who drive and employ others, this same capacity exists within the contemplation of the *yathābhūta-darśana* (viewing things as they truly are), yet it is inferior and weak;

because the matter is the same as being worn out and decrepit, it is said that "there are also those who are worn out and decrepit. Although these people employed are not in their prime, they are still capable of labor and service;
therefore, it is said that "those who require them shall be provided. △ Fourth, the analogy for the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
"Set your mind at ease; I am like your father, so do not worry further.
"Set your mind at ease" means that you have attained the five faculties, such as faith, which are stable and difficult to destroy.

"I am like your father" means that because you have already attained the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) and understanding, you are close to realizing the truth; however, since this is still a semblance and not yet the reality itself, it is said to be "like a father. It is also [said] because...
"Be like a son and do not worry further," he said, intending to set their minds at ease and destroy their views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
△ Fifth, the analogy of the five powers (*pañca-bala*). Why is this so? "I am old and you are young; when you work, you never show deceit or indolence."
"Your anger, resentment, and complaints—I do not see these various evils in you at all, as one might find in other laborers.
From this day forward, you shall be like my own son.

The Buddha stands at the end of the Path, having fully perfected both wisdom and abandonment; thus he says, 'You are old' (meaning senior). You stand at the beginning of the Path (the stage of the inner ordinary person), and have not yet attained it."

Because one has abandoned [afflictions] through wisdom, one is called "youthful"; this refers to the stage of the Dharma of Patience (*kṣānti*). Having attained these five powers (*pañca-balāni*), one is free from the five unwholesome dharmas:

because of the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*), one does not deceive; because of the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*), one does not become indolent; because of the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*), one does not become angry; because of the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*), one does not harbor resentment;
and because of the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*), one does not speak words of complaint. As for the rest who act as such, they are a remote reference to the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Seeing that those who seek the principle are called "others" and that this text is free from the five faults refers to the five powers (*pañcabala*).

From now on, for one who is like a newborn child, the duration of the stage of lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) is still long—sixteen moments of a *kṣaṇa*. Although the stage of middle patience (*madhya-kṣānti*) has been shortened through contemplation, it is not yet a single *kṣaṇa*.
As for the stage of upper patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) and the supreme worldly dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), they consist of the final single *kṣaṇa*.

Because that mind is adjacent to the Truth and close to the Holy Ones, this stage is called "the son born according to the [True] Nature," which is the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
△ Sixth, the analogy for the Eightfold Noble Path.
Immediately, the elder gave him another name and called him "son.
Because the Dharma of the Supreme Worldly State (*laukikāgradharma*) and the Truth (*satya*) are not far apart, it is said "immediately. The *Āgama* speaks of five kinds of sons of the Buddha:

those of the four fruits and the Pratyekabuddha are called true sons of the Buddha; as for the Bodhisattva, who does not sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the meaning of being a son is not yet established.
Now, because those of the Two Vehicles have attained the Eightfold Noble Path and entered the Path of Seeing, they are called "children. △ Seventh, the parable of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment:
At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter, he still considered himself a lowly hired laborer; for this reason—
For twenty years, he was constantly made to clear away dung.

Because those of the Two Vehicles become sons [of the Buddha] by severing the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*), it is said that although they rejoice in this encounter, their delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) are not yet exhausted;

thus they still dwell in the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*). It is precisely because they must rely on the teachings to practice and exhaust suffering that it is said: "They still, for themselves, consider..."

If a lowly laborer who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) becomes weary of the small [vehicle] and delights in the great, and the capacity for the Mahāyāna is awakened, he should immediately be granted the Mahāyāna;
there is no further need to advance to sever the remaining residual fetters (*anuśaya*). This is precisely because, by not abandoning the small [vehicle], his great capacity does not awaken.
For this reason, he is first made to rely on the teaching to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*); thus it is said, "For this reason, [two]."

For ten years he constantly had him remove filth; for twenty years—because he had severed the view-based afflictions through one unimpeded path and one liberation, and severed the cultivation-based afflictions through nine unimpeded paths and nine liberations—it is said that it was "twenty years.

This is combined with the third verse below, which says "twenty," yet the meanings are each different; they may be explained according to the respective texts. △ Fourth, the parable of entrusting the family estate, in two parts.
First, taking charge of the family business; second, first, mutual trust in mind and character. First, clarifying that mutual trust:
"After this, they mutually trusted one another in mind and character, so there were no difficulties in their coming and going.
This marks the period of receiving the Vaipulya [sūtras]. "After this" means after the period of the Tripiṭaka at the Deer Park.
This refers to the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings. "The mind and its characteristics are mutually understood and believed" means that father and son fully comprehend and trust one another;
it signifies that within the Tripiṭaka teachings, they have obtained the price of Nirvāṇa.

Since this was not false, the present teaching of this Mahāyāna for the sake of the Bodhisattvas is likewise not false—this is the son believing his father. The Buddha knows that such individuals have already severed their views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*).

Hearing the Great [Vehicle], one does not slander it; with sharp faculties for the untainted roots (*anāsrava-indriya*), hearing it will necessarily give rise to faith—this is the father’s faith in the son.
Regarding "entering and exiting without difficulty": by virtue of this, seeing the *vairocana-kāya* (the body of sublime marks) and hearing the teachings of the Mahāyāna is called "entering";

furthermore, being rebuked while still seeing the sixteen-foot body and hearing the preaching of the Hīnayāna dharma is called "exiting. This constitutes the entering and exiting of the Great and Small [Vehicles].
And they have no doubts or difficulties. △ Second, "still dwelling in their original positions.

Although they remain in their original places, even though the followers of the Two Vehicles encounter no difficulty in entering and emerging from the Great and Small Vehicles, upon hearing the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, they say it is [the path of] Bodhi...

Regarding the Bodhisattva’s affairs, because [the Śrāvaka] considers them beyond the scope of his own wisdom and is unwilling to turn from the Small toward the Great, he remains at the rank of an Arhat and does not say that he shall attain Buddhahood in the future;
therefore it is said that "he still abides in his original place. This summarizes the teachings on the "ghee" stage found in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* and the *Vimalakīrti*.
△ Second, the detailed account of leaving the household life, in two parts: first, the fourfold command to take charge of the affairs. 4.
First, the time is clarified.
At that time, the World-Honored One, a certain elder was ill and knew for himself that he would soon die.
From this point downward, it concerns the occasion when [the Buddha] received the command to turn and teach the *Prajñāpāramitā*. "Soon to die" means that there was an opportunity [for the teaching].
That which should be brought forth is called birth; that which should cease is called death. Now, as the transformative function is nearing its end, its cessation will not be long in coming.
△ Second, instructing the son regarding the family estate:
He said to the impoverished son, "I now possess much gold, silver, and rare treasures, filling my storehouses to overflowing. How much is there within them?"
You should know that all that is to be grasped is fully contained herein:

gold represents the specific (pṛthag) teaching and principle, while silver represents the universal (sāmānya) teaching and principle. The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) elucidated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* does not exceed these two;

yet, when it is said that there are "many," this is not because the principle itself is manifold, but rather that it may be described as "many" by way of various approaches (*mukha*). This is the analogy.
Just as space is not eighteen [in itself], yet by negating the eighteen dharmas it is called the "eighteen emptinesses";

so too, in the "Chapter on Encouraging Study," it is clarified that all dharma-gates are treasuries of jewels: the gate of concentration (*samādhi*) is the storehouse of the one hundred and eight samādhis, and the gate of wisdom (*prajñā*) is the realm of the eighteen emptinesses.
Thus, the storehouses of concentration and wisdom encompass both the universal and particular teachings.
Because all meditative concentrations and wisdoms are without deficiency, overflowing from within and surging outward, it is said they "overflow within.

Regarding the measure of this—whether much or little—it is explained that in the Prajñāpāramitā there are two gates: the extensive and the concise. The concise is "little," while the extensive is "much.

Taking [the teachings] for one's own practice is "receiving," while bestowing them upon others for their transformation is "giving. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "You should [cultivate] for the sake of Bodhi..."
Because Śākyamuni spoke thus, he said, "You all know this. Third, the admonition to realize the mind:
"My mind is such; you should embody this meaning. Why is this? Because now I and you are no different."
Regarding the admonition "one who embodies my mind," the Buddha takes *prajñā* as his mind; you, now teaching in turn, should speak according to the Buddha’s intention.
As for the statement "now I and you are not different," there are three ways to explain this: first, being empowered to teach such that one is not different from the Buddha;
second, from the perspective of principle (*li*), because all phenomena are *tathatā*, they are not different; third, from the perspective of...

Now, for the first time, one realizes that the natural affinity between father and son is fundamentally no different [from that of others], whereas those of the Two Vehicles merely claim to have received a distinct empowerment.
△ Fourth, the command to avoid the loss of the outflow-free state.
You should apply yourself with diligent care so as not to let it leak away or be lost.

Regarding "not letting it leak away or be lost," there are two aspects: first, in terms of the teaching, you must preach the Prajñāpāramitā teachings for the sake of the bodhisattvas without letting them leak away or be lost;
second, in terms of the principle, this is your own dharma which you shall utilize at a later time; therefore, do not let it leak away or be lost.
This is an error. △ Second, receiving the mandate and taking charge of the four [treasuries]. First, the formal reception of the mandate and the knowledge [of the assets]:
At that time, the impoverished son immediately accepted the instructions and took charge of the various goods, gold, silver, precious gems, and all the storehouses.
△ Second, his mind was free from seeking or grasping;
he lacked even the slightest intention to seek a single morsel of food.
Although Subhūti taught by turning the Dharma wheel and spoke of the Prajñāpāramitā, he said of himself, "This is the dharma of a bodhisattva; I have no share in it. △
Third, they have not yet abandoned their original station;
because they still dwell there, their inferior mind has likewise not been relinquished.
Thus, those who remain in their original station—though they may aspire to the Great [Vehicle] while abiding in the stage of an Arhat—have not yet definitively resolved to become [a Buddha].

Even though a bodhisattva has not yet abandoned the inferior mind, although he feels shame for the small [vehicle], he has not yet definitively declared that he will abandon the realization of the small.
△ Fourth, the contempt for the inferior and the seeking of the great:
After a short time had passed, the father knew that his son’s mind had gradually become open and at ease, having achieved a great resolve and come to despise his former thoughts.

This refers to the parable of receiving the neck-rope and carriage, which signifies the casting aside of one's former, inferior mind and the desire to seek the Great Way—the awakening of the great capacity.

Question: When is this called "a short time"? Answer: One interpretation states that it is when, upon the conclusion of the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, one reflects upon the Mahāyāna Dharma-gates one has received and gives rise to a mind of longing and joy, pondering such matters as whether this constitutes a loss or no loss; such reflection is precisely what is meant here.
The time when the capacity [for understanding] arises is the present moment; since at this time one is not far from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is said that "after a short while.
Furthermore, when the *Anantamukhanirhāra* (The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings) was being preached, the capacity for the Mahāyāna arose. How is this known?

Within the *Anantamukhanirhāra*, it is clarified that the seven kinds of skillful means and the immeasurable gradual and sudden teachings arise from a single Dharma. Having heard this teaching, one reflects upon the three [vehicles] of the past.
The three vehicles within the treasury all arise from a single dharma; these three vehicles should likewise enter into that one.

When one contemplates in this way, the mind gradually becomes unobstructed and expansive, and the great resolve is immediately awakened; therefore, it is said that "the great aspiration is accomplished.
II. Entrusting the Family Business (in two parts): A. First, entrusting the business (in four parts): 1. First, clarifying the time of entrusting the business.

"At the time when he was about to pass away" refers to the period following the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* when he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. "At the time when he was about to pass away" clarifies that the season had arrived and his karmic conditions for transformation were nearing their end;
it marks the moment on Vulture Peak after eight years of preaching the *Lotus Sūtra*, as he announced his entry into *nirvāṇa*.
△ Second, the command to assemble the witnesses.
He commanded his son, and all the kinsmen, kings, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders were gathered together.
Those who had been transformed by twenty trillion Buddhas and were called "sons" were the Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body from the ten directions.
As for those influenced by kinship, it is because the multitude influenced by kinship was vast;
these were Śākyamuni’s former fellow-practitioners who, together with the Tathāgata, had jointly converted them at the abodes of twenty trillion Buddhas.

Since they were all of the status of uncles and cousins, he used this [kinship] as the basis for those who are kings of his kin. There is not a single gradual or sudden sūtra that does not [bear witness to this].

That which is designated as the locus of the expressed meaning is called the "King of Sūtras. Because it benefits sentient beings according to their capacities, its arising and ceasing occur at specific times;

as each section differs, they are termed "kingdoms," all of which claim to be the foremost, and thus are called "kings. Since this present sūtra synthesizes and harmonizes all teachings, is it not the gathering together of these various kings?
In the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, it was previously stated that those [teachings] were first expounded as four.

Having first taught the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, he next taught the twelve divisions of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) sutras, and subsequently taught the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
This is the universal gathering of all sutras, wherein the gradual and sudden teachings are harmonized and integrated; for this reason, it is called the "Assembly of the King.
Maitreya and the other great Bodhisattvas are all those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-sambodhi), serving as his ministers from the first to the ninth bhūmis.

Di was born into the lineage of the Kṣatriya Dharma-kings; those who have attained the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten transferences are householders—all of these were transformed by Śākyamuni.
△ Third, the conclusion: the reunion of father and son.
He then made this proclamation: "Gentlemen, you should know that this is my son, begotten by me.
Having abandoned me in such-and-such a city, he fled and wandered in hardship for more than fifty years. His original name was so-and-so, and my name is so-and-so.
While formerly in that city, I searched for him with deep anxiety; now, unexpectedly meeting him here, I have found him. This is truly my son."
I am truly his father;
he has indeed received instruction from me and is truly my son. Having attained understanding through me, he was born from me.
Because I have constantly taught the Great Dharma in the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas, I am truly his father in such-and-such a city.
As for the "medium" version, the text of this sutra in the Western lands (India) was extensive, but the translation here is very brief;

perhaps it could have included the ancient names of the countries and lands, such as those in the *Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū-sūtra*, but now the names are abbreviated, mentioning only a certain city and a certain person.
It is said that these sentient beings turn their backs on this Mahāyāna, giving rise to the darkness of ignorance and fleeing into the cycle of birth and death.

"Having abandoned me and fled, he has undergone the various experiences of the six realms; therefore, it is said 'for more than fifty years. As for the phrase 'formerly in his native city' and so forth:
since ancient times, within the stage of the Dharmakāya, the Tathāgata has constantly used both provisional and ultimate wisdoms to observe and seek those with the capacity for conversion.
Only beginning today have cause and response met in harmony; hence it is said, 'Suddenly, on this day, we have encountered one another.'"
"Having found him, he truly says, 'This is my son,'" etc., which judges that their nature is fixed as father and son. △ Fourth, the formal entrustment of the family estate:
"Now all the wealth and property I possess are the son's; what was previously spent or brought in is known by the son."
Because it encompasses all the myriad practices and myriad virtues of the Mahāyāna, it is said that "all that exists" refers to what was previously brought forth and internalized;

this is what the son knows. This is a retrospective reference to the extensive and abbreviated *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings—both common and uncommon—that were entrusted to him during his reception of the instructions in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Since these are what you know, they are indeed what you possess; therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* clarifies only the Buddha’s [wisdom].
The knowledge and vision [of the Buddha] do not further elaborate upon all the various modes of practice. △ Second, rejoicing:
At that time, the impoverished son, hearing these words from his father, was filled with great joy at having attained what he had never experienced before, and he thought to himself:
"Originally, I had no intention of seeking anything; yet now, this treasure store has come to me spontaneously."
Each of them mounted a great carriage and experienced what they had never known before; looking back at themselves, they felt no aspiration for the Buddha-way.

Now, suddenly hearing that they have received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, it is said that "it was obtained spontaneously without being sought. In the *Tripiṭaka*, their original minds did not seek it;

in the *Vaipulya* (Vaipulya-sūtras), they were ashamed of the Lesser Vehicle and their hopes were severed, so they did not seek it; in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, although they understood it, it was not within their own capacity.
Therefore, although one did not seek it in the past, though not sought, it is now spontaneously attained. △ Second, the combined analogy, in four parts.
First, the combined analogy of the father and son losing each other:
"The World-Honored One, the great wealthy elder, is the Tathāgata; we are all like the sons of the Buddha."
When the Tathāgata unites with the father, he likewise unites with the son; this "resemblance" has two meanings:

first, taking those of great capacity as sons—since they previously fled and have not yet attained the true stage, remaining instead at the level of external ordinary beings, they are said to be "resembling" [the son];

second, taking those of small capacity as sons—since their small capacity resembles the nature of the Mahāyāna faculties, they are said to be "resembling" [the son]. Once the son has turned his back on the father...
Because he fled, [the father] disparaged him by saying, "He merely resembles [a son]. △ Second, combining this with the analogy of the father and son meeting:
the Tathāgata constantly says that we are his sons;

this corresponds to the elder seeing his son and immediately recognizing him. △ Third, combining this with the analogy of the father’s command to pursue and entice [the son], in two parts: first, the combination.
The bystanders pursued the two initial points, yet both the gates of admonition and exhortation found no responsive capacity in them.
[They said: "World-Honored One, because of the three kinds of suffering, we undergo various torments within birth and death, being deluded and ignorant."

The three types of suffering arise from the three feelings: from painful feeling arises the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); from pleasant feeling arises the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*);

and from neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). The *Miaole* (Sublime Joy) commentary states: "Because of these three sufferings, the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) are intensified.

Therefore, the two gates of exhortation and admonition lack any great-capacity practitioners; they are only fit for those who can be transformed by the Small Vehicle. Being oppressed by the five turbidities is precisely what constitutes the three [sufferings]."

Because they are shrouded by the ignorance of suffering, they are simply ignorant. △ Second, regarding the combined summary of the transformation [of beings], there are those with small aspirations who delight in and cling to minor teachings.
This combines the aforementioned "small aspirations" but does not combine "abandonment. △ Second, the two combined analogies for the two types of guidance.
First, summarizing the teaching in two parts: first, collectively presenting the aforementioned matter.
Today, the World-Honored One has commanded us to contemplate and eliminate the dung of conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena.
The dung of frivolous conceptualization refers to the afflictions of views and thoughts. △ Second, the combined removal of dung and the taking of payment:
"Within this [work], we applied ourselves with diligent vigor and obtained the day’s wage of reaching nirvana.
Having obtained this, our hearts were greatly rejoiced and we considered ourselves sufficient; we then said to ourselves: 'Because of our diligent vigor within the Buddha-dharma...'"
The gain obtained is vast and great.
"Among these, we shall apply ourselves with diligent vigor" corresponds to the upper section on clearing away the filth to attain *nirvāṇa*;
"first taking the price" corresponds to the lower section. △ Second, combining the exploration and reception, in three parts: first, combining the initial intent to deliberate.
However, the World-Honored One had already known us beforehand;
whereas previously he spoke of seeing us from afar, now he speaks of having known us in advance. △ Second, [he addresses] their attachment to skillful means:
their minds are attached to base desires and they take pleasure in inferior teachings.
Previously it was said that they were emaciated and haggard; now it is said that their minds are attached to base desires.

△ Third, one should first know that [the Buddha] praised the chariot, yet he immediately showed them indifference and did not make a distinction, saying: "You all shall have a share in the treasure-store of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision."

The previous statement said that he immediately cast off his necklaces and put on coarse, tattered clothes; the present statement says that he was seen to abandon them freely, making no distinction between them and the treasures of the storehouse.

△ Fourth, the analogy of inheriting and being entrusted with the family estate has two parts: first, the analogy of inheriting the family estate; second, [the analogy of being entrusted]. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, the analogy of causing one to realize and believe; second, [the analogy of entrusting]. Within the first section, there is the analogy of causing one to realize and believe.
The World-Honored One, by the power of skillful means, speaks of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

Because he teaches the true reality of the Mahāyāna while employing the skillful means of the three vehicles, it is said that "by the power of skillful means, he preaches the Mahāyāna dharma before us.
This also accords with the preceding statement that he "enters and emerges without difficulty," for by the power of skillful means, he brings forth and elucidates [the truth].

If those of the Two Vehicles had entered into the clear realization of the true mark through the Buddha’s power of wisdom, yet did not embody or believe it, how could they have manifested the Buddha’s wisdom before me?
△ Second, returning to their original places.
"We have obtained from the Buddha the price of one day's worth of nirvāṇa and consider this a great gain; thus, we have no aspiration or pursuit regarding this Mahāyāna.
△ Second, the collective command to receive and take up the karma, in two parts: first, the collective reception and taking up of the karma.
Furthermore, because we have been taught and expounded the Tathāgata’s wisdom for the sake of all bodhisattvas, there is both life-force (*jīvita*) and sensation (*vedanā*).
Now, however, one should only accept the sensation; there are four types of such sensation: first, accepting the life-force through the power of karma;

second, having no desire for acquisition; third, not abandoning what is inferior; and fourth, the mind gradually becoming expansive and serene. Now, however, one should only accept the first two and not the latter two.
2. △ Second, combining [the two] to show there is no aspiration or grasping. Part one: the actual combination.
"Yet, regarding this, I have no personal aspiration.
To say "no aspiration" clarifies that it is through the Buddha’s bestowed power that he speaks in accordance with the Buddha’s own mind; therefore, "I do not aspire."
This is the prayer. △ Second, the explanation of the intent:
Why is this so? Because the Buddha knows that our hearts delight in the Lesser Dharma, he employs the power of skillful means to teach us accordingly;
yet we do not realize that we are truly the sons of the Buddha.

"The Buddha speaks according to our capacities through the power of skillful means" means that the Buddha, employing the power of skillful means, teaches the Dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) in common with those of the Two Vehicles.
We did not recognize his intention of not teaching in common; thus, we did not know that we were truly sons of the Buddha.
II. Entrusting the Family Business in Common. A. Entrusting the Business in Common. 1. Explaining the Absence of Reluctance.
"Now we have finally come to know that the World-Honored One has no begrudgingness regarding the Buddha's wisdom.

It was simply because we delighted in the small [vehicle] that he did not bestow the Great [Vehicle] upon us early on; how could it be that he truly begrudges the Buddha-wisdom and does not speak of it for our sake?
△ Second, the explanation of having no begrudgingness.
Why is this? Because we have been true sons of the Buddha from of old, yet we took pleasure only in the Lesser Dharma.
Had we possessed a mind that delighted in the Great [Dharma], the Buddha would have taught us the Mahāyāna Dharma. In this sutra, he speaks only of the One Vehicle;
yet in the past, before the bodhisattvas, he disparaged the śrāvakas who delighted in the Lesser Dharma. However, the Buddha truly [taught] with the Great...
This is the vehicle of transformation.

Within this sutra, the following section cites the present to verify the past; since the principle of the present is one and the same, we know that the three [vehicles] of the past were not real, but were merely taught because [beings] were not yet capable.
Thus, before the Great Vehicle, the Lesser Vehicle was disparaged in order to cause them to abandon the false and grasp the true, thereby establishing certainty.
Knowing this was not out of stinginess, [we realize] that the Buddha has indeed used the Mahāyāna to teach and transform us. II.
Harmonizing with Joy: "Therefore, we say that originally we had no mind to seek anything;
now the great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously, and all that a son of the Buddha ought to obtain has already been attained."
This also refers to the meaning of the three "not seeking" mentioned above regarding the foremost among the monastic community. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts:
first, seventy-three and a half lines in verse summarize the prose; second, the first part summarizes the Dharma-exposition.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Today we have heard the Buddha’s teaching and are filled with joy and exultation, having attained what we never had before. The Buddha has declared that we śrāvakas shall attain Buddhahood;
this unsurpassed mass of jewels is obtained spontaneously, without being sought."

He does not praise [the father] nor seek him out, but praises only what he has attained himself. △ Second, the verse on the parable, in two parts: first, the verse opening the parable, in four sections;
first, the verse on the son turning his back and leaving his father, in four parts; first, the direct verse on the son turning his back and departing from his father.
For example, it is like a young boy who, being immature and ignorant, abandons his father and flees, wandering far away to other lands and traveling through various countries for over fifty years.
While the "blazing house" clarifies the kingdom, cities, and villages ruled by the elder, this section clarifies the impoverished son.
Transmigrating through the three realms is called "various lands," and passing through the six destinies is called "fifty-odd years.
To speak of "wandering" means to drift through the five paths, undergoing birth and death like a floating duckweed or a broken twig, reaching everywhere without exception.
△ Second, the actual verse on failing to find a son, in two parts: first, the verse on his searching.
His father, filled with anxiety and concern, searched in all four directions.
This "searching in all four directions" differs from the previous instance;

whereas the former four directions refer to investigating according to the Four Noble Truths, the present four directions refer to seeking among the four types of birth for a sentient being who can be saved. △ Second, the cessation within the verse.
Having exhausted his search for it, he stopped at a city and built a residence there, enjoying himself with the five desires. His family was immensely wealthy,
possessing much gold, silver, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearls, lapis lazuli, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, palanquins, and various vehicles.

His fields, estates, servants, and subjects were numerous; his income and profit from lending and trade extended throughout other countries, and there was no place where his merchants and traders did not exist.
Surrounded and revered by thousands of millions of followers, he was constantly cherished and remembered by the king.
All the ministers and noble clans alike honored and esteemed him. Because of these various circumstances, those who came and went were many; such was his great wealth and prosperity.
It possesses great power and majesty.
The construction of dwellings refers to the *parinirvāṇa* in other lands; the building of the house of compassion relies upon the dwelling of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
The multitude of those who come and go refers to the Bodhisattvas from various lands coming and going to hear the Dharma. △ Three.
The father’s grief and anxiety grew even deeper.

As he grew old and advanced in years, his concern for his son increased all the more. Day and night he thought only of how the time of his own death was approaching, lamenting, "My foolish son has abandoned me for over fifty years;
what shall become of the treasures and goods in my storehouses?"
This merely summarizes the previous suffering of losing one's son; because there was no one to whom he could entrust [the child], he was thus filled with grief.
△ Fourth, the subsequent summary of the son’s arrival at his father’s city, in two parts: first, the summary of the causes for approaching his father.
At that time, the impoverished son sought food and clothing, traveling from town to town and from kingdom to kingdom;
sometimes he obtained something and sometimes he obtained nothing, until he became emaciated by hunger and malnutrition, and sores and scabs broke out upon his body.
To travel from village to village means that the faculties and their objects intermingle like villages; the eighteen realms are like nations.
To cultivate the contaminated goodness of the three realms is like having something to attain; to cultivate the uncontaminated goodness of the two vehicles is like having nothing to attain.
Not obtaining the Dharma-food of the Great Vehicle is like being hungry; lacking great power of function is to be weak; lacking great merit and virtue is to be emaciated.
The existence of views and afflictions regarding good and non-good arises like sores and scabs. △ Second, the verse on finally arriving at the father’s city:
gradually passing through various places, he arrives at the city where his father resides.
△ Second, the verse on the meeting of father and son: Part One, the verse on the son seeing the father; Part Three, the verse on the causes for seeing the father.
Through successive stages of hired labor, he eventually arrived at his father’s house.
△ Second, the verse on the signs of seeing his father:
At that time, the elder was inside his gate, seated upon a lion throne beneath a great jeweled canopy, surrounded by his retinue.
Among those attending him, some were calculating gold, silver, and precious objects, and recording the accounts of income and expenditure on scrolls and documents.

Above, one clearly saw his father; in every place by the side of the gate, it was now said that the elder was within that gate—this indicates that the characteristics [of the father] and the location are both attained.
The Dharma-body is the Teacher and the King; the retribution-body is the elder who bestows great gifts.
The jeweled canopy is the place where the father of Right View resides; the "notes on the vouchers" (*zhùjì quànshū*) refer to the bestowal of prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), clarifying the practice.
Zhiyi says: "To extensively reveal what is concise constitutes the 'notes' (*zhù*); to bestow a decisive resolution constitutes the 'prophecy' (*jì*).
The Four Great Vows constitute the 'vouchers' (*quàn*); cultivation of practice constitutes the 'commentary' (*shū*). △ Third, verses on generating a mind of fear and avoidance.
When the impoverished son saw his father’s great wealth, nobility, and majestic dignity, he thought him to be a king or someone of royal rank;
filled with alarm and wondering at himself for having come there, he reflected: "If I remain here long, I may be coerced or forced into labor.
Having thought this, he fled and went away, seeking out a poor neighborhood where he wished to go and seek work as a hired laborer.
According to the *Supplemental Translation*, if this were a single version [of the text] for kings and others, it would be used as the national standard. II.
Verse on the Father Seeing the Son. Part One: Verse on the Place Where He Saw His Son.
At that time, the elder was seated upon the lion throne.
△ Second verse: Recognizing the son upon seeing him.
Seeing his son from afar, he recognized him silently.
△ Third verse: The father’s command to pursue and entice him. Part one: A verse on bystanders pursuing him. Part two: A verse on calling the son, which does not succeed.
"Come! He immediately commanded his messengers to pursue and seize him; the impoverished son was startled and cried out.
This verse praises the fact that the gate of exhortation found no responsive capacity [in him]. △ Second, the verse on the failure to come despite being called again.
He fainted and fell to the ground.
This verse admonishes that the gate [of the teaching] was without affinity for him. △ Third, the verse on immediately letting go:
"This man clings to the self, thinking 'I shall certainly be killed'; what use have I for food and clothing to bring me to this state? The elder knew his son..."
"Deluded, narrow-minded, and inferior, they do not believe my words; they do not believe that he is their father.

This summary verse exhorts through two gates regarding those who lack the spiritual capacity (*agotra*); because they lack such capacity, the Buddha’s transformative activity ceases, which is why it is said that "he releases them and abandons them.
The mention of "seeing them killed" has the same meaning as the aforementioned "certain death. △ Second, the verse on the two types of people who entice [the children].
Part Two: First, a verse on hiring laborers (which corresponds to the formal instruction); second, a verse on employing skillful means (which corresponds to the preliminary proposal).
By means of these skillful means, he further dispatches another person—one who is blind in one eye, short of stature, and lacking in majesty—and says to him: "You may speak to them thus:
'I shall hire you to clear away all filth and excrement, and I will pay you double wages.'"

Since the great transformation has ceased, he employs skillful means to preach the Dharma of the Small Vehicle to entice and guide them. The "blind eye" is a metaphor for the partial emptiness perceived;
because what is seen is not correct, one cannot vertically exhaust the source of the true mark (*dharmatā*).

Because there is no horizontal adornment of the manifold virtues of the Great Vehicle, it is like being short and ugly; this is called lacking majesty, as it is not the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
"Blissful, self, and pure" are names for that which lacks virtue. △ Second, accepting the price and removing filth (which corresponds to the aforementioned "fulfilling his wishes"):
Upon hearing this, the impoverished son rejoiced and followed along, removing the filth and purifying the various rooms and dwellings.
The "purity of the six sense organs" refers to the house of the five aggregates (skandhas). △ Second, the verse on the teaching through analogy (i.e., the introductory summary), in four parts;
first, the verse on the window:
The elder constantly sees his son from within the window.
△ Second verse: [The mother] is emaciated;
she thinks of her son who is foolish and inferior, delighting in base deeds.
△ Third verse: [The mother] changes her clothes.
Thereupon, the elder put on worn and soiled clothes, took up a dung-removal tool, and went to where his son was.
△ Fourth, the actual instruction for labor:

He approached him through skillful means and spoke to him, urging him to work diligently, saying, "This will increase your wages, and you shall also receive oil for your feet and sufficient food and drink."
The mats and bedding are so thick and warm; [the Buddha] spoke these harsh words, saying, "You should work diligently," and then used gentle words, saying, "As if you were my own son.
The superior teachings given to the elder consist of seven categories of Dharma-gates; what is here called "speech" corresponds to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
"Causing him to work diligently" corresponds to the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). Since this benefits the following, one verse-line encompasses the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Anointing the feet with oil so as to be able to walk in deep water is analogous to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); furthermore, oil can dispel wind, which is analogous to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Abundant food and drink represent superior rice and flour; thick and warm mats and bedding represent the four types of meditative cultivation—namely, *vipaśyanā*, *bhāvanā*, *vāsana*, and *abhyāsa*.
By practicing these concentrations, one is able to eliminate distracted movement. Such are the bitter words [spoken] halfway through.

The fourth section of the preceding summary verse on practice is "Consolation," which refers to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*); the fifth is "Absence of Faults," which refers to the five powers (*pañcabala*).

Once the faculties and powers are perfected, one is then capable of speaking words of admonition. Furthermore, the sixth section of the preceding summary verse on practice is "Forming Characters," which refers to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*);
the seventh is "Causing Constant Practice," which refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). These constitute the stage of the "son."
