Regarding these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), according to conventional discourse, the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*) precede the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*);
however, here, because they are arranged according to their sequential order, the eightfold noble path is placed before the seven factors of awakening. IV. Verse on Entrusting the Family Business:
Part One—The Verse on the Reasons for Entrusting the Task; Sub-part One—The Verse on the Mind’s Characteristics and Embodied Faith.
The elder, possessing wisdom, gradually allowed him to enter and exit.
△ Second, the verse on the detailed entrustment of the family estate has three parts; first, the verse on receiving the command.
For twenty years he managed the household affairs, demonstrating to him the flow of gold, silver, pearls, and crystal.
He caused all to know this.
Some say that for twenty years he taught the Mahāyāna teachings to the bodhisattvas of the two vehicles, severing their individual views and individual thoughts;
others say that the period during which he preached the *Prajñāpāramitā* lasted for twenty years, as stated in the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā Prajñāpāramitā*.
In the eighteenth year, he preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. △ Second, he still remained in his original position.
Still staying outside the gate, he dwelt in a thatched hut and thought to himself regarding his poverty: "I have no such thing."
Because he had not yet abandoned his inferior mind, he stayed in the grass hut. △ Third, the realization of the great resolve:
The father knew that his son’s mind was gradually becoming expansive;
as it became increasingly expansive, the capacity for the Mahāyāna was activated. △ Second, the verse on entrusting the family business, in two parts: first, the verse on the actual entrustment.
Regarding the three types of karma, the first verse assembles the kinsmen:
wishing to bestow wealth and goods, he immediately gathers his relatives, kings, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders.
△ Second, the verse determines the nature of the realm of rebirth.
To this great assembly he said: "This is my son, whom I lost fifty years ago when he left me to travel elsewhere.
It has now been twenty years since I saw him come here. Long ago, in a certain city, I lost this son; having wandered everywhere in search of him, I have finally arrived at this place."

These words were spoken because the Buddha was moved by the presence of those with the capacities for the two vehicles; thus it is said, "Since you first came as my son, twenty years have already passed.

The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "He merely establishes these two names [of Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha], and they are called 'twenty years'. △ Third, the verse on the formal entrustment.
"All my houses and people I entrust entirely to him, to be used by him as he pleases.
△ Second, the verse on the joy of being entrusted with the inheritance:
"The son reflects that formerly, in his poverty, his aspirations were lowly; now, from his father, he has obtained great treasures as well as houses and lands."
He was filled with immense joy over all his wealth and possessions, having attained what he had never experienced before.
△ Second, the verse that combines the parable, in four parts; first, the verse combining the loss of father and son:
"The Buddha is also like this."
The *Myōraku* states: "If one takes only the single phrase 'the Buddha is likewise so,' it does not yet fully reveal the meaning of the father and son losing sight of each other;
next, the phrase 'knowing that I am small' does not yet fully reveal the meaning of the father and son seeing each other. Why?
Because the preceding phrase relies on the succeeding phrase to establish the sense of 'knowing that [I] am small,' and thus its meaning would be lost; next, the succeeding phrase relies on..."

The first phrase establishes that because they delight in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), they are able to see one another; their delight in the Lesser arises from their regression from the Great Vehicle, which is why they lose sight of one another.

Their regression from the Great arises from their delight in the Lesser, which is why they are able to see one another. Thus, these two phrases mutually establish one another and encompass all eight phrases.
△ Second verse: The union of father and son meeting;
knowing that I delight in the Lesser Vehicle, the meaning is naturally understood.
△ Third verse: The union of the father’s command to pursue and entice; first, the verse on the union with the bystanders who pursue.
I have never said to you, "You shall become Buddhas.

Although I sent forth attendants to pursue you, because you lacked the spiritual capacity (*indriya*), I desisted; this was because I had not yet declared that you would become Buddhas. △ Second, the verse:
△ Second, the two [sons] are enticed, and it is said that they have attained all outflows-free states and become disciples of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) Śrāvakas.

△ Fourth, the four verses on the collective entrustment of the family estate, divided into two parts: first, the verse on the collective entrustment of the family estate; second, the long verse. First, the long verse:
He commanded them to take this to heart.
The Buddha instructed us, saying: "If you practice this supreme path, you shall attain Buddhahood.
This supreme path is none other than the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*); there is nothing superior to it. △ Second, the actual verse.
Regarding the two aspects of receiving [the teaching] without seeking anything for oneself: first, one correctly receives the life-force [of the Dharma].
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, I act as a great bodhisattva, using various causes and conditions, diverse parables, and manifold expressions to expound the unsurpassed path.
The sons of the Buddhas, having heard this Dharma from me, contemplate it day and night and practice it with diligent application.
At that time, the Buddhas immediately bestowed upon him this prediction: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood.
Yet, while all Buddhas expound the essential reality of the secret treasury of the Dharma solely for the sake of bodhisattvas, they did not explain these true essentials to me.
That the sons of the Buddha, upon hearing the Dharma, attain the prediction [of enlightenment] clarifies that they turn the teaching to benefit others.

At that time, it is said only that they turn the teaching to transform and instruct bodhisattvas; it does not say it is for their own sake. II. Unifying [the two cases] to show there is no desire for gain. Part One: Citing the preceding analogy to apply it to the present case.
Just as that impoverished son, upon approaching his father, knew of all the various goods yet had no desire to take them;
△ Second, the actual application [of the analogy] regarding the absence of desire to take, in three parts: first, the direct verse on the meaning of the absence of desire to take.
Although we speak of the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha, we ourselves likewise lack any aspiration for it.

△ Second, because they possess both wisdom and abandonment, there is no seeking or grasping; first, the heading; second, the detailed explanation. First, the heading: because they possess the virtue of abandonment, there is no seeking or grasping.
"We have attained internal extinction and consider ourselves sufficient; we understand only this matter and there is nothing further.

"Internal extinction" (*antardhāna*) refers to the internal essence of the afflictions; because the afflictions of view and thought within the three realms have been exhausted, it is called "internal extinction.
Therefore, this section is categorized as the "marking of the virtue of severance. △ Second, marking the virtue of wisdom: being fully endowed with it, there is no further seeking or grasping.
If we were to hear of purifying Buddha-lands and teaching sentient beings, we would feel no joy at all.
Since it is said "if one hears," hearing and being taught belong to the category of wisdom; therefore, this section is classified as the heading for the virtue of wisdom.

Because they possess only small wisdom, they do not rejoice in great wisdom. This, together with the preceding heading on the virtue of abandonment, simultaneously reveals the fault of lacking joy in the Great [Vehicle] and manifests their attachment.
This is the fault of [conceiving] smallness. △ Second, the explanation:
Why is this so? Because all dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent—without arising and without ceasing, without large and without small, without outflows and without conditioned activity.
Reflecting thus, one does not give rise to joy or delight, yet we have for a long night [remained distant] from the Buddha’s wisdom.
Being without greed, without attachment, and without further aspiration, they consider themselves to have reached the ultimate within the Dharma.
Having practiced the dharma of emptiness for a long night, we have attained liberation from the afflictions of suffering within the three realms;
dwelling in our final bodies within *nirvāṇa-with-remainder*, we have realized the Path through the Buddha’s teaching without fail, and thus we have already repaid the Buddha’s kindness.
First, from "Why have we come to joy and bliss" to "relinquishment," it explains severance (*prahāṇa*). Next, from "We have come to the ultimate" to "wisdom," it explains wisdom (*jñāna*).
Next, from "We have come to nirvāṇa" it again explains severance. Finally, from "The grace to which the Buddha has come" it again explains wisdom.

Thus, one knows that the first two sections clarify abiding in the severance of the small [vehicle], while the next one and a half sections clarify the loss of great wisdom, followed by another one and a half sections that re-explain it.
The commentary on the subsequent line concerning the severance of the minor [defilements] explains that those who have lost great wisdom [regard] all phenomena as empty and quiescent;
this means that the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*) is originally empty, eternally abiding, equal, pure, and unconditioned. "Those in their final body" refers to Arhats.

"Nirvana with remainder" means that while the fetters of the "son" (the afflictions) have been exhausted, the fetters of the "fruit" (the aggregates) still remain. "Those taught by the Buddha," and so forth...
By highlighting the faults attained through the loss of great wisdom, one lacks aspiration and joy; yet if one possesses great wisdom, one loses that aspiration and joy.
To cultivate [the path] and thereby attain realization is the way to repay the Buddha’s kindness. △ Third, the conclusion.
"Although we preach the Bodhisattva Dharma for the sake of the sons of the Buddhas and others in order to seek the Buddha-way, we have forever no aspiration or delight [in it].
This explains that he himself has no intention of seeking or grasping [for it]. △ Third, clarifying that the Buddha’s vision of abandonment is consistent with having no aspiration for grasping.
The Teacher, seeing that [the son] had been abandoned [by others], did not initially urge him forward or speak of the actual benefits, because he was observing his mind.

△ Second, the verse on the entrustment of the family business, which has two parts: first, the verse on the formal entrustment of the business; second, the restatement of the parable and its application. First, the restatement of the parable and its application.
Just as a wealthy elder, knowing his son’s inferior disposition, uses the power of skillful means to gently subdue his mind before finally entrusting him with all his wealth.
△ Second, the actual verse on the entrustment of the task.

The Buddha is likewise; manifesting rare and marvelous events, he perceives those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle and, through the power of skillful means, tames their minds before teaching them the Great Wisdom.
△ Second, the verse on the joy of receiving the entrustment.
Today we have attained what we never had before; that which we did not previously hope for, we now receive for ourselves, just as that impoverished son obtained immeasurable treasures.
World-Honored One, today we have attained the Way and the fruit; regarding the untainted Dharma (anāsrava-dharma), we have attained the pure eye.
For a long night we have upheld the Buddha’s pure precepts, and it is only beginning today that we receive their retribution within the Dharma of the Dharma-King.
"Having long cultivated the pure conduct, we have now attained the supreme, great fruit that is free from outflows. We are now truly śrāvakas;
by the sound of the Buddha-way, we cause all to hear. We are now true arhats;
among all the worlds—devas, humans, māras, and brahmās—we are universally worthy of receiving offerings."
"Those who have attained the Way attain the Way of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa); those who have attained the fruit attain the fruit of practice of the Mahāyāna.

This clarifies the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge. "Regarding the untainted dharmas (anāsravadharma), they attain the pure eye. This clarifies the opening of the Buddha’s vision; seeing the principle of the true mark.
Previously, seeing the untainted did not cause one to fall among ordinary beings; today, seeing the untainted does not cause one to fall into the two [vehicles].
Riding upon the wisdom-eye of the past that saw emptiness, one now sees the Middle Way with the pure eye. Regarding those who obtain retribution for upholding the precepts:

in the past, they upheld the precepts and practiced the Brahma-faring life together to manifest the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*); yet, as their physical forms were reduced to ashes and their wisdom extinguished, there was no one to receive this fruit of retribution.

Today, through the Brahma-faring life, one can attain the outflow-free state; this is the meaning of the "revealing cause" (*jñāpaka-hetu*) taking its fruit. Upholding the precepts is the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya*).
The principle perceived by the eye of the purity of causal meaning is precisely the meaning of the true cause;

we who are true śrāvakas are indeed at the true stage of the Mahāyāna. While the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*)—in which a single sound pervades the three thousandfold world-system—are like the path rather than the reality itself, entering the ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*) is the reality.
There are three meanings of a true arhat, all of which are cited here.
One is called an *Arhat* (Worthy of Offerings) only when one is capable of serving as a field of merit for the ten dharma-realms;
furthermore, it is said that one is called "Unborn" (*anutpāda*) only when there is no longer birth through transformation;

and it is said that one is called a "Slayer of Thieves" only when the common and specific views and afflictions (*kleśa*) are completely severed. △ Second, thirteen lines praising the profound kindness of the Buddha.
The World-Honored One, with great kindness, has out of compassion taught and benefited us through this rare occurrence; who could ever repay such a debt over immeasurable billions of kalpas?
Even by providing for our hands and feet, prostrating with our heads at his feet, and making every kind of offering, none could repay it.

Furthermore, even if one were to carry him upon the crown of one's head or on both shoulders for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, serving him with the utmost reverence and the finest delicacies...
Even if one were to use immeasurable precious robes, various bedding, diverse medicinal decoctions, ox-head sandalwood,
and all manner of rare jewels to construct stūpas and temples— spreading such precious garments upon the ground— and were to offer these as worship for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
one still could not repay the Buddhas’ rare, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable great supernormal powers.
The King of all dharmas—taintless and unconditioned—is able to endure such matters for those of inferior capacity;
yet he teaches according to the suitability of ordinary people who grasp at signs. The Buddhas have attained supreme mastery over all dharmas;

knowing the various inclinations, desires, and mental powers of sentient beings, they teach the Dharma through immeasurable parables according to what each can bear, in accordance with the needs of all sentient beings.

Having known through various deliberations and distinctions whether the roots of goodness from past lives have matured or not yet matured, [the Buddha] teaches the Three Vehicles as appropriate within the single vehicle path. Zhanran says:
"The Great Benevolence of the World-Honored One" refers to when the Buddha first established compassion and made great vows to rescue [sentient beings].
The suffering of the six realms and the bliss of the four noble ones universally enter the Four Great Vows throughout the ten dharma realms;

this is the first aspect of the Tathāgata’s room, the grace of bestowing bliss through great compassion. Second, regarding the Tathāgata’s practice: although the Bodhisattva path may cause me to forget the Mahāyāna for a time, my wisdom and vows shall not be lost.
This is because the Tathāgata’s room is cool and warm, providing the grace of great compassion that grants happiness. Second, when sentient beings regress from the Mahāyāna...
When sentient beings encounter suffering, the Buddha observes their capacity and opportunity in the interim—like a calf following its mother—to benefit them by practicing the six perfections.
This is because the Tathāgata’s chamber wards off the cold and obstructs the heat;

with great compassion he uproots suffering, and his grace is such that although the Buddhas have attained enlightenment and ought to enjoy the bliss of unconditioned quiescence, they conceal their spiritual virtues to employ those things that the poor delight in.
1. In the Deer Park, he first used the five precepts and ten wholesome paths to cause them to leave behind the various veils of desire;
this is the Tathāgata’s robe that wards off the heat and affliction of greed. 2. He manifested as an old bhikṣu to skillfully approach them and preach the Three Vehicles for them;
this is the Tathāgata’s robe that removes the cold of wrong views and the heat of craving. 3. Regarding the Vaipulya sūtras, he rebuked and censured them.
To be demoted and disgraced, feeling ashamed of one's smallness while admiring the great—this is the Tathāgata’s robe that conceals ugliness; this is the seventh grace.
To be entrusted with the family business by the command of Prajñā, such that all gold, silver, and treasuries are made known—this is the Tathāgata’s robe that bestows adornment upon me;
this is the eighth grace. At the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, one’s kinship is confirmed as father and son, and the unsurpassed treasury of jewels is attained.
Seeking self-attainment is the Tathāgata’s seat; having sat upon this seat, body and mind are serene and one attains swift peace and stability.
Causing the sound of the Buddha-way to be heard by all, so that all devas and humans everywhere therein should receive offerings, is the Tathāgata’s seat;
it enables me to fulfill my own practice and transform others—this is its grace.
This refers to what is called "the great kindness of the World-Honored One, which cannot be repaid even by bearing it upon both shoulders.
*Fahua jing kezhu*, Scroll Two;
*Miaofa lianhua jing kezhu*, Scroll Three.
△ Chapter Three: The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs (2).

First, the title: *The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma*, Chapter Five: "The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" (*Zhengfahua* refers to it as the "Chapter on Medicinal Herbs"; the *Fahua lun* calls it the "Chapter on Clouds and Rain").
Why is it that this chapter alone, among the mountains, rivers, clouds, and rain, is specifically titled after the medicinal herbs? It is because the land is that which is capable of producing them.

Clouds and rain are that which moisten; grasses and trees are that which are produced by such moistening. Both the moisture and that which is moistened are universally functional, yet medicinal herbs possess a particularly potent efficacy.
Likewise, all conditioned wholesome dharmas (*sāsrava-kuśala*) are capable of eliminating evil, yet they are most effective when directed toward the unconditioned (*anāsrava*).
Among the unconditioned, the four great disciples—using the parable of the impoverished son—comprehended the Parable of the Burning House and deeply harmonized with the Sage’s mind.

For this reason, the Tathāgata describes their attainment of understanding by using them as a metaphor for these people; thus it is called the "Chapter on the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" (the world).
Now, medicinal herbs have grown together for a long time, and upon encountering the clouds and rain, they spread out luxuriantly and flourish;

their sprouts and stems become abundant and lush, with external power nourishing them from without and internal moisture saturating them from within. This is analogous to those who dwell in the final body of no-outflows (anāsrava), who now hear [the Dharma].
The Sūtra, encompassing both the Śrāvaka Vehicle and the Buddha Vehicle, further guides human beings. The text states:

"We who are now truly Śrāvakas [shall] cause all to hear through the sound of the Buddha-way. Because it possesses superior power and function regarding the internal and external, as well as oneself and others, it is titled the "Chapter on the Simile of the Medicinal Herbs" (for the sake of humans).
△ Second, the Explanation of the Text (the Tathāgata’s Confirmation within this Chapter). Part Two: First, the Brief Confirmation; Part One: The Double [Confirmation].
"Excellent! At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa and the other great disciples: "Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!
You have well spoken of the Tathāgata’s true merits; it is exactly as you have said."

The two instances of "Excellent! (sādhu) both express their intent: one describes how they received the reality (*tattva*) at both locations, and the other describes how they received the provisional (*upāya*) at both locations.

Regarding the phrase "well-spoken of the truth" (*satya-sudeśita*): because the phrasing is subtle and skillful, it is called "well-spoken"; because everything is the Buddha-dharma, it is called "truth.
"Truth" describes the merit of receiving the reality, while "reality" describes the sincerity of receiving the provisional.
"What has been stated" refers to the meaning of definitive sealing. *Miaole* says:
"The two locations" refers to the stage of Expedient Means and the Burning House, which correspond to the two cycles of the Dharma and the Parable. △ Second, acknowledging what was not yet reached.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits,
which you would be unable to exhaustively describe even in immeasurable billions of kalpas.

While the teachings of the Two Vehicles are limited such that they only lead those of the Two Vehicles to receive benefits, they do not apply to humans or devas (who may regress), nor to the *zang* and *tong* [teachings].
The benefit for other bodhisattvas (whose progress is insufficient) constitutes the realization of what they have not yet attained. △ Second, the extensive exposition, which consists of two parts:
first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part [the prose] also has two sections: first, the Dharma-exposition; second, first, citing that the Dharma King is not in vain.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas; whatever he speaks is never false.
Although the Buddha-dharma is vast, it does not transcend the provisional and the real; beyond the provisional and the real, there are no other separate dharmas.
As for what was previously called "immeasurable," its meaning is difficult to believe; therefore, by citing the Dharma-King’s words as being true and sincere, he encourages faith.
Furthermore, this serves as the basis for the analogy of the great cloud. △ Second, the exposition of the opening of the three [vehicles] to reveal the one vehicle. Part One:
Clarifying the opening of the provisional to reveal the real according to the teachings. Sub-part One: Explaining the opening of the provisional according to the teachings.
One expounds all dharmas through wisdom and skillful means.
"All dharmas" refers to the seven stages of skillful means (*saptopāya-dharma*).

Although these dharmas are numerous, they are taught according to the various types of sounds through the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*), so that there is nothing that does not accord with and benefit beings. For humans and devas, one teaches the two categories of precepts and wholesome deeds.

The teaching of the [Four] Truths and [Twelve] Conditions is for the Tripiṭaka; the teaching of the Perfections (Pāramitās) of phenomena is for the Shared Teaching; the teaching of Non-arising is for the Distinct Teaching;

and the sequential revelation of the Tathāgatagarbha is what is called the description of its mastery in opening the Threefold [Teachings]. △ Second, describing the manifestation of the Reality according to the Teachings.
The Dharma they teach all reaches the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
"Stage" (*bhūmi*) refers to the ultimate reality-mark (*tathatā*), which is non-dual; because its nature is vast and expansive, it is called "all.
Because it is quiescent yet ever-illuminating, it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). Because it is the foundation of non-abiding that establishes all phenomena, it is called "stage. It is wondrous bliss.

Regarding the phrase "ultimate equality," this clarifies that all provisional [teachings] ultimately return to the true mark (*dharmatā*). Therefore, when the teachings and wisdom of the three vehicles have not yet converged, they are not called "one.
Because it is the ground upon which wisdom relies and from which all wisdoms are produced, it is named the "ground of wisdom" (*jñāna-bhūmi*).
△ Second, clarifying the provisional to reveal the real by means of wisdom, in two parts. First, describing the opening of the provisional by means of wisdom:
The Tathāgata perceives and knows the ultimate destination of all phenomena, and he also knows the profound mental activities of all sentient beings, penetrating them without obstruction.
To contemplate all places of refuge is provisional wisdom; being able to illuminate these provisional knowledges of where one is headed is to be able to identify the medicine.
To know the practices of the deep mind is to be able to recognize the illness—all of these are provisional dharmas. Each provisional dharma has its own destination:

precepts, good deeds, and so forth, lead proximately to the realms of humans and devas; yet, if they serve as distant conditions—such as bowing the head or raising the hands—they lead distantly to the fruit of Buddhahood.
The applications of mindfulness, the factors of enlightenment, and so forth, lead one near to nirvāṇa;

whereas if you cultivate the adornment of merit, that which you practice is the bodhisattva path leading far toward the place of treasure. Thus, from the six perfections to the various specific and general dharmas, the different routes of near and far destinations can be understood.
Regarding the practices of the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*), there are two kinds: if the profound mind is attached to...

Regarding the "reliance on the correct" (the primary body) and the "reliance on the secondary" (the environment): if one gives rise to the ten grave evils that obstruct the vehicles of humans and devas;

or if one becomes attached to the dharmas as being truly existent, giving rise to the four inversions, the three paths, the six obscurations, and the four or five abidings, these will obstruct the four noble vehicles.

One should know that the manifestations of these deep-seated mental afflictions differ; the Tathāgata, by means of his provisional wisdom, illuminates them all with unimpeded penetration. △ Second, [the section] concerning wisdom.
This describes the manifestation of reality.
Furthermore, it exhaustively clarifies all phenomena and reveals to all sentient beings the wisdom of omniscience.
That which is "clarified regarding all phenomena" is that which is illuminated by true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*); for there is no provisional dharma whatsoever that does not enter into reality.
It is said that because it exhaustively investigates what is seen by the Buddha-eye and known by true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), it is "clearly manifest" (*vibhūta*).

If this wisdom illuminates the various distinctions of seeds, it is the illumination of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*); if one wisdom universally illuminates all medicines and all illnesses, it is the illumination of true wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "unimpeded penetration" used for the aforementioned provisional wisdom, this refers to the real in terms of the provisional.

Now, regarding the text on "actual wisdom" (*bhūtajñāna*) and "provisional means" (*upāya*) among all phenomena: this refers to the mutual manifestation of the two—reality and provisionality—in both ultimate discourse and conventional discourse.
It clearly demonstrates that reality is provisional and provisionality is real; one should know that ultimately they are neither provisional nor real, neither differentiated nor non-differentiated.
Through the skillful means of wisdom, although there are distinctions within provisionality, once one reaches the ground of wisdom, there is no longer any differentiation.
...Also. △ Second, the illustrative explanation, which has two parts: first, the actual clarification; second, the opening of the analogy.
First, the analogy of having distinctions, which illustrates the wisdom of the provisional teaching. Sixth, the analogy of the land.
Kāśyapa, it is like this: the mountains, rivers, valleys, and terrain of a trichiliocosm are used as a metaphor for the world of sentient beings;
the mountains, rivers, valleys, and terrain are a metaphor for the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
There is no separate dharma that constitutes the terrain of the world, just as there is no separate dharma that constitutes sentient beings other than the five aggregates.

The land being level represents the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), while the mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys represent the other four aggregates. The *Yaojie* (Essential Explanation) states:
"The great trichiliocosm is a single expanse of earth, yet it contains the elevations and depressions of mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys;
this is like how the one true realm contains the distinctions of the three realms and the various destinies. 2. The Simile of the Herbs and Trees.
The various species of flowers, trees, forests, and medicinal herbs that arise differ in their names and forms.

Flowers and grasses are collectively termed "herbs," while trees are generally called "woods"; when many herbs form a thicket and many trees form a forest, those with superior power to cure diseases are designated as "medicines.
Just as wholesome dharmas can all cure evil, so too do untainted wholesome states have the function of curing afflictions.
Because they are superior, they are likened to medicinal herbs, trees, and forests whose branches and trunks provide vast shade;
using this great metaphor for the two types of bodhisattvas, it is said that because the causes and fruits of the five vehicles and seven wholesome qualities are not identical, they are "various.

Thus, each type has its own designation and its own essential characteristics, which are precisely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); therefore, they are said to be "distinct. △ Third, the metaphor of the dense clouds.
Dense clouds spread everywhere, completely covering the three thousandfold world system.

These "dense clouds" are a metaphor for the Buddha’s Three Mysteries (sanmi). That the clouds possess form and color is a metaphor for the Buddha’s appearing in the world, which is the Mystery of Body (shinmitsu).

That the clouds can provide shelter and shade is a metaphor for the Buddha’s compassion, which is the Mystery of Mind (imimitsu). In the following passage, the distant thundering of the voice is a metaphor for the Buddha’s... [text continues]
The teaching itself is the secret of speech; because it permeates the manifested body with compassion to preach the Dharma throughout the ten dharma-realms, it is said to be "pervasively spread.
△ Fourth, the analogy of raining down:
at one time, it pours equally upon all.
It is like the Buddha using the eightfold voice and four types of eloquence from his secret mouth to proclaim and pour down the rain of Dharma, benefiting and nourishing sentient beings.
△ Fifth, the analogy of receiving nourishment:
Its moisture universally saturates the grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and all medicinal herbs—those with small roots, small stems, small branches, and small leaves.
There are middling roots, middling stems, middling branches, and middling leaves, as well as great roots, great stems, great branches, and great leaves.
When the rain of Dharma universally moistens the ground of the hearts of these seven kinds of sentient beings, all the seeds of habitual causes immediately sprout;

this is called the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). That which is named "universally nourishing the roots, stems, branches, and leaves" refers to faith as the root, precepts as the stem, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as the branch.
Wisdom is the leaf; because they mutually support one another in succession, these four are used as analogies. The small roots and stems represent the faith and precepts of humans and devas;
the medium roots and stems represent the faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom of the two vehicles;
and the great roots and stems represent the faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom of the bodhisattvas. △ Sixth, the analogy of growth.

The various trees, according to their size—whether superior, middling, or inferior—each receive what is appropriate; rained upon by a single cloud, they grow and flourish according to their respective natures, putting forth flowers, fruits, and seeds.

This clarifies that just as grasses and trees receive moisture according to their capacity, so too do the seven classes of sentient beings, through the two causes of habituation and retribution, [cultivate] wholesome dharmas.

"Receiving the rain of the Dharma, both the fruits of practice (*śikṣā*) and retribution (*vipāka*) each attain growth according to their respective natures" clarifies the provisional application of means (*upāya*) to suit the capacities of beings:

for those of small capacity, they do not exceed their measure, and for those of great capacity, they are not diminished. This refers precisely to the seven kinds of causes of practice and retribution.
"The flowers and fruits unfold and bear fruit" refers precisely to the two kinds of fruits of practice and retribution. △ Second, the Absence [of Defilement].
The three analogies illustrating the distinction between the teaching of reality and the wisdom [that realizes it]: first, the analogy of what is produced by a single stage.

Although it is produced within a single stage, that which is produced from the "mind-ground" prior to the Path ultimately depends upon the "wisdom-ground" subsequent to the Path. Second, the analogy of the rain showered by a single cloud.

Moistened by a single rain and proclaimed with a single voice, the Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle develops the five kinds of roots of goodness; ultimately, it is the teaching of a single, equal voice.
△ Third, the analogy of the three types of grass and two types of trees.
Yet each of these grasses and trees has its own distinctions.

Just as the three types of grass and two types of tree receive nourishment without being aware of it, so too do those with the five kinds of good roots grow according to their respective capacities under the rain of the Buddha-dharma without realizing it;
nor do they realize that these five causes all rely upon the single Buddha-nature.
Knowing that the teachings of the five vehicles are all Mahāyāna, yet not knowing for oneself that they all return to the Buddha-wisdom—only a Tathāgata can know this.
△ Second, the combined analogy, in two parts: first, combining the analogy of differentiation;
second, the formal combination in six parts. First, combining the dense clouds.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is likewise so when appearing in the world:
like the rising of a great cloud, he pervades the world with a great voice for the sake of devas, humans, and asuras; just as that great cloud completely covers the trichiliocosm.
First, it is raised that the Buddha’s body is like a secret cloud that manifests in form within the world;

this precisely corresponds to the appearance of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) in the world, just as a great cloud arises. This immediately provides a simile to clarify that the Tathāgata, through his great compassion, manifests a body to cover and nourish all beings.
"With a great voice" refers to the Buddha’s secret speech (*vākmudrā*), which is like the sound of a cloud. Heaven... [text ends].
Regarding "humans and asuras," this separately cites the three wholesome realms to illustrate the benefit of the secret of speech;

that is, those with the distinct capacities of the three vehicles receive the benefit of the voice accordingly. "Like that great cloud" is a metaphorical illustration, corresponding to the fact that clouds possess sound.
"Pervasively covering the great trichiliocosm" generally refers to all beings, who are equally the children of the Buddha and thus all receive the secret of speech.
...the benefit thereof. △ Second, combining the notes on the two rains. First, the initial presentation of the chapter headings. Sixth, the first proclamation of the ten titles.

Among the great assembly, he uttered these words: "I am the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
△ Second, the proclamation of the Four Great Vows:

Those not yet crossed over, may I cause them to cross over; those not yet liberated, may I cause them to be liberated; those not yet at peace, may I cause them to find peace; those not yet in nirvana, may I cause them to attain nirvana.

The *Bie xing xuanyan* states: "The great vows are fundamentally established through compassion; since compassion takes suffering and pleasure as its object, the great vows likewise rely upon the Four Noble Truths.
If one perceives the truth of suffering—its oppression and agonizing torment—one gives rise to a vow on this basis, hence it is said:
'Those not yet crossed over, may they be crossed over. If one perceives the truth of origination—the inverted flow and circulation through birth and death, vast and boundless—"
Out of compassion for them, he makes this vow: "Those who have not yet understood, may they understand the path of purity;

those sentient beings who do not recognize that by practicing this path one can transcend birth and death to reach the ground of peace and bliss—desiring to establish these beings upon this path, he says:
'May those who have not yet found peace find peace. The place where afflictions are extinguished is called Nirvana, the fruition of the child."
Having severed the bonds and attained the two types of nirvana, he makes this vow on their account; therefore, it is said that what has not yet been attained shall be attained.
△ Third, the proclamation of the threefold knowledge:
he knows the present life and future lives as they truly are.

The *Shanjian* (Commentary on Difficulties) states: "Past-life knowledge (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) reaches the past; the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) reaches the future; and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*) reaches the present life.
These are the three penetrations (*trividya*), also called the three insights (*tisro vidyāḥ*). △ Fourth, the single mind and the three knowledges.
I am the All-Knowing One.
The All-Knowing One is one who is fully endowed with the three types of knowledge. △ Fifth, proclaiming that he possesses the five eyes:
the All-Seeing One.
"One who sees all" is one who is fully endowed with the five eyes. △ Sixth, the three karmas are conjoined with wisdom.
"One who knows the Way," "one who opens the Way," and "one who speaks the Way.
"One who knows the Way" refers to non-restraint of the mind; "one who opens the Way" refers to non-restraint of the body; "one who speaks the Way" refers to non-restraint of speech. As it is said:
Because his three karmas are always conjoined with wisdom and thus free from error, there is no need for him to guard them; this is called the "threefold non-guarding.
△ Second, the exhortation to listen and receive:
"You multitudes of devas, humans, and asuras should all come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma."
From a general perspective, it is appropriate to encourage others to go and listen to the Dharma in order to follow the three wholesome paths. △ Third, the gathering of the assembly:
At that time, countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings came to where the Buddha was to listen to the Dharma.

"Grasping at retributive fruits, there are sentient beings," as if depending upon mountains and rivers (that is, the land), one obtains worlds numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis—this refers precisely to the sentient beings of the ten dharma-realms;
here, we are simply speaking of the distinctions among the sentient beings of the seven stages of expedient means.
△ Fourth, combining [the analogy with] herbs and trees.
At that time, the Tathāgata observes the sharpness or dullness of the faculties, and the diligence or indolence of these sentient beings.

Just as in the preceding analogy there were differences among the herbs and trees in their size and variety, here, in the combined explanation, it is clarified that there are sharp and dull faculties and progressions of practice;
this refers precisely to the depth of the causes of cultivation, which is identical in meaning to the analogy of the herbs and trees, and is not an extraneous addition.

Regarding "at that time": if one discusses the gradual beginning, it refers to the time of preaching the Three Vehicles at the Deer Park; if one discusses the intermediate period, it may be discussed in various places.
Regarding "sharp and dull faculties": if judged generally, those in the three miserable realms—whose causes are evil and whose fruits are suffering—and who cannot receive the Way are called "dull";
those who, through the seven kinds of skillful means, gain benefit upon hearing the teaching are called "sharp. If...
Regarding the distinct classification: those among humans and devas who only receive karmic retribution and are unwilling to accept the Path are termed "dull";

those of the three vehicles' root-natures who sever delusions and exit the realms are termed "sharp. Furthermore, Śrāvakas who contemplate arising and ceasing are termed "dull," while Bodhisattvas who contemplate non-arising and non-ceasing are termed "sharp.
By discussing sharpness and dullness across the three teachings—Shared, Distinct, and Perfect—their relative subtlety and coarseness can be precisely understood.

Those who advance toward diligence are those who abandon the three miserable realms; negligence is called indolence for humans and devas, while upholding the precepts and performing good deeds is called diligence for humans and devas.
Not being weary of suffering is indolence for the Two Vehicles, while fearing impermanence is diligence for the Two Vehicles.

Greedily seeking realization without aspiring to become a Buddha is indolence for Bodhisattvas, while resolving to seek the Buddha-way is diligence for Bodhisattvas. △ Fifth, receiving moisture together.
He preaches the Dharma according to their respective capacities, in various and immeasurable ways, causing them all to rejoice and swiftly obtain wholesome benefits.
"According to their respective capacities" means that he accords with their individual aptitudes, free from the faults of excess or deficiency;
"rejoicing and obtaining wholesome benefits" means that each receives the nourishment of the Dharma and gains its benefit. (6) This is the sixth section: Increase and Growth.
When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they will attain peace and security in the present life and be reborn in favorable realms,
experiencing happiness through the Path and further hearing the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, they will be free from all obstacles and, according to their individual capacities,
gradually enter the Path among all dharmas.
"Attaining peace and stability in the present life and rebirth in a good realm" refers to the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) that brings about the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*).

"The blossoming and growth of the combined flowers, as well as hearing the Dharma and even entering the Path" refers to the causal condition of practice (*abhyāsa-hetu*) that draws forth the fruit of practice (*abhyāsa-phala*).
Just as the Buddha is like a great cloud that universally covers all three realms of suffering, causing them to be moistened and grow; it is as described in the *Panna*.
If the Vaipulya sutras also clarify that one gains benefit from the hells—such as when the fire is extinguished and the boiling water cools—this constitutes peace and security in the present life;
or if one is reborn among devas or humans, this constitutes a favorable rebirth in future lives. To cultivate the Path while among devas and humans is to experience happiness through the Path.
If humans or devas hear the Dharma and maintain the precepts, their merit will sustain their bodies; this is [the benefit].

Peace and security in the present life, or the rebirth of devas among devas, humans among humans, or mutual rebirth between devas and humans—this is birth in a good destination in future lives and the attainment of awakening.
To hear the Dharma and attain *nirvāṇa* with remainder through the Two Vehicles is peace and security in the present life;
to be born in a land of skillful means is birth in a good destination in future lives.
Hearing the sutras there, one receives joy through the Way;

if a bodhisattva with a birth-body hears the Dharma preached by Vairocana Buddha and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), this is security in the present life. Birth in the Land of True Reward is birth in a good realm in the future.
To be free from all obstacles and receive joy through the Way is security in the present life according to one’s capacity.
Entering the Way is precisely receiving happiness through the Way in future lives. △ Second, the application [of the analogy].

Just as that great cloud rains upon all the herbs, trees, thickets, forests, and various medicinal plants, each receives its full nourishment according to its own nature and attains growth accordingly.
The Great Cloud Sutra, Fascicle One: "Form and Sound Both Benefit" (The Rain Falls Upon All). Fascicle Two: "The Sixfold Chapter Dharma Gate.

Fascicle Four: "Grasses, Trees, and Forests. Fascicle Five: "Sentient Beings Receiving Transformation—According to Their Sharpness or Tardiness, Diligence or Indolence, and the Depth or Shallowness of Their Causes for Practice;
According to Their Seed-Nature, They Fully Receive Moistening. Fascicle Six: "Receiving Moistening and Attaining [Realization]."
Furthermore, each attains growth and increase; this is the sixth [section], on the increase of peace and stability in the present life. △ Second, the combination of the two without distinction:
first, the combination of one earth and one rain.

The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma has but one characteristic and one flavor; that is to say, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation, ultimately reaching the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

As for the "one characteristic," the minds of sentient beings are identical to the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*); this is the One Ground (*ekabhūmi*). As for the "one flavor," it is as follows:
The Dharma of the One Vehicle explains the same single principle; this is the "one rain. In the past, through skillful means, the one true reality was opened up into seven aspects.
Within the Dharma of the One Vehicle, it is distinguished and taught as seven teachings, yet the Buddha knows that they ultimately converge into a single aspect and a single flavor.
This is what is meant by the following double explanation of the single aspect and single flavor regarding the nature of the minds of sentient beings.
This refers to the three characteristics of the liberation of intrinsic virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*): remoteness, tranquility, and cessation.

Regarding these, the characteristic of liberation is the absence of the characteristic of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); the characteristic of detachment is the absence of the characteristic of nirvāṇa; and the characteristic of cessation is the absence of characteristics, even the absence of absence, wherein there is only the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, it is called the "one characteristic. Within this one characteristic, these three characteristics are present. Thus, the Tathāgata is one...
Master Yin explains that these three marks are, within a single flavor, three flavors;

these three marks serve as the objective conditions for the practice of the Middle Way arising from conditions, which ultimately results in the fruit of omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Therefore, it is said that one "ultimately reaches all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Furthermore, he further explains that the single mark is the foundation of non-abiding upon which all phenomena are established.
Non-abiding and signlessness are without differentiation; the establishment of all dharmas involves differentiation.
Differentiation is like that of herbs and trees, while non-differentiation is like the single earth and single taste. This is the True Teaching (Shijiao), which is pure and without admixture;

by taking this as an analogy for the "One Aspect" (Yixiang), it can be understood. II. The Meaning of Differentiation. This corresponds to the preceding section on the differentiation of grasses and trees. Part Five: First, Sentient Beings.
They do not know it.
There are sentient beings who, upon hearing the Dharma of the Tathāgata, uphold, read, recite, and practice it according to the teaching,
yet they do not themselves realize or know the merit thereby obtained.
Regarding those who possess the notion of a "sentient being," they are all ignorant of the Dharma of persons and dharmas;

that is to say, even if they hear the Dharma of a single sound and uphold or explain it, they correctly clarify that their understanding of upholding and explaining is not the same, and their practice is likewise different.

Those in the realms of humans and devas form an understanding of precepts and wholesome deeds, while those of the Three Vehicles form an understanding of the Truths, Conditions, and Means of Deliverance. Since these understandings are already different, this constitutes the differentiation of what is attained.
Those who do not know are clarified as follows: although these five people each received the teaching, they did not realize that the Buddha’s teaching is of a single flavor and without distinction.
They failed to recognize the reality and were unaware of the seven kinds of skillful means and their distinct teachings;
yet, each clung to their own understanding as the truth because they did not understand the provisional. Therefore, it is said that they "do not awaken to themselves. △ Second, the Tathāgata.
One is able to know through four initial points based on four dharmas. Why is this?
Because only the Tathāgata knows the lineage, characteristics, and essential nature of these sentient beings.
As for "lineage," it refers to the three paths; these are the seeds of the three virtues. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that they are the "multitude of all afflictions. They are like...

To cultivate this illumination through the path of afflictions is precisely the presence of *prajñā*. Furthermore, it is said that all five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) give rise to the appearance of liberation;
this is because from the unwholesome there arises the wholesome dharma of liberation.

All sentient beings are themselves the appearance of *nirvāṇa* and cannot be further extinguished; this is the taking of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as the *dharmakāya*. This is explained in terms of relative opposition.
Regarding the discussion of seeds: if one discusses seeds according to their categories, all bowing the head and raising the hands are seeds of liberation;
all worldly wisdom and the minds of the three vehicles seeking liberation are seeds of Prajñā. Indeed, all who possess a mind shall become Buddhas; this is the seed of the Dharmakāya.
The various distinctions among these seeds are themselves non-distinct, and that which is non-distinct is itself distinct. Thus is the Tathāgata able [to manifest them].

Regarding the knowledge of characteristics and essence, this is explained in terms of the ten realms and the ten suchnesses. If one discusses their differentiation, it refers to the characteristics of the ten realms;
if one discusses their non-differentiation, it refers to the characteristics of the single Buddha-realm. Differentiation is non-differentiation, and non-differentiation is differentiation.

That the Tathāgata is likewise able to know their essence and nature can be understood by analogy. △ Second, knowing the three [realms] by means of the three dharmas. First, the explanation of the three.
The objects of wisdom:
what is recollected, what is contemplated, and what is cultivated?
These three factors are precisely the three types of wisdom—those of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. "Objects" refers to the spheres of these three wisdoms, namely that which is heard.
That which is contemplated and cultivated refers to the dharmas of the various characteristics, aspects, and essential natures explained in the preceding teachings;

the phrase "all say" indicates the objects of apprehension, and according to the teachings, there are differences in contemplation and cultivation. △ Second, clarifying the essence of the three types of wisdom.
What is mindfulness, what is reflection, and what is cultivation?
As for mindfulness: mindfulness is the recording of the Dharma one has heard; it is precisely the essence of mindful wisdom (*smṛti-prajñā*).
△ Third, the causes and conditions for the three types of wisdom (*trividya*).
By means of what dharma does one recollect, by means of what dharma does one contemplate, and by means of what dharma does one cultivate?
These are the three wisdoms that apprehend their objects; hearing the Dharma is their cause and condition. Thus, these three vehicles possess the three wisdoms from of old.
That is to say, when the essence of objects arises from differing causes and conditions, there is distinction; yet upon entering the perfect and subtle threefold wisdom, there is no distinction.
This distinction and non-distinction the Tathāgata is able to know. △ Third, knowing by means of two dharmas.
By what dharma does one obtain what dharma?
By what dharma is the cause obtained, and by what dharma is the fruit obtained? The causes of the five vehicles each obtain their respective fruits;
this is "differentiation. That all Buddhas are of one suchness and non-dual is "non-differentiation. Differentiation is non-existent.
The Tathāgata can know distinctions, yet he knows that distinction is itself non-distinction, and non-distinction is itself distinction; the Tathāgata can also know this.
△ Fourth, knowing by means of a single dharma:
Sentient beings abide in various stages, but only the Tathāgata perceives them as they truly are, with clarity and without obstruction.
Because the seven stages of the preparatory practices (*saptopāya*) consist of seven distinct positions, they are called "various grounds. This constitutes their differentiation.

The Tathāgata perceives them with his Buddha-eye of reality (*yathābhūta-buddhacakṣus*), seeing that once they have entered the ocean like the confluence of rivers, they lose their original flavors and become undifferentiated.
While he speaks according to the inclinations of others through the skillful means of wisdom (*jñānopāya*), the Tathāgata is nonetheless able to know their distinctions.
The Dharma he teaches all reaches the stage of omniscience; thus, the Tathāgata knows them as being without distinction.
△ Third, the application of the analogy of not knowing:
just as those herbs, trees, forests, and various medicinal plants do not themselves know their own superior, middling, or inferior natures.
This is analogous to those who practice the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*), each of whom cannot know for themselves;
because they do not know, it serves to manifest that only the Tathāgata is able to know. △ Fourth, reiterating the preceding point to explain "ability to know."
The Tathāgata knows that this is the dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor— namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment,
the characteristic of cessation, and ultimate nirvāṇa, which is the characteristic of eternal quiescence and ultimately returns to emptiness.

The single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) and the single flavor (*ekarasa*) have already been explained as above. Taking characteristics, flavors, liberation, detachment, cessation, and so forth as conditions for conceptual differentiation is precisely the infinite within the one, which is ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
Ultimately returning to emptiness is precisely the one within the infinite.
This is a restatement of the previous point to re-explain non-differentiation. Why? Because the single characteristic and single flavor are liberation.
If "detachment" and "cessation" were the essence of the Dharma-body of the Two Vehicles, they would still be described as distinct terms;
yet now, by establishing the ultimate *nirvāṇa* of the Mahāyāna, it ultimately returns to emptiness—this universally encompasses the non-distinctive ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

The preceding phrases all refer to what is not the *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) or *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder) of the Two Vehicles, but rather the ultimate *nirvāṇa*, which is eternally quiescent and extinguished.
The various phrases above concerning "mutual binding" do not refer to the quiescence of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), but rather to eternal, abiding quiescence.
As stated in the preceding text: "All dharmas have from the beginning been eternally and spontaneously characterized by quiescence"—this is precisely that meaning.
That which "ultimately returns to emptiness" is not the emptiness of annihilation, but rather the emptiness of the primary truth of the Middle Way. △ Fifth, explaining its...
The assembly was filled with doubt.
The Buddha, knowing this, observed the inclinations and desires of sentient beings and, in order to protect them, did not immediately preach the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
This explains away the doubts of sentient beings: "Since the Buddha already knew from the beginning to the end that all is one, why did he not immediately preach the Truth at the Deer Park?
The explanation says: He observed the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings and, in accordance with the three *siddhāntas*, sought to protect them;
fearing they might slander [the Dharma], he did not preach it immediately. II. Reaffirming the Thesis and Praising [It] (also called the Concluding Praise), Part One: The Exposition.
[The Buddha] sighed:
"O Kāśyapas, it is truly rare that you are able to know the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and that you are able to believe and accept it.
He spoke thus to reaffirm his point and to resolve their doubts. As for those who have doubts, having heard of the Buddha’s immeasurable merits, they [suspect] the four younger brothers...

In the teaching of "Equalizing" (Samatā), understanding is attained through guidance; why must it necessarily be the ultimate reality? Therefore, although the Buddha’s description has not yet reached the stage of Buddhahood, the teaching of Equalizing is not false.
Furthermore, this is intended to inspire those of inferior capacity to likewise attain awakening. As for why he first praises its rarity:

ordinary beings, having previously experienced setbacks, can gain benefit upon hearing it again; whereas for Bodhisattvas, who have already realized this as their own business, there is no longer much wonder in the understanding.
To be able to renounce and realize the true state is most rare;

to be able to know and rejoice in the one who preaches the Dharma describes their capacity for reception, while the three subsequent statements describe their realization. To be able to believe and accept describes their reception, thereby manifesting the one.
△ Second, the explanation of the praise.
Why is this so? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; it is difficult to understand and difficult to know.

This clarifies that while the Buddha speaks of three [vehicles] within the One Way—profound, mysterious, and difficult to comprehend—you are nonetheless able to believe and accept it; therefore, he praises you.
How rare! △ Second, the verses in praise, which are divided into two parts. First, the verses praising the Dharma-exposition. First, the verses praising that the Dharma King does not speak in vain.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The Dharma King who shatters existence appears in the world.

Because the twenty-five kings of samādhi have shattered the twenty-five existences, and because the Tathāgata has shattered this king within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), he is called the "Dharma King who shatters existence";
this refers to the meaning of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*). △ Second, the verse on opening the three and revealing [the one].
The first two lines of the initial verse [discuss] the second: the teaching. First, the verse on the provisional teaching:

preaching various doctrines according to the desires of sentient beings, and employing skillful means to teach according to their inclinations—this is the worldly intention. Second, the verse on the ultimate teaching.
The Tathāgata honors wisdom that is profound and far-reaching; he has long remained silent on this essential point and did not strive to speak of it hastily.

Because he does not disparage what he teaches, he says he "honors" it. Having deeply discerned that those of limited capacity were not yet able to receive it, he remained silent for more than forty years without speaking.
Now that the great capacity has been awakened, he finally speaks for their sake. △ Second, the verse:
Regarding the two types of wisdom, the first verse explains provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*):
"Those with wisdom who hear this will be able to believe and understand; those without wisdom will doubt and regret, thereby suffering eternal loss.
Question: Since it is said that "those with wisdom who hear this" must refer to those with the capacity (*yogyatā*), how can it be said to belong to the Buddha's provisional wisdom? Answer: If...
Since it is not for the sake of those who lack wisdom that one speaks—asking how one could cause those with wisdom to believe—it belongs to the Buddha.
This refers to the intention of the person [who spoke]. The three *siddhāntas* above are verses on what was previously explained through wisdom and skillful means.
△ Second, the verse explaining true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Therefore, Kāśyapa, according to their capacities, I teach using various causes and conditions to enable them to attain right view.

This verse means that from the point of reaching the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), one teaches various doctrines through various causes and conditions solely for the purpose of enabling others to attain the right view of the Mahāyāna;
prior to this, all are termed wrong views. This is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate established tenet).

This is the meaning. △ Second, the verse on the parable, in two parts: first, the verse on the opening of the parable; second, the verse on the distinctions [of the parable]. First, the verse on the distinctions, in six parts; first, the verse on the dense clouds:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that it is like a great cloud arising in the world, pervading and covering all things; the cloud of wisdom contains moisture."
Flashes of lightning dazzle and the sound of thunder reverberates afar, bringing joy to the multitude; the sunlight is eclipsed and the earth becomes cool.
The clouds hang low and spread out as if they could be grasped.

The clouds are likened to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), for the response body follows the movement of wisdom; thus it is called the "Wisdom Cloud" (*prajñā-megha*), capable of possessing the twelve divisions of the scriptures.

Because it is the Dharma of the Sūtras, it is said to contain moisture; if the *saṃbhogakāya* were not to preach the Dharma—as in the cases of Suśānta and Prabhūtaratna—this cloud would lack moisture.
Its body emits great radiance like a flash of lightning, and its mouth resounds with the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) like the sound of thunder.
Because sentient beings hear the Dharma and rejoice, it is said to be "joyful"; because the ninety-five kinds of heterodox lights do not appear, [it is so called].
The phrase "concealing and removing" refers to the removal of the ninety-eight kinds of afflictions of view and thought, which are like a heat; it is like the coolness upon the earth.

The Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) descends into the world appearing as if identical to the three realms of existence, and though one might go with a mind to grasp it, it is truly unobtainable; therefore, it is said to be "like something that can be grasped.
△ Second, the verse on the pouring of rain.
That rain falls equally upon all four directions, streaming down in immeasurable torrents to saturate the entire land.
Because the Dharma-rain is proclaimed and poured forth through the eight tones and four analytical knowledges, heard simultaneously by all, it is said that "it falls equally upon the four directions.
Because all who possess a mind receive its benefit and profit, it is said that "the entire land is saturated. This both completes the preceding [section] and establishes what follows.
Mountains and rivers are metaphors for this. △ Third, the verse on the land:

"Mountains, rivers, and perilous valleys" refers to the aforementioned land, which consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings in the seven stages of expedient means; they now receive the rain of the Dharma, [purifying] their bodies and speech.
"Supple and soft like the earth, it receives moisture. △ Fourth, the verse on herbs and trees:
"The herbs, trees, and medicinal plants produced in the deep recesses.

Regarding "produced in the deep recesses," this verse refers to the aforementioned differences in the habitual causes of sentient beings, illustrating how sentient beings have [existed] for a long time.
Because the planted causes of habituation lie hidden within the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas), they are said to be "profound and remote";
now, having encountered the rain of the Dharma, they have all been brought to full development, and thus they are said to be "that which has grown. △ Fifth, the verse on receiving nourishment.
The great and small trees, the hundred grains, the seedlings and crops, the sugarcane, and the grapes—all were made abundant and sufficient by the moisture of the rain.

Even the parched lands were universally moistened, and medicinal herbs and trees flourished together. From that cloud issued water of a single flavor, yet the grasses, trees, and forests received its nourishment according to their respective capacities.
The "hundred grains" are taken collectively to represent the five grains, which serve as a metaphor for the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*) being able to produce a hundred virtues.

The sugarcane and grapes represent meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). The thorough moistening of dry land represents causing those who have not yet attained faith to believe. The remaining metaphors are as explained in the text.
△ Sixth, the verse on growth.
All the trees—whether superior, middling, or inferior—each grow according to their respective size;
their roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, as well as their luster and color, all become fresh and radiant wherever the single rain falls.
△ Second, the verse on non-differentiation. Part one: the actual verse on non-differentiation.

Just as their essence and characteristics are such that their nature, divisions, and magnitude result in a single moisture, the first two lines of the verse praise what is produced and what is moistened;
the next line praises the agent of moistening—this is the verse on non-differentiation.
Separate. △ Second, the verse on the ignorance of their differences, yet each flourishing luxuriantly.
△ Second, the verse on combining the analogy; first, the verse combining the differences (of the six); first, the verse combining the dense clouds. First, [part one].
This perfectly accords [with the analogy].
The Buddha likewise appears in the world in this same manner.
△ Second, the application [of the analogy].
For example, it is like a great cloud that universally covers all.
△ Second, the verse on the combined annotation regarding the raining of the two [teachings]. First, the presentation of the topical headings. First, the verse on the Ten Epithets:
Having appeared in the world for the sake of all sentient beings, the Great Sage, the World-Honored One, analytically expounds the reality of all dharmas.
In the midst of all the assemblies of devas and humans, he proclaims these words: "I am the Tathāgata, the Honored One among two-legged beings;
having appeared in the world like a great cloud.

This verse summarizes the ten epithets; the phrase "appearing in the world" contains the meaning of "Unsurpassed One" (Anuttara) and "Buddha," while "for the sake of preaching" refers to the "Teacher" (Śāstṛ).

The Perfectly Enlightened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha), the One Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct (Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna), the World-Honored One (Bhagavat)—the tenth title—among gods and humans is the Tamer of Men (Puruṣadamyasārathi) and the Teacher of Gods and Humans (Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām);

the Tathāgata—the first title—who has come from the well-gone (Sugata) and has departed well (Sugata), having emerged from the world, is the Knower of the World (Lokavid). II. Verses on the Four Great Vows.
To moisten and nourish all withered sentient beings, causing them all to leave suffering behind and attain the peace and joy of worldly happiness as well as the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
To moisten and nourish all— that is, those whom one has vowed to deliver— causing them all to leave suffering behind and cause them all to leave their causes behind.
The suffering of the fruit is the vow to sever afflictions; the attainment of secure bliss is the vow to study the Dharma-gates;

and the bliss of nirvana is the vow to accomplish the Buddha-way. All five vehicles possess worldly bliss, yet [the Bodhisattva] causes them all to attain the supreme bliss of nirvana. △ Second, the exhortation to listen and receive.
All you multitudes of devas and humans, listen with single-minded devotion; all should come here to behold the Unsurpassed Honored One.

I am the World-Honored One, whom none can equal, appearing in the world for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings. For the great assembly, I shall preach the pure Dharma of ambrosia.
This Dharma is of a single flavor—liberation and nirvana—and with one wondrous voice, I shall expound this meaning, always for the sake of the Mahāyāna.

Thus, as a causal condition, he exhorts [the audience] to listen and receive the teaching. This section has two parts; the first part consists of the initial two lines, which first praise the Buddha, and subsequently, from "for the sake of the great" onwards, praises his discourse.
Because the speaker—the Honored One—is supreme, the Dharma he teaches is the wondrous nectar (*amṛta*). This medicine is now heard as the wondrous Dharma, which sustains the life of wisdom.
Because it prevents untimely death, it is called the "Amṛta Pure Dharma. Since the seven virtues all return to the One Vehicle (the single flavor), one is exhorted to listen and receive it.
△ Third, the verse on the convergence of mountains and rivers.
I contemplate all things as universally equal, without a mind of attachment or aversion toward self or others;
free from greed and without obstruction, I constantly preach the Dharma with impartiality for all.

Mountains and rivers are like the seven kinds of five-aggregate sentient beings; the rain falls without distinction between ravines and valleys, for the Buddha’s teaching is impartial. Thus, there is no "this" or "that":
those with the capacity [to receive] it are "this," while those without the capacity are "that"; those who plant roots of goodness are "loved," while those who create evil are "hated.
Because one does not harbor love for the Buddha's capacity while hating the capacities of others, there is no greedy attachment or limitation.
Whether for one person or for many, he constantly expounds the Dharma without ever engaging in other matters;
whether going, coming, sitting, or standing, he never grows weary, sufficing the world like rain that universally moistens all.
Buddha-activity is for oneself and Mara’s activity is for others; the former corresponds to coming, and the latter corresponds to departing.

Entering into reality is sitting, and emerging through skillful means is standing. When the Buddha observes sentient beings with such equality, this is precisely the meaning of raining [the Dharma] equally upon mountains and rivers.
This verse summarizes the aforementioned countless billions of sentient beings. △ Fourth, the verse on the convergence of herbs and trees.
Whether toward the noble or the lowly, the high or the low, those who maintain the precepts or violate them, those whose dignified conduct is complete or incomplete,
and those with right view or wrong view, whether of sharp or dull faculties— to all these he rains down the Dharma rain without weariness.
Nobility and meanness refer to the station; upholding and violating refer to conduct; sharpness and dullness refer to habituation.

From nobility and meanness to sharpness and dullness, one must also fully traverse the five vehicles and seven wholesome practices, explaining them in their successive progression. △ Fifth, the verse on the harmonious reception of moisture, in three parts:
first, a general clarification of receiving moisture.
All sentient beings who hear my Dharma abide in various stages according to what they receive through their respective capacities.
△ Second, a specific explanation of receiving nourishment, in five parts: first, small grasses, humans, and devas.
Those who dwell among humans and devas as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), Śakra, or the various Brahmā kings are the "small medicinal herbs.
Since both humans and devas have not yet severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), they are collectively categorized as small herbs. △ Second, the "medium herbs" are the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Those who know the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), are able to attain *nirvāṇa*, give rise to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), and obtain the three insights (*tisro vidyāḥ*);
dwelling alone in mountain forests, constantly practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and attaining the realization of a *pratyekabuddha*—these are the medicinal herbs.

The two vehicles both possess wisdom and abandonment; these combined constitute the middle and small medicinal herbs. The six supernormal powers and threefold clear knowledges are explained in the "Parable" chapter.
△ Third, the superior medicinal herbs:
the *saṃghāṭa* bodhisattvas who, seeking the state of World-Honored One, resolve, "I shall become a Buddha," and practice the concentration of vigor—these are the superior medicinal herbs.
The Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections, who aspire to attain Buddhahood and transform others, surpassing the Two Vehicles, are therefore alone designated as the "superior grasses.
△ Fourth, the small trees are the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching.
Furthermore, these sons of the Buddha single-mindedly devote themselves to the Buddha-way, constantly practicing compassion, and know with certainty that they will become Buddhas without any doubt.
This is called the "small tree.

The Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) have already severed the delusions common to the two vehicles; yet, they vow to sustain their remaining habits while entering the realm of existence to transform others. Compared to those below, they are superior;
compared to those above, they are inferior. Therefore, they are called "small trees. △ The fifth is the "great tree," referring to the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).
Abiding securely in supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma and deliver immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings;
such Bodhisattvas are called "Great Trees.

According to the Separate Teaching (*pṛthag-deśanā*), because the Bodhisattvas' own practice and their transformation of others are superior in their height and breadth, they are named "Great Trees. Thus says the *Myōraku* (The Wondrous Joy).

In the *Great Tree* (Dajù zhōng), it is stated that the "wheel of non-retrogression" (*avivartana-cakra*) is turned; since those of the Separate Teaching (*biejìe*) at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) are able to turn the wheel of Dharma, this refers to "non-retrogression through mindfulness.
In the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings (*zàngtōng*), one only turns the wheel of Dharma upon reaching the final fruit.

How, then, could they be called "such Bodhisattvas"? Therefore, we know this refers to the Separate Teaching. △ Third, the conclusion regarding the moistened and the moister. First, the topical explanation of the moistened.

The Buddha teaches with impartiality, like a rain of a single flavor; yet according to the dispositions of sentient beings, what they receive differs, just as the various plants and trees each absorb nourishment differently.
△ Second, clarifying that which provides moisture.
