these evolve every seven days to form mind and form (*nāmarūpa*). Because this mind and form constitute the substance, it is said that "consciousness conditions name-and-form.

As for the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*), once the six faculties have been formed within the womb, they possess the capacity to admit sensory objects; thus they are called "bases. Since they exist...
Because mind and form (*nāmarūpa*) accomplish the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), it is said that "name-and-form conditions the six bases. As for "contact" (*sparśa*) conditioned by the six bases:
from after birth until the age of three or four, because the faculties encounter their objects yet one is not yet able to discern them, this is called contact;

hence it is said, "the six bases condition contact. As for "feeling" (*vedanā*) conditioned by contact: the experiencing [of an object] is called feeling; this lasts from the age of five or six until twelve or thirteen.
When the six sense objects contact the six sense faculties, one immediately experiences the qualities of the external objects, such as their being pleasant or unpleasant;
although this constitutes discernment, it does not yet give rise to a mind of craving. Therefore, it is said that "contact conditions feeling. These five [links] belong to the present result.
As for craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it refers to the period from ages fourteen or fifteen up to eighteen or nineteen, during which one covets various excellent and wonderful requisites.
Regarding objects such as forms and desires, although one has not yet extensively and universally pursued them, because of their being experienced, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) immediately arises;

therefore it is said that "feeling is the condition for craving. As for "craving is the condition for grasping" (*upādāna*): from the age of twenty onwards, whenever one sees any object, a mind of grasping and attachment arises;
because attachment arises from craving, it is said that "craving is the condition for grasping. Furthermore, this craving and grasping...
That which belongs to the cause of future birth and death and is associated with afflictions, being identical to past ignorance, is called "clinging conditions becoming" (*upādāna-pratyaya-bhava*);
this is because, having become attached to various objects, one gives rise to wholesome and unwholesome karma, which accumulates and draws forth rebirth in the three realms of existence.
Furthermore, that which belongs to the cause of future birth and death and is associated with karma, being identical to past formations (*saṃskāra*), refers to:
Rebirth within the six realms of existence arises from *bhava* (existence), as one undergoes further birth in future lives; therefore, it is said that "conditioned by existence, there is birth.

Because the body that has undergone birth matures and decays, it is called old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*); thus, it is said that "conditioned by birth, there is old age and death. These two [links] belong to the future fruit.

Regarding the mention of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction at the end of the text, as stated in the *Myōgen* (Wondrous Profundity): [it refers to the suffering experienced during the process].

Old age and death inevitably entail sorrow and lamentation. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease;

with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases.
When craving ceases, grasping ceases; when grasping ceases, becoming ceases; when becoming ceases, birth ceases; when birth ceases, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease.

The twelve links of dependent origination are simply the detailed observation of the Four Noble Truths in their distinct aspects; regarding suffering and its origin, they are respectively "existence" and "non-existence."
From ignorance up to old age and death, regarding their cessation through the Path, there is the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death.
Whether observing in reverse or in forward order, all are rooted in ignorance;
therefore, when ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease, and so on, until birth ceases, whereby old age and death cease. △ Third, attaining the Path upon hearing the Dharma.

When the Buddha preached this Dharma amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, six million billion nayutas of people attained liberation of the mind from all outflows (*āsrava*) by way of not grasping at any phenomena;

they all attained profound and wondrous meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and were endowed with the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). During the second and third preachings of the Dharma, ten million [people attained these].
Sentient beings numbering as many as billions of nayutas of Ganges sands likewise attained liberation of the mind from all outflows (*āsrava*) by way of not grasping at any phenomena;
from that time forward, the assembly of śrāvakas became immeasurable, boundless,
and incalculable.
One who does not accept any phenomena does not accept various views and realizes the first fruit;

one who attains liberation is liberated from the two bonds of the "fruit" and the "seed" and attains the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). One with profound and wondrous concentration is a person of "double liberation" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), who is fully endowed with the practice of contemplation, refinement, and cultivation;
such concentration is termed "profound and wondrous. The three types of higher knowledge (*trividyā*) and so forth are explained as before; the four [fruits] are mentioned first.
When he expounded the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, six hundred trillion nayutas of people attained the Way;
during the second, third, and fourth preachings of the Dharma, those who attained awakening became even more numerous than before, such that they could not be numbered.
△ Second, the Turning of the Wheel of the Full-Syllable Dharma: Part One, The Prince’s Renunciation.
At that time, the sixteen princes all left the household life as youths to become śrāmaṇeras; their faculties were keen and their wisdom was clear,
for they had already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, purely cultivated the Brahma-faring,
and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"The various faculties" refers to the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Because these six faculties are pure, they are said to be "penetrating and sharp.

Furthermore, because the six faculties function interchangeably, they are said to be "penetrating," and because they reach the realm of the Buddha, they are said to be "sharp. "Clarity of wisdom" refers to opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
△ Second, the request to practice and study the Dharma.
They all addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of great and virtuous śrāvakas have already achieved [their goals].
World-Honored One, you should also preach for us the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
having heard it, we shall all practice and study it together. World-Honored One, our aspiration is the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, the profound mind..."
He realized this through his own mindfulness of the Buddha.
The sixteen sons requested once more that he set aside half [of the teaching] to reveal the full [truth], just as the present Buddha now preaches the Lotus Sūtra.
That Buddha first taught the perfect and sudden Mahāyāna, wherein all merits are fully complete; yet he further took pity on those who rely on expedient means.
For the sake of ultimate realization, they again entreat the Buddha to reveal the provisional and manifest the real.
That "the śrāvakas have all already achieved" clarifies that their obstacles have been removed and the capacity for the Mahāyāna has been activated; thus, they make this request.

When it says, "We aspire to the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision," this means that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* solely elucidates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; to aspire only to this is the formal request.
The manifestation of the full-character script as it supersedes the half-character script is clearly like this. △ Third, those he led forth to leave the household life:
At that time, among the multitude led by the Wheel-Turning Sage King, eighty trillion people saw the sixteen princes leave the household life and also sought to leave the household life;
the King immediately granted them permission.
△ Fourth, accepting the invitation to preach the Dharma.

At that time, after that Buddha had accepted the śrāmaṇera’s invitation for more than twenty thousand kalpas, he preached this Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wonderful Law* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*)—a teaching for bodhisattvas and protected by the Buddhas—amidst the fourfold assembly. He preached this sūtra.
The sixteen śrāmaṇeras had already collectively received, maintained, recited, and mastered [the teachings] for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
After twenty thousand kalpas had passed—
referring to how the Buddha previously taught the doctrines of the Truths, the Conditions, and so forth for the sake of the three vehicles— he subsequently accepted his sons.
Please consider that because he requested the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, we know that he could not have remained silent without speaking during this interval;

for within these twenty thousand kalpas, he must have preached the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras. Thus, the subsequent verse states: "He preached the six pāramitās as well as the matters of various supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Prajñā is the practice, while supernatural powers are the manifestations. Indeed, many of the current Vaipulya sūtras clarify these points extensively.
Because he deliberated upon various supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), it is known that this is the Vaipulya spoken by that Buddha.

Furthermore, because the verse says, "Discerning the true Dharma," which clarifies the meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Great Perfection of Wisdom) regarding the reality-mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of prajñā, it is known that this is the Prajñā spoken by that Buddha.
△ Fifth, the understanding or lack thereof among the assembly.
When this sutra was being preached, all sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras believed and accepted it; among the assembly of śrāvakas, there were also those who believed and understood;
yet among the other beings of thousands of myriads of koṭis, all gave rise to doubt and confusion.

The sixteen śrāmaṇeras and those of the two vehicles constitute the assembly of those who have attained faith and understanding; the remaining ten million are all members of the assembly who harbor doubts and are thus not yet resolved.
This latter assembly is precisely that which, while listening to the sixteen sons’ re-expounding of the Dharma, established the karmic conditions for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
△ Sixth, the time and occasion of preaching the sutra.
The Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand kalpas without ever ceasing or resting.
△ Seventh, after finishing the preaching, he entered meditative absorption.
Having finished preaching this sutra, he immediately retired to a quiet chamber and dwelt in dhyāna-concentration for eighty-four thousand kalpas.
After that Buddha had preached the Lotus Sutra, he entered into meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This was precisely the proximate cause for establishing karmic connections.
Because the Buddha had entered concentration and did not emerge for thousands of myriads of koṭis of years, those who possessed various doubts and perplexities had no one to consult.

Therefore, the sixteen śrāmaṇeras lectured on the *Lotus Sutra* for them as a substitute. △ Second, the actual establishment of karmic connections, in two parts: first, the establishment through the Dharma-exposition.

Regarding the first section of the initial passage on the analogy of forming karmic connections through two examples, there are three parts. First, it clarifies how they previously formed a connection together.

Within this, the first part concerns knowing that the Buddha had entered meditative absorption: at that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha had entered his chamber and was in silent, tranquil dhyāna-concentration.
△ Second, the two princes gave a recitation of the teaching.
Each ascended the Dharma seat and, for eighty-four thousand kalpas, extensively expounded and analyzed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the fourfold assembly.

Because the Buddha had entered meditative absorption, he was able to know that his transformation of one being was nearing completion and that this particular group of people would no longer be ripened;
thus, he caused the prince to form a karmic connection with them.

Furthermore, knowing that these individuals would certainly attain ultimate liberation through the prince, he remained in absorption for a long time without emerging. △ Third, the benefits obtained by the assembly.
Each one delivered six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, instructing, benefiting,
and gladdening them, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Because they have all resolved their minds on Bodhi, it is said they are "saved. When one first resolves the mind [on enlightenment], vowing to become a Buddha, one has already transcended the mundane world;
this is the meaning of having crossed to the other shore of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidhopāya*).

The "nayuta" of sentient beings refers to the aforementioned masses who do not understand. "Showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening" means: "showing" is pointing out; "teaching" is instructing and admonishing.
To instruct them so that they obtain benefit is "benefit" (*hita*); to cause their minds to rejoice is "joy" (*sukha*). △ Fourth, the praise upon emerging from meditative concentration, in two parts:
first, praising the Bodhisattvas.
After eighty-four thousand *kalpas*, the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū arose from his samādhi and proceeded to the Dharma-seat.
Sitting serenely, he addressed the great assembly: "These sixteen śrāmaṇera bodhisattvas are truly rare;

their faculties are keen and their wisdom is lucid. They have already made offerings to immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, and under those Buddhas they have constantly cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya).
Having received and upheld the Buddha-wisdom, they reveal it to sentient beings, causing them to enter therein."
The Buddha arose from samādhi and praised the bodhisattvas merely to encourage his followers.
"Tranquil" (*ānāpāna*) means peaceful, composed, and elegant; this is truly rare. This is precisely a praise of the bodhisattvas.
II. Exhorting others to draw near. 1. First, the exhortation to draw near.
"You all should repeatedly draw near to and make offerings to them.
This is an exhortation regarding those whom the Bodhisattvas transform. Second, the explanation of the intent behind the exhortation:
Why is this so? Because if Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Bodhisattvas can believe in these sixteen [Bodhi]-...
Those who receive, uphold, and do not disparage the sutras and dharmas spoken by the Buddha shall all attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata, which is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
△ Second, clarifying the intermediate encounters.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These sixteen bodhisattvas always delight in preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Each of these bodhisattvas has transformed six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

wherever they are born from lifetime to lifetime, they are accompanied by these bodhisattvas, and hearing the Dharma from them, they all believe and understand it. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they have encountered [the Buddhas]."
The forty trillion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, are not yet exhausted.
This clarifies that after the initial formation of karmic connections, they constantly encounter one another during the intervening period. There are three types of such encounters:
first, those who meet and constantly receive the Mahāyāna; this class has all already attained accomplishment in the interim and has not reached the present [time]. Second... [text truncated]
If they encounter one another, and those who have encountered the Great [Vehicle] yet regressed are still received by means of the Small,

this class of people remains, as it were, not yet exhausted; now that they are able to hear the teaching of the Mahāyāna again— though this discussion concerns only encountering the Small and does not mention encountering the Great—
it follows that those not yet saved in the interim will likewise not be exhausted at present, but will only now begin to receive the Great [Vehicle], continuing until after my parinirvāṇa.
The Way is this very thing. [Question: For as many eons as there are motes of dust, it was only now that he first attained arhatship;

if this is so, how can the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) be so easily ascended? [Answer: The Great Sage, through his skillful means (*upāya*), speaks thus according to the four *siddhāntas*.
Or, for those who would grow weary of the long duration of the Buddha-way, he speaks of its brevity, lest they develop a sense of contempt for the Buddha-way.

To those whose conceptions are easily transformed, one speaks of "long" as a *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (remedial tenet). Or, for the purpose of generating past roots of goodness, one speaks of long and short;
this is the *pudgala-siddhānta* (tenet for individuals). Or, according to what the world desires, one speaks of long and short; this is the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly tenet).
Or, so that upon hearing the discourse on long and short one may immediately enter into the principle, this is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (ultimate tenet).

Regarding the *siddhānta*, one should know that the statement that it was only after such kalpas that he attained arhatship is a provisional practice (*upāya*) of the four *siddhāntas* used to lead those of true practice (*satyavādins*) into the Way. △ Third, explaining that he now returns to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Part two: First, reconciling the past and present; first, reconciling the teacher’s past and present.
"O monks, I now tell you: those sixteen śrāmaṇeras who were disciples of that Buddha have all now attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
they currently reside in buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, preaching the Dharma, with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as their retinues.
Of those two śrāmaṇeras, one has become a Buddha in the eastern direction."
The one named Akṣobhya resides in the Land of Joy; the two Buddhas in the southeast are the first, Siṃhaghoṣa, and the second, Siṃhadarśana;
the two Buddhas in the south are the first, Gaganastha, and the second, Nityapraśānta;
the two Buddhas in the southwest are the first, Indradhvaja, and the second, Brahmaketu; the two Buddhas in the west are the first, [Akṣobhya]...
Amitābha has two names: [the first is Amitābha] and the second is Sarvalokaduḥkhapramocana (Deliverer from All Worldly Suffering). To the northwest are two Buddhas:

the first is named Tamālapatrakālānusāricandanagandhābhijña (Supernormal Knowledge of the Fragrance of Tamāla-leaf and Kālānusāri Sandalwood) and the second is named Merudhvaja (Sumeru-mark). To the north are two Buddhas:

the first is named Meghasvara (Cloud-Sovereign) and the second is named Meghasvararāja (King of Cloud-Sovereign). To the northeast is a Buddha named Sarvalokabhayavidhvamsanakara (Destroyer of All Worldly Fears).
Sixteenth: I, Śākyamuni Buddha, have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the Sahā world-system.
The *Akṣobhyavyūha Sūtra* states: "There is a land named Abhirati, and the Buddha there is named Akṣobhya. The commentary (*shù*) explains: "A—" [referring to the phonetic component of the name].
"Speechless" refers to his speech and actions; "Amitābha" is translated as "Pure and Equal Enlightenment," while "Amitāyus" is translated as "Immeasurable Purity and Immeasurable Life.
"Śākyamuni": "Śākya" is translated as "Capable Benevolence" (Nengren), which is his clan name; "Muni" is translated as "Silent Stillness" (Jimo), which is his personal name.
"Capable Benevolence" signifies compassion that benefits all things, while "Silent Stillness" signifies wisdom that penetrates the profound principle.
Because he benefits sentient beings, he does not abide in nirvana; because he accords with the profound principle, he does not abide in saṃsāra.
As for the names of other Buddhas, since I have not seen where they originate, I dare not provide a speculative interpretation. Saha is also called *Sokha*;
this means "Endurance," referring to the trichiliocosm as the field of transformation for a single Buddha. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* asks: "Why is it named Saha?"
Because these sentient beings endure the three poisons and all afflictions, and are able to tolerate such evils, this land is named "Endurance Land" (Sahā).
△ Second, the assembly of followers, both ancient and modern; first, the assembly of present followers, in four parts; first, those dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression.
"O bhikṣus, when we were śrāmaṇeras, each of us converted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who heard the Dharma from us and [set their minds] upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
This statement refers to those who, after the great elements have subsided, do not regress from their dwelling in the unsurpassed path. △ Second, regarding those who regress and dwell as śrāvakas:
"Among these beings, there are those who currently dwell on the stage of the śrāvaka; I constantly teach and transform them toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi: these people should enter the Buddha-way gradually by means of this Dharma.
This means that after having planted the seeds [of enlightenment], they subsequently regressed from the Great Vehicle toward the Small, dwelling in the stage of a śrāvaka;
the Buddha then taught them through the Mahāyāna so that they may now gradually enter the Buddha-way. △ Third, explaining the intent behind their regression and dwelling.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.

This explains the intent behind those who retreat from and abide in [the Lesser Vehicle]: although they possess the great seeds [of the Mahāyāna], because the Buddha’s wisdom is difficult to believe and understand, they retreat from the Great Vehicle and turn toward the Small.
△ Fourth, the formal conclusion connecting the ancient and the present.
The "immeasurable sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" who were transformed at that time refer to you, all you bhikṣus.
"At that time" points to the period when the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū planted the seeds for them.
II. Gathering Future Disciples. Part One: The Actual Gathering.
These are the śrāvaka disciples who will exist in future ages after my parinirvāṇa.
△ Second, resolving doubts:
After my parinirvāṇa, there will again be disciples who do not hear this sutra and thus neither know nor realize the conduct of bodhisattvas.
Regarding the merits they have attained, they will give rise to the thought of extinction and think that they shall enter nirvana;

yet I shall become a buddha in another land under a different name. Although these people harbor thoughts of extinction and enter into nirvana, they shall seek the wisdom of a buddha in that land and hear this sutra, attaining extinction solely through the Buddha-vehicle, with no other vehicle existing.
Setting aside the skillful means by which the Tathāgatas preach the Dharma, those who harbor doubts may say:

"Those in the present age who hear the Buddha preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and enter the One Vehicle are indeed part of the stream of those with whom [the Buddha] has established a karmic connection;
however, as for those in the future who enter parinirvāṇa without hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, how could such people possibly [attain this]?"

"Abandoning the Lesser Vehicle to enter the One Vehicle" is explained as follows: although they have entered parinirvāṇa, I shall cause them to become Buddhas in other lands so that they will ultimately hear this sutra.
"Other lands" refers to those where the teachings common to the Three Vehicles remain.
"Excluding the expedient teachings of the Tathāgatas" serves to sever doubts; the Three Vehicles are merely expedient teachings, for in reality there are no three.
△ Second, explaining the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra. First, the purity of the assembly at that time:

If the Bhikṣus know that the Tathāgata’s time for parinirvāṇa has arrived, and if the assembly is further pure, possessing firm faith and understanding, having thoroughly realized the dharma of emptiness and deeply entered meditative concentration.

Regarding "the time for *nirvāṇa* having arrived": when the Buddhas appear in the world and their work of transforming beings through the Path is about to be completed, they preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Just as Kāśyapa Buddha, Candrasūryapradīpa Buddha, and others appeared in pure lands, preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and then entered *nirvāṇa*, Śākyamuni appeared in this defiled land, preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and then further proclaimed that he would soon enter extinction.

Furthermore, regarding the purity of the assembly of those in *nirvāṇa*: having obtained the benefits of the Tripiṭaka teachings, they are freed from the calamities of the five turbidities and the eight sufferings.
Those with firm faith and understanding have mutual trust in the essence of the mind through the Vaipulya (*fangděng*) teachings.

Those who have fully realized the dharma of emptiness, upon hearing the preaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, attain full realization within the dharma of emptiness; this is precisely the turning [of the wheel of Dharma].
This is the intended meaning of the teaching. △ Second, the formal exposition of the Lotus Sūtra:
He immediately assembled the multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas and preached this sūtra for them, saying: "In the world there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction;
it is only through the Single Buddha Vehicle that one attains extinction."
The gathering of all bodhisattvas constitutes the assembly of kinsmen, and the assembly of śrāvakas constitutes the summoning of his sons;
thus, the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body are designated as the retinue of "influences and echoes. To verify this meaning through the present text, it is clear:
regarding the statement that "there are no two vehicles in the world," according to reason, there is not a single person in the world who is fit to enter parinirvāṇa permanently.
They must ultimately return to the Great [Vehicle]. △ Third, explaining the three previous points of the opening:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata, through his skillful means, deeply penetrates the nature of sentient beings.

Knowing that they aspire to inferior teachings and are deeply attached to the five desires, for their sake he speaks of *nirvāṇa*. If these people hear it, they will immediately believe and accept it."
This follows the meaning of the preceding text: if there were no followers of the two vehicles who attained extinction (nirvāṇa) in the world, for what reason did the Tathāgata teach the three?

The explanation says: "Bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata, through his skillful means and provisional wisdom, deeply understands that sentient beings have small capacities and desires, are attached to the five sensory objects, and are defiled by the five turbidities; therefore, he first preached the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles."

First, the explanation after escaping the peril of the ruined city. △ Second, the parable of establishing a connection. This has two parts: first, the opening of the parable; second, the application of the parable.
The first section further has two parts. First, the analogy of the guide. Within this, there are five points, the first being the analogy of the five hundred *yojanas*.
For example, five hundred yojanas.
These five hundred yojanas represent the various abodes within the cycle of existence where sentient beings above [the desire realm] who have not yet attained liberation are attached;

this corresponds to the "vast house" within the *Fire Simile* chapter. The "Three Realms" represent the lack of peace, which corresponds to the "insecurity" in the *Expedient Means* chapter, as opposed to "safety."
This refers to the meaning of "steadfastness. To speak in terms of lands (*bhūmi*): the Land of Common Abode of the Three Realms is three hundred;
the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder is four hundred; and the Land of True Retribution is five hundred. This is clearly explained in the subsequent allegory which states:
"Knowing all births and deaths—births and deaths themselves are the dwelling place. To speak in terms of afflictions (*kleśa*): the afflictions of views constitute one hundred.
The five lower-tier fetters constitute two hundred; the upper-tier fetters constitute three hundred; the *rajas* (dust-like) delusions constitute four hundred;

and the delusions of ignorance constitute five hundred. The subsequent passage provides a combined analogy, stating that "afflictions" and "the dangers and difficulties of the evil realms" support one another in their meaning.

Speaking in terms of contemplation: entering the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) allows one to transcend three hundred, while entering the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya*) allows one to transcend [the remaining].
The four hundred [stanzas] enter into the Middle Way and can surpass the five hundred [stanzas]; the subsequent text provides a combined analogy, stating:

"One who well knows the characteristics of the obstructions and openings of a perilous path" refers to simultaneously knowing both cause and effect—the two types of meaning of the five hundred [stanzas] mutually support one another.
The term *yojana* is explained as before. △ Second, the perilous and evil paths.
A perilous and evil path, vast and desolate, devoid of people, and a place of terror.

This perilous and evil path is analogous to the multitude of beings above who have not yet crossed over; their afflictions and defilements are heavy, which corresponds to the fire breaking out within the burning house.
It represents the contrast between the unstable dharmas and the secure [state], namely the two types of suffering: *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative).
The various forms of birth and death are the perils of the result; the afflictions of view and thought, the dust-like delusions, and ignorance are the perils of the cause.
Because of these causes and results, they are called "evil paths. Regarding the absence of people, there are two kinds of paths:
first, those that are desolate yet have people who can be relied upon; second, those that are desolate and have no one to rely upon. That which has people to rely upon is illustrated by analogy:
Within birth-and-death there is nirvana, and within afflictions there is bodhi;
though these may appear vast and remote, there is a person who can rely upon them—this generally refers to the three teachings of the Mahayana.

If, however, within birth-and-death and afflictions there were no nirvana and bodhi, it would be like having no illness within medicine or no medicine within illness; this would be a vast and remote void where no one could be relied upon. Much more so!
These three baskets of the two vehicles, according to principle, are common to the two vehicles of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao).
△ Third, the analogy of many people: "If there are many people..."
This is like the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings transformed by the prince, all of whom give rise to doubt and confusion and fail to understand;

it corresponds to the thirty sons within the burning house and the five hundred people in the "Expedient Means" chapter, through which one comes to know the inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings.
△ Fourth, the analogy of desiring to reach the place of treasure.
Desiring to pass beyond this path to reach the place of rare treasures:
because the followers of the Two Vehicles have severed the afflictions of views and thoughts and emerged from the triple world, it is said they "desire to pass beyond this path";

furthermore, because they seek to sever the dust-like afflictions and ignorance to attain the unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment, it is said they "desire to reach the place of rare treasures. △ Fifth, the analogy of the single guide.
There was a guide who was wise, intelligent, and discerning, well-acquainted with the characteristics of the dangers and the passabilities of the perilous path.
This "guide" is none other than the sixteenth prince. That his eyes and ears are pure is called "wisdom" (*cōng*);
that his faculty of mind is pure is called "discernment" (*míngdá*). Taken together, this refers to the purity of the six sense faculties. "Wisdom" (*huì*) refers to single-mindedness.
The three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) are the fulfillment of the five eyes, and furthermore, the three knowledges serve as illumination while the ten powers (*bala*) serve as penetration.
△ Second, the analogy of the guide, in three parts: first, the analogy for the multitude of people being led.
He leads the multitude, intending to pass through this peril.
This is like those who originally formed a karmic connection but have not yet attained deliverance; because their original connection has not been lost, they are led by the Guide.
△ Second, the analogy of those who grow weary and retreat midway. Part one: The great retreat midway. First, the weariness and retreat midway.
The multitude of people he leads becomes weary and regresses along the way.
This "multitude of people" is precisely a metaphor for those who, encountering circumstances midway, abandon the Great Vehicle and take up the Small Vehicle.
"Along the way" does not refer to the literal midpoint; rather, it refers to the period beginning from the initial generation of the bodhicitta and ending with the attainment of Buddhahood.
Because this space between the two pillars gives rise to the intention to withdraw from the Great [Vehicle], it is therefore called the Middle Way.
△ Second, addressing the Guide:
"We are utterly exhausted and filled with fear," they said to the Guide.
Regarding the term "Guide" (Nāyaka), there are three types: first, the Universal Guide of Compassion, as the text says, "There was a guide who led a great multitude";
second, the Guide for Establishing Karmic Connections, as the text says, "The people being led said to the guide";
and third, the Guide of Expedient Wisdom, as the text says, "The guide was many."
These are the various skillful means (*upāya*). There is also the Guide of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), as the text says: "The Guide knows that these people are [such-and-such].
Now, when we speak of the "White Guide," we specifically mean the Guide who establishes karmic connections (*kṣetra-bandha*).

Because he causes those who have regressed from the Great Vehicle to undergo extinction in the Great, and those who have been received into the Small Vehicle to be born in the Small, his birth and extinction move the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
This is called the "White Prince. Knowing that he is retreating from the Great [Vehicle] means that his roots of goodness from hearing [the Dharma] are weak and obscured by ignorance;
therefore, it is said that he is "exhausted" and "dreads birth and death," which is termed "fear.
△ Third, being unable to advance further.
"Unable to proceed further, the path ahead is still long; now I wish to turn back.
"Unable to proceed further, the path ahead is still long" means that the afflictions of view and thought, the dust-like and river-like [afflictions], and ignorance are difficult to sever abruptly.
By employing the Lesser Vehicle to receive them, one does not allow them to return immediately to their original state; thus, there is also the sense of "progressing. △ Second, Receiving.
The young child initially employs many skillful means;
the Guide likewise possesses many skillful means.
This analogy illustrates the principle of "meeting [the disciple] with what is small," which is appropriate for the occasion. △ Second, lamenting the loss of the treasure.
And he formed this thought: "These people are to be pitied; how can they wish to turn back and abandon such great treasures?
It is tragic that they lose the treasure—this is like knowing there is the small while being unaware of the great. △ Third, the manifestation of a city, in two parts: first, the manifestation itself.
Having formed this thought, by the power of skillful means, he manifested a city within the perilous path three hundred *yojanas* away.

This is precisely the teaching of skillful means used to transform those of the two vehicles, enabling them to sever the delusions of views and afflictions and escape the suffering of the triple world.
Therefore, it is said that he led them past three hundred *yojanas* and caused them to provisionally realize the *nirvāṇa* of true emptiness;
thus it is said, "he conjured a city. △ Second, the teaching of the transformation:
He addressed the multitude, saying, "Do not be afraid, and do not retreat. You may now dwell within this great city."
"Act as you wish; if you enter this city, you will quickly attain peace and security, and if you can proceed further, you may also reach the place of treasure.
This parable is intended to encourage and demonstrate the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma. "Do not be afraid; do not retreat."
"Exhorting to turn" means exhorting them to enter the city; "this great city" and so forth indicate the turning that shows the city as a place where one may dwell.
"If one enters this city, one will swiftly attain peace and stability" indicates the turning that realizes the peace and stability of the city.
"One may also proceed to the precious destination" refers to the meaning of advancing forward, which is not discussed in the Tripiṭaka teachings but exists within the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the two meanings of the "Jewel Mine" (ratnākara) shared by the gatekeeper and the Bodhisattva: if one takes the ultimate sense, the "Jewel Mine" refers to the supreme fruit;
thus the preceding text states, "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

If one distinguishes the stages of entry, the "Jewel Mine" refers to the first stage, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādabhūmi*); thus the preceding text states, "The unsurpassed accumulation of jewels."
"Seeking nothing, they attained it spontaneously. It is further said: "They have obtained their share of the Buddha-dharma; all that sons of the Buddha ought to obtain, they have already obtained.
△ Fourth, the Parable of Entering the City.
At that time, the exhausted multitude felt great joy and marveled at this unprecedented event, saying: "We have now escaped this [suffering]."

Having quickly attained peace and security from the evil realms, they entered the illusory city before the multitude; having done so, they conceived the thought that they had already crossed over and the thought of peace and security.

With great joy, they immediately heard of this unprecedented wisdom: the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata), which frees one from the evil realms, and the stage of "Summit" (mūrdhan), which brings swift liberation.

"Safety" refers to the stage prior to the position of patience (*kṣānti*); "entering the city" refers to the stage of seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*); and "having already crossed over the perception" refers to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
This is because it accords with the sons' wishes within the burning house; thus, it is the same as their courageous and vigorous pushing themselves out of the house.

The perception of having "already crossed over" is like attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); the perception of "safety" is like attaining the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Furthermore, being endowed with wisdom and virtue is like [the state] already attained.
The virtue of having attained liberation and realization is like being at ease. △ Third, leading them to the place of treasure, part one: knowing they have rested.
At that time, the guide knew that this multitude of people had already attained rest and were no longer fatigued.
Having attained rest and no longer experiencing fatigue is like reaching the time of supreme *nirvāṇa*, when the assembly is further purified and they escape the calamity;
thus, the great capacity [for awakening] shall be activated. △ Second, heading toward the place of treasure.
He immediately causes the conjured city to vanish and says to the multitude: "Come, you all! The place of treasure is near.
That great city you saw before was merely a conjuration of mine for the sake of providing rest.
By thus vanishing the conjured city and leading them toward the place of treasure, he illustrates the aforementioned correct teaching of the Lotus Sūtra, which reveals the true nature of the jewel.
Regarding those situated near the great city of the ultimate, I manifest a provisional transformation;
this is an analogy for setting aside the provisional to reveal the real. As stated above: "These people should enter the Buddha-wisdom through this Dharma gradually. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is difficult to believe and difficult to understand; thus, within the context of skillful means, it is said: "I cause them to be liberated from suffering."
Question: For those bound who attain *nirvāṇa*, the Buddha uses the power of skillful means (*upāya*) to manifest the teachings of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*).

When it is said that he reveals the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) by opening up the three at five locations, what is the difference between these? Answer: Generally speaking, there is no difference; specifically speaking, there are distinctions.

In the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paryāya*), regarding the teaching that opens up the three and reveals the one, the text states: "The Tathāgata teaches only by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*)."
In preaching the Dharma for sentient beings, there are neither two nor three [vehicles]. Regarding the burning house, the three are opened up through practice to reveal the one;

"vehicle" carries the sense of transport, and transport serves as a metaphor for practice. As the text says: "Each riding upon a great vehicle, they travel in the four directions, sporting and enjoying themselves in happiness.
In the *Śraddhāparivarta* (Chapter on Faith and Understanding), the three are opened up according to persons to reveal the one, thereby reconciling the allegory of the hired laborers.
"The person" refers to the elder’s son; the text states, "We have from of old truly been sons of the Buddha.

In the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs, the distinction between the provisional and the real is clarified through the categories of differentiation and non-differentiation, yet there is no sense of rejecting one and grasping the other. It simply clarifies that sentient beings do not know the Buddha and thus causes them to know him.
If one understands the seven types of differentiation, one realizes that the provisional and the real are identical in their reliance upon the single principle.
Non-differentiation is itself the knowledge of actual differentiation; non-differentiation is non-differentiation yet differentiated—this is merely intended to make this meaning known.
It is never said that there is "neither one nor many. This is because, regarding his own practice, the Buddha’s dual knowledge of the provisional and the real follows his own intentional speech;
thus, the Buddha is able to know both what sentient beings know and what they do not know, encompassing both the preceding and the subsequent.
It is not understood that [this teaching] clarifies the provisional and the real. Now, the "City of Transformation" (pariṇāmika-nagara) specifically concerns the principle (*li*):

it opens up the three to reveal the one, and both the treasure-land and the city of transformation consist of the two principles of the Great and Small Vehicles. By negating the transformative principle of the Two Vehicles, the real principle of the treasure-land—the single principle—is revealed.
What follows, from the "Five Hundred Disciples’ Realization of Understanding" through the parable of "Tying the Jewel," also concerns the principle.
△ Second, the actual application of the two parables. First, the actual application of the parable of the guide. Fifth, the actual application of the aforementioned guide:
"O bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is also like this."
△ Second, the combination of "many multitudes of people":
"Now, for your sakes, I act as a great guide.
This uses that which leads to manifest that which is led. △ Third, the combination of "perilous and difficult evil paths."
He knows that the various births and deaths, afflictions, and evil realms are perilous and difficult;
they extend for four hundred and fifty *yojanas* and are vast and far-reaching.
△ Fifth, those who are wise, intelligent, and discerning are likewise fit for the place of the most precious jewels;
they should go there and be delivered.

Those who are superiorly wise, intelligent, and discerning, and who well know the characteristics of dangerous paths—whether they are passable or obstructed—are likewise fit for the aforementioned desire.

Having traversed the perilous path, they arrive at the place of precious treasures. △ Second, the combined analogy of leading and guiding, in three parts: first, the combination of the people being led.
"If sentient beings... [and so forth].
△ 2. Combining the "Retreat from the Great Path" with the "Connection to the Small Path. First, combining the "Retreat from the Great Path" at the midpoint:
"Those who hear only the Single Buddha Vehicle" corresponds to the aforementioned retreat at the midpoint;
it indicates the absence of the great capacity for enlightenment. △ 2. Combining the phrase "addressing the Guide": [The text continues with the disciples] addressing the Teacher.
Consequently, they do not wish to see the Buddha nor wish to draw near him;
together with the preceding, this refers to those who address the Guide but do not accept his exhortations and admonitions. △ Third, being unable to advance further, they think thus:
"The path of the Buddha is long and distant; only after enduring diligent suffering for a long time can it be accomplished."

Having joined [the palms], one cannot proceed further; this is the intention to cease the transformation. △ Second, joining to connect with the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). First, joining to accord with the skillful means of the Teacher:
The Buddha knows this mind.

The meaning of joining the upper [part] while withdrawing the intermediate [part] and returning to the great by reconnecting with the small is illustrated by the fact that although there are originally four conjunctions, there are now only three;
this precisely represents the intention of the Guide’s many skillful means (*upāya*) to adapt to what is appropriate. △ Second, the conjunction of these who are to be pitied.
Those who are timid and inferior are, by the power of skillful means, joined with the superior [vehicle];
these pitiable ones are known to possess small faculties. △ Third, they are joined and manifested as a conjured city (*nirmāṇa-pura*) so that they may find rest midway;
for this reason, two types of *nirvāṇa* are taught.

This collectively illustrates the analogy of the conjured city (*nirmāṇa-pura*). Within this, the teaching of two types of *nirvāṇa*—distinguishing between *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* at these two intermediate stages—refers to the *nirvāṇa* of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, it refers to the two deaths (*dvimaraṇa*): while the death of the segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*) has been exhausted, the death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-bhava*) has not yet been eliminated, and the delusions of the triple world have been exhausted while the sands-of-samsara ignorance (*avidyā*) remains unbroken.
Because it is judged as being with remainder or without remainder within this interval, it is called the Middle Way. △ Third, the convergence leading toward the treasure place.
Part one: Convergence through knowing that breathing has ceased.
If sentient beings abide in these two stages...
△ Second, proceeding toward the place of treasure.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately spoke for their sake: "That which you have accomplished is not yet complete; the stage upon which you abide is near to the Buddha-wisdom.
You should observe and deliberate that the nirvāṇa you have attained is not the ultimate reality; it is merely [the teaching] of the Tathāgata."
The power of skillful means causes him to differentiate and preach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
△ Second, citing a parable and applying it to the text, in two parts: first, citing the parable of turning back to apply it to the bestowal of the three vehicles.
It is like that guide who, for the sake of providing rest, conjured a great city.
△ Second, citing the analogy of the extinguished transformation to bring it back for a unified explanation:
Having known that [the city] has ceased, he tells them, "The place of treasure is near; this city was not real; I created it by transformation."

△ Second, the two verses in praise [of the formation of the karmic connection]. First, the verse summarizing the causes for forming the connection; second, the verse on the actual formation of the connection. The first section further has two parts: first, the verse on the remote causes;
second, the verse on the Great Universal Penetration attaining Buddhahood. The first of these further has three parts: first, the verse on events prior to attaining Buddhahood.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas; yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood.
The devas, nāga kings, asuras, and their hosts constantly rained down celestial flowers as an offering to that Buddha."
The devas beat celestial drums and performed various musical offerings; fragrant winds blew away the withered flowers and rained down fresh, beautiful ones.
△ Second, the verse on the actual attainment of the Way:
After ten intermediate kalpas had passed, he finally attained the Buddha-way; the hearts of all the devas and the people of the world were filled with exultation.
△ Third, the request for the Dharma combined with making offerings:

The poisonous beasts are a metaphor for delusions; the absence of water and grass is a metaphor for not cultivating the path to bodhi.
The clarity and stillness of the water represent meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the variety of the grass represents wisdom (*prajñā*). △ Second, the verse on the multitude of people.

possessing strong memory and wisdom, with a clear mind and firm resolve, one rescues the multitude from perils.

featuring multi-gated towers and lofty pavilions, all filled with men and women.

The various houses and residences are the objects of the contemplation of emptiness. The gardens and groves are the groves of the untainted dharmas of the total retention (*dhāraṇī*) of the two vehicles.
The nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) are the channels; the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) are the bathing pools.

The triple gate is the triple gate of emptiness, which is also the samādhi of the "repeated emptiness. The towers and pavilions rising high above are the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). The men...
The woman represents concentration and wisdom. One who understands through contemplating the mind possesses the essence of wisdom in its entirety, like a city wall;

wholesome dharmas are perfectly complete, like the surrounding moat; ultimate emptiness serves as the dwelling; and true goodness enables the accomplishment of one's own practice, like a man managing domestic affairs.
Compassion and kindness transform others externally, like a woman marrying out. △ Second, the verse on transforming others.
Having thus performed this transformation, he comforted the multitude, saying: "Do not fear; you all may enter this city and each may go wherever you please.
△ Fourth, the verse on entering the city:

△ Section Three: Two Verses on the Cessation of the Transformation and the Direction toward the Jewel Place. △ First Verse: Knowing that [the beings] have rested.
The Guide, knowing they have rested...
△ Second Verse: Ceasing the transformation and leading them to the place of jewels.

Now, exert yourselves with diligence, and together we shall reach the place of treasure."
△ Second, the two verses that synthesize the parable, divided into two parts: first, the actual synthesis; second, the synthesis of the analogy of leading the way.
First, the synthesis of the five hundred *yojanas*. "I, likewise, am the guide for all.

thus, through the power of skillful means, for their sake he preaches Nirvana, saying: "Your suffering has been extinguished, and that which was to be done is already accomplished."
△ 2. The combined destruction and transformation leading to the place of jewels. Part one: Having combined, they know the cessation of breath;
once they know they have reached nirvāṇa, they all attain arhatship.
△ 2. The combined destruction and transformation leading toward the place of jewels.
Thereupon, he gathered the great assembly and preached the Dharma of reality: "The various Buddhas, through the power of skillful means, have distinguished and taught the three vehicles;
yet there is only the single Buddha-vehicle. Because it is a place of rest, they spoke of two. Now I shall preach the truth for you: that which you have attained is not extinction.
You must arouse great diligence to realize the all-knowledge of a Buddha—the ten powers and other Buddha-dharmas."
To be endowed with the thirty-two marks is the true cessation.
This verse contains the meaning of the secret treasury of the three virtues: your realization of omniscience is *prajñā* (wisdom);
your possession of the thirty-two marks is the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body); and this true cessation is *vimukti* (liberation).
That these three dharmas are neither vertical nor horizontal is precisely the seeing of the Buddha-nature. △ Second, the verse provides an analogy and applies it to the teaching:
