△ Second, the bestowal of predictions for the final two chapters. Part One: The Chapter on the Bestowal of Predictions upon the Five Hundred Disciples; Part Two: The Bestowal of Predictions upon the Thousand [Disciples].
The Chapter on the Prophecy for the Two Thousand Disciples Who Have Been Taught, both Learners and Those Beyond Learning; Part One of the Hundred Chapters. Furthermore, there are two sections:
first, the title.
*The Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Dharma*, Chapter Eight: "The Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples."
Although this chapter fully records the titles for one thousand two hundred śrāvakas, it only indicates five hundred;

this is because these five hundred received their predictions under the same names, and as they all spoke aloud to express their understanding, the chapter is titled accordingly. △ Second, the scriptural text has two parts:

first, the bestowal of the prediction upon Pūrṇa; second, the bestowal of the predictions upon the one thousand two hundred. The first part further has two sections: first, the narration of his silence.

The first part, "Understanding the Two Tathāgatas’ Narration of the Prophecy," is further divided into two sections. The first section, "Narrating the Joy of Attaining Understanding," is further divided into two parts.

The first part, "Narrating the Causes for Attaining Understanding," is further divided into four sub-sections. The first sub-section, "Hearing the Dharma," concerns the two stages of the revelation and clarification.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, having heard from the Buddha this teaching on wisdom and skillful means for preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate,

upon hearing this wisdom, immediately grasped the skillful means; he understood how the reality was revealed in two ways within the burning house as a skillful means for preaching according to what is appropriate.
The preaching of the Dharma is precisely the summary of the opening of the provisional at both locations. △ Second, hearing the bestowal of predictions upon the five great disciples:
Furthermore, he heard the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon all the great disciples.
The various great disciples refer to Śāriputra and the four principal disciples;
"receiving the provisional and being granted the prediction of Bodhi" implies receiving the revelation of the ultimate truth. △ Third, hearing the account of past-life causes and conditions.
Furthermore, they hear of the events concerning their past causes and conditions.

Upon hearing the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter regarding these past causes and conditions, they immediately comprehend the manifestation of the ultimate reality. △ Fourth, they hear that through the Buddha’s power, their contemplation has been as if for a long time, yet it is as if just now.
Furthermore, one hears that all Buddhas possess the power of great sovereign supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).
The Tathāgata’s threefold penetration (*trividyā*) is unimpeded; he perceives the distant past as if it were today—this is precisely the power of great sovereign supernormal faculties.
By "rejecting the two vehicles" (*dvayayāna*), he establishes the limit at eighty thousand [kalpas], which signifies the opening of the provisional (*upāya-kauśalya*). △ Second.
The narrative of attaining understanding and rejoicing has two parts; first, it clarifies the internal joy of realization.
One attains a state never before experienced, with a pure mind leaping for joy.

Because one has now heard what was previously unheard—the revelation of the provisional to manifest the ultimate—it is said that "one attains what was never before attained. (Excluding the following.)
Because this love that guarantees nirvana severs the sands and pebbles of ignorance and secondary delusions, it is said that the mind is purified and the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened;
therefore, one leaps with joy. △ Second, clarifying external expressions of reverence.
He immediately rose from his seat, went before the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, he did not for a moment cast his eyes away.
This was because he attained understanding through the Buddha, and thus gave rise to reverence. △ Second, the narration of silent contemplation and realization; first, the main part.
They silently reflected and understood, thinking:
"The World-Honored One is most extraordinary; his deeds are rare and marvelous.
In accordance with the various dispositions of those in the world, he employs skillful means and insight to preach the Dharma, drawing sentient beings out from their attachments everywhere. We..."
The Buddha’s merits cannot be fully proclaimed in words.
During the first two rounds [of teaching], Śāriputra and the others attained awakening and all spoke out to acknowledge their understanding; why then do they now remain silent?

This is because Śāriputra and the others were of inferior faculties and had not yet awakened; it was necessary to use explicit words to exhort and move them. Now that those of inferior faculties have already awakened, [there is no need for such encouragement].
Because he was moved by what had been exhorted, he remained silent and did not speak. That which the World-Honored One has done is most extraordinary and rare:

namely, to lead with the wisdom of reality (*tattvajñāna*) while conforming to the seven kinds of expedient means (*upāya*) according to the faculties and natures [of beings] and thereby preaching the Dharma;

this is to lead with the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyajñāna*), which leads through the "Expedient Means" chapter to reveal the reality by opening up the expedients. Thus, he pulls sentient beings out from their various places.
"Attachment" refers to the passage in the "Burning House" parable where the provisional means are opened up to reveal the ultimate reality.

"We cannot proclaim the Buddha’s merits with words" refers to the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," wherein it is said that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable merits that even the four great disciples, such as Kāśyapa, cannot exhaustively describe;
this is the reference to what is beyond their reach. Now, the intention of Pūrṇa is as follows:

This means that when the four great disciples heard the parable of the burning house, they fully grasped such matters as the Tathāgata’s transformative teachings across five periods and his discernment of capacities through the stage of the Dharmakāya;
yet the Tathāgata still rebuked them for what their grasp had failed to reach.
Now, although I have heard this and wish to comprehend it, how could I possibly surpass those four great disciples? One should know that beyond what has been grasped, there remains more.
Furthermore, because his dwelling place is manifold, he is also said to be "inexpressible by words. Since it is said that he cannot be expressed by words, he is likewise beyond the reach of thought.
△ Second, silently seeking the revelation of his true identity and requesting a prophecy.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can know our profound inner resolve and original vows.
The phrase "we" refers generally to all those who have called upon him to manifest; this profound inner resolve is the foundation, while what is currently manifested here is its outward trace.
The "original vow" refers to the vow of great compassion. Because great compassion transforms those below, I have made a vow to seek the Way above.

Because he acts as a Buddha, my vow requests that he seek the supreme [attainment], which is the request for the prediction (vyākaraṇa); it requests that he preach for the sake of the lower transformation, which is the request for the revelation of his origins.

Furthermore, because of his profound mind, it clarifies how he assists the Buddha in proclaiming the transformation throughout the three periods of time; because of his original vow, he is then granted the prediction.
II. The Tathāgata’s Narration of the Prediction. A. First, the prose section. B. Second, the verse section. 1. Initial prose text.

Furthermore, regarding the first of the two [sections], the description of the original and the manifested; within this, first is the manifestation of the origin through the practice of causes during the world of Śākyamuni.
First, the person is pointed out:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "Do you see this Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra?"
"Do you see?"—does this phrase contain two meanings? First, it asks whether you see his manifestation as being small; second, it asks whether you see his fundamental merit.
The multitude only sees the manifestation as that of a śrāvaka and cannot know that he is fundamentally a bodhisattva;
therefore, it says, "Do you see? △ Second, the general presentation of the fundamental and the manifested, in two parts: first, the presentation of the manifestation.
I have always praised him as the foremost among those who preach the Dharma.
To designate his traces as the foremost among those who preach the Dharma implies that were it not for the wondrous essence of the Dharmakāya, he could not have manifested these supreme traces.
Hitherto, it has only been said that he was the foremost in preaching the Dharma among [those who manifest] traces; now, however—
This is not so; having long since attained the foremost state among the unsurpassed dharmas, this [passage] cites the traces to reveal the fundamental.
△ Second, it indicates that fundamental nature:
"He also constantly extols its various merits."
Because it designates the dharma-gates of the myriad practices of merit and wisdom within their original ground (*mūla-bhūmi*), it says "various kinds.
Since there are various dharma-gates in the original ground, how could there be only two vehicles in the traces (*vyañjana*)? This cites the original to clarify the traces.
△ Third, the separate explanation of the original and the trace, in two parts: first, the assistance in proclaiming the *ardha* (half) and *pūrṇa* (full) teachings within the traces.
Diligently upholding and assisting in the proclamation of my Dharma, they are able to instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly;
they fully explain the Buddha’s true Dharma and bring great benefit to their fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Those who assist in proclaiming my Dharma are those who, within the provisional traces, assist in proclaiming the teachings of both the Half and the Full.
At the Deer Park, as a trace for those of inferior capacity, he acted as a śrāvaka; this was to protect and assist in proclaiming the teachings of the Tripitaka and the Half-letters.

At the stage of the Vaipulya, he manifested himself as being subject to rebukes and censures; this was to protect and assist in proclaiming the teachings that clarify the Full by contrast with the Half.
The trace [teaching] that leads to the *Prajñāpāramitā* is precisely the protection and assistance in proclaiming the Dharma that "retains the half and clarifies the full";
the trace that attains awakening through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is precisely the protection and assistance in proclaiming the Dharma that "discards the half and clarifies the full.
The passage in the previous text stating, "I constantly praise various merits," refers to this very meaning: that one inherently possesses the merits of both the provisional and the real. And yet...
Appearing in the world through the five flavors to assist the Buddha in maturing sentient beings of true practice—is this not the intent of diligent assistance in proclaiming the Dharma?
To demonstrate, instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly is to distinguish the teachings of the "half-syllables" (the *neyārtha*).
To provide complete explanations is to assist in proclaiming the "full-syllables" (*nītārtha*) of the Prajñāpāramitā. And to bring great benefit is to assist the Buddha in bestowing abundance.

He benefits those disciples of both the partial and complete teachings among his fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring; these are the disciples of both the partial and complete teachings who are transformed within the sphere of his manifested traces.
△ Second, a specific description of the unfathomable merits of his fundamental ground.
Since his renunciation, no one except the Tathāgata has been able to exhaust the eloquence of his discourse.
From those who have descended from the Buddha back to the practitioners of the seven stages of expedient means, none can know the eloquence of his fundamental ground.
△ Second, revealing his original practices by reference to the past.
"You should not think that Pūrṇa is merely able to protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming my Dharma;

he has also, in the presence of ninety billion Buddhas in the past, protected, upheld, and assisted in proclaiming the Buddha’s True Dharma, being the foremost among those who preached the Dharma therein.
Furthermore, regarding the teaching of emptiness spoken by all those Buddhas, he has clearly and thoroughly penetrated it, attaining the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge."
He was always able to preach the Dharma with careful discernment and purity, free from all doubt, and was fully endowed with the supernatural powers of a bodhisattva.
Throughout his entire life, he constantly practiced the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). To those Buddhas and the people of that world, he was universally regarded as being truly a śrāvaka.
Yet, through these skillful means, Pūrṇa benefited immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings and further transformed countless others.
He causes incalculable numbers of people to establish themselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of purifying Buddha-fields,
and thus constantly performs the work of a Buddha to teach and transform sentient beings.
It is said that Pūrṇa did not merely assist me in proclaiming the teachings of the Half and the Full [Tripitaka], but has also, for a long time...

To travel far to where the Buddha was and later assist in proclaiming the teachings of both the Half- and Full-Chariot [vehicles], taking the assistance in proclamation today as the manifestation of his trace (*japō*), and taking the assistance in proclamation in the past as the revelation of his origin (*honji*):
there are two ways of revealing the origin. First is the distant origin; second is the near origin.
Because the distant origin is profound and remote, it is difficult for people to believe; therefore, for now, we shall speak only of the ninety billion near origins that exist.

Because the wisdom of knowing past lives can know that which is near by its very nature, he cites what is near to testify to what is distant, thereby causing others to give rise to faith, uphold, and assist in proclaiming it.

This refers to assisting in the proclamation of the "half-syllable" (vyavahāra) teachings; this refers to assisting in the proclamation of the Dharma of the Buddha’s True Teaching, which clarifies the "full" (pūrṇa) in contrast to the "half.
It clarifies that the six pāramitās mutually encompass one another, revolving without obstruction. Furthermore...
To clearly understand and thoroughly penetrate the dharma of emptiness is precisely to assist in proclaiming the Dharma that carries half-illumination toward full illumination.

The four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are the four unhindered analytical insights; because these knowledges reside in speech: (1) the unhindered knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) knows the meanings of all dharmas with perfect clarity and without obstruction;
(2) the unhindered knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) is the wisdom for the purpose of knowing all meanings.
The unimpeded knowledge of the non-obstruction of all phenomena and the three types of expression,
which enables one to cause each and every sentient being to understand their own respective dialects and languages— whether those of men or women—

and to expound them with unimpeded eloquence such that all who hear it fully comprehend the speech; and the fourth, the unimpeded knowledge of joyful exposition, wherein the Bodhisattva is able to expound [the Dharma] within a single syllable.
Within a single word among all words, one can speak all words; within a single dharma, one can speak all dharmas.

All that is taught is entirely true and provides benefit according to those who are to be saved—namely, the twelve divisions of the scriptures and the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma, which accord with the inclinations and capacities of all sentient beings.

Having heard the Dharma, he expounded it for others; those who heard it never grew weary. By virtue of his possession of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), he was able to practice pure conduct throughout the Buddha’s entire lifespan.
During that Buddha’s era, as he had not yet revealed his true identity, all people regarded him as a mere *śrāvaka* and did not say he was a great *bodhisattva*.
He transformed immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to establish themselves in the Three [Vehicles].
Bodhi is precisely that which assists in proclaiming the Dharma that discards the partial and clarifies the complete;

thus, those who assist in proclaiming the Buddha-Dharma are indeed forming the karmic conditions for a Pure Land with all beings. If one does not form such conditions with beings, then when the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, his land will be defiled and devoid of sentient beings capable of being transformed.
△ Third, [the section] concerning the causal practices cultivated by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The bhikṣu Pūrṇa was also foremost among those who expound the Dharma under the seven Buddhas; now, he is likewise foremost among those who expound the Dharma under me;
and in the future, he will also be foremost among those who expound the Dharma under all the Buddhas yet to come in this Bhadrakalpa.
He shall protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma, assisting in its proclamation, and he shall continue to do so in the future as well.
To assist in proclaiming the Dharma of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, to teach and benefit immeasurable sentient beings,
and to establish them in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of purifying Buddha-fields, he constantly exerts himself with diligence in teaching and transforming sentient beings.

This also follows the previous examples regarding the benefits for sentient beings of varying capacities through the methods that assist in proclaiming the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Full) and *Ardhadharma* (Half) teachings.
As for the Seven Buddhas, according to various texts, they are: first, Vipaśyin Buddha; second, Śikhin Buddha;
third, Viśvabhū Buddha; fourth, Krakucchanda Buddha; fifth, Kanakamuni Buddha; sixth, Kāśyapa Buddha; and seventh, Śākyamuni Buddha.

Regarding the Seven Buddhas, Śākyamuni Buddha takes the last three of the thousand Buddhas of the *Bhadrakalpa* (the Auspicious Aeon) and the first four of the thousand Buddhas of the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa* (the Adorned Aeon) as these seven. However, according to this present sutra, where Śākyamuni himself declares,
"Among those who speak the Dharma under me, you shall also be the foremost," he thereby treats the [previous] seven Buddhas as belonging to the past.
Śākyamuni is the present [Buddha], while Maitreya and others are the future ones;
these should be identified as the latter four Buddhas of the *Rucirakalpa* (Adorned Aeon) and the first three Buddhas of the *Bhadrakalpa* (Auspicious Aeon), who constitute the seven past Buddhas.

However, in various texts, Śākyamuni is sometimes included with the preceding six Buddhas to form the seven past Buddhas; this is likely because the intent was to refer to the chapter on the aeons (*kalpa*).
The fact that the sutra was compiled after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni also indicates that Śākyamuni is regarded as a Buddha of the past.
△ Second, the bestowal of predictions, in seven parts:
first, clarifying the perfection of causes—gradually fulfilling the path of a bodhisattva.
△ Second, the fulfillment of the fruit:
After immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in this land,
with the name Dharmaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid.
The Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
△ Third, the purity of the land; first, the great majestic purity of the land.
That Buddha takes as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River to constitute a single buddha-field, with the seven treasures forming [its ground].
The ground is as level as the palm of a hand, without mountains, hills, streams, ravines, or gullies;
towers and pavilions made of the seven treasures fill it, and the palaces of the devas are situated close to the void, such that humans and devas meet and can see one another.

Regarding the phrase "the ground is as level as a palm," the sutra simply says "as a palm" without specifying "a hand-palm. Since the surface of a hand-palm is not inherently level, this cannot be the intended reference.
There is a stone at the bottom of the ocean called "Palm" (*pāṇi*); this stone does not have even a speck of dust's worth of unevenness, and it must be that the ground is like this "ocean-palm.
Furthermore, the *Bhadrapāla-kalpa-sūtra* (or *Bhadrakalpa-sūtra*) explicitly clarifies that it is like the palm of a Buddha’s hand; it is not a citation from [that source].
"Human beings have palms [for hands]. △ Second, it clarifies that this is purely a realm of goodness.
There are no evil realms, nor are there women; all sentient beings are born by transformation and are free from sexual desire."

Regarding those realms where there are no evil destinies (*apāya*), there are likewise distinctions and differences among them: some realms where there are no women and consequently no evil destinies;
others where there may be women but still no evil destinies—such as the land of Akṣobhya Buddha, where although there are women, there is no female defilement;
and the land of Amitāyus Buddha, where both [women and evil destinies] are absent. △ Third, the explanation of merit and wisdom.

He was fully endowed with great supernormal powers; his body emitted radiance, and he traveled through the air with ease. His resolve and mindfulness were firm, and his diligence and wisdom were all golden in color.
He adorned himself with the thirty-two marks of a great man. The sentient beings in that land always partook of two kinds of food.
First is the food of Dharma-joy (*dharmaprīti-bhakṣa*), and second is the food of dhyāna-delight (*dhyānaprīti-bhakṣa*).
The ninth fascicle of the *Candragarbha-sūtra* clarifies the sutra text on the food of Dharma, the food of joy, and the food of dhyāna;

while the text speaks of them collectively as "Dharma-joy" and "dhyāna-delight," when divided specifically, there should be three distinct varieties. △ Fourth, it clarifies that the number of disciples is vast.
There were immeasurable, incalculable, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas who had attained great supernormal powers and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge,
and were well able to teach and transform sentient beings; their number could not be known even by calculation or reckoning among the assembly of śrāvakas,
for all of them were fully endowed with the six supernatural faculties, the three types of clear knowledge, and the eight liberations.
△ Fifth, the accomplishment of the merits of the five precepts.
The Buddha-land is thus adorned and accomplished with immeasurable such merits.
The *Candragarbha-sūtra*, fascicle 5, clarifies that each of the ten wholesome actions possesses ten merits; first, by not killing, one obtains ten merits.
First, one attains fearlessness toward all sentient beings; second, one attains a mind of great compassion for sentient beings;
third, one severs evil habitual karma; fourth, one is free from illness; fifth, one enjoys a long life; sixth, one is protected by non-human beings;
seventh, one has no bad dreams; eighth, one has no enemies; ninth, one does not fear the evil realms; and tenth, after death, one is reborn in a good realm and subsequently becomes a Buddha.
The land is free from harmful weapons, and its people enjoy long lifespans; furthermore, by the tenth [virtue], through the absence of wrong views, they obtain ten merits:

first, a mind that is gentle and virtuous, and so on, up to the tenth, being reborn in good realms after death and becoming a Buddha, at which time the people of the land possess right faith—this constitutes the adornment of immeasurable merit. △ Fourth, the name of the kalpa and the land.
The kalpa was named Precious Radiance and the land was named Pure Excellence.
△ Fifth, the Buddha’s lifespan:
that Buddha’s life span lasted for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
△ The six dharmas will endure for a long time;
the Dharma will remain for a very long time.
△ Seventh, making offerings to the śarīra.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, stupas made of the seven treasures will arise and fill his entire land.
△ Second, the verses in praise, in two parts: first, the verses praising the revelation of origins; second, the general revelation of the origins of all śrāvakas, in five parts;
first, explaining the inconceivable Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Listen attentively, O bhikṣus! The path traversed by the sons of the Buddha is inconceivable, for they have skillfully trained in expedient means."
This indicates that the disciples, having already attained the method for manifesting traces after practicing inconceivable deeds, [are now revealed].

△ Second, explaining the reason for manifesting traces: Knowing that the multitude delights in inferior dharmas and fears great wisdom, the bodhisattvas therefore manifest as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
△ The third: the descent of the traces to benefit others.
By means of innumerable skillful expedients, he transforms all classes of sentient beings. He says of himself, "I am a śrāvaka;

I am far removed from the Buddha-way," yet he delivers immeasurable multitudes, causing them all to achieve fulfillment. Although they may have few desires or be indolent, he will gradually cause them to become Buddhas.
To those with few desires, he demonstrates the seeking of the Small Vehicle; to those who are indolent, he demonstrates the retrogression from the Great Vehicle.

Through these provisional practices, he guides those of true practice to transform all sentient beings, gradually leading them to become Buddhas. △ Fourth, explaining the inner secrecy and outer manifestation.
Internally they keep secret their bodhisattva practices, while externally they manifest as śrāvakas with few desires who loathe birth and death; yet in reality they purify their own buddha-fields.
They manifest the presence of the three poisons to the assembly and even display the appearance of false views; my disciples employ such skillful means to deliver sentient beings.
It is not only that he manifests as a śrāvaka; he also manifests as an outsider (tīrthika) and as an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) under the influence of the three poisons.

Śāriputra manifesting anger, Nanda manifesting greed, and Devadatta manifesting delusion are all examples of this category. △ Fifth, clarifying the brief indication and the suppression of the extensive.
If I were to fully describe the various manifestations of my transformations, sentient beings who heard this would harbor doubts and confusion.
△ Second, the distinct manifestation of the traces of fulfilling vows, which has two parts: first, a verse revealing the past origin.
Now this Pūrṇa, having diligently practiced the path under a thousand billion Buddhas in the past, has proclaimed and protected the teachings of those Buddhas;
seeking unsurpassed wisdom, he has appeared as a chief disciple among those Buddhas, possessing great learning and wisdom,
speaking with fearlessness and ability to gladden the masses, never experiencing weariness as he assists in the Buddha’s work.

Having already attained great supernormal powers and being endowed with the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom, they know the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all beings and constantly preach the pure Dharma,
expounding such meanings to instruct thousands of billions of assemblies, causing them to abide in the Mahāyāna Dharma while purifying their own Buddha-lands.
△ Second, the verse on the causes for practice throughout the three periods of time:
In the future as well, they shall make offerings to immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas, protect and assist in proclaiming the True Dharma, and personally purify their own Buddha-lands.
Constantly employing various skillful means, they shall preach the Dharma with fearlessness, deliver an incalculable multitude of beings, and achieve all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).
△ Second, the prediction in four verses: the first verse concerns the perfection of causes—making offerings to all Tathāgatas and upholding the treasury of the Dharma Jewel.
△ The second verse concerns the fulfillment of results.
Thereafter, he attained Buddhahood, and his name was called Dharmaprabhāsa (Dharma-Illumination).
Third, the names of the eon and the land:
that land was named Suviśuddha (Excellently Pure), composed of the seven treasures; the eon was named Ratnaprabhāsa (Jewel-Illumination).
△ Four verses on the purity of the land:
The assembly of bodhisattvas is vast, numbering immeasurable billions; they have all attained great supernormal powers and are fully endowed with majestic virtue.

Their land is filled with them, and the śrāvakas are likewise countless, having attained the three knowledges (*traividya*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
With such as these as their Saṃgha, all sentient beings in that land will have already severed lustful desire;

they will be born solely through transformation, possessing bodies adorned with the marks of excellence, nourished by the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna, having no further thought of food, and being without women or any evil realms.
Bhikṣu Pūrṇa, when his merits are fully perfected, he shall attain such a pure land.
The assembly of noble sages is so vast that such immeasurable matters I now describe only in brief.
△ Second, the conferral of predictions upon the twelve hundred [Arhats]. 3. First, the initial thought and request.
At that time, the twelve hundred Arhats who had attained mastery over their minds thought to themselves: "We have attained this with great joy..."
"It would be truly wonderful if the World-Honored One were to grant a prediction of enlightenment to each of us, just as he has done for the other great disciples.
These twelve hundred people have all already attained the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle; because they are no longer afflicted by the outflows of views and thoughts, their minds are at ease.
Having heard the Dharma taught during the three turnings of the wheel and having seen the prediction granted to Pūrṇa, they are now filled with joy and desire [to hear more]."
Please take note. △ Second, the bestowing of predictions, in two parts. First, the prose section, in three parts. First, the general prediction for the twelve hundred [monks].
Knowing the thoughts in the minds of these [disciples], the Buddha addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"These twelve hundred arhats, I shall now, before your very eyes, confer upon them in succession the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
△ Second, the specific bestowal upon Kauṇḍinya:
"Among this assembly, my great disciple, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya, shall make offerings to sixty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas;
thereafter he shall attain Buddhahood, and his name shall be the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vairocana."
The One Perfected in Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One—
because Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the first to realize the Way and sat at the head of the assembly, he was specifically granted this prediction. △ Third, the specific bestowal upon the five hundred men.
These five hundred arhats— Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa,
Kālodāyin, Udāyin, Aniruddha, Revata, Kapphiṇa, Bakula, Cunda, and Śāgata—
all shall likewise attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi together.
The first was named Puming (Universal Radiance).
Kālodāyin means "Black Light" in this language, or alternatively "Coarse Black," because his complexion was black yet radiant.
Cūḍapanthaka, or as some say Zhouli, means "Born by the Side of the Great Road. The *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sutra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds) states that his mother followed [her husband]...
A man traveled to another country and, after a long time, became pregnant. As she was about to give birth, she thought of returning home;
while traveling halfway there, she gave birth to her child. This happened twice, resulting in two sons. She distinguished them by their size:
the elder was named Cūḍapanthaka, and the younger was named Śāḍha, also called Panthaka, which means "by the side of the small path."

Śāriputra asked: "The Buddha previously granted sequential predictions to twelve hundred [disciples]; why now do you grant predictions to only five hundred, and not see the other twelve hundred receiving them?
Answer: These five hundred are precisely within the number of twelve hundred.
In the verse, at the very end, the line "Kāśyapa, you already know" and so forth, collectively grants the prediction to seven hundred; therefore, they constitute the twelve hundred. △
The two verses [commenting on] the first part record the names of Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the five hundred [monks].
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya shall see immeasurable Buddhas; after an incalculable number of kalpas, he will then achieve Equal and Perfect Enlightenment."
Constantly emitting great radiance and fully endowed with all supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), his fame pervades the ten directions and he is revered by all;
because he constantly proclaims the unsurpassed path, he is named Samantaprabha (Universal Radiance). His land is pure, and its bodhisattvas are all valiant;
they all ascend exquisite pavilions to travel through the lands of the ten directions, offering unsurpassed articles of worship to all Buddhas.
Having made this offering, his heart was filled with great joy, and in an instant he returned to his own country.

Possessing such supernatural power, the Buddha’s lifespan was sixty thousand kalpas; the True Dharma remained for twice that duration, and the Semblance Dharma for twice that again. When this Dharma had perished, gods and humans were filled with grief.
Those five hundred bhikṣus will successively become Buddhas, all sharing the same name, Samantaprabha, as they receive their predictions in turn.
"After my parinirvāṇa, such-and-such a person shall become a Buddha; the world he transforms shall be as majestic and pure as my own land today,
and his supernormal powers, the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma,
and the duration of his lifespan in kalpas shall all be exactly as described above."
△ Second, the general bestowal of predictions upon all śrāvakas:
"Kāśyapa, you already know that this applies to the five hundred masters; the rest of the assembly of śrāvakas shall likewise receive such predictions.
As for those who are not present in this assembly, you should proclaim it to them."
The first two lines conclude the previous section on the five hundred who have already received their predictions;
the next two lines are a verse on the seven hundred, hence it says, "The rest of the assembly of śrāvakas shall likewise be so.

Furthermore, the final two lines are for the sake of those not present in this assembly, so that Kāśyapa may proclaim [the teaching] on their behalf; thus it says, "For those who are not here in this assembly, you should act as their representative."
In the "Chapter on Upholding after Proclamation," it says: "I have previously stated in general that all śrāvakas have already received their predictions.
This specifically refers to the current one and a half verses, and does not mean that the prediction was restricted only to seven hundred śrāvakas.

△ Third, the Acceptance and Understanding, in two parts: First, the prose; second, the narrative by the sūtra compiler regarding joy, in two parts: First, rejoicing because of having attained understanding now, hence being joyful.
Joy: Part One clarifies the inner rejoicing of the mind.
At that time, the five hundred arhats, having received their predictions before the Buddha, leaped for joy with exultation.
△ Part Two clarifies the outward expression of reverence.
He immediately rose from his seat, went before the Buddha, and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet.
△ Second, he reproached himself for his past lack of understanding;
he repented and self-reproached.
△ Second, the personal statement of realization. Part one: Explanation by way of Dharma. Sub-part one: Repenting of being content with little.
"World-Honored One, we have constantly harbored this thought, saying to ourselves that we had already attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*."

This is the remorse for having previously been deluded, considering the attainment of the small to be sufficient and failing to know how to seek the great. △ Second, the reproach for dull faculties that were difficult to awaken;
now one finally knows.

This rebuke implies that one's faculties are dull and that one has only now realized what was not known before; it means that one now understands that the small [vehicle] is not ultimate, while the Great [Vehicle] is the true reality.
△ Second, the illustrative explanation, which has two parts: first, the brief illustration; second, the initial brief presentation of the analogy. First, the brief presentation of the analogy:
They are like those who lack wisdom.
△ Second, explaining the meaning of "lack of wisdom":
Why is this? We ought to attain the wisdom of a Tathāgata, yet we instead consider our own meager wisdom to be sufficient.
△ Second, the actual illustration, in two parts: First, the opening of the illustration; second, the analogy of the poor man intoxicated with wine.
First, the analogy of the kinsman tying the jewel.
"World-Honored One, it is as if there were a person who went to the house of a close friend and lay down, intoxicated by wine. At that time, the friend [had business] with the authorities..."
He should then take an invaluable jewel, tie it inside the person's garment, and depart.

The act of tying the jewel is a metaphor for the Prince’s establishment of karmic affinity with those on the neck; "a certain person" refers to those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas);
the "close friend" is the sixteenth prince from former times; and the "house" represents the Mahāyāna teaching.

As for "lying drunk at home": this refers to a time when the great capacity [of the mind] is momentarily activated and ignorance is temporarily subdued, such that upon hearing the sutra, there is a subtle internal understanding.
It is like being in the house of a close relative; however, because ignorance is heavy, one again becomes lost and confused, like lying drunk at home.
There are two meanings to "drunkenness": first, heavy drunkenness, where one has no awareness at all; second, light drunkenness.

Even if one who is intoxicated regains a slight awareness only to forget it again, this is still termed "non-awareness. Although there are these two meanings, they ultimately result in the "tying of the jewel," which is like a poisonous drum.
When official business is to be carried out, the Prince clearly perceives the conditions arising elsewhere; he approaches and responds to those conditions according to the occasion.

Therefore, it is said that [the task] "should be carried out. Propagating the Dharma and transforming others is not a private matter; hence it is called "official business. This refers to the priceless jewel.
This is the jewel of the wisdom of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

"Tying it within his robe" means that shame (*hrī*), remorse (*apatrāpya*), and patience (*kṣānti*) can conceal ugliness, anger, and resentment, and prevent external evils; this constitutes the outer garment. A mind of faith and joy, which internally enwraps the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), constitutes the inner garment.
At that time, hearing the Dharma and having a slight faith and desire constitutes the wisdom of the "cause of understanding" (*vyañjanahetu-jñāna*) and the seed of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bīja*).
This is the child. △ Second, the analogy of lying drunk and unaware:
That person lies drunk and remains entirely unconscious.
This refers to those who, in the interim, become indolent and regress, failing to receive the Great Dharma. "Lying drunk and unaware" signifies ignorance (*avidyā*).
The mind, though it seeks again, does not recall it. △ Third, the parable of setting out and wandering:
Having set out and wandered, he arrives in another country; for the sake of food and clothing, he strives and seeks with great difficulty, and if he obtains even a little, he considers it sufficient.

This refers to the middle section of the upper garment, which signifies receiving the transformation of the Three Vehicles through minor capacities. Because their roots of goodness are about to sprout and they seek happiness while wearying of suffering, it is said that "having arisen, they wander. Being shrouded by ignorance, they do not know how to return to the source to seek the Great Vehicle; thus, it is said they "go toward other lands to seek the sustenance of the Small Vehicle. If one compares this to the perspective of Māra versus the Buddha: [The text continues: ...it is like a person who, having lost their way, wanders in the wilderness and encounters a great city. Having entered the city, they see various merchants selling goods such as clothing, food, and drink. Seeing these things, they feel joy and say to themselves, "I have now obtained clothing, food, and drink; I shall no longer suffer from hunger and cold. They do not yet realize that this is merely a small city, nor do they know that there is a great capital city beyond. They take what they have obtained as sufficient and do not seek further. This is called "seeking the sustenance of the Small Vehicle. Furthermore, it is like a person who, having been struck by a severe illness, seeks a physician and obtains medicine. Upon taking the medicine, they recover slightly and feel well. Thinking they have already been cured, they do not seek further treatment. This is called "seeking the sustenance of the Small Vehicle. Furthermore, it is like a person who, having fallen into a deep pit, climbs out using a rope. Once out, they think they have escaped danger and do not seek to ascend to a high place. This is called "seeking the sustenance of the Small Vehicle. Furthermore, it is like a person who, having been bound with ropes, is released. Once released, they think they are free and do not seek to break the ropes completely. This is called "seeking the sustenance of the Small Vehicle. Furthermore, it is like a person who, having been imprisoned, is released. Once released, they think they are free and do not seek to escape the prison entirely. This is called "seeking the sustenance of the Small Vehicle. Furthermore, it is like a person who, having been beaten with a staff, receives a remedy. *The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Nine: The Chapter on Bestowing Predictions upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training (the main text calls it the Chapter on the Decision for Ānanda and Rāhula).

Those who investigate reality, sever delusions, and aspire toward superior vision are called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*), namely the four stages of approach and the three fruits of the path; they are truly without [delusion].

When outflows are exhausted, wisdom is perfected, delusions are eradicated, and superior insight has reached its ultimate limit such that there is nothing further to be learned, this is called "no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣa*), which is the fruit of Arhatship.

Regarding the teaching, the meaning of the Tripitaka is as follows: to analyze phenomena and investigate the truth is called "learning"; when delusions are exhausted and the truth is fully realized, it is called "no-more-learning.
In the sense of the Dharma-body (the essence of phenomena), to investigate the truth is called "learning," while being without falsehood and without delusion is called "no-more-learning."

"Attaining understanding" (*tongyi*) refers to progressing from the shallow to the deep; when the delusions of both the specific and general categories are exhausted and the provisional and ultimate principles are fully realized, it is called "no-more-learning" (*wuxue*).

This is the meaning of the specific [teaching]. To investigate the Tathāgatagarbha—whether the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or that which is neither in training nor beyond training—is to realize that through learning one reaches no-more-learning;
this is the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching]. These two thousand people may be either those in training or...

yet their original ground (*honji*) is inconceivable. By this analogy, each of the other two thousand disciples should likewise have their own provisional and ultimate aspects; this chapter concerns them.

this is taught for the sake of ordinary beings (*bālapṛthagjana*) of weak faculties, so that by relying upon it they may propagate the Dharma without fearing harm. The first section consists of two parts:

The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Preacher (*Dharmabhāṇaka*).
This chapter elucidates five kinds of dharma-preachers: first, receiving and upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, explaining and expounding; and fifth, copying and writing.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* elucidates six kinds of dharma-preachers: first, receiving through the power of faith; second, upholding through the power of mindfulness; third...
To examine the text is "reading" (1); to recite it without forgetting the four [aspects] is "recitation" (2); to proclaim it to others is "exposition" (3).

Since the scriptures of the sages are difficult to understand, they require interpretation; thus, receiving and upholding the present sutra constitutes one [aspect], and interpreting and explaining it constitutes another.

Opening [the text] for reading and reciting makes two, and adding the transcription of the book makes five. If discussed separately, these four constitute self-cultivation, while interpretation and exposition constitute one [aspect].

These five types constitute the transformation of others. If discussed generally, the five practices that serve as one's own model are called the "Dharma Master of Self-Cultivation," while the five practices used to instruct others are called the "Dharma Master of Transformation.
Why is this so? "Dharma" (dharma) refers to a standard or rule, and "Master" (ācārya) refers to a teacher or craftsman.
Although the Dharma serves as a standard, its essence does not propagate itself; it depends on people. These five types of masters all penetrate the sutras.
One is called a "Dharma Master" (dharmabhāṇaka) because they take the sublime Dharma as their teacher and accomplish their own practice through it;

since they take the sublime Dharma as their teacher and achieve perfection in their own practice, they are named a Dharma Master. Furthermore, there are five kinds of persons who can instruct and mold others with the sublime Dharma;

thus, by taking the Dharma as the standard for the teacher, one is named a Dharma Master. Whether it be modeling the Dharma oneself or acting as a craftsman of the Dharma for others, both constitute this title.
This concludes the section titled "Attaining the Title of Dharma Master. △ Second, the main text of the sūtra has two parts: first, praising the five kinds of dharma masters who uphold the Dharma;
second, praising the Dharma they uphold and demonstrating the power of the universal sūtra.

The first part further divides into two: first, the profound merit and heavy blessings of disciples who have received the Way; second, [the disciples] during the Buddha's lifetime. The first of these further begins by selecting and identifying the class of people.

"Because" (*yin*) means to entrust; it means that he wished to entrust the wondrous Dharma to the Medicine King so that he might receive and uphold these instructions, ensuring that all eighty thousand would cause them to circulate. You see this great assembly?
The phrase "and so forth" indicates those who receive blessings by upholding this sutra. △ Second, the specific conditions for receiving the prediction:

"All such persons as these—who, in the presence of the Buddha, hear even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, or even for a single moment rejoice in it—I shall all grant them the prediction that they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Those who attained wondrous awakening according to their capacity before the Buddha—namely, the five hundred and two thousand who were deeply learned and possessed profound understanding—are all those for whom the general and specific predictions have already been bestowed in person.

Those now being selected are the eight classes of beings, the fourfold assembly, and the various types belonging to the three vehicles; therefore, it is said that "the Tathāgata and his like" are all present before the Buddha.
"Knowing that the time coincided with the Buddha being seated" means that [the teaching] was at its most minimal, consisting of a single phrase or a single verse;

"even down to a single thought-moment" means that the duration was the briefest possible. "Rejoicing" means that although one has not yet personally practiced, one merely rejoices in the Dharma and rejoices in the person [who teaches it].
That "all are given the prediction that they shall attain Bodhi" clarifies their future attainment.

If even hearing for an extremely brief moment or a very short duration brings about the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) such that one subsequently attains the fruit of Buddhahood, how much more so for those who hear it in its entirety, uphold it throughout their lives, propagate it through the five methods of transmission, and make offerings with the three karmas?

If those who hear but little and understand shallowly can still remember it, how much more so those who hear much and understand deeply? If the universal benefit is thus when it comes to the lower grade, what need is there to mention the middle and upper grades?
This is likewise something that can be understood through one's own mind and does not require further explanation. △ Second, the disciples after the extinction [of the Buddha], in two parts:
first, identifying the categories of disciples.
The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja: "Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, if there should be someone who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*..."
As for those who, even for a single verse, a single phrase, or a single thought, rejoice with sympathetic joy:
△ Second, they are also granted a prediction.
I likewise grant them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

It should be understood that even hearing a very small amount of the Dharma and receiving a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) yields merit and retribution as previously explained. △ Second, clarifying the profound merit and heavy blessings of the teacher who bestows the Way.
This has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part [the prose] also has two sections: first, the specific [explanation]; second, the general [explanation].

The first section [the specific explanation] further has two parts: first, clarifying the present life; second, clarifying future lives. The first part [clarifying the present life] further has two sections: first, clarifying the teacher of inferior grade; second, clarifying the characteristics of the teacher.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
and treats this scripture with reverence as if it were the Buddha, making various offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense,
unguents, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and music, and even joining their palms in reverent salutation;
The above clarifies the disciples who receive the Way; from here below, it clarifies the teachers who transmit the Way.

Now, we clarify the characteristics of the present-day teachers of the lower grade, which consist of the five kinds of Dharma-preachers and the ten kinds of offerings. △ Second, clarifying the karmic rewards.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that these people have already made offerings to ten trillion buddhas;
having fulfilled their great vows in the presence of those buddhas, they have out of compassion for sentient beings been born into this human world.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if anyone asks, "What kind of sentient beings will attain buddhahood in future ages? you should point to these very people as those who will attain buddhahood in future ages.

They will certainly attain Buddhahood. Why is this? If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and makes various offerings to the scripture—such as flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointment incense, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, flags, robes, and music—and with palms joined in reverence, such a person...
All the world should look up to and honor them, and they should be honored with the same offerings as the Tathāgata.
You should know that such a person is a great bodhisattva who has accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and out of compassion for sentient beings,
has made a vow to be born in this world to extensively expound and analyze the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The phrase "having made offerings" clarifies that the causes from previous lives were profound.

The phrase "out of compassion for sentient beings, he was born into this human world" clarifies that his merit in the present life is great. The section beginning with "If someone asks... clarifies that the retribution in future lives will be heavy.
The section beginning with "Why is this? explains the characteristics of such heavy retribution. △ Second, explaining the teacher of the highest grade: first, illustrating the superior by comparison.
How much more so for those who are able to fully receive and uphold various offerings.
△ Second, clarifying the superior karmic reward.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such a person, having voluntarily relinquished their own pure karmic retribution, will, out of compassion for living beings after my parinirvāṇa,
be born in an evil age to widely expound this sutra.
This person, having personally relinquished their pure retribution, is drawn by the power of the great compassionate vow to leave the pure lands and be born within a defiled and evil world;
this is still birth through karma, for it has not yet reached the stage where the vow supersedes karma, and thus birth occurs as a combination of both vow and karma.
This is as explained in the "Excellence of Retinue" section of the *Miaoxuan*, regarding the retinues born through karma and those born through vows. △ Second.
Clarifying the two types of teachers in future ages: first, clarifying the teacher of inferior grade; second, first clarifying the characteristics of such a teacher.

If there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, after my parinirvāṇa, is able to secretly preach even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for the sake of a single person.

If one were to explain a single phrase for a single person, although that person might attain an understanding of that one phrase, it would not be based on broad learning or the mastery of diverse meanings;
thus, it would be impossible to address various challenges within a public assembly, and there would be points where the discourse fails to penetrate.
Consequently, the true principle would not be able to be proclaimed and propagated. If one wishes to expound this one phrase of correct speech, it should only be done in private.
As clarified in the *Śāstra*, one who possesses wisdom but lacks learning is like a light rain without thunder. △ Second, clarifying the merit and retribution:
It should be known that such a person is an emissary of the Tathāgata, dispatched by the Tathāgata to perform the work of the Tathāgata.

This sutra is that which was spoken by the Tathāgata’s wisdom of suchness, teaching according to suchness. Today, when a practitioner upholds this teaching and proclaims it according to suchness, they are an emissary of the Tathāgata.
One who performs the work of the Tathāgata is one whom the Tathāgata—through his wisdom of suchness—illuminates as performing the work of suchness;
today, when a practitioner relies on the teaching of suchness and practices according to suchness, this is precisely practicing suchness.
This is the activity of the Tathāgata (explained in terms of one’s own practice).

Furthermore, just as the Tathāgata takes it as his task to transform sentient beings through the wisdom of suchness and the principle of suchness, if a practitioner today possesses great compassion and explains the principle of true suchness found in this sutra for the sake of sentient beings, enabling them to attain benefit, this is also called performing the activity of the Tathāgata (explained in terms of transforming others). △ Second, clarifying the above.
How much more so for one who extensively explains it to the great assembly?
This is because the merit and retribution of the superior grade are not briefly measured by comparing the previous inferior grade with the present superior grade; this is the intended meaning.
This can be understood. △ Second, the general [explanation] has two parts. First, clarifying that those who act in opposition incur sin:

"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there were an evil person who, with a malevolent mind, stood before a Buddha for an entire kalpa constantly reviling and abusing him, their sin would still be light compared to a person who, with a single evil word, disparages those—whether lay or ordained—who recite and study [this sūtra]."
The offense regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is extremely grave.

In this case, the gravity of the offense or merit is not determined by the richness or barrenness of the field of merit; rather, it is clarified according to the initial and subsequent states of mind.

If a practitioner who has only recently begun their studies and recites the sūtra already possesses afflictions, yet they further disparage or create obstacles for others, [the offense is particularly heavy].
Because it causes the matters one has studied to fall into ruin, the offense incurred is great. Since the Buddha’s delusions are exhausted, he regards enemies and kin with equality;
as evil cannot disturb or obstruct him, the offense is said to be light. The same applies to making offerings:

if such a person is in need, and if they receive an offering, the task they are cultivating will succeed; therefore, the merit of giving to them is superior. The Buddha, however, has no needs, unlike the assembly [of ordinary beings].
Although the ritual matters have been fulfilled, because making offerings to the Buddha would yield no further benefit, it is said that the retribution is inferior.
Second, explaining that those who comply obtain merit:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that anyone who reads and recites the Lotus Sutra is adorned by the adornments of the Buddha."

Adornment: The Buddha, adorned with meditative concentration and wisdom, preached this sutra. If there are those who read and recite this sutra, they are able to cultivate the meditative concentration and wisdom of the Buddha;
therefore, it is said that they adorn themselves with the adornments of the Buddha.
One shall then be carried upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata.
To be on the back is to be "borne" (hē), and to be on the shoulder is to be "carried" (dàn).

If a person reads and recites this sutra, they will be able to attain the Dharma-body of the Buddha, which is neither provisional nor ultimate; this very body is what is borne upon the back of the Tathāgata, and one will likewise be able to attain it.
The Buddha’s application of the two wisdoms— the provisional and the ultimate— is what is borne upon the two shoulders of the Tathāgata.
To whatever place he goes, one should follow him, pay homage with a single-minded focus, join the palms in reverence, and offer worship, respect, praise, and veneration through flowers,
incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and various delicacies.
One should provide the highest offerings of music and dance to make offerings to them, holding celestial jewels to scatter over them and presenting heaps of heavenly treasures as an offering.
Why is this? Because these people joyfully preach the Dharma, and by hearing it for even a moment, one immediately attains ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Regarding the direction one is heading toward, one should direct one's salutation toward those worthy of honor. Previously, it was clarified that the Dharma is the teacher; now, it is clarified that there are those capable of being teachers for sentient beings.
Whatever these persons may turn toward is entirely in accord with the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), and all such individuals are worthy of veneration and compliance.

"Compliance" (*śuǎn*) is equivalent to "direction" (*xiàng*), and "veneration" (*jìng*) is equivalent to "salutation" (*lǐ*). One should comply with them and offer them worship and so forth. Why is this so? [Because...]
This explains below the meaning of "Worthy of Offerings" mentioned above. △ Second, the verse summary in three parts: first, exhorting self-cultivation and benefiting others.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way and achieve spontaneous wisdom, one should always diligently make offerings to and uphold those who receive and maintain the Lotus Sutra.
Those who wish to quickly attain the wisdom of all modes should likewise receive and maintain this sutra and make offerings to its upholders.

△ Second, the verses on the distinctions among teachers, which are twofold: first, the general [summary], and second, the specific [details]. First, the verses on the specific [details], which are twofold: first, the verses on teachers of the present age, which are twofold:
first, the verses on teachers of inferior capacity, which begin with the clarification of their characteristics:
"If there should be those who are able to receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*..."
△ Second, explaining the merits:
One should know that the Buddha’s emissaries take pity upon all sentient beings.
△ Second, the verse on the superior teacher; first, explaining the characteristics of the teacher.
Those who are able to receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
△ Second, explaining the merit and retribution:
Having abandoned the pure lands, they are born here out of compassion for the multitudes; it should be known that such persons are sovereign over where they wish to be born.
One who is able to extensively proclaim the unsurpassed Dharma in this degenerate age should honor the teacher of the Dharma with celestial flowers and incense,
celestial precious robes, and heaps of exquisite celestial jewels.
△ Second, the two verses on future lives: first, the verse skipping ahead to those of superior grade; second, the verse on the teacher’s characteristics.
"After my parinirvāṇa, in the evil age, those who can uphold this sutra...
△ Second, the verse on the karmic reward.
One should join the palms in reverent salutation as if making offerings of the finest delicacies, various sweets, and diverse garments to the World-Honored One;
these sons of the Buddha hope to hear [this teaching] for even a brief moment.
In the prose section, the retribution for merit was originally missing, whereas it is now present in this verse. △ Second, the subsequent verses on the teacher of the lower grade:
First, the verses introducing the person:
"If one is able to receive and uphold this sutra in future ages..."
△ Second, verses on the merit and retribution:
"I dispatch [them] to act as Tathāgatas among those who dwell in the human realm.
△ Second, verses summarizing the two [sections]; first, verses on the transgressions incurred by those who oppose [the teaching].
If one were to harbor an unwholesome mind for an entire kalpa, assuming an angry countenance and reviling the Buddha, one would incur immeasurable and grave sin;
yet if someone who reads, recites, and upholds this Lotus Sūtra should be subjected to malicious speech for even a moment, their sin would exceed that of the former.
△ Second, a verse on how those who comply obtain merit:
Suppose there were someone seeking the Buddha-way who, for the duration of an eon, stood before me with palms joined and praised me with countless verses;
because of this praise of the Buddha, they would obtain immeasurable merit. Yet, the merit of one who extols and holds this sutra surpasses even that.

If, for eighty billion kalpas, one were to make offerings of the most exquisite forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and textures to a holder of this sutra—and having made such offerings—were then to hear it for even a single moment, one should rejoice within oneself, thinking: "I have now attained a great benefit."
△ Section Three: Praising the Sublimity and Excellence of the Sūtra in Three Verses.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you: among all the sūtras I have spoken, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the foremost.
△ Section Two: Praising the Dharma to be Upheld through Prose and Verse, and Showing the Method for Propagating the Sūtra. Part One: Prose.
The opening text of the two verses on practice also has two parts. First, the praise of the Dharma of the sutra, which has five sections. First, the praise according to the Dharma:
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja:

"Of the immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of sūtras I have spoken—those already spoken, those currently being spoken, and those yet to be spoken—among them, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most difficult to believe."
It is difficult to understand.
Having already [discussed] what has been said, I shall now explain that this sutra is the most supreme; this is a praise based on the Dharma.

"Already" refers to the gradual and sudden teachings from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Great Perfection of Wisdom) onwards. "Now" refers to being in the same assembly, namely the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings). "Shall" refers to...

This refers to *nirvāṇa*. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts, various explanations—whether gradual or sudden—are all accompanied by skillful means (*upāya*) so that they may be easily accepted with faith.
In the *Anantamukha-sūtra*, the one gives rise to the immeasurable, yet the immeasurable does not return to the one; this too is easy to believe.

Now, in the *Dharmaparyāya* (Lotus Sūtra), regarding the Dharma, all differences are harmonized and integrated into the One; regarding the person, both teacher and disciple, as well as their original and manifested aspects (*honji-suijaku*), are likewise unified.
Because all these people and dharmas are entirely different from those of the past, they are difficult to believe and understand;
yet when faced with such difficult matters at the front lines, once the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has been preached, the subsequent *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* can indeed be believed.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, this sutra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas; it must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others.
That which is called the "secret and essential treasury" is "secret" because it is concealed and not spoken of; it is "essential" because it encompasses all dharmas;

and it is a "treasury" because it contains within it the true suchness and the reality-mark. It "must not be distributed" because the Dharma is subtle and difficult to believe, and can only be entrusted to those of profound wisdom.
Because those who lack wisdom and harbor disbelief will incur sin by slandering it, it must not be spoken of recklessly.
It is protected by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and has never been revealed since ancient times.

That which has never been explicitly taught since antiquity is this: within the Tripiṭaka, it is not stated that those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) attain Buddhahood, nor is the relationship between teachers and disciples, or their original and manifested forms, clarified.

Although the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras speak of the treasury of the true reality (dharmatā), they have not yet declared that those of the five vehicles attain Buddhahood, nor have they revealed the original ground to manifest the basis; thus, across all the sutras of the sudden and gradual teachings, they have not yet been harmonized.
Therefore, it is called "secret. This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* fully expounds the Dharma that was previously kept secret;
it is precisely the opening of the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*), and it is also the secret treasury itself. Such a secret treasury was guarded from of old, and is now finally revealed.
Furthermore, as for this sutra, even while the Tathāgata is currently present, there are still many who harbor resentment and jealousy; how much more so after his parinirvāṇa?
That the Tathāgata was beset by such resentment and jealousy during his lifetime is evident from the fact that for over forty years he did not preach it immediately.

Although he wished to preach it now, five thousand people rose from their seats and departed. If this was the case even during the Buddha’s own era, how much more so will it be in the future? This is the logical conclusion.
They are difficult to transform. △ Second, praising by way of persons:

"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who are able to write, uphold, read, recite, make offerings to, and explain it to others—the Tathāgata will cover them with his robe, and they shall be protected by the Buddhas currently residing in other directions."
One should know that because this person possesses the power of great faith, the power of aspiration, and the power of all roots of goodness,
they dwell together with the Tathāgata, and it is as if the Tathāgata’s own hand were stroking their head.
This is a praise based on the person. When this Dharma resides in a person, that person becomes noble and honored.

"Clothed by the Tathāgata’s robe" means that if one can uphold and expound this sutra, one is practicing and learning the Great Patience; this constitutes being clothed by the Tathāgata’s robe, which is what was referred to above as the "Tathāgata’s adornment.
"Protected by the Buddha’s mindfulness" means that the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the Buddha, and true wisdom is the Buddha.
If a disciple reveres the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and gives rise to true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), they will be protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.

The fourfold faith constitutes the power of faith (namely, faith in the Three Jewels and the precepts); the four great vows constitute the power of aspiration; and great wisdom constitutes the power of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

As for faith, it is faith in the principle (*li*); this principle is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Aspiration is the establishment of practice; this practice is liberation (*vimukti*). When the roots of goodness are firm, they are difficult to uproot.
To move this is precisely Prajñā; one should know that these three powers are the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
When those with the initial resolve (*ādikarmika*) dwell herein, they are no different from the Buddha; therefore, it is called "dwelling together with the Tathāgata.

As for "rubbing the head," it means that this person, through the power of their vows, the power of goodness, and their own practice of the provisional and the real (*upāya-tattva*), acts as the stimulus and response. This "stimulus and response" is what is meant by the "head."

Coming now with the two wisdoms of provisional and real [knowledge] used to transform others, he is called "the hand" because he develops the "head"—representing the provisional and real wisdom of the practitioner's own practice—thereby causing a mutual resonance between teacher and disciple.
Thus it is said, "rubbing the head" (*mòtóu*); "rubbing the head" is precisely the bestowal of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). △ Third, praising by way of location.

Bhaiṣajyarāja, wherever this [sūtra] is taught, read, recited, written down, or where its scrolls are kept, one should erect a stupa made of the seven precious substances, making it exceedingly high, wide, and magnificently adorned. It is not necessary to enshrine relics therein. Why is this?
Because within this very place resides the entire body of the Tathāgata. This stupa should be honored with all manner of flowers, incense, and necklaces.
With silk canopies, banners, streamers, music, songs, and hymns, they shall offer worship, pay homage, show respect, honor, and praise.
If there are those who see this stūpa, prostrate before it, and make offerings, you should know that all such persons draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is a praise based on location. When this Dharma resides in a place, that place is noble.
The locations where the Buddha was born, attained enlightenment, turned the wheel of the Dharma, and entered parinirvāṇa—places where the Dharma King has traveled—all should have stupas erected.

This sutra is the birthplace of the Dharma-body, the site where the Way is realized, the very essence of the turning of the wheel of the Dharma, and the cave of Great Parinirvāṇa; wherever this sutra is found, [it is so].
Regarding the statement that one need only perform offerings at the stupa without needing to enshrine śarīra, the *Śāstra* explains: "Crushed bone is the śarīra of the physical body (*janma-kāya*);
a scripture is the śarīra of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*). This sutra is the śarīra of the Dharma-body; it is not necessary to further enshrine the śarīra of the physical body.
Both the physical and Dharma-bodies may exist in either their whole or crushed forms; this can be understood accordingly. (And so forth. △
Fourth, the praise based on causes:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, there are many people, both lay and ordained, who practice the bodhisattva path;
yet if they are unable to see, hear, read, recite, copy, uphold, or make offerings to this Lotus Sūtra, you should know that these persons have not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path."
If there are those who hear this sutra, they will then be able to skillfully practice the path of a bodhisattva;

this is a praise based on the causal stage. If one has not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path and has received only the three preceding teachings, one is unable to deliver others with skillful means;
however, upon hearing this sutra, one immediately enters the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya), which is called "skillful delivery. Skillful delivery constitutes skillful practice.
[End of section. △ Five: Praising the five [aspects] by way of the fruit. First, clarifying "nearness":

If there are sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way, and they either see or hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and having heard it, believe, understand, receive, and uphold it—know that such persons have drawn near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
It should be known that those who will certainly attain the fruit of *sambodhi* are called "proximate" within the practice of peaceful conduct (*anulomika-caryā*).
This fruit of *bodhi* has as its essence the sphere of the Buddha’s eye and the Buddha’s wisdom of knowledge and vision; it is of two kinds:

first, the *bodhi* of the initial mind, which is the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*); second, the *bodhi* of the final mind, which is the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*su-prabuddha*). What is now referred to as "proximate" refers to this.
This refers to being truly close to the initial stage of awakening (*bodhi*). △ Second, the opening of the analogy:
Medicine King, suppose there is a person who, parched with thirst, requires water;

they dig for it on a high plateau and see only dry earth, knowing that the water is still far off. Yet, without ceasing their exertion, they gradually see moist earth and eventually reach mud. Their mind—
One knows with certainty that water must be near. Regarding this, there are two interpretations:
first, the perspective of the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*); second, the perspective of the gate of scripture (*āgama-mukha*). As for the gate of contemplation:

the minds of sentient beings are possessed of all afflictions (*kleśa*), which is likened to a high plateau; the cultivation of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) is likened to digging and excavating, through which one eventually realizes the flavor of the ultimate principle (*tattva-rasa*). As it is said:

Obtaining clear water is like relying on general contemplation: when one observes the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*) as being like dry soil, and recognizes that it is actually moist earth and mud, one knows that water must be near;
seeing the Truth (*satyadarśana*) is like obtaining clear water. If, however, one relies on specific contemplation, one first enters emptiness from the conventional;
seeing only emptiness and not non-emptiness, one cuts off the delusions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*), which is like digging into dry soil—the water is still far away.

Next, emerging from the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) through the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*), one first realizes that it is not provisional and now realizes that it is not empty.

By means of these two contemplations, one enters the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), whereby one can subdue ignorance (*avidyā*). When the perception of moist earth disappears and water appears, one is close to the First Ground (*prathamā-bhūmi*); this is the attainment of clear water.

If one relies on the Perfect Contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*), the Middle Way is neither empty nor provisional, yet it illuminates both emptiness and the provisional; thus one approaches [the goal] gradually.
Having exhausted the four stages of the moist mud and having subdued ignorance, one attains a semblance of the perfect understanding of the Middle Way;
