Furthermore, diligently practicing the wholesome dharmas of generosity (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*) is bodily diligence, while diligently practicing patience (*kṣānti*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) is mental diligence.
Fifth is the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, which is translated here as "cultivation through contemplation."
This refers to all forms of training in samādhis through the gathering of the mind and the binding of mindfulness, which are termed "cultivation through reflection" (bhāvanā).

This also has two types: first, the mundane; second, the supramundane. First, mundane dhyāna refers to the four fundamental dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and so forth;
these are the dhyānas practiced by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Second, supramundane dhyāna... [still]...
There are two kinds: first, supramundane dhyāna; second, supramundane and unsurpassed dhyāna.

"Supramundane" refers to the Six Wondrous Gates, the Sixteen Special Victories, the Universal Clarity, the Nine Contemplations of Foulness, the Eight Recollections, the Ten Recollections, the Eight Liberations, the Eight Bases of Mastery, the Ten Totalities, the Dhyāna of Refining, the Fourteen Transformations, the Dhyāna of Vow-Knowledge, the Summits of Dhyāna, the Samādhi of Non-contention, and the King of Samādhis.
The Samādhi of the Lion’s Boundless Leaping, the Samādhi of Transcendence, and so forth, up to the three supernormal knowledges and six supernatural powers—

all such categories are termed supramundane dhyāna and are also termed the dhyāna shared by the two vehicles. Furthermore, the supramundane dhyāna of the highest order refers to the nine kinds of great dhyānas,
such as the *svabhāva-dhyāna*, the one hundred and eight samādhis such as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, and those not [shared] by the Buddhas.
The one hundred and twenty-three samādhis, such as the "moving" [samādhi], are all termed supramundane, supreme dhyāna;

they are also called uncommon dhyāna, meaning they are not shared with ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles. Regarding loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—these four are all termed "immeasurable minds" (apramāṇa-citta) because they derive their name from their objects;
for since the sentient beings who are the objects of focus are immeasurable, the cognizing [minds] that take them as objects are likewise so named.

Because the mind also becomes immeasurable in accordance with its objects, all four are designated by the name "immeasurable mind": first, loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which is the mind capable of bestowing happiness upon others;

second, compassion (*karuṇā*), which is the mind capable of uprooting the suffering of others; third, sympathetic joy (*muditā*), which is the mind that gives rise to gladness and rejoices when others obtain happiness;
and fourth, equanimity (*upekṣā*), which is the mind that regards others without feelings of either aversion or attachment. These are the four.

The mind that is free from anger, hatred, resentment, and affliction, vast and immeasurable, pervading the ten directions, is called the Four Immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*), also known as the Four Immeasurable Samādhis (*catur-apramāṇa-samādhi*).
Each of these four has three distinct types: those conditioned by sentient beings (*sattvālambana*), those conditioned by phenomena (*dharmālambana*), and those without conditions (*anālambana*).

Regarding these, the Tripitaka masters hold that the first two types—those conditioned by sentient beings—are practiced by the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) merely for their own self-discipline; they can thus be subsumed under the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*).

The Bodhisattva, in order to deliver all beings, separately cultivates the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). When these reach fruition, they are termed Great Loving-kindness, Great Compassion, Great Sympathetic Joy, and Great Equanimity.
While the general teaching holds that these are cultivated equally by those of the three vehicles, there is also a distinction between self-benefit and the benefit of others.

In the gradual teachings, one cultivates them sequentially through the three stages; in the Perfect Teaching, they are fully and instantaneously perfected within a single mind. Thus, the four traces are fundamentally one. △
Second, the perfection of the fruit:
possessing the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, a purple-golden complexion, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses,
the four means of integration, the eighteen unique qualities, and the power of the divine path, he attains equal and perfect enlightenment and extensively delivers sentient beings.
The thirty-two marks, eighty minor characteristics, eighteen unique qualities, ten powers, and four fearlessnesses are explained extensively in various sutras and treatises;
therefore, I shall not trouble you by citing them here. As for the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*):

first, the Bodhisattva attracts others through generosity (*dāna*) by practicing the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—with a mind that has nothing to relinquish. If, for the sake of those who delight in material wealth...
One gathers beings through the gift of material wealth as soon as they are born;
if they are beings who delight in the Dharma, one gathers them through the gift of the Dharma. Second, gathering through pleasant speech:
if a bodhisattva uses words that are virtuous and gentle to accord with all beings, comforting and instructing them, then all beings will joyfully listen to it, and from this, [faith] arises.

The three types of beneficial conduct (*hitacaryā*)—loving-kindness, affection, and reliance on the Dharma—encompass the physical, verbal, and mental actions that arise in accordance with the Bodhisattva’s state, enabling all sentient beings to each receive benefit.
The fourth, the gathering through common purpose (*samānārthatā*), involves the Bodhisattva using the clarity of the Dharma-eye to perceive the faculties and conditions of sentient beings;
whenever there are those who share a common joy, the Bodhisattva immediately divides their form and disperses their shadow to universally harmonize with them.
Their light is equal to those activities, each bringing benefit to its respective object; these four are collectively termed "attraction" (*saṃgraha*).

That which sentient beings cherish in their hearts is precisely these four dharmas. If one employs these four dharmas to approach and guide them with sympathetic concern, sentient beings will then come to rely upon them.
Only after that can one lead them by means of the Great Vehicle's true path to deliver them across. Therefore...

It is said that "first using the hook of desire to entice, and later causing entry into the Buddha-way" means that being free from the deviant is called "correct," and turning one's back on delusion is called "enlightened.
△ Third, the conclusion regarding the benefits:
all are due to the spiritual friend Devadatta.
△ Second, explaining that the wondrous fruit for the Dharma Master shall be realized. Part one:
Explaining the realization of the fruit. He addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta, after the passing of immeasurable kalpas, shall attain Buddhahood;
his name shall be Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara."
The World-Honored One, the Buddha, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Charioteer of Men, dwells in a world named Heavenly Path (Devamārga).
Second, the explanation of his transformative deliverance:

At that time, the Buddha King of Heaven (Devarāja) remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, extensively preaching the wondrous Dharma to sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Innumerable sentient beings attained the fruit of Arhatship; immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the mind of a Pratyekabuddha;
and sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gave rise to the mind of the Unsurpassed Way, attained the patience of non-arising, and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
△ Third, the benefits after the parinirvāṇa:
After the Tathāgata Devendra-buddha enters parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remains in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*).

A stupa made of the seven precious gems is erected over his entire bodily relics (*śarīra*), sixty *yojana* in height and forty *yojana* in length and breadth; all the devas and human beings [revere it].
With various flower powders, incense, burning perfumes, ointments, robes, necklaces, banners, streamers, precious parasols, music, and hymns,
they prostrated and made offerings to the wondrous stupa of the seven jewels; thereby immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of Arhatship,
immeasurable sentient beings realized Pratyekabuddhahood, and inconceivable numbers of sentient beings resolved upon Bodhicitta and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
△ Third, dispelling doubts and exhorting faith.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "In future ages, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the 'Devadatta Chapter' of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, develop a pure heart of faith and reverence and do not give rise to doubt or confusion, they shall not fall into hell."
Those born as hungry ghosts or animals will be reborn before the Buddhas of the ten directions; wherever they are reborn, they will constantly hear this sutra.
If they are reborn among humans or devas, they will experience supreme and wondrous bliss; if they are before a Buddha, they will be born by transformation upon a lotus flower.

Regarding those born through transformation from a lotus, the *Tāisheng jing* (Sūtra on Birth from a Lotus) states: "Those born from a lotus are not among the [four modes of birth]—womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, or transformation-born;
they are called 'transformation-born' only because they are not [born by] transformation. The *Guanshiyin pusa pumen pin jing* (Sūtra of the Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva) states:

"Birth from a lotus is for those who have no parents. The *Wuliangshou jing guan jing* (Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Infinite Life) states: "Those who remain long upon the lotus pedestal are said to be womb-born, yet in reality they are not womb-born. These are the examples.
Those born from lotuses are also called "moisture-born" or "egg-born," yet they are neither moisture-born nor egg-born;
they are not the same as the "transformation-born" (upapāduka) among the four modes of birth within the realms.

For instance, while the transformation-born gods are still born upon the laps of their fathers and so forth, how could they be the same as those within the four destinies? What is here termed "transformation-born" refers to those who appear instantaneously.
As it says in the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*: "He was suddenly born by transformation into the family of King Śuddhadeva.

Furthermore, regarding those described as being born from moisture or eggs, this refers simply to being born from a lotus; because it is moist and not yet split open, it is like moisture or an egg contained within a flower—this is the sense of being like a fetus.
△ Second, clarifying how Mañjuśrī today transmits the sutra and the dragon girl attains Buddhahood. Part one.
The fifth section of the first chapter, "Mañjuśrī’s Mastery of the Sūtra," begins with the Request for Departure by Jñānakūṭa:
At that time, a bodhisattva named Jñānakūṭa, who had come from below from the presence of the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna, addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, saying,
"I shall now return to my own land."

Jñānākūṭa said that because the Prabhūtaratna Buddha had emerged as a witness for the sake of the sutra’s propagation, and since the exhortation to circulate it was now complete, he requested to return.
II. Śākyamuni Buddha’s Intervention:
Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Jñānākūṭa, saying, "Good man, wait a moment; here is a bodhisattva."
"It is said that Mañjuśrī may come to meet you and discuss the sublime Dharma; he may then return to his own land.
Although the World-Honored One Śākyamuni restrained him, this was because the events of the *jirimon* (trace gate) had concluded while the *honmon* (essential gate) had not yet been revealed;
thus, he entrusted Mañjuśrī with the task of preserving the secret intent of Buddha Prabhūtaratna, which is beyond the knowledge of ordinary bodhisattvas. △ Third, Mañjuśrī immediately arrives.
At that time, Mañjuśrī sat upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel; the bodhisattvas who had come together with him likewise sat upon precious lotus flowers.
They emerged spontaneously from the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King in the great ocean and remained suspended in mid-air.
Proceeding to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, they descended from their lotuses to the place where the Buddha was, and prostrated themselves at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones in reverence.
Having completed his prostrations, he went to where Zhiji was and exchanged greetings with him. They sat down to one side, and [Zhiji] asked Mañjuśrī:
"According to the introductory account, you were seated here; why have you now come from the sea? Please answer this:
how could you possibly cross the realm of the sages with ordinary sentiments? What fault is there in not remaining at this assembly to transform sentient beings in the ocean?"
Furthermore, it may also be that after the benefits of the first period have been completed and [the Buddha] has departed, one must inform others;

yet how could great benefit arise only upon his arrival? He came from the ocean together with the assembly, or perhaps there was a detailed text containing the words of the *saṃnipāta* (assembly) which reached us here in an abbreviated form.
Question: Beyond the three thousandfold world-system, each contains four hundred trillion [worlds].
Question: Since there is no longer a great ocean, why does Mañjuśrī still say he has "emerged from the sea"? Answer: This explanation based on the facts is not erroneous;

moreover, it is now explained through three points regarding the inconceivable. First, since both the devas and humans have been moved and the great ocean transformed, if [Mañjuśrī] were to come from the place where they were moved, he would be subject to the same limitations as those who were moved.
Second, even if the assembly in the ocean were moved, the dragons... [text fragment ends].

As for the Dragon King Akṣobhya not moving: it is said that while he does not move, his dwelling has already been transformed. What is there to prevent him from coming from that place which, though transformed, remains unchanging?
Thirdly, regarding those without karmic connection who were moved and those with karmic connection who have now arrived here:

this inconceivable mountain and sea remain exactly as they were, yet the multitude does not see them. This is merely a transformation of perception (*darśana-pariṇāma*), not a change in the substance (*bhāva*) itself; such is the nature of Mañjuśrī.

Since that land is both defiled and pure, it does not require one to arise and travel there; thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that when beings are transferred to another land, no one has the perception of coming or going.
Here, however, people are made to have the perception of coming and going while, in reality, there is no movement.

Therefore, we know that for those who possess the karmic capacity (*mārga*), the lands transform and the multitudes shift, yet they still come [to this realm] because they lack the necessary conditions.

As for this land, many more have come yet do not arrive; the reason is that while the principle remains unmoving, the manifestation of events follows a fixed pattern, causing what is seen to differ and the timing of arrivals and departures to vary.
If even the transformative protocols of Bodhisattvas are thus, how could the transformations established by the Buddha be the same as those of ordinary beings?
△ Fourth, Zhizhi asks about the transformation.
The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa asked Mañjuśrī, "O Benevolent One, how many sentient beings were converted by you during your visit to the Dragon Palace?
5. Mañjuśrī’s Definitive Answer (in seven parts): First, the answer that those benefited were exceedingly numerous.
Mañjuśrī said: "Their number is immeasurable, beyond calculation, not to be proclaimed by mouth nor fathomed by mind;
wait but a moment, and you shall know it for yourself."
△ Second, the assembly of those who have received benefit and attained realization.
Before these words had even concluded, countless bodhisattvas sat upon precious lotus flowers, emerged from the ocean, and proceeded to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa,
where they remained suspended in the air.
△ All three are emanations of Mañjuśrī.
These bodhisattvas have all been transformed and delivered by Mañjuśrī; they are fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva and together discourse upon the six pāramitās.
△ 4. Śrāvakas who previously received the Lesser [Vehicle]:
Originally, these śrāvakas spoke of the practices of śrāvakas while in the void;
having previously received the provisional teachings, they dwelt in the path of the Two Vehicles and spoke only of severing birth and death. △ 5. Now hearing the Reality and Abiding [therein].
Great! Now all practice the meaning of the Mahāyāna emptiness.
Having now heard the teaching of reality, they all abide in the Dharma of the Mahāyāna. △ Sixth, Mañjuśrī concludes on the benefits.
Mañjuśrī said to Jñānakūṭa, "Such was the manner of his teaching and transforming beings within the sea.
7. Jñānakūṭa’s Verses of Praise.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa praised him with a verse, saying:
With great wisdom, virtue, and heroic vigor, you have transformed and delivered immeasurable multitudes;

now this entire great assembly and I have all witnessed you expound the meaning of the true mark and reveal the Dharma of the One Vehicle, widely guiding all sentient beings so that they may swiftly attain Bodhi.
△ Second, explaining the benefits for the dragon girl (nine sections). First, explaining Mañjuśrī’s own account.
Mañjuśrī said: "In the midst of the ocean, I have always exclusively preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*."
△ Second, the inquiry of Prajñākūṭa.
Prajñākūṭa asked Mañjuśrī: "This sutra is extremely profound and subtle, a treasure among all sutras, rare in the world.
Are there any sentient beings who, by applying themselves with diligent vigor and practicing this sutra, can quickly attain Buddhahood?"
△ Third, Mañjuśrī’s actual response. Mañjuśrī said:
"There is the daughter of the Dragon King Sāgara, who is eight years of age.

She possesses sharp faculties and wisdom, well understands the faculties, karmic actions, and practices of sentient beings, has attained dhāraṇīs, and has realized the profound secret treasury taught by all Buddhas."

They are able to receive and uphold [the teachings], enter deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and thoroughly penetrate all phenomena (*dharmas*). In a single instant, they give rise to the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and attain non-retrogression.
Their eloquence is unimpeded; they regard all sentient beings with compassion as if they were their own infants.

Fully endowed with merit, they express through both thought and speech that which is subtle, wondrous, vast, compassionate, benevolent, and yielding. With minds harmonious and refined, they are able to reach the state of *bodhi*.
△ Fourth, Zhizhi raises a specific objection.

Bodhisattva Zhizhi said: "I have seen the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, throughout immeasurable kalpas, performing difficult practices and asceticism, accumulating merit and virtue while seeking the path to Bodhi without ever ceasing. I have observed the three-thousandfold world system, and even..."
There is not even a space the size of a mustard seed where this bodhisattva has not sacrificed her body and life for the sake of sentient beings;
it is only after this that she shall attain the path of enlightenment. Do not disbelieve that this woman will achieve perfect awakening in a mere moment.
Practicing the path for immeasurable kalpas is the distinct teaching of the Dharma-knowledge; it is difficult to attain.

Now, that the Dragon Girl attains Buddhahood in an instant is the distinct response to the doubt regarding the perfection [of the teaching]; therefore, they do not believe. △ Fifth, the Dragon Girl explains through the Perfect [Teaching], in two parts:
first, the narrative by the Sūtra compiler.
Before his speech had concluded, the Dragon King’s Daughter suddenly appeared before him; she prostrated with her head at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and praised him in verse:
Part Two: Praise in Verse (Three sections) 1. Clarifying that upholding this sutra leads to liberation.
Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, one shines universally throughout the ten directions.

Regarding the "characteristics of sin and merit," these are discussed in terms of the mutual relationship between sin and merit across the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*). Now that the provisional teachings have been opened, there is neither sin nor merit;

there is only the single true reality (*ekasatyatā-lakṣaṇa*), which is called "profound penetration. "The ten directions" refers to the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*), all of which are equally perceived through true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*).
Because it is luminous, it is called "pervasive illumination. △ Second, explaining the accomplishment of the two bodies:
The subtle and pure Dharma-body is endowed with the thirty-two marks and adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics;
this Dharma-body is venerated by devas and humans, revered by dragons and spirits, and there are no classes of sentient beings who do not revere it.
One who possesses the thirty-two marks has deeply realized the principle of the Dharma-body and is thus fully endowed with its primary and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies, if one wishes to attain all dharmas, one should study Prajñā, just as one obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).

The followers of the Two Vehicles, however, merely attain emptiness-emptiness and lack these marks and characteristics. This is because that great wisdom of equality in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* is precisely what is present now.
This is cited as scriptural evidence because it accords with the principle of the single true reality (*eka-lakṣaṇa*). △ Third, the citation of the Buddha as proof:

Furthermore, having heard that the realization of *bodhi* is such that only a Buddha can witness and know it, [the Bodhisattva] declares: "I shall open the Mahāyāna teaching to deliver sentient beings from suffering."
△ Section Six: The Objections of Śāriputra. Part Two: The Initial General Objection Regarding Faith.
At that time, Śāriputra said to the dragon girl, "What you say—that you will attain the unsurpassed path before long—is difficult to believe.
Why is this? The female body is defiled and impure; it is not a vessel for the Dharma. How could it possibly attain unsurpassed bodhi?"

The path of the Buddha is vast and remote; only after diligently accumulating practices through hardships for immeasurable kalpas and fully cultivating all the *pāramitās* does one finally achieve it.
△ Second, the exposition of the five obstructions:
Furthermore, the female body still possesses five obstructions: first, one cannot become a Brahmā King; second, [one cannot become] Śakra Devendra.
Third is the Māra King; fourth is the Cakravartin Sage-King; and fifth is the Buddha-body. How can one quickly attain Buddhahood?
These five hindrances are the five obstacles of the female body, which thereby cause lingering obstructions and difficulties.

The Brahmā King is the Lord of the First Dhyāna Heaven; Śakra is called the Way of Brahmā, meaning the Jade Emperor. In reality, these are one person with two titles, each following its respective context.
The teachings of that school describe [the cosmos] as terminating at the Nine Heavens; beyond the Nine Heavens, there is nothing heard of at all.

This is because those heavens possess speech, perception, and reflection, and are thus able to issue commands. Consequently, when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they are preceded by the Brahma King and followed by the Heavenly Emperor (Śakra).
Śakra is the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who dwells in the Sudarśana Palace and exercises sovereign rule.
The King is the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the Māra King is the Lord of the Āsaṃjñika Heaven, or perhaps he is one who has converted a host of followers as his retinue.
He is the sovereign of those multitudes. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"Powerful Great Māras are all Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages who have realized the Dharma-gate of inconceivable liberation. They manifest evil to reveal the right, and they uphold the Buddha's mission as Universal Monarchs."
The four [types of bodies] cannot be fully enumerated; they are merely designated by the title of a Golden Wheel-Turning King who rules over the four continents.

The Buddha-body, however, is the fruition that fully encompasses all. △ Seventh, the Dragon Girl explains through reality in two parts: first, she offers a pearl to symbolize her attainment of perfect understanding.
At that time, the Dragon Girl possessed a precious jewel worth as much as the three-thousandfold world-system;
she offered it to the Buddha, who immediately accepted it. The Dragon Girl then addressed the Bodhisattva Zhijie and the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

"Was this matter—the offering of the precious jewel by me and its acceptance by the World-Honored One—not swift? They replied: "It was exceedingly swift. The girl said: "Observe with your supernatural powers—"
My attainment of Buddhahood shall be even swifter than this.
The perfect sphere represents the cultivation of the perfect cause; offering it to the Buddha signifies that through this cause, the fruit will be realized.

The Buddha’s swift acceptance of it symbolizes the Dragon Girl’s rapid attainment of the fruit. This is precisely the non-falsity of attaining Buddhahood by sitting at the site of enlightenment in a single thought-moment.
△ Second, the correct demonstration of the perfection of cause and the fulfillment of fruit:
At that time, the entire assembly saw the dragon girl suddenly transform into a man, complete with the practices of a bodhisattva,
and immediately proceed to the Stainless World in the south, where she sat upon a precious lotus flower and attained equal and perfect enlightenment, endowed with the thirty-two marks.
Possessing the eighty minor marks, he universally expounds the wondrous Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
The *Tāi jīng* (Womb Sūtra) states that Māras, Brahmās, Śakras, and goddesses do not discard their current bodies nor receive new ones, yet all attain Buddhahood in their very present bodies.
Thus, a verse from that sūtra says: "The nature of phenomena is like a great ocean; it does not say 'this is' or 'this is not,' nor does it distinguish between ordinary persons and sages."
For the noble and sagely person, there is equality without high or low; it depends solely on the extinction of mental defilements, where realization is attained as easily as turning over one's hand.
△ Section Eight: The Assembly Gains Benefit upon Hearing and Seeing, Part One: Properly Explaining What is Seen and Heard.
At that time, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings, as well as humans and non-humans of the Sahā world,
all saw from afar that dragon girl had attained buddhahood and was preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly of gods and humans.
△ The two beings rejoiced;
their hearts were filled with great joy, and they all paid homage from afar. Immeasurable sentient beings, hearing the Dharma, attained realization and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
Immeasurable sentient beings received the prediction of attaining the Way. The World of Stainless shook in six ways, as did the Sahā world.
Three thousand sentient beings dwelt on the stage of non-retrogression; three thousand sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and received their predictions of enlightenment.
Immeasurable sentient beings in that land received benefit, as did those in the Sahā world who received benefit here.
In the south, conditions were ripe and it was appropriate for him to manifest the eight phases of enlightenment; in this land, conditions were thin, so he used only the dragon girl.
This teaching is the power of skillful means, the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body, which attains one body as all bodies.
△ Ninth: Zhizhi and Śāriputra silently accepted it.
The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa, Śāriputra, and the entire assembly accepted this in silence.
Having heard and seen it, they were sustained by direct experience; through their faith and reverence, they immediately attained the removal of doubt and joy, benefiting both gods and humans equally.

△ Chapter Thirteen: The Chapter on Upholding (The Chapter on Exhortation in the Main Text), Explaining the Accomplishment of the Power of Patience through Propagating the Sūtra in This Land and Newly Attaining Retention while Propagating the Sūtra in Other Lands.
First, the Title: *Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra*, Chapter Thirteen: The Chapter on Upholding.

Two hundred thousand bodhisattvas were commanded to propagate the sutra; hence it is called the "Chapter on Upholding" (*Dhāraṇī-parivarta*). Eighty quadrillion nayutas of bodhisattvas were further exhorted to propagate the sutra;
hence it is called the "Chapter on Exhorting to Uphold" (*Anuparindanā-parivarta*). Why is this so?

Because the number "two hundred thousand" refers to the specific count of those individually commissioned at the beginning of the "Chapter on the Dharma-Master," who received the mandate to uphold [the teaching]. As for the "eighty quadrillion nayutas," [this refers to the subsequent exhortation].
As previously stated, there was no separate injunction for this; it was merely a general search. Now, by beholding them with the Buddha-eye, he causes them to make a vow.
Because the transmission of the sutra in this land carries profound verification and the Buddha’s intention is earnest, they propagate it upon receiving his exhortation.
Thus, there are two meanings. △ Second, the text of the sutra has two parts: first, clarifying the upholding [of the sutra], which has three sections; first, the twenty thousand [beings].
The Bodhisattvas having received this command, they shall propagate this sutra in this land.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna, together with a retinue of twenty thousand bodhisattvas, all made this vow before the Buddha: "We pray only that the World-Honored One will not..."
We reflect that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall uphold, recite, and expound this sutra.
Although sentient beings in the future evil age will have diminished roots of goodness, will increase in overweening pride, will crave gain and offerings, and will increase unwholesome roots—
making them difficult to transform and far removed from liberation— we shall nevertheless arouse the power of great forbearance to read, recite, uphold, and expound this sutra.
They transcribe [the scriptures] and perform various offerings, not sparing even their own bodies or lives.

Sentient beings have little merit; this is the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). Arrogance increases greatly; this is the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Greed for profit and offerings; this is the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
The increase of unwholesome roots; this is the defilement of life-span (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*). Being far removed from liberation; this is the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). If...
How could anyone other than a Bodhisattva of the profound stages, who has perfected the power of patience, be able to propagate this sutra in this world of five turbidities?
△ Second, the great Śrāvakas vow to propagate it in other lands.
At that time, five hundred arhats within the assembly who had received their prediction of enlightenment addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, we too vow to extensively expound this sutra in other lands.

Furthermore, eight thousand persons—both those still in training and those beyond training—who had received their predictions rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and made this vow: “World-Honored One, we...”
Furthermore, you should also preach this sutra extensively in other lands. Why is this? It is because the people in this Sahā world are for the most part corrupt and evil;
they harbor overweening pride, their merit is meager, and their minds are turbid with anger, deceitful, and insincere.

Question: Since these śrāvakas, having already received their predictions, have ascended to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), shattered the delusions of ignorance (*avidyā-āvaraṇa*), attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and become great bodhisattvas, why are they unable to propagate the sutras in this evil world? Answer:

It is because they are intended to lead those bodhisattvas who have newly resolved upon the path and are beginning their practice; furthermore, it is because they wish to inspire others to undertake the practice of austerities in this evil world and propagate the sutras.
This leads to the opening of the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct. △ Third, the Bhikṣuṇīs request the prediction of enlightenment.
Fourth, the initial request by the maternal aunt:
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with bhikṣus who were both in training and beyond training... [end of fragment]
Six thousand bhikṣuṇīs rose from their seats, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, and gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance without averting their eyes for a moment.

Regarding the maternal aunt, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (The Collection of Former Deeds) states that when King Śuddhodana was born to the Śākya clan member Suprabuddha, eight daughters were born. At that time, King Śuddhodana...
The four brothers each took two daughters as wives; Queen Māyā and Mahāprajāpatī were the consorts of King Śuddhodana.
Seven days after giving birth to the Bodhisattva, Māyā passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Because Mahāprajāpatī was her maternal aunt, she is called "Aunt" (Yipo).
△ Second, the record.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Gautamī: "For what reason do you look upon the Tathāgata with a face of sorrow?
Does it not occur to your mind that I have failed to mention your name when bestowing the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Gautamī, I have previously spoken in general terms that all śrāvakas have already received their predictions; if you now wish to know your own prediction, listen."
In a future age, amidst the teachings of sixty-eight thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, you shall become a great Dharma-master;
together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), you shall all be Dharma-masters.
Thus, gradually perfecting the path of a bodhisattva, you shall attain Buddhahood under the name Tathāgata Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, World-Knower, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans,
Buddha, World-Honored One Gautamī, and six thousand bodhisattvas— all beings who delight in seeing—
successively transmitted the prediction of their attainment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What I previously stated in summary—that all śrāvakas have already received their predictions—refers to the verse in the "Chapter on the Five Hundred Disciples" which says:
"Kāśyapa, you already know," and so forth, for one and a half lines of verse. II. Yaśodharā Requests Her Prediction.
Part One: The Request.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, thought to herself:
"Among those who have received predictions [of enlightenment], the World-Honored One alone has not mentioned my name.
△ Second, the prediction.

The Buddha told Yaśodharā: "In the future, amidst the teachings of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, you shall cultivate the bodhisattva path as a great Dharma teacher, gradually perfecting the way to Buddhahood.
In the land of Sukhāvatī, you shall attain Buddhahood, named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Endowed with Thousands of Myriads of Radiant Marks."
The Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has a lifespan of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
△ Third, the nuns’ realization and understanding.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, and their retinues were all filled with great joy at having attained what they had never experienced before; they then spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, Guide, we, the gods and humans, having heard this prediction, our minds are at peace and fully satisfied.
△ Fourth, the nuns make their vows.
After the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken these verses, they addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, we too are able [to go] to other regions.”
The kingdom shall widely proclaim this sutra.
△ Second, explaining the exhortation to uphold [the sutra], in two parts. First, the prose section, in five parts. First, explaining that the Buddha gazes with his Buddha-eye:
At that time, the World-Honored One gazed upon eighty quadrillion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The Tathāgata has silently exhorted them with his gaze without speaking;

although he has not specifically commanded the bodhisattvas above, he has already cited the profound depth of the merit of upholding this sutra as clear evidence, and the many-body emanations of Prabhūtaratna have come from afar to urge them on.
Since these earnest matters and principles are sufficient, those who wish to respond to the summons should depart immediately.

I vow not to trouble you with further words; moreover, because of my aspiration to protect the śrāvakas and to propagate the sūtras in other directions, I do not extol the matter of propagating the sūtras in this land. △ Second, the Bodhisattvas’ request and announcement.
All these bodhisattvas were *avaivartika*, having turned the wheel of non-retrogression and attained all *dhāraṇīs*.
They rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, and thought:
"If the World-Honored One commands us to uphold and expound this sutra, we shall widely proclaim this Dharma in accordance with the Buddha's teaching."
△ 3. The Buddha of the Three Knowledges remained silent.
Again, [the Bodhisattva] thought: "The Buddha now remains silent and does not issue an instruction;
what should I do? △ 4. The Bodhisattva knew his intention.
At that time, the bodhisattvas, out of reverence for the Buddha’s intention and desiring to fulfill their own original vows, △ fifthly, made a vow to propagate the sutra.
They then uttered a lion’s roar before the Buddha and made this solemn declaration: “World-Honored One, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction...”
Thereafter, as we travel back and forth through the worlds of the ten directions, may we enable sentient beings to copy this sutra,
receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain its meaning, practice according to the Dharma, and maintain right mindfulness—
all through the majestic power of the Buddha. We pray that the World-Honored One, remaining in other lands, will behold us from afar and provide protection.
△ Second, the four verses in praise; first, donning the robes and propagating the sutra. Third, a general discussion of the time and season to clarify the donning of the robes.
At that moment, all the bodhisattvas together raised their voices and spoke these verses:
I only pray that you will not be concerned; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall extensively expound [this Dharma] amidst the terrors of the evil age.
△ Second, specifically clarifying the objects of endurance. Part three: First, a general clarification of those with false views.
"We shall endure all instances where ignorant people revile us with harsh words or attack us with knives and staves.
The following nine lines specifically clarify the objects of endurance; now, this one line generally clarifies those with wrong views, namely the worldly masses.
△ Second, regarding those with overweening pride concerning the path.

In this degenerate age, there are bhikṣus whose minds are characterized by perverse wisdom and crookedness; having not attained anything, they claim to have attained it, and their hearts are filled with arrogance.
△ Third, those who falsely claim to be sages through overweening pride.
There may be those who, though dwelling as forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*) in seclusion wearing robes of rags (*pāṃśukūla*), claim to practice the true path while looking down upon worldly people;
yet because they are greedily attached to gain and offerings, they preach the Dharma to laypeople and are venerated by the world like arhats with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijña*).
Such persons harbor evil intentions and constantly dwell on worldly affairs; they merely bear the name of "forest-dweller" and take pleasure in exposing our faults.
And they spoke these words: "These bhikṣus, for the sake of craving gain and offerings, preach the doctrines of external paths and compose these sūtras themselves to delude the people of the world.
Seeking fame and renown, they discriminate against this sūtra and, desiring to disparage us within the great assembly, approach kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders."

Furthermore, other groups of bhikṣus slandered me, speaking ill of me by claiming that I was a person of false views who propounded the doctrines of non-Buddhists. Regarding the term *āraṇya*—sometimes called *ālanya*:
in Chinese it is translated as "unoccupied" (*wushi*); in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is translated as "a place of seclusion" (*yuǎnlí chù*);

in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra*, it is translated as "a quiet and peaceful place" (*xiánjìng chù*), or alternatively as "a place of non-contention" (*wúzhèng*). The *Zuòchán sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on Dhyāna and Samādhi) states: "Un... [The text here is incomplete].

"Those who dispute" refers to protecting sentient beings so as not to cause them to engage in contention. The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states: "An araṇya is a place where one does not contend with the world;
it is neither too near nor too far, convenient for begging for food, possessing tree shade, abundant flowers and fruits, and sufficient pure water;
it is free from difficulties, lacks rugged obstacles, and is easy to ascend; it is solitary and without companions, where one recites what has been heard. [In such a place], there is no king.
When ministers, householders, and others come seeking him out, he should say to them: "Welcome, welcome!
When you reach your dwelling, you should invite me to sit; do not sit alone. If they do not accept his humble seat, he should comfort them in various ways and preach the Dharma for them.
If they do not wish for an extensive explanation, he should provide a brief explanation, and so forth. If he does not act thus...

This is not the practice of an araṇya-dweller; one who merely resides in an araṇya to subdue their own afflictions while exalting themselves and despising others does not practice the conduct of non-contention.
Not knowing that true tranquility lies elsewhere, they treat teachers and friends with contempt and show arrogance toward kings and ministers;
how much more so for the ignorant, whom they lead to call them "sages," causing those with eyes to feel cold dread. Rāhula’s conduct has forever departed from emptiness.
Wherein lies the virtue of one who is born? It is simply that the mind lacks internal substance while the body is exclusively occupied with external affairs;

though they earnestly discourse upon the Way, there is nothing substantial to be said. If it is truly as Piṇḍola knows—that the king lost his kingdom for seven years—or as the Dhyāna Master Chou [was aware of] whether he was fit to be king, then adjusting one's conduct to the times is appropriate;
how can one be consistently designated by the name of an *āraṇyaka* (forest-dweller)?
"If one points out their unwholesome bodily actions," "or points out our faults," "or points out their unwholesome mental actions," and says such things as these—
this refers to their unwholesome verbal actions. △ Third,
the meaning of putting on the robes collectively.
Out of reverence for the Buddha, we shall endure all these evils; even when they treat us with contempt, saying, "You are all Buddhas," we must accept such insults and arrogance.
"Revering the Buddha while enduring insults is identical in intent to that of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging. A commentary on this difficulty states:

"Regarding the insults mentioned here, there are two types—those concerning the Dharma and those concerning persons. To insult a person by saying 'you are all Buddhas' is an extreme form of disparagement."
In this turbid age of evil, there will be many terrors and malevolent spirits who enter our bodies to revile and insult us.
Out of reverent faith in the Buddha, we shall don the armor of patience; for the sake of expounding this sutra, we shall endure these various hardships.
We do not cherish our own bodies or lives, but only regret that we might fail to attain the Unsurpassed Way. In future ages, we shall protect and uphold what the Buddha has entrusted to us.

"Blessed One, you yourself should know that in this defiled age there will be wicked bhikṣus who do not understand the Buddha’s skillful means and the teachings spoken according to what is appropriate;
they will speak with harsh words, frown, and be repeatedly expelled and kept away from stūpas and monasteries.
Because of such various evils, we shall all endure these matters out of respect for the Buddha’s instructions."
△ Second, entering a room to propagate the sutra:
"In all villages and cities, wherever there are those who seek the Dharma, I shall go to their respective places and preach the teachings entrusted by the Buddha.
△ Third, sitting upon a seat to propagate the sutra.
"I am the messenger of the World-Honored One; standing amidst the assembly, I am fearless. I shall skillfully preach the Dharma; may the Buddha remain in peace.
(4) Summary of the Request for Knowledge:
"Before the World-Honored One and all the Buddhas who have come from the ten directions, I have made this vow. The Buddha himself knows my heart."

△ Chapter Four: On Peaceful Conduct. This chapter explains the Dharma upon which those of external ordinary capacity and weak power should rely, so that they may propagate [the teaching] without fearing danger or suffering.
First, the title: The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Fourteen: On Peaceful Conduct.
The commentary on the text has three parts: first, based on the facts; second, following the text; and third, the dharma-gate. Regarding "based on the facts":
because the body is free from danger, the mind is at peace; because there is no sorrow or affliction, there is joy. When body and mind are peaceful and joyful, one is able to progress.
This "progress" refers to the path to *nirvāṇa*, named after its cause. "Peace and joy" refers to Great *Nirvāṇa*, named after its fruit. Thus, these are the cause and the fruit.

There are four permutations regarding suffering and pleasure: 1. There is cause and effect that are both suffering, such as when those of the eternalist heretics practice asceticism and yet receive a painful retribution.
2. There is a cause that is pleasure and an effect that is suffering, such as when those of the nihilist heretics indulge their desires to seek pleasure and later receive a painful retribution.

3. There is a cause that is suffering and an effect that is pleasure, such as when those of the Three Vehicles who follow the Dharma of disintegration employ unskillful means and exert effort [to attain liberation].

If one enters nirvana only when suffering arrives, whereas cause and effect are solely blissful, then the present practice of peaceful dwelling is precisely the "Great Vehicle" (Mahāvaipulya) of skillful and true deliverance.
All else is not the practice of peaceful dwelling; only this wondrous cause and wondrous fruit are called the practice of peaceful dwelling.
As for those who attach themselves to the text: they don the robe of the Tathāgata and abide on the ground of patience; thus, the Dharma-body peacefully enters into suchness.
Because one enters the chamber [of meditation] without sudden violence, the mind is liberated and delights in sitting upon the Tathāgata-seat;

because one contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, Prajñā leads the way as one proceeds. Taking these three virtues collectively as the object of practice, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"From the first generation of the bodhicitta, the Bodhisattva constantly contemplates Nirvāṇa; when practicing the causes of the Path, he employs these three."
The Dharma guides the three karmas as practice; when the three karmas are purified, the six sense faculties are purified.

When the six sense faculties are purified, one gives rise to a semblance understanding and attains entry into the true cause, until finally reaching that which is beyond all dependence, termed the "Peaceful and Blissful Practice" (*anraku-gyō*).
As for the dharma-gate: "peace" means immovability, "bliss" means non-reception, and "practice" means non-action. Immovability means not being affected by birth-and-death or nirvana.
That which is moved by the two extremes of saṃsāra is precisely that which abides immovably. "Non-acceptance" refers to not accepting the vast functioning of samādhi;
it is that which neither the ordinary nor the sagely five types of sensation accept. Where there is acceptance, there is suffering; where there is no acceptance, there is no suffering.
To be without suffering and without pleasure is called the practice of Great Bliss, the practice of non-practice. If there were anything accepted, it would not be so.

Thus, there is that which is practiced and that which is not practiced; because ordinary beings practice what is not practiced while noble sages do not practice it, this is the Middle Way of practicing through non-practice.
△ Second, the scriptural text has two parts: first, the question; second, first, praising the profound practice of the bodhisattvas who can thus propagate the sutra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
it is truly rare for these bodhisattvas to have such reverence and compliance toward the Buddha that they have made great vows to protect,
uphold, read, recite, and preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in the future evil age."
This praises the Bodhisattvas of profound practice in the preceding chapter for being able to uphold the command and propagate this sutra in a defiled and evil world.
△ Second, the question regarding how Bodhisattvas of shallow practice should expound this sutra.
"Bhagavān, how can Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas preach this sūtra in the future evil age?
This question asks how bodhisattvas of shallow practice can propagate the sūtra in an evil age. △ Second, the answer has three parts:

first, a general presentation of the four categories of practice; second, an explanation of the methods of cultivation; third, a general clarification of the characteristics of the perfection of practice. Now:
First,
the Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to preach this sutra in the evil age to come,
they should abide securely in four dharmas."
The "four dharmas" provide a general outline of the four peaceful practices (*anurakṣaṇā-pratipatti*) of body, speech, mind, and vow.
II. Explanation of the Methods of Practice (in four parts): 1. Peaceful Practice of Body; 2. Peaceful Practice of Speech; 3. Peaceful Practice of Mind; 4. Peaceful Practice of Vow.
Regarding the first [the Peaceful Practice of Body], there are two sections: A. Prose Exposition; B. Verse Recitation. Regarding the prose exposition, there are further [subdivisions].
Second, first, the brief indication of the practice of proximity.
First, one who dwells securely in the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice (*caryā-vihāra*) and sphere of proximity (*upaniṣad*) is able to expound this sūtra for the sake of sentient beings.

"Practice" refers to advancing toward [the goal], while "proximity" refers to cultivation. Furthermore, the sphere of practice is the garment of patience (*kṣānti-vastra*), and the sphere of proximity is the Dharma.
To practice patience while sitting in emptiness and inwardly harboring the ultimate principle is called "practicing the Dharma of emptiness.

To endure circumstances and events while physically attaining realization of external conditions and dwelling in the true realm is called "being near. △ Second, the explanation of practicing and being near, in two parts:
first, the explanation of the place of practice.
Mañjuśrī, what is called the "sphere of practice" of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the ground of patience, being gentle, compliant, and harmonious, neither impetuous nor startled in mind;

furthermore, if they do not engage in any activity regarding phenomena, yet contemplate all phenomena according to their true nature, and neither practice nor discriminate—this is called a bodhisattva.
This is the sphere of activity of the Mahāsattva.
To explain this, there are three [stages]: first, it refers to a single dharma, namely the one true reality (*ekasatyatā*);

second, it refers to two dharmas, namely the two patiences regarding arising and dharmas (*utpāda-dharma-kṣānti*); third, it refers to three dharmas, namely the three inconceivable truths (*acintya-trisatyatā*). First, as for the one true reality: for...
That which is the refuge of all serves as the foundation for all, yet it is pervasive and without discrimination;
because it is the refuge of all, it is called "abiding on the ground of patience" (*kṣānti-bhūmi*). Since all dharmas take refuge therein, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*);

because all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) come to rest within it, it is called "patience. This is precisely the practice of non-practice, the robe of the Tathāgata, which serves as the foundation for all.

Therefore it is said that through various practices such as gentleness, flexibility, and docility, one attains the Principle and achieves fulfillment. This is like all things that grow when they obtain the earth.

If one attains the fundamental Principle, being firm yet capable of yielding, being contrary yet capable of compliance, being violent yet capable of governance, and being startled yet capable of tranquility, immeasurable merits arise from this ground of the One Reality of the Middle Way—a ground where there is no arising.
The arising of merit is precisely the practice of non-practice; it is the Tathāgata’s chamber because it is universally non-discriminative.
Furthermore, regarding the equality of dharmas, it means to realize that the nature and characteristics of practice and non-practice are non-dual.
To perceive the reality of all dharmas is called "non-discrimination," yet there is also no characteristic of non-discrimination to be grasped; this can be termed "also non-practice."
Non-discrimination is the Tathāgata’s seat—the practice that is neither practice nor non-practice.
Because there are no three practices yet there are three practices, it is called "practice. Because it is identical with the single ultimate truth, it is called the "place.

Furthermore, the two types of patience regarding arising and dharmas are precisely the two emptinesses of arising and dharmas. This differs from that of the Two Vehicles; for the Two Vehicles [possess] only the emptiness of arising...

The two emptinesses of the Two Vehicles break the self-clinging within the realm of conditioned existence (*dhātu*) and break the clinging to false causes and conditions and to causeless phenomena within that realm.
Now, the two emptinesses of the Perfect Teaching are explained in relation to the provisional names of the ten realms as being the Middle Way;

therefore, no further provisional names of the ten realms can be found, and this is called the emptiness of living beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Furthermore, they are explained in relation to the real dharmas of the ten realms as being the Middle Way.

Because no real dharmas can be found within the ten realms, it is called the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmasūnyatā*). If one were to further expand upon this, there would be four types of patience (*kṣānti*):

namely, the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*), the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*), the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*), and the patience of cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*) (the five patiences, six patiences, and forty-two patiences are abbreviated here).
Furthermore, when one does not engage in any activity regarding dharmas and contemplates all dharmas as they truly are, that is the patience of non-arising; nor is it...

Practicing non-discrimination is the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*). The first two are called patience toward beings (*sattva-kṣānti*), and the latter two are called patience toward phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*).
From beginning to end, one endures all phenomena through the principle of the two kinds of emptiness. Wearing the robe of the Tathāgata means abiding in the principle of the two kinds of emptiness;
sitting on the seat of the Tathāgata means having compassion for all sentient beings. These are the two kinds of emptiness and the four patiences.
Because the principle of practice is itself the locus, it is said that this is the "place of practice" for Bodhisattvas. Third, regarding the three inconceivable truths (*trīṇi satyāni*):
dwelling on the ground of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*) generally refers to the three truths; only when one has a ground upon which to rely can one truly exercise patience.

Being "gentle, compliant, and harmonious" means being well-compliant with the truth of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*), thereby being able to endure both within and beyond the realms of existence (*saṃsāra*).

Regarding "delusory views [of] loving cold, heat, and so forth": although one does not act with sudden violence and the mind is not startled, this is because one is at peace within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), enduring the conditions of the various faculties and responding appropriately to their capacities; thus, one does not act with sudden violence.

Because one physically endures both opposition and compliance, the mind is not startled. Regarding "having no practice toward phenomena," etc.: this refers to abiding in middle truth (*madhyama-satya*), being able to endure the two extremes.
It is said that there is "no place of practice" because one correctly abides in the Middle Way; it is said that one "contemplates the true aspect" yet does not even attain the middle reality.

It is said that one "neither practices nor discriminates. This refers to the stage of the Three Truths, which is called the "Abiding in Patience," and to the fifth dwelling, which is called the "Practice of Practice.
This practice is also threefold: the practice of cessation (*śamatha*), which is practicing while not practicing.

"Clad in the Tathāgata’s robe," the practice of contemplation is neither practicing nor not practicing; "seated upon the Tathāgata’s seat," the practice of compassion is practicing without practicing;
"entering the Tathāgata’s chamber"—this is the explanation of the Bodhisattva’s sphere of action (*caryā-viṣaya*) by means of three dharmas, clarifying the method for propagating the sūtra.
△ Second, the explanation of the proximate spheres (*upaniṣad*). Part one: Explaining the proximate by way of what is distant. (10)
First, one distances oneself from their power and influence (which is the condition for arrogance).
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s proximity and what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s non-proximity?
[It is that] a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not draw near kings, princes, ministers, or high officials.
The following explains the "near abodes" (*upasthāna*) by clarifying that the ten afflictions which cause disturbance are "distant," yet are discussed here as being "near.

This is also an attachment to the gate of precepts (*śīla-dvāra*) that assists meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*). Whereas the preceding section directly took the principle (*tattva*) as its object and dwelt on the ground of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), the present gate of precepts extensively sets forth the various conditions for humiliation;
one should practice distancing oneself from them. This is not like ordinary people who merely defend themselves against weapons and staves, nor is it the same as the [two] previous [approaches].

One abandons them by not observing them, but rather distances oneself from them through right wisdom; because this involves distancing oneself from the distant in order to approach the near, it is called the "place of intimacy.
△ Second, distancing oneself from false persons and dharmas (which are the conditions for false views).
One does not associate with various non-Buddhist practitioners, such as brahmins and Nirgranthas, nor with those who compose secular writings,
praise foreign scriptures, or engage in the Lokāyata and Prati-lokāyata doctrines.
This is the second remote category of persons who follow heterodox teachings. When people are defiled by heterodox doctrines, they become deluded regarding correct principles;

as their right contemplation has not yet been established, they must urgently strive to prevent and sever such views. Because they do not receive the internal teaching, they are called *bāhiraka* (outsiders) or *brahmacārin* (those of pure conduct);
this is also translated as "pure lineage. As for their kind, they claim that they were born from the mouth of Brahmā.
Those who dwell at home and serve Brahmā are called *brahmacārin* (Brahmins). Those who have left the home life and follow non-Buddhist paths are collectively termed *nirgrantha*;

"nirgrantha" here means "one who is free from bonds. Regarding the terms "wen" (文) and "bi" (筆): "wen" refers to genres such as songs and poetry, while "bi" refers to categories such as inscriptions and rhapsodies.
As for "praise" (*zanyong*), that which manifests virtue is called "praise," while that which expresses sentiment is called "verse" (*yong*). *Lokāyata* is translated here as "the evil [view]."
The treatise also states: "The 'contrary path' (*viloma*) refers to a discourse that opposes one's sovereign or father;
furthermore, *Lokāyata* is called a 'virtuous discourse' when it is the teacher refuting the disciple, and it is called a 'vile discourse' when it is the disciple refuting the teacher.
3. Remote, Fierce, and Dangerous Games (these are conditions for distraction).
Furthermore, one should not associate with various violent games such as boxing, wrestling, and the various performances of the *nara* and others.
This is the third [precept]: staying far from violent games. Boxing and wrestling are violent games; *nara* here means...
"Power" (*bala*) refers to wrestling and other displays of physical strength.

The commentary states that *Nārāyaṇa* refers to upper-body acrobatics, or painting one's body to create various transformative appearances, as well as activities such as climbing poles and performing acrobatic flips.
△ Fourth, the far-off Caṇḍālas (who are the conditions for evil karma).
Furthermore, he does not associate with outcastes (caṇḍāla), nor with those who keep pigs, sheep, chickens, or dogs, nor with hunters, fishermen, or those engaged in other evil occupations;
yet, should such persons ever come to him, he preaches the Dharma for them without any expectation of reward.
This is the fourth type of distant *caṇḍāla*. *Caṇḍāla* is translated here as "butcher" (*túzhě*) or "fierce" (*yánchì*);
it refers to one who adorns themselves with fiercely blazing evil karma. To associate with such a person causes others to lose their compassion;
they raise pigs, sheep, chickens, and dogs, and engage in hunting, trapping, and fishing—all of which involve the act of killing.
The mind is called "non-restraint"; when such a person comes, one should skillfully preach the Dharma for them to turn their intent toward killing, and one must not harbor any expectation of reward.
△ Fifth, distancing oneself from those of the Two Vehicles (this is the condition for the Lesser Nirvana).
Furthermore, they do not associate with, nor do they inquire after, śrāvaka bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās.
Whether in a cell, on a walking path, or in a lecture hall, they do not dwell together with them;
yet, if they should occasionally come, they preach the Dharma as appropriate, without seeking anything for themselves.

This is the fifth [point]: staying far away from those of the Two Vehicles. Because people of the Two Vehicles stagnate in emptiness and quiescence and are unable to give rise to the bodhicitta, one must remain distant from them.
△ Sixth: staying far away from the signs of desire and conceptualization.
Mañjuśrī, furthermore, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not take up the signs within a woman’s body that give rise to thoughts of desire when preaching the Dharma to her;
nor should he delight in seeing her. If he enters another's home, he should not converse with young girls, virgins, widows, or the like.
This is the sixth [meditation], the perception of the distance from desire (*dūra-kāma-saṃjñā*).

Because the perception of desire can destroy the bodhicitta, or because it may defile one’s physical appearance, gestures, speech, laughter, deportment, and every movement—whether turning, bending, or bowing—one must treat this with the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*).
A "virgin" (*kanyā*) refers to a girl living at home who has not yet been married.
A "widow" (guǎnǚ) is one who has no husband. △ Seventh, regarding those distant from "eunuchs" (wúzhìcāo zhī yuán):
furthermore, one should not draw close to or form intimate bonds with the five kinds of eunuchs.
This seventh [category] refers to those who are "distantly impotent" (*pārājika-śaṇḍha*). Because they corrupt and disrupt the resolve for enlightenment, there are five types of impotents:

the "born," the "violent," the "jealous," the "transformed," and the "half. "Born" means that from birth onward one has been without male organs. "Violent" means having one's virility removed by means of a blade.
"Jealous" means that only upon seeing another engaged in sexual intercourse does a mind of envy arise, and immediately thereafter sexual desire is ignited. "Transformed" means...
In this life, they transform into "half-men," meaning those who are male for half the month and non-male for the other half.
△ Eighth, avoiding harm:
Not only when entering the homes of others, but even when one must enter alone due to some necessity, one should simply maintain single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha.
This is the eighth [point]: being far removed from harm and peril, for it is improper to enter places where harm and peril abound. △ Ninth:
being far removed from matters of censure and suspicion (which serve as conditions that give rise to others' attachment).

If one preaches the Dharma to women, one should not show one's teeth when smiling nor reveal one’s chest; even for the sake of the Dharma, one should not become overly intimate, let alone for other matters.
This is the ninth point for avoiding censure and suspicion.
To show one's teeth when smiling or to reveal one’s chest increases the unwholesome thoughts of others.
When preaching the Dharma for women, one should avoid causing scandal or suspicion; it is not even appropriate to be intimate with them, much less engage in other matters.
△ Ten: Avoiding the Pleasure of Keeping [Women] (the condition that gives rise to self-love).
One does not delight in keeping young disciples, śrāmaṇeras, or children, nor does one delight in having them share the same teacher.

This is the tenth [precept] on distancing oneself from those one keeps as dependents. Generally, keeping young children hinders the cultivation of the primary practice; therefore, they must be distanced.
From the first distancing from the powerful and influential to this distancing from those kept as dependents, these ten types of disturbances are divided into two extremes.
Nine are birth and death, and one is nirvana; to distance oneself from both is merely another name for quiescence (*śānti*).
These ten dharmas are consistent across all teachings, yet they differ slightly from those of the Two Vehicles.
This is because the present practitioner of the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*) propagates the uniquely wondrous sutras of the Mahayana; therefore, one must distance oneself from [the Lesser Vehicle].
[This refers to] those who hear [the teachings] and follow the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, which is the Lesser Vehicle. △ Second, the immediate proximity regarding the proximate place:
"Constantly delighting in sitting meditation, dwelling in a secluded place to cultivate and restrain the mind—Mañjuśrī, this is called the first proximate place."

Now, cultivating the gathering of the mind is discussed in terms of what is proximate; this is also an auxiliary to meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*) attached to the gate of concentration (*samādhi*).

Previously, distancing oneself from the ten kinds of disturbances was the cultivation of ethical discipline (*śīla*); now, constantly delighting in sitting meditation is the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi*).
In the subsequent text, contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena is the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*). Within the present cultivation of concentration, there are three intentions.
This refers to concentration of mind, concentration of place, and concentration of gateway. "Mind" refers to the mind capable of aspiration;

aspiring to break through obstacles and manifest the principle is precisely the cultivation and gathering of the mind. "Place" refers to dwelling in a quiet location among the five conditions; this is being in a secluded place now.
"Gateway" refers to the essential gateways for cultivating concentration; it is, among the five matters, the regulation of the mind so that it is neither sunken nor agitated.
Fú was one who, even now, constantly delights in sitting in meditation. △ Third, the section on "Neither Far Nor Near," Part One: First, a general indication of the object and the wisdom.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas as empty.
This contemplation that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty is neither distant nor near; yet, in speaking of it as "near," it serves as an auxiliary to contemplation by way of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The initial character "contemplation" (*guan*) indicates the wisdom—the contemplative wisdom of the Middle Way that is capable of observing.

The intermediate three characters "all phenomena" indicate the object—the realm of the ten dharma-realms that is the object of observation. The final character "empty" [indicates the nature of the object].
However, when one forms the realization that both the wisdom which is the subject of observation and the object observed by that wisdom are unattainable, then both object and wisdom are empty.
△ Second, the specific explanation of object and wisdom.
It is according to reality, non-erroneous, immovable, non-retrogressive, and non-reversing; like space, it is of a nature of non-existence;
all paths of language are cut off; it is unarisen, unproduced, and unoriginated; it is nameless and signless;
it is truly non-existent, immeasurable, boundless, unobstructed, and unimpeded.
The three characters "yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa" (the reality-as-it-is) provide a distinct explanation of the object. Emptiness and the provisional side correspond to the Middle Way;

they are neither identical nor different, and are not merely provisional names for the seven stages of expedient means. Because the real is taken as the characteristic, it is called "yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa.

The various phrases such as "not inverted" provide a distinct explanation of the contemplation. Regarding "not inverted," ordinary beings [perceive] the two aspects of the environment and its inhabitants...
The nature of retribution is fundamentally impermanent, yet ordinary beings perversely cling to it as permanent; it is fundamentally suffering, yet they perversely cling to it as pleasure;
it is fundamentally without self, yet they perversely cling to it as a self; it is fundamentally impure, yet they perversely cling to it as pure. These are the four inversions of ordinary beings.
The followers of the Two Vehicles, conversely, perversely cling to the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity as being suffering, impermanence, non-self, and impurity.
These two vehicles possess four inversions; because Bodhisattvas lack these eight inversions, they are said to be "non-inverted.

"Immovable" means they are not moved by the two types of birth and death: the *pariccheda* (segmented) and the *pariṇāma* (transformative). "Non-retrogressive" means they accord with the principle of quiescent extinction;
with each thought-moment extinguished, they enter the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience). "Non-revolving" means they do not act like ordinary beings.
Now, transmigrating through birth and death is not like the Two Vehicles' transformation from the ordinary to the holy.

That which is "like space" means that space has only a name, and this name cannot be found when sought; likewise, the wisdom of the Middle Way contemplation also has only a name and cannot be found when sought.
"The nature of non-existence" means realizing that all phenomena lack self, other, or both.
To be free from the attachment to the four natures is the characteristic of the arising of emptiness (*utpatti-śūnyatā*).
That all paths of linguistic expression are cut off is the characteristic of the emptiness of the cessation of speech and thought (*prapañca-śūnyatā*).

It is "unborn" because both the delusions to be negated and the wisdom that negates them are entirely in accord with reality; it is "unemerging" because it is the very essence of what the Tathāgata has remedied.

For this very reason, there is nothing that can emerge, nor anything that arises, because one has entered into principle (*li*). Thus, the skillful means (*upāya*) and the teachings on principle are all quiescent.
This principle of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) cannot be named, and therefore its nature is empty; it cannot be characterized by marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and therefore its marks are empty.
Hence, it is said to be "nameless" and "markless. This reiterates the previous statement regarding "non-existence" and so forth. There is nothing.
The owner deeply sighed, [reflecting that] the essence of the wisdom of the Middle Way contemplation possesses no existence of the two extremes.
It is "immeasurable" because it is not a numerical dharma among the aggregates, elements, or sense bases; it is "boundless" because it is not a limited dharma like those that are partial or small;
it is "unobstructed" because it universally enters all dharmas; and it is "unimpeded" because nothing can hinder or stop it—even though...
Furthermore, these many phrases can only mean that one contemplates the signless (*animitta*) and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) as being in accord with the object;
they also merely refer to all phenomena by the name "all-empty" (*sarva-śūnya*). △ Third, the conclusion establishing the object and wisdom.
Because that which exists arises from causes and conditions and from inversion, one should always joyfully contemplate such characteristics of phenomena;
this is called the second station of intimacy for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

The preceding section clarified that the wisdom of contemplating the Middle Way is neither understanding nor delusion, transcending the characteristics of the two extremes. Now it is clarified that [wisdom] illuminates both extremes simultaneously:
from the causes and conditions of delusion, birth and death arise; from the causes and conditions of understanding, nirvana arises.
Furthermore, existence arises from causes and conditions, while within nirvana, that which arises from inversion gives rise to birth and death. This is what constitutes simultaneous illumination.
This clarifies that those who constantly delight in contemplating such dharmas refer to the dharmas of the three truths and so forth.
Furthermore, the phrase "arising from inversion due to conditions" concludes the inconceivable realm of the three truths;
thus, "the teaching" refers to the inconceivable teaching, and "those who constantly delight in contemplating" concludes the inconceivable three contemplations. △ Second, the verse in praise.
First, the initial verse establishes the chapter title.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If there is a bodhisattva who, in the evil age to come, desires to preach this sutra with a mind free from fear."

The preceding verse states that one who wishes to expound this sutra should abide in four dharmas; because the mind abides in the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*) and is not startled or terrified, it is said to possess a "mind free from fear.
△ Second, the verse on the practice of cultivation has two parts; first, the verse on the distance and proximity of the object.
One should enter places of practice and places of association, while always remaining far removed from kings, princes, ministers, and high officials;

from those who engage in violent games, as well as from *caṇḍālas* and non-Buddhist brahmins; and one should not associate with those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) or those who are greedily attached to the study of the Tripitaka of the Lesser Vehicle.

From "One should naturally enter the sphere of practice" below, there are fourteen verses; above, the ten afflictive matters were discussed in terms of the distant, whereas here they are discussed in terms of the proximate.
These include:
bhikṣus who break the precepts, those with the name of an arhat, bhikṣuṇīs who delight in frivolous laughter, and those who are deeply attached to the five desires.
One must not associate with any upāsikās who seek manifest parinirvāṇa;
those called "arhats" by name are merely nominally so and have not attained it through actual realization.
Those who seek manifest parinirvāṇa are close to the Hīnayāna and are not vessels for the Great Dharma; therefore, one who propagates the Mahāyāna sūtras must not associate with them.
They are near [to liberation].
