If such persons come to the bodhisattva with a sincere heart desiring to hear the Buddha-way, the bodhisattva,
with a mind free from fear and without destroying their aspirations, shall preach the Dharma for them— even for widows, virgins, and those who are neuter.
Do not associate with them or treat them as close friends.

To have no expectations is as follows: the Venerable Zuoxi never spoke a single word of Dharma for the sake of profit, nor did he ever accept so much as a hair’s breadth of wealth on account of the Dharma.
Only by maintaining such a mindset can one be said to be without expectation.
Furthermore, do not associate with butchers, executioners, hunters, fishermen, those who kill for profit, those who sell meat for their livelihood, or those who traffic in women;
do not associate with such people at all.
To slaughter is to butcher; to carve meat is called *tu-kuai*, which refers to finely mincing flesh. To peddle means to buy at a low price and sell at a high price;
to hawker means to advertise oneself for sale. Since these activities are all not pure conduct, one ought to distance oneself from them.
One must not associate with fierce wrestlers, various performers, or courtesans;

one must not preach the Dharma to women in private or secluded places. When preaching the Dharma, one must not engage in joking or laughter. When entering a village to beg for food, one should be accompanied by another bhikṣu;

if no other bhikṣu is present, one should single-mindedly recollect the Buddha. These two—walking and dwelling—are called the "range of conduct" and the "range of proximity. By means of these two ranges, [one attains the goal].

One who is able to preach with ease and enters a village for alms, as stated in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*: "There was once a sheep that went to a dung heap, ate its fill, and returned to the flock, conceitedly thinking, 'I have obtained excellent food.
Monks are also like this; having received the four types of offerings, they become arrogant."
Attached to perceptions and ignorant of the way out, he treats the other bhikṣus with arrogance and contempt, thinking, "I have attained what they have not attained.
This is the sheep-like bhikṣu who goes for alms. A lion king, upon encountering a large beast, devours it without savoring it or becoming attached;
upon encountering a small beast, it devours it without disdain or disparagement. The bhikṣu is also like this when he receives [alms].

Having made offerings with these four things, one should not give rise to thoughts of attachment, knowing for oneself that there is liberation from the cycle of existence and that the mind is neither increasing nor decreasing;
this is the alms-round of the Lion King Bhikṣu. Furthermore, before a bhikṣu has obtained food while on his alms-round, he should reflect:
"For the sake of cultivating the Path, I must mend the wound of hunger by going on alms-round. Once he has obtained food, it is for the purpose of repaying the kindness of those who have given.
He maintains mindfulness of the Way without ceasing. △ Second, the verse on what is neither distant nor near:
Furthermore, he does not practice the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas, nor the conditioned or unconditioned, nor the real or unreal dharmas;
nor does he discriminate between male and female, nor grasp at any dharmas, nor know or see them—this is called the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice.

Regarding the superior, middling, and inferior teachings: in terms of the classification of doctrines (*jiao*), the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) is superior, the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*) is middling, and the Treasury Teaching (*zangjiao*) is inferior.

In terms of persons, this may refer to those of the Three Vehicles or the Bodhisattvas of the three teachings; however, as this section concerns the "abolition of the provisional" (*feiquan*), it speaks of "not practicing" and so forth.
As for "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*): because they are worldly dharmas, they are unreal; [the opposite] is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Regarding the phrase "Because this is a supramundane dharma, it is in reality also non-discriminative," the *Avalokiteśvara-ṭīkā* uses male and female as symbols for wisdom (*prajñā*) and concentration (*samādhi*), respectively—wisdom being symbolized by male and concentration by female.

It specifically cites these two lines to clarify that the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of concentration and wisdom is fundamentally beyond words and cannot be discriminated; hence, it immediately follows with the statement, "one does not apprehend any dharmas."
All phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty and non-existent; they neither abide eternally nor undergo arising and ceasing. This is called the sphere of intimacy for the wise.
To conceptually discriminate all phenomena through inversion—regarding them as existent or non-existent, real or unreal, or produced or unproduced—is [the domain of the ignorant].
Dwelling in a secluded place, one cultivates and collects the mind, abiding immovably like Mount Sumeru;
observing that all phenomena are non-existent, like empty space, lacking solidity, neither arising nor emerging, neither moving nor receding,
eternally abiding in a single mark— this is called "near-dwelling."
This verse summarizes the preceding passages concerning his constant fondness for sitting in meditation and contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena, as can be seen in the text.
△ Third, the verse on the accomplishment of practice has three parts;
first, the heading: "If there be a bhikṣu who, after my parinirvāṇa, enters this sphere of practice and this sphere of intimacy when preaching this sutra..."
"There is no timidity.
This indicates that when practice is perfected, the external demeanor does not fail; when principle is perfected, the internal mind has no obstructions.
Therefore, it is said that at the time of preaching the sutra, there is no timidity. △ Second, the explanation.
At times, a bodhisattva enters a quiet chamber and, with right mindfulness, contemplates the Dharma according to its meaning; rising from meditative concentration,
he teaches and expounds this sutra for kings, princes, ministers, subjects, brahmins, and others,
his mind remaining peaceful and free from any timidity.

This explains the cause of peace and happiness: by entering a quiet chamber to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one ceases transgressions and attains the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
Outwardly, because one does not harm others and practices wisdom through correct mindfulness, one is free from all grasping and attains the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Inwardly, being free from inversion, the mind is not timid; this lack of timidity is called "peace."
This is the joy. △ Third, the conclusion:
"Mañjuśrī, this is called the Bodhisattva abiding in the first dharma, who is able to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in future ages.
This verse summarizes the prose section; "the first dharma" refers specifically to the practice of physical ease (*kāya-sukha-pratipatti*). △ Second, the peace of speech.
Regarding the first part, the practice of joy, there are two sections: first, the prose exposition; second, the initial presentation of the chapter.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the period of the Final Dharma, those who wish to preach this sutra should abide in the Practice of Peaceful Joy.
△ Second, the two practices of the Dharma; first, the practice of tranquility (śamatha), in four parts. First, not speaking of faults:
when proclaiming [the Dharma] orally or reading the scriptures, one does not delight in speaking of the faults of persons or of the scriptures.
This commentary explains that within the practice of oral tranquility (*śamatha*), there are both the practices of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Regarding the practice of tranquility, one should initially refrain from speaking of the faults of either the listener or the scripture being heard.

This is because the provisional teachings (*upāya*) of the seven stages of skillful means prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* were spoken by the Buddha according to the capacities of others and in accordance with their intentions; thus, they are termed "indefinitive" (*neyārtha*). If...
If one listens to and accepts the teaching that there may be the fault of partiality toward the Lesser Vehicle, what fault is there? This is a teaching given according to the capacities of beings;
how could it have any fault? To say that the Dharma has a fault would be to disturb those who listen and receive it;
it is not the characteristic of practicing with peace and happiness of mouth and mind. △ Second, not being arrogant or contemptuous.
Furthermore, one must not treat other Dharma masters with contempt.

This means that those who propagate the sutra must not rely on the perfection of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* they propagate to despise the Dharma masters of the partial, provisional, and Hinayana teachings;
for even when the Buddha was in the world, he still employed various skillful means and other profound [teachings].
The Dharma-activity assists the true path of perfect reality; how could later students, following the teachings, willfully contravene it?
They must accord with the Buddha’s intent and protect the capacities of sentient beings. △ Third, neither praising nor disparaging.
One does not speak of the good or evil, the long or the short of others; nor does one mention by name the faults or evils of even a śrāvaka, nor does one mention by name to praise their excellence.
From the outset, one does not speak of all people in general, but specifically mentions the śrāvaka; this is what is meant by "not speaking of the long or the short of others."

Because people dislike hearing of their own faults, they do not speak of others' shortcomings; because those who love praise will surely be skilled at disparagement, they do not extol others' virtues.

Thus, the *Dīrgha-āgama* (or *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*) states: "During the first, middle, and last watches of the night, diminish sleep and apply yourself with diligence to sitting in meditation, reciting the sūtras, and cultivating the Way.
Turn your back on birth-and-death and head toward the path of Nirvāṇa. Do not speak of others' shortcomings, nor speak of yourself."
Long. △ Fourth, freedom from resentment and aversion.
Furthermore, one does not give rise to a mind of resentment or aversion.

"Resentment" (yuan) refers to the sound of enmity; when one's own interests are harmed, it is called resentment, and when it opposes one's feelings, it is called aversion (xian). If one considers the person from whom one has received [benefits], and...
If the Dharma one has received hinders my path, that is a mind of resentment; if I consider another’s person or Dharma to be inferior, that is a mind of aversion.
Once the mental faculty is stirred, verbal expression immediately follows. Therefore, by blocking the source of such speech, resentment and aversion do not arise.
If even those who practice for peace and happiness abandon joy that accords with their own desires, how much more so should one refrain from constructing resentment?
Regret. △ Second, the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Because he has skillfully cultivated such a mind of peace and bliss, all who hear him do not oppose his intent;
when they pose difficult questions, he does not answer with the teachings of the *Hīnayāna*, but explains them solely through the *Mahāyāna*, causing them to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Since the Master has already contemplated that all phenomena are empty and his mind dwells in the principle of ultimate emptiness, he is free from grasping and attachment;

he certainly does not hold the Great Vehicle in high regard while disparaging the Small Vehicle. Rather, he accords with the dispositions of sentient beings and does not contradict the characteristics of the Mahāyāna teachings.
Thus, when faced with difficult questions, he does not speak of the Small Vehicle but answers solely by means of the Mahāyāna. There are those who ask: why is this so? [The answer follows: Because...

Second, regarding the two intentions: if one perceives that a person lacks the great capacity (*mahā-ākṣepa*) and teaches them the Small Vehicle merely to provide the limited benefit of expedient means, there is no fault;
however, if one does not perceive the lack of great capacity yet teaches the Small Vehicle, it obstructs their connection to the Great Vehicle.
Therefore, by teaching only the Great Vehicle, one avoids the fault of these two [situations]. △ Second, the verse summary, in three parts: first, the verse summarizing the headings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Bodhisattva always delights in preaching the Dharma with peace and stability. Upon a pure ground, he provides seats and couches;
he anoints his body with oil and bathes away all dust and impurities, putting on fresh, clean robes so that both his inner and outer selves are purified."
These two verses constitute the initial presentation of the chapter on the "Practice of Peaceful Abiding" (*anuvartana-sukha-vihāra*). Above, it was stated generally that one "should abide";
now, within these verses, the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of this practice are set forth. There are three such characteristics:

first, the first half-verse intends to enable present beings to attain the path and its fruit of peace and security, which is the meaning of "entering the Tathāgata’s chamber. Second, the latter half-verse refers to "sitting upon the Tathāgata’s [throne]."

The meaning of "sitting" follows; the single line immediately following refers to the meaning of donning the Tathāgata’s robe. Guiding one's verbal karma through these three dharmas is called the "Practice of Peaceful Dwelling.
△ Second, the verses on the methods of practice, in two parts. First, the verses on the practice of cessation, in four parts. First, the verse on not being disrespectful.
Seated securely upon the Dharma-seat, he explains according to the questions asked.
Now, this half-verse states that one must not be disrespectful; for if one is disrespectful, he will not explain according to the questions asked.
△ Second, not speaking of long or short [lives].

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, as well as kings, princes, ministers, officials, or commoners, he shall explain the subtle and profound meanings to them with a serene countenance;
and should they pose difficult questions, he shall answer them in accordance with the meaning.
△ Third, not speaking of others' faults.
Through causes, conditions, parables, and detailed expositions, by these skillful means, he causes all to resolve their minds toward enlightenment,
gradually increasing their merit until they enter the Buddha-way.
If one speaks of another's faults, it gives rise to poisonous thoughts in that person;

by not speaking of their faults now, one causes them to resolve their mind on entering the Buddha-way, for the Buddha-way arises from joy. △ Fourth, the verse on being free from resentment and dislike.
Having eliminated slothful intent and thoughts of indolence, and being free from all sorrow and affliction, one preaches the Dharma with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
When a mind of resentment or aversion arises, there is laziness, sorrow, and affliction; now, by preaching the Dharma with a mind of loving-kindness, one is free from resentment.

This is because one who is without resentment is diligent and free from sorrow. While the preceding prose section was explained in terms of the excellence of *śamatha* (calming), the verses herein are all explained in terms of... [the excellence of *vipaśyanā*].
This is the practice of goodness. △ Second, the verse on contemplative practice:
Day and night he constantly proclaims the unsurpassed Way of the Buddha, using various causes, conditions, and immeasurable parables to reveal it to sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice;
yet regarding clothing, bedding, food, drink, medicine, and other necessities, he harbors no expectations therein.

If one simply focuses the mind on the causes and conditions for preaching the Dharma, aspiring to attain the Buddha-way and causing all beings to do likewise, this constitutes a great benefit, peace, and bliss as an offering.
While the preceding prose states, "Answer solely by means of the Mahāyāna," the present verse says, "Preach the Unsurpassed Way. As stated above...

To cause [beings] to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), the present verse says: "May they achieve the Buddha-way and cause the multitudes to do likewise. This means causing others also to achieve the Buddha-way.
△ Third, the verse on the accomplishment of practice has four parts; first, the verse marking the accomplishment of practice.

"After my parinirvāṇa, if there should be a bhikṣu who is able to expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this single line establishes the 'Peaceful Practice of Speech. II. Freedom from Obstacles and Difficulties."

The mind is free from envy, anger, and all afflictive hindrances; it is likewise free from sorrow and those who revile, and it is without fear of being struck with weapons or staves, nor of being expelled, because it abides in patience.
These two lines clarify that when there are no faults within, external difficulties do not arise; it is like flies not coming to a place where there is no foul odor.
△ Third, the accomplishment of virtuous conduct:
A wise person who thus skillfully cultivates the mind can abide in peace and happiness, as I have explained above.
△ Fourth, the evaluation of merit:
The merit of such a person cannot be fully exhausted even by means of calculation, analogy, or parable throughout ten million billion *kalpas*.
△ Third, the practice of mental peace and happiness, in two parts: First, the prose section; third, first, the presentation of the chapter.
Furthermore, regarding those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas Mañjuśrī who, in the future final age when the Dharma is about to perish, shall receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra.
△ Second, the four practices of the Dharma; first, the four practices of cessation; first, freedom from envy and flattery.
One should not harbor a mind of jealousy, flattery, or deception.

Now, because those of the Two Vehicles seek to transcend birth and death, they first eliminate greed and desire; because Bodhisattvas seek to transform others, they first eliminate anger, views, and jealousy.
Jealousy is a defilement of anger, and flattery is a defilement of views. Jealousy violates the mind of loving-kindness and compassion; it is not [the path].
The method of converting others through flattery and deception deviates from the path of wisdom and is not the method for one's own practice.
If wisdom is obstructed, how can one seek the Buddha-way above? If compassion is hindered, how can one transform sentient beings below?
Therefore, a Bodhisattva who wishes to cultivate the Practice of Mental Peace and Bliss must most certainly abandon these [methods]. △ Second, [the section on] Not...
Do not revile others lightly.
Furthermore, do not revile those who study the Buddha-way by seeking out their faults.
Regarding the phrase "do not revile others lightly," this precept means that a Bodhisattva should not rely upon their own perfect practice [to look down on others].

One should not reprimand practitioners of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) who study the Buddha-way by relying on the superiority of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) to seek out the shortcomings of their provisional teaching.
One should discern the capacity [of the practitioner] before reprimanding; do not revile those who lack such understanding.

This is because if one does reprimand or revile them, there is the possibility that it will cause them to lose their roots of goodness; hence the instruction to "also not [reprimand]," and so forth. △ Third, not causing disturbance.

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who seek the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the bodhisattva path, one must not disturb them or cause them doubt and regret by saying to them:
"You are very far from the Way; you will never be able to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Why is this? Because you are negligent."

Because such people are indolent regarding the Path, and because the four assemblies of bhikṣus and others all possess the capacities for the three vehicles, it is said that they "seek the śrāvaka [vehicle]," and so forth.

This precept should not be used to reprimand those of the Three Vehicles in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) by means of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao); for their fundamental capacity is not that of the Great Vehicle, yet one would be forcibly reprimanding them with the Perfect Teaching.

To act contrary to one's mind results in affliction; having been rebuked by the Shared [Teaching], yet not yet understanding the Perfect [Teaching], one suffers both prior regret and subsequent remorse, losing both the Small and the Great.
Thus, the path to Buddhahood becomes circuitous and exceedingly remote. This affliction pertains specifically to practitioners of the Separate Teaching.

Although the present text speaks of rebuking the Shared Teaching, this is because within the Shared Teaching there are also those of the Separate capacity. If one were to hastily seek realization, one would sink...
To remain stagnant in emptiness and silence, unable to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), is a vexation that applies to practitioners of the Shared Teaching;

it is called indolence because one loathes birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and is lazy in guiding and transforming others. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* clarifies that those of the Lesser Vehicle are indolent.
△ Fourth, non-contention.
Furthermore, one should not engage in frivolous speculation regarding all phenomena nor contend with others.
△ Second, the four aspects of contemplative practice: First, giving rise to great compassion to counteract envy and flattery.
One should conceive the thought of great compassion toward all sentient beings.
The following four sections clarify the practice of contemplative cultivation (*vipaśyanā*); that is, initiating virtuous conduct in response to the aforementioned four types of evil.
△ Second, giving rise to the mind of a compassionate father when encountering contempt and abuse.
One should conceive of all Tathāgatas as one's compassionate fathers.
Anyone who seeks the Buddha-way is a student; they should be revered and studied as Buddhas and must not be treated with contempt or reviled.
△ Third, one should conceive of them as Great Teachers and avoid causing them distress or disturbance.
One should conceive of all bodhisattvas as great teachers and should always, with a profound mind, pay respect and prostrate to the great bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
According to principle, those of the three vehicles all possess the virtue of transforming and instructing others; they are all [to be regarded as] sentient beings.
One should regard such teachers as one's own teacher and must not speak of their shortcomings. △ Fourth, preaching the Dharma with equanimity and avoiding contentious debate:
one preaches the Dharma with equality toward all sentient beings in accordance with the Dharma, neither too much nor too little, even unto the profound.
One who loves the Dharma also does not speak excessively.
Because the fundamental nature of the Dharma is equality that shatters the disputes of biased attachments, it is said that one accords with the Dharma by speaking neither too much nor too little;
this measures the sharpness or dullness of the recipient's faculties. △ Third, the conclusion in two parts: first, by means of *śamatha* (calm abiding).
Evil cannot affect them. Mañjuśrī,

when this Dharma is being taught, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished this third practice of peace and happiness will be unable to be disturbed or troubled during the final age at the end of time when the Dharma is about to perish.
△ Second, because of the excellence of their contemplative practice, superior persons gather together.
They obtain excellent fellow students with whom they may jointly read and recite this sutra; they also draw a great assembly to listen and receive it.

Having heard it, they are able to retain it; having retained it, they are able to recite it; having recited it, they are able to explain it; and having explained it, they are able to write it down or cause others to write it, and thereby make offerings to the sutra.
Roll: Reverence, Respect, and Praise.
Because of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), superior persons gather, and one obtains good companions for study. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts:
first, the summary of the methods of practice; second, the summary of the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*). Fourth, the summary of freedom from envy and flattery.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to preach this sutra, one should abandon jealousy, anger, pride, flattery, deceit, and a false mind; one should constantly cultivate a straightforward and upright conduct."
△ Second, two verses on not disparaging or reviling others;
not looking down upon people.
△ Third, three verses on not engaging in contention or rivalry.
Nor does one engage in frivolous discourse regarding the Dharma.
△ Fourth, the verse on non-disturbance:
not causing others to doubt or regret by saying, "You shall not attain Buddhahood."
△ Second, the four verses on contemplative practice. The first verse concerns the arousal of great compassion toward all beings:
"This son of the Buddha, when teaching the Dharma, is always gentle and patient; with compassion for all, he never gives rise to a mind of indolence."
△ Second, the verse on conceiving the thought of the Great Teacher regarding Bodhisattvas:
"The great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions practice the path out of compassion for sentient beings; one should give rise to a mind of reverence, thinking: 'These are my Great Teachers.'"
△ Three verses on conceiving of the Tathāgata as a compassionate father and generating the thought of the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, as one’s supreme father.
△ Four verses on preaching the Dharma with equanimity to quash disputes.
Having destroyed the mind of pride, he preaches the Dharma without obstruction.
△ Third, the verse on the perfection of practice:
"The wise one who thus protects this Dharma should dwell in the single-minded practice of peace and bliss, and will be honored by immeasurable multitudes."
△ Four: The Practice of Peaceful Conduct Based on Vows. Part One: The Long Exposition. Part Two: Clarifying the Method of Practice. Part Three: Indicating the Chapter.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in the future final age when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be those who uphold...
Regarding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*:
it is because one practices with body, speech, and mind in conjunction with compassion and kindness, making a vow for peaceful and happy conduct (*sukha-vihāra*), and vowing to circulate this sutra.
△ Second, the practice of the Dharma has two parts: first, the designation of the object of the vow; second, the compassionate object of the vow.
One gives rise to great compassion toward both householders and those who have left the home life.
This includes all who have previously developed the mind of skillful means but have not yet transcended the triple world; these are termed "householders.

Those who have exhausted the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃjñā-kleśa*) and have transcended the triple world are termed "those who have left the home life. This encompasses the two vehicles (*yāna*) of the two teachings and the bodhisattvas of the three teachings.
Since these individuals all possess ignorance and sufferings that can be uprooted, they should also be objects of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

However, because they have all previously given rise to partial or limited minds (*hīnayāna*) corresponding to vows of benevolence (*maitrī*), one must provide them with the bliss of the perfect path and perfect fruit;
therefore, it is said that one gives rise to a mind of great benevolence (*mahāmaitrī*), for benevolence is able to bestow bliss. △ Second, Compassion (*karuṇā*).
The object of the vow:
to give rise to great compassion toward those who are not bodhisattvas.
Here, "those who are not bodhisattvas" refers generally to those who have not yet generated the mind of skillful means; this category includes all beings within the three realms.

Since these individuals have never once given rise to the provisional mind of the Hīnayāna, much less been able to give rise to the true mind of the Mahāyāna, it is known that they are all members of the class who transmigrate within the realms of saṃsāra;
they too must be granted happiness. However, as their transmigration is boundless, it accords precisely with the vow of compassion that one should uproot the causes of their suffering.
Because it is the fruit of suffering, one speaks of giving rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), for through compassion one is able to uproot suffering.
△ Second, the arising of vows has two parts: first, the cause for giving rise to the vow of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
One should reflect thus: "Such a person has suffered a great loss regarding the Tathāgata’s skillful means and his teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
This is the reason for giving rise to compassion. "Such a person" refers to those mentioned above who previously gave rise to the mind of skillful means;
because they delight in the Lesser Vehicle, they cling to the Buddha’s skillful means as being ultimate reality and do not realize the Perfect Path; therefore, it is said that their loss is "great."
To lose [the Dharma] is the reason for losing this vow of great compassion. △ Second, the reason for giving rise to the vow of compassion:
not hearing, not knowing, not perceiving, not inquiring, not believing, and not understanding.

Those who have not yet given rise to the mind of either the partial or the perfect on their fingers—because they have not given rise to such a mind, they do not hear the two paths of the partial and the perfect.

Not hearing the path of the partial constitutes a lack of *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing); not knowing the path of the partial constitutes a lack of *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from reflection);

and not awakening to the path of the partial constitutes a lack of *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from cultivation). Furthermore, they lack the three perfect wisdoms. Why? Because they do not inquire.
Because they do not hear the Perfect Way, they do not believe in the Perfect Way; because they do not hear the Perfect Way, they do not contemplate or understand the Perfect Way;
because they do not hear the Perfect Way, they do not cultivate the three wisdoms of the partial and the perfect. Since both the provisional and the real are absent for them, they are truly pitiable;

this is the reason for giving rise to compassion. Question: How can one know that the first three are provisional and the latter three are real? Answer: According to the text of the "Correct Vow," it is simply...

By extinguishing the sorrows and afflictions of the present life, they eliminate the retribution of painful sensations; this is the mind that transforms future retribution into present retribution. There is none [who does not attain this].

The fact that the complexion during illness is bright and white is the manifestation of the color of the present retribution. △ Second, the transformation of karmic obstacles results in the non-arising of the retribution of future births;

This is the transformation of evil karma. Because the causes of evil karma ought to result in evil fruits, by the power of upholding this sutra, one transforms the evil causes to obtain good fruits;

For these three reasons, the Tathāgata halted [the proclamation]. [However, he] summoned those from the lower regions to come.
There are also three meanings: first, that as my disciple, you should propagate my Dharma;

second, that because your conditions are profound and vast, you can benefit this land universally and also benefit other lands afar; third, that you have attained the opening of the near and the manifestation of the distant.
△ Third, the emergence from below. Part One: The Sūtra Master’s Description of the Signs. Section Five: The Initial Emergence.

At the time when the Buddha spoke these words, the earth throughout the three-thousandfold world system of the Sahā universe quaked and split open, and from within it, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of *bodhisattva-mahāsattvas* simultaneously surged forth.

Regarding "the earth cracks": the earth had previously covered its own manifestations, as when a footprint conceals its origin; now, by opening the traces to reveal the fundamental, it cracks the earth to symbolize this.
△ Second, the physical marks: the bodies of these bodhisattvas are all golden in color, possessing the thirty-two marks and immeasurable radiance.
△ Third, the dwelling place.
Initially, they all resided beneath this Sahā world, within the void of this realm.

As for the dwelling place, it is the Constant, Quiescent Light (*nitya-śānta-prabhā*). "Constant" refers to the virtue of permanence; "quiescent" refers to the virtue of bliss; and "light" refers to the virtues of purity and self.
Regarding these two virtues, this secret treasury of the four virtues is their dwelling place.
Because they abide by means of the dharma of non-abiding within the secret treasury, it is called "the lower direction.
This "lower" does not belong to this space, nor does it belong to that; being neither that nor this, it is precisely the Middle Way. Furthermore,
They emerged neither from above nor from below, but dwelling in mid-air, neither above nor below—this too is the Middle Way.
△ Fourth, hearing the command:
When these bodhisattvas heard the sound spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha, it issued forth from below.
Regarding the reasons for their coming: they come because they have heard the mandate; they come to propagate the Dharma (for the world); they come to shatter attachments (as an antidote);
and they come to reveal the fundamental nature (the ultimate truth). All of these are as explained above. △ Fifth, the retinue.
Each and every bodhisattva was a leader at the head of a great assembly, each leading a retinue as vast as sixty thousand Ganges-sands;
how much more so those leading retinues of fifty thousand, forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand Ganges-sands?
How much more so those leading even down to a single Ganges-sand, half a Ganges-sand, a quarter, or even ten million Ganges-sands?
How much less those who have a retinue of a hundred million nayutas; how much less those with a retinue of ten million;
how much less those with a retinue of one million, a hundred thousand, or even ten thousand; how much less those with a retinue of one thousand, one hundred, or even ten;
how much less those who lead only four, five, four, three, two, or one disciple; and how much less those who dwell alone, delighting in solitude?
Their practices are beyond measure and boundless, such that they cannot be known through calculation or analogy.

As for the retinues they lead, if one were to judge by human standards, leading sixty thousand or fifty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [as many as the sands of the Ganges] would be considered many, while leading three, two, or one would be considered few;
those who travel alone are solitary individuals. If one follows the literal text to investigate this:
Sixty thousand and fifty thousand are few; those who are alone are many. Therefore, the verse below states: "Those who dwell alone and solitary are even more numerous than that.
If one relies on the Dharma-gate, each and every one is a guide capable of leading the multitude to the place of treasure.
One should know that "one" does not mean only sixty thousand, nor does "many" mean only fifty thousand.
First is the single path of purity; second is concentration and wisdom; third is precepts, concentration, and wisdom; fourth is the Four Noble Truths;
fifth is the five eyes; sixth is the six perfections. Each perfection encompasses the ten dharma-realms, and as each realm mutually encompasses the others, they form one hundred dharma-realms.
Within each realm, the ten suchnesses are present, forming one thousand suchnesses. And within each suchness, the ten wholesome acts are present, resulting in ten thousand wholesome acts.
Once the ten thousand and six perfections are complete, these constitute sixty thousand Dharma-gates;
many are not considered many, and one is not considered few—it is neither many nor few, yet it is both many and few. △ Second, the Great Assembly’s Inquiries, Part Five, Section Three:
Offerings of the Three Karmas.
Once these bodhisattvas had emerged from the earth, they each proceeded through the air to the sevenfold solid and wondrous stupa where the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni Buddha were located.
Upon arriving, they bowed their heads at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones;

likewise, they went before the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the various jeweled trees and paid homage to them all, circumambulating them three times to the right with palms joined in reverence.
Praising the two World-Honored Ones with various dharmas of praise used by the bodhisattvas, they stood to one side, joyfully gazing up at them.
The seats beneath the trees were those upon which the emanated bodies of the Buddhas sat; [the bodhisattvas] bowed to and circumambulated these bodies while praising the dharmas.
This mouth gazes up at this mind.

From the moment these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first surged forth, they praised the Buddha with various kinds of bodhisattva eulogies for a period of time lasting fifty intermediate kalpas; at that time, Śākyamuni Buddha remained silent.
However, those seated there and the fourfold assembly likewise remained silent for fifty minor kalpas;
through the Buddha’s spiritual power, he caused the great multitude to perceive this duration as being like half a day.
Although it was fifty minor kalpas, it appeared to the fourfold assembly as if it were only half a day; thus, the long was concealed and the short was manifested.
To borrow the power of his supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*) so that what is narrow may appear vast—both of these are inconceivable.
That fifty intermediate *kalpas* were but half a day is an inconceivability regarding time. What the Tathāgata perceives is not by means of dualistic marks;
the bodhisattvas from the lower regions constantly praise him face-to-face, and the Tathāgata remains silent, always accepting their offerings.
To praise the one who explains is to take the short as long, referring to the fifty minor kalpas; to mislead the deluded is to take the long as short, referring to it being like half a day.
This serves as a preliminary lead-in for the fundamental and the manifested. When the Tathāgata has not yet spoken, one remains in darkness regarding the fundamental and clings to the manifested;
when the Buddha reveals and clarifies, one awakens to the near and reaches the far, thereby knowing that the inconceivable is one.
At that time, the fourfold assembly, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, also saw the bodhisattvas filling the empty space of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands.
That the fourfold assembly saw the bodhisattvas everywhere was because the Tathāgata, by borrowing his supernatural power, caused what was narrow to become vast.
To see so extensively is itself inconceivable. Indeed, what is seen by the fleshly eye or the divine eye does not extend far;
yet now that which is beheld fills all of space. Seeing the intensity of the rain, one knows the greatness of the dragon; seeing the abundance of the flowers, one knows the depth of the pond.
Since one knows that the marks of the Bodhisattva’s response are so numerous, they must have simultaneously realized the true principle of the entire Dharma-realm. △
Second, the presentation of the words of inquiry. First, the designation of the four leaders:
among this assembly of bodhisattvas, there are four leaders—first, Superior Conduct; second, Boundless Conduct; third, Pure Conduct;
and fourth, Established Conduct. These four bodhisattvas are the foremost leaders within that assembly and speak forth.
Regarding the "Guiding Teachers," only four individuals are mentioned because they are intended to represent the forty stages of "Opening, Showing, Awakening, and Entering.
This is analogous to how the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* mentions only Dharmamati, Guṇakara, Vajradhvaja, and Vajragarbha to explain these forty stages. △ Second.
The formal presentation of the questions, in two parts: first, the prose; second, the questions regarding the Tathāgata’s well-being.
First, [the assembly] before the Great Multitude each joined their palms together, gazed upon Śākyamuni Buddha, and inquired after him, saying:
"World-Honored One, are you free from illness and affliction? Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?"
△ Second, the question regarding the ease with which sentient beings may be delivered:
"Are those who are to be delivered easy to instruct, so as not to cause the World-Honored One weariness?
△ Second, the verse summary, consisting of two parts: first, the verse summarizing the question concerning the Tathāgata’s well-being.
At that time, the four great bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
"World-Honored One, you are at ease, with little illness and little affliction, teaching and transforming sentient beings without ever experiencing weariness.

World-Honored One, you have already transcended the worldly outflows and the five aggregates; how could there be illness or affliction? It is only because you wish to manifest equality with ordinary people."
Since the Dharma accords with the constant conventions of the land, it was necessary to inquire, "Is there illness or distress? △ Second, the verse asks whether sentient beings are easy to deliver:
"Furthermore, are the various sentient beings easy to transform, so as not to cause the World-Honored One weariness?"
△ Third, the Buddha’s response regarding peace and happiness, in two parts: first, the response regarding peace and happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "So it is, so it is, O all [bodhisattvas]..."
"Good son, the Tathāgata is at ease, with little illness and little affliction.
II. Answering that [beings] are easy to deliver: First, their faculties are sharp and their virtues are profound.
All these sentient beings can be easily transformed and delivered without any fatigue. Why is this? Because these sentient beings..."
"Throughout successive lifetimes, they have constantly received my transformation and have planted various roots of goodness by revering and honoring past Buddhas;
as soon as these sentient beings see my body and hear what I say, they immediately believe and accept it,
entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata."
Those whose faculties are sharp and whose virtues are profound have constantly received the Great Transformation since time immemorial;

upon first seeing my body, they immediately receive the *Avataṃsaka* and enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Since their fruit has ripened and is easily shed, this class of sentient beings is easy to deliver.
△ Second, those with dull faculties and meager merit—
except for those who have previously practiced and studied the Lesser Vehicle— I now likewise cause such persons to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
Those with dull faculties and meager virtue have, from lifetime to lifetime, failed to receive the Great Transformation.

For the sake of such people, it was necessary to open up the gradual teaching; through the Tripiṭaka, Vaipulya, and Prajñāpāramitā, they were tamed. Now, by hearing the Lotus Sūtra, these same individuals enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
Compared to what preceded it, although this is difficult for them, it is exceedingly easy for the Buddha—regardless of whether their faculties are sharp or dull.

The entry [into the truth] is identical, yet it is explained by briefly citing ten points of meaning. First, "seeing at the beginning" versus "seeing now" (the time of initial attainment of the Way is called "seeing at the beginning"; the true reality after a long period is called "seeing now").

Second, "opening and closing" versus "neither opening nor closing" (when the sun shines upon a high mountain, it is spoken of as sudden; this is "neither opening nor closing" for those who have not entered.

To open up the sudden teaching and speak of the gradual, using samādhi to tame and transform them so they may gradually return to the sudden, is "opening and closing"). Third, "vertical breadth" versus "horizontal brevity," where both horizontal and vertical are combined.

Fourth, "The One Fundamental and Many Traces" versus "The Fundamental Alone": [The former] is called "fundamental" because it is a single platform; it is called "traces" because there are many thousand-petaled lotuses. It is called "shared" because the traces are common to all other sutras; it is called "unique" because the fundamental is distinct from all other sutras. Fifth, "With Added Exposition" versus "Without Added Exposition": [The former] is called "with added exposition" because four bodhisattvas are added to preach the forty stages; [the latter] refers to the self-exposition that reveals and shows [the truth]. Regarding "Broad" (vast): it is called "vertical breadth" because it enters directly and immediately into the Dharma-realm; it is called "horizontal brevity" because it does not pass through expedient means. Now, passing through the five flavors constitutes "horizontal breadth," and attaining entry into the Buddha-wisdom constitutes "vertical breadth. (Note: The term *jue* [頓] is rendered as "immediate/direct"; *zhi* [直] as "straight"; *shu* [竪] as "vertical"; *ru* [入] as "entering"; *fa jie* [法界] as "Dharma-realm"; *yan* [言] as "to say/call"; *shu guang* [竪廣] as "vertical breadth"; *bu li* [不歷] as "not passing through"; *fang bian* [方便] as "expedient means"; *yan* [言] as "to say/call"; *heng lue* [橫略] as "horizontal brevity"; *jin* [今] as "now"; *li* [歷] as "passing through"; *wu wei* [五味] as "five flavors"; *ji shi* [即是] as "is precisely"; *heng guang* [橫廣] as "horizontal breadth"; *de ru* [得入] as "attaining entry"; *fo hui* [佛慧] as "Buddha-wisdom"; *ye shi* [亦是] as "also is"; *shu guang* [竪廣] as "vertical breadth"; *di si* [第四] as "fourth"; *ben yi* [本一] as "one fundamental"; *ji duo* [迹多] as "many traces"; *ji gong* [迹共] as "traces shared"; *yu zhong jing tong* [與眾經同] as "same as other sutras"; *yu* [故] as "because"; *yan* [言] as "to say/call"; *gong* [共] as "shared"; *ben yu* [本與] as "fundamental with"; *zhong jing yi* [眾經異] as "different from other sutras"; *gu yan du* [故言獨] as "therefore called unique"; *di wu* [第五] as "fifth"; *jia shuo* [加說] as "with added exposition"; *bu jia shuo* [不加說] as "without added exposition"; *jia si pu sa* [加四菩薩] as "adding four bodhisattvas"; *shuo* [說] as "preach"; *si shi wei* [四十位] as "forty stages"; *gu yue jia shuo* [故曰加說] as "therefore called with added exposition"; *zi shuo kai shi* [自說開示] as "self-exposition that reveals and shows").

1. Entering Awakening without adding anything to others (it is called "not adding" because nothing is added to others). 2. Transforming the land versus not transforming the land (because it is the Flower King World [Padmavati], it is called "not transforming";

because the three lands are transformed, it is called "transforming the land"). 3. Many locations versus not many locations (the seven locations and eight assemblies constitute "many locations"; because Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain is distant and the assembly is in the open sky, it is "not many locations"). 4.

Expelling and taking away versus not expelling and taking away (because the phantom city is extinguished and the hired labor is changed, it is called "expelling and taking away"; because there is no such matter here, it is "not expelling and taking away"). 5. Direct manifestation.

Truly, this is the opening of the provisional to reveal the real (practicing the great direct path is called "directly revealing the real"; definitively resolving the Śrāvaka dharma is called "opening the provisional to reveal the real").

Tenth, those with sharp faculties mature first, while those with dull faculties mature later (those with sharp faculties mature first as they initially enter the Buddha-wisdom; those with dull faculties mature later as they now enter the Buddha-wisdom).

Because the conditions and suitability differ, there are briefly ten distinctions; yet since the *sarvajñatā* and the *dharmadhātu* are without differentiation, this sutra says: "Only now do I see my body and hear..."
All that I have spoken you should believe and accept, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
except for those who previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna, who now, upon hearing this sutra, shall enter the Buddha-wisdom. The clear evidence is found herein, so there is no need for doubt.
△ Fourth, the verses in praise of sympathetic joy.
At that time, the great bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
"Excellent, excellent, Great Hero, World-Honored One! Sentient beings can easily be transformed and delivered. You have been able to inquire about the profound wisdom of the Buddhas;
having heard it, they will believe and practice it. We rejoice in this."
The "questioner" refers to the four great bodhisattvas in the *Avataṃsaka* and Śāriputra’s three requests in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; both are capable questioners.
The "subject of inquiry" refers to questioning the Buddha regarding his wisdom. △ Fifth, the Tathāgata’s praise and exhortation.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the foremost great bodhisattvas, saying: "Excellent, excellent, sons of good family!
You are able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata."

The Tathāgata’s praise differs significantly from the preceding section. Why? In the previous passage, those who were able to ask with sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) were all bodhisattvas or those being transformed by them;
having heard [the teaching], they practiced with faith, which is to say they gave rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the bodhisattvas and others.
Now, why does the Tathāgata’s praise instead say, "You are able [to practice] toward the Tathāgata"?
The arising of a mind of sympathetic joy (anumodanā) means that those who are able to inquire are all ancient Buddhas;
that you are able to rejoice is precisely to rejoice in the Tathāgata. Thus, the Bodhisattva rejoices in his traces, while the Tathāgata praises his source.
This also secretly indicates [the Buddha’s] lifespan. Why? For if one now praises a Bodhisattva as being an ancient Buddha, it secretly indicates that the present Buddha is not [merely so].

Since that which is accomplished now is not accomplished by means of the present, there must necessarily be a remote origin; because this has not yet been made manifest, it is therefore a subtle indication.
△ Second, the doubts and questions, part two: first, the doubting thoughts of the bodhisattvas in this land; second, the doubt expressed in prose.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assembly of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers, all had this thought:

"Since the distant past, we have never seen nor heard of such a great multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas emerging from the earth to stand before the World-Honored One, joining their palms in worship and inquiring after the Tathāgata’s well-being. At that moment, Maitreya Bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva knew the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers, and also desired to resolve his own doubts.
From this point downward is the second introductory section on inquiry; all those who harbor doubts, including Maitreya and the other bodhisattvas, are as follows:

There are four intentions: first, from the time I attained quiescence at the site of enlightenment until this present assembly, the great beings from the ten directions have gathered here without ceasing;
though they are beyond limit, by the power of my wisdom as a Bodhisattva of the final birth, I see them all and know them all—how could I not recognize even a single person among this multitude?
Furthermore, as I travel and transform throughout the ten directions, I pay homage to and behold all the Buddhas of the entire ocean of worlds.
That which everyone knows and understands is not recognized even within one’s own career; whether coming or going, one seeks it and does not find it.
Because there is no world if it is not known, one must inquire about these two points.
Second, those great beings were advanced predecessors, while Maitreya is a junior student of a later generation; the latter does not know the former, as the text states.

Little do they realize that the realm of women who have entered meditative concentration is unknown to ordinary women, and the realm of the Bodhisattva Abandoner of All Coverings (Sarvāvaraṇaviskambhin) is unknown because it is not recognized.
Because they do not know this, they do not understand the inner goodness within him, nor do they give rise to their own goodness;

thus, there is no benefit for those who dwell in the state of non-being, and for this reason, there must be questioning regarding these three points. Furthermore, these Great Beings fundamentally penetrate the bottom of true reality (bhūtatathatā) and manifest throughout the ten directions.
Furthermore, regarding the separate teaching of all true and responsive manifestations, none of these fall within the realm of Maitreya.

Since he does not recognize the path for benefiting sentient beings, he likewise does not recognize their afflictions and lacks the means to provide remedial benefit; therefore, it is necessary to pose questions.

Fourthly, the Buddha entrusted the propagation of the sutra and summoned the great bodhisattvas; as these bodhisattvas respectfully fulfilled their master’s solemn command, they came to secretly reveal the duration of the Buddha's life.
Since the assembly at that time did not recognize the Tathāgata’s esoteric intent, they would have lacked the benefit of the ultimate truth (paramārtha);

therefore, it was necessary for them to pose questions. Furthermore, although Maitreya’s manifest status as the Regent (upapadya) implies he must inherently possess deep realization, why is it that he appears thus ignorant?

There are two meanings to this: first, if one speaks according to the ultimate reality (tattva), his recent attainment of the position of Regent does not mean he is unaware of his long-standing fundamental nature.
If one discusses this from the perspective of provisional means (*upāya*), then the fundamental [state] being high and the trace [manifestation] being low gives rise to doubts among sentient beings.
△ Second, the verse portion of the formal inquiry, in five parts: first, asking from where he has come.
With palms joined toward the Buddha, he asks in verse:
"O Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, these immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of great assemblies of bodhisattvas have never before been seen;
we pray that you will tell us from where they have come.
△ Second, the question regarding the cause for their arrival.
By what causes and conditions has he gathered such a massive body, great supernormal powers, and inconceivable wisdom?
His resolve is firm and steadfast, and he possesses the power of great patience; he is a joy for all sentient beings to behold—from where has he come?
△ Third, describing their numbers:
Each of these bodhisattvas is accompanied by an immeasurable retinue, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
some great bodhisattvas lead as many as sixty thousand times the sands of the Ganges. Such a great assembly seeks the Buddha-way with a single mind.
These great masters, numbering as many as sixty thousand Ganges-sands, all came together to make offerings to the Buddha and to protect and uphold this sutra;
there were also fifty thousand Ganges-sands, whose number exceeds that [of the former], as well as forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand,
down to ten thousand, one thousand, one hundred, and so on, until reaching one Ganges-sand, half a Ganges-sand, a third or a fourth part of a Ganges-sand, and even a billionth part of a Ganges-sand.
There were hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of disciples, even up to fifty million; their number further exceeded one hundred thousand,
reaching ten thousand, one thousand one hundred, one hundred and fifty, and ten, down to three, two, and one—
those who were solitary and without retinue, delighting in dwelling alone— all came together to the place where the Buddha was, their number surpassing the former by far.
If one were to count these great assemblies by means of tally sticks, they would not be fully known even after more kalpas than the sands of the Ganges.
△ Fourth, asking who their teacher was:
"Who taught and transformed these bodhisattvas of great majesty and diligence, so that they attained accomplishment?"
From whom did you first resolve to attain enlightenment? What Buddha-dharma do you extol? Whose sutras do you uphold and practice? And what path of the Buddhas have you cultivated?
△ Fifth, Maitreya’s summary request, in five parts: first, a summary praise of his supernatural power.
Such is the great power of the supernormal knowledges and wisdom of these bodhisattvas.
II. Requesting an Answer Regarding Their Origin:
The earth in the four directions cracked open, and from within it they all surged forth, saying, "World-Honored One, we have never before seen such a thing."
I pray that you will tell us the name of the land from which they come; though I have constantly traveled through various lands, I have never seen such an assembly.
△ Third, the request for an explanation of the cause of their arrival:
"Among this assembly, I do not recognize even a single person; how is it that they have suddenly emerged from the earth? I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions thereof."
△ The Four Great Assemblies join in this request:
"In this great assembly, these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas all desire to know the causal conditions regarding the origins and the end of these bodhisattva hosts."
△ 5. Request for the Teacher’s Response:
O World-Honored One of Immeasurable Virtue, we pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly.
△ 2. Doubts of the Bodhisattvas from Other Lands.

At that time, the various Buddhas who were emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha and had come from immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands in other directions sat cross-legged upon lion thrones beneath the jeweled trees in the eight directions.
Each of those Buddhas’ attendants saw this great assembly of bodhisattvas in the four quarters of the trichiliocosm.

Emerging from the earth and abiding in the void, they each addressed their respective Buddhas, saying, "World-Honored One, from where have these immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable assemblies of bodhisattvas come?
At that time, each of those Buddhas spoke to his attendant, saying, "Good sons, wait but a moment; there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Maitreya, and Śākyamuni..."
The Muni Buddha has already bestowed a prediction that you shall become Buddhas next; having asked about this matter, the Buddha now answers it, so that you yourselves shall hear it through this.
That Buddha’s attendant is none other than a Bodhisattva from another direction, a member of his retinue who has manifested as a division-body pervading the ten directions.
Maitreya and the others shared the same doubt, none knowing that the Tathāgata had attained Buddhahood in his original ground long ago.

Thereupon, each presented their doubts to their own Buddha, and every Buddha suppressed them, awaiting Maitreya; thus it is said that Maitreya has already asked about this matter, and you yourselves shall hear it because of him.
This refers to the Buddhas of the emanated bodies who spoke as if they themselves were answering the questions.
Since the benefit does not reside within myself, I do not provide an answer; rather, it is because I await Śākyamuni’s response to Maitreya’s question that I say, "I await Maitreya.
Why is this? The matters concerning which Maitreya inquires are no trivial ones; throughout the entire career of the World-Honored One, they have never been explicitly taught.
It is through this exchange of questions and answers that the long life [of the Buddha] is extensively revealed. This profound mystery of the present dispensation resides with the Buddha himself.

"Open [your ears], for you shall hear that I should not answer. △ Second, from this half-chapter down to the end of the verses spoken by Maitreya in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," the second section of the main exposition of the Root Gate has two parts: first, the admonition and permission; second, the actual exposition.
The first part [the admonition] further has two sections: first, the prose; second, the initial admonition, which begins with the description of praise.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "Excellent, excellent, Ajita!
You are indeed able to ask the Buddha about such a great matter.
△ Second, the formal admonition.
"You all should together with one mind don the armor of diligence and resolve upon a firm intention.
With a single mind, admonish yourselves not to be distracted; having donned the armor, admonish yourselves not to be indolent; being firm, admonish yourselves not to retreat.
△ Second, the promise, which has two parts. First, indicating the fruit of wisdom.
The Tathāgata now desires to manifest and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas.
△ Second, the teaching for the transformation and edification of the three periods of time:
the power of the sovereign spiritual penetrations of all Buddhas; the power of the lion’s majestic display of all Buddhas; the fierce and awesome power of all Buddhas.
The power of great majesty (*mahābhijñājñānabala*).

The commentary states: "Opening and transforming through teaching" refers to the proclamation [of the Dharma]. "Sovereign spiritual power" (*vaśitā-ṛddhibala*) refers to benefiting beings in the past.
"The lion’s vigorous leap" (*siṃhavikrīḍita*) refers to the places where the emanated bodies reach throughout the ten directions; it refers to benefiting beings in the present. Furthermore:
"Powerful and majestic" refers to the future benefit of sentient beings. Zhan’an privately comments: "The Tathāgata’s sovereignty" is the virtue of self;
"supernatural powers" are the virtue of bliss; "the lion’s vigorous display" is the virtue of purity through the vigorous removal of defilements;
and "great power and majesty for the future benefit of beings" is the virtue of permanence. △ Second, the verse summary, in two parts: first, the summary of the prose.
Admonition.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"You should be diligent and single-minded; I wish to speak of this matter, so do not harbor doubt or regret."
△ Second, the two verses on the acceptance [of the teaching]. First, the verse on the fruit of wisdom:
"The Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable.
△ Second, the verse on the transformations throughout the three periods of time.
"Now that you have brought forth the power of faith and abide in the goodness of patience, you shall now hear all those dharmas never heard before.
I now comfort you: do not harbor doubt or fear. The Buddha’s words are never untrue;

however, even there, the explicit term "three periods" did not appear, but rather the force of the meaning corresponded to the three periods. This verse is likewise:
it directly employs half a line of verse—“The Buddha has no speech that is not true”—to encompass the entire point. Since his words are not false, one knows the three periods.
This is also truly beneficial. △ Second, the actual exposition has two parts: first, one chapter and a half that directly opens up the near to reveal the far;

Regarding the statement that those dwelling in the space below [attain] the *adhas-vikīrṇa-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Dispersion Below), the *Śāstra* explains it as follows: "Below" (*adhas*) means downward; "dispersion" (*vikīrṇa*) means emptiness (*ākāśa*).

This merely clarifies the terminology; if one were to define its essential nature, it should be explained in four ways: 1. "Existence" (*asti*) refers to the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*). 2. "Below" (*adhas*) refers to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naiva-saṃjñā-nāsaṃjñāyatana*).

This is the "bottom" (*adhas*) because it is the ultimate limit of the outflows (*sāsrava*). [This is according to the *Hīnayāna* teachings. 3. Furthermore, "existence" (*asti*) refers to names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*). 4. "Below" (*adhas*) refers to... [text fragment].

"Emptiness" (śūnyatā) is the bottom (the ultimate ground of the True Truth). Because it is empty and quiescent, it serves as the bottom (Shared Teaching). Furthermore, "that which exists" refers to the two extremes of the conventional;
"bottom" refers to the fulfillment of the wisdom of the limit (the ultimate ground of the Conventional Truth), and thus it serves as the bottom (Distinct Teaching).

In this present sutra, taking the emptiness of the lower direction as the bottom—neither the upper realm nor the lower realm—symbolizes the Middle Way as the bottom (Perfect Teaching). Among these four interpretations:
It is simply said that "there is" and not that it is "dispersed," because that which exists is itself dispersed. △ Second, the dual explanation:

"Profound wisdom that is unimpeded" refers to relying on inconceivable wisdom. "Delighting in the Buddha-Dharma" [is as follows].
This is delighting in the inconceivable realm; since the realm and wisdom are profoundly subtle, this is not the practice of a bodhisattva of shallow capacity.

△ Second, the Chapter on the Lifespan (*Āyus-pramāṇa-parivarta*), which extensively reveals the near while manifesting the far, thereby severing doubt and engendering faith. Part One: The Title.
*The Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Law*, Chapter Sixteen: “The Lifespan of the Tathāgata” (the main text refers to it as the “Chapter on the Manifested Lifespan of the Tathāgata”).

“Tathāgata” is the general title for all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—whether they be the two Buddhas, the three Buddhas, the fundamental Buddha, or the manifested Buddha.
Regarding the "Life Span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*): this explains and measures the virtues of the Buddha.

Since we are now specifically explaining the virtues of the three Buddhas of the Original Ground (*mūla-bhūmi*), it is called the "Chapter on the Life Span of the Tathāgata. The meaning of "Tathāgata" is manifold; here, two or three aspects will be clarified. The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Because one comes by means of the path of reality (*yathābhūta-mārga*) to achieve perfect enlightenment, one is called a Tathāgata. This refers to the vehicle (*yāna*).

The wisdom that accords with the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatājñāna*) is in reality the very object that is the suchness of phenomena. When object and wisdom are in union, there is cause and effect:

when the illumination of the object is not yet exhaustive, it is called the "cause"; when the source is fully exhausted, it is the "fruit. When the cause is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled, one comes by means of the path of reality (*yathābhūtamārga*) to achieve perfect enlightenment;
this is the True Body (*dharmakāya*). By means of the wisdom of reality, one comes to be born through the path of reality.

Third, there is the manifestation of attaining perfect enlightenment, which refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body); this is the meaning of the two bodies, the *dharmakāya* (truth body) and the *nirmāṇakāya*.

Regarding the "Tathāgata," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because he understands according to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and explains according to the nature of phenomena, he is called Tathāgata.

"Tathā" (Thus) refers to the *tathatā* (suchness), the realm of reality that is neither cause nor fruit; whether a Buddha appears or not, its essential characteristics remain eternally as they are, pervading all things.
Abiding without change is "as" (如); reaching without moving is "coming" (來).
This Dharma-body Tathāgata is the Dharma-suchness; the wisdom-vehicle of suchness is the true path of suchness. Coming to achieve perfect enlightenment, his wisdom accords with principle.
Following principle is "as"; following wisdom is "coming. This is the Reward-body (Sambhogakāya) Tathāgata. Thus, the Treatise says: "In accordance with the characteristics of phenomena."

Because he has realized [this], he is called the Tathāgata. Since his wisdom is united with the realm of suchness (*tathatā*), he is able to manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment in every place.
Just as mercury mixed with pure gold can coat various forms and images, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) conjoined with merit manifests everywhere;
proceeding through the eight phases of enlightenment and turning the wheel of the Dharma is the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata. Therefore, the Treatise says:
Because he teaches according to the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he is called the Tathāgata. The Dharmakāya Tathāgata is named Vairocana, which translates as "Pervading All Places.
The Sambhogakāya Tathāgata is named Rocana, which translates as "Pure and Full.
The Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata is named Śākyamuni, which translates as "Deliverer from the Swamp of Reeds. These are the three bodies; if one takes them individually, they are incomplete.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The Dharma-body is neither prajñā, nor is it liberation, nor is it the three dharmas.
When these three are fully possessed, it is called the Secret Treasury and named Great Nirvāṇa. It cannot be characterized as one or many, nor as vertical, horizontal, simultaneous, or separate;

it is the perfect contemplation of the three dharmas, designated by the provisional name 'Tathāgata. Question: This chapter does not mention the names of the three Buddhas; why then do you provide this explanation? Answer: [As follows...]
Although the specific name is not mentioned, its meaning is fully contained in the text: "Neither identical nor different; unlike the three realms, one perceives the three realms.
This indicates that it is not a partial identity, but reveals this perfect identity (*pariniṣpanna-tathatā*), which is precisely the meaning of the Tathāgata as the Dharma-body. Furthermore, it says:
"The Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the three realms as they truly are" (*yathābhūtam*); this is the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*) corresponding to suchness itself.

The "object" (*viṣaya*) refers to the meaning of the *saṃbhogakāya* Tathāgata. Furthermore, it is said that either manifesting one's own body and one's own affairs, or manifesting the bodies and affairs of others, constitutes the meaning of the *nirmāṇakāya* Tathāgata.
If the three Tathāgatas consist solely of the virtues of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*), they are horizontal;

if they consist solely of the virtues of cultivation (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), they are vertical. First the *dharmakāya*, then the *saṃbhogakāya*, and subsequently the *nirmāṇakāya*—this too is vertical. Now...
The Sūtra speaks of the three Tathāgatas in their perfected sense as being neither vertical nor horizontal. The Śāstra states: "It manifests three kinds of bodhi:
first, the bodhi of the nirmāṇakāya; second, the bodhi of the saṃbhogakāya; and third, the bodhi of the dharmakāya.

Therefore, since the Sūtra contains the meaning and the Śāstra provides the names, how could one not accord with both the Sūtra and the Śāstra by providing the aforementioned interpretation? This is its lifeblood.
"Measure" (*pramāṇa*) refers to the meaning of "reception" (*vedanā*). Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is not separated from all phenomena, it is called reception;

because object and wisdom are in correspondence, it is called reception; and because the retribution obtained throughout a single lifetime continues without interruption for a hundred years, it is called reception.

"Measure" also means "to define. In defining phenomena, the Tathāgata takes suchness as his life; whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, the nature and characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are eternally constant.

However, whether in terms of association (*saṃprayukta*) or non-continuity (*asaṃtati*), there is neither measure nor immeasurability. As the text says: "It is not like, not different, not real, and not false.
This explains that the fruition of the Tathāgata is suchness-wisdom (*tathatājñāna*) which accords with the realm of suchness (*tathatāviṣaya*).

When the realm gives rise to wisdom, it constitutes fruition-wisdom; when wisdom merges with the realm, it constitutes the received realm (*anubhūta-viṣaya*). Since this is already immeasurable and boundless, [it is beyond calculation].
The wisdom that is eternally abiding and indestructible is also like this. As the *Sūtra* says:
"The power of my wisdom is such that its light of insight illumines immeasurably; it is obtained through long-cultivated practice over the course of countless kalpas.

This explains that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) accords with conditions: when conditions are long, it is long; when conditions are brief, it is brief. Thus the text states: "It manifests birth again and again."

Regarding the repeated manifestation of extinction and so forth: from that perspective, it is either the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) within me, or it is the case that their names differ and their ages vary in seniority.
The *dharmakāya* is neither measurable nor immeasurable; the *saṃbhogakāya* is measurable prior to the *vajra* [stage] and immeasurable thereafter;
and the *nirmāṇakāya* is measurable according to conditions, yet its application is uninterrupted.
There are four propositions—eternal, non-eternal, and so forth—to be analyzed in detail first and then generally.
That which is neither eternal nor non-eternal is the *dharmakāya*. That which is eternal is the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is likewise neither eternal nor non-eternal.
That which is both eternal and non-eternal is the *nirmāṇakāya*; because its applications are inexhaustible, it is "eternal," and it is also frequently designated by the name "Nirvāṇa."
Regarding the general explanation of impermanence according to the universal principle: each and every Tathāgata is fully endowed with the fourfold dharmakāya.

First, that which is neither permanent nor impermanent is so because it simultaneously refutes the eight inversions of both ordinary beings and sages. Second, "permanent" means it is as permanent as space.
Third, "impermanent" means it is free from the inversion of birth and death held by ordinary beings, and is thus also permanent. Fourth, "both permanent and impermanent" refers to its quiescence...
The fourth [aspect] of the *saṃbhogakāya* is that it is neither permanent nor impermanent: because the object and wisdom are in profound union (*amita*), it is permanent;

because it transcends the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is impermanent; and because it is free from the inversion of arising and ceasing, it is both permanent and impermanent, as it can simultaneously illumine both.
The fourth [aspect] of the *nirmāṇakāya* is that it is neither permanent nor impermanent: because it is neither the *saṃbhogakāya* nor the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is permanent.

Since that which is eternal must always be identical [to itself], and that which is impermanent is likewise identical in its impermanence, and that which is both eternal and impermanent exists as both, this chapter generally clarifies the means of evaluating the three bodies (*trikāya*).
However, from a specific perspective, it primarily concerns the *saṃbhogakāya*. Why?

Because the meaning is facilitated and the text is harmonized; regarding the facilitation of meaning, the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* is "concordant above" and "in accord below" with the three bodies.

This is because it is perfectly complete. As for the convergence of the texts: since my attainment of Buddhahood has been exceedingly long ago, I have been able to benefit sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
That which is accomplished is the Dharmakāya; that which accomplishes it is the Saṃbhogakāya;
and the union of the Dharma- and Saṃbhoga-kāyas constitutes the Nirmāṇakāya, which benefits all things. Inferring from this, the primary intent is to discuss the merit of the *saṃbhogabuddha*.
This is virtue. △ Second, the main text has two parts. First, the exhortation to believe, which has four sections. First, the initial exhortation:
At that time, the Buddha addressed all the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly: "O sons of good family, you should believe and understand the true and sincere words of the Tathāgata.

Combining the preceding and following sections, there are five admonitions and seven requests. These matters are extraordinary and momentous, treated with such earnestness and gravity. "Sincere" (sei) refers to loyalty and integrity; "truth" (tei) refers to—

Examining reality without deceiving others, his words reach the truth. Formerly, when he was among those of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*), whatever he spoke was all speech conforming to the intentions of others (*parāśaya-vāk*), not a declaration of ultimate sincerity.
Now, the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—pure, perfect, and fully revealed—is precisely speech conforming to his own intention (*svāśaya-vāk*).
Because it reveals the essential core, it is called "truthful and sincere. △ Second: The Request.
