The color of the sunlight gradually diminishes over approximately one month; as for its increase and decrease, these pertain to the Dharma-body, specifically to wisdom and the abandonment of afflictions.
△ Third, the assembly’s offering:
When the Buddha spoke of how these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had attained great benefit from the Dharma, a rain of *maṇi* jewels fell from the void.
With *tāla* flowers and great *mandārava* flowers, they scattered them over all the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of jewel trees;

they also scattered them over Śākyamuni Buddha and the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna—who had long since entered parinirvāṇa—seated upon the lion throne within the stupa made of the seven precious substances;
and they also scattered them over all the great bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.

Furthermore, the assembly rained down fine powders of *candana* and aloeswood incense, and so forth; in the midst of space, celestial drums resounded of their own accord with wondrous sounds deep and far-reaching.
They also rained down a thousand kinds of celestial garments, draped with various necklaces:

necklaces of pearls, necklaces of *maṇi* jewels, and necklaces of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*), pervading the nine directions. Countless precious incense burners burned priceless incense of their own accord.
Furthermore, throughout the great assembly of offerings, above each and every Buddha,
there were bodhisattvas holding banners and canopies that ascended in succession up to the Brahma Heaven; these bodhisattvas, with wondrous voices, sang immeasurable verses in praise of the Buddhas.
At that time, the assembly, having heard the profound and far-reaching Dharma and attained great benefit, desired to repay the Buddha’s kindness and thus established offerings.

This was also a figurative act intended to manifest their realization. While the previous "Gate of Revealing the Expedient and Manifesting the Real" had been opened, the Bodhisattvas also attained awakening, yet their great task was not yet complete;
therefore, they did not present offerings to manifest their realization. Now, in this "Root Gate," the near [expedient] is opened.

Since the manifestation of the distant [realms] has been completed, Maitreya provides a comprehensive summary and exposition for the sake of understanding; thus, he expresses this by means of offerings.

As for the various bodhisattvas holding banners and canopies who ascend in succession until reaching the Brahma Heaven: "banner" (dhvaja) signifies "turning," and "canopy" (chattra) signifies "covering.
"Earth" (bhūmi) signifies "beginning," and "Brahma" (brahman) signifies "purity. Wisdom and severance turn successively, and compassion turns successively.
Covering from high to low and deep to shallow without losing their proper order, reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven;

manifesting the increasing of the Path and the diminishing of births for all Bodhisattvas, they approach the Subtle Enlightenment and reach the ultimate purity. △ Second, Maitreya articulates his understanding and realization, in three parts:
first, a verse on the assembly’s understanding and realization.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"The Buddha has preached a marvelous Dharma, such as has never been heard before. World-Honored One, you possess great power, and your lifespan is immeasurable."
When countless sons of the Buddha heard the World-Honored One distinguish and explain those who have attained the benefit of the Dharma, joy filled their bodies to overflowing.
△ Second, the verse on the Tathāgata’s distinctions:
Some abide in the stage of non-retrogression; some have attained *dhāraṇīs*; some possess unimpeded eloquence and the *koṭis* of *parivartas* of the *dhāraṇī*.
There were bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a great trichiliocosm, each capable of turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma;
there were bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a medium chiliocosm, each capable of turning the pure wheel of Dharma;
and there were bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm, who each had eight births remaining before they would attain the path of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms within four, three, or two such worlds of four continents who attain Buddhahood after successive births;
or there are bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms within one world of four continents who shall become omniscient after only one more birth.
When such beings hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is so long and far-reaching, they obtain the immeasurable, untainted, and pure fruit of retribution.
Furthermore, sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds, upon hearing the Buddha’s discourse on his lifespan, all resolved their minds upon supreme enlightenment.
The World-Honored One has expounded immeasurable and inconceivable dharmas, bringing vast benefit that is as boundless as space.
Regarding "attaining immeasurable, outflow-free, and pure karmic fruition": it is called "immeasurable" to distinguish it from the limited [fruition] of the two vehicles;

it is called "pure" because it is evoked by sublime causes; and it is called "karmic fruition" because it is a realm of non-obstruction, distinguishing it from the absence of fruition in the two vehicles.
△ Third, verses on the offerings of the assembly at that time.

It rained *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* flowers; Śakra and Brahmā, along with countless buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, arrived raining sandalwood and aloeswood that fell in profuse, swirling abundance like birds flying down from the sky to scatter as offerings before the Buddhas.
From the midst of space, celestial drums spontaneously produced wondrous sounds, and tens of millions of varieties of heavenly garments swirled down.
With exquisite incense burners made of various jewels, they burned priceless incense that spontaneously pervaded everywhere as an offering to all the World-Honored Ones.
The great assembly of Bodhisattvas held banners and canopies made of the seven treasures, high and sublime in ten trillion varieties, which reached successively up to the Brahma Heaven.
Before each and every Buddha, jeweled standards suspended excellent banners, and they likewise sang praises of the Tathāgatas with ten million gāthās.
Such various matters as these have never before been heard; hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable, all are filled with joy.
The Buddha’s name is renowned throughout the ten directions, extensively benefiting sentient beings, so that all may be endowed with roots of goodness to assist their unsurpassed resolve.

△ Section Three: Dissemination (Tri-āvatāra-varga). Part Two: First, from the end of the third chapter and a half, clarifying the profound merit of propagating the sutra and exhorting its dissemination;
second, from the "Divine Power" (Ṛddhi-anuśaṃsā) chapter downward through eight chapters, clarifying the entrustment and dissemination. The first text [of the second part] further has three sections:

first, from here down to the end of the "Rejoicing" (Anumodanā) chapter, clarifying the exhortation for dissemination based on the causal merit of the first chapter; second, the merit of the Dharma Master...

The Chapter on Merits: Clarifying the Initial Chapter’s Fruits and Virtues, Exhorting the Circulation [of the Text]. Part Three: The Chapter on Never-Slighting, Quoting Those Who Believe and Those Who Slander to Prove the Exhortation to Circulate.
The initial section has two parts: first, the four types of faith during the present life; second, the five grades after the extinction of the Tathāgata.
The first of these has four parts: first, a single thought of faith and understanding; second, a brief explanation of the verbal approach; third, an extensive [explanation]; fourth, [the conclusion].

He says that the contemplation of the four profound faiths constitutes the first section, which is further divided into two parts. First, the prose explanation; within this, first, he identifies the person:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya Ajita: "If there are sentient beings who hear the Buddha..."
Their lifespan shall be long and far-reaching, even to the point that they can give rise to a single thought of faith and understanding.

One should know that from this point until then, this constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding. Regarding the statement "a single thought of faith and understanding" in the context of the four present faiths:
it means that wherever one hears [the teaching], there is a sudden and clear illumination; one enters according to the words without any obstruction.
To believe that all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma; and to believe that the Buddha-dharma is not separate from any phenomenon—
neither attaining the Buddha-dharma nor attaining any phenomenon, yet seeing all phenomena as the Buddha-dharma, such that they are three in one and one in three—
to thus walk upon non-paths while penetrating the Buddha-path, is to walk upon the Buddha-path itself.
The Way penetrates all paths; without attaining the Buddha-way, it penetrates all paths as the Buddha-way.
All paths are non-existent, yet they exist; they exist while being non-existent, neither existent nor non-existent.
It is like a road before a gate that penetrates all directions—east, west, south, and north—without any obstruction, even for the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue.
Whatever is encountered by the tongue, body, or mind is likewise without obstruction; this is called faith (*śraddhā*), and its clarity is called understanding (*adhimukti*).
This constitutes the single-moment mind of faith and understanding. Such faith and understanding is termed the stage of the Iron Wheel (*ayaścakra*).

According to another explanation, this is not yet the fully perfected Iron Wheel, but rather the initial mind of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*); such a person has not yet attained the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
Because it is pure, it is not the formal stage of the iron wheel. △ Second, clarifying its merits, in two parts: first, a general discussion of its immeasurability.
The merits attained are without limit.
△ Second, the measurement of the quantity [of merit]. Part one: First, citing the five perfections as the basis for measurement.

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, practice the five pāramitās—namely, dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, [kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, and dhyāna-pāramitā]—for eighty quadrillion nayutas of kalpas...
The *pāramitās* of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditation—excluding the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Since *prajñā* itself is the correct wisdom that serves as the standard for evaluating these five perfections, it is said here to be excluded. △
The second correct calculation shows that it falls far short;
compared to this merit, the previous merit does not equal even one hundredth, one thousandth, one hundred-thousandth,
or one ten-millionth part, nor can it be known through calculation, number, or analogy.
△ Third, non-retrogression in practice.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family possesses such merit, it is impossible for them to regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), when one at the initial stage of the ten stages of faith (*shixin*) hears of the merit of the lifespan, they receive external support through the perfect and compliant faith-understanding, while internally being perfumed by it;

thus, they do not regress. Regarding the classification of stages as "non-regression in practice" (*xing bu-tui*): the text judges that those who have attained the four stages of faith are thereby established in the ten stages of faith.
Consequently, from the first stage of faith up to the seventh is "non-regression in position" (*wei bu-tui*), while from the eighth stage onward is "non-regression in practice."
The "Chapter on Non-Retrogression" clarifies that there are bodhisattvas who regress and those who do not, as well as those with demonic interference and those without.

In the Perfect Teaching, even at the initial stage of the mind, demons cannot find an opportunity; how much more so for those in the stage of non-retrogression. II. Verse Summary (in three parts): 1. First, the comparative measurement of quantity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Suffering beings seek the Buddha’s wisdom; for eighty million billion nayutas of kalpas, they practice the five pāramitās.
Throughout all these kalpas, they give alms and make offerings to Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas and their disciples, as well as to the assemblies of bodhisattvas."
If one gives various kinds of rare and exquisite food and drink, superior garments, bedding, and dwellings made of *candana* sandalwood, adorning them with gardens and groves—
dedicating such diverse and sublime acts of giving throughout the duration of these kalpas toward the Buddha-way;
or again, if one maintains the precepts with purity and without flaw, seeking the unsurpassed path praised by all Buddhas.
Furthermore, if one practices patience and dwells in the stage of gentleness, such that even when various evils are inflicted upon them, their mind does not waver;
and if they are thus slighted or troubled by those who have attained dharmas and harbor overweening pride, they are likewise able to endure it.
Moreover, if they are diligent and energetic, with a will and mindfulness always firm and steadfast, for immeasurable billions of eons they remain single-mindedly without slackening or rest.
Furthermore, throughout incalculable kalpas, dwelling in secluded places— whether sitting or walking— to dispel drowsiness and constantly restrain the mind, by these causes and conditions,

I am able to give rise to various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). For eighty billion *koṭis* of kalpas, my mind remains undisturbed as I abide in this single-minded merit and vow to seek the Unsurpassed Way,
so that I may attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and reach the ultimate limit of all meditative concentrations.
This person shall practice these various merits as described above for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
△ Second, a verse summarizing the characteristics of such persons:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing my teaching on the span of life, believe in it for even a single thought-moment, their merit shall exceed that [of the former]."
If a person is entirely free from all doubt and regret, and with a profound mind believes for even a moment, their merit shall be such as this.
△ Third, non-retrogression in practice and stage:
If there are bodhisattvas who have practiced the Way for immeasurable kalpas and hear me speak of this lifespan, they will then be able to believe and accept it.
May all such persons as these receive this sutra upon the crowns of their heads and make this vow:

"May I, in the future, possess long life to deliver sentient beings, just as the World-Honored One, the King of the Śākyas, now delivers them; may I, like the Lion’s Roar at the site of enlightenment, preach the Dharma without fear.
May I, in all future ages, be honored by all, and when sitting at the site of enlightenment, may my preaching of the lifespan likewise be thus."
If there are those with a profound mind who are pure and upright, who have heard much and are able to retain it,
and who understand the Buddha’s words according to their meaning— such persons will have no doubt regarding this.

"One who has practiced the Way for immeasurable kalpas" refers to one who has long cultivated the various *pāramitās*. "May I, in the future... and so forth, expresses the arising of vows of compassion.
Having already heard the vow for longevity, one should now align oneself with it;

even if one hears this sutra for the first time, the merit of a single moment of faith and understanding is equal to, or even exceeds, that of long-term practice. "The teaching of longevity is likewise" means that it speaks of the eternal.
If his lifespan were eternal, it would surely exceed this limit even until the end of the future world; how could it be otherwise?

Now, the Tathāgata’s lifespan is spoken of as being established according to reality, and thus it is permitted to be so for the time being. Regarding "the profound mind" (*śuddhacitta*) and so forth: "profound" means exhausting the principle of non-duality;
"direct" means that from beginning to end there is a single standard. One who has no doubt regarding this is perfected within the Ground (*bhūmi*).
The gate still possesses five dharmas before doubt can be severed. △ Second, a brief explanation of the meaning of the words, in two parts: first, indicating the characteristics of the person.
Furthermore, Ajita, if there are those who hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching and understand the meaning of these words—
△ Second, the formal evaluation:
The merit obtained by this person is limitless and can give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of a Tathāgata.

This is the second concise explanation of the meaning of the faith; whereas previously one merely had faith and understanding, one was unable to elaborate upon it, as the explanation would have been too extensive.
One must be well-versed in terminology and dialects; since this [text] is complete in these respects, it is said that "understanding the meaning of its words" constitutes explaining them for others.
By the power of such explanation, one is able to give rise to unsurpassed wisdom in both oneself and others. △ Third, extensively explaining it for others, in two parts:
first, indicating the characteristics of the person.
How much more so for those who extensively hear this sutra, whether they cause others to hear it, uphold it themselves, or cause others to uphold it;

whether they write it themselves, or cause others to write it; or whether they make offerings to the scroll with flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, flags, silken canopies, fragrant oils, and ghee lamps.
△ Second, the formal evaluation:
This person’s merit is immeasurable and boundless, capable of giving rise to all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This is the third [stage]: faith that is extensive, explaining it extensively to others—meaning hearing it extensively, understanding it extensively, and explaining it extensively to others.
By practicing offerings, one causes external conditions to support internal wisdom so that it may swiftly enter and give rise to all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
△ Fourth, the accomplishment of profound faith through contemplation:
"Ajita, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears me speak of the long duration of my lifespan and believes it with a deep heart..."
Upon understanding this, one sees that the Buddha is constantly on Vulture Peak, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as he preaches the Dharma;
furthermore, one sees this Sahā world with its ground of lapis lazuli, level and even, with Jāmbūnada gold marking the eightfold paths,
rows of jewel trees, and all the terraces and towers made entirely of precious gems— such is the Bodhi [tree].
If all the assembly of bodhisattvas were to dwell within this, and if anyone is able to contemplate in such a manner, one should know that this is the mark of profound faith and understanding.

This is the fourth stage: the accomplishment of the contemplation of deep faith, which means adding the cultivation of contemplative practice to the three aforementioned types of faith and thereby entering [the path].

In the practice of dhyāna, through the application of wisdom and conceptualization, one gives rise to the perception of the characteristics of the two lands: the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*) and the Land of True Retribution (*vipāka-bhūmi*).
To see the Buddha together with the assembly of bhikṣus constantly residing on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is the characteristic of the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder.

Furthermore, to see the Sahā world consisting purely of bodhisattvas is the characteristic of the Land of True Retribution. The first two stages of faith are the stage of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*), which is extensive.

Hearing this extensive exposition constitutes the stage of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); the accomplishment of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) constitutes the stage of wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Progressing from the shallow to the deep, one achieves the six faculties of purity; this is the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). △ Second, the extinction of the subsequent five grades. This has two parts:

first, listing the five grades and weighing the merit of the four grades; second, weighing the merit of the grade of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*). First, the text on weighing the merit of the initial grade.
Furthermore, regarding the two [sections], in the first [section] of the prose portion, there are five [sub-sections]: first, directly giving rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).

Moreover, if, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, one hears this sutra and does not disparage it but gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, one should know that this is already a sign of profound faith and understanding.
The five grades are categorized as follows: first, those who simply give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy; second, those who additionally practice upholding, reciting, and chanting themselves;

third, those who additionally exhort others to uphold, recite, and chant; fourth, those who additionally practice the six perfections concurrently; and fifth, those who additionally engage in the correct practice of the six perfections.
These five types of persons are collectively considered to both practice for themselves and transform others; thus, the "Chapter on Sympathetic Joy" below refers to them as "fifty people."

They teach one another in succession; because they all possess their own practice, they are collectively called "disciples" (śrāvaka), and because they all possess the capacity to transform others, they are collectively called "Dharma-teachers" (dharmabhāṇaka).
If discussed specifically, the former two types engage only in their own practice, while the latter three types both transform others.
Regarding the title "Dharma-teacher," it applies to those in the third [category] rather than the fifth; since their own practice is universal, [the title applies accordingly].
Since all are referred to as "disciples," the current text is merely the first "Chapter on Rejoicing," which only identifies the individuals;
it is only in the subsequent "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing" that the merit is formally compared. Question: Why is this so? Answer:

The latter four chapters provide a rough estimation of the merit here, whereas the first chapter provides a detailed estimation there. Having provided a detailed estimation there, it serves to further magnify [the value] here by comparison.
The Victor’s intention is this: if the merit of even the first chapter is already such, how much more so for the four subsequent chapters?

Thus, the Buddha skillfully explains them without burdening the text with excessive words. II. Encouraging Personal Upholding, Retaining, Reading, and Reciting. 1. First, identifying the characteristics of the person.
How much more so for those who read, recite, accept, and uphold it!

Since the first chapter merely involves rejoicing with a straightforward mind, those who go further to accept, uphold, read, and recite it constitute the second chapter, "On Reading and Reciting. △ Second, the formal comparison.

Such a person is one who bears the Tathāgata upon their crown; Ānanda, these sons and daughters of good family need not build stūpas or temples for me, nor construct monasteries, nor provide the four requisites to the Saṃgha. Why is this?
Because those sons and daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sūtra have already built a stūpa.
To construct monasteries and provide offerings to the Saṃgha is equivalent to erecting a stūpa of the seven treasures for the Buddha’s relics,
high and vast, gradually tapering upward to the Brahma-heaven, adorned with hanging banners, canopies, various jeweled bells, flowers, incense, necklaces,
powdered incense, ointments, burning incense, great drums, music, flutes, pipes, lutes, and all manner of dances and performances, accompanied by exquisite sounds.
To sing hymns and offer praises is equivalent to making such offerings for immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of kalpas;

this is the second grade of merit when compared. Fearing that those of initial resolve might be distracted by worldly conditions and hindered from cultivating their primary practice, if they simply recite and uphold this sutra with single-minded devotion, it is as if they were bearing the Tathāgata upon the crown of their heads and making offerings to him.

Regarding the support of the Sangha: this sutra is the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata. If one focuses solely on reading and reciting it, one is thereby "wearing the scripture upon one's head" (*śīrṣa-parigraha*).
Since the scripture is the means of expression (*vācaka*), it is like a stupa that can contain [relics]; thus, there is no need to construct a physical stupa.

The true reality (*dharmatā*) is the object of expression (*vācya*), which is the Dharma-body relic; therefore, there is no need to enshrine the relics of the physical body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The scripture is capable of... [text ends]
Because it honors the Sangha of the ultimate meaning (paramārtha-saṃgha), there is no need to offer worship to the conventional Sangha that follows worldly forms.
△ Third, exhorting others to receive, uphold, read, and recite [this sutra], in two parts: first, identifying the person;
"Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa anyone hears this sutra and is able to receive and uphold it—whether by writing it themselves or by teaching others to do so—"
Regarding the person who writes [the text]:
one who merely recites and maintains it themselves, yet is now further able to teach others, is of the third grade. △ Second, the formal evaluation.
He then established monasteries and constructed thirty-two halls made of red sandalwood, each eight *tāla* trees in height, magnificent and well-adorned in both height and breadth.
Within them resided hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus;
the gardens, bathing pools, walking paths, meditation caves, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions—all such articles of comfort—were fully provided therein.
These monasteries, halls, and pavilions number in the hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions, their count being immeasurable;

by these, one makes offerings before me and the community of bhikṣus. Therefore, I say that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, or explain [this sutra] for others, or who write it themselves or instruct others to write it, and make offerings to the scripture scrolls, they need not rise again.
They build stupas and temples, as well as monasteries, to provide offerings for the assembly of monks.
△ Fourth, regarding those who additionally practice the six perfections: First, the description of their characteristics.
Furthermore, suppose there is a person who can uphold this sutra while additionally practicing giving, morality, patience, diligence, and single-mindedness.
Wisdom. From the first chapter up to this point, if the contemplation of principle has matured, external affairs will not hinder internal matters;

they will instead support the Path, like a fire that blazes more fiercely when there is abundant oil, or a sail raised with the current that gains even greater speed through the application of further effort. △ Second, the formal practice.
Its measure is most supreme, immeasurable and boundless, like space— without limit or boundary in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below;
the merit of this person is likewise immeasurable and boundless, swiftly reaching all.
The Knowledge of All Modes.
△ Fifth, adding its correct practice: the six perfections. First, indicating the characteristics of the person:
if a person reads, recites, receives, and upholds this sutra, explains it for others, writes it themselves, or teaches others to write it; furthermore...
They are able to erect stupas and construct monasteries to make offerings to and praise the assembly of *śrāvaka* monks;

they also praise the merits of bodhisattvas by means of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of methods of praise. Furthermore, for the sake of others, they explain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in various ways according to its meaning.
Moreover, they are able to maintain the precepts purely and dwell together with those who are gentle and harmonious.
Abiding in patience and free from anger, their resolve is firm; they constantly value sitting in meditation and attain all profound concentrations.
With diligent vigor, they gather all wholesome dharmas; possessing sharp faculties and wisdom, they skillfully answer difficult questions.

Regarding the summary of the five stages (*pañca-varga*): the first three stages constitute the stage of wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*); the stage where one concurrently practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) constitutes the stage of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*);

and the stage of correctly practicing the six perfections constitutes the stage of wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*). All of these belong to the period prior to the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Alternatively, it is said that the first "Stage of Rejoicing" (*anumodana-varga*) represents the section on entering the mind of faith; this single stage is divided into two minds, such that the five stages comprise the ten minds of faith.
This is precisely the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties of the Iron Wheel-turning King. △ Second, the formal comparison:

"Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa there are good sons or good daughters who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and who further possess such virtuous merits, you should know that these people have already entered the site of enlightenment and are close to [Buddhahood]."
Under the Bodhi tree where one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, wherever this good man or good woman sits,
stands, or paces back and forth, a stūpa should be erected there; all devas and humans should make offerings to it just as they would to a stūpa of the Buddha.
△ Second, the four verses in verse form; first, the verse for the second chapter.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If, after my parinirvāṇa, one is able to uphold this sutra, the merit of such a person shall be immeasurable, as described above."

This constitutes the fulfillment of all offerings: constructing a stūpa for the śarīra adorned with the seven treasures, its pinnacle exceedingly high and wide, tapering gradually to reach the Brahma-heaven, with billions of precious bells that emit sublime sounds when stirred by the wind;
furthermore, making offerings to this stūpa throughout immeasurable kalpas with flowers, incense, various necklaces, celestial robes, and manifold musical performances.
Furthermore, by constantly illuminating the surroundings with lamps of fragrant oil and ghee throughout the degenerate age at the end of the Dharma,
one who can uphold this sutra will have already provided all the aforementioned offerings in their entirety.
△ Second, the verse on the third chapter:
If one can uphold this sutra, it is as if the Buddha were present in person;

one would establish a monastic residence (saṅghārāma) using gośīrṣa-candana, and provide a hall for offerings thirty-two *tāla* trees high, fully equipped with exquisite food, fine clothing, and bedding.
The dwellings of hundreds of thousands of beings, the gardens, the various bathing pools, the walking paths, and the meditation caves—all were adorned in every way with exquisite beauty.
△ Third, the verses on the fourth chapter:
If there is one who, with a mind of faith and understanding, upholds, recites, copies, or further teaches others to copy [this sutra], and makes offerings to the scripture scrolls.

By scattering flowers, incense, and powdered incense, and by constantly burning perfumed oils such as *sumana*, *campaka*, and *atimuktaka* to make offerings in this manner, one attains immeasurable merit;
its extent is like the boundlessness of space, and the same is true for the merit [of the practitioner].

How much more so for one who upholds this sutra while simultaneously practicing generosity, maintaining the precepts, enduring patience, delighting in meditative concentration, being free from anger, and refraining from harsh speech!
△ Chapter Five: Four Verses.
One who shows reverence to stūpas and shrines, remains humble toward all bhikṣus, stays far removed from self-exaltation, and constantly contemplates wisdom;
one who does not become angry when questioned or challenged, but explains the teachings in accordance with the truth—if one can practice such conduct, their merit shall be immeasurable.
If one sees this Dharma-master endowed with such virtues, one should scatter celestial flowers over him and cover his body with celestial robes;
one should bow one’s head to his feet and pay homage, conceiving of him as a Buddha. Furthermore, one should reflect:

"Before long, he will go to the Tree of Enlightenment and attain the outflow-free and unconditioned state, bringing vast benefit to all humans and devas. One should regard wherever he dwells—whether walking, sitting, or lying down—as a sacred site.
Even for the sake of reciting a single verse therein, one should erect a stūpa, adorning it exquisitely and making various offerings to it.
A Son of the Buddha dwelling on this stage is constantly present within the enjoyment of the Buddhas, walking, sitting, and reclining therein.
Regarding "one who gives rise to the thought of the Buddha": this refers to the person upon whom the first part of this fifth stage relies, and is therefore designated as a Tathāgata.
Regarding "before long he approaches the Tree of Enlightenment": the position of this person in the fifth stage is already within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the iron wheel;
before long, they will enter the first abode (*prathamā bhūmi*) and the copper wheel, capable of manifesting the eight aspects of a Buddha. This is the fifth stage.
Being identical to the fourth stage of faith, this is the stage of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*);

however, regarding the entry into this stage, it is the same as the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*), differing only in that there is a distinction between the period when a Buddha is present in the world and the period after his parinirvāṇa.
△ Second, the Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing (Anumodanā-puṇya). First, the title of the chapter:
*The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Eighteen: The Merit of Rejoicing* (the main text calls it the "Chapter on Encouragement and Assistance").

"Rejoicing" (*anumodanā*) means to celebrate both oneself and others upon hearing the profound and mysterious Dharma, in accordance with the non-dual and undifferentiated nature of phenomena and principle.

The merit of accord with principle consists of substantial virtue; the merit of accord with phenomena consists of skillful means. To rejoice in one’s own attainment is wisdom, while to rejoice in others is compassion.
Because these—skillful means and reality, wisdom and abandonment—are explained in conjunction, it is called the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing.

Furthermore, to accord with principle means that upon hearing of the Buddha’s profound and remote original ground, one believes and follows it without opposition, free from even a hair’s breadth of doubt or obstruction.

One who accords with the practice hears that the Buddha benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, pervading all places both vertically and horizontally, without even a hair’s breadth of doubt or obstruction.
Thus, they penetrate the profound principle through extensive phenomena, and penetrate extensive phenomena through the profound principle.

Though non-dual, there is duality; though not distinct, there is distinction. Yet, despite this duality and distinction, there is neither duality nor distinction. To have such faith and understanding is to accord with the practice.

This is called "Following the Tathāgata’s Appearance in the World": for over forty years, he did not reveal the reality, nor did he speak the ultimate truth regarding the seven stages of skillful means.
Now, this sutra reveals and clarifies it, bringing joy to myself and others.

By using the mind of an ordinary person to equalize what the Buddha knows, and by employing the eyes produced [by this practice] to see as the Tathāgata sees, such knowledge and vision ultimately penetrate the Dharma-realm. Furthermore...
There is nothing superior to this; it is called "Rejoicing. The Buddha now speaks of this, and because I have heard it, it is named the "Fifty-first Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing.
Among these five grades of practice, this is the initial chapter on Rejoicing.
At the very first thought, there is but a single moment of understanding and a single moment of celebrating oneself and others; as yet, there is no matter of actual practice or grace.
The merit obtained by others cannot compare to that of the Tathāgata’s skillful parables, which surpass even those of the Aśaikṣas;
how much more so for those who hear them for the first time within this assembly, and how much more so for those who hear them in the second, third, fourth, or fifth assemblies?

The Tathāgata has spoken of these profound and wondrous merits to inspire people with admiration, as detailed in the "Chapter on the Excellence of the Dharma Master," the "Chapter on Upholding," and the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits."
When the fourfold faith and the five stages were praised for the merit of upholding this sutra, the assembly could not fathom the greatness of the merit of those at the initial stage of the path;
they all believed these individuals had already entered the rank of the true cause (bhūta-hetu). Yet, such virtue was produced from the very first moment of the initial mind.

They suddenly conceived a notion of weakness and insignificance, yet they heard that the roots of a tree planted in good soil have already reached a girth of a hundred spans, and the kalaviṅka bird within its egg possesses a voice more excellent [than any other].
Because of this, the assembly of birds now demonstrates that while their practice is shallow, their merit is profound, thereby revealing the rare and extraordinary power of the sutra;

thus, light doubts are dispelled. Those outside the Way who have attained the five supernatural powers can move mountains and dry up the oceans, yet they cannot subdue the fetters of views and craving, nor reach the stage of "warmth.
Even the disciples of the Two Vehicles who are beyond training, having attained liberation in both cause and fruit, are still bound by *nirvāṇa*.

Knowing that both cause and effect are provisional, those who follow the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) may employ skillful means in their cultivation of the cause, yet they do not recognize the five hundred *yojanas* when first resolving their minds;

thus, upon attaining the fruit, they merely eliminate the four abodes (*catur-vāsa*). Although the distinct teaching (Biren) is superior to the two vehicles, its cultivation of the cause is partial and its approach is clumsy;
it is not praised by the Buddha and does not equal the person who rejoices at the beginning. △ Second, the scriptural text has two parts.
First Question:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, rejoice in it, how much merit do they obtain? And he spoke these verses:
After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, if there are those who hear this sutra and are able to rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain?
△ Second, the answer, which has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. In the first part, there are again two sections.
First, the answer for those who rejoice inwardly, which has five sub-sections. The first is the successive teaching.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ajita: “Ajita, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or other wise persons— whether old or young— who, having heard this sutra, rejoice in it,
and then depart from the assembly to another place, whether it be a monastery or a secluded spot;”
If, in cities, market streets, villages, and rural hamlets, one expounds this according to what has been heard for the sake of parents,
kinsmen, good friends, and acquaintances to the best of one's ability, and these people, having heard it, rejoice and in turn teach others;
and those others, having heard it, likewise rejoice and teach others— thus it is passed on in succession until the fiftieth person.
The two schools, North and South, explain that fifty people do not understand the intent of the sutra; the present explanation divides them into two categories.

First, regarding the horizontal correlation with the various teachings: for example, within the Three Baskets (Tripitaka), there are four gates, and each gate contains the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus and so forth.
If one further distinguishes śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, this makes six persons per gate; across the four gates, this results in twenty-four people. Furthermore, this is correlated with faith...
Regarding the practice of the Dharma-practice (dharmacaryā), there are forty-eight people; including the first and the last, there are fifty people in total.

This applies equally to the four gates of both the general and specific teachings. If one calculates directly according to the Perfect Teaching (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa) gate, the method of counting consists of seven small sevens, seven large sevens, and seven times seven, totaling forty-nine.
All of these represent the successive instruction between teacher and disciple, wherein each is fully endowed [with the teaching].
Regarding the virtue of benefiting oneself and others, it applies only to the very last individual;

however, because this person possesses only the virtue of self-liberation and lacks the virtue of teaching others, the lower category is set aside to manifest the excellence of the higher. △ Second, the comparative evaluation of the fundamental [categories].
Ajita, I shall now describe the merit of the rejoicing performed by those fifty million sons and daughters of good family;
you should listen well. Suppose there were beings in four million *asamkhyeya* worlds—beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth:

born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether they have form or are formless, possess perception or are without perception, or are neither—[if all these beings were to...]
Regarding those beings included within the category of sentient beings— whether they possess no thought, or have one thought, two feet, four feet, or many feet—
if there is someone seeking merit who provides them with all the articles of enjoyment according to their desires, giving to each single being as much gold,
silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, and various other exquisite treasures as would fill the entirety of Jambudvīpa.
Jewels, elephants, horses, carriages, and palaces and towers made of the seven treasures—such was the great donor’s practice of giving.

After he had practiced such generosity for eighty full years, he thought to himself: "I have already bestowed upon sentient beings all manner of articles for their enjoyment, according to their every desire.
Yet these sentient beings are all in decline; they are over eighty years old, with white hair and aged faces."
"Chou will die before long; I shall instruct and guide him with the Buddha-dharma.

He then gathered these sentient beings and proclaimed the transformation of the Dharma, teaching, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, so that at once they all attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the stage of *anāgāmin*, and the stage of *arhat*.
They exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and attained mastery over profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
The eight liberations.
△ Third, raising the intention to inquire:
"What do you think? Is the merit obtained by this great donor much or not?"
△ 4. Answering with Sincerity.
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the merit of such a person is exceedingly great, immeasurable, and boundless.
If a donor were to bestow all manner of articles of pleasure upon sentient beings, their merit would already be immeasurable; how much more so if they cause them to attain arhatship?"
The Result.
△ Fifth, the formal comparison.
The Buddha said to Maitreya: "I shall now distinguish and tell you: suppose this person were to bestow all manner of articles of pleasure upon the four [classes of beings]..."
The merit obtained by all sentient beings of the six realms throughout hundreds of billions of asaṃkhyeya worlds, even if they were to attain the fruit of arhatship,
would not equal that of the fiftieth person who hears a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and rejoices;
it does not approach even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-billionth part of that merit, nor can it be reached by any calculation, analogy, or comparison.
Ajita, you cannot know the measure of the merit of the fiftieth person who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* through successive transmission and rejoices in it;
it is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).
How much more so for those who hear it and rejoice at the very beginning of the assembly—their merit is even more supreme, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable, beyond all comparison.
In this comparative evaluation, first one bestows worldly happiness to extract the suffering of the fruits [of karma], and subsequently bestows *nirvāṇa* to extract the suffering of birth and death;
this is a brief enumeration of Brahma-merit used for comparison. To speak more extensively, the merit of all people filling Jambudvīpa does not equal the merit of a single person in Aparagoyānī;
the merit of all people filling Aparagoyānī does not equal that of a single person in Pūrvavideha.
The merit of one person in Pūrvavideha is equal to the merit of all people in the three continents; the merit of all people in the four continents is not equal to that of one person in Uttarakuru.
The merit of all people in the four continents is not equal to that of one Cāturmahārājakāyika deva; the merit of the Cāturmahārājakāyikas is not equal to that of one Śakra;
and so on, up to the sixth heaven, which is not equal to the merit of one Brahmā. The merit of all those in the Brahma realm is not equal to [the merit of] one... [Brahmā].
Furthermore, the merit of the noble ones of the three vehicles within the Tripitaka teachings does not equal that of the Shared [Vehicle]; the Shared does not equal the Distinct;
and the Distinct does not equal the merit of a person who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* from the very beginning in the "Chapter on Rejoicing.

Why is this? Because those former three belong to the three vehicles and are not the Buddha-dharma; they are provisional and not ultimate; they are partial and not perfect. Although one may abide in the latter [stages], [the merit of the former] is inferior.
The meaning is that the fruit does not equal my initial resolve; it is thus. △ Second, directly clarifying those who listen as outsiders, part four:
first, going oneself to listen.
Furthermore, Ajita, if a person, for the sake of this sutra, goes to a monastery and sits or stands there for even a brief moment—
Through the condition of hearing and receiving [the Dharma], by virtue of this merit, one will be reborn with excellent and sublime elephant and horse carriages,
precious palanquins, and celestial palaces. (2) Second,
the section on sitting upon seats.
Furthermore, if there is a person sitting at a place where the Dharma is being taught, and another person comes and encourages them to sit and listen, or offers them a seat to sit upon,
the merit of this person will cause them to obtain, in their next rebirth, the seat of Śakra, the seat of Brahmā,
or the seat of a Wheel-Turning King.
△ Third, exhorting others to listen:
"Ajita, if there is another person who says to someone else, 'There is a sutra named the Lotus Sutra;
we should go together to hear it,' and that person accepts this instruction and hears it for even a brief moment, the merit of this person will cause them to obtain the *dhāraṇī* upon rebirth."
A bhikṣuṇī and a bodhisattva dwelling together in one place will possess keen faculties and wisdom;

for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, they shall never be mute or speech-impaired, their breath shall not be foul, and their tongues shall always be free from disease. Their mouths shall likewise be free from ailment;

their teeth shall not be stained or black, nor yellow, nor sparse, nor missing, nor uneven, nor crooked; their lips shall not hang down, nor be drawn back, nor be coarse and rough, nor afflicted with sores.
The nostrils are neither deficient nor damaged, neither crooked nor slanted; they are neither thick nor large, neither dark nor black, and free from all loathsome qualities.
The nose is not flat or bulbous, nor is it curved or distorted; the facial complexion is neither black nor narrow and long, nor is it sunken or twisted—there is not a single disagreeable feature.
The lips, tongue, teeth, and gums are all perfectly beautiful, and the nose is long and prominent.
With a face of perfect symmetry, high and long eyebrows, and a broad, level forehead, he was endowed with all the marks of a superior person;
in every birth throughout his successive lives, he beheld the Buddhas, heard the Dharma, and faithfully accepted their teachings.
Zhang’an says: This passage also contains the merits of the six sense organs. Sharp faculties and wisdom are the merit of the mind; not being mute or speech-impaired is the merit of the tongue;
the nose being well-cultivated, elevated, and straight is the merit of the nose; seeing the Buddha is the merit of the eyes;
hearing the Dharma is the merit of the ears; the remainder are the merits of the body. The preceding [section] concerns the merits of the stage of semblance.
This merit is merely the preliminary virtue of the stage of semblance. △ Fourth, the merit of listening and practicing:
"Ajita, you should observe that the merit of exhorting even a single person to go and listen to the Dharma is such as this;
how much more so for one who listens with a single mind, hears, recites, and explains it in detail for the sake of the great assembly, and practices according to what has been taught?"

"The merit obtained by the person at the end shall now be analyzed.
Suppose there were a great donor who provided immeasurable necessities for eighty years, fulfilling every desire; yet, seeing that person’s signs of aging—hair white and face wrinkled—"
With teeth sparse and his form withered, he knew that his death would not be long. "I should now instruct him so that he may attain the fruit of the Path.
He then employed skillful means to preach the true Dharma of Nirvana: "All things in the world are not solid; they are like foam, bubbles, and flames.
You all should swiftly give rise to a mind of weary detachment. Upon hearing this Dharma, all those people attained Arhatship.
They are fully endowed with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣāḥ*).

△ Second, the verse on those who listen to the Dharma from outside, in four parts: first, the verse that anticipates the exhortation to listen.
If there is someone who encourages another person to go and listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, saying, "This sutra is profound and subtle;

it is difficult to encounter even in ten million kalpas," and that person follows this instruction and goes to listen—even for a mere moment—the merit and reward of such a person shall now be explained in detail:

from lifetime to lifetime, they will have no afflictions of the mouth; their teeth will not be sparse, yellow, or black; their lips will not be thick, curled, or cleft; and they will possess no loathsome features.
His tongue was not dry, black, or short; his nose was high, long, and straight; his forehead was broad and even; and his entire countenance was upright and majestic, pleasing to all who beheld him.
His breath was free from foul odors, and the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus constantly issued from his mouth.

If, at a place where the Dharma is being expounded, one encourages others to sit and listen to the sutras, through this causal condition of merit, one will obtain the seats of Śakra, Brahmā, or a Cakravartin King.
△ Fourth, the verse on listening and cultivation.
How much more so for one who listens with a single mind, explains its meaning and intent, and practices according to those teachings—their merit would be beyond measure.
△ Third, the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" clarifies the merits of the fruit of the first chapter and exhorts the circulation [of the sutra]. Part One:
The Title of the Chapter.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Nineteen: The Merits of the Dharma-Preacher (the main text calls it the Chapter Praising the Dharma-Preacher).
Regarding the meaning of "Dharma-preacher," it is as explained in the Chapter on the Dharma-Preacher.

As for "merits," the previous chapter discussed the merits of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), which refers to the merits at the very beginning of the first of the five stages, situated prior to the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*). This present chapter concerns the Dharma-preacher.

"Merit" refers to the merit of the purification of the six sense faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi) belonging to the five grades above [the ten abodes], which corresponds to the stage of semblance within the ten faiths (daśa-śraddhā).

By means of this merit, one is adorned both internally and externally: the purification of the five sense faculties is called external adornment, while the purification of the mental faculty (manas) is called internal adornment.
Furthermore, it encompasses all forms and images from the hells upward, up to the Buddha.

That which manifests entirely within the body is called internal adornment; that which externally transforms all forms and images from the hells up to the Buddha through the Samādhi of Universal Manifestation is called external adornment. Just as it is with the faculty of the body, so it is with the other five faculties.
Just as reciting and chanting results in the purification of the six faculties, so too do upholding, explaining, and transcribing [the teachings].
Now, within the five grades, if the purification of the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*) in the first grade is already thus, it is even more so for the subsequent four grades.
If the semblance purification of the six faculties is already thus, it is doubly so for those of partial realization (*bhūta-tattva*). (For the world:

When practitioners hear of these merits and benefits, they rejoice beyond measure, seeking them with tireless diligence, their faith and progress doubling. (For others: They clearly recognize that there exists the Mahāyāna.

Possessing great power, one is decisively free from the net of doubt (the antidote). At the very beginning of what appears to be understanding, one surpasses the ultimate limit of the two vehicles by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
This indicates the beginning and reveals the end; it is a suspended liberation that culminates in the inconceivable ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
What is elucidated in this chapter is fully endowed with these four meanings, and because they constitute the merit of the Dharma Master, it is so stated.
This is the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master. △ Second, the main text has two parts. First, a general enumeration of the expansion and contraction of the merits of the six sense organs.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Constantly Diligent: "If a good man or a good woman receives..."
Whoever upholds this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*— whether by reading, reciting, explaining, or transcribing it— shall obtain eight hundred merits of the eye,
twelve hundred merits of the ear, eight hundred merits of the nose, twelve hundred merits of the tongue, eight hundred merits of the body,
and twelve hundred merits of the mind; by these merits, they shall adorn the six sense faculties.
All are rendered pure. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Because form is pure, prajñā is pure; because prajñā is pure, form is pure. Because form is pure, the five faculties are pure;
because prajñā is pure, the mental faculty is pure. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is fully endowed with six thousand merits.
The Treatise states: "Ordinary people, by the power of the sutras, attain superior sensory faculties;
although they have not yet entered the First Stage (bhūmi), they can see the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm with the physical eyes born of their parents. The Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
"A single faculty of the Tathāgata is able to see forms, hear sounds, smell fragrances, distinguish flavors, perceive tangibles, and know dharmas. Now, in this sūtra, the six faculties are purified.

It shares with the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dapin) that these merits adorn the six sense faculties; it shares with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Zhengfahua) regarding the smelling of odors, seeing forms, hearing sounds, and the faculty of cognition;
it shares with the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* regarding the functions of the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom-eye, and the Dharma-eye;

and it shares with the treatises regarding the enumeration of the six thousand merits. If one clarifies these six thousand merits, they are established according to the three karmas of the *Anrakugyō* (Practice of Peaceful Conduct).

There are ten wholesome acts; each one of these ten contains ten, which makes one hundred wholesome acts. Within these one hundred wholesome acts, each one further contains ten, thus making one thousand wholesome acts.

When these are categorized according to self-cultivation and transforming others, they become two thousand. Taking into account the Tathāgata’s chamber, the Tathāgata’s robe, and the Tathāgata’s seat, they total six thousand.
The five kinds of Dharma-preachers all possess the purity of the six sense faculties, and each individual faculty is [complete].
There are one thousand merits. Furthermore, within a single mind, the ten dharma-realms are fully present;
each realm possesses ten suchnesses, which together constitute one hundred. When each of these roots universally encompasses the six sense objects, there are six hundred.
By combining the two adornments of samādhi and prajñā, they become one thousand two hundred. Each and every root is thus fully endowed with the adornments of both samādhi and prajñā.
There are one thousand two hundred. If one discusses the purity of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*), that purity is not described in terms of merit—whether it be much or little.
If one speaks of adornment, it can be expanded and can be contracted, yet it can also be made equal;

this "equal adornment" means six thousand for each organ. If one speaks of one thousand two hundred, it manifests its capacity for expansion; if one speaks of eight hundred, it manifests... [its capacity for contraction].

If one can understand that [the faculties] can contract, and that they are pure, without expansion or contraction, and without equality—because the six sense organs function interchangeably, because the organs are sovereign, and because this is inconceivable—then to judge it from a partial perspective would be to lose the essential meaning.
△ Second, the separate composition of six chapters; the first is the analysis and explanation of the eye organ (1). First, the long prose section.
These sons and daughters of good family, with the pure physical eye born of their parents, see all that exists within and without the trichiliocosm—
from the mountains, forests, rivers, and seas down to the Avīci Hell, and up to the Peak of Existence—
and they see all sentient beings therein, as well as their karmic causes and conditions, their retributions, and their places of birth, seeing them all clearly.
[The Buddha] knew.
△ Second, the verse summary:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
If one preaches this Lotus Sūtra amidst the great assembly with a mind free from fear, listen to its merits:
such a person shall obtain eight hundred meritorious and preeminent eyes;

because they are adorned by these, their vision is exceedingly pure, and with the eyes born of their parents, they see the entirety of the three thousandfold world-system, including the inner and outer Mount Merus, Mount Sumeru, and the Iron Ring Mountains.
Furthermore, all sentient beings within the various mountains, forests, great oceans, rivers, and streams— from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence above—
shall all see [him], even though they have not yet attained the divine eye and their power of physical vision remains as it was.

That which is produced by one's parents is called the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*); yet, if it can see both the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm, then what is seen exceeds that of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*).
The divine eye obtained as a karmic reward by Brahmā kings is able to see throughout the great trichiliocosm within their own realm;

however, beyond the great trichiliocosm there is a wind-wheel that acts as an obstruction to the eye, preventing them from seeing what lies outside. If they were in another realm, this would not be the case.
Because the entire trichiliocosm is not under one's own governance, a Lesser Arhat sees a small thousand-fold world system, while a Great Arhat sees a great thousand-fold world system;
a Pratyekabuddha sees a hundred Buddha-worlds. These are not obstructed by wind-circles, nor are they separated by the boundaries of self and other realms.
In this sutra and treatise, the eye that can see the interior and exterior of a great thousand-fold world system must be the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), yet it is still so named [as "the eye"].

Regarding the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*): within the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-avasthā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), by the power of the sūtras, it possesses the function of a superior eye;
yet, as true reality has not yet been manifested, it cannot be called the "heavenly eye" (*divya-cakṣus*). Although it is called the fleshly eye, it possesses the functions of all five eyes:

it sees the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm with the function of the heavenly eye; it sees all sentient beings along with their karmic causes and conditions with the function of the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*); its vision is exceedingly [vast]...
The function of the pure eye of wisdom (*vimala-prajñā-cakṣus*) is to see all at once the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm, seeing both karma and purity;
it is also perfectly able to subdue the delusions of ignorance within the Middle Way. The function of the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) is vast; as the Mahāyāna sūtras state:
"Though one possesses the fleshly eye, it is called the Buddha-eye. Because the Buddha-eye is named "pure" and is endowed with the five eyes, it is said that its adornment is capable of fulfillment.

Since "capable of contracting" is termed the "superior faculty" (*indriya*) and its function is termed "mastery over the faculties" (*indriyavaśitā*), how could it be interpreted merely as eight hundred or twelve hundred [yojanas]?
△ Second, the Ear Faculty (2): First, the prose section.

they will attain the merit of twelve hundred ears. With these purified ears,
they will hear all the various sounds within and without the trichiliocosm, from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above.
The various kinds of speech and sounds: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of oxen, the sound of chariots, the sound of weeping,
the sound of lamentation, the sound of conchs, the sound of drums, the sound of bells, the sound of gongs, the sound of laughter, the sound of conversation, the voices of men, the voices of women,

The voices of devas, the voices of nāgas, the voices of yakṣas, the voices of gandharvas, the voices of asuras, the voices of garuḍas, the voices of kiṃnaras, the voices of mahoragas;

Regarding the sounds of Buddhas, to speak briefly:
although one has not yet attained the divine ear, one hears and knows all internal and external sounds within the trichiliocosm with the pure, ordinary ear born of one's parents;
