△ Second, the verses in praise.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"With the ears born of one's parents, pure and free from turbidity or defilement, with these constant ears one hears the sounds of the three thousandfold world-system."
The sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and oxen; the sounds of bells, gongs, conchs, and drums; the sounds of lutes, harps, and *konghou* zithers; the sounds of flutes and pipes;
the sounds of pure and beautiful songs—listening to these, one is not attached to them. One hears the voices of countless kinds of people and can understand them all.
Furthermore, one hears the subtle and wondrous singing voices of the devas, as well as the voices of men and women, and the voices of boys and girls.
In the midst of mountains, rivers, and perilous valleys, the cries of the kalaviṅka, the jīvajīvaka, and all other such birds are heard;
the sounds of various agonies and bitter torments of the beings in the hells; the sounds of hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst, seeking food and drink;
and the great sounds produced when the asuras dwelling on the shores of the great ocean converse among themselves.
Thus, the teacher of the Dharma dwells here and hears these various sounds from afar without his faculty of hearing being impaired;
he hears all the cries of birds and beasts calling to one another throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
as well as the voices and speech of the Brahma heavens, including those of Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, and up to the pinnacle of existence (Bhavāgra).

Wherever the Dharma Master dwells, he hears them all: whether it be the entire assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs reciting the sūtras or preaching the Dharma to others, wherever the Dharma Master dwells, he hears them all;
furthermore, wherever there are bodhisattvas reciting the sūtras and teachings, or preaching them to others, or compiling and explaining their meanings, [he hears them all].
All such sounds and voices are heard: those of the Great Holy Buddhas who teach and transform sentient beings as they expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma within great assemblies;
and all who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* shall likewise hear them.
Furthermore, all sounds within and without the trichiliocosm—from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above—are heard.
All hear their voices without their faculty of hearing being impaired; because their ears are keen and sharp, they are all able to discern and understand them.
Thus, even though those who uphold this Lotus Sūtra have not yet attained the divine ear, the merit of the ears with which they were born is already such as this.

The faculty of hearing also possesses the five functions of the ear; therefore, it is able to universally hear the sounds of the ten dharma-realms, both internal and external, throughout the great trichiliocosm.
Hearing the sounds of the six realms of existence is the function of the fleshly ear and the heavenly ear; hearing the sounds of the two vehicles is the function of the wisdom ear;

hearing the sounds of bodhisattvas is the function of the dharma ear; and hearing the sounds of the Buddhas is the function of the Buddha-ear. Furthermore, that which is produced by one's parents is...

The fleshly ear can hear both the internal and external; this is the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*). Hearing without attachment is the wisdom ear (*prajñā-śrotra*), which is fully capable of discernment;
this is the Dharma ear (*dharma-śrotra*). Hearing simultaneously and mutually is the Buddha ear (*buddha-śrotra*). By analogy with the ear, it is the same for the eye:
seeing humans and devas is the fleshly eye and the divine eye; seeing the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) is the wisdom eye; seeing Bodhisattvas is the Dharma eye.
To see the Buddha with the eye is the Buddha-eye. △ Third, the faculty of the nose (2): First, the prose section.

Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if good sons or good daughters receive and uphold this sutra—whether reading it, reciting it, explaining it, or copying it—they will accomplish eight hundred merits of the nose.
By means of this pure faculty of the nose, they shall hear...
Within the trichiliocosm, there are various kinds of fragrances— above, below, and within and without— including the scents of *sumanā* flowers,
*jāti* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *pāṭala* flowers,
red lotuses, blue lotuses, and white lotuses; as well as the scents of flowering trees, fruit-bearing trees, sandalwood, and aloeswood.
Whether it be tagara incense, tamāla-patra incense, kālānusāri incense, or ten million varieties of blended perfumes— whether in powder form, pill form, or as unguents—
one who upholds this sutra, while dwelling in this world, is able to distinguish them all; furthermore, they specifically know the scents of sentient beings,
the scents of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and goats, as well as the scents of men, women, boys, and girls.
Whether near or far, all fragrances— those of incense, herbs, grasses, and groves— he shall perceive without error;
one who upholds this sutra, even while dwelling here, shall likewise smell the scents of the various devas in the heavens,
the fragrance of the pārijātaka and kovidāra trees, and the scent of the māndārava and mahāmāndārava flowers.
He perceives and knows every fragrance produced from the blending of celestial incenses—
such as the fragrance of *roca*, *māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*, sandalwood, aloeswood, various powdered incenses, and diverse flower perfumes—
as well as the bodily fragrances of the devas. He also perceives Śakra Devānām Indra enjoying the five desires within his magnificent palace.

Whether the fragrance is present when they are sporting in the Sudharmā Hall while preaching the Dharma to the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, or when they are sporting in the various gardens, or the fragrance from the bodies of the male and female deities of other heavens—all these are smelled from afar.
In this manner, it extends successively even to the Brahma worlds and up to the Akanistha heaven; the fragrances from the bodies of all those gods are likewise smelled. And...
They smell from afar the incense burned by the devas, as well as the fragrance of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the bodily fragrance of the Buddhas;
they know their locations even as they smell these fragrances. Yet, although they smell these fragrances, their faculty of the nose is neither impaired nor deluded;
if they wish to discern them and explain them to others, their recollection is unerring.
△ Second, the verses in praise.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The nose of this person is purified; within this world, whether it be fragrant or foul things, he perceives and knows all varieties."
The fragrance of various flowers and fruits— such as sumana, jāti, tamāla, sandalwood, aloeswood, and cinnamon— as well as the scents of sentient beings,
including those of men and women, and the scent of the Dharma-preacher, allow one who dwells afar to perceive their location upon smelling these odors.

Furthermore, the scent of the great powerful universal monarchs, the minor wheel-turning kings, their sons, ministers, and palace attendants allows one to know their whereabouts upon smelling their fragrance.
By smelling the fragrance, one knows the location of the precious jewels worn upon the body, the treasures hidden in the earth, and the precious women of the wheel-turning kings;
by smelling the fragrance, one knows the ornaments for the body, the clothing, the necklaces, and the various types of ointments applied by people;

and by smelling the fragrance, one can fully know whether the devas are walking, sitting, sporting, or performing spiritual transformations—all this is known by those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The fragrances of the flowers, fruits, and kernels of all trees, as well as the scent of clarified butter—those who uphold this sutra dwelling here shall know their locations entirely.
In the deep and perilous places among the mountains where sandalwood trees are in bloom and sentient beings dwell therein, they shall be able to know them all by scent.
Within the Iron Ring Mountains, the great oceans, and the earth, all sentient beings who hear the fragrance shall have their locations known by those who uphold this sutra.
When the male and female asuras and their various retinues engage in combat or sport, they can know [all things] by smelling their fragrance.

In vast wildernesses and perilous narrow passes, they can smell the scent of lions, elephants, tigers, wolves, wild oxen, water buffaloes, and the like, and by smelling their scent, they know their locations.
If there are those who are pregnant, they can know whether it is a boy or a girl; they can also smell and fully discern those who are rootless or non-human beings.
By the power of smelling fragrances, they know whether a woman has recently conceived and whether she will achieve a safe delivery or give birth to a blessed son;
by the power of smelling fragrances, they know the thoughts of men and women—whether their minds are stained by desire, delusion, or anger—and they also know those who cultivate goodness.
They can perceive all hidden treasures within the earth, such as gold, silver, various precious gems, and copper vessels, simply by smelling their fragrance.
There are various kinds of necklaces whose prices no one can appraise, yet by smelling their fragrance, one knows their value, origin, and location;
likewise, by smelling the fragrance of the celestial flowers such as the *māndārava*, *mañjūṣaka*, and *pāriyātraka* trees, one is able to know them all;
and by smelling the fragrance of the celestial palaces distinguished as superior, middling, or inferior, adorned with various precious flowers, one is able to know them all.

In the midst of the celestial gardens, excellent palaces, and various pavilions, there is a Hall of Sublime Dharma where they find entertainment; by smelling their fragrance, he can know all the devas—
whether they are listening to the Dharma or indulging in the five desires, as they come and go, walk, stand, sit, or lie down—
and by smelling their fragrance, he can know all the celestial maidens, adorned with fine garments and exquisite flowers and perfumes, as they move about and sport.
In this manner, proceeding upward through successive stages as far as the Brahma-world, those who enter and emerge from dhyāna can perceive all by means of their sense of smell;
they can perceive all by means of their sense of smell, from the Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna heavens up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), including those first born there and those passing away.
As for the assembly of bhikṣus who are always diligent in the Dharma—whether sitting, walking, or reciting the scriptures—they too can perceive them all by means of their sense of smell.
Or those who, beneath forest trees, sit with single-minded devotion in meditation or uphold the sutras—their locations are all known by the scent.
Whether Bodhisattvas of firm resolve sit in meditation, recite and chant, or preach the Dharma for others, their presence in every direction is fully known by the scent.
O World-Honored One, those whom all revere, who preach the Dharma out of compassion for the multitudes—their presence is likewise fully known by the scent.
When sentient beings hear this sutra before the Buddha, they all rejoice and practice in accordance with the Dharma. By smelling [this fragrance], they are able to know all things;
although they have not yet attained the bodhisattva’s untainted dharma (anāsrava-dharma), those who uphold this sutra first attain this mark of the nose.
The faculty of the nose likewise possesses five functions: the fleshly nose born of one's parents; the celestial nose that perceives all fragrances within and without the great trichiliocosm;
the wisdom nose that is untainted and unattached; the dharma nose that discerns without error;

and the Buddha nose that employs these functions simultaneously and interchangeably. As for the interchangeable function of the nose faculty, it is the nose that knows the good and the bad and distinguishes the noble from the base.

When one of low station beholds the adornments of the celestial palaces, the nose possesses the function of the eye; when reading scriptures or preaching the Dharma, one is able to know through the scent, so the nose possesses the function of the ear;
when knowing the fragrances of various flowers, fruits, and essences such as ghee and oil, the nose possesses the function of the tongue;

and upon entering or emerging from dhyāna—wherein there are the eight tactile sensations (*spraṣṭavya*) and the play of the five desires—all these are likewise the phenomena of touch, which are heard.

If the nose can perceive fragrance, it possesses the bodily function; if it also perceives a mind stained by desire, delusion, or anger, as well as the cultivation of wholesome states and so forth, then the nose possesses the mental function.
If the sovereign and superior function of the nose faculty is such as this, then the same applies to the other five faculties.
△ Fourth, the faculty of the tongue; Part Two: First, the prose section.

Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they shall obtain twelve hundred merits of the tongue.
Whether [the food] be pleasant or unpleasant, delicious or not...

Whatever delicious, bitter, or astringent things come into contact with his tongue-root, they all transform into the supreme flavor, like celestial nectar (*amṛta*), such that there is nothing that is not delicious.
If he uses his tongue-root to deliver discourses within a great assembly, he produces a profound and wondrous sound that can enter their hearts, causing them all to rejoice and experience happiness.
Furthermore, when the sons of gods, daughters of gods, Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas hear him...
When this profound and wondrous voice delivers any discourse or explanation, the sequence of its teachings is heard by all who come to listen:

nāgas and nāga daughters, yakṣas and yakṣa daughters, gandharvas and gandharva daughters, asuras and asura daughters, garuḍas and garuḍa daughters, kiṃnaras and kiṃnara daughters, mahoragas and... [mahoraga daughters].
The *hūlaga* women all came to approach, revere, and make offerings for the sake of hearing the Dharma;
as did the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; kings, princes, ministers, and their retinues;

minor wheel-turning kings (*kṣudra-cakravartin*), and great wheel-turning kings (*mahā-cakravartin*) with their seven treasures, their thousand sons, and their internal and external retinues—all arrived together upon their palaces to hear the Dharma.
Because this bodhisattva skillfully expounds the Dharma, the brahmins, householders, and all the people within the kingdom attend upon and make offerings to him for as long as they live.
Furthermore, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas always delight in seeing him.
In whichever direction this person resides, all the buddhas turn toward that place and preach the Dharma; he is able to receive and uphold it all.
The Buddha-dharma can also produce the sounds of profound and wondrous Dharma.
The faculty of the tongue likewise possesses the functions of five tongues, capable of producing the speech of the six realms;

specifically, the three tongues of flesh, heaven, and wisdom can produce the speech of the two vehicles; and the tongue of Dharma can produce the speech of Bodhisattvas—all functioning simultaneously and interchangeably.
This is the Buddha’s tongue. △ Second, the verse recapitulation:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The tongue-faculty of such a person is pure; they shall never again experience foul flavors. Whatever they consume or eat shall all become nectar."

Using a profound, pure, and wondrous voice, he preaches the Dharma to the great assembly; through various causes, conditions, and parables, he guides the minds of sentient beings, so that all who hear it rejoice.

They offer all manner of supreme offerings, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others all come together with reverent hearts to listen to this Dharma. If this preacher of the Dharma wishes to employ a wondrous voice...

Pervading the trichiliocosm, he can reach any place at will; the great and small wheel-turning kings, along with their retinues of a thousand sons, constantly come with palms joined in reverence to hear and receive the Dharma.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas also constantly delight in coming to make offerings with joyful hearts. So too do Brahmā-deva, Māra-rāja, Īśvara, and Maheśvara.

Thus, the hosts of devas constantly come to his abode; the Buddhas and their disciples, hearing the sound of his preaching the Dharma, always keep him in mind and protect him, and sometimes manifest themselves before him.
△ Section Five: The Body-Faculty (Kāyendriya), Part Two:

Initial Prose Exposition. Furthermore, Constantly Diligent One, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they shall obtain eight hundred merits of the body and attain a pure body like clear lapis lazuli.
Because the body of the sentient being Joy-to-See was pure, the births and deaths of all beings in the trichiliocosm— whether high or low, beautiful or ugly,
born in good or evil realms— all appeared within it; likewise, the Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains,
Mount Meru, Mount Mahāmeru, and all other mountains, as well as the sentient beings dwelling therein, all appeared within it.
From the Avīci Hell below to the Peak of Existence above, all things and all sentient beings appear within it;
the forms and images of the Dharma teachings preached by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas all appear within his body.
The body-faculty possesses the five functions of the body: all that exists in the world manifests within the body as the function of the physical body;

reaching upward to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it manifests within the body as the function of the celestial body; for the followers of the Two Vehicles, it manifests within the body as the function of the wisdom-body (*prajñā-kāya*);
for Bodhisattvas, it manifests within the body as the function of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*); and for Buddhas, it manifests within the body as... [the Buddha-body].
The functions of the Buddha-body: at one time they manifest perfectly; at one time they function reciprocally; at one time they are without error;
at one time they are without attachment. △ Second, the verse summary:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
If one upholds the Lotus Sūtra, their body becomes exceedingly pure, like that clear lapis lazuli which all sentient beings joyfully behold;
it is also like a pure, bright mirror in which all forms and images are fully seen.

Within this pure body, the Bodhisattva perceives everything that exists in the world, clearly understanding it alone while others do not see it—the entirety of all living beings within the three thousandfold world system.
The forms of devas, asuras, hell-beings, pretas, and animals—all such images appear within his body.

The palaces of the devas and others, up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), as well as the Iron Ring Mountains (*cakravāḍa*), Mount Meru, Mahāmeru, and all the great oceans, all appear within his body.
Furthermore, the Buddhas, śrāvakas, and bodhisattvas, the sons of the Buddha, all appear therein.

Whether alone or in the midst of a multitude, they manifest when preaching the Dharma; although they have not yet attained the wondrous body of the untainted dharma-nature, all things appear within it by virtue of its pure and eternal essence.
△ Sixth, the faculty of mind (manas-indriya), part two: first, the prose section.

Furthermore, Constant Diligence, if a son or daughter of good family, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they shall obtain twelve hundred merits of the mental faculty. By means of this purity...
With a purified mental faculty, from hearing a single verse or a single line until one penetrates immeasurable and boundless meanings,
having understood these meanings, one is able to expound upon a single line or a single verse for a month, four months, or even a year;
all the teachings thus spoken accord with their intended meaning and do not contradict the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), whether they speak of worldly scriptures or...
Whether it be writing, worldly discourse, or activities for sustaining life—all such things accord with the True Dharma.
He fully knows the mental activities, the movements of the mind, and the conceptual proliferations of all sentient beings throughout the six realms within the trichiliocosm.
Although he has not yet attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), his faculty of mind is thus purified; this is how that person reflects upon all things.
All deliberations and speech are the Buddha-dharma; none are not true, and this is also what was spoken in the sutras of former Buddhas.
The faculty of mind (*manas*) likewise possesses the five functions of the mind. All worldly livelihoods and productive enterprises accord with the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
That which is the purification of human intent is the practice of the heavens; that which is the movement of the heavens is the purification of heavenly intent. The four months are the four.
The first month of the year consists of twelve days; these are the twelve links of dependent origination, which do not contradict the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Thus, the purity of the mind of wisdom is attained. The second month consists of one day; this is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which is the purity of the Bodhisattva’s mind.

All that can be measured in this way has been taught in the sutras of the former Buddhas; it is the purity of the Buddha-mind. It is perfectly luminous all at once, and perfectly interpenetrating all at once.
At one time they are unstained; at one time they are unerring; their faculties and functions are sovereign, able to expand, able to contract, able to equalize, and able to purify.
△ Second, the verse summary:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
This person’s mind is pure, clear, sharp, and free from turbidity or defilement;

by means of this wondrous faculty of the mind, they know the superior, middling, and inferior dharmas, and even upon hearing a single verse, they penetrate immeasurable meanings and explain them in successive order according to the Dharma.
Whether it be for a month, four months, or a year, they [perceive] all sentient beings within and without this world—whether devas, nāgas, humans, yakṣas, or spirits.
While within the six realms of existence, whatever various dharmas they contemplate, the retribution of upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* causes them to know all at once;

they see the marks of the countless Buddhas of the ten directions adorned with a hundred merits as those Buddhas preach the Dharma for sentient beings, hearing it all and being able to receive and uphold it;
they contemplate immeasurable meanings and their preaching of the Dharma is likewise immeasurable, never forgetting or erring from beginning to end because they uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
He fully knows the characteristics of all phenomena according to their meanings, understands their sequence, and masters names and language; he expounds them exactly as he has realized them.
Whatever this person says consists entirely of the Buddha’s prior teachings, for by expounding these dharmas, they possess no fear among the assembly.

For one who upholds the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the faculty of the mind is purified to such an extent that, although they have not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), they already manifest such signs.
This person, upholding this sutra, dwells securely in a state of rarity; they are joyful toward all sentient beings and are loved and respected by them,
for they are able to expound the Dharma through thousands of myriads of skillful modes of speech, because they uphold the Lotus Sutra.
*Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra*, Fascicle Six;
*Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra of the Wondrous Dharma*, Fascicle Seven.
△ Third, the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging," which encourages the circulation [of the sūtra] by citing the karmic retribution of faith and slander. Part Two: First, the title of the chapter.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty: The Bodhisattva Never Disparaging (the original title being "The Chapter on Constantly Being Despised").
Although this is a case of encouraging the circulation [of the Dharma] through compliance rather than converting through opposition, the Buddha cites the past as proof.

Internally harboring the realization of "Never Disparaging," he externally honors the objects of that "Never Disparaging" attitude; thus, his body, speech, and mind are brought into accord with his realization and practice.

Regarding the arousal of the intent to teach and transform, the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra) states: "Because sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, one does not dare to treat them with contempt. There are five kinds of Buddha-nature:

the *zhengyin foxing* (causal Buddha-nature), which pervades the fundamental and original state; and the *yuan*, *liao*, and *zhongzi* (conditional, developmental, and seed) natures, which are inherently present and not merely acquired in the present.
If it is the *guoxing* (fruition nature) and *guoguxing* (fruition-of-fruition nature), one will certainly attain it; this is by no means in vain.
Although he was subjected to insults and humiliation, he thoroughly perceived this principle and did not disparage them; now having realized the fruit of Buddhahood, he is named Śākyamuni.

His original and manifested traces are inconceivable, and his responses to adversity and favor are unfathomable; therefore, the chapter is titled accordingly. △ Second, the scriptural text has two parts:

first, the prose (long-form), and second, the verse (gāthā). The first part [the prose] further has three sections. First, a double reference to the offenses and merits of the preceding chapter. First, the reference:
...a transgression.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta:

"You should now know that if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and if someone should speak to them with harsh words, revile them, or slander them..."
The grave retribution for slandering [this teaching] is as previously described.
△ Second, pointing out the merit:
the merit one thereby attains is as previously described—the purification of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
△ Second, the dual opening of this chapter concerning faith and slander: first, clarifying the origin of the matter in seven parts; first, the time period.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, in the remote past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago...
△ Second, the names and titles:
There is a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (*Vaiśvānara-rāja*), Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
△ Third, the kalpa and the land:
the kalpa is named Free from Decline, and the land is named Great Achievement.
△ Fourth, the teaching of the Dharma.
In that world, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna preached the Dharma for devas, humans, and asuras;
for those seeking to become śrāvakas, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths to deliver them from birth, old age, sickness, death, and ultimately lead them to nirvāṇa;

for those seeking to become pratyekabuddhas, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; and for all bodhisattvas, [he taught] by means of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The teaching on the three types of *bodhi* should be understood as the ultimate Buddha-wisdom according to the Dharma of the six *pāramitās*.
△ Fifth, regarding lifespan:
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the lifespan of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna was four hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sand eons.
△ Sixth, the periods of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma:

The number of kalpas that the True Dharma remains in the world is equal to the number of dust motes in one Jambudvīpa; the number of kalpas that the Semblance Dharma remains in the world is equal to the number of dust motes in the four continents.
After that Buddha has extensively benefited sentient beings, he then enters parinirvāṇa.
△ Seventh, the subsequent Buddha:
After the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma have been extinguished, another Buddha shall appear in this land,
likewise named Vimalacandra-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi.
The World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, has appeared in this sequence as twenty thousand billion Buddhas, all bearing the same name.
△ Second, explaining the past events (pūrvayoga), part one: first, a general indication of the time period.
First, after the Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound had already entered parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma had ceased, △ Second, the names of the individuals are presented together:
during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there were monks of overweening pride who possessed great power; at that time, there was a bodhisattva...
The name of this Bhikṣu was Constantly Not Disparaging.
△ Third, a dual explanation of gain and loss, in two parts: first, discussing that the believer gains [merit].
By what causes and conditions did Mahāsthāmaprāpta receive the name Constantly Not Disparaging? This Bhikṣu, whenever he saw anyone—whether a fellow monk... [text continues]
The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās all paid homage and praised him, saying:
"We deeply revere you and do not dare to treat you with contempt. Why is this? You all practice the bodhisattva path and shall surely attain Buddhahood.
Yet this bhikṣu does not specialize in reading or reciting the sūtras, but instead practices only prostrations and so forth.
Seeing the fourfold assembly from afar, he likewise went there to pay homage and offer praise, saying these words:
"I do not dare to treat you with contempt; you shall all become Buddhas."
Regarding those who possess faith, "attainment" refers to obtaining the great principle of the true teaching and its wondrous benefit of circulation.
This person is named "Never-Disparaging. First, whenever they see anyone, this is the single principle; second, they prostrate to all of them, which is the single practice;
third, they speak these words, which is the single teaching. These constitute the four aspects of the Trace Gate (*jimon*) that reveal the provisional to manifest the real (*kaiken*).
First, seeing the fourfold assembly from afar is the "oneness of principle"; going to pay homage is the "oneness of practice";
and speaking these words is the "oneness of teaching. Even for those with limited capacity, the meaning is understandable;

this constitutes the fourfold oneness of the "Final Gate" (Hōmon), which reveals the distant by opening the near. Those who do not specialize in recitation and study but solely practice prostration are the first [category].
To rejoice in others is the station of a person; to rejoice in all dharmas as having the nature of peace and bliss, and as being all of one true mark;

to rejoice in all people as possessing the three Buddha-natures—wherein the recitation and study of the scriptures constitute the *vijñapti-hetu* (revealing cause), the practice of the Bodhisattva path constitutes the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause), and not daring to treat them with contempt while instead maintaining deep reverence constitutes [the nature of the fruit].
The fundamental cause is to respect persons and respect the Dharma, refraining from contention and strife; this is the seat of the Tathāgata, characterized by a profound mind of sympathetic joy.
To endure being struck or reviled is to wear the robe of the Tathāgata. To constantly practice compassion without ceasing is the hall of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, profound respect is the mental action (*manas-karma*); not disparaging speech is the verbal action (*vāk-karma*).
Therefore, going to pay homage is a bodily action; these three, when conjoined with compassion, constitute the vow for the practice of peaceful dwelling.
How could such threefold and fourfold [practices] not be the circulation of wondrous benefits? △ Second, clarifying the losses of those who disparage [the teaching].
Among the fourfold assembly, there were those who gave rise to a mind of anger and impurity, reviling him with harsh words, saying:
"This ignorant bhikṣu has come from where? He says of himself, 'I do not slight you; I bestow upon you the prediction that you shall become a Buddha.
We have no need for such false predictions. Thus it continued for many years, and they were constantly...
Even when reviled, he did not give rise to anger, but constantly spoke these words: "You shall all become Buddhas.
When he said this, some among the crowd struck and pelted him with sticks, wood, tiles, and stones; yet he fled and stayed at a distance, still shouting aloud:
"I do not dare to slight you; you shall all become Buddhas. Because he constantly spoke these words, [his merit] increased.
The arrogant bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās called him "Never-Disparaging.
Those with impure minds did not accept his four [teachings] or his single [truth]. They reviled him, saying he was ignorant;

yet, though they knew the principle that he was ignorant, because they said he was ignorant, they would not accept his single truth. Thus, the bhikṣu did not receive their single truth. From where did this come?
First, not accepting and practicing [the teaching]; second, not receiving the instruction of false predictions;
third, being constantly reviled over many years, which constitutes the fourth "one" among the traces of opening up the provisional and revealing the real;

fourth, fleeing to dwell far away, which constitutes the fourth "one" among the original ground of opening up the near and revealing the far; and because he always speaks these words, for this reason...
To bestow the name "Not-Light" (Māndāravat) upon the fourfold assembly is to bind them with deep faith without ceasing;

this concludes the section on not abiding in disparagement. Question: When Śākyamuni appeared in the world, he hesitated and did not speak [of this practice]; why then, upon meeting Not-Light, did he speak of it so impulsively? Answer:
Those who already possessed roots of goodness were protected by Śākyamuni through subtle means. As for those who had not yet produced such goodness, [he spoke thus].

One should not, out of arrogance regarding one's own greatness, forcibly oppress them. △ Third, the dual exhortation concerning the latter two [types of people]—the contrary and the compliant—is also called the dual clarification of the retribution for praise and slander.

First, the clarification of the retribution for those who believe; second, the clarification of obtaining the fruit of that retribution. First, the clarification of obtaining the fruit of that retribution.

When this bhikṣu was about to pass away, he heard in the midst of the void all twenty quadrillion verses of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* previously preached by the Buddha Prabhūtaratna (King of Majestic Sound).
He was able to receive and uphold them all, immediately attaining the aforementioned purity of the faculty of the eye, as well as the purity of the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Having attained this purity of the six faculties, his lifespan increased further.
For two hundred trillion nayutas of years, he extensively preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of others.

At that time, the fourfold assembly of arrogant monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who had treated him with contempt and given him the name "Not-Disdainful" (Adīnamati) saw that he had attained the power of great supernormal faculties, the power of eloquence in joyful exposition, and the power of great, sublime tranquility. All who heard what he taught believed, were subdued, and followed him. This Bodhisattva further transformed thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings, causing them to dwell in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
After his life came to an end, he encountered two thousand koṭis of Buddhas, all named Candrasūryapradīpa (Sun-Moon-Lamp).
Within their teachings, he preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. By these causes and conditions, he further encountered two...

A thousand billion Buddhas, all bearing the same name Cloud-Sovereign-Lamp-King, within the teachings of these Buddhas, upheld, recited, and expounded this sutra for the sake of the fourfold assembly;
therefore, he attained this constant purity of the eye, and the purity of the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Among the fourfold assembly, he preached the Dharma with a mind free from fear and attained great power—this is his constant state.
Light Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have made offerings to this many Buddhas, honoring, respecting,

they will achieve such merit that they shall attain Buddhahood.

In this present life, they attain the purification of the six sense faculties; in their future lives, they encounter the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; and in lives thereafter, they encounter the Buddha Meghasvarendrarāja.

Through the power of supernormal knowledges, their physical actions are purified; through the power of eloquence in teaching, their verbal actions are purified; and through the power of sublime tranquility, their mental actions are purified.
△ Second, the correlation of the ancient and the modern, in two parts. First, the formal correlation:

Because one explains this sutra for others, one will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Mahāsthāmaprāpta, at that time, because the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās treated me with contempt out of a mind of anger and malice,
for two hundred billion kalpas they never encountered a Buddha, did not hear the Dharma, and did not see the Saṅgha.
After enduring great suffering in the Avīci Hell for a thousand kalpas, once their transgressions were exhausted, they again encountered the Tathāgata Never-Disparaging.
The Bodhisattva teaches and transforms others toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This clarifies that those who disparage [the Dharma] obtain both good and evil fruits; because they slander, they fall into the evil realms.

Yet, by hearing the name of the Buddha-nature, which is like the power of a "poison drum," they obtain the retribution of a good fruit. This is what is meant by saying that even slander constitutes a seed. It is like a person who has fallen...

Those who do not regress from the three types of enlightenment.

Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you should know that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* brings great benefit to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and is able to cause them—
Since this pertains to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should,
after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, constantly uphold, recite, explain, and transcribe this sutra.
The sutra possesses great power and will ultimately bring about great results; one must diligently practice the five kinds of conduct.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

△ Second, the verses on the original narrative (nidāna), in three parts. First, the verse that introduces both individuals together:

At that time, the fourfold assembly was attached to the teachings.
To speak of "clinging to dharmas" means that dharmas cannot be demonstrated. If one definitively asserts that they exist, this is clinging to dharmas;
if one definitively asserts that they neither exist nor do not exist, this too is clinging to dharmas. Therefore, the *Buddhapiṭaka* states:
"The harm caused by a wheel of swords to the people of Jambudvīpa is still minor compared to the sin of those who preach the Mahāyāna with a mind of grasping."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "To cling to existence and dispute with non-existence, or even to cling to that which is neither existent nor non-existent and dispute with existence and non-existence—these are like a cowhide rope and a dragon-rope;
both cannot avoid the affliction. The *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* states:

"The Buddhas taught the Dharma of emptiness primarily to transform those who cling to existence. If there are those who become attached to emptiness, they cannot be transformed by the Buddhas. If one definitively asserts that all phenomena are..."

To hold that "it exists" rather than "it does not exist" is called the discourse of ignorance; if one grasps the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*, then whether acting for oneself or transforming others, there will be no attachment.

the foremost teaching— to instruct and lead others so that they might abide in nirvana,

After billions of billions of kalpas, even unto inconceivable time, one may hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
After billions of billions of kalpas, even unto inconceivable time, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have preached this sūtra. Therefore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the practitioner—

Upon hearing this sutra, do not give rise to doubt; you should with single-minded devotion widely proclaim this sutra, so that in life after life you may encounter Buddhas and swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood.

This is because it is encountered only once in hundreds of millions of births and is difficult to hear even throughout vast kalpas; those who are able to receive and uphold it will certainly attain Buddhahood.
How can one not believe and comply with these parables and instead strive toward them?
This chapter, it seems, concerns how the Tathāgata, in a past kalpa, encountered the appearance of a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvāsana-rāja).

Under that Buddha, he cultivated the bodhisattva practice known as Constantly Not Disparaging (Sadāparibhūta), sowing seeds of bitter poison among the fourfold assembly; yet the faculties of those fourfold assemblies were meager.
Being inferior and unable to endure the great transformation, they instead struck and pelted him with tiles and stones; thus, through their transgressions, they fell into the *niraya* hells.
Within those hells, they gave rise to three thoughts and said to one another: "By what causes and conditions have we now fallen into this place?
They further said to one another: "It is because in our previous lives we were foolish and ignorant, and we reviled [the Buddha]."

Furthermore, because Ajātaśatru treated [the Bodhisattva] with contempt and even inflicted upon him the torments of staffs and wooden cudgels, he sank into the depths of suffering due to these evil deeds.
Subsequently, by cultivating goodness and reforming his wickedness, he was forever freed from the three miserable realms and immediately attained a supreme fruit.
This is like parched wood sprouting in spring or cold ashes igniting once more; such is the sublime and wondrous power and function of this sutra.

The general purport is as follows: When the Bodhisattvas who have emerged from the earth gaze upon the Honored Countenance and make their vows, the ancient and wise sages dwelling here behold his supernatural power and increase in joy.
The Dharma Lord of Vulture Peak extends his long tongue to the Brahma world;

beneath the trees, all Buddhas radiate light from their pores throughout the Dharma-realm. The sound of his clearing his throat reaches everywhere in the ten directions, and the resonance of his snapping fingers shakes the earth.
By shaking these six kinds [of earth], the sentient beings of the ten directions behold the assembly of the Dharma in this Sahā world;
the boundless multitudes of living beings hear the wondrous voice from the void, and each person increases their mindfulness of the Buddha while scattering various precious objects.
In every land, the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) are melted away, becoming a single Buddha-field (buddhakṣetra). (And so forth.)

△ Section Two: The Eight Chapters from "The Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (Rddhy-abhisaṃskāra-parivarta) downward clarify the entrustment and circulation [of the teaching]. This section has three parts: first, two chapters clarify the entrustment through supernatural powers;

The Bodhisattvas Receiving the Mandate to Propagate the Sūtra; Chapter Two on Entrustment. Regarding the first section, the text of the Tathāgata’s Entrustment, it is further divided into two parts.
First, the chapter title:
*The Lotus Sūtra of the Wonderful Dharma*, Chapter Twenty-one: "The Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers."
As explained above, regarding "the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers" (*ṛddhi*): "supernormal" (*śen*) refers to the unfathomable, and "power" (*li*) refers to the sovereign function.
Being unfathomable, it is the profound essence of spontaneity; being a sovereign function, it is the great power of transformation.

Herein, because the profound Dharma is entrusted [to the Bodhisattvas] by manifesting ten kinds of great supernormal powers, it is called the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernormal Powers. △ Second, the Sūtra Text.
The text has two parts: first, the prose exposition; second, the verse summary. The first part [of the prose] also has two sections: first, the Bodhisattvas receiving their charge;
second, the narrative of the occasion.
Regarding the first, the narrator describes the scene: "At that time, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a thousand worlds, who had emerged from the earth, all..."
Before the Buddha, with single-minded devotion, they joined their palms and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance.
△ Second, the vow to propagate the sutra, in three parts: First, the time.
They addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, after the extinction of the Buddha..."
△ Second, the locations:
the lands and places of parinirvāṇa where the World-Honored One’s emanation bodies reside.
△ Third, the vows.
Why should this sutra be explained in detail? It is because we ourselves also desire to obtain this truly pure Great Dharma, to receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, copy, and make offerings to it.
△ Second, the Buddha manifests his supernatural powers. Part one: The assembly present.

At that time, the World-Honored One [addressed] Mañjuśrī and countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had long resided in the Sahā world, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Before the entire assembly of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
△ Second, the actual manifestation of supernatural power, in ten parts; first, the mark of protruding the tongue.
He manifests great supernormal power, extending his broad and long tongue upward as far as the Brahma-world.
Now, what is expounded in this sutra reveals the Three to manifest the One; internally it is secret while externally it is manifested.

It sets aside the near to reveal the distant, clarifying how he benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time with truthfulness and without falsehood. The tongue of one of great merit reaches the tip of the nose; that of a Buddha of the Tripitaka reaches the hairline.
Now, those who have reached the Brahma Heaven transcend both ordinary beings and sages, reaching the very summit of the Pure Heavens.
△ Second, the entire body emits light:
from every pore, immeasurable and innumerable rays of light of various colors are emitted, universally illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.

When Śākyamuni Buddha and the Buddhas beneath the jewel trees manifested these supernatural powers, a full hundred thousand years passed.
Light radiates from every pore throughout his entire body, pervading the ten directions so that there is nowhere it does not illuminate; this signifies the full exhaustion of the realm of wisdom.

In the preceding *Jikimon* (Trace Gate), the brilliance of the ūrṇā-kośa first shone toward the east, signifying the initial vision of the single principle by those on the seven stages of expedient means (*sapta-upāya*).
Now that the present *Honmon* (Essential Gate) has concluded, he emits light from his entire body to illuminate all lands, enabling those at the initial stage of the cause [to attain realization].
Finally, the ultimate Buddha-wisdom of Equal Enlightenment and the emanated Buddhas are likewise so.
△ Third, the sound of clearing the throat:
thereupon, he withdraws his tongue-mark and simultaneously clears his throat.
Coughing is the manner of one about to speak; it is also a sign of unobstructed flow.
For over forty years, the truth has been concealed and hidden, but now it is finally extended and laid bare without any lingering obstruction. This is my great task for appearing in the world:
this thorough unblocking. Therefore, I cough so as to entrust this Dharma to the bodhisattvas, so that they may guide and benefit the multitudes in future ages.
The Master was about to speak of this matter; therefore, he cleared his throat and again cleared his throat. There are two meanings to this clearing of the throat:
first, to signal that the matter is concluded; second, to entrust it to another. △ Fourth, the sound of snapping the fingers.
Together they snapped their fingers.

To snap the fingers means to rejoice in those of the seven stages of expedient means as they enter the Perfect Path together; to rejoice in the Perfect Path for increasing wisdom and diminishing birth;
to rejoice in all Bodhisattvas upholding the Great Dharma of True Purity; and to rejoice in the attainment of the Unconditioned in future lives.
This supreme jewel is that which, in a single snap of the fingers, penetrates vertically through the three periods of time and extends horizontally across the ten directions.
△ Fifth, the sixfold earthquake:
these two sounds reach throughout the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and the earth everywhere shakes in six ways.

therein dwell sentient beings—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and so forth.

they all rejoiced greatly, having attained what they had never experienced before.
This signifies that the path of all Buddhas is identical; from this day forward, it shall likewise be so.
The five thousand who rose and departed and those moved by the three transformations had lost their original minds and were unable to provide manifest benefit.

It is appropriate to manifest extinction where there is no extinction, so that by following the various Bodhisattvas who propagate the sutra and attain the Way, they may enter the Buddha-wisdom, no different from the present assembly. This also signifies the future.
First, there is the occasion for its appearance. △ Seventh, the proclamation of sound from mid-air:

The Bhikṣuṇī now preaches for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wonderful Law*,
which instructs bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas. You all should, with deep hearts, rejoice in it and also pay homage and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.

with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and various ornaments for the body, as well as rare jewels and exquisite items, they are all scattered together from afar toward the Sahā world.

Answer: As the text below states: "If I were to use this supernatural power to preach the merits of this sutra for the sake of entrustment throughout immeasurable kalpas, I would still be unable to exhaust them.
This clearly demonstrates that the ten aspects represent the past, while the fourfold unity clarifies the meaning of the future.

At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of Bodhisattvas, including Upariṣṭha and others: "The supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of all Buddhas are thus immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.

△ Second, the summary and formal entrustment:
To state it briefly, all the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata—
"All are the Buddha-dharma" refers to the fact that this seal is entirely wondrous in name.
"The Tathāgata’s all-encompassing sovereign spiritual powers,
penetrating without obstruction and possessing the eight masteries" refers to the wondrous function of this seal.
The Tathāgata’s treasury of all secret essentials pervades all places as the true reality; this is the wondrous essence of this seal.
It is the Tathāgata’s all profoundly deep matters.
"This is the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle; this concludes the wondrous thesis.
All of these are proclaimed and clearly expounded within this sutra.
In summary, the entire sutra consists of only four [sections], which capture its essential pivot and are handed down. △ Third, the Exhortation.
I entrust this to you.
Therefore, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, you should with a single mind receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, copy, and practice according to the teaching.
In whatever land there may be those who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, or copy [this],...
Wherever this discourse on practice is kept— whether in a garden, in a grove,
at the foot of a tree, in a monastery, in a layperson’s house, in a hall, or in a mountain valley or wilderness—
one should erect a stūpa there to pay homage.

Exhorting the fourfold assembly to circulate [this scripture] everywhere, it states that in whatever place it may be, one should erect a stupa, for this sutra is itself the true body and śarīra-relics of the Tathāgata. △ Fourth, the explanation of the intent behind the entrustment.
Why is this so? You should know that this very place is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
This explains the profoundly deep matter:
it is here that all Buddhas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is the Dharmakāya, which is the treasury that explains the secret essentials.
It is here that all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma;
it is this very Prajñā that explains all dharmas.
The Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa herein;
this is the power of the sovereign liberation of Śakra. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts: first, the summary of the ten powers of sovereignty.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas, the saviors of the world, abide in great supernormal powers. To delight sentient beings, they manifest immeasurable spiritual transformations:
their tongue-reaches extend to the Brahma-heaven, and from their bodies they emit countless rays of light. For those who seek the Buddha-way, they manifest such rare and wondrous events."
The coughing sounds and the snapping of fingers of all Buddhas resound throughout the lands of the ten directions, causing the earth to quake in six ways;
because they are able to uphold this sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all Buddhas rejoice and manifest immeasurable supernatural powers.
△ Second, the summary in verse and the entrustment (in three parts): First, the general verse on the four dharmas.
Because this is the entrustment of the sutra, it praises those who receive and uphold it, stating that even throughout immeasurable kalpas one could not exhaust their merit;
it is boundless and inexhaustible, like the ten directions of empty space, for which no limit can be found.
△ Second, the separate verses on the four dharmas; first, the verse on all dharmas:
"One who can uphold this sutra shall have seen me, as well as the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and all his emanations, and shall also see me today teaching and transforming the bodhisattvas."
△ Second, the verse on sovereign spiritual power:
"Those who can uphold this sutra shall cause me, as well as my emanations, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna who has entered parinirvāṇa, and all others to rejoice.
They shall also see and make offerings to the Buddhas currently present in the ten directions, as well as those of the past and future, and cause them all to attain joy."
△ Three verses on the treasury of the secret essentials:
The secret essential Dharma attained by all Buddhas when seated at the site of enlightenment—those who can uphold this sutra shall likewise attain it before long.
△ Four verses on the matter of profound depth.
Those who can uphold this sutra will possess inexhaustible eloquence in explaining the meanings, names, and phrases of all dharmas, just as the wind moves through space without any obstruction.

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, they will know the causes, conditions, and sequence of the sutras spoken by the Buddha, and will explain them according to their true meaning as they really are. Like the light of the sun and moon, they are able to dispel all darkness.
Such a person, moving through the world, is able to extinguish the darkness of sentient beings and teach immeasurable bodhisattvas to ultimately abide in the One Vehicle.
△ Third, the general verse concluding the meaning:
Therefore, those with wisdom who hear these merits and benefits should, after my parinirvāṇa, receive, uphold, and recite this sutra.
Such a person will certainly encounter no obstacles on the path to Buddhahood.
△ Second, the Entrustment Chapter, which clarifies the Tathāgata’s entrustment by stroking the head; first, the chapter title:
*The Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Dharma*, Chapter Twenty-two: "Entrustment."
"Entrustment" (*zhù*) refers to what is entrusted by the Buddha; "cumulative charge" (*lèi*) refers to your being troubled by the task of proclaiming it.

This derives its name from the Buddha’s own intent. "Entrustment" refers to receiving the entrustment upon the crown of one's head; "cumulative charge" refers to accepting it with joy rather than weariness. This derives its name from the Bodhisattva’s respectful compliance.

"Entrustment" refers to what is entrusted by the Tathāgata’s golden mouth; "cumulative charge" refers to the Bodhisattva’s sincere heart bearing it upon the crown of the head. This derives its name from the transmission.

Because it is based on the *Śāstra on Receiving and Harmonizing*, it is called the "Entrustment. Furthermore, as the Tathāgata rose from his seat in person, he stroked [the crown of] their heads and conferred [the teaching] upon the great assembly.
Because they were earnestly instructed by the World-Honored One, saying, "You should practice this," and because it was received with such diligence, it is called the "Chapter on Entrustment.
Part Two: The Sūtra Text. Section One: The Proper Clarification of the Entrustment. Subsection One: The Tathāgata’s Entrustment. Part One: The Actual Entrustment.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha rose from his Dharma-seat and manifested great supernormal power;
with his right hand, he stroked the heads of immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and spoke these words:
"I have cultivated this rare Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas; now, by means of it—"
"I entrust this to you; you should with one mind disseminate this Dharma and cause it to flourish and increase extensively.
Having thus placed his hand upon the heads of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he spoke these words:
"For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have practiced and cultivated this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is so difficult to obtain."
I now entrust this to you; you should receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and widely proclaim this Dharma so that all sentient beings may universally hear and know it.
With the skillful hands of his expedient wisdom, the Buddha stroked three thousand three hundred nayutas of lands.

The Bodhisattvas who fill the void possess the crown of true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*). Because the Tathāgata bestows the Way upon them to transform others, they are called the Bodhisattvas of Expedient Wisdom Hands.
Because they receive the Way through their own practice, they are called the Crown of True Wisdom. Extending his hand to touch their crowns is the entrustment of the body;
expedient wisdom facing true wisdom is the entrustment of the mind; and speaking these words is the entrustment of the mouth.
Furthermore, this teaching contains the fourfold intention of the *siddhāntas*. I have cultivated the Dharma that is difficult to attain over immeasurable kalpas;
I received its instruction from previous Buddhas and now transmit it to you. You, in turn, shall bestow it upon others as the succession of the Three Times—this is the *loka-siddhānta*.
To cause it to flow forth with a single mind is the *pudgala-siddhānta*. To cause it to be widely propagated and further increased is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*. As for "increasing," it is...
This is the primary meaning. △ Second, the explanation of the entrustment.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata possesses great compassion, is free from all stinginess, and has no fear;
he is able to bestow upon sentient beings the Buddha-wisdom, the Tathāgata-wisdom, and the self-existent wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*). The Tathāgata is [the father] of all sentient beings.
O great donors among living beings, you too should follow and learn the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and do not give rise to stinginess.
Great compassion is the chamber of the Tathāgata; being free from all stinginess is the robe of the Tathāgata; fearlessness is the seat of the Tathāgata;
Buddha-wisdom is all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); Tathāgata-wisdom is the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*); and natural wisdom is—
The knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) can bestow the three kinds of wisdom upon sentient beings within the Tathāgata’s chamber, and it is likewise so even within his seat; such is the donor.
Because he is without stinginess and without fear, you should study this Dharma of the Tathāgata. This is called explaining the Buddha’s intention and entrusting it to you. △
The third entrustment:

In a future age, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who have faith in the Tathāgata’s wisdom, you should expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them so that they may hear and know it, in order to enable those people to attain the Buddha-wisdom. If there are...

If you are able to act in this way, you will have repaid the kindness of all Buddhas."

If their roots are deep and their wisdom sharp, explain the Buddha’s wisdom directly; if they are not yet capable, then within other profound dharmas, instruct, benefit, and gladden them regarding the Buddha’s wisdom.
This Buddha’s wisdom is profound but not the others; the six provisional means are "other" but not "profound";

At that time, having heard the Buddha speak these words, all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas were filled with great joy that pervaded their entire bodies;
they increased their reverence even further, bowing their heads low with palms joined toward the Buddha, and together they spoke aloud: "As the World-Honored One [has said]..."
"We shall respectfully carry out the instructions as commanded; indeed, World-Honored One, we pray that you have no further concern.

All were filled with great joy; this was the mental reception. They bowed their bodies and lowered their heads; this was the physical reception. Together they raised their voices and spoke; this was the verbal reception.
"As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall receive [this teaching]. The Tathāgata is the Great Giver.

Entering the Tathāgata’s chamber, we shall mentally fulfill and carry out [his instructions]. This is the reception free from all stinginess and attachment. "Wearing the Tathāgata’s robe," this is the mental vow.

Without further deliberation, he accepted [the invitation] with a mind free from fear, seated upon the Tathāgata’s throne. △ When these three matters were concluded, the announcement for dispersal was made.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha commanded all the emanated Buddhas who had come from the ten directions to each return to their own lands, saying:
"May the various Buddhas each return to their respective abodes, and let the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna return to its former state."
Because Prabhūtaratna has come to bear witness to this sutra, the two gates of the Trace and the Origin have now been completed;

therefore, it is necessary to respectfully dismiss him and close the stupa as before. Although he divided his body to open the stupa, that task having been finished, he causes the emanations to each return to their own lands, for the stupa cannot be opened again.
Thus, while the emanations depart and no longer appear, the stupa continues to listen to the Dharma.

Therefore, although it was closed, it remained; if one were to inquire whether the stupa listened to the Dharma, the answer is that it was closed because it had already realized the truth, yet it remained present so as to facilitate its circulation. △ Second, the assembly rejoices.
When these words were spoken, the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions who were seated beneath jeweled trees upon lion thrones,

It is said that all rejoice greatly.
The Buddhas rejoice because they have accomplished the task of transforming others; the Bodhisattvas rejoice because they have attained the Dharma for their own practice;
and they also rejoice because the person who can preach it is pure—this refers to the Buddha. Furthermore, they rejoice because they have heard the pure Dharma, which is wondrous.
This refers to the sutra itself; furthermore, it refers to those who have attained realization upon hearing the Dharma and rejoice; and it refers to those who will benefit in the present and future.
Because these three matters are complete, there is great joy. 2.
From the chapter on Bhaiṣajyarāja downward, five chapters concern exhorting others to circulate [the teaching]. First, Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva.
This chapter clarifies the teacher who exhorts others toward transformation. It is my sole wish that the Great Dharma may be widely proclaimed and that all sentient beings may obtain great benefit.
Therefore, I exhaust my spiritual power and the full span of my life, with earnest and devout devotion, yet my resolve remains undiminished.
I hope to cause my disciples to revere the Dharma as I do my teacher; I shall transmit this clarity to you, and you, in turn, shall transmit this clarity to others.
The "Manifesting" (Míngmíng) chapter reveals the resolve of one who has no teacher; thus, it should be known that this section exhorts those masters who propagate the Dharma.

Next, the two chapters on "Wondrous Sound" (Miàoyīn) and "Avalokiteśvara" (Guānyīn) clarify how the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) of other directions receive the mandate to propagate the sutra, universally manifesting their physical forms with no fixed standard;
they cannot be viewed with the eyes of cattle or sheep, nor can they be fathomed by the consciousness and understanding of the ordinary and ignorant.
Do not give rise to thoughts of contempt regarding that from which you hear [the Dharma]; for if one harbors such contempt, the Dharma will not permeate the mind.

Thus, it is known that these two sections exhort the disciples who receive the Dharma. 3. The Chapter on Dhāraṇī: This clarifies that in the evil age, the propagation of the sutra will encounter many afflictions and difficulties;

The attainment of the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies is precisely the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Bodies.

This has three meanings: first, internal manifestation, as described in this sutra, wherein the body-faculty is purified such that the ten dharma realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—manifest within the body, like various forms appearing in a clear, bright mirror; second, external manifestation, as in the case of [the Bodhisattva] Wondrous Sound.

Regarding the third point, Avalokiteśvara manifests the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the ten realms according to the capacities of beings. This is manifested both internally and externally, as described in the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*:

The Great Dhyāna Master Zhizhe of the Tiantai school was named Zhiyi; he was a native of Huāróng in Jīngzhōu and belonged to the Chén clan.
His mother, Lady Xú, dreamed of five-colored clouds coiling around her womb on the day she conceived him. On the day of his birth, auspicious light illuminated the room.

At the age of seven, while at Guòyuàn Monastery, he heard a monk reciting the *Pǔmén Pǐn* (Universal Gate Chapter) and recited it along with him, spontaneously remembering the entire seven-fascicle text.
His literary compositions were flawless and free of error. At eighteen, his parents passed away, and he entered Fruit Monastery (*Guo-yuan-si*) to become a monk.

At twenty, he received full ordination under Vinaya Master Kuang (*Kuang lǎoshī*), through whom he became thoroughly versed in the Vinaya-piṭaka. Hearing of the reputation and virtue of Meditation Master Huisi (*Huisi Chánshī*) of Mount Dàsū in Guangzhou, he traveled there despite the perilous journey.
When Huisi first saw him, he smiled and said, "In the past, we together listened to the teachings at Vulture Peak (*Vulture Peak Mountain*)."

"Pursued by karmic conditions from past lives in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you have now returned once more. He then showed him the practice of the *Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra* at the site of Samantabhadra’s enlightenment;
after practicing the path and reciting the sūtra for fourteen days, they reached this chapter where all Buddhas together praised Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying, "This is true diligence;
this is called the true offering of the Dharma. At that moment, he attained sudden and great awakening, clearly illuminating and comprehending the Dharma.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, World-Honored One, you still remain in the world.

the moment of my final extinction is at hand. You should prepare a seat, for tonight I shall enter parinirvāṇa.

I entrust this to you, as well as to all the bodhisattvas, great disciples, and the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
I also entrust to you the three-thousandfold great thousand-world system of seven-jeweled worlds, with its jeweled trees, jeweled terraces, and the attendant devas.
After my parinirvāṇa, all my relics shall likewise be entrusted to you; you must cause them—
After the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa had thus instructed the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana to propagate [the teaching], establish extensive offerings,
and erect several thousand stūpas, he entered parinirvāṇa during the latter part of the night.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, seeing that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, was overcome with grief and distress, longing for the Buddha.
He immediately used *candana* sandalwood from this side of the sea to construct a pyre as an offering to the Buddha’s body, and burned it with fire.

For example, [the light] pervades the trichiliocosm: from the small chiliocosm up to the first dhyāna, the middle chiliocosm up to the second dhyāna, and the great chiliocosm up to the third dhyāna;

"You all should focus your minds with single-mindedness as I now perform this offering."
After the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa-śrī had spoken these words, he burned his arm,
adorned with a hundred blessings, before eighty-four thousand stupas for seventy-two thousand years as an act of worship.
△ Third, the benefit:

to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and enables them all to dwell in the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies.

Having made this vow, they were naturally restored once again by virtue of this.
This was brought about by the profound thickness of the Bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom;
at that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the heavens rained down precious flowers, such that all devas and humans experienced what they had never known before.

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva宿王華 (Śubhavyūha): "What do you think? Is the Bodhisattva 一切衆生憙見 (Sarvasattvapriyadarśana) anyone else?

It measures hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas.
△ Second, the exhortation to practice:
"O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, if there are those who resolve their minds and wish to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are able..."
It is superior to offer one's own fingers, even up to a single toe, as an offering to a Buddha stūpa, rather than offering kingdoms,

To light a single finger-tip [of incense] is superior to giving away one’s external body, for while the external is light, the internal is heavy; thus, their merits differ.

As for "wife and children," these are the external body; "kingdoms, cities, and so forth" are external wealth. △ Second, praising the excellence of the sutra, in three parts: first, praising those who can uphold it.

great bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and arhats, the merit obtained by that person would not equal that of one who upholds even a single four-line verse of this Lotus Sūtra; the latter’s merit is far greater.
△ Second, the praise of the Dharma he upholds, in two parts.
First, the praise of the essence of the Dharma: "O Śubhavyūha, for example, among all streams, rivers, and great waters, the ocean is foremost;
