This Dharma Flower teaching is like an ocean of *amṛta* (clarified butter); its exposition of the ultimate fundamental ground constitutes its profundity, and its pervading of all places constitutes its greatness.
It is also like the earthen mountains, the Black Mountains, the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains, the Greater Iron Ring Mountains, and the ten jewel mountains among the various mountain ranges.
Just as Mount Sumeru is the foremost among [the mountains] therein, so too is this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* likewise;
it is the most supreme among all sūtras.
As for the ten precious mountains, their names appear in the *Avataṃsaka* and other sūtras; the dark iron perimeter mountains (*cakravāḍa*) are not made of jewels.
Although mountains may contain treasures, they are but one or two, and various divine dragons dwell therein; Mount Sumeru, however, is composed of the four jewels and is the abode of pure devas.
Likewise, the true principle of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—constantly blissful, self, and pure—is like that which is formed of the four jewels;
it is the reliance for those who have opened, shown, awakened to, and entered [the truth].
Furthermore, just as among the many stars the Moon Deity is the most preeminent, so too is this Lotus Sutra;
among the hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of various sūtras and dharmas, it is the most illuminating.
The stars and the moon are both of the nature of *yin* (darkness/substance), yet they both appear at night; while the stars do not wax or wane, their brightness does not equal that of the moon.

Various sutras state that provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) cannot be autonomous, whereas this sutra clarifies that provisional wisdom is identical to reality (*tattva*) and reality is identical to the provisional.
Their waxing and waning refer to one another as non-dual yet dual. In this way, this provisional wisdom surpasses that of other teachings.
Furthermore, just as the Sun Deva is able to dispel all darkness, so too is this sutra able to destroy the darkness of all unwholesome states.
The sun, being the essence of solar heat, can alone dispel darkness; yet even the luminous true wisdom of other sutras does not equal its power to immediately shatter delusion.
Since the ultimate and the provisional are not separate, and the provisional is itself the ultimate, one knows that this sutra clarifies that ultimate wisdom is the most supreme.
Just as among all minor kings, the Wheel-Turning Sage King is the most supreme, so too is this sutra.
Among all the sūtras, this is the most honored, just as Śakra is the king among the thirty-three gods;
so too is this sūtra the king among all sūtras.
The commands of a Wheel-Turning King extend only over the four continents, while Śakra rules equally over the Heaven of the Thirty-three. Likewise,
just as the Great Brahmā King is the father of all sentient beings, so too is this sutra the father of all noble ones—
both those in training and those beyond training— as well as those who have resolved to attain the mind of a bodhisattva.

The Sanskrit title serves as a general heading for what follows, serving as an analogy to other sutras which state that the three truths and the three samādhis are each distinct and do not encompass one another, nor can they attain self-mastery.
What is taught in this sutra, however, is that by entering the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) through the ultimate truth, one decisively understands the Dharma of the śrāvakas;
this is the king of all sutras. By entering the conventional truth through the true reality, all activities of livelihood and production are not in conflict with it. This is the reality.
Among all phenomena that mutually interpenetrate, there is none that is not the Buddha-dharma; this is as the text says:
"He is the father of all those in training and those beyond training, as well as those who have resolved to attain the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, it is like the relationship among all ordinary persons, from stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats...
The Pratyekabuddha is the foremost; this sutra is likewise the most supreme among all the sūtras and dharmas spoken by all Tathāgatas, whether spoken by Bodhisattvas or by Śrāvakas.
"Ordinary beings, the four fruits [of the śrāvaka], and pratyekabuddhas— these are foremost because they are spontaneous and effortless (*anābhoga*).
This clarifies that while other sūtras require effort to enter the stream— just as those who have attained the four fruits must first rely on hearing,

reflection, and cultivation to achieve realization— this sūtra elucidates the Four Truths of Non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), which, being untainted by expedient means, naturally flow into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
The ocean is like a great white ox, fat and strong, walking with steady gait as swift as the wind.
One who is able to receive and uphold this sutra is likewise so: among all sentient beings, they are the foremost;
among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattva is the foremost; and this sutra is likewise so.
This is the foremost among all the teachings of the various sūtras; just as the Buddha is the King of all dharmas, so too is this sūtra the king among all sūtras.
Among the two vehicles, the bodhisattva is the foremost—this clarifies the cause; the Tathāgata is the foremost—this clarifies the fruit. As for the rest...

The sutra clarifies that the fruit is near by pointing to the site of enlightenment; this sutra clarifies that the fruit is far-reaching by pointing to the Original Ground, and is therefore the most supreme.
△ Second, praising the function of the Dharma, in three parts: first, praising its function of uprooting suffering.
"O Rājanvatsapuṣpa, this sūtra can save all sentient beings; this sūtra can cause all sentient beings to be free from all suffering and affliction.
△ Second, praising its function of bestowing happiness.
This sutra can greatly benefit all sentient beings and fulfill their aspirations;
it is like a cool pond that satisfies all who suffer from thirst, like fire for those in the cold, like clothing for the naked,
like a master for merchants, like a mother for a child, like a boat for those crossing over, like a physician for the sick, like a lamp in the darkness, and like wealth for the poor.
The jewel is like the people obtaining it; the king is like the merchant obtaining the sea; the torch is like that which dispels darkness.
△ Third, the summary of bestowing and extracting:
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is also like this, for it can cause sentient beings to leave behind all suffering and all ailments.
It can untie all the bonds of birth and death.
△ Third, the merit of upholding the sutra, in two parts: first, the merit of hearing the sutra in its entirety.
If a person hears this Lotus Sutra, whether by writing it themselves or instructing others to write it, the merit they obtain—
The Buddha’s wisdom cannot be measured in its extent; its limits cannot be found.

If one were to write out this sutra scroll and offer it flowers, incense, necklaces, burnt incense, powdered incense, ointment incense, banners, canopies, robes, and various kinds of lamps—such as ghee lamps, oil lamps, lamps of various fragrant oils, *campaka* oil lamps, *sumanā* oil lamps, *pāṭala* oil lamps, and *vārṣika* oil lamps.
The merit obtained from making offerings of *nāgamallī* oil lamps is likewise immeasurable.

"Sudāṣa-puṣpa, if there is anyone who hears this 'Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva,' they shall also obtain immeasurable [merit]."

there are women who hear this sutra and practice according to its teachings, they will, upon the end of life here, immediately go to the world of Sukhāvatī.
Born within a lotus flower upon a jeweled throne in the abode where Amitābha Buddha dwells, surrounded by a multitude of great bodhisattvas,
one will no longer be afflicted by desire, nor afflicted by anger or delusion, nor afflicted by the defilements of pride and envy;

Having attained this patience, his faculty of the eye became pure; with this purified faculty of the eye, he beheld seven million two hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sand-like Buddhas, Tathāgatas.
At that time, all those Buddhas praised him from afar in unison, saying:

The merit obtained from contemplating this sutra and expounding it for others is immeasurable and boundless; fire cannot burn it, nor can water wash it away.
Even if a thousand Buddhas were to speak of your merit together, they could not exhaust it.
You have now been able to defeat the mara-enemies, destroy the army of birth and death, and utterly annihilate all other adversaries. Good son, [this is] the hundredth...
A thousand Buddhas, through their supernormal powers, together protect you;
among all the devas and humans in every world, there is no one like you, except for the Tathāgata.

Among all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even bodhisattvas, none possess wisdom or meditative concentration equal to yours. O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, this bodhisattva has accomplished such merit.
By the power of virtue and wisdom, if there be anyone who, upon hearing this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," can rejoice in it and praise it as excellent,

that person shall, in their present life, constantly have the fragrance of blue lotuses issue from their mouth and the fragrance of gośīrṣa-candana issue from the pores of their body; the merit they obtain shall be as described above.
The fragrance emanating from the mouth is a reward received in the present life; all other [benefits] are rewards to be received in future lives. △ Second, the entrustment:
"Therefore, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, I entrust this 'Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva' to you.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, you must widely proclaim and disseminate it throughout Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be cut off."
Māras, Mārakāyikas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others will find an opportunity to harm [those who do not protect it].
Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, you should use the power of your supernatural faculties to protect this sutra. Why is this?

Because this sutra is the excellent medicine for the illnesses of the people of Jambudvīpa. If a person with an illness hears this sutra, their illness will immediately be extinguished, and they shall not grow old.
"Amṛtāyus-kusuma-rāja, if you see anyone who receives and upholds this sutra, you should take blue lotuses filled with powdered incense and scatter them upon that person.
Having scattered them, you should form this thought:

'This person will, before long, surely take grass to sit upon at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), shatter the armies of Māra, blow the dharma-conch, beat the great dharma-drum, and deliver sentient beings.'"

Since all sentient beings are in the ocean of old age, sickness, and death, those who seek the Buddha-way and see anyone who receives and upholds this sutra should give rise to a heart of such reverence.
Regarding "neither aging nor death," this must be understood through contemplative insight: "not aging" refers to bliss, and "not dying" refers to permanence.
This means that upon hearing this sutra, one attains the realization of permanence and bliss, which remains peacefully within the heart, free from all fear or dread.
Furthermore, "neither aging nor death" is spoken in reference to the realized *dharmakāya*; it does not refer to the illusory, deluded karma of the provisional combination of the four great elements.
[The] Body. △ Second, explaining the attainment of benefits:

When this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" was being preached, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the dhāraṇī for understanding the languages of all sentient beings.

The Tathāgata Many Treasures, from within the jeweled stupa, praised the Bodhisattva King of Hosts of Stars, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, King of Hosts of Stars! You have accomplished inconceivable merit, being able thus to question Śākyamuni Buddha regarding..."
This matter benefits all sentient beings immeasurably.

"The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara," the text itself explains that because he formerly offered one hundred thousand kinds of musical instruments to the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararāja,
he now has music following him as he travels to transform others; and because he formerly offered eighty-four thousand precious bowls, he now possesses such a multitude of ritual vessels.
Surrounded by his retinue, he had previously attained the *dhāraṇī* of the languages of all sentient beings;

now, by universally manifesting his physical form and wondrous voice to roar throughout the ten directions, he widely proclaims this teaching. Therefore, this chapter is named "The Chapter on Wondrous Sound" (*Ghoṣadatta-parivarta*).
This chapter clarifies how the Bodhisattva, through inconceivable power, communicates the sutras according to the various types of beings, such that all who behold his traces [are transformed].
To fathom its source yet only savor its flavor without discriminating against its form;

to treat the ground as lowly while damming its own flow—this is the second meaning within the section on transforming others. II. The Scriptural Text has six parts: First, emitting light to summon from the East;

Chapter Six: The Six Realms Hear and Enter the Path. Now begins the first part.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted the light from the *uṣṇīṣa*—the mark of a Great Man—and emitted the light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which shone throughout the east, illuminating as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in one hundred and eight million *nayuta* of *gaṅgā* rivers.
Beyond this number of worlds, there is a world named Pure Light Adornment (*Vimalaprabhālaṃkāra*). In that land dwells a Buddha named Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men,
Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One, who [is surrounded] by immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas.
Surrounded by a multitude who paid him respectful homage, Śākyamuni Buddha preached the Dharma for them. The radiance from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows illuminated that land entirely.
The marks of a Great Man constitute an ocean of great characteristics; the merit of all the hairs on his body does not equal the merit of even a single secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*).

The merit of all other excellent marks does not equal the merit of a single mark; each successive mark from the bottom upward is superior to the one below it, yet they do not equal the merit of the *ūrṇā* (white tuft of hair).
The merit of the *ūrṇā* does not equal the merit of the *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protrusion);

therefore, these are called the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). As for the karma of this mark, it arises from filial obedience toward teachers and elders. Now, he emits this light to summon [them].
"I, this disciple, shall propagate the sutras of the Middle Way to benefit those of great capacity. The white tuft of hair arises from the single path of purity;
now, emitting this light, it causes this Dharma to be propagated. Question: "The Buddha’s individual marks are each the ocean of the Dharma-realm;
why then do you speak of victory and defeat? Answer: "This is merely a provisional teaching intended for other sutras. Question: "O Buddha..."

Question: Since there are disciples with whom he has a karmic connection filling the ten directions, why does he summon those in the east and speak of the west, rather than addressing all eight directions?
Answer: This has a symbolic significance. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* asks: "For what purpose do the sun and moon travel over Jambudvīpa?

It is because they desire to use their radiance to dispel the deep darkness of the masses. The east is the beginning of light, and the west is the end of light. To have a beginning and an end—this is the way of the Sage alone.

For those among humanity who have not yet resolved their minds for enlightenment, cause them to resolve their minds; for those who have not yet reached the ultimate goal, cause them to reach the ultimate goal.

As it is with one bodhisattva, so it is with all bodhisattvas; as it is in one direction, so it is in all directions. II. Receiving the Command and Coming from the West. This section has two parts: A.

The Introduction, Part One: Describing the Field of Merit.

At that time, in the land of Universal Pure Light Adornment, there was a bodhisattva named Gadgadasvara who had long since planted the roots of all virtues and had made offerings to, and drawn near to, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of buddhas.
△ Second, the description of wisdom:

He attained the Samādhi of the Wondrous Banner Mark, the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra, the Samādhi of Pure Virtue, the Samādhi of the Constellation King’s Play,
the Samādhi of Objectless Wisdom, the Samādhi of the Seal of Knowledge, the Samādhi of Understanding the Languages of All Sentient Beings,
the Samādhi of Gathering All Merit, the Samādhi of Purity, the Samādhi of the Play of Supernatural Powers, the Samādhi of the Torch of Wisdom, and the Samādhi of the Adorned King.

He attained hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great samādhis, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River, such as the Samādhi of Pure Radiance, the Samādhi of the Treasury of Purity, the Samādhi of Unshared Qualities, and the Samādhi of the Revolving Sun.

The Bodhisattva Sarvauṣadhi-rāja, the Bodhisattva Śūradatta, the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña,
the Bodhisattva Viśiṣṭacāritra, the Bodhisattva Vyūharāja, and the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.
△ Fourth, the admonition on sincerity.
At that time, the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña addressed the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara: "Do not despise that land by conceiving thoughts of inferiority.
Good son, that Sahā world is uneven with high and low ground, filled with mountains of earth and stone, and replete with filth and impurity;
the bodies of the Buddhas there are short and small, and the forms of the assembly of bodhisattvas are likewise small, whereas your own body is forty-two [yojanas tall]."
"My body is one thousand yojanas in height, while yours is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas.

You are preeminent in physical beauty, possessing hundreds of thousands of millions of merits and exquisite radiance; therefore, go there and do not disparage that land, nor harbor thoughts of inferiority toward the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or the realm."
However, although a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body is inherently majestic without needing formal solemnity, those whom he leads as his retinue may not yet have attained such realization;

therefore, he relies upon that [external form] to guide them toward this [inner truth]. Indeed, the Buddha-body is in perfect correspondence with ultimate principle (*tathatā*); one must not perceive its humble appearance and thereby forget its sublime majesty.
This is a warning based on the Tathāgata’s seat. Furthermore, regarding the wisdom and the abandonment [of afflictions] of both teacher and disciple:
The Master, having fully employed skillful means, likewise conceals his true reality from his disciples; this is a warning based on the Tathāgata’s robe.

Since the land of the external environment (*upapatti-bhoga*) is entirely induced by the primary retribution (*pradhāna-vipāka*), and the Tathāgata presides over the great trichiliocosm with compassion, one must attend both to what is high and what is low;
do not behold only the external environment and neglect the primary retribution—this is based on the Tathāgata’s dwelling.
This is an exhortation; this Buddha’s propagation of the sutra also commands three intentions, for that Honored One exhorted and constrained [them] by noting that the Way of all Buddhas is the same.

Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound addressed his Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I shall now go to the Sahā world; it is entirely as [you have said]."
The power of the Tathāgata’s arrival is the power of the Tathāgata’s playful mastery of supernormal powers (*ṛddhivikrīḍita*); the power of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom is the adornment.
The power of the Tathāgata is the power of this seat; the power of supernormal mastery is the power of this chamber; the power of adornment is the power of these robes.
Because this receives the great purport of the extensive sūtra and constitutes the essential core for benefiting sentient beings, one is able to travel while remaining unmoved from this assembly.
He transforms the ten directions. △ Sixth, Manifesting the Signs of Arrival. First, the Sending of the Lotus.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, without rising from his seat and without moving his body, entered into samādhi.
By the power of that samādhi, he manifested eighty-four thousand precious lotuses not far from the Dharma-seat on Vulture Peak Mountain.
The lotus has Jambūnada gold for its stem, white silver for its petals, diamond for its filaments,
and Vaiḍūrya (Karketana) jewels for its pericarp.
△ Second, Mañjuśrī’s inquiry.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, seeing these lotuses, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this auspicious omen first appeared?
There are many tens of millions of lotuses, with stems of Jāmbūnada gold, leaves of white silver, filaments of diamond, and pedestals made of karketana gems."
△ Third, Śākyamuni’s response:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying,
"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara wishes to come from the land of the Buddha Śubhavyūha-rāja-saṃkusumitābhijña, surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas."
Having arrived here in this Sahā world, they have made offerings to, drawn near to, and paid homage to me; now they also wish to make offerings to and hear the Lotus Sūtra.
△ Fourth, the request to see his form.

Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what roots of goodness has this bodhisattva planted, and what merits has he cultivated, that he is able to possess such great supernormal powers?
What samādhi does he practice? We pray that you will tell us the name of this samādhi;
we also wish to diligently cultivate and practice it, for only by practicing this samādhi can one see this bodhisattva."

Regarding his physical appearance, stature, dignified demeanor, and movements, I only pray that the World-Honored One, by means of your supernormal powers, will cause that Bodhisattva to come so that I may behold him.
Question: If Mañjuśrī’s rank were lower, it would be inappropriate to request an audience; if his rank were higher, why would he come to such a place?

Suddenly not recognizing [the answer], although they share the same rank, there is a beginning, middle, and end; by stopping at this single matter, one remains ignorant and yet does not disgrace the high position.
Furthermore, seeing an auspicious sign among the assembly, [the Buddha] did not understand its cause, so he posed a question to initiate [the explanation] and bring about understanding.
△ Fifth, explaining the attribution of merit.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "This Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who entered parinirvāṇa long ago, shall now manifest his form for you all.
△ Sixth, the command to come.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed those bodhisattvas, "Sons of good family, come! Mañjuśrī, the Prince of the Dharma, wishes to see your body.
△ Second, the actual departure and arrival, in six parts: first, the journey with his retinue.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land and set out together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas;
as they traveled through the various lands, the earth shook in six ways, and everywhere there rained down lotuses made of the seven treasures,
while hundreds of thousands of celestial musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
△ Second, the description of his physical appearance as he ascends the platform:
This Bodhisattva’s eyes are like the broad petals of a vast blue lotus; even if a hundred thousand million moons were joined together, his countenance would be more upright and handsome than they.
His body is the color of pure gold, adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of meritorious qualities.
With majestic power blazing forth and radiant light illuminating all, his physical marks were fully perfected like the firm body of Nārāyaṇa.
Entering a pavilion of the seven precious gems, he ascended into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees above the ground;
surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas who paid him respectful homage, he came to this Sahā world, to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
△ Third, the inquiry after his health and the transmission of the message.

Having arrived, he descended from the seven-jeweled terrace, took a necklace worth hundreds of thousands, went to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, presented the necklace, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom..."

The Buddha inquired after the World-Honored One: "Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy? Do you dwell in peace and happiness? Are the four great elements in harmony?
Can you endure worldly affairs? Are sentient beings easy to deliver? Are they free from much greed, hatred, delusion, envy, stinginess, and pride?
Are they free from lack of filial piety toward their parents, disrespect for śramaṇas, wrong views, and unwholesome thoughts?"
He gathers his five senses; the World-Honored One can subdue all Māras and enemies, and before long he will enter parinirvāṇa.

The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna is within the stupa made of the seven treasures, coming to listen to the Dharma. Furthermore, he inquires after the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna’s well-being, asking if he has little affliction, if he is enduring, and if he dwells long.
△ Fourth, the request to see Prabhūtaratna:
"World-Honored One, I now wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna; I only pray that the World-Honored One will show it to me so that I may behold it.
Once the emanated bodies had dispersed and the stupa was closed as before, and since Prabhūtaratna resided within the stupa, [the assembly] prayed that he be revealed.
[He] saw [him]. △ Fifth, the World-Honored One acts as an intermediary.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha said to the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, "This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara wishes to meet you."
△ It was well-spoken within the six stūpas.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed Gadgadasvara, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
You have come here for the sake of making offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, for the purpose of hearing the Lotus Sutra, and to behold Mañjuśrī and the others."
△ Section 30: Propagation of the Sūtra in the Ten Directions, Part 2: Questions and Answers on the Power of Roots of Goodness, Part 1: The Questions, Part 1:
Questioning What Roots of Goodness Were Planted.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what roots of goodness did this Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound plant?"
This question concerns the past. △ Second, the question regarding the existence of this supernatural power:
"By cultivating what merit does one possess such supernatural power?
This question concerns the present. △ Second, the answer, which has two parts; first, the answer concerning the planting of roots of goodness.
The Buddha told Flower-Virtue Bodhisattva: "In the past, there was a Buddha named Cloud-Thunder-Sound King (*Meghadundubhisvararāja*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
His land was named Manifesting All Worlds, and his eon was named Joyful Sight.
During that time, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣavasu*) made offerings to the Cloud-Thunder-Sound King for twelve thousand years with a hundred thousand varieties of musical instruments."
The Buddha also presented him with eighty-four thousand bowls made of the seven treasures.

By virtue of these causes and conditions and their karmic retribution, he has now been born in the land of the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom and possesses such supernatural powers. Flower Virtue, what do you think?
Is the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound—who at that time performed musical offerings before the Buddha Cloud Thunder Sound King and presented those precious vessels—anyone other than this person?

O people, this present Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara is that same Flower-Virtue (Puṣpadatta). This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara has already made offerings to and drawn near countless Buddhas,
long planting the roots of merit, and has further encountered hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
△ Second, answering regarding his supernatural powers:
"Puṣpadatta, you see only that the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara’s body is here;

however, this bodhisattva manifests various kinds of bodies everywhere to preach this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings—sometimes manifesting as the body of Brahmā, sometimes manifesting as Śakra."
The body may manifest as the form of Īśvara, or manifest as the form of Maheśvara, or manifest as the form of Deva Senāpati,
or manifest as the form of Vaiśravaṇa Rāja, or manifest as the form of a Cakravartin King, or manifest as the form of various minor kings,
or manifest as the form of a householder, or manifest as the form of a lay devotee, or manifest as the form of a government official, or manifest as the form of a brahmin...
They may manifest as the bodies of Brahmins, or appear as the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās;
they may appear as the bodies of elders, laymen, or women; they may appear as the bodies of female officials, or female Brahmins;
they may appear as the bodies of boys or girls; or they may appear as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, or asuras.
He preaches this sutra with the bodies of garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans;
he is able to rescue all those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and other places of great suffering, even transforming into a female body within the royal harem to preach this sutra.
Flower Virtue, this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara can provide protection and salvation for the Sahā world.

The various sentient beings of the Sahā world see the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara manifesting such diverse transformations of his body here in this Sahā land to preach this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings;
yet, in his supernormal powers, transformations, and wisdom, there is no diminution whatsoever. By means of his manifold wisdom, this bodhisattva illuminates the Sahā world.
All sentient beings each obtain what they know; it is likewise so throughout the worlds of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If there are those who should be delivered by appearing in the form of a śrāvaka, he manifests in the form of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.

If there are those who should be delivered by appearing in the form of a pratyekabuddha, he manifests in the form of a pratyekabuddha and preaches the Dharma for them. If there are those who should be delivered by appearing in the form of a bodhisattva...
To those who are to be saved by the form of a bodhisattva, he manifests in the form of a bodhisattva and preaches the Dharma for them;
to those who are to be saved by the form of a Buddha, he immediately manifests in the form of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma for them.

In this way, he manifests various forms according to what is appropriate for each being to be saved, even manifesting his own parinirvāṇa for those who are to be saved by means of parinirvāṇa—such is the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue Wondrous Sound.
Such is the manner in which Mahāsattvas accomplish the power of great supernatural penetrations (*ṛddhi*) and wisdom.

This response to the question regarding supernatural power demonstrates the thirty-four [states]—the four ordinary bodies and the four noble bodies—which constitute the ten dharma-realms and the six paths of existence.
△ Second, the question and answer concerning "In what concentration do you currently abide? Part one: the question.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound has deeply planted roots of goodness.
World-Honored One, in what samādhi does this bodhisattva abide, such that he is able to manifest transformations in various places to deliver and liberate sentient beings?”
Question: "In what meditative concentration (*samādhi*) do you currently abide to be able to thus freely benefit others? Part Two: The Answer.
The Buddha told Flower Virtue Bodhisattva: "Good son, this samādhi is named 'Manifesting All Physical Bodies.
It is by abiding in this samādhi that the Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound is able to thus bring benefit to immeasurable sentient beings."
The Buddha answered as recorded in the text. △ Fourth, the benefits obtained in the two lands:

When this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached, the eighty-four thousand people who had come together with the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara all attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms;
likewise, immeasurable bodhisattvas in this Sahā world also [attained it].
He attained this samādhi and dhāraṇī.
△ Fifth, returning to his own country.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and Prabhūtaratna Buddha.

Having finished with the stupa, he returned to his own land. As he passed through the various countries, the earth shook in six ways, jeweled lotuses rained down, and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kinds of music were played.

Upon arriving in his own country, surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, he went to the presence of the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have reached the Sahā world..."
Furthermore, he caused the sentient beings to see Śākyamuni Buddha and to pay homage and make offerings to the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna;
they also saw the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, as well as the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja,
Vīryadatta, and Sūradatta, and likewise enabled these eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas to manifest [the Buddha] before their eyes.
The Samādhi of the Body of All Colors.
△ Sixth, advancing on the Path through hearing the chapters.
While this "Chapter on the Coming and Going of Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached, forty-two thousand devaputras attained the dharma of non-arising.
The Bodhisattva Endowed with the Virtue of Patience attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
*Commentary on the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Fascicle Seven.
*Commentary on the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Fascicle Eight.
△ Second, the Universal Gate Chapter on Avalokiteśvara.
Part One: The Title of the Chapter. *The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Twenty-Five: "The Universal Gate of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.

According to the Tiantai commentary, this chapter has a distinct *xuanshu* (profound commentary). Summarizing that commentary on the chapter, there are both general and specific [explanations]. The general [explanation] is as follows:

This constitutes ten pairs; specifically, there are five single items and ten pairs. Regarding the "ten pairs": the first is the person's method, up to the tenth, which is the wisdom that abandons this category [of afflictions].
This chapter combines the person's method and the Universal Gate (Pumen) method as its title.

There are two rounds of question and answer. As for "Avalokiteśvara," it refers to one who extracts suffering through great compassion, based on the previous discussion of the hundreds of thousands of sufferings.

Regarding "Universal Gate" (Pumen): it refers to great compassion that bestows happiness; based on the subsequent question and answer, one should preach the Dharma according to what is necessary for deliverance.

As for the "five modes of contemplation": first, there are many types of contemplation, namely, the contemplation of disintegration (*zhé*), the contemplation of the emptiness of essence (*tǐkōng*), the sequential threefold contemplation (*cìdì sānguān*), and the perfectly integrated threefold contemplation (*yuánróng sānguān*), and so forth. Now, excluding the former three, this refers exclusively to the perfectly integrated contemplation.

Furthermore, there are many kinds of "worlds" (*loka*) across the two lifetimes: namely, the conditioned world (*saṃskṛta-loka*), the unconditioned world (*asaṃskṛta-loka*), the world of the two extremes, and the inconceivable world (*acintya-loka*).
Here, we take the inconceivable world. Regarding the three sounds, "sound" refers to the capacity (*indriya*). Capacity is also of many kinds:

the capacity of humans and devas, the capacity of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), the capacity of bodhisattvas, and the capacity of Buddhas. Now, we respond by employing only the capacity of the Buddha.
"Also four: 'Universal' (pǔ) means all-pervasive. If the immeasurable dharmas do not attain universality, they are partial dharmas;
if they attain universality, they are perfect dharmas. Universality is defined according to the ten dharmas (*yúmǎ*) [and so forth]. As for the five gates:

the gate of emptiness, the gate of the provisional, and the gate of the middle. Now, because it penetrates the true reality (*dharmatā*) and simultaneously illuminates the two truths, it is called such."
Because it is universally able to provide access, it is called a "gate"; the Universal Gate (Pumen) is precisely the gate of perfect penetration.

Therefore, the title of this chapter signifies that the Bodhisattva, by means of the wondrous contemplation of perfect interfusion, contemplates the sounds of the Buddha’s responsive capacity within inconceivable worlds, universally causing all to enter the gate of perfect penetration. Hence, it is titled the "Universal Gate Chapter of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. △

The second part, the scriptural text, has two sections: first, two rounds of question and answer; second, the benefits gained upon hearing this chapter. The first section [of the scriptural text] further has two parts:
first, the prose; second, the verses. The first part [the prose] further has two sections: first, one round of question and answer; second, another round of question and answer.
The first of these further has two parts: first, the question; second, the initial narration by the scribe of the scripture.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"Akṣayamati" means neither exhausted nor inexhaustible; this is taught in contrast to the Hīnayāna, which clarifies exhaustion. The Hīnayāna clarifies... [text fragment ends].
"Exhaustion" refers to the cessation of the emptiness of form-attachment through the wisdom that realizes non-arising; thus, it possesses the meaning of being inexhaustible.
Space is inexhaustible, all dharmas are inexhaustible, and neither the empty, the provisional, nor the middle can be reached to their limit.

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Form itself is emptiness; it is not that form is extinguished to become emptiness. Because emptiness is such, it is inexhaustible. △ Second, the formal posing of the question.
For what causes and conditions is the World-Honored One, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, named "Observer of the Sounds of the World"?
There are two rounds of question and answer; this is the first. First, the person who is Avalokiteśvara is questioned, and subsequently, the Dharma of the Universal Gate is questioned.

This section constitutes the first round of questioning. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Because you possess the two kinds of adornment, you are able to question me, who likewise possess the two kinds of adornment."

Because it is solemn, one is able to answer. The *Vyākhyā* (Śāstra) says: "There are many kinds of questions; there are those asked because of a lack of understanding, those asked as a test, and those asked to accord with the capacities [of beings].
The present case is a question asked to accord with their capacities. Regarding the phrase "by what causes and conditions," its meanings are very numerous; for now, I shall speak briefly.

As for the relationship between the object (*viṣaya*) and wisdom (*jñāna*), sentient beings' two capacities—wholesome and unwholesome—serve as the cause, while the Bodhisattva’s spiritual... [is the condition].
Wisdom and compassion serve as the conditions; for these reasons, he is named Avalokiteśvara. II. The Response (in three parts). A.
General Response to the Capabilities and Responses of Sentient Beings. 1. Indicating the Number of People.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati: "Good son, if there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings..."
The statement that "the capacities of the ten dharma realms are immeasurable, numbering in the hundreds, thousands, myriads, and billions," refers generally to those who share the same karma.

By citing multiple types, it clarifies that among those encountering suffering, some invoke the Name at one time, while the capacity to respond exists at another time. △ Second, explaining the encounter with suffering.
They undergo various sufferings and afflictions.

Because hundreds of thousands of karmas are identical [in nature], they are called "various sufferings and afflictions. This arises because the fruits of accumulated karma are many and the causes are likewise many;
thus, while the text of the general answer is concise, its meaning is extensive. △ Third, hearing the name and title.

"Hearing this and single-mindedly invoking the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" clarifies that the arising of goodness and the presence of both good and evil together constitute the spiritual capacity (*ki*). If one can penetrate this, "hearing" is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);

"the mind being free from dwelling or attachment" is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and "single-mindedly invoking the name" is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Single-mindedness possesses...

When one focuses on an object, maintains mindfulness of its characteristics, practices counting the breath, or binds the mind through recollection so that the single mind is undisturbed—all these constitute "single-mindedness in regard to phenomena" (*sāsrava-ekacitta*).
If one can penetrate this, one realizes that the nature of the mind—whether self, other, or both—is ultimately unfindable;
being without mind and without thought, one accords with the wisdom of emptiness. This is "neither single-mindedness nor mind. One then knows that the characteristics of sound are all empty.
The echo is not real; both the one who calls and that which is called cannot be apprehended. This is called "namelessness," which is precisely the single mind of principle.
△ Fourth, attaining liberation:
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately observes their voices, and all attain liberation.
When those suffering in the higher realms simply invoke the Name, this is the swiftness of the capacity [of the practitioner]. When the invocation is made now, there is an immediate response;
this is the swiftness with which the response accords with the capacity and reaches the invocation. Therefore, all attain liberation. △ Second, the specific answer regarding the three karmas.
Part three: first, the response to the capacity of speech. Part two: first, clarifying the seven calamities. Part seven: the calamity of fire. Section four: first, those who hold the Name.
"If there are those who hold the name of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara":
the practitioner must remember and maintain the name; this is what is meant by "holding the name. △ Second, encountering suffering.
Even if one enters a great fire,
△ third, as a dark response,
the fire cannot burn them.
△ Fourth, the conclusion.
It was due to the majestic spiritual power of this Bodhisattva that such traces were left.
The man of Jin, Xie Fu, who possessed profound faith in the Great Dharma, transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* during his daily life and composed [the *Guānyīn*]...
According to tradition, Zhu Changshu was struck by a spreading fire during the Yuankang era of the Jin dynasty. With single-minded devotion, he invoked the Buddha’s name;

the wind shifted and the flames turned away from his neighbor's dwelling, and the fire was extinguished. Fayuan observed that there are three kinds of fires: the fire of karmic retribution (*vipāka-agni*), the fire of karma (*karma-agni*), and the fire of afflictions (*kleśa-agni*).
The fire of karmic retribution extends as far as the First Dhyāna Heaven; the fire of karma pervades the three realms; and the fire of afflictions [pervades all].
Because it applies to those who follow the three vehicles, from the first dhyāna downward, no one can escape the fire of karmic retribution when the kalpa of destruction is exhausted.
As for the fire of karma: the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions are burned by the fire of the three poisons, which consumes all roots of goodness. As for the fire of afflictions:
if a śrāvaka grows weary of birth and death and views the triple world as being like a burning house, they diligently seek skillful means.

Rushing out of the burning house, one immediately attains liberation. For Pratyekabuddhas, there are the six pāramitās; for those of the Separate, Shared, and Perfect Teachings, there is the practice of the path by those in the land of transformation.

Those who cultivate the Way are scorched by the fires of the afflictions and delusions of the five abodes; as their skillful means are not yet perfected, they are constantly beset by the perils of fire.
By invoking the Name, they immediately attain liberation. The Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattvas is immeasurable, yet it is not outside the two: the Separate and the Perfect.
Because he contemplates the original arising of compassion, he is able to respond universally. △ Second, the peril of water:
if one is being swept away by a great flood, by invoking his name, one will immediately find shallow ground.
The *Account of Verified Miracles* (*Shiji Yingyan Zhuan*) states that a man of Haiyan who was drowning called upon the name of the Bodhisattva and encountered a rock, thereby escaping death.

Furthermore, when Liu Cheng was traveling to serve as the Governor of Guangzhou, he encountered a storm at sea; his mother and two nuns called upon the name of the Bodhisattva and were likewise delivered from the peril.
According to the *Yueguan jie*, there are karmic fruits for such acts: water reaches up to the second dhyāna heaven, while the earth extends down to the hells.

None can escape the waters of difficult and evil karma that flood the three realms, submerging and destroying the roots of goodness; nor the waters of affliction (*kleśa*) that sweep through those of the Three Vehicles.

As the Sūtra says: "The great river of affliction can sweep away fragrant elephants; the waters of craving and desire increase false views, drowning one in the hardships of birth and death, making it difficult to reach the further shore of Nirvāṇa.
For those of the Two Vehicles who cut across the river of birth and death, the path ahead remains far."
Chanting the name and giving rise to true insight into the truths is called "reaching the shallow shore and arriving at the further shore of no-more-learning.
The sequence for Pratyekabuddhas, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), and so forth, is likewise the same. △ Third, the difficulty of the *rākṣasa*.
If there are hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings who, seeking treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, tridacna shell, agate, coral,
amber, and pearls, enter the great ocean, and if a black wind should blow their ship and cast it adrift into the land of the rākṣasa demons—
if among them even a single person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara—
All these people attain liberation from the perils of the rākṣasas; for this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
The Āgamas state that "wind" refers to the extreme terror of black karma; a rākṣasa is a ghost that devours humans.

According to the commentary on the *Guān* (Contemplation) Sūtra, it is not only the winds of the mundane world, but black karma itself that is called "wind. The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra speaks of the "fierce winds of resentment and hatred."
The wind of the mind’s afflictions constantly blazes, blowing the merchants of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) into the evil destinies.

They lose the precious jewels of the human path and the wealth of the untainted Dharma (*anāsrava-dharma*). Furthermore, from the hells up to the third dhyāna heaven, there are the perils of the winds of karmic retribution:
in the hells, there are fierce winds and violent waves; in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), cold winds split the bones; and among animals...
When the Asuras face the calamity of the wind that overturns nests and destroys eggs, and when the wind-disaster at the end of the kalpa arises,
such that all mountains collide and strike one another until the palaces of the third dhyāna heaven are crushed into fine dust—
at that time, if one single-mindedly invokes the name of Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva will, by the power of the King Samādhi, either shield them with his hand or...
By means of the mouth, one inhales immeasurable skillful means to bring about liberation.

Furthermore, the black winds of evil karma blow away the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, blowing the vessel of the ship down into the three miserable realms, the four modes of existence, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the sphere of craving and views.

When those of the Two Vehicles gather the treasures of the noble wealth, they are blown by the winds of affliction, causing their ship of compassionate practice to fall into the sphere of views and craving; this constitutes "view."

Those harmed by the demon Āḷavaka were delivered from suffering through the mere utterance of his name; those who have forever escaped the twenty-five states of existence within the two wheels of craving and views;
those Pratyekabuddhas and those practicing the six perfections—whether following the Shared, Distinct, or Complete teachings—who enter the sea of afflictions to gather the jewel of omniscience;

and those whose ship of conditioned formations is tossed by the violent winds of the eight inversions, falling into the ghost-realm of the two extremes. [All these] rely upon... (the power of the name).

By correctly contemplating the essence of the mind and realizing that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, one enters the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and immediately attains liberation.

The *Account of Miraculous Responses to Deeds* relates that more than a hundred people from foreign lands were traveling by sea from Siṃhala Island when they encountered a violent wind and fell into a realm of ghosts.
At that time, as the rākṣasas intended to devour them, the entire ship’s company together invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara; among them was...
There was once a śramaṇa of the Hīnayāna who did not believe in Avalokiteśvara and refused to invoke his name. When a ghost seized this śramaṇa, he was in a state of panic;
however, when he learned to invoke the name, he attained liberation. △ Fourth, the peril of the Four Kings.
If there is another person who, when about to be harmed, calls upon the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
the swords and staves held by their assailants will immediately break into pieces, and they shall attain liberation.
By way of contemplation, it is explained that evil karma can likewise harm the wholesome body and life-force. The six sense-objects and the three poisons are all termed "swords and arrows";
they destroy the wholesome mind, sever the skin of precepts, and cut through the flesh of meditative concentration, such that for ten thousand kalpas one does not again give rise to a heart of fear.
If one invokes Avalokiteśvara, one immediately receives protection; the three poisons cannot cause injury, and one ascends purely to receive bliss—this is the power of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, if Śrāvakas weary of birth and death and contemplate the three realms, they perceive that their afflictions of view and thought are more piercing than knives and arrows.

For Pratyekabuddhas and those practicing the six pāramitās—whether following the Shared, Distinct, or Complete teachings—their afflictions of the five abodes are like the wounds of knives and arrows that injure the Dharma-body and damage the life of wisdom.

If one can invoke the name [of the Buddha], one will immediately receive the response of the Sage and be liberated from the two kinds of birth and death associated with the Shared and Distinct vehicles, as well as from the knives and staves of these afflictions.
The *Account of Miraculous Responses to Past Deeds* states that during the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, a man from Pengcheng was captured by bandits and placed in shackles.
This man habitually made offerings to a golden image of Avalokiteśvara, which he wore within his topknot. When he was under the blade, he heard only the sound of metal;
though the blade struck his neck three times, it remained uninjured. Upon untying his topknot to examine the image, he found three marks upon it. Because of this, he was granted release.
5. The Peril of Ghosts.

If the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were filled with yakṣas and rākṣasas wishing to come and harass people, yet they hear someone reciting the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, these evil ghosts would not even be able to look upon them with malevolent eyes, let alone [harm them].
Furthermore, as for "filling [the vessel]":

it is because the mental consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*) of the ghosts extends throughout it that they fill its interior. As for the statement that one cannot inflict harm upon someone who calls out their name:
this is either because they fear their majesty or because they harbor gratitude toward them. This is explained according to the *Guān* (Contemplation) school.
Regarding the discourse on retribution: there are powerful ghosts who torment sinners in the hells; among animals, there are ghosts that devour other animals;
and the same can be understood regarding humans. As for the devas, since they already preside over ghosts, how could those ghosts cause them distress?
The Āgama states: "There was a powerful ghost who suddenly sat upon Śakra’s throne; when Śakra became angry, the ghost’s radiance grew even more intense."
When Śakra develops a mind of compassion, the light of the ghost immediately extinguishes and it departs at once.

If even the Lord of Devas is thus afflicted, how much more so the Four Heavenly Kings and the asuras? In such places, ghosts may be numerous, yet by invoking the name of Avalokiteśvara, they cannot inflict harm.
Furthermore, those who cultivate causes but possess their own evil karma are themselves called "ghosts. As the Āgamas state: "The lust-ghost..."
They enter into people's hearts, causing them to become licentious and immoderate, or inducing anger, ignorance, and the like.

These three poisons are, in their very essence, demons. For instance, lust destroys the precept of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); anger destroys the precept of loving-kindness and compassion; the demon of greed afflicts the precept of non-stealing;

and the demon of craving afflicts the precept of non-intoxication. This applies even to the ten wholesome paths of action and the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*); they are all likewise rendered evil by these [demons].
If one can invoke their names, the karmic ghosts will not inflict harm upon the karma of humans and devas, whether moving or unmoving.
Furthermore, as for the ghosts of affliction (*kleśa*): the perception of the mind is the male ghost, and the craving of the mind is the female ghost.

Since there are eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) throughout the three realms and ninety-eight cravings throughout the three realms, how could they not be pervasive, coming to torment [beings]?
This applies to practitioners of the Two Vehicles, as well as those who practice the six pāramitās, whether in their general or specific aspects, up to the Perfect Teaching (Vipula-yāna).
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "We only pray that the World-Honored One, acting as a virtuous master of spells, will eliminate for us the demon of ignorance.
It further states: "The rākṣasa of folly dwells therein. Is this not indeed the demon of afflictions? If one invokes the name and recites it, the wisdom of contemplation will be accomplished.
This enables one to cause the afflictions of views and craving to turn according to one's will, so that they cannot cause harm.
△ Sixth, the hardship of shackles and fetters:
Suppose there is a person, whether guilty or innocent, whose body is bound and constrained by cangues, manacles, and neck-shackles; this is called "contemplation."
All those who hear the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva shall have their bonds severed and immediately attain liberation.
The *Shilu Yingyan Zhuan* (Records of Miraculous Responses from the Path) relates that a man from Hushan Yang was imprisoned and sentenced to death;

for three days and three nights he invoked the name of the Bodhisattva without ceasing, whereupon he received the illumination of Avalokiteśvara’s light, his shackles fell away, the prison door opened, and he followed the light.
After traveling twenty li, the light faded. He observed that the essence of hell is like a prison;
ghosts and animals are likewise confined in cages, and even asuras are bound by the five fetters. Yet, in the northern continent and the heavens, there should be no such suffering of subjugation;
from these places downward, none can escape the calamities of the dark realms. If one can invoke the Name, all such sufferings shall be severed.
Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of causes: evil karma is nothing other than shackles and fetters. Although karma possesses power, it depends on whether or not one acts;
yet once a cause has been created, its fruit is never lost. Therefore, it is called an "indestructible dharma" (*avipraṇāśa-dharma*), like a promissory note.
If a person cultivates various virtues, they may be obstructed by evil karma, just as a great mountain casts a shadow that covers the mind.
If one further increases evil karma through good that has been ruined, one will immediately encounter the bonds of retribution from which there is no way to escape.
Those who wish to be liberated should invoke Avalokiteśvara to cause their evil karma to be destroyed. Thus, a sutra says: "Wives and children are shackles;

wealth and property are prisons; and royal law is a penal register. These obstruct the practitioner, preventing them from cultivating the Way; this is the retribution experienced in the present life."
The bondage of longing for the past is itself karma. △ Seventh, the difficulty of hostile bandits:

Suppose the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were filled with hostile bandits, and a certain caravan leader, leading many merchants and carrying heavy treasures, was passing through a perilous road.
Among them, one person raised this cry: "O virtuous sons, do not..."
"If you encounter fear, you should with one mind invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
This Bodhisattva is able to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings; if you invoke his name, you shall be liberated from these hostile bandits.
Upon hearing this, all the merchants raised their voices together and said, "Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva," thus invoking his name.
Therefore, one immediately attains liberation.

The term "fulfillment" (*pūrṇa*) is used here as a metaphorical designation. An enemy-thief (*vairi-caura*) represents a grave peril; while a thief originally seeks wealth, an enemy originally seeks to take one's life.

Thus, the term "enemy-thief" refers here to the dual pursuit of both wealth and life. This account is recorded in the *Yijing Yingyan Zhuan* (Records of Verified Miracles) as being told by Śikṣānanda.

In the second year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, Huida was carrying a hoe and gathering medicinal herbs on the northern slopes of the Long Mountains when the Qiang people, who were starving, began capturing and eating humans.
Huida was seized by the Qiang and confined within a stockade; they selected the fattest among them to eat first.
Thereupon, Huida called upon the Buddha with utmost sincerity and recited the sutras. When the Qiang had finished eating all the other captives, only Huida and... [the text continues].
The child remained there throughout the night, praying with such earnest sincerity that he hoped for a divine response.

At dawn, just as the Qiang were about to take him, a tiger emerged from the edge of the grass, roaring; the Qiang scattered in all directions. The tiger then bit through the fence, making a hole, and departed.

The general Da took the child and fled into rebellion, thereby escaping the disaster. Later, when they met again, the general witnessed the retribution of his past enmity. From this, one can observe the fruits of karma. Thus ends the account of the rebel.
From the hells up to the sixth heaven, there is everywhere strife and contention; by reciting this name, one is delivered from such encounters with enmity.
Furthermore, when practicing virtue, evil thoughts are often numerous; these are called "enemies.

If one can recite this name, evil will retreat and goodness will increase, darkness will perish and light will arise. Furthermore, all afflictions are enemies and thieves to those seeking the supramundane Dharma.
The Master is the caravan leader; receiving the precepts through the *karmavācanā* is the merchant; the unmanifested precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*) are the precious jewels;

the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are the enemy bandits. Alternatively, the Dharma Master is the caravan leader; the assembly of disciples is the merchant; the principles and teachings are the precious jewels;

and the demonic activities of the two extremes (*antadvaya*) are the enemy bandits. Alternatively, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is the caravan leader; the mental factors (*caitasika*) are the merchants...
When one correctly contemplates this, wisdom is the precious treasure and discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) is the enemy;

alternatively, Prajñāpāramitā is the caravan leader and the ten thousand practices of the five perfections are the merchants, while the true reality of the *dharmatā* is the precious treasure and the six obscurations are the enemies.
With these many perspectives, one traverses all the teachings, and by merely invoking the name, one attains liberation. △ Second.
[The Buddha] said:
"Akṣayamati, such is the majestic and sublime power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
'Majestic and sublime' (*weiwei*) is a term denoting loftiness and height, used here as a metaphor for the power of Avalokiteśvara, which transcends the two [vehicles]."
This refers to those who erect the vertical banner outside the enclosure. II. The Intentional Mechanism of Response. Part One: Explaining the Three Poisons.
If there are sentient beings who abound in lustful desire, yet constantly keep in mind and pay reverent homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they shall immediately become free from desire.
If they abound in anger, yet constantly keep in mind and pay reverent homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they shall immediately become free from anger. If they abound in... [the text continues].
If a person of delusion constantly recollects and pays homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they will immediately be freed from delusion.
Since the three poisons frequently assail practitioners, it can be known that even those with the greatest [afflictions] may attain liberation, let alone those with fewer.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Women who violate the precepts, defile themselves, slander the Dharma, and fall into subsequent calamities—discarding no distinction between humans and beasts, and knowing no avoidance—"
High walls bring about the ruin of families and the destruction of nations, and their calamity extends to one's own person. A Great Sūtra states:
"If one habitually associates with greed and desire, when the retribution ripens, these are the signs of excessive lust. One who harbors much anger causes others to find them unpleasant to behold;
the *Śāsanānuśāsanī* states: "No thief of merit surpasses anger. The *Avataṃsaka* states: "The arising of a single thought of anger obstructs a hundred dharmas."

For those who are deluded regarding the gate of illumination and abound in ignorance, who perversely paint various views, deny cause and effect, and slander the Mahāyāna—one should single-mindedly maintain the visualization of Avalokiteśvara and shall thereby attain liberation.
By constant mindfulness, one attains right mindfulness;

by penetrating the nature of afflictions as being non-existent, one abides at the limit of greed and hatred, which is the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Having extinguished subject and object, one realizes that the nature of thought is fundamentally pure.
This refers precisely to concentration and wisdom. △ Second, the conclusion on the benefits:
"The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Infinite Intent possesses such great majestic spiritual power and brings benefit to many;
therefore, sentient beings should constantly keep him in mind."
△ III. The Response of the Three Bodies to the Capabilities [of Sentient Beings] (2). Part One: Clarifying the Two Types of Seeking (2).
Part One: Seeking a Son (3). Part One: Establishing the Vow.

If there is a woman who wishes to seek a son—since among human wishes none is more weighty than the continuation of one’s lineage, and the succession of a son is the greatest thereof—a woman must necessarily follow her husband.
Seeking the birth of a son. △ Second, the practice:
prostrating to and making offerings to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
△ Third, the virtue for giving birth to a son.
One will then give birth to a son endowed with merit, virtue, and wisdom.
Merit brings high status and rank; wisdom brings broad renown and profound understanding. If one is ignorant, unwholesome, and lacks these qualities, what benefit would there be?
△ Second, seeking a daughter, part one: making a vow.
If one desires to seek a daughter,
she shall be born upright and possessed of auspicious marks; having planted roots of virtue in past lives, she will be loved and respected by all.
"Being upright and possessing auspicious marks" means that she possesses the marks of physical beauty and lacks the marks of wickedness or depravity;
this is the virtue of a woman that has been manifest from an early age. Therefore, people love and revere her because she has planted the roots of merit in previous lives.
△ Second, the conclusion that [the results] are not in vain.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, of Inexhaustible Intent, possesses such power that if there are sentient beings who reverently pay homage to Avalokiteśvara,
their merit shall not be in vain.
If one pays homage with such supernatural power as that of a Bodhisattva, all shall obtain merit that will not go to waste.
△ Third, the exhortation to uphold the name, which has three parts; first, the exhortation to uphold it.
Therefore, all sentient beings should receive and uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
△ Second, the comparative evaluation:
"O Akṣayamati, if there were someone who received and upheld the names of bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty-two billion Ganges Rivers, and furthermore—"
"If one were to provide offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine for as long as one lives—what do you think, Unfailing Mind?
Would the merit of such a good man or good woman be great? "It would be very great, World-Honored One," Unfailing Mind replied. The Buddha said:
"If there is another person who upholds the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, even for a single moment, and pays him homage and makes offerings to him—"
The merit of these two persons is exactly equal and without distinction; it cannot be exhausted even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.

Although one person upholds many names, possesses many fields of merit, acts for many periods of time, and provides many of the four requisites of support, while the other upholds but a single name, worships for but a short time, and offers but a small amount—like a mere seed—their fields of merit are both small, yet the merit of these two persons is exactly equal.
The Buddha, weighing this with the Buddha-eye, finds it neither increased nor diminished. △ Third, the concluding praise:
"If one receives and upholds the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, one shall obtain such immeasurable and boundless benefits of merit."

The merit of reciting the name at one time is inexhaustible. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If one scatters a single flower into the air, its merit will not be exhausted until the end of suffering.
△ Second, the second round of question and answer, in two parts: first, the question, in three sections; first, the question regarding the body.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara traverse this Sahā world?
Having previously asked for what reason the Bodhisattva received his name, the Buddha replied: "It is because the three karmas of sentient beings manifest as responsive conditions."

The objective realm, the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-body, and spiritual wisdom are in profound stillness; they respond through the harmonious union of the conditions of compassion and wisdom, which is why he is named Avalokiteśvara.

Now, as to the question of how he wanders through this world, the Buddha answers with ten points, beginning with the manifestation of the three karmas through the Universal Gate to respond to the latent capacities of sentient beings. First, regarding the question of wandering through this world:
This concerns the appropriate physical action (*kāyakarman*). △ Second, the question concerning speech:
"How does one preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?
Next, the question regarding preaching the Dharma refers to the appropriate verbal action (*vākkarman*). △ Third, the question concerning the mind.
What are the matters regarding the power of skillful means (*upāya*)?
The three questions concerning skillful means correspond to the mental action (*manas-karman*). These three actions of the Sage transform beings without deliberation and respond to all;
they are also called the "three non-failures," meaning the inconceivable three wheels (*trimaṇḍala-acintya*). They are also called the three... [text fragment].
Regarding "not guarding" (the three karmas): when Avalokiteśvara dwells in the Dharma-gate of the inconceivable perfect sound, he truly does not engage in deliberate mental calculation;
rather, like a clear mirror that manifests images according to whatever is set before it, he responds universally and simultaneously. Therefore, it is said that his three karmas are "not guarded.
Regarding "the three non-losses": although the capacities of sentient beings have varying depths, Avalokiteśvara, while not engaging in deliberate mental calculation, adapts to their faculties.

Because phenomena and principle are in profound accord and their relative heights and depths correspond perfectly, one’s words do not miss the mark. Regarding the inconceivable transformation of the three wheels—
such as manifesting in the form of a Buddha-body while simultaneously revealing the mind and speech of a Buddha,

and even manifesting as a Vajrapāṇi deity while likewise revealing the mind and speech of a Vajrapāṇi— the universal manifestation of the form-body (rūpakāya) does not, however, depart from the wisdom of the dharma-body (dharmakāya).
"Without any diminution"—the Pure Name says this means being well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena while remaining unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);
this is inconceivable transformation. △ Second, the answer in three parts; first, the individual answers in eight sections;
first, the Holy Body in three parts; first, the Buddha-body.

The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati: "Good son, if there are sentient beings in any land who should be liberated by means of a Buddha-body, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately manifests in the form of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma for them."
"Answering according to what is appropriate" refers to the power of skillful means (*upāya*). One should understand that this refers to the mental faculty (*manas-karma*):
observing the capacities of beings on the level of the mind, seeing what they require, determining which body to manifest, and teaching whatever Dharma is suitable to transform them accordingly.

"Manifesting a body" answers bodily action (*kāya-karma*), and "teaching the Dharma" answers verbal action (*vāk-karma*). The same applies to all subsequent instances. Nevertheless, within these specific answers, there are generally thirty [points].
The three bodies and nineteen modes of preaching are condensed into the ten dharma-realm bodies; why, then, are two realms missing from the text?
Some say that since Avalokiteśvara is already the bodhisattva body, there is no need for him to manifest further [as other realms];

furthermore, as for the absence of the hell realm, although it is not mentioned in the specific explanations, the general response contains the text stating: "He wanders through all lands in various forms."

How can it be said that [the Buddha-body] does not exist? Furthermore, the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-sūtra* states that he may "sport in the hells," and the *Śāstra* (Treatise) says that when a Bodhisattva transforms the hells, he frequently manifests in the form of a Buddha.

Inferring from this, one sees that he possesses bodies corresponding to all ten realms of existence (*daśa-dharmadhātu*). Question: Is the manifestation of the Buddha-body a response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) or a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*)?
Answer: That which suddenly appears where there was previously nothing is called a "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*); as for the "response" (*nirmāṇa*), they are ultimately the same.
First, regarding the "name" (nāman): if the Dharma-body is the true Buddha, it is not the transformation body that preaches the Dharma.
△ Second, the body of the pratyekabuddha:
for those who should be saved by the body of a pratyekabuddha, he immediately manifests the body of a pratyekabuddha and preaches the Dharma for them.
This is like Mañjuśrī, who for twenty trillion kalpas acted as a pratyekabuddha to transform sentient beings. △ Third, the śrāvaka body:
for those who are to be delivered by means of a śrāvaka body, he immediately manifests a śrāvaka body and preaches the Dharma for them.

Alternatively, within the two teachings of the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya*, or according to the transformation through the five flavors, he secretly conceals [his true nature] while manifesting outwardly to adorn the four withered and the four flourishing states, thereby guiding sentient beings.
△ Second, the celestial bodies, sixfold: first, the body of Brahmā-rāja.
To those who are to be saved by the body of a Brahmā King, he manifests as a Brahmā King and preaches the Dharma for them.
He is the Lord of the Form Realm named Śikhin-alaṃkāra; it is understood that each of the four dhyānas has its own king, and this Brahmā King is likely the one of the first dhyāna.
Since he still possesses vitarka and vicāra and the faculty of speech, he is able to serve as the sovereign of a thousand worlds. — Avalokiteśvara.
Because he cultivates the white-colored samādhi without grasping, he does not follow the birth of the dhyānas;
yet because he does not abandon them, he manifests as a Brahmā King to lead beings from the provisional to the real. △ Second, the body of Śakra.
To those who are to be saved by the body of Śakra, he manifests in the form of Śakra and preaches the Dharma for them.
He is the Lord of the Earth-dwellers; his full name is Śakradevendra, which means "The Able Heavenly King," signifying one who is able to act as the sovereign over all the devas.
Avalokiteśvara, having cultivated the Samādhi Difficult to Subdue, manifests his body [in this way].
Using the provisional to lead to the ultimate. △ Third, the body of Maheśvara:
For those who are to be delivered by means of the body of Maheśvara, he immediately manifests the body of Maheśvara and preaches the Dharma for them.
This summit of the desire realm is named the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations; it is the Māra King who accomplishes his own pleasure by means of what others have created.
Avalokiteśvara dwells in the red-colored samādhi and should manifest as the Māra King, so that the realm of Māra is immediately the realm of the Buddha.
△ Regarding the body of Maheśvara:
for those who are to be delivered by means of the body of Maheśvara, he manifests the body of Maheśvara and preaches the Dharma to them.
This is Maheśvara at the summit of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). The *Loutan jing* calls him the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; the *Huayan jing* calls him the Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*).
The commentary states that he rides a white ox and possesses eight arms and three eyes, serving as the general of all the devas.
△ This is the body of the Great General of the Five Heavens.
To those who are to be saved by means of the body of a Heavenly Great General (*deva-mahāsenapati*), he immediately manifests the body of a Heavenly Great General and preaches the Dharma for them.
Within the light, he takes Vaiśravaṇa as his great general; as the *Mahāsūtra* says, "The eight *kumbhāṇḍas* possess the power within the heavens."
Regarding the *Śāstra-vyākhyā*, it says: "Kumāra means 'youth' (tóngzǐ); he carries a rooster, holds a rattle-drum, and grasps a red banner.
△ Sixth, the body of Vaiśravaṇa:
For those who are to be delivered by the body of Vaiśravaṇa, he immediately manifests the body of Vaiśravaṇa and preaches the Dharma for them.
This is called Bahudhāraṇī (Much-Hearing), who dwells on the northern face of Mount Sumeru; he is one of the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings.
△ Third, regarding the five types of human bodies: first, the body of a minor king.
For those who are to be saved by the body of a minor king, he manifests as a minor king and preaches the Dharma for them.
Some say that [the Buddha] manifests as a great king or a minor king; some say it is because there are great and small nations, or that he is a prince.
△ Second, the body of a householder:
for those who are to be saved by the body of a householder, he immediately manifests in the body of a householder and preaches the Dharma for them.
The elder possesses the virtues of a leader; the ten similes have already been set forth in the text. △ Third, the householder body:
