for those who should be liberated through the body of a householder, he manifests as a householder and preaches the Dharma to them.
This refers to those who possess great wealth and engage in business; some say it refers to scholars who dwell in the Way, dwell in the mountains, or dwell in wealth.
4. The Body of a Minister:
For those who are to be saved by the body of a minister, he manifests the body of a minister and preaches the Dharma for them.

"Zai" (宰) means "ruler," and "guan" (官) means "to govern. Taken together, they signify one who presides over and manages; this refers to those with meritorious achievements who assist and govern the sovereign.
Furthermore, the chief officials of commanderies and districts are all called *zai-guan* (宰官). △ Fifth, the body of a Brahmin.
To those who are to be saved by means of a Brahmin body, he immediately manifests a Brahmin body and preaches the Dharma for them.
This is called the "Pure Conduct" (śuddha-carita), the lineage at the beginning of the kalpa;

it refers to one of the four castes of the Western Regions, specifically those who dwell in seclusion in forests and fields, living in reclusion like the hermits of India and China—a general designation for such sages. △ Fourth, the bodies of the fourfold assembly.
To those who are to be saved by the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, he immediately manifests the bodies of bhikṣus,
bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās and preaches the Dharma for them.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" has been explained following the listing of the assembly in the introductory chapter. A *bhikṣuṇī* is simply a woman who has left the household life (*pravrajitā*).
An *upāsaka* is a male lay follower (*upāsaka*), and an *upāsikā* is a female lay follower (*upāsikā*);

this is because they have received the precepts of refuge and are capable of drawing near to and serve the two groups of the ordained. Alternatively, they may be translated as "male and female pure believers," and so forth. △ Five.
Fourth, regarding the female body:
for those who are to be liberated by appearing in the form of a woman— whether she be the wife of a householder, a lay official, or a brahmin—
he manifests in the form of a woman and preaches the Dharma for them.
This is as stated in the "Chapter on Sublime Sounds" (*Ghoṣadatta-parivarta*): "Within the royal harem, he transformed into a female body and preached the Dharma.
△ Sixth, regarding the bodies of boys and girls:
for those who are to be liberated by the body of a boy or a girl, he manifests the body of a boy or a girl and preaches the Dharma for them.
Regarding the Dharma,
Master Fasheng stated that those from seven or eight years of age upward may all be termed "children" (tóngzǐ). △ The eighth [section] concerns the bodies of the eight classes.
He manifests the bodies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, and non-humans— whichever forms are necessary to deliver beings— and preaches the Dharma to them accordingly.
Having already explained the Mahātejas-deva, those mentioned here again may be the ones who govern the human realm among the constellations.
As for the *nāgas*, they are the leaders among scaly creatures and are of four kinds: first, those who guard the celestial palaces;
second, those who raise thunder and bring forth rain; third, the terrestrial *nāgas* who open and regulate rivers and streams; and fourth, those who guard hidden treasures.
The *nāgas* are those who guard the precious treasuries of the Wheel-Turning Kings (*cakravartin*). The *yakṣas*—translated here as "swift spirits" (*jiéjí guǐ*)—dwell in three places:
on islands in the ocean, in the air, and in the heavens; it is traditionally said that they do not eat humans.

These are the very same spirits who, from the time the Buddha first attained enlightenment until he turned the wheel of the Dharma, proclaimed [the teachings] upward as far as the Brahma Heaven. The *gandharvas*—translated here as...
Gandharva (the second character pronounced with a departing tone) is a celestial musician deity who dwells within the Vajra Cave on the southern face of Mount Sumeru.
Asuras are beings who may have a thousand heads and two thousand arms, or ten thousand heads and twenty thousand arms, or three heads and six arms;
they are called "Deities of No-Wine" because they formerly observed the precept against drinking. Their males are ugly while their females are beautiful; they reside on Mount Manasottara.
Regarding those who dwell in the middle: some say they reside beneath the ocean, supported by the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala) which holds the water like clouds, and they live below that.

*Garuda* is translated here as "King of the Golden-Winged Birds" (*jīnqishiwang*); this has been explained above. As for *kiṃnara*, they are the deities of the celestial emperors who play stringed and bamboo instruments;
this has been explained in detail above. Regarding *mahoraga*, Master Kumārajīva says they are terrestrial dragons (*dilon*), while Sengzhao [says they are]... [text fragment].
The Dharma Master says that this "great python that crawls on its belly" is neither a human nor a non-human, but refers to the *kiṃnara*;
it is a general term for the eight classes of beings, each of whom leads their own retinue. △ Eighth: The Body of the Vajra-Wielder (*Vajrapāṇi*).
To those who should be saved by means of the Vajrapāṇi deity, he manifests as the Vajrapāṇi deity and preaches the Dharma for them.
This Vajra is not among the eight classes of spirits; rather, it is a precious object held in the hand to protect the Dharma.

Alternatively, it is said that he dwells in the heavens of the desire and form realms to teach and transform the various devas, and is thus a deity of great transformative power (mahopāya). △ Second, the general response.
Aksayamati, it is because the Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara has accomplished such meritorious virtues that he travels through various lands in manifold forms to deliver sentient beings.

Transversely pervading the ten directions and vertically penetrating the three realms, he manifests transformations according to the capacities of beings; his manifestations do not stop at merely thirty-three bodies.
Third, the exhortation to make offerings, in two parts. First, the exhortation to offer:
"Therefore, you all should with one mind make offerings to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to bestow fearlessness amidst terror and urgent distress; for this reason, in this Sahā world..."
The world all calls him the "Bestower of Fearlessness.

The Buddha’s answer to the former question is general at first and specific later; his subsequent exhortation to uphold the name implies that although sentient beings rely upon and receive his hidden benefits, they need only maintain the name itself.
The Buddha’s answer to the latter question is specific at first and general later; it concludes with an exhortation.
One should make offerings because sentient beings look up to and rely upon [the Buddha] for manifest benefit; seeing his form and hearing his voice, one is thus exhorted to offer worship.
A Bodhisattva is able to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings, acting as the one who enables them to be liberated from fear. This is what is meant by "forming these characters."
△ Second, receiving the mandate, in six parts; first, accepting the command.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I shall now make an offering to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
He immediately untied from his neck a necklace of many precious jewels worth hundreds of thousands of taels of gold and presented it to him, saying:
It is said that the benevolent one receives this precious jeweled necklace as a gift of Dharma.
The *Necklace Sutra* states that the first stage is a copper necklace, up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), which is a mani-jewel necklace.
Although the Inexhaustible Intent (*Akṣayamati*) occupies such a high rank, the statement that its value is "worth hundreds of thousands of taels of gold" is a concise expression.
In terms of the contemplative explanation, the neck represents the principle of the single reality of the Middle Way, adorned with the various dharmas of non-attachment.

"Explanation" (*jie*) signifies the practice of constant relinquishment; because one reaches the state of Bodhi through the merit of vows and conduct without dwelling, clinging, or dependence, it is called "explanation.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that precepts, concentration, wisdom, and *dhāraṇī* constitute the necklace.
The adornment of the Dharma-body with hundreds of thousands [of merits] represents one hundred thousand, signifying the first stage (*bhūmi*); ten thousand merits represent the ten stages.
The "Dharma-gift" (dharma-dāna) is so called because it communicates the Dharma through material wealth. △ Second, not receiving.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva was unwilling to accept it;
because he does not accept the vast application of samādhi, there is nothing for him to receive. △ Third offering.
Akṣayamati again addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "O Benevolent One, out of compassion for us, please accept this necklace.
I offer it to you for the sake of the fourfold assembly; out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, you should accept it—accepting it by way of non-acceptance."
...Thus it is. △ Fourth, the Buddha’s exhortation:

At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying, "You should take pity upon this Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, as well as the fourfold assembly, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas."
Because they were humans, non-humans, and so forth, they accepted these necklaces.
The Buddha’s intention was that a bodhisattva should accept offerings for the sake of sentient beings. △ Fifth, the acceptance:
At that moment, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly as well as the devas, nāgas, humans, non-humans, and others, accepted them.
He divided the necklace into two parts: one part he offered to Śākyamuni Buddha, and the other part he offered to the stupa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha.
Offering these two parts symbolizes the two causes of phenomena and principle; offering them to the two Buddhas symbolizes that the two causes lead to the two fruits.
One should know that the perfection of principle is the activity of the Dharma-Buddha, and the perfection of phenomena is the Reward-Buddha.
△ Sixth, the conclusion: Thus does the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, with such sovereign spiritual powers, roam throughout the Sahā world.
△ Verse Section, Part Three: Initial Pair of Verses on the Two Questions, Part One: Praising Virtue.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati asked in verse: [The text notes:
"These verses were translated by Śīladharma (Jñānagupta). When the Wise One (Xuanzang) produced his version, these verses had not yet circulated; therefore, they are not present here."

Since the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) by Jingxi cites the passage "returning to attach to the original person," Ciyun has divided the text into sections corresponding to the two types of question-and-answer found in the prose;
these correspond like the halves of a tally. Now, I shall explain the text according to his topical outline.
"The World-Honored One is endowed with wondrous marks" praises the Buddha’s marks and virtues.
△ Second, the double inquiry: first, it incorporates the two preceding questions:
"I now ask him again."
In the prose section, he first asked about the causes and conditions for obtaining the name, and subsequently asked about the manner of his wandering and transforming through the three karmas;
now, this verse reiterates that single line, encompassing both meanings. △ Second, a separate verse on the initial question.
"Son of the Buddha, by what causes and conditions is he named Avalokiteśvara?
△ Second, the double verse for the two answers. First, the sūtra-narrator’s account:
"The Honored One with Perfectly Endowed Wondrous Marks replied in verse to Akṣayamati."
These are the words compiled by the scribe of this sutra. II. Verses on the Buddha’s Response, Part Two: First, a general verse on the practices and vows.
Listen to the practices of Avalokiteśvara, who responds skillfully to all places. His great vows are as deep as the ocean;
throughout inconceivable kalpas, he has served many thousands of billions of Buddhas and made vast, pure aspirations.
The practice of Avalokiteśvara is the wisdom-practice of the three contemplations within a single mind, which brings sentient beings to liberation.
"All directions" refers to the lands of atoms; "vast vows" refers to the practice of the four great vows.
Throughout the long duration of kalpas, he encountered many Buddhas and made pure aspirations. II. Specific Verses on the Two Answers. Part One: Verses on the General Answer regarding Avalokiteśvara.
Regarding the name, the first verse provides a general response:
"I shall briefly explain for you that hearing the name and seeing the body and mind are not in vain; they are able to extinguish the suffering of all existences.

This explains that hearing [the name] is vocal action (*vākkarman*), seeing the body is physical action (*kāyakarman*), and mental recollection is mental action (*manaskarman*); because these three actions are purified, one is able [to attain liberation].

It extinguishes the suffering of all states of existence. △ Second, the verses that provide specific answers to the two [sections]; first, the verses on the seven calamities. (12) First, the calamity of fire:
Even if someone with a malicious intent were to push one into a great pit of fire, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, the fiery pit would transform into a pond.
△ Second, the peril of water:
Whether drifting upon the vast ocean or facing the dangers of dragons, fish, and various spirits, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one cannot be submerged by the waves.
△ Third, an added verse on the peril of falling from Mount Sumeru.
Or if one is on the peak of Mount Sumeru and is pushed over by someone, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one will remain in the sky like the sun.
△ Fourth, an added verse concerning the peril of falling onto a diamond-hard surface.
Or if pursued by evil men and falling down Mount Vajra, through the power of calling upon Avalokiteśvara, not even a single hair can be harmed.
△ Fifth, the verse on the peril of bandits:

Or if encountered by hostile bandits surrounding one and each wielding blades to inflict harm, through the power of calling upon Avalokiteśvara, they will all immediately give rise to a compassionate heart.
△6. A supplementary verse on the peril of swords and staves:
Should one encounter the suffering of royal punishment and face execution at the end of one’s life, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, the sword shall be shattered into pieces.
△7. A supplementary verse on the peril of shackles and fetters.
Or if one is imprisoned and shackled, with hands and feet bound by cangues and fetters, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one shall be released and attain liberation.
△ Eighth, a summary verse on the peril of spells and poisons:
Should various poisonous drugs used for curses and incantations seek to harm one’s body, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall return to the person who cast them.
△ Ninth, the verse on the peril of rākṣasas:
Should one encounter evil rākṣasas, venomous nāgas, various ghosts, and the like, when one calls upon the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall all dare not cause harm.
△ Tenth, the added verse on the peril of wild beasts.
If one is surrounded by fierce beasts with terrifying, sharp teeth and claws, by recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, one will flee swiftly to boundless directions.
△ Eleven: An added verse on the peril of venomous snakes.
The venomous vipers, scorpions, and centipedes, whose poisonous breath is like a blazing fire, shall upon recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara turn back at the mere sound of his name.
△ Twelfth, the verse on the peril of thunder:
When clouds and thunder roll, lightning flashes, and hail falls in torrential rain, by the power of recollecting Avalokiteśvara, they shall be dispersed and vanish in that very moment.
△ Second, two verses on the three poisons and the two types of seeking:
Sentient beings are beset by calamities and oppressed by immeasurable suffering; with the wondrous power of wisdom, Avalokiteśvara can rescue the world from its pain.
Sentient beings abound in greed, hatred, and false views within the realms, as well as the three poisons outside the realms, which yield no retribution.

Because men and women internally lack the dharma-wealth of concentration and wisdom, they invite the two kinds of birth and death; hence it is said that "immeasurable suffering oppresses their bodies.
If one can take the primary and auxiliary practices as the occasion, one will immediately respond to the manifestation of the True Body to rescue them from the sufferings of the two kinds of worlds.
△ Second, the verse on the subsequent answer regarding the universal manifestation; first, the direct verse on the manifestation.
The first part presents a summary answer in verse regarding the manifestation of the two [bodies].

"Possessing the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhibala*) and extensively cultivating the skillful means of wisdom (*jñānopāya*), there is no land in the worlds of the ten directions where he does not manifest his body.
This verse describes his wandering through various lands in diverse forms. △ Second, the subsequent verse provides a detailed answer in three parts; first, the body.

Through the universal response of karma, the various sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death within the diverse evil destinies—namely those of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—are gradually and completely extinguished.
These various evil destinies, which pervade the nine realms, are all termed "evil" from the perspective of the Buddha; thus, these evil destinies are collectively included herein.

This is to cause the extinction of suffering and the attainment of the Way. △ Second, the universal contemplation of mental karma, which has two parts: first, the fundamental contemplations of compassion and loving-kindness.

These are the contemplation of reality, the contemplation of purity, the contemplation of vast wisdom, the contemplation of compassion, and the contemplation of loving-kindness; one constantly vows and constantly gazes upward toward them.

These five characters for "contemplation" (guān) are all pronounced with the departing tone (*qùhū*). They fully clarify the three contemplations as well as the two contemplations of compassion and mercy. "True" (*zhēn*) refers to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*);

"pure" (*qīngjìng*) refers to the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), for when the provisional arises from emptiness, it is free from the defilements of view-tendencies and thought-tendencies, and is thus pure.

"Vast and great wisdom" (*guǎngdà zhìhuì*) refers to the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*), which simultaneously negates and illuminates both extremes, transcending all dependence and attaining absolute equality—the Great Wisdom.
Furthermore, all three contemplations are compassion; they are like the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) and the four dhyānas, for dhyāna is itself contemplation.
Avalokiteśvara contemplates sentient beings with unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*); this is called the contemplation of compassion (*karuṇā-vipaśyanā*).

Using the three contemplations to extract suffering is called the contemplation of pity (*karuṇā-vipaśyanā*); using the three contemplations to bestow happiness is called the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-vipaśyanā*). One must constantly cultivate and constantly revere them.
This is the contemplation. △ Second, the pervasive illumination of the light of wisdom:
"The stainless, pure light of the sun of wisdom destroys all darkness; it can subdue calamitous winds and fires, universally illuminating the world."
The light of wisdom shines universally to benefit beings at the stage of fruition. The stainless pure light illuminates the ultimate principle and examines its fundamental source.

If the three poisons and various darknesses were not destroyed, and the fires and winds of the two deaths were not extinguished, how could one universally benefit the capacities of the two kinds of worlds?
△ Third, the universal teaching through verbal karma; Part One: A verse on the two wheels for the sake of transformation.
The foundation of this is the essence of compassion. With the thunderous resonance of the precepts as its body and the wondrous great cloud of a compassionate mind,
the Dharma-body first employs the virtue of the precepts to awaken beings, like the thundering of heaven’s lightning such that there is nothing that does not respond.
"Sustaining the Great Cloud of Compassion" means taking compassion as one's cloud; it impartially covers all things without exception, just like that great cloud.
Once the two wheels have been bestowed, the nectar rains down according to the Dharma that should be granted—this refers to the turning of the wheel of Dharma through speech.
△ Second, the verse on the turning of the wheel of Dharma through speech.
It pours down the Dharma-rain of ambrosia to extinguish the flames of affliction.
Regarding "ambrosia," Tiantai says it is the divine medicine of immortality possessed by the various heavens;

that which is proclaimed as the ultimate principle is necessarily non-arising, and non-arising is precisely immortality. Thus, the Dharma-rain of ambrosia is poured for the sake of sentient beings who suffer from the three delusions.
Because the "Flame-Extinction" chapter takes these three universals as the gateway for entering the Path, the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) should be praised separately. 2.
[The second part] adds verses to manifest the capacities of sentient beings:
"In places of litigation before government officials, or amidst the terrors of military arrays, by recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, all enemies shall retreat and disperse."
Formerly, when the śramaṇa Daoying was surrounded by bandits, he and his disciples together recited [the name]. In an instant, from within a black cloud, a deity clad in golden armor appeared;
thereupon the bandits fled, and they were spared from harm. △ Third, the two verses on the dual exhortations.
First, the exhortation to receive and uphold. First, the exhortation to maintain constant mindfulness by clarifying the object of wisdom.
The wondrous voice, the Avalokiteśvara-voice, the Brahma-voice, the ocean-tide voice—these surpass the voices of the world; therefore, one should always keep them in mind.

Because the Bodhisattva observes with wondrous wisdom the sounds uttered by sentient beings, they all become wondrous objects. Because the three wisdoms illuminate them, the sounds become the three objects.
When both emptiness and existence are simultaneously negated, it becomes the wondrous voice; when both emptiness and existence are simultaneously illuminated, it becomes... [the wondrous voice].

Regarding these two sounds of the two worlds, they are the realm of wisdom. The "Brahma-sound" refers to the four immeasurables—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—which constitute the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The "ocean-tide sound" refers to responding to the capacities of sentient beings according to the conventional;
whether they are ripened or liberated, the timing never errs. These two sounds are the realm of provisional wisdom. They surpass those sounds of the world. Thus it is concluded.

The ultimate wisdom of emptiness emerges from the nine realms; its compassionate illumination reaches the voices of sentient beings, transcending both worlds. This single voice is precisely the realm of the wisdom of emptiness.
Although the words appear to follow a sequence, the contemplation resides within the single mind: outside the mind there is no sound, and outside sound there is no realm of wisdom.
Wisdom and its object merge into one, and discursive thought is suddenly forgotten. Therefore, one must maintain constant mindfulness; this is the meaning of the exhortation to uphold [the teaching].
Although these sounds are produced by the vocal karma of sentient beings, when those sages illuminate my three truths with their three wisdoms, they are precisely the three bodies.
Therefore, I exhort practitioners to keep these three bodies in mind; to "constantly keep them in mind" is what is meant by "right mindfulness.
△ Second, clarifying the response to resonance and exhorting against doubt.
"Do not give rise to doubt in every thought-moment; Avalokiteśvara, the Pure and Holy One, can act as a refuge in the face of suffering and the perils of death.

This clarifies that the response of the Buddha is unfathomable in order to quell doubt. In the preceding passage, the objective realm and wisdom were first presented, followed by an exhortation to maintain constant mindfulness;

here, the exhortation not to doubt comes first, followed by the description of the response. This serves to mutually illustrate what is meant by "continuous succession from thought-moment to thought-moment."
One also contemplates that profound and wondrous realm of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom. Although one attains the state of permanence, one cannot avoid the flux of conditioned phenomena;
yet, within this very flux, one contemplates the constant realm and wisdom. Thus, in every thought-moment, one is never separated from Avalokiteśvara. This is as Tiantai taught to the assembly:
"The true mind accords with the true realm; true conditions arise in succession; true and true mutually infuse one another, spontaneously."
Entering into the true principle, the actual conditions are momentary thoughts that arise in succession; each and every one is a condition for the true contemplation.
One must guard against these thoughts giving rise to doubt. If doubt arises, it will obstruct the realm of principle;
even if you seek it thereafter, it will not respond. You must have faith that the subtle assistance of the pure sages is never in vain, for they can be relied upon like parents.
O Protector, by mindful recollection and upholding [this teaching], a response will surely be manifested. △ Second, the verse on exhorting offerings:
"Possessing all merits, gazing upon sentient beings with eyes of compassion, an ocean of merit immeasurable; therefore, one should pay homage."
△ Second, the merit of hearing this chapter, in two parts. First, the Bodhisattva Earth-Holder praises the merit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Earth-Holder rose from his seat, came forward, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings who hear this 'Chapter on Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,' concerning his sovereign activities and the supernormal powers manifested through the Universal Gate,"
One should know that the merit of such a person is not small.
△ Second, the benefits obtained upon hearing this chapter.
When the Buddha preached this "Universal Gate" Chapter, eighty-four thousand sentient beings within the assembly all gave rise to the aspiration for the peerless and equal [enlightenment].
Regarding the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, Jingxi says that it is only by means of the eightfold teaching that one can properly apply this to the present sutra.

"Hearing of Avalokiteśvara" refers to the question concerning the preceding section on secret benefits; the "Universal Gate Chapter" (*Pumenpin*) is the answer concerning the section on manifest benefits.
Regarding "sovereign karma": the karma of ordinary beings is moistened by craving; because it is conditioned by outflows (*āsrava*), they lack sovereignty.
Avalokiteśvara, in order to harmonize the ten dharma realms, manifests these three types of karma.

Moistened by the power of his compassion, he undergoes birth according to conditions without being deluded or burdened by afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, it is called "sovereign karma. Thus it was heard.
Because one is able to attain the subtle and wondrous merits of both the true and semblance stages of contemplative practice, it is said that they are "not few.

As for the eighty-four thousand sentient beings who give rise to the "unequaled" mind: this refers to taking the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction within the mind as the seeds of the Tathāgata, giving rise to the mind of the true mark (*dharmatā*) which is equal to the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates; thus, they are "unequaled" (*asama-sama*).
Although those of the two vehicles have emerged from the triple world, they still possess superior dharmas; it is not that they lack equality with the Buddha, for this is the ultimate stage.
Because they have resolved to seek Buddhahood, they are "equal to the unequaled," meaning they are equal to the Buddha.

As the Sūtra says: "The initial resolve and the ultimate [attainment] are not two different things. Of these two minds, the former is more difficult. Since the present initial resolve is equal to the final mind, it is so stated.
The "Incomparable" (asama-sama) is designated as such in the final mind; this clarifies the arousal of the bodhicitta according to the intent of the four *siddhāntas*.
One should know that there are three types of arousing the mind: first, the nominal arousal, which refers to the five ranks of disciples;

second, the semblance arousal, which refers to the purification of the six sense faculties; and third, the true arousal, which refers to those from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward—this is called the true arousal of the mind.

[End of section. ○ I personally maintain that the main text of this chapter is entirely devoted to compassion—extracting beings from suffering and bestowing upon them happiness—up until the section on receiving offerings.

It is only when [the Buddha] honors Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna that it clearly manifests the stage of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s circulation, wherein all Bodhisattvas are compassionate, and Avalokiteśvara manifests through the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*), possessing sovereign supernatural powers and the ability to grant fearlessness.
Regarding those who bestow [this teaching] upon sentient beings, their response through the resonance of its name and the manifestation of its compassion are particularly manifest;
there is no one in the world who does not first read this chapter before reading the entire Lotus Sūtra. For this reason, it has been specially printed and widely distributed.
△ Chapter Twenty-Six: The Chapter on Dhāraṇīs (In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this is titled "The Chapter on Total Retention") **Part One:
Title** *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Six: The Chapter on Dhāraṇīs (in the root text, it is called "The Chapter on Total Retention").
*Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "total retention" (*saṃgraha*). It means that evil does not arise and good is not lost. [It is also used for] worlds. Furthermore, it is translated as "capable."

It is because it obstructs that which can maintain [evil] and maintains that which is good while obstructing evil (as an antidote for persons). Furthermore, it obstructs the evils of the two extremes and maintains the goodness of the Middle Way (the ultimate truth).
The applications of "opening" and "obstructing" in various sutras differ: some are used exclusively to treat illness, such as in the case of the householder Nātha;
some are used exclusively to protect the Dharma, as in this text; and some are used exclusively to extinguish transgressions, such as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Whether it be the *Samanta-dhāraṇī* (Universal Dhāraṇī), or those used generally for curing illness, extinguishing transgressions, and protecting scriptures— such as the *Dhāraṇī for Invoking Avalokiteśvara to Subdue Poisonous Harm*,
or the "Great Bright Mantra," the "Unsurpassed Bright Mantra," or the "Incomparable Bright Mantra"—

if these are not specifically for curing illness, extinguishing transgressions, or protecting scriptures, yet are universal in application, they should also be employed concurrently; however, if they are specific [to a particular purpose], they should be used separately.
The commentator must fortunately rely upon the sūtra and not deviate from its teaching. △ Second, the Sūtra Text, in four parts: First, the question regarding the merit of upholding the sūtra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
The Buddha said, “World-Honored One, if there are good men or good women who are able to receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
or read and recite it until they have mastered it, or transcribe its scrolls, how much merit will they obtain?”
△ Second, the answer concerning the vastness of merit, in four parts. First, establishing the basis for comparison:
The Buddha told Bhaisajyarāja: "If there were good men or good women who made offerings to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in eight hundred million nayutas of Ganges Rivers..."
△ 2. Raising the question of whether it is much or not:
"In your opinion, how is it? Is the merit obtained therein truly great?
△ 3. Answering truthfully that it is exceedingly much.
"Very much so, World-Honored One.
△ Fourth, the enumeration of merits:
The Buddha said, "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family is able to receive and uphold even a single four-line verse from this sutra..."
The merit of reciting and chanting these verses, understanding their meaning, and practicing according to the teachings is exceedingly great.
△ Third, the request to protect by means of mantras, in five parts; First, the request by Bhaiṣajyarāja.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I shall now provide for the speaker of the Dharma with a *dhāraṇī*..."
The bhikṣuṇī protected him by means of a mantra.
△ Second, the recitation:

After practicing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for this long, he attained the Samādhi of Adornments with All Pure Merits.

He immediately rose into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, these two sons of mine have already—"
Performing Buddha-work through supernatural transformations and manifestations, they turned my perverse mind and caused me to dwell securely within the Buddha-dharma;
I have now been able to see the World-Honored One. These two sons are my spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);
desiring to arouse my roots of goodness from past lives and to benefit me, they have come to be born in my family.

At that time, the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom addressed King Wondrous Adornment, saying: "So it is, so it is!

Great King, you should know that a spiritual friend is a great causal condition;

These two sons have already made offerings to sixty-five hundred thousand million billion nayutas of Ganges-sands of Buddhas;

The Buddha praised that spiritual friends possess great significance and are able to perform the work of a Buddha.

Those who provide instruction, guidance, benefit, and joy are spiritual friends as external protectors (*bāhya-pālaka*). Those who transform and lead others so that they may see the Buddha are spiritual friends of common practice (*sahāya*).
Those who cause one to enter into Bodhi are spiritual friends of the ultimate reality and true mark (*bhūtārtha-bhūtalakṣaṇa*). These are the external protectors.
Having taught these three kinds of practices, [the text] concludes with the chapter on Sudatta. △ Tenth, the praise of the Buddha’s own vow:
King Subhavyūha immediately descended from the midst of the void and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata is most rare and extraordinary;
by virtue of his merit and wisdom, the light from the flesh-turban (uṣṇīṣa) upon his crown shines forth brilliantly, and his eyes are long and wide."
The hair-treasure between his eyebrows was deep blue, while his teeth were as white as a conch or the moon, even and closely set, and constantly radiant;
the color of his lips was a beautiful crimson, like the *bimba* fruit.

At that time, King Subhavyūha, having praised the Buddha for such immeasurable hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of virtues, joined his palms with single-minded devotion before the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha once more:
“World-Honored One, it is unprecedented! The Dharma of the Tathāgata is fully accomplished with inconceivable, subtle, and wondrous merits.
The teachings, precepts, and practices are secure, peaceful, and wholesome.

From this day forward, I shall no longer act according to my own whims, nor shall I give rise to wrong views, arrogance, anger, or any other evil thoughts. Having spoken these words, he prostrated before the Buddha and departed.

The King Subhavyūha and his retinue were born as those two sons;
they are none other than the present Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.

Having accomplished such great merits as these, the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata have planted the roots of all virtues under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas and have perfected inconceivable wholesome merits.

When the Buddha spoke this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment," eighty-four thousand people became free from dust and removed from defilement.

Regarding the "purity of the Dharma-eye" mentioned in the benefits of the *Shouwen-pin* (Chapter on Hearing), some say it refers to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).
Since the King, the Queen, and the eighty thousand others all upheld this sutra and were all destined to become Buddhas, how could those who heard the *Wenpin* have obtained only a minor fruit?

Although the names are identical, their meanings differ; one must exercise careful discernment. The commentator also states that "the vision is pure," but does not say it refers to the stage of the first fruit of the Śrāvaka vehicle (*śrāvakaphala*).
In my private opinion, although the term "Dharma-eye" (*dharmacakṣus*) is used, its substance is different; it certainly cannot be the first fruit.
It must be judged as the stage of the Dharma-eye of the "purity of the six sense organs" (*ṣaḍindriyaviśuddhi*), which is at least from the seventh stage of faith (*saptama-śraddhā-bhūmi*) upward.

Second, this chapter exhorts propagation by highlighting the greatness of Samantabhadra’s power of vows. First, the title of the chapter.
The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Exhortation of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (the "Correct Scripture" refers to this as the "Chapter on Rejoicing in Samantabhadra").
Both the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* name him Pien-chi (遍吉), while this scripture calls him Pu-hsien (普賢).

These are all Chinese transliterations of the Sanskrit name *Samantabhadra*. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-bhadrakalpa-vyākaraṇa* states: "I vow to practice the bodhisattva path within a defiled and evil world."
To cause you to attain such solemn purity, my practice must surely surpass that of all other Bodhisattvas. The Buddha said:

"For these reasons, I now change your name and call you Samantabhadra (Universal Worthy). This refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), which stands at the summit of all subduing paths.

Because the path of subduing is all-pervasive, it is called 'Universal' (*samanta*); because the path of severance has just reached its end, there is little remaining to be compared, and one is adjacent [to Buddhahood]."
Because it reaches the ultimate limit, it is called "Worthy" (Bhadra). These words of encouragement are the expressions of one who yearns for the Dharma.

Having heard this sutra from beginning to end in its entirety while staying far away in that land, and desiring to practice it himself and transform others forever without end, he has come from the east and from the west to offer this encouragement.
This text contains the intent of the four *siddhāntas*, as it says: "I have come to make offerings."
Because of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, he manifests his own body; if one sees my body, one will experience great joy.
Because of seeing me, one further applies oneself with diligence and immediately attains samādhi and dhāraṇī.
Because one has attained this dhāraṇī, no non-human being can destroy them, nor will they be deluded by women.

The Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in three thousandfold world-systems, who counteract [afflictions] and are fully endowed with the path of Samantabhadra—this explicit text is an exhortation issued from the four *siddhāntas*.
△ Second, the main text has four parts; first, the narrator’s account has three parts;
first, the higher offerings.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, accompanied by an immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable number of great bodhisattvas,
arrived from the east through the power of his sovereign spiritual penetrations, majesty, and renown; all the lands he passed through trembled,
rains of precious lotus flowers fell, and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various kinds of musical instruments played.
Mastery (*vaśitā*) is the one principle; supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are the one practice; majesty and virtue (*prabhāva*) are the one person;
and renown (*yaśas*) is the one teaching. Furthermore, mastery is permanence (*nitya*); supernormal powers are bliss (*sukha*);
majesty and virtue are self (*ātman*); and renown is purity (*śubha*). When expressed in this way, there is the One, and the four virtues are fully present.
By the power of mastery, flowers rain down; by the power of joy, music is played; by the power of supernormal faculties, the earth trembles;
and by the power of sovereignty, they rain, move, and play according to their will—following wherever they go, wherever they rain, wherever they move, and wherever they play.
It is like a great dragon that flies without ceasing, from whose body clouds and rains arise in an endless flow, as do Samantabhadra and his retinue.
Using the body of a Bodhisattva, he employs the power of the four virtues to come and exhort the four types of beings;
as for the places he visits, he personally makes offerings to them, and his conduct therein is as described above. △ Second, the downward transformation.
Furthermore, he was surrounded by a great assembly of countless devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, each manifesting their majestic power and supernormal abilities.
In the places he traverses, he descends to transform and benefit others according to what is appropriate for them, manifesting the forms of the eight classes of beings.

He briefly employs two powers according to their respective capacities; such is the nature of his deeds. In the preceding text, the four qualities beginning with mastery were used to represent the four virtues;
here, they are abbreviated, omitting mastery and renown, as two [qualities] subsume two [others]. Since the sutra text states:
Regarding the statement that "each, together with immeasurable [attendants], manifests two powers," one should know that what they follow is the Dharmakāya;
because both the principal and the retinue are fully endowed with the four virtues, it is said "each. △ Third, paying homage.
Arriving at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the Sahā world, he prostrated with his head at the feet of Śākyamuni Buddha and circumambulated him seven times to the right.
△ Second, explaining the exhortation to practice, which has two parts: first, the inquiry regarding the exhortation; second, the inquiry itself. First, the inquiry.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, from afar in the land of the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja, I have heard that in this Sahā world the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is being preached.
Together with immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas, I have come to hear and receive it.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it for us. If a good man or a good woman, regarding the Tathāgata..."
"How can one obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* after [the Buddha's] parinirvāṇa?

This inquiry and exhortation within the section of questions and answers concerns how Samantabhadra, having heard the conclusion of the sutra from afar in that land, was filled with such longing for the Dharma that his resolve to travel a great distance arose; his intent being to exhort others to come together to listen and receive it.

This is a further request for the correct exposition, which encourages the practice of one's own cultivation; if there are sons of good family and others, this is a further request for the circulation [of the teaching], which encourages the transformation of others.
Since the Tathāgata has granted both paths (the *zhengzong* and the *liutong*), he again manifests light upon light in infinite measure;
therefore, these two requests are made together. △ Second, the Buddha’s response, in three parts: first, the general [response].
The Buddha told Samantabhadra Bodhisattva: "If good sons or good daughters accomplish four dharmas, they shall obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
△ Second, the specific [explanation].
First, they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas; second, they plant the roots of all virtues; third, they enter the stage of right determination;
fourth, they give rise to the mind that seeks to rescue all sentient beings.
Since Samantabhadra had made his dual request, the Tathāgata gave a skillful response by briefly citing four points to encompass all others.

What are these? The essentials of these four dharmas comprehensively cover the correct and pervasive path. Although the Buddha is without partiality, if one can distance oneself from evil and follow what is good, turn back from delusion and return to correctness, and open up provisional means and insights to reveal the Buddha’s own knowledge and vision, then one will accord with the holy mind of all Buddhas.
If the Buddha’s protective mindfulness, knowledge, vision, and opening [of the Dharma] illuminate through Prajñā, this is the planting of the roots of all virtues;

it is also entry into the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). It is neither distracted, nor savoring, nor grasping, nor abandoning; it is also the arousal of the resolve to save sentient beings.

One should know that these four—along with the "opening of the provisional to reveal the real"—differ in name but are identical in essence, being non-dual and without distinction. Furthermore, the Buddha’s protection...
"Mindfulness" is the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; "planting the roots of all virtues" is the demonstration of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

"arousing the intent to save sentient beings" is the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; and "entering the stage of right determination" is the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. These four encompass the essentials of the gate of the traces.

Furthermore, since the traces have their source in the fundamental, there is an opening, demonstrating, awakening to, and entering [the truth] from the perspective of the fundamental; thus, they exist within the traces.
"Revealing, awakening, entering, and now revealing the provisional to manifest the fundamental: the fundamental and the provisional are non-dual and without distinction.
Thus, answering his request with these four dharmas makes the meaning perfectly clear. To answer with four dharmas means to explain the propagation [of the teaching].

The methods for propagation are only three or four. As for the three: first, to bring forth the salvation of sentient beings is to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, which is to enter right concentration.
To be gathered within the Buddha’s protective mindfulness is the wearing of the Tathāgata’s robe; to plant the roots of all virtues is the sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat.

This is the essential method for widely proclaiming [the Dharma]: it consists of four aspects, yet three of them are one. Specifically, "setting forth to rescue sentient beings" is the Practice of Peaceful Conduct through Vow;
"entering the stage of right determination" is the Practice of Peaceful Conduct through Mind; and "planting the roots of all virtues" is the Practice of Peaceful Conduct through Speech.
It should be known that "joyfully practicing mindfulness" refers to the peaceful practice of this body; the latter four [sections] are identical to the former four.

First, he responds to the two requests by citing the four [sections] as a comprehensive summary: the re-expounding of the *Lotus Sūtra* (the *Zhengzong*) and the re-proclamation of this sūtra (the *Liutong*).
The meaning of the encouragement for those who have come from afar is thus established. △ Third, the conclusion.
Good sons and good daughters who thus accomplish these four dharmas will certainly obtain this sutra after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata;
they will certainly obtain this sutra after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata. (The old translation states: "Those who can practice these four dharmas in future ages...")
When one physically obtains this sutra, it is not as it was previously thought. As stated in the preceding text:

"The meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena has already been explained for you," and again, "To cause all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Indeed, the essential body (*samyaktva*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* consists in the ability to practice these four dharmas; by necessarily attaining this understanding, it is called a "sutra of understanding" (*prativedha-sūtra*). This concludes that [point].

I request that you rectify this: If one can transmit these practices of understanding and application to others, and those others, upon attaining such faith and understanding, become the first type of person;

and if they further attain true understanding and become the second, third, and fourth types of persons—does not the intent of this request for circulation preclude the pointlessness of making other explanations? △ Second, the Vow.
I vow to exhort and inspire [others]. First, regarding the protection of people: first, warding off external calamities. First, a general warding off of such calamities.

At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, during the final five hundred years of the turbid and evil age, for those who receive, uphold, and recite this sutra, I shall provide protection, eliminate their afflictions and misfortunes, and cause them to attain peace and security."
To prevent anyone from seeking an opportunity to find an advantage over them.
△ Second, specifically warding off difficulties:
whether it be Māra, or the sons of Māra, or the daughters of Māra, or the subjects of Māra, or those possessed by Māra, or yakṣas...
Neither rākṣasas, nor kumbhāṇḍas, nor piśācas, nor kiṭibhas, nor pūtanas, nor vetālas,
nor any other such beings who afflict people, shall find any opportunity to cause them harm.
△ Second, instructing him in the internal Dharma: First,
if this person walks or stands while reading and reciting this sutra, at that time I shall mount the six-tusked White Elephant King and,
together with a great assembly of bodhisattvas, go to where he is, manifest my own body before him, and provide offerings, protection, and consolation for his mind.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of making offerings to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
△ Second, as for sitting, one contemplates its meaning.
If this person sits and contemplates this sutra, at that time I shall again mount the King of White Elephants and appear before that person.
If that person should forget or lose even a single word or a single verse of the Lotus Sūtra, I shall instruct them and read and recite it with them until they have mastered it again.
At that time, those who uphold, read, and recite the Lotus Sūtra will behold my body and experience great joy;
through this increased diligence and because they behold me, they will immediately attain samādhi and dhāraṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇī attained such dhāraṇīs as the Dhāraṇī of Revolving, the Dhāraṇī of Hundreds of Thousands of Myriads of Billions of Revolutions,
and the Dhāraṇī of Skillful Means of the Dharma-Sound.

The *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī* (revolving dhāraṇī) refers to revolving from the conventional into emptiness; the "hundred thousand revolutions" refers to revolving from emptiness back out into the conventional.
"Skillful means" refers to using these two as the path of skillful means to enter the Middle Way, the Supreme Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
△ Third, single-minded diligent practice for twenty-one days.
“World-Honored One, if in a future age, during the final five hundred years of a turbid and evil world,
there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who seek, uphold, read, recite, or transcribe this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and desire to practice it,
they should for twenty-one days apply themselves with single-minded diligence. Once those twenty-one days are complete, I shall— ”

Riding upon a six-tusked white elephant and surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas, he manifests before those beings with a body that all sentient beings delight to behold, preaching the Dharma for them to instruct, benefit, and gladden them. Furthermore, he bestows upon them dharanis;
because they have obtained these dharanis, no non-human being can destroy them, nor shall they be... [afflicted].
"My body has also been constantly protected from the delusions and disturbances caused by women;
I only pray that the World-Honored One will allow me to speak this dhāraṇī mantra. Thereupon, before the Buddha, she spoke the mantra, saying:

he covered them with his supernormal power.
World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas who hear this dhāraṇī, they should know that it is the supernatural power of Samantabhadra.
If the Lotus Sūtra circulates in Jambudvīpa and there are those who receive and uphold it, they should form this thought:
"All of this is due to the majestic spiritual power of Samantabhadra."
△ Fourth, showing its superior causes: If there are those who receive,
uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, and understand the meaning and intent [of this teaching], and practice according to what is taught,

it should be known that such persons perform the practices of Samantabhadra, have deeply planted roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, and are [the disciples] of all Tathāgatas.
He came and stroked his head with his hand.

If one can cause the *Lotus Sūtra* to circulate for the sake of these five kinds of Dharma-preachers, this person has, before the Buddhas of the three periods of time, planted, ripened, and attained liberation;
because they will attain liberation together with the Buddhas of the future, it is said that they are equal to Samantabhadra.
Because this person has planted wholesome roots under previous Buddhas, it is said that they have "deeply planted wholesome roots.
Because this person has been brought to maturity by the present Buddha, it is said that he "touches their head with his hand. △ Fifth, showing their proximate fruit.
If one merely copies it down, at the end of that person's life they shall be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

at that time, eighty-four thousand celestial maidens will perform various musical performances to welcome them, and that person will immediately don a crown of the seven treasures and enjoy themselves with pleasure among those court ladies.
How much more so for one who receives, upholds, reads, recites, correctly contemplates, and understands its meaning and intent as it has been taught!

If there is anyone who practices, upholds, reads, recites, and understands the meaning and intent [of this teaching], at the end of their life, a thousand Buddhas will extend their hands to them, ensuring they are not terrified and do not fall into the evil realms.
They shall immediately go to the presence of Maitreya Bodhisattva in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Maitreya Bodhisattva possesses the thirty-two marks and is surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas numbering one hundred [thousand].
Therein, among the retinues of billions of celestial maidens, such merits and benefits as these arise.
Merely being able to transcribe [this sutra] brings one near to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where one possesses the five qualities of a Dharma Master; next, one dwells in Tuṣita.
△ Sixth, the summary of merits.
Therefore, the wise person should single-mindedly write it themselves, or cause others to write it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it,
correctly contemplate it, and practice according to its teaching.
△ Second, protecting the Dharma.

World-Honored One, by means of my supernormal powers, I shall now protect this sutra and cause it to be widely circulated within Jambudvīpa after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, so that it shall not be interrupted.
△ Third: The Narration of the Emission [of Samantabhadra]. Part One: An Interpolated Account of the Protection of the Dharma.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Samantabhadra!
You are able to protect and assist this sutra, bringing peace, happiness, benefit, and aid to many sentient beings. You have already accomplished inconceivable merit."
Having long ago given rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* out of profound and great compassion,

you are able to make such vows of supernatural power (*abhijñā*) to protect this sutra; I, too, shall use my own powers of supernatural penetration to protect those who are able to receive and uphold the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
The Tathāgata, extolling the superior to establish the inferior, encourages those who practice with increasing vigor to propagate the teaching with courageous resolve.

First, he describes the protection of the Dharma, saying: "Since you are thus able to bring great benefit to others externally while accumulating compassion within, and have been providing such protection for many kalpas, I too shall protect this Dharma through the supernatural power of a Buddha; how much more so for you?"
Yes. △ Second, the retrospective account of those who protected [the Dharma], in five parts. First, the retrospective presentation of the teachings on the person’s body:

"Samantabhadra, if there be anyone who receives, upholds, reads, recites, correctly contemplates, practices, or transcribes this Lotus Sūtra, you should know that such a person shall see Śākyamuni Buddha; it is as if they have heard this sūtra directly from the Buddha’s own mouth."
Know that this person has made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha; know that this person is praised by the Buddha as "well done";
know that this person has been stroked on the head by Śākyamuni Buddha with his own hand;
know that this person has been covered by the robe of Śākyamuni Buddha.
You should know that when it is said that such a person has seen Śākyamuni Buddha, this describes his manifestation of the body and his teaching of the Dharma;
if he has already seen my fruition-body endowed with myriad virtues, how much more so have you, who in the causal stage were a six-tusked white elephant?

If he has already heard the sutras in their entirety from the Buddha’s own mouth, how much more so have you, who were taught by him, forgotten the chapters and verses? If he was even praised by the Buddha’s own mouth, how much more so are you?
If even one who merely touches the Buddha’s robe is thus protected, how much more so one who is covered by the *dhāraṇī* of this person?
△ Second, skipping ahead to describe the superior causes:
such a person no longer clings to worldly pleasures, does not take pleasure in the scriptures or writings of non-Buddhists, and likewise...
One does not delight in associating with such people or with those who are evil—such as butchers, those who raise pigs, sheep, chickens, or dogs, hunters, or those who traffic in female beauty.
Such a person’s mind is upright and straightforward, possessing right mindfulness and the power of merit;
they are not afflicted by the three poisons, nor are they overcome by envy, pride, or false pride.
A person afflicted by pride may yet possess few desires and be content, thereby able to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra.

This extensively cites the absence of all faults and evils within the causal stage as the means to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra with few desires and contentment, thereby describing the superior causes.
△ Third, transcending the description to indicate the proximate fruit.
Samantabhadra, if after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there should be anyone who sees another receiving,
upholding, reading, or reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you should form this thought: "This person shall before long proceed to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
destroy the hosts of Māras, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, turn the wheel of Dharma, beat the drum of Dharma, blow the conch of Dharma, and rain down the Dharma."
"Rain, when seated upon the lion Dharma-throne amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, [I declare]:
if anyone in a future age upholds, maintains, reads, or recites this sutra, that person shall no longer be greedily attached to clothing, bedding, food, drink, or the necessities of life;
their aspirations shall not be in vain, and they shall likewise obtain their karmic rewards in the present life."
Such a person shall surely attain the distant fruit upon reaching the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), let alone the proximate fruit;
they shall obtain that proximate fruit even in the present life, not merely rebirth in heaven. △ Fourth, recounting the warding off of external calamities.

If there are those who disparage them, saying, "You are merely a madman; practicing such deeds in vain, you shall gain nothing," they will suffer this karmic retribution by being born blind life after life.
Conversely, if there are those who make offerings to or praise them, they shall obtain manifest rewards in this very life.
Furthermore, if one sees someone who upholds this sutra and speaks of their faults—whether those faults be real or not—[they shall likewise suffer].
Indeed, such a person will contract leprosy in this present life; furthermore, those who mock them lightly shall, in every successive birth, suffer from gaps and missing teeth,
deformed lips, flat noses, contorted hands and feet, squinting eyes, a foul-smelling and filthy body, malignant sores with pus and blood, abdominal dropsy,
and various other grave and evil illnesses.

The Buddha extensively reveals the transgressions of those who disparage [this scripture] so that they may recognize their faults and surely reform them, ensuring they do not cause further affliction or confusion.

It is not only those who uphold the sutra who find it difficult to extinguish [their karmic obstacles], but even those who wish to disparage it can give rise to merit. When there is neither disparagement nor difficulty, both parties attain peace and happiness;

this vast salvation without partiality is the ultimate expression of compassion. I reflect deeply that the Supreme Sage has already manifested these warnings as a mirror for reflection, serving as a lamp for all.

How could the towering and encompassing protection of its benevolent nurturing be surpassed? Why is it that the karma of sentient beings is so deep that it is suddenly difficult to prune and sweep away?
Those who see someone with sincere devotion to this Way seek out flaws in a hundred ways, exerting all their strength to revile and destroy them;
this may indeed bring momentary gratification, but it will surely leave behind calamity for vast eons. How tragic!
Now, fifth, describing the merit of those who possess faith:
Therefore, Samantabhadra, if you see one who receives and upholds this sutra, you should go out to welcome them from afar, treating them with the same reverence as you would the Buddha.
△ Fourth, the manifestation of benefits in two parts: first, attaining the Way upon hearing this chapter.

When this "Chapter on the Exhortation of Samantabhadra" was being preached, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, immeasurable and boundless, attained hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *vartanī-dhāraṇīs*, and bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms within a trichiliocosm were fully endowed [with these].
The Path of Samantabhadra:
The hundred thousand million koṭis of *parivarta-dhāraṇīs* constitute the Path of Samantabhadra at the first stage (*bhūmi*), and this constitutes the tenth stage.
△ Second, the benefits of hearing the sutra.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the entire great assembly— including Samantabhadra and the other bodhisattvas, Śāriputra and the other śrāvakas,
as well as the devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans— all rejoiced greatly, received and upheld the Buddha’s words,
paid homage, and departed.
That the great assembly rejoices is the benefit gained from hearing this sutra.
That they are still referred to here as "śrāvakas" is merely because the compilers of the sutra preserved their original status.
Furthermore, that the compilers refer to them as "Mahāyāna śrāvakas"—causing all to hear the sound of the Buddha-way—makes this meaning even more evident.
Annotated Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Eight (End)
